title: Ukrainian Attacks Kill 5 in Belgorod and Lipetsk, Hit Perm Industrial Plant
description: Overnight Ukrainian drone attacks killed four people in southwestern Russia’s Belgorod region, one in the Lipetsk region and damaged an industrial site in the Perm region of the Ural Mountains, officials said Sunday.
content:
Overnight Ukrainian drone attacks killed four people in southwestern Russia’s Belgorod region, one in the Lipetsk region and damaged an industrial site in the Perm region of the Ural Mountains, officials said Sunday.
In the city of Belgorod near the Russian border with Ukraine, an attack killed three people and injured 13, said Belgorod regional governor Alexander Shuvayev.
The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities, Shuvayev said.
In a separate incident on Sunday morning, one person was killed and another injured when a Ukrainian drone struck a car in the village of Voznesenovka near the town of Shebekino, local authorities said.
A drone attack on Russia's Perm region damaged an industrial facility, injuring five of its workers, regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said on Sunday.
Emergency services were at the scene and the injured people received the necessary medical help, he said on the state-backed MAX messaging app without providing further detail on the nature of the damage.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk during an overnight attack.
The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian army.
Russian forces also hit a logistics center, a distribution center and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv. The ministry said the facilities had been used for storage and distribution of dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian military.
Reuters could not independently verify the Defense Ministry's information.
Later on Sunday, southwestern Russia's Lipetsk region Governor Igor Artamonov said a Ukrainian missile strike on an industrial zone in the city of Yelets killed a security guard and injured a paramedic.
Artamonov said the security guard worked at one of the industrial facilities located on the site. The paramedic at the medical center was taken to hospital, where she was receiving the necessary treatment, the governor said.
The governor did not identify the facility that was hit in the strike.
Reuters could not independently verify the report. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

title: Moscow to Host 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, IWF Says
description: Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Sunday.
content:
Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Sunday.
No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, originally awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were later moved to Singapore.
“Concerning the IWF Senior World Championships, Ahmedabad (India) will host the 2029 edition and Moscow (Russia) will host the 2030 edition,” the IWF said in a statement.
It will be the first time since 1983 that Moscow has hosted the World Weightlifting Championships.
“All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the Championships in your respective countries will be a huge success,” said IWF General Secretary Jose Quinones.
Russian and Belarusian weightlifters have been eligible to compete in IWF events since the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July, a step seen as advancing Russia's gradual return to international sport.
The IOC Executive Board, when it lifted the suspension, said athletes should not be held responsible for the actions of their governments. No decision has yet been taken on whether Russian athletes will compete under their national flag, colors and anthem at the Olympic Games.
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine has appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport against the IOC's decision.
The ROC was suspended in October 2023 after recognizing regional Olympic councils in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russia's return to international competition also comes against the backdrop of one of the biggest doping scandals in Olympic sport.
The country has been under scrutiny since a 2015 World Anti-Doping Agency-commissioned report found evidence of systematic doping in Russian athletics, while subsequent investigations uncovered a state-backed cover-up linked to the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics.
The IOC said all Russian athletes now returning to international competition would have to ⁠meet relevant anti-doping ​requirements.

title: Europe Should Be Included in Ukraine Peace Discussions, Kremlin Aide Says
description: Europe should be included in discussions on a peace settlement in Ukraine because its position could be crucial, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said on Sunday.
content:
Europe should be included in discussions on a peace settlement in Ukraine because its position could be crucial, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said on Sunday.
The U.S. has been unable to put pressure on Kyiv to agree to a peace deal, Ushakov said in an interview with state television correspondent Pavel Zarubin.
“Before, it seemed after Anchorage, that the U.S. administration might be able to dictate something and force Kyiv to comply. But so far, this hasn't really worked out,” Ushakov said, referring to a 2025 meeting in Alaska between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“That's because it's not enough to talk only to Kyiv; we need to talk to the whole of Europe, which fully supports Kyiv.”
After initially leaving it to Trump to try to broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, the EU has made cautious approaches to Russia. The leaders of Britain, Germany and France have said they supported a proposal for talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Putin to try to secure a ceasefire, and that Europe would play a role.
Russia, meanwhile, has said it would be open to dialogue but not ultimatums.
On Sunday, Ushakov said that Russia was ready to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Russia's National Unity Day on Nov. 4, echoing Kremlin comments this week on Putin's willingness to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
Zelensky said on Friday that peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. had agreed to meet at a technical level in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, adding that he hoped a meeting of their leaders would follow.
Ushakov also commented on a potential meeting between Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, saying that preparations had already started. The proposed meeting is set to be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China over Nov. 18-19.
A separate meeting between Putin and Trump in Shenzhen had not been agreed upon, Ushakov said.

title: Saudi Arabia Will Not Host Russia’s Intervision Song Contest This Year, TASS Reports
description: Saudi Arabia will not host the Russian-backed Intervision song contest this year, with the event potentially postponed until 2027, the state-run news agency TASS reported, citing an unidentified source.
content:
Saudi Arabia will not host the Russian-backed Intervision song contest this year, with the event potentially postponed until 2027, the state-run news agency TASS reported , citing an unidentified source.
The source said a “combination of circumstances” had made it impossible to stage the competition in Saudi Arabia in 2026, without elaborating.
The decision leaves the future of Russia’s alternative to Eurovision uncertain a year after Moscow revived the Soviet-era competition.
A source in Riyadh had already cast doubt on the event in August, telling TASS that its dates, participants and program remained unclear.
Saudi Arabia was announced as the next host during the final of the September 2025 contest in Moscow. Saudi officials later said Russia had yet to formally hand over responsibility for organizing the event.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov expressed hope in May that escalating tensions in the Middle East would not disrupt plans for the second edition.
Russia revived Intervision after being barred from Eurovision in 2022 following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Eurovision’s organizers said Russia’s participation could bring the competition into disrepute.
Culture Minister Olga Lyubimova subsequently proposed bringing back Intervision, which was held in the Polish city of Sopot in the late 1970s and early 1980s and featured performers from the Soviet Union and other socialist countries.
President Vladimir Putin signed a decree ordering the competition’s revival in February 2025, with Russian authorities allocating 750 million rubles ($9.3 million) to stage it.
Organizers said the Moscow contest drew participants from 22 countries. Russia was represented by the pro-Kremlin singer Shaman.
Vietnamese singer Duc Phuc, who won his country’s version of “The Voice” a decade earlier, took first place. Kyrgyzstan’s Nomad group finished second, followed by Qatar’s Dana Al Meer.

title: Starlink in Ukraine Back to Normal After Week of Throttling
description: Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the U.S.
content:
Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the U.S.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometers per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelensky, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive U.S. intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the U.S. government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, U.S. administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out."

title: Russia Says Drone Attack Damages Tolyatti Facilities, Ukraine Says Petrochemical Plant Hit
description: Several industrial facilities were damaged in a drone attack on the Russian city of Tolyatti on Saturday, local authorities said, while Ukraine said it had struck a major petrochemical plant there.
content:
Several industrial facilities were damaged in a drone attack on the Russia n city of Tolyatti on Saturday, local authorities said, while Ukraine said it had struck a major petrochemical plant there.
Togliatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said preliminary reports indicated no fatalities or injuries. He did not specify which facilities had been hit.
Ukraine's General Staff said it had struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant, one of Russia 's largest producers of synthetic rubber.
The General Staff also reported a strike on the Proton electronics plant in Russia 's Oryol region, which Kyiv says manufactures components for cruise and ballistic missiles.
Oryol regional Governor Andrei Klychkov said three people were killed on Friday in a Ukrainian missile strike on an unspecified civilian facility in the region.
Ukraine's military also reported hitting an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in southern Russia . Local authorities confirmed an attack in the area but said it caused only minor damage to two apartment buildings.
Russia 's Defense Ministry said on Saturday that air defenses had destroyed 1,297 drones, one French-made SCALP cruise missile and four Ukrainian Neptune missiles over the previous 24 hours.

title: 3 Tankers of Russian Diesel Headed for North America, Russian Deputy PM Says
description: Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their way to North America, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.
content:
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their way to North America, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.
Novak, in a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, said the cargos were part of a deal to supply U.S. and world markets.
"The first three fuel tankers are already on their way to the eastern coast of the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the RDIF [Russian Direct Investment Fund]," Novak said.
Novak said Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tons in October.
Under a deal announced this month by U.S. President Donald Trump, Russia agreed to supply ​diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. The Trump administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its ‌war on Ukraine.
The deal as announced by Trump provided for 300,000 metric tons in October and more later.
A Reuters exclusive story published earlier on Friday, quoting ship-tracking data, said the first Russian diesel was on board a tanker headed for New York.

title: Russia, Ukraine Agree on Ceasefire in Embattled Oleshky, Plan New Peace Talks Next Month
description: Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through U.S. first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.
content:
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through U.S. first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.
The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine,” Melania Trump said in a statement.
The first lady noted that her intervention allowed both Russia and Ukraine to assign teams to work on the technical terms of the process, including de-mining the heavily mined roads. “All parties have worked around the clock since that moment,” she said.
Amid a U.S. push to organize new talks aimed at ending the 4.5-year-old war, Zelensky said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A U.S. official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland.
Zelensky said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow.
Previous rounds of talks headed by the United ​States ​stalled in February ⁠with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War II. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas ​region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.
The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia.
A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest U.S. midterm elections.
On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America.
In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.
The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defense Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time on Oct. 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.
Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already used drones twice to send food into the town.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also said the ceasefire would go into effect on Oct. 27 and told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians.
Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"Oleshky is a frontline war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water."
The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war.
Moscow and Kyiv both accuse each other of blocking supplies to the population of the town, which Ukrainian forces have been trying to retake.
Earlier, the Kremlin said that President Vladimir Putin had discussed the situation in Oleshky with U.S. President Donald Trump and told him that Russia’s human rights commissioner was working on humanitarian efforts there.
Putin also told Pope Leo in a phone call last Friday that he supported a Vatican initiative to help deliver supplies to civilians in Oleshky and was ready to cooperate on the matter. At the same time, he laid blame for the dire humanitarian situation in the town on Ukraine.
Zelensky's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St. Petersburg.
Zelensky said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and U.S. envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelensky told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialized.
Zelensky spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks.
Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required.
"If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since Oct. 13.
Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defense Ministry said. Zelensky described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result."
Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago.

title: Russia, U.S. Deny That American Hubbard Was Released in Exchange for Russian War Blogger
description: Russia and the U.S. have both denied that Russia had released American national Stephen Hubbard from prison in exchange for the recent release of a Russian war blogger detained in Montenegro whom the U.S. has accused of election interference.
content:
Russia and the U.S. have both denied that Russia had released American national Stephen Hubbard from prison in exchange for the recent release of a Russian war blogger detained in Montenegro whom the U.S. has accused of election interference.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that Hubbard, a 74-year-old U.S. citizen held in Russian custody since 2022, had been freed in what the Kremlin called a humanitarian goodwill gesture.
U.S. President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard and that Russia had not asked for anything or anyone in return for letting the retired U.S. schoolteacher return home.
But some people, including a former U.S. ambassador, suggested that Hubbard may have been freed in connection with the case of Mikhail Zvinchuk, a high-profile Russian war blogger who was briefly detained in Montenegro earlier this month before being let go.
"This case had no connection to Stephen Hubbard’s release," a State Department spokesperson said. "The Russian government made the unilateral decision to release Mr. Hubbard. Mr. Hubbard’s release was not part of an exchange, and no other concessions were provided."
In October 2024 the U.S. State Department offered $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of employees of the Russian media organization Rybar, listing Zvinchuk as its director.
The department's Rewards for Justice program says on its website that Rybar was previously funded by the late Russian mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin and managed social media channels promoting Russian government political interests in the U.S., including by stoking divisions over immigration in the run-up to the 2024 presidential election. Britain imposed sanctions on Zvinchuk and others linked to Rybar in July, having already designated the media company for spreading false narratives about Ukraine and interfering in European elections.
Moscow has regularly denied accusations of misinformation and sabotage campaigns, saying the ​West is spreading anti-Russian propaganda.
Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defence Ministry official, was detained in Montenegro on charges of spreading "Russian influence," then expelled with three other Russians on Oct. 9.
The State Department spokesperson declined to say whether Washington was involved in Zvinchuk's detention by U.S.-ally Montenegro or whether it had requested his extradition.
Asked to comment on Friday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Hubbard was not released in exchange for Zvinchuk.
"That's not right," Peskov said of the claim.

title: Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport Resumes Operations After Ukrainian Drone Threat
description: Moscow's largest airport, Sheremetyevo, resumed operations on Friday after it was forced to briefly suspend its work and ask passengers to move to safe locations due to a Ukrainian drone threat.
content:
Moscow's largest airport, Sheremetyevo, resumed operations on Friday after it was forced to briefly suspend its work and ask passengers to move to safe locations due to a Ukrainian drone threat.
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a statement on Telegram that air defense forces had shot down 21 Ukrainian drones that were headed to the Russian capital over a two-hour period.
Sheremetyevo said earlier on Friday that it had asked passengers to seek shelter and had evacuated certain areas and got passengers to disembark aircraft during an alert.
Rosaviatsia, Russia's aviation watchdog, said earlier on Friday that three of Moscow's four airports had temporarily suspended flight operations, something they do when there is Ukrainian drone activity.
Earlier, the state-run TASS news agency reported that all four airports serving the capital had halted arrivals and departures, citing aviation authorities and the Transport Ministry.
Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports were also accepting arrivals and departures in coordination with the relevant authorities following changes to temporary airspace restrictions, Rosaviatsia said. It warned that flight schedules could still change.
At one point during the disruption, 69 flights across Moscow’s airports were listed as canceled and another 164 as delayed, according to the flight-tracking website Airports.ru.
St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport received 25 flights diverted from Moscow, the local news outlet Fontanka reported . Passengers were either kept on board or allowed into the terminal, depending on their airline’s decision.
The Telegram news channel Shot reported that an Emirates Airbus A380 flying from Dubai to Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport was circling over the Penza region as it awaited clearance to land.
Residents and local monitoring channels reported explosions and air defense activity across Moscow’s suburbs, including Khimki, Dolgoprudny, Balashikha and Podolsk. There were also reports of explosions near the Sokol metro station and in the Zyuzino district within the capital.
Photos circulating on social media appeared to show drone debris on a runway at Sheremetyevo.
Authorities also evacuated the IQ Quarter tower in the Moscow City business district, which houses the Digital Development, Economic Development and Industry and Trade ministries, the news outlets MSK1 and Ostorozhno Novosti reported , citing eyewitnesses.
The attack followed several days of major disruptions to air travel in the capital. More than 500 flights were canceled at Moscow’s airports between Oct. 16 and 18, according to Airports.ru data.
Ukrainian drone attacks have repeatedly prompted temporary airport closures in Russia, with aviation authorities restricting flights while air defenses respond.

title: The Digital Ruble Gives the Kremlin a Kill Switch for Dissent
description: Opinion | Russians deserve to know what their own Central Bank is asking them to opt into.
content:
Russians deserve to know what their own Central Bank is asking them to opt into. The Russian central bank digital currency (CBDC) began its nationwide rollout in September.
The digital ruble is not an app, a card, or simple electronic cash. Instead, it is a direct connection to the Central Bank.
The risks of CBDCs are many. Under ordinary circumstances, governments have to go through commercial banks to access citizens’ money. But the default state of a CBDC is that the government has ultimate surveillance and control over people’s finances and how they use their money. Tracking purchases, freezing funds and locking people out of the economy become only a click away.
Rather than address these concerns head-on, Central Bank official Alla Bakina simply dismissed them as fake news. But how can that be true when the Central Bank itself has said it is investigating how to attach conditions to the digital ruble so that money can only be spent in ways the regime deems acceptable? Moreover, how can that be true when the Central Bank has already imposed restrictions limiting people to a monthly balance of 300,000 rubles ($3,660)?
You don’t need a crystal ball to see how such surveillance and control will be harnessed. Russians who dare to speak out against the Kremlin often find themselves on the state’s list of “terrorists and extremists” and their bank accounts frozen.
Anna Chekhovich , financial d irector of the Anti-Corruption Foundation (ACF), watched powerlessly as the regime went after her organization’s funds. It was only after the fact that she learned that the Anti-Corruption Foundation had been targeted by the Justice Ministry with accusations of money laundering. However, what appears much more likely is that the ACF was targeted for being critical of the regime. Since then, the regime has repeatedly frozen the accounts of both the organization and its employees, even going so far as to designate them as a terrorist organization in 2025.
In such cases, the state used the financial system to go after its opponents. The key difference with a CBDC, however, is that the state has immediate access to people’s money. No more tracking down banks or payment services. It’s in the government’s hands from the beginning.
And the Kremlin has rarely had less reason to loosen its grip. On Oct. 16, United States President Donald Trump waived nearly all of the new sanctions and tariffs Congress had passed to punish Russia’s war on Ukraine. A ruler who feels unchecked, who no longer fears consequences abroad, will not hesitate to use new tools at home to crush any type of dissent.
Despite the Central Bank’s best efforts to stress that the digital ruble is voluntary, it’s worth asking just how voluntary it really is or will become in practice. Banks and retailers are forced to support the CBDC . The regime recently began paying public employees with the digital ruble and the Central Bank announced that peer-to-peer cryptocurrency trading will be illegal starting in July 2027.
That is a lot of pressure for a currency few Russians say they want. In a 2025 state-run poll, 40% of Russians saw no benefit, and 37% struggled to identify how the digital ruble could possibly benefit them. Today, despite the launch of the digital ruble, Russians are using cash in record numbers .
History shows what can happen when demand falls short. In Nigeria , the hybrid authoritarian regime orchestrated a cash shortage in an attempt to spur CBDC adoption. It didn’t go well. Lines outside the banks turned into protests — and those protests turned into riots. In the end, CBDC adoption among the population rose from just 0.5% to 6% .
Nigeria is not an outlier. Around the world, more than 150 governments are exploring CBDCs, which is why the Human Rights Foundation built the CBDC Tracker in 2023 to document the proliferation of these digital currencies and the human rights concerns their implementation amplifies. One finding stands out above all else — the governments that are pursuing CBDCs more aggressively are authoritarian regimes .
Russians deserve to know that the digital ruble isn’t just another form of money. It’s tyranny technology being spearheaded by authoritarian regimes in a bid to secure control over money. That is what the Russian people are being asked to opt into.

title: Russian Subsidiary of German Retailer Metro Donates $12M to Military Fund
description: The nationalized Russian subsidiary of German wholesale giant Metro announced Friday that it donated 1 billion rubles ($12.4 million) to a pro-war charitable foundation linked to the Kremlin.
content:
The nationalized Russian subsidiary of German wholesale giant Metro announced Friday that it donated 1 billion rubles ($12.4 million) to a pro-war charitable foundation linked to the Kremlin.
The funds were sent to a foundation called “People’s Front. Everything for Victory!” — which is managed by President Vladimir Putin’s political coalition, the All-Russia People’s Front (ONF).
“As part of Russia’s economic system, we consider it important to participate in the state’s strategic initiatives,” Metro Russia CEO Johannes Tholey said.
Metro’s donation will be used to buy tactical gear, off-road vehicles, communications equipment, intelligence hardware and anti-drone systems for Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine, according to senior ONF executive Sergei Gorbunov.
Metro AG, the parent company of Metro Russia, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The move comes after Putin signed an executive order on Sept. 28 placing Metro Russia under “temporary management” of the state. Tholey is the CEO of the state-appointed entity that now manages Metro Russia, Torg Rus.
Metro’s takeover comes alongside similar seizures of major Western companies in recent weeks, including retail chain Auchan, food giant Nestlé and logistics operator FM Logistic.
Putin has defended the moves as a symmetrical response to Western sanctions and the freezing of Russian state assets there. He said control of the companies could be returned under favorable conditions.
Earlier in October, The Bell reported that the Russian government expects businesses to pay $5.7 billion in voluntary contributions to plug a widening budget deficit amid record war spending.

title: Romania Blames Russia for Deadly Drone Attack on Cargo Ship
description: Romania said Friday that one sailor had died and three were missing after a drone struck and sank a ship in the Black Sea, with the country's president blaming Russia for the attack.
content:
Romania said Friday that one sailor had died and three were missing after a drone struck and sank a ship in the Black Sea, with the country's president blaming Russia for the attack.
The cargo ship Khoryv, flying the Comoros flag, was "struck by a drone and sank near Romanian territorial waters," President Nicușor Dan wrote in a Facebook post.
Speaking to reporters, Dan said the attack was "clearly part of the escalation that Russia is carrying out in the context of the war in Ukraine."
Romania launched a rescue operation after the Khoryv sent a distress signal around 10:00 am local time, 13 nautical miles from the Romanian port of Constanta.
Romanian authorities said 10 Ukrainian and three Azerbaijani crewmembers were on board.
"Of the 13 people on board, 10 were rescued by another commercial vessel in the area, nine of whom were alive and one of whom had died. Three others are still missing," Romania's interior ministry said in a statement.
It added that the vessel "sustained major damage and capsized."
"Due to adverse weather conditions and poor visibility, an aerial rescue operation by helicopter is not possible," the Romanian Naval Authority said in a separate statement.
Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Facebook the attack was "unacceptable and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law."
The strikes on civilian shipping in the waters off NATO and EU members Bulgaria and Romania have left scores of sailors missing or dead.
Seven ship crewmembers went missing on Oct. 15 off the coast of Romania when the Wine Trader, a chemical tanker, caught fire after a drone attack.
Romanian fighter jets also shot down two Russian drones over the Black Sea last weekend.
On Thursday, following a meeting of Romania's Supreme Council for National Defense, the presidency said that "threats to freedom of navigation and critical infrastructure have increased significantly."
Romania is looking into "accelerated development of maritime surveillance capabilities, mine countermeasures and effective countermeasures against drones that intrude unauthorized into national airspace and territorial waters," the presidency said.
NATO said after talks on Black Sea security on Tuesday that it was deploying additional planes, drones and radar systems to the area because of the attacks on ships.
Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu said Romania was working with NATO allies including Bulgaria and Turkey to "fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities."
In his Facebook post, Dan said it was "time for Russia to take the peace initiatives put forward by the United States and Europe seriously, to accept the proposals for a ceasefire and to bring the war to an end."

title: FSB Orders Critical Infrastructure Operators to Shutter Websites Over PHP Bug – RBC
description: The FSB security service’s cybersecurity division has told Russia’s critical infrastructure operators to temporarily take down websites if they cannot immediately patch critical flaws in the PHP programming language that were uncovered using AI, the RBC outlet reported Thursday.
content:
The FSB security service’s cybersecurity division has told Russia’s critical infrastructure operators to temporarily take down websites if they cannot immediately patch critical flaws in the PHP programming language that were uncovered using AI, the RBC outlet reported Thursday.
Operators were ordered to apply emergency software patches, run full antivirus scans and report any suspicious activity.
“Consider temporarily restricting external access to vulnerable web servers up to and including shutting them down,” the security alert reportedly stated.
The FSB order applies to communication networks and information systems across government agencies, as well as financial, energy, transportation, medical and other companies.
Its directive mirrors that of the U.S. National Security Agency, as well as authorities from the EU and China, after PHP programmers released a fix for the critical vulnerability on Wednesday.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Global firms and governments rushed on Thursday to patch PHP flaws as cloud firms reported a surge of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.
As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare and Amazon.
Tech experts warned in comments to RBC that “tens or hundreds of thousands” of Russian websites remain vulnerable to cyberattacks due to widespread reliance on PHP across the country.
More than 90% of Russian-language websites and almost 70% of the web globally run on PHP, according to the W3Techs platform.

title: Russia and Ukraine Exchange 540 POWs
description: Russia and Ukraine exchanged 270 prisoners of war each in the second consecutive repatriation effort in as many days, the Russian Defense Ministry said Friday. “On Oct. 23, 270 Russian servicemen were returned from territory controlled by the Kyiv regime,” the military said. “In exchange, 270 POWs of the Ukrainian armed forces were handed over.” The swap took place at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus, according to Belarusian state media.
content:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged 270 prisoners of war each in the second consecutive repatriation effort in as many days, the Russian Defense Ministry said Friday.
“On Oct. 23, 270 Russian servicemen were returned from territory controlled by the Kyiv regime,” the military said. “In exchange, 270 POWs of the Ukrainian armed forces were handed over.”
The swap took place at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus, according to Belarusian state media.
While in Belarus, the Russian soldiers are being provided with mental health and medical support, after which they will return to Russia for further treatment. Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova is accompanying them, the Defense Ministry said.
On her Telegram channel, Lantratova said that 12 families were also reunited across the border, with seven civilians returning to Russia and seven others departing for Ukraine. She did not mention the POW exchange.
Lantratova said the family reunification was a joint effort with her Ukrainian colleague Dmytro Lubinets. She also thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for helping mediate the initiative.
Friday’s exchange comes a day after Russia and Ukraine repatriated the remains of 277 fallen soldiers at the same Belarusian border crossing.

title: Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Perm Region Chemical Plant
description: A Ukrainian drone strike damaged an industrial plant in the Ural Mountains region of Perm, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said Friday.
content:
A Ukrainian drone strike damaged an industrial plant in the Ural Mountains region of Perm, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said Friday.
Makhonin said air defense systems intercepted 20 drones over the Perm region overnight, with falling debris shattering windows in residential buildings in the city of Berezniki and the nearby town of Solikamsk.
“An industrial facility also sustained minor damage,” he wrote on Telegram without identifying the site.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of rising smoke from the purported area of the attack to identify the targeted facility as the Azot chemical plant in Berezniki. Azot is part of Uralchem, a corporation controlled by billionaire Dmitry Mazepin.
The facility is Russia’s sole producer of higher aliphatic amines, sodium nitrate and crystalline sodium nitrite, and manufactures ammonium nitrate, liquid ammonia, urea, nitric acid and nitrite-nitrate salts.
Ammonium nitrate is widely used as fertilizer and is also a component in explosives.
The Azot plant, which employs around 2,500 people and is located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from the border with Ukraine, was previously targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks in September 2026 and October 2025.
Russian civil aviation authorities issued airspace restrictions during the air raid alert in the Perm region on Friday.
The Defense Ministry said it intercepted 443 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

title: Russian Central Bank Holds Key Interest Rate Steady
description: Russia’s Central Bank decided to hold its key interest rate at 14% during its latest meeting on Friday, weighing inflation risks against the need to lower currently high borrowing costs for businesses and consumers as the Kremlin prioritizes spending on the war against Ukraine.
content:
Russia’s Central Bank decided to hold its key interest rate at 14% during its latest meeting on Friday, weighing inflation risks against the need to lower currently high borrowing costs for businesses and consumers as the Kremlin prioritizes spending on the war against Ukraine.
The Central Bank reported that annual inflation hit 6.8% earlier in the week. Policymakers slightly increased their full-year inflation forecast, now at 7.1% to 7.6%, but they still expect price growth to fall toward the 4% target next year.
Inflation expectations remain high, the Central Bank said, though officials have argued that some of the more recent price increases are rooted in one-time factors, like Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries raising the cost of gasoline and diesel.
“Underlying price growth has not yet decreased… primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacities in certain sectors,” it said in a press release, while also alluding to inflation risks associated with the war in Iran and its impacts on global energy markets.
Policymakers also hiked the projected key rate range for next year by two percentage points, now at 12.5 to 13.5%.
The rate hold, which analysts widely expected, comes as spending on the war in Ukraine continues to strain the Russian government’s finances, while Ukrainian drone and missile attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial sites in recent months have raised the cost of some goods and services.
Despite its more bearish outlook on inflation, the Central Bank raised its forecast for economic growth this year, with GDP now expected to come in at 0.5% to 1% by the end of 2026, according to Friday’s press release.
Sofia Donets, chief economist at T-Investments, said policymakers appeared to leave room for another rate cut this year, “ especially since the signal in the press release remained neutral with no explicit guidance on the future direction.”
Inflation is a growing concern across the globe as the war in Iran drives up the price of oil, which rose above $116 per barrel for the first time since May on Friday. For Russia, Ukrainian attacks against oil refineries have compounded the problem since it can sometimes take up to several months to repair the complex facilities.
“The speed at which [production] capacity is restored is itself an element of uncertainty,” Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina said at a press conference later on Friday.
“Another factor of uncertainty is the full range of secondary effects — namely, how this will feed into prices across a broad spectrum of goods and impact inflation expectations,” she said.
A long period of high borrowing costs has weighed down economic growth in Russia, leaving business leaders pressing for a lower key interest rate to stimulate investment. But the Central Bank has so far prioritized keeping price growth subdued.
“There were individual opinions in favor of raising the rate, but only one option was discussed in detail: keeping the rate unchanged,” Nabiullina said of the key rate decision on Friday.
The Central Bank ’s next rate meeting takes place on Dec. 18.

title: Russia Vows Retaliation After Austria Expels Its Diplomats
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry has vowed to issue an “inevitable” response to Austria expelling four of its diplomats, the state-run TASS news agency reported Friday.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry has vowed to issue an “inevitable” response to Austria expelling four of its diplomats, the state-run TASS news agency reported Friday.
Austria’s foreign ministry said earlier that it declared the Vienna-based Russian diplomats personae non gratae over “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status,” a term usually used for spying.
“A response will follow inevitably,” Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky told TASS without providing further details.
Three of the expelled diplomats worked at Russia’s Embassy in Vienna and one at the Russian delegation to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on military security and arms control, the Austrian ministry said.
The move brings the total number of Russian diplomats expelled in Austria over the past six years to 18. While Austria is a neutral country, politically its governments have sided with Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In May, Austria expelled three Russian diplomats, citing an “antenna forest” on the roofs of Russian diplomatic buildings that could be used for spying.
Moscow routinely issues tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats from the host country’s embassy in Moscow.
Vienna is a major diplomatic center, hosting the OSCE and UN organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency.

title: First Shipment of Russian Diesel Departs for the United States Under Trump Deal
description: The Kremlin confirmed Friday that the first shipment of diesel to the United States left port the day before as part of an energy deal made between President Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. “The first tanker is on its way to buyers,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. “From here on out, shipments will continue on a regular schedule.” Reuters, citing shipping data, confirmed the tanker was loaded with 40,000 tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in the Baltic port of Primorsk.
content:
The Kremlin confirmed Friday that the first shipment of diesel to the United States left port the day before as part of an energy deal made between President Donald Trump and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
“The first tanker is on its way to buyers,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. “From here on out, shipments will continue on a regular schedule.”
Reuters, citing shipping data, confirmed the tanker was loaded with 40,000 tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in the Baltic port of Primorsk. It is expected to arrive in the United States on Nov. 7.
Trump announced the diesel deal on Oct. 9, saying that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.
The following day, Russia partially lifted its diesel export ban — first introduced in the summer due to domestic shortages.
Most experts agree that the agreement will have little effect on global energy markets in the near future. The 300,000 tons scheduled to hit the U.S. market this month cover only three-quarters of the country’s daily consumption, according to calculations by The Guardian.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Wednesday that subsequent shipments “will satisfy all the U.S. requirements within our capacity.” Deliveries to other international buyers, he added, will depend on how quickly Russian refineries can restore output following Ukrainian drone strikes.
“If, according to the schedule, we can reach full volume only by the end of the year, then other countries will receive the volumes they previously received,” Novak said.
Turkey’s energy minister said this weekend that Ankara had negotiated to secure a share of the Russian diesel under the Trump agreement.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European allies have criticized the U.S.-Russian agreement, arguing that it will bolster the Russian economy and strain transatlantic relations.
By most accounts, the diesel deal is designed to boost support for Republicans going into the midterm elections in early November. Polls show that surging energy costs in the United States, largely triggered by the war in Iran, are driving voter frustration and hurting the chances of Trump allies being elected to office.

title: Moscow to Present New ‘Anti-Drone Dome’ at Upcoming Russia-Africa Summit
description: Russia’s state exporter Rosoboronexport will reveal a planned air defense system called the “Anti-Drone Dome” at next week’s Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported Friday.
content:
Russia’s state exporter Rosoboronexport will reveal a planned air defense system called the “Anti-Drone Dome” at next week’s Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported Friday.
The multilayered system combines radar detection, electronic jamming, weapons and physical barriers, Rosoboronexport said in a statement.
The “Anti-Drone Dome” is designed to protect civilians and military personnel, as well as bridges, buildings and energy and industrial facilities. Rosoboronexport said a separate system offers protection for mobile convoys and cargo.
“All the tools and solutions used in it have proven their effectiveness in real conditions,” Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheyev said.
The system relies entirely on Russian-manufactured equipment and is “adaptable to a specific partner and specific facility,” the state arms exporter said.
Moscow hosts the Russia-Africa summit next Wednesday and Thursday.
The upcoming presentation for Moscow’s African partners comes as Russia itself continues to struggle against Ukrainian drone attacks that have repeatedly overwhelmed air defense systems, targeting oil refineries, warehouses and data centers.
Earlier this spring, President Vladimir Putin replaced the head of Russia’s Aerospace Forces following a series of destructive Ukrainian drone strikes. Its new chief, Alexander Chaiko, narrowly survived a suicide bomb attack at an upscale Moscow restaurant in August.

title: She Was a Leading Arctic Ornithologist. Now She’s Imprisoned for $25 in Donations.
description: Sofya Rozenfeld dedicated her life to following Arctic birds across the tundra, counting flocks from a small seaplane and advocating for the species she studied.  When her colleagues urged her to leave Russia as she faced criminal investigation for donating to Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), she struggled to imagine a life away from that work. “For Sofya, leaving her geese would have been like abandoning her children,” Alexandra Panyutina, who studied with Rozenfeld at Moscow State University and later worked alongside her, told the independent media project Veter.
content:
Sofya Rozenfeld dedicated her life to following Arctic birds across the tundra, counting flocks from a small seaplane and advocating for the species she studied.
When her colleagues urged her to leave Russia as she faced criminal investigation for donating to Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), she struggled to imagine a life away from that work.
“For Sofya, leaving her geese would have been like abandoning her children,” Alexandra Panyutina, who studied with Rozenfeld at Moscow State University and later worked alongside her, told the independent media project Veter.
Even as she awaited sentencing, Rozenfeld continued her fieldwork, securing court permission for a 10-day expedition to the Russian Arctic.
“The first piece of advice [from her colleagues] was to leave Russia,” her friend Artur Ryabitsev said . “But she was against it: ‘No, I live here; I work here; everything I have is here. What would I do outside Russia?’”
On Oct. 7, a Moscow court sentenced the ornithologist to 3.5 years in a penal colony for making two donations totaling 2,000 rubles ($25) to the FBK.
Rozenfeld, 50, is now the third woman in Russia to be imprisoned for donating to the late Kremlin critic’s organization, which was banned as “extremist” in 2021. The Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights organization Memorial has designated her a political prisoner.
The sentence has stunned friends and colleagues, who describe a scientist devoted to studying and protecting Arctic waterfowl.
By spring 2026, authorities had opened more than 200 criminal cases over donations to the FBK, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported. The average donation amounted to just 400 rubles ($5).
For Rozenfeld, a researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Ecology and Evolution, the case threatened to sever a passion for the Arctic that stretched back to her time as a student.
After her family emigrated to Israel in the late 1980s, she returned to Moscow at 15, finished school and enrolled in Moscow State University’s biology faculty. She holds dual Russian-Israeli citizenship.
Panyutina recalled witnessing Rozenfeld’s determination early on.
“Imagine a second-year student organizing her own expedition to Wrangel Island to study snow geese,” she told Veter. “You could say that was the start of her fieldwork. And it continued right up until she was handcuffed.”
Rozenfeld chose to focus her research on the Arctic, particularly geese, swans and related waterfowl that breed in the Far North before migrating thousands of kilometers south.
To track those journeys, one must determine where the birds nest, where they stop during migration and where they spend their winters. But the real challenge lies in determining how many birds there actually are.
Previously, such counts often relied on rough estimates that varied wildly among researchers. Colleagues describe Rozenfeld as one of the few specialists capable of producing more reliable population counts across vast, remote territories.
“She could say: This is how many birds of a particular species we have, this is where they live, and this is where they go for the winter,” Mikhail Kalyakin, director of Moscow State University’s Zoological Museum, told Veter. “To do that, she had to fly over the tundra.”
Working with colleagues, Rozenfeld developed a survey method in which the team would take detailed photos of birds while flying an ultralight seaplane built by a fellow researcher at low altitudes and speeds. These photos would then be used to count populations.
She also got involved with conservation policy, serving on a commission assessing birds for Russia’s Red Data Book of threatened species and helping inform decisions about their protection.
“She fought for their conservation, for their survival, so that we could learn more about them and protect them,” Panyutina said. “She felt responsible for them.”
That sense of responsibility helped keep Rozenfeld from leaving Russia after investigators raided her Moscow apartment and interrogated her in December 2025.
“The first advice she received was to leave Russia,” her friend Artur Ryabitsev told Veter. “But she was against it: ‘No, I live here, I work here, everything I have is here. What would I do outside Russia?’”
Relatives said she could not imagine how she would continue her profession from another country.
She continued her work as the criminal case progressed, including on the court-approved expedition to the Yamalo-Nenets autonomous district shortly before her final hearing.
According to her colleagues, Rozenfeld feared going to prison but remained hopeful that she would receive a lighter punishment.
In court, she explained that she had signed up for recurring donations to FBK “out of a desire to fight corruption.”
“Don’t we have law enforcement agencies for that?” the judge interrupted .
“I believe that any public help is needed here,” she replied. “Because I have seen the horrific forms this evil can take in my own work related to scientific research and environmental protection. It seemed to me that any help in combating corruption would be a good thing.”
While the verdict shocked her friends and family, Panyutina recalled that Rozenfeld herself appeared composed and focused in court — “like someone in an extraordinarily difficult situation trying with all her strength to keep composure and maintain dignity.”
As soon as the sentence was announced, uniformed officers approached Rozenfeld to take her into custody.
“They handcuffed Sofya and pushed her into the cage,” Ryabitsev recalled. “The judge finished reading the verdict, and then they took her away.”
Her relatives have since set up a support website and appealed to the Israeli authorities for assistance. Israel’s Foreign Ministry told Newsru.co.il that it was in contact with her family, but did not say whether a consular official had visited her.
Rozenfeld is one of a growing number of Russian academics, scientists and engineers who have been prosecuted for donating to FBK.
Andrei Dymov, an associate professor at the Higher School of Economics and senior researcher at the Steklov Mathematical Institute, are among those who have been prosecuted. Physicist Yevgeny Onishchenko, a former researcher at the Lebedev Physical Institute, received 18 months of compulsory labor for a 5,000 ruble ($60) donation.
“I think, until the very last second, none of us could really take in the possibility that she would actually go to prison,” Panyutina said. “Including Sofya herself.”

title: Putin Says Renewed Peace Talks Must Focus on Security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe Overall
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that future talks on ending the war against Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe.
content:
Russia n President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that future talks on ending the war against Ukraine should focus on security guarantees for both countries and an overall framework for security throughout Europe.
Putin, interviewed on Russia n state television a day after meeting U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, confirmed that Russia was ready to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Ukraine next month.
He restated longstanding Kremlin policy that Russia never wanted to launch its full-scale invasion, but had run into hostile reactions from Ukraine on key issues of concern to Moscow.
Talks on a variety of matters could lead to a positive outcome, Putin said, but Russia remained intent on resolving the conflict once and for all rather than agreeing to a short-lived ceasefire.
"The goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said.
The Russia n president said Witkoff also stressed that discussions had to extend to "the architecture of European security as a whole. And I agree with that too. Well, let's see how things develop in the coming days."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who met Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ready for talks likely to take place by early next month. Ukraine, he said, supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives."
The United States has led efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, but talks have stalled since Trump ordered attacks against Iran in February.
Many of the disagreements about how to end the Ukraine war focus on territory, with Russia demanding Ukraine cede all of eastern Ukraine's Donbas region. Kyiv rejects any deal that would include giving up land it currently holds.
In his comments on Thursday , Putin said any discussion on territory in eastern Ukraine had to consider what he said was the fact that the area was "historically Russia n land."
And residents there, he claimed, had voted to be a part of Russia in referendums staged seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
"Firstly, my attitude on this matter is that this is not their territory. It’s the territory of historical Russia ," Putin said.

title: Trump Says Musk Restored Ukraine's Starlink Access, Declines to Say if They Spoke
description: Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access but the U.S. president declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter.
content:
Donald Trump said on Thursday that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had restored Ukraine's Starlink access but the U.S. president declined to comment when asked whether he had spoken to the billionaire about the matter.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Thursday that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
"I don't want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference, I guess. The bottom line — he put it back," Trump told reporters when asked if he spoke to Musk. Trump did not elaborate further.
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country's attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.
The Starlink system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after the Trump-Musk conversation, the WSJ reported earlier, citing U.S. and Ukrainian officials.
Some Ukrainian officials told the newspaper the system had not been restored to full functionality but was working at higher speeds than under the cap.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier on Thursday that speed on Starlink systems had not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the coming days.
Trump told Musk he was frustrated the system's speeds remained capped, according to the newspaper.
Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown. Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that decisions regarding Ukraine's access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House.
Zelensky's relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskiy.
Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow on Thursday, as the warring sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest U.S. push to end the conflict. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Trump had promised to end the war when he took office but the goal has remained elusive.

title: AvtoVAZ Output, Sales Could Fall Up to 25% as State Subsidies Run Out
description: Russia’s largest carmaker AvtoVAZ could see production and sales fall by 20% to 25% by the end of the year after funding ran out for government programs subsidizing car purchases, a senior Industry and Trade Ministry official said.
content:
Russia’s largest carmaker AvtoVAZ could see production and sales fall by 20% to 25% by the end of the year after funding ran out for government programs subsidizing car purchases, a senior Industry and Trade Ministry official said.
Dmitry Klementyev, deputy head of the ministry’s automotive and railway engineering department, linked the projected decline to the suspension of subsidized car loans, Interfax reported .
The program offered discounts on Russian-made vehicles ranging from 10% for families with children to 35% for buyers of electric cars.
This year’s allocations of 20 billion rubles ($244 million) for subsidized car loans and 30 billion rubles ($366 million) for vehicle leasing were exhausted in September. No additional funding is planned this year, as military spending puts pressure on the federal budget.
The Industry and Trade Ministry said the programs had supported sales of 178,200 vehicles, including more than 123,000 purchased through subsidized loans, and had met their targets for supporting the market.
Analysts expect AvtoVAZ, which sold 244,600 vehicles in the first nine months of the year, to be particularly exposed to the withdrawal of state support because subsidized purchases account for a larger share of its sales.
The funding shortfall comes as Russia’s car market loses momentum. New passenger car sales fell 7% year on year in August and were virtually unchanged in September. Weekly figures for October also show little sign of a recovery: sales from Oct. 12 to 18 were 9% below the same period last year.
Analysts and dealers say demand is too weak to make up for the loss of government-backed discounts.
The withdrawal of subsidies is pushing manufacturers to offer their own discounts and subsidized loans, potentially bringing down average car prices in October, according to Sergei Tselikov, head of market research agency Autostat.
AvtoVAZ has fewer resources for a price war than its Chinese competitors. During last year’s market downturn, company president Maxim Sokolov complained that Chinese manufacturers were offering discounts approaching 1 million rubles ($12,200), roughly the starting price of a new Lada Granta.
Sokolov called for greater state support. The Industry and Trade Ministry subsequently raised Russia’s vehicle recycling fee again, affecting high-powered foreign cars, including those imported by individuals for personal use.
Lada’s share of Russia’s new car market has fallen to about 24% this year, below the 25% threshold Sokolov previously described as critical for the company.
Its market share stabilized at 24.7% in September, when it sold about 30,300 vehicles, according to Avtostat. Overall, Russia recorded 122,800 new passenger car sales that month and about 968,000 in the first nine months of the year.
Analysts say the growing market share of locally manufactured cars has benefited producers assembling Chinese models more than Lada. These include Haval and Tenet, which assembles Chery models in Russia, as well as the Belarusian brand Belgee, a joint venture with China’s Geely.
Russian-made vehicles accounted for 65% of new passenger car sales in September.
State support is set to shrink further. The draft budget allocates 7 billion rubles ($85.4 million) annually for subsidized car loans over the next two years, roughly a third of this year’s funding.
AvtoVAZ is already reducing its Moscow dealership network.
The Industry and Trade Ministry has pledged to seek more funding for automotive support programs, but broader budget cuts leave little room for an increase.
“Everything that could be cut has been cut,” Alexander Ivanov, chief economist at Ingosstrakh Investments, said of the 2027 budget.

title: Moscow to Build ‘Veterans Palace’ Rehab Center for Ukraine War Vets
description: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin on Wednesday revealed plans to build a “Palace of Veterans” rehabilitation center for Russian soldiers who served in the war against Ukraine.
content:
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin on Wednesday revealed plans to build a “Palace of Veterans” rehabilitation center for Russian soldiers who served in the war against Ukraine.
Located at the former war veterans social rehabilitation center in central Moscow, the renovated Palace of Veterans will feature state-of-the-art medical, physical, as well as social and creative facilities, Sobyanin said.
“This will be a single complex with a first-of-its-kind full-fledged infrastructure for the recovery and rehabilitation of [Ukraine war] veterans,” he wrote in a post on Telegram.
The Palace of Veterans will feature diagnostic equipment, a “walking school,” physical therapy and kinesitherapy halls, as well as a water wellness complex and spaces for yoga and martial arts.
Sobyanin said the space will be designed for “daytime and short-term” rehabilitation visits, with art therapy workshops, libraries, as well as music and dance classrooms.
He did not disclose the facility’s capacity.
The Palace of Veterans will consist of two reconstructed buildings covering 22,000 square meters (236,806 square feet).
Renovation work began in January, with its completion scheduled by the end of 2027.
The nearby Yekaterininsky Park is also being renovated, with a family center, sports fields and a refurbished waterfront with a boat station and amphitheater set for completion by late 2026.

title: Regions Calling: More Questions Than Answers After Latest Black Sea Oil Spill
description: Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
content:
Hello and welcome to Regions Calling , your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
In this week’s edition, we are putting the spotlight on the southern Krasnodar region , home to Russia’s vast Black Sea coast, which is reeling from the environmental fallout of a Ukrainian drone attack on the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio tanker — while officials have offered few details.
For more of the latest news from the regions, subscribe to our biweekly email newsletter here or on Substack .
On the evening of Oct. 6, apocalyptic photos of a thick plume of smoke rising from the burning sea against a bright dusk sky flooded the Russian internet.
These images showed the result of one of Ukraine’s most successful drone attacks on the energy infrastructure along Russia’s Black Sea coast as the 247-meter, Liberian-flagged Afromax Rio oil tanker had been hit off the shore of the resort city of Sochi.
Environmental specialists were quick to sound the alarm over the fire's potentially catastrophic consequences, saying its ecological impact could exceed that of the massive 2024 spill near the resort city of Anapa, which left beaches coated in heavy fuel oil and mobilized thousands of volunteers.
Two weeks after the attack, as locals find oil-covered birds and pollution builds up along the coast, there are still more questions than answers.
“I would be a bad expert if I were to outline the [exact environmental] consequences right now,” one prominent environmentalist told The Moscow Times. “Why? Because it is not known how much oil has spilled as a result of this attack. And that is the main problem.”
Though regional authorities initially denied that the attack had caused an oil spill, Krasnodar Governor Venyamin Kondratyev warned of a potential emergency in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk one week after the attack.
The regional Emergency Situations Ministry also said it “detected minor oil spills” along the shoreline near Novorossiysk last week, but denied they were linked to the Aframax Rio.
The environmentalist, who requested anonymity for safety reasons, said officials’ reluctance to publicize details of the attack’s environmental impact comes amid mounting evidence of a spill and contradicts Russian legislation that “prohibits classifying information about the environment and environmental pollution.”
The Afromax Rio was towed to Novorossiysk, Russia’s largest Black Sea port, the day after the attack — a move decried by prominent local environmental campaigner Tatiana Tribat, who pointed to the already heavy environmental burden borne by the city.
Satellite images analyzed by Greenpeace showed the damaged vessel leaving an oil slick that covered around 25 square kilometers by Oct. 8.
Independent environmental monitor Prozrachny Mir also dentified an oil slick stretching along the coast from Novorossiysk toward the town of Arkhipo-Osipovka some 70 kilometers (43 miles) south in images dated Oct. 10.
Meanwhile, residents of Novorossiysk, Sochi and smaller coastal towns along the tanker’s route have reported finding oil-covered birds and traces of pollution washing ashore.
“Every day we receive reports [of contamination] from Yuzhnaya Ozereevka, Limanchik, Dyurso and elsewhere. If it wasn’t the Aframax Rio that fouled the coastline, then who is responsible for the pollution?” Tribat told a local newspaper.
For coastal residents who remember the Anapa disaster, the images were causes for concern. Yet evidence available from local media and volunteers “suggest that the spill from Afromax Rio was, in fact, significantly smaller” than that disaster, the environmental expert told The Moscow Times.
The Anapa spill happened in December 2024 when two Russian-flagged oil tankers were damaged during a storm, releasing over 9,000 tons of heavy fuel oil, known as mazut, into the Black Sea. Pollution from the spill stretched from annexed Crimea to Georgia, though Russia’s Krasnodar region was hit the worst.
“What we see now is incomparably smaller coastal pollution,” the Russia-based expert said.
“Back then, hundreds — even thousands — of birds were affected. In this instance, the number is in single digits. Back then, about 60 kilometers [37 miles] of coastline was covered in…a continuous strip of fuel oil,” he said.
Though the Afromax Rio can carry up to 100,000 metric tons of oil — nearly 10 times the combined load of the two tankers that caused the 2024 Anapa spill — this leak’s less pronounced impact on the environment is likely the result of the apocalyptic fire documented in the initial images.
“Of course, burning oil pollutes the air, then the combustion products…fall into the sea,” the expert said. “But this amount of damage and consequences are incomparable to what would have happened if all that oil poured out unburnt into the sea.”
Authorities reopened beaches affected by the 2024 Anapa spill this summer, but the disaster is far from over.
Images analyzed by satellite imagery monitor Sky Eye in July identified a fresh oil slick coming from the sunken bow of the Volgoneft-239 tanker in the Kerch Strait.
Meanwhile, authorities have long denied any ongoing leaks coming from the wreckage — sometimes in statements accompanied by photos of divers emerging from inspections covered in oil.
The consequences of the Afromax Rio spill could be shorter-lived, as some reports suggest authorities have already started pumping the remaining oil out of the tanker.
But the ongoing war in Ukraine, which has seen an escalation in maritime drone activity in recent months, means that a new oil disaster threatening the Black Sea’s ecosystem could be just around the corner.
“In recent months, Ukraine has significantly intensified its attacks on civilian vessels [in Black Sea], including tankers. While there do not appear to have been any major spills…some level of pollution has nonetheless occurred,” the expert said.
“And yet no damage from a military strike can compare to a disaster caused by negligence of officials and vessel operators, corruption and the like — which is precisely what led to the 2024 accident,” he said.
Authorities in the Far East port of Vladivostok removed a statue of Nobel Prize-winning writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn from the city’s central embankment on Tuesday to relocate it to the city outskirts.
Vladivostok city hall had ordered the Soviet dissident’s statue to be relocated earlier this year after deeming its presence among the warships “inappropriate.”
But just a day later, the 2.5-meter-tall monument reappeared on the embankment after it was found to be too large for its new location. It is unclear if the authorities will proceed with the plan after this week’s mishap.

title: Communist Party Leader in Komi Republic Arrested for ‘Justifying Terrorism’
description: Russian law enforcement authorities have arrested former State Duma lawmaker from the Communist Party Oleg Mikhailov on charges of publicly justifying terrorism, his regional party team said Wednesday.
content:
Russian law enforcement authorities have arrested former State Duma lawmaker from the Communist Party Oleg Mikhailov on charges of publicly justifying terrorism, his regional party team said Wednesday.
Mikhailov has headed the Communist Party branch in the northern republic of Komi since 2014 and served as a State Duma member between 2021 and September 2026. In last month’s parliamentary elections, he lost his seat to a rival from the ruling United Russia party.
Komi’s Communist Party branch said in a social media post that Mikhailov was arrested at a Moscow airport after returning from a vacation.
The charge against Mikhailov of publicly justifying terrorism stems from old social media posts in which he allegedly supported jailed sociologist Boris Kagarlitsky and leftist activist Sergei Udaltsov .
“We believe the charges are revenge by Goldshtein and United Russia,” the party wrote on the VKontakte social media platform, referring to the regional head of Komi, Rostislav Goldshtein.
A court hearing where a judge will decide whether to place Mikhailov in pre-trial detention is scheduled for Thursday. He could face up to seven years in prison if found guilty.
Mikhailov’s arrest follows the August detention of Communist Party firebrand Nikolai Bondarenko in the southern Saratov region on “extremism” charges over an old social media post featuring a photo of the late opposition activist Alexei Navalny.
