title: What Is Russia Trying to Achieve by Arresting a Japanese Journalist?
description: Opinion | After bursting into the hotel room in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Oct. 13, the masked FSB agents quickly pressed the suspect to the floor and handcuffed him.
content:
After bursting into the hotel room in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Oct. 13, the masked FSB agents quickly pressed the suspect to the floor and handcuffed him. The FSB video then shows the man being whisked from Sakhalin to Moscow, where he was placed in pre-trial detention for two months at Lefortovo Prison.
Was this some dangerous terrorist? Not at all. The suspect is Imai Yuki, a 34-year-old Japanese journalist from the Hokkaido Shimbun, a regional newspaper on Japan’s northernmost main island. The FSB accuses him of espionage on behalf of Japan’s intelligence service.
The charges are almost certainly trumped up. Japan does not even have an external intelligence service.
The FSB also failed to produce any proof of its allegations. They weakly suggested that he had gathered information about residents of the Southern Kuril Islands sent to fight in Ukraine. This is not espionage but legitimate journalism, especially since Japan claims these disputed islands as its own territory. Ludicrously, one of the supposedly suspicious documents displayed by the FSB is a Japanese taxi receipt.
The Russian security services do, of course, have a record of detaining foreigners for use as diplomatic leverage. In March 2023, Evan Gershkovich, an American journalist for The Wall Street Journal , was detained on similarly flimsy espionage charges.
Sentenced to 16 years in a maximum-security penal colony, Gershkovich was freed after 491 days thanks to a multinational prisoner exchange that saw several Russian intelligence officers and criminals returned to Moscow.
This tactic of hostage diplomacy is not even a secret. On Oct. 9, Deputy Chair of the Russian Security Council Dmitry Medvedev posted on Telegram that, in response to the detention of Kremlin propagandist Mikhail Zvinchuk in Montenegro, Russia needs to “fill up the exchange pool with European and American idiots in order to pull our own people out.”
In the case of Japan, there is no obvious person whose release the Kremlin is seeking. On Oct. 6, it was reported that Japan had detained a Russian citizen suspected of being a member of Qilin, a Russian cybercriminal group accused of multiple ransomware attacks, including against Asahi Holdings, the Japanese brewer. The suspect has, however, already been extradited to Germany.
There remains the possibility that Imai could be part of a multinational prisoner exchange, with Japan’s Western partners releasing Russian citizens — most likely more spies and criminals — in return for Imai and other unfortunate Westerners.
Yet, Russia’s recent policy toward Japan suggests there is more to Imai’s detention than the Putin regime refilling the exchange pool.
On Aug. 13, President Putin visited Iturup (known as “Etorofu” in Japanese), the largest of the Southern Kurils. While other Russian politicians, including Dmitry Medvedev, have visited the disputed islands, Putin had never done so. The trip was therefore a significant escalation and was condemned by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi as “absolutely unacceptable.”
Other confrontational steps followed. On Sept. 4, a new monument to the Soviet victory over Japan in 1945 was unveiled in Khabarovsk. It controversially features a Soviet soldier smashing the Imperial Japanese chrysanthemum, the symbol of the much-revered imperial family.
Later that month, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov lambasted Japan (and Germany) at the United Nations General Assembly for taking “the path of militarization and revanchism.” Russian military activity around Japan has also intensified, including bombing drills on Japan-claimed Iturup from Oct. 13-17.
Another Oct. 13 provocation came when Russian media reported that a delegation from China’s Heilongjiang Province had visited Iturup. This is sensitive because Japan strongly opposes the involvement of third countries on what it claims to be inherent Japanese territory. It is especially worrying that the delegation was Chinese since Japan’s government fears Moscow and Beijing uniting against it in East Asia.
At first glance, this Russian barrage is puzzling since, earlier this year, Japan’s government had tentatively explored re-engagement with Russia. Unlike Fumio Kishida, who led Japan from 2021 to 2024, Prime Minister Takaichi has few strong feelings about Ukraine. She rarely speaks about the war and has yet to visit Kyiv.
This gave a green light to those within the government who favor re-engagement. In May, Japan’s Economy, Trade and Industry Ministry led a business delegation to Moscow. Japan’s Foreign Ministry also resumed sending young Japanese to Russia for short-term study. The first of these arrived in St. Petersburg just one day before Putin’s visit to Iturup.
It seems perverse that Russia should unleash a hardline campaign just when Japan was seeking rapprochement. What prompted this?
Scanning the period before the start of Russia’s campaign, two things stand out. First, thanks to the initiative of Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan announced on May 29 that it had contributed 2.2 billion yen ($14.7 million) to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). Through this scheme, countries can fund the purchase of United States-manufactured military equipment for provision to Ukraine. Japan also announced it would deploy four Self-Defense Force personnel to the headquarters of NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine in Wiesbaden, Germany.
Japan’s contribution to PURL is limited to non-lethal military equipment. Yet, even this level of cooperation with NATO is strongly opposed by Moscow since it views it as an attempt by the Atlantic alliance to extend its influence to East Asia. For helping Ukraine in this way, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Japan of supporting “the terrorist Zelensky regime” and seeking the “strategic defeat” of Russia.
The second factor was the deployment to Japan in mid-June of U.S. Typhon missiles, a ground-launched mid-range system that can fire missiles that were prohibited under the now-defunct INF Treaty. Officially, Washington deployed them to Japan for the joint U.S.-Japan Orient Shield drills in September. However, Moscow is convinced that this is a pretext for the permanent deployment to Japan of missiles with the range to strike targets in the Russian Far East.
In response to the Typhon deployment, Zakharova warned on Sept. 1 that Moscow would take “compensatory countermeasures.”
Moscow’s intention is clear. It intends to impose pain on Tokyo and thereby compel it to back away from further steps that the Russian government opposes.
This was made explicit on Oct. 20, when senior Japanese diplomat Kimitake Nakamura visited Moscow to seek the release of the detained Japanese journalist. He was told that the deterioration in bilateral relations was the direct result of Japan’s “unfriendly stance.” Moreover, normalization would require Japan “to abandon anti-Russian activities” and to show greater “consideration for Russia’s national security concerns.”
This places Japan’s government in a bind. Of course, it wishes to do everything to secure the release of Imai Yuki, an innocent victim of Russia’s geopolitical games.
At the same time, if Japan makes concessions on key issues such as cooperation with NATO and missile deployments, it will have allowed its security policy to be taken hostage by Russia. Concessions would also encourage the Putin regime to repeat these criminal tactics.
As tragic as the situation is for Imai, Japan’s government should demonstrate that it cannot be bullied. It should respond not with concessions, but with punitive measures against the Putin regime, including fresh sanctions and additional support for Kyiv.

title: As the Kremlin Seizes Control of European Companies, U.S. Rivals Remain Largely Spared
description: Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing U.S. firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russian officials and U.S. businesspeople said.
content:
Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing U.S. firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russia n officials and U.S. businesspeople said.
Of the 20 foreign-owned firms President Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since U.S. President Donald Trump's inauguration in January 2025, only three were linked to the United States, with the rest controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.
A person close to Russia n financial regulators said that it is not in Moscow's interest to take a tough line on American companies while business negotiations with Washington are underway.
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russia n news agencies reported that Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the United States.
Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the U.S. is backing away from its support of Kyiv, and Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russia n oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russia , citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities," has taken control of the local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro since last month.
Last week, the Kremlin seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russia n property."
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia , declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than U.S. firms were being targeted.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Commenting on the report after its publication, the Kremlin said that U.S. companies were better treated than their European rivals because of Trump's efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine.
"The American administration is doing a lot to help bring about a peaceful settlement. The European capitals are doing nothing to help while doing a lot to prolong the military action," Peskov told reporters.
Russia 's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed. The U.S. announced a deal this month to buy Russia n diesel, and other deals, including those on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months.
Trump also signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russia n goods.
Russia n negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a U.S.-educated investment banker who heads the Russia n Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of American firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment."
Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of peace talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week that Russia and the U.S. would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends. The U.S. has previously signaled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russia n officials who do not support peace efforts could still push for the Kremlin to seize more American firms.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a U.S. company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tire factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving U.S. business in Russia .
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped protect the interests of American companies, two U.S. businesspeople in Moscow said.
American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European foreign policy. The chamber estimates there are around 300 U.S. firms remaining in Russia .
"We have Trump, and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russia n media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.
Russia did target some mid-sized U.S. firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated that the Kremlin seized more than $50 billion worth of private property from both Russia n and foreign owners.
The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to U.S. ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name."
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the moves showed " Russia is not a safe environment for business."
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," the spokesperson added.

title: Moscow Court Upholds Detention of Political Analyst Alexander Kynev Despite Serious Injury
description: A Moscow judge has rejected political analyst Alexander Kynev’s appeal against being held in pre-trial detention on drug trafficking charges despite growing concerns about a serious injury he sustained when he was arrested, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported Thursday.
content:
A Moscow judge has rejected political analyst Alexander Kynev’s appeal against being held in pre-trial detention on drug trafficking charges despite growing concerns about a serious injury he sustained when he was arrested, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported Thursday.
Kynev was arrested at his Moscow apartment last month on charges of attempting to sell a large amount of drugs. He was later hospitalized inside a Moscow detention center for bone fractures and other injuries.
A lower Moscow court ordered Kynev to be placed in pre-trial detention until Nov. 24, with details of the case remaining withheld from the public. He denies the charges, which carry a punishment of up to 20 years in prison if convicted.
Kynev appeared at the Moscow City Court appeal hearing via video link with his leg in a cast. Kynev’s defense team warned that he faces permanent disability without proper medical care and crutches .
“If Kynev doesn’t get medical help soon, he’s going to end up disabled,” his attorney Vera Goncharova told the judge.
However, the judge rejected the defense’s request for house arrest or other forms of restrictions, ruling that Kynev will remain in custody until at least Nov. 24.
Kynev, who wrote regular opinion columns for The Moscow Times before it was designated an “undesirable” organization in 2024, has worked as a political consultant since the 1990s, when he was first involved with the campaigns of the liberal Yabloko party.
Over the years, he has worked for a number of independent political organizations, including the now-disbanded election observer Golos.
He remained in Russia despite growing political oppression following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Kynev was a leading commentator on the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections before his arrest
He estimated a far lower turnout and vote share for the ruling United Russia party than the official results, warning that the party’s record haul of 349 out of 450 seats could backfire on the Kremlin.

title: Who Is Stephen Hubbard, the U.S. Citizen Released by Russia?
description: American national Stephen Hubbard has arrived back in the United States, following his release from detention in Russia by President Vladimir Putin at the start of talks with U.S.
content:
American national Stephen Hubbard has arrived back in the United States, following his release from detention in Russia by President Vladimir Putin at the start of talks with U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, on Wednesday.
Hubbard, 74, a retired schoolteacher, grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the U.S. Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by the New York Times.
He earned a master’s degree in English and lived in Japan for 25 years where he taught English before moving to Cyprus and then, in 2014, to Izium in eastern Ukraine with a Ukrainian partner, according to his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox.
Fox told Reuters in 2024 that Hubbard subsisted on a pension of about $300 a month and had few connections with local people. The siblings last spoke in September 2021.
Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izium two months later. Ukrainian forces retook the city in September 2022, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody by then.
Russian state media said Hubbard had been detained in April 2022 and alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture.
Fox said she recognized her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the videos were recorded.
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison. Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defense unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced.
Fox questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his 70s.
Martin De Luca, his U.S.-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.
In January 2025, Washington designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, enabling the U.S. government to pursue negotiations for his release.
The State Department has said Russia refused to grant U.S. officials consular access.
The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centers before his trial.
His lawyer said Hubbard's legal team found out only in April 2025 that he was being held in a facility in the republic of Mordovia, east of Moscow.

title: Russia and Ukraine Exchange Bodies of Nearly 300 Soldiers
description: Russia and Ukraine exchanged the remains of 277 soldiers killed fighting in the war, the RBC outlet reported Thursday, citing a Russian lawmaker.
content:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the remains of 277 soldiers killed fighting in the war, the RBC outlet reported Thursday, citing a Russian lawmaker.
Russia returned 252 bodies to Ukraine and received 25 fallen Russian soldiers in return, said Shamsail Saraliyev, a State Duma lawmaker from the ruling United Russia party and member of a parliamentary group dedicated to the conflict.
The exchange took place at the Novaya Guta border crossing in Belarus, according to Belarusian state media.
Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War later confirmed the exchange. It thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help facilitating the repatriation.
Earlier this month, Kyrylo Budanov, the head of the Ukrainian president’s office, estimated that more than 26,000 bodies and human remains had been repatriated to Ukraine through exchange operations since the start of the war.
Russia and Ukraine previously exchanged the bodies of fallen soldiers in September and August .
Thursday’s repatriation came a day after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff concluded talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss renewing trilateral peace negotiations that have stalled since February.

title: Ex-Deputy PM Grigorenko Nominated as Sberbank Deputy Board Chairman
description: Russian state lender Sberbank confirmed Thursday that former Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of Government Staff Dmitry Grigorenko has been nominated to serve as deputy chairman of its board of directors.
content:
Russian state lender Sberbank confirmed Thursday that former Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of Government Staff Dmitry Grigorenko has been nominated to serve as deputy chairman of its board of directors.
The announcement immediately followed President Vladimir Putin’s decree officially relieving Grigorenko of his duties in the government cabinet. First Deputy Finance Minister Irina Okladnikova is set to succeed him, becoming the first woman to take on the role of chief of government staff.
At Sberbank, Grigorenko is expected to oversee strategic initiatives, including government relations and the deployment of artificial intelligence and digital services across the public sector, the lender said.
“His arrival will strengthen Sber and give impetus to the development of our systemic dialogue with the state and regions,” Sberbank CEO Herman Gref said in a statement.
Sberbank’s supervisory board is scheduled to formally vote on Grigorenko’s appointment at its next meeting on Nov. 10.
Sources close to the Kremlin and in Russia’s tech industry told the newspaper Vedomosti that Grigorenko could take charge of Sberbank’s entire digital agenda.
Russian political analysts have speculated that Grigorenko’s departure from the government will reduce Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin’s power in the cabinet given the close working relationship between the two men over the years.
Meanwhile, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, whom Putin promoted to deputy prime minister alongside his ministerial position, and other economic officials have seen their influence in government grow as balancing state finances has taken on greater importance amid surging war spending, rising inflation and high interest rates.
Grigorenko previously served as deputy head of Russia’s Federal Tax Service, which Mishustin headed for several years, before joining the prime minister’s cabinet in January 2020 as chief of government staff, where he led the digitalization of government affairs.

title: Ukraine and Russia Trade Deadly Strikes After U.S. Tries to Reboot Peace Talks
description: Ukraine and Russia exchanged a flurry of drone and missile attacks overnight, leaving at least seven dead across Ukraine and one person killed in southwestern Russia, officials in the two warring countries said Thursday morning.
content:
Ukraine and Russia exchanged a flurry of drone and missile attacks overnight, leaving at least seven dead across Ukraine and one person killed in southwestern Russia, officials in the two warring countries said Thursday morning.
Authorities in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine said a man was killed when a Ukrainian drone crashed into the truck he was driving. In a separate strike in the region, a man riding a motorcycle was wounded.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 Ukrainian drones had been tracked in the skies above the wider Moscow region overnight, with air defense systems intercepting 163 of the unmanned aircraft that were on a direct approach to the city. Two people were wounded in the Voronovo district, located to the southwest of central Moscow.
There were also reports of an explosion and fire south of the capital. The exiled news outlet Astra, using eyewitness footage of the fire, identified the targeted facility as a storage and logistics facility belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry’s Main Missile and Artillery Directorate, located in Serpukhov.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify those reports.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 808 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
Russian officials reported injuries in the border regions of Kursk amid the overnight air barrage. Residential buildings in the Lipetsk region were also damaged. Power lines were knocked down in the Voronezh and Kaluga regions.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed at least seven people across the country, including three in Zaporizhzhia, two in Donetsk, one in Sumy and a woman in the Kharkiv region.
The exchange of attacks came just hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff concluded talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to discuss renewing trilateral peace negotiations that have stalled since February.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that Kyiv supported a U.S. proposal for three-way talks with Moscow and Washington. The Kremlin said Putin had agreed to resume the U.S.-mediated talks as early as next month.

title: Kazakhstan's Orthodox Churches Remain Under Russia's Thumb. An Anti-War Priest Paid the Price.
description: Opinion | Earlier this month, a court in Almaty, Kazakhstan sentenced Yakov Vorontsov, a former priest who publicly opposed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, to four years in prison.
content:
Earlier this month, a court in Almaty, Kazakhstan sentenced Yakov Vorontsov, a former priest who publicly opposed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, to four years in prison. Officially, he was found guilty of illegally acquiring and possessing, without intent to sell, 2.44 grams of an analogue of a psychotropic substance.
Although this is far from the first case in which a Russian Orthodox priest has faced repression for criticizing the Church leadership or for expressing pacifist views on the Russo-Ukrainian war, it sets a new precedent in Kazakhstan.
Yet it would be wrong to ignore the roles that the structure of the Orthodox Church, Russian history and the former Fr. Yakov’s life story all play in his case. One also has to take into account the legacy of Stalin’s repressions and why Kazakhstan cannot, at present, have an Orthodox Church independent of Moscow.
Vladimir Yuryevich Vorontsov was born in the capital of Soviet Kazakhstan, then still called Alma-Ata, in 1986. He wouldn’t be known as Fr. Yakov until many years later, in 2018, when he was tonsured as a monk by His Eminence Alexander (Mogilev), Metropolitan of Astana and Kazakhstan — the very same cleric who signed the decree suspending him from priestly ministry in 2023.
The list of charges behind his suspension was extensive. Fr. Yakov was accused of “violating his priestly oath and perjury, abandoning his ministry without authorization, engaging in public political activity, disturbing the peace of the Church, slandering the Orthodox Church in the media, incitement to schism and fomenting interreligious and interethnic discord, as well as additional negative circumstances that have come to light.”
A year later, Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church (ROC), would personally approve the Kazakhstani ecclesiastical court’s decision that Yakov should be defrocked.
In 2008, the then 22-year-old Vorontsov was known in Almaty literary circles as a poet and writer, as well as a qualified Russian language and literature teacher.
Just two years later, on Dec. 2, 2010, Vorontsov would be ordained and appointed second priest at the Church of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos in the village of Sarymoldayevo, Zhambyl region.
To those unfamiliar with the institution, it may seem strange that the only Orthodox churches in Kazakhstan fall under the Moscow Patriarchate. The Christian presence on the territory of modern Kazakhstan goes back centuries, but only gained a secure foothold from the mid-18th century under Russian rule. St. Petersburg sent thousands of peasants and garrisons of soldiers to the Kazakh Khanate, for whom they built churches. Initially, these were built exclusively for Russians, without any aim of proselytizing and converting the locals.
To understand why the lone voice of Fr. Yakov was silenced by a system he had served for so long and so diligently, one has to understand the structure of the Orthodox Church itself.
Unlike the Catholic Church, there is no absolute authority like the Pope. Unlike Protestantism, with its decentralized congregations, Orthodoxy is organized as a family of independent churches, the most honored of which is considered to be the Patriarchal Church of Constantinople.
Over the past four years of Russia’s war, Constantinople has become a refuge for Russian priests who have been defrocked or suspended for criticizing church leadership or for expressing pacifist views, including Andrei Kuraev and the former Moscow priest Ioann Koval .
In 2022, five priests in Lithuania who expressed their disagreement with Patriarch Kirill’s position on the invasion of Ukraine were defrocked by the head of the Moscow Patriarchate’s Diocese of Vilnius and Lithuania. In 2023, the Archbishop of New Rome and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew of Constantinople restored them to clerical rank. In January of this year, they established an Orthodox exarchate in Lithuania under the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople.
Moldova also saw an exodus of priests from the Russian Orthodox Church’s Metropolis of Moldova, with clergy joining the Metropolis of Bessarabia within the Romanian Orthodox Church.
A few years ago, Yakov and his supporters wrote to Patriarch Kirill, asking for the establishment of an Orthodox church in Kazakhstan independent of the ROC.
Why can an anti-war Orthodox Christian not simply remain a parishioner of the ROC in Kazakhstan? The Church has made no public statement condemning the invasion of Ukraine, but nor has it directly supported it. Broadly speaking, any Kazakhstani priest is ultimately subordinate to Patriarch Kirill. But individual parish priests usually have no direct connection to the Russian authorities.
Fr. Yakov made his views clear. “Orthodox Christians in Kazakhstan have the right to profess faith in Christ without the admixture of idolatry. Because the narratives of the ‘Russian World’ ideology are precisely that: idolatry. Moreover, we do not want the Church to be an instrument of Russian political influence over Kazakhstan’s internal affairs,” he said in an interview. “As I have already said, the hierarchs of the Russian Orthodox Church have betrayed Christ.”
So for some of his supporters, it is a matter of principle. Fr. Yakov’s sister Svetlana said her brother wanted to resist the system that was trying to force him to repent. Kazakhstani poet and journalist Vadim Dergachev, who attended every hearing in Yakov’s case, says the priest was determined to follow Christ’s example, not merely thinking about his authority in the church. Another supporter, an ethnic Kazakh, told me that the ROC’s backing for the war in Ukraine was the main reason he did not get baptized into the church.
The ROC leadership takes a different position. After Constantinople’s 2018 decision to grant autocephaly — independence — to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, the ROC severed relations with the Church of Constantinople.
But unlike Ukraine, which has sought to cut off all ties with Russia amid its invasion, Kazakhstan does not have an Orthodox Church independent of Moscow.
The main reason is political. Astana’s relationship with Russia is far less hostile than Kyivs, so it has no need to establish its own Orthodox Church. Nor has such a desire been publicly expressed by other, less prominent Kazakhstani priests.
Alexander Suvorov, archpriest of Almaty’s main Orthodox church, told me in an interview a couple of years ago that an attempt to open a Constantinople representation in Kazakhstan would amount to “raiding in the most literal sense,” because Constantinople has no historic connection to Kazakhstan.
In Suvorov’s view, potential “interference” by the Patriarchate of Constantinople in Kazakhstan would also be “politically motivated,” since Constantinople has close ties to the U.S. and its patriarch is perceived by the Orthodox world as a vector of American influence. This assertion is somewhat difficult to verify, although it would be hard to call the opinion unusual.
Yet Kazakhstan already has at least two Orthodox communities that are predominantly Russian. The Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia (ROCOR), specifically the part that refused to recognize reunification with the ROC in 2007, has one parish in the southern Zhambyl region. It had another in Kostanay until 2023, when the Moscow Patriarchate seized the church’s land from the parish.
Kazakhstan’s government was supposed to settle the question of an independent Orthodox church in the country by either permitting or banning the initiative. No direct answer was given, but the idea wasn’t officially outlawed. Was Fr. Yakov persecuted because of his interest in the idea? Notably, instead of being tried for political statements or actions, he was officially tried for drug offenses. Of course, not everyone agrees with the court’s framing. In March, Yakov was included by the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom in its database of people persecuted for their faith, which appears to have had almost no effect on the judge’s decision. Will Yakov’s followers be able to continue this work without him? Only time will tell. In any case, they appear determined to do so for now. They attended the court hearings wearing T -shirts in support of him, write actively about the case on social media and remain convinced that he is innocent.
If the archived page of the Metropolitan District in the Republic of Kazakhstan is to be believed, Vladimir Vorontsov, as he was then known, had been a source of pride for the church in the 2010s, before his fall. At first, he served as a sacristan, reader and general handyman. He then worked his way up to become the rector of a rural church. For years, he organized a children’s camp for pupils of Sunday schools and remotely taught the history of the Russian Church and the history of the local Churches.
In March 2018, the once-ordinary village priest was appointed a staff priest at the Ascension Cathedral in Almaty at just 32 years old. Moreover, he was appointed head of the Department for the Canonization of Saints of the Astana Diocese, made responsible for museum affairs and appointed custodian of antiquities for the Astana Diocese.
Eight days later, he was tonsured as a monk in Almaty. How would the newly appointed Yakov differ from Vladimir? Instead of simply celebrating liturgies in a provincial church, he would study the New Martyrs, Orthodox Christians who suffered at the hands of the Bolsheviks.
What happened to Yakov after the full-scale invasion? Did he remain faithful to God to the end? Or was he tormented by a demon to cause a schism in Kazakhstan’s already small Orthodox community? Is he sowing unnecessary discord, or is he attempting to bleed the community in order to heal it?
By December 2018, Fr. Yakov had joined the Publishing Council of the ROC and later took part in creating Turkestan Golgotha , the largest electronic database of clergy and lay members of the ROC who were subjected to repression and whose lives were connected with Central Asia. At that time, he wanted to become a hieromonk , renounce everything worldly and devote himself forever to God and His Church.
Vorontsov was tonsured in March 2018 in honor of Archbishop Yakov. Known as the Hieromartyr Yakov of Barnaul, he was an innocent man who was shot by atheist Bolsheviks, yet displayed steadfastness and dignity in the face of those who no longer felt any reverence toward him. It is precisely the example of Yakov of Barnaul and many other New Martyrs that, as Yakov Vorontsov says , prevents him from acting against his conscience.
The supporters of the disgraced Fr. Yakov and his opponents already have their clearly articulated positions, which are unlikely to change any time soon. Is Fr. Yakov’s case unique and isolated, or is it a symptom of something more far-reaching?
The answer to that question lies beyond the walls of his Almaty prison. But at least one thing can be said with certainty: the era in which Christianity in Central Asia could rhetorically exist in an absolute ideological vacuum, far removed from the storms of the outside world, has gone forever.

title: Japan Sends Senior Diplomat to Russia to Seek Release of Arrested Journalist
description: Japan sent a senior diplomat to Moscow this week to discuss the release of a journalist arrested in Russia on spying accusations, Tokyo said Wednesday.
content:
Japan sent a senior diplomat to Moscow this week to discuss the release of a journalist arrested in Russia on spying accusations, Tokyo said Wednesday.
Russia’s FSB security service said last week that a Japanese national had been arrested on the Far Eastern island of Sakhalin.
The individual was later identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, who faces accusations of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory."
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has denied that Japan conducts spying activities in Russia, while the Hokkaido Shimbun has stressed its independence from the government.
On Tuesday, Kimitake Nakamura, Japan's top diplomat for Europe, met Lyudmila Vorobyova, the head of the department at the Russian Foreign Ministry dealing with much of East Asia, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.
"We lodged a request... that calls for the earliest possible realization of consular access to the Japanese national detained in Russia, as well as the individual's immediate release," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Wednesday.
Japan also summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a formal protest over the arrest, while its foreign ministry has urged Moscow to provide him "fair and impartial treatment."
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls "unfriendly" countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
Kihara said the meeting on Tuesday was also held to discuss tense bilateral relations.
"Japan-Russia relations are in a difficult state," he said. "Precisely for that reason, it is necessary for the diplomatic authorities to engage in exchanges on the various issues."
For decades, Russia and Japan have been locked in a territorial dispute over the southern Kuril islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan — which are located northeast of Japan’s Hokkaido prefecture and southwest of Far East Russia’s Sakhalin. The Soviet Union seized control of the islands at the end of World War II.
Japan has also sanctioned Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Fighter Jet Crashes in Kaliningrad Region During Training Flight
description: A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed in the western Kaliningrad region during a routine training flight, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday.
content:
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed in the western Kaliningrad region during a routine training flight, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday.
The two-member crew successfully ejected from the aircraft and was later found by a search and rescue team, the ministry said, adding that “there is no threat to the lives of the pilots.”
It added that the fighter jet crashed in an unpopulated area and was not carrying any weapons on board.
The cause of the incident was not immediately clear.
Some Russian news outlets reported that the Su-30 went down in an area surrounding the Chernyakhovsk naval airbase, a hub for the Russian Navy’s Baltic Sea Fleet.
An eyewitness video circulating on social media showed a fireball and a thick column of smoke rising in the air following the crash.
In the video, a group of men in military uniforms are seen standing at a cemetery, which is located east of the airbase, looking toward the site of the incident.
A similar military air crash took place in the Far Eastern Amur region late last month when six crew members on board a Russian bomber plane were killed.

title: Armenia Appeals to Eurasian Economic Union for Removal of Russian Trade Restrictions
description: Armenia has asked the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to designate Russia’s growing trade restrictions on Armenian goods as illegal market barriers, the newspaper Kommersant reported Wednesday, citing the South Caucasus country’s economic minister.
content:
Armenia has asked the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) to designate Russia’s growing trade restrictions on Armenian goods as illegal market barriers, the newspaper Kommersant reported Wednesday, citing the South Caucasus country’s economic minister.
Russia has issued sweeping bans on a range of Armenian products this year as Yerevan, Moscow’s historical ally, began the process of joining the European Union. Amid the mounting restrictions, the EU relaxed tariffs on around 80% of Armenian exports for the next two years.
“We consider the [Russian] restrictions against us to be unlawful,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan told reporters, according to the Kommersant.
“If these restrictions are recognized as a barrier, then Russia is obliged to remove them within 30 days per EAEU procedures,” Papoyan was quoted as saying.
He added that Armenia has already submitted individual appeals to each trade restriction introduced in recent months, and in one case, it allegedly secured the support of three other members of the economic union. However, Russia has used its veto power to block those appeals, Papoyan said.
A translation of Papoyan’s comments cited by Kommersant states that the EAEU will consider Armenia’s latest, more sweeping appeal on Nov. 3. “We’ll see if there will be a tangible result,” he was quoted as saying.
Meanwhile, a joint report released Tuesday by the remaining EAEU members Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan warned that Armenia’s exit from the economic union or alignment with the EU would hit Yerevan’s trade, labor and energy markets.
Relations between Russia and Armenia have soured in recent years after neighboring Azerbaijan took control of the disputed Nagorno-Karabakh region in September 2023. Officials in Yerevan accused Russian peacekeepers of failing to protect the region and its Armenian population from advancing Azerbaijani forces during a shock offensive.

title: Solzhenitsyn Statue Temporarily Returned to Original Vladivostok Site After Relocation Mishap
description: Authorities in the Far Eastern port city of Vladivostok have temporarily returned a controversial monument to Nobel Prize-winning Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn to its original location after a failed attempt to relocate it.
content:
Authorities in the Far Eastern port city of Vladivostok have temporarily returned a controversial monument to Nobel Prize-winning Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn to its original location after a failed attempt to relocate it.
The statue was dismantled from the waterfront promenade in central Vladivostok on Tuesday, with plans to place it in a nearby, smaller square.
However, on Wednesday, the Vladivostok city hall’s press service told Interfax that workers realized the statue was too large for the smaller square when attempting to install it there.
“The monument visually overloads the small recreational zone,” a press spokesperson was quoted as saying.
Officials confirmed that the Solzhenitsyn monument will remain at the original Ship Embankment until architects finish modifying the Faith and Hope Square, where it was intended to be moved. They did not provide a timeframe.
Solzhenitsyn, the Soviet Union’s most famous literary dissident who spent years in prison camps before being exiled to the United States, passed through Vladivostok when he returned back to Russia by plane in May 1994.
Some local activists have criticized the statue, which was installed in 2015, for depicting Solzhenitsyn stepping off a ship gangway.
Vladivostok’s city hall had agreed in March to move the Solzhenitsyn monument following complaints from the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet, which argued that a statue dedicated to a Soviet dissident was out of place on a waterfront reserved for World War II memorials and warships.

title: Putin Releases American Jailed in Russia, Agrees to Trilateral Peace Talks as Witkoff Visits
description: President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday announced the release of Stephen James Hubbard, an American teacher who was taken from his home in Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion, as the Kremlin leader met with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St.
content:
President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday announced the release of Stephen James Hubbard, an American teacher who was taken from his home in Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion, as the Kremlin leader met with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg to discuss restarting negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard, convicted in Russia on allegations of serving as a mercenary for the Ukrainian military, was already preparing to board a flight back to the United States. Washington had maintained that the 74-year-old Michigan native and former teacher was wrongfully detained and sentenced to six years in prison.
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters at the Oval Office earlier in the week that he had personally asked Putin to release Hubbard ahead of Witkoff's trip to St. Petersburg. "I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him," Trump said.
Trump, writing on Truth Social following Hubbard’s release, said the U.S. was “not required to give anything in return,” as he sought to quell speculation that Moscow and Washington had agreed to conduct another tit-for-tat prisoner exchange.
“This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin,” Trump wrote in a post. “Stephen is on his way back home.”
Witkoff, who has engaged in a frenzy of shuttle diplomacy on both the wars in Ukraine and Iran in recent months, was met by Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev at Pulkovo International Airport before meeting with Putin at the lavish Constantine Palace on Wednesday afternoon.
Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who is also a key mediator in Ukraine peace negotiations, did not join Witkoff for the latest Russia trip after falling sick with the flu. Witkoff confirmed that Kushner would participate in the talks with Putin via video link.
Putin told Witkoff in St. Petersburg that he was grateful to Trump for the "attention paid to the settlement of the Ukrainian crisis," referring to the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "I know that President Trump attaches special importance to this, most importantly due to humanitarian concerns."
Witkoff said that he hoped Wednesday's meeting would help to restart trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine that have been stalled since February, when Trump ordered attacks against Iran.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process, so that we can begin to have technical teams discuss what are those next steps," the U.S. envoy told Putin. "Even if we don't have resolution today... I think that will be important. And I think the world is waiting to hear that.
Earlier, a U.S. official told Reuters that Witkoff held "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a meeting in Oslo, Norway, on Tuesday.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the talks in Oslo, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland, as well as European and NATO representatives, and that participants made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia.
Those talks were said to have covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff would aim to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the U.S. official said.
Speaking to the U.S. envoy in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Putin said he was "curious to learn about the outcomes" of the discussions in Norway.
The Russian president also offered to help Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address U.S. concerns about Iran's nuclear program.
In addition, Russia could supply large quantities of fertilizer to the United States to help American farmers, Putin told Witkoff, adding he wanted to discuss a ​potential meeting in China next month with Trump, which the Kremlin has suggested could also include Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Kremlin later said renewed peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo.
"These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting, which lasted nearly three hours.
Zelensky traveled to Oslo this week in hopes of mending ties with the Trump administration, which have once again hit rocky waters in recent weeks after Trump blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel costs in the United States, though analysts say the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is the main cause of high energy prices globally.
Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine earlier this month, which neither side said they had agreed to beforehand. That apparent pause in strikes collapsed immediately as the Russian army continued its attacks against Ukraine's power grid.
Ukraine had accused the United States in recent days of withholding critical military support and intelligence amid the renewed attacks on Russian refineries.
However, Zelensky told a news conference after the Oslo meeting and an earlier phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Ukraine was again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks.
"Now it works, it's great," he said, adding he and Rubio had discussed supplies of Patriot missile interceptors, as well as the satellite-based Starlink system, which Kyiv said had stopped working when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said that the Oslo meeting had been constructive. Similarly, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said he believed Ukraine peace talks were "back on track."
On Tuesday, Trump, who has leveled increasingly harsh criticism at Zelensky, called on Ukraine to make a deal to settle the war and claimed Putin was interested in signing a peace agreement. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," he told reporters.
Trump also suggested Russia had the upper hand on the battlefield since "Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land."
Zelensky so far has resisted pressure from the White House to turn over his country's land in exchange for peace with Russia, arguing that doing so would only encourage further Russian aggression.
Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the partially occupied Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.

title: FSB Arrests German Accused of Fighting for Ukraine
description: Russia’s FSB security service has arrested a German citizen accused of serving as a mercenary for the Ukrainian military before deserting his unit, Russian state media reported Wednesday.
content:
Russia’s FSB security service has arrested a German citizen accused of serving as a mercenary for the Ukrainian military before deserting his unit, Russian state media reported Wednesday.
The man, who was identified only by his birth year of 1976, is reportedly a former German military veteran with a history of combat deployments in Afghanistan, Somalia and Syria.
The FSB claimed the man also served as a sniper in a Ukrainian territorial defense unit between 2016 and 2018 near the Russian-occupied city of Donetsk.
In a video interrogation published by the state-run TASS news agency, the German national said he had left for Switzerland after completing his contract.
He said he re-entered Ukraine in November 2025 and signed a new three-year contract in December.
“I was promised 100,000 hryvnias ($2,200). However, I didn’t receive the money and was forced to flee the ranks of the armed forces of Ukraine,” the man said.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify whether the confession was made under duress.
Russia’s FSB did not specify when or where his detention took place. It said investigators were preparing to charge him with mercenary activities under Russian law.
The arrest follows a similar incident last Thursday, when the FSB announced the detention of a Swedish national in the northwestern Pskov region on allegations of illegal border crossing and sabotage.

title: Kremlin Hopes Witkoff Will ‘Brief’ Putin on Talks With Ukraine and Europe
description: The Kremlin said Tuesday that it hopes U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will “brief” President Vladimir Putin in the coming days on his talks with Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo amid ongoing efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
content:
The Kremlin said Tuesday that it hopes U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will “brief” President Vladimir Putin in the coming days on his talks with Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo amid ongoing efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff arrived in the Norwegian capital earlier in the day for a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, top British, French, German and Polish representatives, as well as EU and NATO officials.
The New York Times reported that Witkoff plans to meet Putin on Wednesday in St. Petersburg, where he is expected to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American who is accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine when he was captured in 2022.
“We hope that a meeting can be arranged in the very near future, and that the American negotiators, Mr. Witkoff, will be able to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that it was in talks with officials in Washington about a possible prisoner release but did not provide further details.
U.S. President Donald Trump said later on Tuesday that he and Putin had discussed Hubbard and hinted at a possible release.
"Everybody's been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here, and just remember that question for a couple of days from now. You know why? Because I do things that nobody else can," he told reporters in the Oval Office.
Peskov told reporters at a Tuesday press briefing that the Kremlin seeks to “continue the exchange of views on a range of very important issues” with Witkoff.
“We consider such meetings to be of great importance on every occasion. They are always timely and very substantive, and we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators,” he said.
A U.S. official told Axios correspondent Barak Ravid that Witkoff hopes to “present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners.”
“President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia,” the official was quoted as saying.
Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who has also been involved in peace negotiations, participated alongside Witkoff virtually during the talks in Norway after having contracted the flu.
The New York Times reported Monday that Trump is seeking to “force a deal” on Zelensky, “even one written largely on Russia’s terms.”
Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.
Sources close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg last month that Putin expects Russian forces to take full control of the Donetsk region by late February 2027.
Witkoff and Kushner last visited Russia on Sept. 5, when subsequent reporting claimed Putin raised the prospect of a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the U.S. negotiators.
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump called on Ukraine to make a deal to end the war.
"Ukraine has to want to settle this war," Trump said.
He suggested Moscow had the upper hand in the fight because " Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land."

title: Russia’s Gold Reserves Fall to Lowest Since 2019 as Budget Deficit Widens
description: Russia’s Central Bank sold gold from its reserves for a 10th consecutive month in September as part of operations linked to financing a budget deficit expected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles this year, twice the original target.
content:
Russia’s Central Bank sold gold from its reserves for a 10th consecutive month in September as part of operations linked to financing a budget deficit expected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles this year, twice the original target.
Gold holdings fell by 200,000 troy ounces, or about 6.2 metric tons, to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019, according to Central Bank figures released Tuesday.
The Bank has reduced its holdings by 2 million ounces, or about 62 tons, since December, when it began its largest sustained sell-off in decades.
International Monetary Fund data show that Russia has drawn down its gold reserves more rapidly only once in its modern history, during the 1998 financial crisis, when the government defaulted on domestic debt and the ruble collapsed.
The Central Bank sold 3.8 million ounces, or about 118 tons, over three months that year. It later bought back some of the gold, leaving its holdings down 1.6 million ounces, or about 50 tons, for the full year, less than the decline recorded since the current sell-off began.
Russia subsequently built up its reserves, increasing its gold holdings more than fivefold from their late-1990s level. By early 2022, it held about 74 million ounces, or 2,300 tons, the world’s fifth-largest stockpile.
The latest sales are linked to Central Bank operations that mirror earlier transactions by the Finance Ministry involving the National Wealth Fund, Russia’s rainy-day fund, Reuters has reported.
Under that mechanism, the Central Bank sells gold into the market to offset earlier sales by the ministry from the fund to finance the budget deficit.
Alexander Potavin, an analyst at investment firm Finam, said falling oil and gas revenue had increased the government’s reliance on the fund’s assets, including gold.
The Finance Ministry uses accumulated reserves to cover budget shortfalls when revenue falls short, he said.
Gold sales could also help the Central Bank address shortages of foreign currency liquidity, Potavin said, adding that high global gold prices had probably encouraged it to step up sales.
Separately, Russian gold exports to China have risen sharply. About 100 tons of Russian-origin gold entered Hong Kong between January and July, three times the volume recorded in the same period a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.
Those trade figures do not establish how much, if any, of the exported gold came from Central Bank reserves.
Russian suppliers have redirected exports eastward since losing access to London, the world’s largest gold trading hub, LSEG analyst Debajit Saha said.
Shipments to China surged in the first year of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian gold worth about $35 billion has since passed through Hong Kong, according to calculations by the Financial Times.

title: Russia’s Anti-War Theater Artists Search for a New Stage in Exile
description: BERLIN — By the time the lights went down at the Komische Oper Berlin, there was hardly an empty seat left.
content:
BERLIN — By the time the lights went down at the Komische Oper Berlin, there was hardly an empty seat left. Tickets for Kirill Serebrennikov’s 10-day festival of theater had sold out months in advance.
Last month’s festival brought together theater, film and public discussions featuring Russian artists now working abroad, with performances moving between German, Russian and English.
For Serebrennikov, one of the best-known Russian theater directors in Europe, exile has opened a new chapter in an already international career. But for many less-established actors and directors who left Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, exile has meant struggling to find their place in the theater world.
Maya Dorozhenko, 30, had been building a career in Moscow when the invasion began. A director and screenwriter, she graduated from the prestigious GITIS theater school and received invitations to work with leading theaters in the capital.
When the war started, she had been planning to stage an anti-war play based on philosopher Hannah Arendt’s life and work, but venues there appeared unwilling to take the risk.
“The play was reviewed and they said it wasn’t going to happen. So my actress and I left,” she recalled. They moved to Yerevan, Armenia, and rented a room where there was barely enough space to rehearse.
“There was a very narrow space between the bed and the wall. It was a one-woman show, so my actress would perform right in front of me and I would just sit there and watch her performance," she said.
Since the invasion, Russian theaters have faced tighter censorship and state control. Artists who oppose the war have had to weigh the risks of speaking out against the prospect of abandoning careers built over years.
In 2024, theater director Yevgenia Berkovich and playwright Svetlana Petriychuk were sentenced to six years in a penal colony for "justifying terrorism" over their award-winning play about Russian women who fall in love with Islamist militants and plan to join them in Syria. Supporters believe Berkovich’s statements against the Ukraine invasion and anti-war poetry were the real reasons for their arrests.
For those who left, Armenia and Georgia, with visa-free entry and large Russian-speaking communities, became hubs for actors and directors.
Among them was actor Yegor Rybakov, 43, who moved to Tbilisi in 2022 after receiving threats on social media that he would be reported to the authorities for his criticism of the Kremlin and support for Ukraine. At the time, he was performing in four productions, including a play ranked in the top 10 best in Moscow.
“I had productions for audiences of around 35 people and others for 5,000. It was a huge, very memorable contrast, and as an actor I loved it,” Rybakov told The Moscow Times.
But in Tbilisi, regular acting work was harder to find. He said he took on side jobs as an event host and acting teacher to make a living in between acting gigs.
Opportunities in Russian-language video production were also limited, while working in the local Georgian theater scene meant building new professional connections and often learning another language, he said.
Beyond the language barrier, theater workers told The Moscow Times they also face a choice between making work for Russian-speaking audiences in exile or trying to integrate into the local theater scene and reach new audiences.
Paris-based director Anastasiia Anisimova is one of the few who have managed to break into the international theater scene. Her play “ Deep Fake ,” which is staged in both Russian and English, has been staged in Tbilisi, Berlin and the prestigious Avignon Festival in France, with an Amsterdam performance planned.
But she said that funding and bureaucratic requirements — even to take part in international festivals — remained major challenges.
“Theater in exile is not about making money at all,” Anisimova said. “You just want to make art and stay in the profession.”
Much of Russian theater in exile reflects on the realities of war and emigration. “ Vanya Is Alive ” tells the story of the mother of a Russian soldier who was drafted to the war in Ukraine, while “ Inostranka ” (The Foreigner) and “ Letters Home ” explore what it means to leave your country.
For some, exile is a way to address political subjects that would otherwise be impossible inside Russia.
Yet not all exiled theater is explicitly political. Anisimova said she “firmly opposed political theater because, for me, it’s simply not how I hear or see the world.” Although she said art and politics are intertwined, she argued that “they don’t necessarily have to be so closely linked.”
The instability of exile has also made it difficult to sustain a production or plan a new one.
“People [in the theater community] are constantly changing. Some move to another country, some stay. That has a huge impact on what you can plan and what you can count on when it comes to rehearsals and projects,” Rybakov said.
Dorozhenko said she has faced many of the same problems. Leaving Russia meant losing the professional environment that had made her work possible, from colleagues and audiences to the networks she had spent years building.
“For four years, you were almost in [professional] isolation. You see people who are also trying to find a way to work, to say something important as artists, but also working as animators, as teachers, doing whatever they can [to survive]. It is still very difficult,” Dorozhenko said.
Theater festivals offer a key way for the community to stay connected after being dispersed by emigration.
Lubimovka, originally a Moscow festival founded in 1990 and dedicated to new Russian-language drama, has developed into an international network of readings and collaborations after the invasion following its decision to move the festival abroad to avoid wartime censorship and to protect writers.
Its representatives said the independent and nonprofit festival operates mostly as a grassroots initiative from people across the world who want to keep the play reading going and also creates opportunities to reach non-Russian audiences, including across Europe , Asia and in the U.S.
“These festivals [called Echo of Lubimovka] started to emerge quite spontaneously in exile — it was no longer possible to hold a large event as in Moscow, so people began approaching us with ideas of their own: ‘Let’s do readings of three plays in Tbilisi, let’s read three plays in Tel Aviv.’ And the whole thing kept growing, like a snowball,” Lubimovka said.
“Starting with Echo of Lubimovka in Paris in 2022, we decided to translate the plays into the local language,” the festival’s representatives said, adding that one of the recent examples is an event in Tokyo, where the readings were performed in Japanese and selected by Japanese curators.
“Step by step, these small initiatives across Echo of Lubimovka festivals, in different languages, are also beginning to build connections outside the Russian-speaking world,” they added.
“There is a strong urge to speak out and express ourselves, as well as a need to connect with colleagues and rebuild professional ties in exile,” Lubimovka said.
For the actors and directors interviewed by The Moscow Times, despite the difficulties abroad, they wanted to stay in theater and they still cannot imagine working in wartime Russia.
For Rybakov, the connection with an audience is what makes that effort worthwhile.
“When you feel that response from people, when you see that they’ve been touched by what you’re doing, especially during this terrible time we’re living through, it turns you inside out,” Rybakov said.
“What I love most in the world is when I have acting work, when I’m rehearsing and performing, when I’m shooting. That’s when I’m happy.”

title: Crypto Exchanges Bitget, MEXC End Services for Customers in Russia and Belarus
description: Two major cryptocurrency exchanges, Bitget and MEXC, are ending services for customers in Russia and Belarus, further limiting their access to international crypto markets.
content:
Two major cryptocurrency exchanges, Bitget and MEXC, are ending services for customers in Russia and Belarus, further limiting their access to international crypto markets.
MEXC said Tuesday it would stop serving users in both countries to comply with international regulatory requirements. Affected customers will receive individual notices setting deadlines for closing trading positions and withdrawing their cryptocurrency.
The announcement follows similar restrictions by Bitget, which added Russia and Belarus to its list of prohibited jurisdictions alongside Kazakhstan.
Bitget barred affected customers from opening new trades and using new products from Oct. 18. Customers have been told to close their positions and withdraw their assets by 10 a.m. Moscow time on Monday, after which the exchange will begin forcibly closing positions and restricting account access.
The moves could signal a broader retreat by international crypto exchanges from the Russian market as regulatory pressure mounts, industry figures said.
Nikita Zuborev, senior analyst at cryptocurrency exchange comparison service BestChange, told the RBC news website that the threat of secondary sanctions and rising compliance costs were making Russian customers increasingly risky for international exchanges.
Earlier this year, the EU sanctioned HTX for allegedly helping Russians evade sanctions and barring EU companies from conducting transactions with the exchange.

title: Putin’s Daughter Says Fear of Death Will Drive Advances Against Aging
description: President Vladimir Putin’s daughter Maria Vorontsova said advances in medicine could help address aging within the next 10 to 20 years, driven by humanity’s fear of death, the Vedomosti newspaper reported.
content:
President Vladimir Putin’s daughter Maria Vorontsova said advances in medicine could help address aging within the next 10 to 20 years, driven by humanity’s fear of death, the Vedomosti newspaper reported .
Vorontsova, an endocrinologist who heads Moscow State University’s Medical Research and Education Institute, spoke at a forum marking the launch of a laboratory at the Skolkovo Moscow School of Management to study how longer lifespans affect public policy, the economy and the labor market.
She said efforts to extend life should be divided into two stages. The first involves reaching what she described as humans’ natural lifespan of 85 to 90 years through healthy habits developed in childhood, proper nutrition and regular medical checkups.
The second involves trying to “cheat God or nature” by living beyond that natural limit, she said, acknowledging that scientific progress in this area remained limited.
Vorontsova said one obstacle was that aging is not classified as a disease, complicating drug development, which requires a clearly defined diagnosis and clinical trials.
Still, she said, the “universal human fear of death” would push medicine toward tackling aging within the next 10 to 20 years.
Her remarks come as Russia invests in research aimed at extending life, an area that has drawn interest from Putin and members of his inner circle.
Deputy Science and Higher Education Minister Denis Sekirinsky previously said Russian researchers were developing what he called a vaccine against aging that is designed to block a gene associated with age-related changes in cells.
Deputy Prime Minister Tatyana Golikova said Russia planned to begin producing an anti-aging drug between 2028 and 2030.
The research forms part of the national project New Health Preservation Technologies, which was launched in 2025 at Putin’s direction.
An unidentified source close to the Kremlin told the exiled news outlet Meduza in 2024 that the initiative stemmed from an obsession with eternal life on the part of Mikhail Kovalchuk, a Putin associate who heads the Kurchatov Institute.
Kovalchuk oversees a federal program supporting Russian genetics research in which Vorontsova also participates .
Putin has never publicly acknowledged Vorontsova and her younger sister Katerina Tikhonova as his daughters, while the Kremlin has kept details of their lives a closely guarded secret.
Russia plans to spend more than 2 trillion rubles ($12 billion) in total on the health technology project and a separate national project, Long and Active Life, also launched in 2025 at Putin’s direction.
Putin has set targets to raise Russian life expectancy to 78 by 2030 and 81 by 2036, from a reported 74.2 years. Male life expectancy is about 68.
Putin, 74, has long been interested in rejuvenation treatments, according to media reports.
During a visit to Beijing in September 2025, he was overheard discussing the prospect of achieving immortality through medical technology and organ transplants with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

title: Latvia Emerges as Top-5 Importer of Russian Grain, Consultancy Says
description: Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has emerged as one of the top five importers of Russian grain this marketing season despite strained political ties, as Moscow redirects exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to Baltic ports.
content:
Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has emerged as one of the top five importers of Russia n grain this marketing season despite strained political ties, as Moscow redirects exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to Baltic ports.
Latvia imported 431,700 metric tons of Russia n grain between July and October, consultancy ProZerno said.
Iran remained the largest buyer of Russia n grain during the period, importing 1.716 million tons, helped by strong purchases of barley and corn.
Russia has been reshaping its grain export routes after shipments through the Azov-Black Sea basin, its main export corridor, largely stalled in mid-August.
Deep-water Baltic ports have become the main outlet, particularly for wheat. According to railway carrier and grain analyst Rusagrotrans, the Baltic route accounted for 65% of Russia n grain exports in September.
Exports are being shipped through both Russia n Baltic ports and ports in the Baltic states, chiefly Latvia.
Estonia has banned the transit of Russia n grain through its territory, while the Baltic states proposed earlier this month a European Union ban on Russia n grain exports through the bloc.
Shipments via the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most cargoes destined for Iran.
Egypt, once the largest importer of Russia n wheat and a key destination for Black Sea shipments, imported 1.35 million tons of Russia n grain between July and October, according to ProZerno.
Azerbaijan imported 545,000 tons and Nigeria 420,900 tons, placing them among the five largest buyers of Russia n grain this season.

title: Russia Slams U.S. Arrest Warrant for Cuba’s Raúl Castro
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday condemned a Florida arrest warrant for 95-year-old former Cuban President Raúl Castro over a 1996 military shoot-down of two civilian planes manned by anti-Castro pilots.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday condemned a Florida arrest warrant for 95-year-old former Cuban President Raúl Castro over a 1996 military shoot-down of two civilian planes manned by anti-Castro pilots.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that a state judge had approved an arrest warrant charging Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
The charges are connected to the Feb. 24, 1996, shooting down of two civilian aircraft operated by the humanitarian group Brothers to the Rescue. Castro, the younger brother of the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro, was Cuba’s defense minister at the time.
“Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood,” Uthmeier said in a statement.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry expressed “categorical rejection and decisive condemnation” of the arrest warrant.
“Bringing a baseless and contrived accusation more than 30 years later looks like nothing other than an act of vengeance by the anti-Cuban lobby in Miami,” the ministry said.
The Foreign Ministry warned that Washington’s legal actions against Cuba risked provoking wider regional instability.
Monday’s arrest warrant comes after the Trump administration issued a federal indictment against Castro in May over the same airplane shoot-down. At the time, the Kremlin called the U.S. indictment “bordering on violence.”
The Cuban government said that the 1996 shoot-down was “legitimate self-defense” against an airspace violation. Four people died in the incident.
Cuba, an ally of Russia going back to the Soviet period, has faced widespread fuel shortages and recurring blackouts in recent months as U.S. President Donald Trump has ramped up pressure on the country, including through a blockade on fuel imports.
Trump has vowed to conduct a “friendly takeover” of Cuba if authorities in Havana do not undertake a series of sweeping political and economic reforms that would greatly favor the United States.
In March, Russia sent an oil tanker to Cuba to provide what it called humanitarian assistance, effectively defying the U.S. blockade.
Trump said at the time that he was not opposed to shipments of oil to Cuba, including from Russia, despite his own administration tightening economic sanctions on the island as part of his “maximum pressure” strategy.
