title: Khabarovsk Scraps Direct Mayoral Elections
description: Lawmakers in the Far Eastern city of Khabarovsk have voted to abolish direct mayoral elections in favor of an appointment system controlled by the regional governor, the Interfax news agency reported Tuesday, leaving Russia with just two major cities where voters can still elect their mayors. “In accordance with federal law, city Duma lawmakers will elect the head of the city based on candidates presented by the governor,” the Khabarovsk regional assembly said in a statement quoted by Interfax.
content:
Lawmakers in the Far Eastern city of Khabarovsk have voted to abolish direct mayoral elections in favor of an appointment system controlled by the regional governor, the Interfax news agency reported Tuesday, leaving Russia with just two major cities where voters can still elect their mayors.
“In accordance with federal law, city Duma lawmakers will elect the head of the city based on candidates presented by the governor,” the Khabarovsk regional assembly said in a statement quoted by Interfax.
The move comes weeks after Khabarovsk’s Mayor Sergei Kravchuk stepped down after winning a seat in the lower-house State Duma in parliamentary elections held last month.
Khabarovsk is the latest city in Russia to cancel direct mayoral elections as part of a nationwide campaign launched by the Kremlin in the late 2000s to exert greater control over local government. Dozens of regional capitals have since eliminated direct mayoral elections, triggering protests in some places.
In 2024, the State Duma passed controversial local government reform which, among other things, allows regional lawmakers to abolish mayoral elections to create a so-called “ unified system of public authority.” The law grants smaller municipalities the right to keep direct elections.
Abakan in Siberia’s republic of Khakassia and Anadyr in Far East Russia’s Chukotka autonomous region are now the only remaining regional capitals to retain direct mayoral elections.

title: Kazakhstan Drops Drug Charges Against Russian Rapper Navai
description: Authorities in Kazakhstan have dropped drug smuggling charges against popular Russian hip-hop artist Navai and deported him from the country, local police said Tuesday.
content:
Authorities in Kazakhstan have dropped drug smuggling charges against popular Russian hip-hop artist Navai and deported him from the country, local police said Tuesday.
Navai Bakirov was arrested last Tuesday while entering Kazakhstan from neighboring Kyrgyzstan after border guards found 2.5 grams of marijuana in his vehicle. A court placed him in pre-trial detention for two months.
Bakirov reportedly admitted during interrogation to purchasing the cannabis in Bishkek prior to crossing the border, triggering an internal investigation in Kyrgyzstan.
“The criminal case against the Russian rap artist was terminated on non-rehabilitating grounds,” Kazakhstan’s Zhambyl regional police department told the Tengrinews outlet.
Kazakh authorities took into account Bakirov’s “active repentance” and the fact that it was his first offense.
“The foreign citizen has been deported,” the police department said in comments quoted by Russia’s state-run TASS news agency.
Bakirov’s defense team said earlier it was seeking to secure his release on bail.
The arrest forced the cancellation of Bakirov’s concert in Astana scheduled for last Wednesday, while organizers postponed his remaining tour dates.
Bakirov, a native of southern Russia’s Samara region, rose to prominence across the post-Soviet space as part of the hit-making duo HammAli & Navai before launching a solo career.
His legal trouble in Central Asia came nearly one month after he resolved a separate civil dispute in Moscow by compensating the city for damages caused when he crashed his Ferrari in the center of the Russian capital in May.

title: Ukrainian Drone Strike Sparks Fire at Oil Transit Hub in Tambov Region
description: A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at an oil pipeline hub in central Russia’s Tambov region, authorities said early Tuesday.
content:
A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at an oil pipeline hub in central Russia’s Tambov region, authorities said early Tuesday.
Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov confirmed that a blaze had broken out at “one of the enterprises in the Michurinsky district” without identifying the facility. He said no one was hurt in the attack.
The district is home to the state pipeline operator Transneft’s Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station, a key transit node along the Druzhba oil pipeline, which supplies countries in Eastern and Central Europe.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of the fire to identify the targeted facility in the Tambov region as the Nikolskoye station.
Nikolskoye receives, stores and transports crude oil and refined products, including diesel, gasoline, jet fuel and fuel oil. Its pumping capacity is estimated at 300,000 metric tons per day.
The attack comes after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement with the Kremlin to increase Russian diesel exports to global markets in order to offset energy prices driven by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, three people were killed after a Russian drone struck near a highway that connects Kyiv to the Black Sea port of Odesa in the south, according to the prosecutor’s office.
More than 32,700 families in the Odesa region were left without electricity after an overnight Russian attack on three facilities of Ukraine’s largest private energy company DTEK.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it struck four commercial cargo vessels, one of them bound for Odesa, alongside logistics hubs in the Volyn and Khmelnytskyi regions.

title: Japan Slams Lack of Access to Journalist Arrested in Far East
description: Japan said Tuesday that it was "extremely regrettable" that its diplomats have been unable to visit a Japanese journalist arrested in Russia despite a bilateral protocol that guarantees the right to consular access.
content:
Japan said Tuesday that it was "extremely regrettable" that its diplomats have been unable to visit a Japanese journalist arrested in Russia despite a bilateral protocol that guarantees the right to consular access.
Russian law enforcement authorities arrested the journalist from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on the Far East island of Sakhalin last week on suspicion of espionage.
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls "unfriendly" countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
Japan has denied the spying allegations and demanded that Russia release the journalist.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said a protocol signed between Japan and the Soviet Union remains in effect with Russia, ensuring the right to consular access within "a period of no later than four days from the time of arrest or detention."
"It is therefore extremely regrettable that, despite this provision, a consular visit was not realized within the prescribed period," Kihara said.
Japan will "continue to strongly urge the Russian side to arrange a consular visit at the earliest possible time," he said, adding that Tokyo was also demanding the journalist's release and fair treatment.
Russian media reported that the journalist would remain in custody at least until Dec. 12.
Last week, the Russian Foreign Ministry identified the arrested reporter as Yuki Imai, with spokeswoman Maria Zakharova saying he was accused of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory."
Russia's FSB security service said a Japanese national was arrested on Sakhalin — near a disputed cluster of islands — but did not name the individual. It said the person had worked for Japanese intelligence services to collect information about Russia's defenses.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi denied the spying claim. Tokyo summoned Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to protest the arrest.
Japan and Russia have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over a string of islands off the northeast coast of Japan's Hokkaido prefecture and southwest of Russia's Sakhalin region.
Russia has controlled the southern Kuril Islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan — since the end of World War II, when the Soviet Union seized them.

title: Russia’s Opposition Urgently Needs to Take Sexism Seriously
description: Opinion | First, let me introduce myself.
content:
First, let me introduce myself. My name is Roxana Kiseleva. I’m an activist with the Feminist Anti-War Resistance movement, a journalist, a radical leftist bimbo and one of the authors of the statement issued by the feminist members of the Peaceful Russia party condemning a sexist joke about when a young supporter would reach the age of consent, made by our party chairman Ilya Yashin and his associate, Roman Levitin.
For years, I made a conscious decision to avoid working with men. I can’t think of a single activist or political organization where women haven’t experienced harassment by male colleagues, whether verbal or physical. Every time we women found the courage to speak publicly about what we had been through, we would try to have a conversation about boundaries, abuses of power and the vulnerable position women occupy in a country where the police can’t always be counted on to help you.
But every time, there were men who would climb onto their soapboxes and loudly proclaim that “None of this matters. What matters is that Putin has seized power in Russia.”
I make my living outside of campaigning. Activism has always been something I did on the side, a form of unpaid work I chose to do, without any ambitions of turning it into more. That meant I could choose who I worked with.
I would have been more than happy to stay in my feminist bubble. I’m already running on empty and I’m not willing to fight yet another battle just to get my colleagues to take women’s issues seriously in politics. But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine made me rethink my rules.
Gender equality doesn’t exist. There isn’t a single country where women enjoy the same rights and opportunities as men. Politics is no exception: power remains firmly in the hands of men, often older and deeply conservative. We women have to elbow our way in and raise our voices just to be noticed, let alone make room for ourselves.
For big and powerful institutions like the European Parliament, the kind of political actor they know how to deal with is a democratic organization that stands for everything good and against everything bad, led by a well-known man whose Instagram is 90% photos of him shaking hands with other respectable political figures. Unless you’re as well-known as, say, Pussy Riot, don’t expect the men in suits to treat your ideas with any reverence.
For me, joining a political party is a way to get through to those men in suits. To tell them about Galina Bekhter , a 68-year-old political prisoner with dementia who can no longer eat without assistance but isn’t receiving the care she needs. Or about Aishat Baimuradova , a Chechen woman who fled her family to Yerevan, only to be found and brutally murdered there. Or about Sofia , a 14-year-old from Samara, the youngest person on Russia’s list of "terrorists and extremists."
When the world finally rids itself of yet another dictator in Vladimir Putin, and Russians have a chance to hope for a better future, I want women to have an equal seat at the table in peace negotiations and in the process of rebuilding Russia. So that when we once again raise issues like abortion rights, sex education, equal access to resources, and legislation against domestic violence, we’re actually listened to instead of brushed aside.
That’s why Russian women need access to international politics now, not someday in a post-Putin future — and why Western institutions must recognize us as political actors in our own right, not as an afterthought or an accessory to the men they already consider their counterparts. And to make that happen, we’ll have to work with men — if only to get a foot in the door in spaces where feminist organizations and women-led groups aren’t very welcome.
I already have so many questions. How will a future Russia tackle its catastrophic demographic decline? What guarantees do we have that a new government won’t turn women into baby-making machines in the name of repopulating the country? And how can it promise peace when so many prominent Russian politicians — men positioning themselves as opposition leaders — still refuse to acknowledge the link between patriarchy and war?
Women shouldn’t just be given a voice. They need to be listened to, and taken seriously. We have to stop pretending that we’ll deal with the war first, put the perpetrators behind bars, establish democracy, and only then, someday, get around to women’s rights, the environment, and Indigenous peoples — everything we’ll be expected to address to qualify for European integration.
Women in Russia aren’t even a minority — we outnumber men by 3%. So why are women’s rights always pushed to the bottom of the agenda? Why do we get a place in politics only through quotas, or when there’s nothing left to lose?
Even in relatively peaceful Europe, you can feel the end of the world creeping closer. The reason we’ve ended up here is that the world has belonged to men for far too long. If women don’t get involved in politics themselves now, the future may have no place for us — or even remember we were there. That’s why I’m not leaving the Peaceful Russia party.
I’m sorry that Ilya Yashin’s public conduct has done so much damage to the party’s reputation and left so many of its members frustrated. It will make it harder for me to do what I joined the party to do. And I suspect this won’t be the last time.
But I want to remind everyone that although Yashin initiated the party’s creation and co-organized its founding congress — giving him an advantage in the election for party chair — he is only a temporary leader. The party does not belong to him. And we, the party’s feminists, have enough influence to get our statement published on its social media without edits from the party leadership. We intend to fight for what matters to us, both in the wider political arena and within the party itself.
I’m also disappointed that some of my male colleagues responded with mockery to the discussions sparked by the scandal. “None of this matters. What matters is that Putin has seized power in Russia.” I’ve heard that line too many times already.
We’re not talking about rookies, here. We’re talking about grown men with a substantial political background. These are people who were active in Russian politics back when opposition politics was still legal, when they had the good fortune to be able to influence what was happening in Russia and change things.
The age-of-consent joke itself is a symptom of a wider problem: the men of the Russian opposition still have a long way to go when it comes to taking gender issues seriously.
I have absolutely no desire to invent new ways to police my colleagues’ behavior. I want the men in the party to show greater awareness and respect for women. Politicians are public servants. If you think the statement by the feminist members of Peaceful Russia is pointless busywork, then you’re not qualified to lead Russia toward a brighter future. Women’s issues are an essential part of any democratic agenda.
You should be grateful to the women who are willing to take on extra work and help educate you. We are literally offering to do the work of remedying your ignorance for you.
I just hope my colleagues will approach our proposal for workshops and discussions on gender issues with the seriousness and sense of responsibility it deserves.

title: From Banking to Taxis, Ukraine’s Data Center Strikes Disrupt Everyday Life in Russia
description: Andrei, a 39-year-old journalist from Moscow, looks at the notification on his smartphone and laughs. “Damn!
content:
Andrei, a 39-year-old journalist from Moscow, looks at the notification on his smartphone and laughs.
“Damn! I can’t log into my Yandex Pay account, but they’re still charging me for a Yandex Music subscription that doesn’t even work,” he says.
When he tried to log in, the app displayed a message that said “Something went wrong” and asked him to try again later.
“It’s a good thing I use another bank’s card for most of my payments,” he says.
Yandex Pay is one of dozens of services whose operations have been disrupted by Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers this month.
For many Russians, these outages have mostly meant temporary inconveniences and changes to their routines. But in a year that has already seen widespread fuel shortages , airport closures and e-commerce disruptions due to the war, they are the latest way in which the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has seeped into everyday life.
The data-center strikes have disrupted everything from taxis and car-sharing services, food delivery and maps to email, banking and streaming platforms.
Problems also arose for state agencies and private firms whose products rely on Yandex infrastructure, from dating apps to access systems for residential complexes and smart homes.
Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30% of normal levels following the Oct. 8-11 strikes, according to internet monitoring group NetBlocks. The disruptions affected 84 cloud services.
Yandex confirmed serious damage to one data center, the shutdown of another and infrastructure disruptions at a third. It has not disclosed the full extent of the damage or given a timeline for recovery.
In addition, all three of Yandex’s supercomputers were likely severely affected, which could set Russia back years in the AI race, the science news outlet T-Invariant said .
After a further strike hit a VK data center in St. Petersburg on Sunday, users also reported disruptions on social network VKontakte, including photos failing to load.
As of Monday, Yandex Pay remained only partially available. The error message had been replaced with a reassurance: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”
The Moscow Times reporter who wrote this article was still unable to access their full Yandex Taxi ride history on Monday.
A senior data analyst at Yandex told The Moscow Times that the company had been preparing for data center outages even before this month’s strikes.
“But the scale turned out to be far more serious than we initially expected,” and Yandex’s rank-and-file employees were caught off guard, said the employee, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal matters.
“We had to drop everything and focus on urgent problems with our services,” he said. “We managed to mitigate some of the effects quickly by switching applications to limited functionality, while in other cases recovery took several days.”
He said it could take much longer to fully restore services.
“I don’t think anyone expects everything to be fully restored within a few days,” the employee said.
The analyst declined to discuss how Yandex was preparing for further Ukrainian strikes, saying that disclosing those plans could create a vulnerability for the company.
While the economic damage and longer-term consequences of the strikes remain unclear, the immediate disruption has been manageable for many users.
The names of the Russians interviewed for this article have been changed for their safety.
Robert, a barista in St. Petersburg, uses Yandex Pay as his main bank account. It’s where he receives his salary and other transfers.
“I use it for payments 99% of the time,” he said. “Luckily, I had almost no money in my account when the outage happened. I’d spent everything on big purchases shortly beforehand. So I wasn’t too worried about losing it forever.”
His access to his digital wallet was restored after several days. He said he has no plans to stop using Yandex.
“I always keep an alternative way to pay just in case — a little cash,” he said.
The attack has nevertheless made him think about the war.
“It’s another reminder that the consequences of the war are getting closer to home — and growing in scale,” he said.
The disruptions also reached Yandex users outside Russia.
Yekaterina, a Russian woman who moved to Georgia after the invasion of Ukraine, said Yandex Go, a taxi service widely used across former Soviet countries, was temporarily unavailable in Tbilisi.
Nikolai, a Russian doctoral student in New Zealand, said he was unable to use Yandex Archives to research his dissertation.
“There weren’t many sources there, but the search was really convenient. So I sat down to write a chapter, wanted to quote something, and the archive was gone!” he said.
The data center strikes have also affected government agencies. The exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported that dozens of court hearings across Russia were disrupted due to technical problems.
Some government websites in the Kaluga region also went offline, Sarkis Darbinyan , an IT lawyer and founder of digital rights organization RKS.global, told The Moscow Times.
The outages have posed particular problems for small and medium-sized businesses whose products run on Yandex’s infrastructure, especially its cloud platform, a Russian equivalent of Google Cloud.
Tatyana, the founder of fitness app FIT&ZEN, told customers that both the app and its web version were temporarily unavailable because of “technical problems at a Yandex data center.”
“A major Yandex outage has affected many companies across the country, so unfortunately we’re not alone in this,” she wrote on the company’s Telegram channel.
A strike on Yandex Cloud hits “thousands of Russian companies at once,” Darbinyan said.
“After the Kremlin pushed Google and all its cloud competitors out of the country, Yandex played a very important role in the Russian internet, even though it did not have a dominant share of the data center market,” he said.
The greatest risks face customers that cut costs by keeping all their data in a single availability zone without backups elsewhere, he added. These include small and medium-sized businesses, regional media outlets and government agencies.
Darbinyan said the vulnerabilities exposed by the strikes are rooted partly in the structure of Russia’s internet and the rules governing where companies can store their data.
Earlier this month, the operator of Ukraine’s Parkovyi data center moved copies of customers’ data to backup sites in the European Union after it was hit by Russian strikes.
By comparison, Russian companies have little scope to do the same, Darbinyan said. Data localization laws and rules governing hosting, authentication services and critical information infrastructure require them to store data inside Russia.
Even so, Darbinyan said it would be difficult to take Russia’s internet completely offline by striking data centers.
Despite the Kremlin’s efforts to isolate it through its “ sovereign internet ” policy, Russia’s internet remains a vast network built along the same lines as the global internet. It encompasses more than 200 data centers, hundreds of telecom network nodes and corporate server rooms.
Its greatest vulnerability is the concentration of commercial data center capacity in Moscow and nearby regions, with much of it owned by a handful of major companies: Yandex, VK, Rostelecom and Sberbank, he said.
Serious disruptions at those companies can therefore affect services nationwide.
Nor will it be easy or quick to replace damaged infrastructure. Russia obtains almost all the necessary equipment through parallel imports, while the AI boom has driven up prices, Darbinyan said.
“If strikes become regular, the market may simply not be able to keep up with replacing what’s been lost,” he said.

title: Annexed Crimea Begins Lifting Fuel Rationing Measures After Months of Shortages
description: Kremlin-installed authorities in Crimea have begun lifting fuel rationing measures introduced months ago in response to shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and supply routes leading to the annexed peninsula.
content:
Kremlin-installed authorities in Crimea have begun lifting fuel rationing measures introduced months ago in response to shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and supply routes leading to the annexed peninsula.
Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Russian-appointed governor of Sevastopol, said Monday that purchase limits in the port city had been officially lifted as of midnight as shipments of fuel began to stabilize.
“We’ve removed the restrictions because the logistics situation with gasoline has practically stabilized,” the Interfax news agency quoted Razvozhayev as saying.
He said Sevastopol had enough fuel to ensure its “smooth sale over a short-term period,” though he said some gas stations ran out of certain fuel grades by midday on Monday before being restocked later in the day.
“Let’s hope the logistics situation will remain this way from now on,” Razvozhayev said.
Crimea began rationing fuel in May after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted military trucks and fuel tankers that supply the region from the north, triggering local gasoline shortages. The supply crisis later spread into mainland Russia as Ukraine ramped up its attacks on refineries, causing two major waves of nationwide fuel shortages.
On Oct. 12, the average price of gasoline in Sevastopol hit 131.76 rubles per liter ($6 per gallon), according to Rosstat data, which tracks the annexed city alongside Russian regions and lists it as being among the places with the highest gasoline prices nationwide.
Across Russia, the average price of gasoline has increased more than 21% since the start of the year.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries began to drive a wedge between the White House and Kyiv this month after U.S. President Donald Trump blamed them for the soaring cost of diesel in the United States, though analysts say the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is the main cause of high energy prices.
Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine earlier this month, which neither side said they had agreed to beforehand. That apparent pause in strikes collapsed immediately as the Russian army continued its attacks against Ukraine’s power grid.

title: ‘The Suicidal Fall of Europe’: Russia Reacts to Riots in France
description: As France picks up the pieces from a weekend that saw violent riots amid wider mass protests over education and the cost of living, reactions in Russia have ranged from outright glee and xenophobia to more muted schadenfreude and patronizing finger-wagging toward its Western adversary.
content:
As France picks up the pieces from a weekend that saw violent riots amid wider mass protests over education and the cost of living, reactions in Russia have ranged from outright glee and xenophobia to more muted schadenfreude and patronizing finger-wagging toward its Western adversary.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Europe was facing a “major crisis.”
“It’s hard to say whether [this] is a systemic or non-systemic crisis, but it’s clear that it’s a major crisis. These are disturbances that are, in fact, already bordering on chaos,” Peskov told reporters. “There is, of course, a clear sign of a crisis here, but, in any case, this is an internal matter for these countries.”
He dismissed accusations that Russia was involved in the protests, saying: “No one anywhere takes such absurd accusations seriously anymore. Not even in Europe itself.”
Elsewhere, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Sunday lambasted Europe’s “double standard” when it comes to dealing with protests.
Zakharova quoted Macron as saying that he would be “unyielding” in dealing with rioters who resorted to violence before asking where “human rights” and “freedom of expression” figured in the equation.
“In other words, when the French are ransacking Paris, it calls for uncompromising condemnation and tough measures, but when protesters in other countries are ransacking cities, we’re supposed to watch silently, re-reading the Élysée Palace’s angry press releases about the unacceptability of suppressing protests,” she wrote on Telegram.
“We need consistent standards, not the West’s endless double standards when it comes to human rights issues and interference in the internal affairs of sovereign nations,” she finished, alluding to Western condemnation of Russia’s crackdown on peaceful protests.
Responding to a question about the student protests on Friday, Zakharova accused the French government of stealing money from their own people to fund the “terrorist regime” in Kyiv.
“Guns and shells instead of school supplies and textbooks — these are the priorities of France’s political leadership today. While billions of euros are being channeled to support the neo-Nazi regime in Kyiv,” she said, repeating a debunked Kremlin talking point that claims Ukraine’s leadership has been co-opted by neo-Nazis.
Kremlin special envoy Kirill Dmitriev took to X over the weekend to call the unrest “The Suicidal Fall of Europe” and blame it on Europe’s migration policies.
“The West has fallen because of an inability to discuss and correct consequential mistakes on migration, energy, and warmongering,” Dmitriev wrote .
Along with his anti-migration rhetoric, Dmitriev reposted several videos showing burning buildings, clashes with police and general unrest.
Senator Alexei Pushkov , head of the Federation Council’s Information Policy and Media Relations Commission, called the scenes from France a “civil war.”
“There’s a civil war in France,” he wrote on Telegram. “They’ve played themselves into a corner with free migration. The country’s president — an irresponsible windbag — sees ‘Russians at the gates of Paris’ everywhere. But the Russians aren’t the French people’s enemies. They should look elsewhere for their enemies.”
RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan posted three side-by-side videos of the protests in France, Italy and Albania on X with the caption, “These are, of course, flourishing countries — France, Italy, Albania — where people live in prosperity, happily hand over their money to Kiev [sic], and enjoy every democratic freedom imaginable to make their wishes known to the government.”
Simonyan also criticized those accusing Russia of meddling in the protests: “Former President of Estonia apparently believes Western Europe needs our help to make a mess out of their own countries. I think they can manage on their own.”
The Kommersant newspaper published a report titled “Robberies on every floor: Oct. 17 was a day of street violence in France.”
“By evening, the demonstrations of discontented protesters had broken up into bewildered activists and roving groups of looters who wandered the streets and attacked anything they could get their hands on,” Kommersant correspondent Alexei Tarkhanov wrote.
“The police can disperse a crowd, detain suspects, and clear the streets,” he continued. “It is much harder to convince people that the president is listening to their everyday problems. Until such a response is provided, the next demonstration may once again begin with slogans about the high cost of living and end with fires in the streets.”
Vedomosti took a similar line, claiming that the French far-right was taking a “win-win” position by opposing the riots.
“All of this can be described as a manifestation of the death throes of Macronism. Macron will leave office in seven months, but not before then. And in the meantime, a lot can still happen in France, including a recurrence of large-scale protests and unrest,” they wrote, quoting Arnaud Dubien, the director of Franco-Russian think tank Observo.
In an interview with the state-run TASS news agency, political analyst Ilya Graschenkov said the protests are a response to “very real” social and economic problems facing European countries.
“They have been building up for years, and the current protests may signal the beginning of a profound restructuring of the European political system,” he said.
He added that the protests could be viewed as an opportunity to influence Europe’s future, as there are “serious ideological differences between Donald Trump’s conservative administration and a significant portion of the European political establishment.”
The pro-Kremlin daily Izvestia focused on French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s announcement of a curfew in select cities, as well as the alleged theft of a Lionel Messi jersey and captain’s armband from a museum in Paris.
State-run outlets also published video showing protesters blocking the entrance to the Louvre.
On the Vesti news program, journalist Yelena Kondratyeva-Salgero also blamed the unrest on migration.
“Where people are marching with French flags, there won’t be smashed storefronts, burning trash piles, torched cars, or looting,” she said. “Those with their faces covered, wrapped in Palestinian keffiyehs, carrying Palestinian, Moroccan, or Algerian flags… [on their part] you’ll see riots, attacks on the police and attacks on journalists.”

title: Putin, Trump and Xi Could Hold Trilateral Meeting on Ukraine War Next Month, Kremlin Says
description: The Kremlin said Monday that President Vladimir Putin, U.S.
content:
The Kremlin said Monday that President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a trilateral meeting focused on ending the war in Ukraine when they gather in China next month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
"Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised," spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in response to a Wall Street Journal report about ongoing talks to end the war.
"It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and substance of that meeting," Peskov added.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the idea of holding a meeting in China without Ukraine's input.
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S. and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia , China and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," Sybiha wrote in a post on X.
Peskov, who told reporters Monday that the U.S. was continuing its efforts to broker an end to the Ukraine war, said it was obvious that Ukraine would ultimately need to be involved in a final peace deal.
"Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility," he said.
The last U.S.-mediated ​peace ⁠talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in February, just before the United States and ⁠Israel ​launched a war ​against Iran. Ukraine and Russia remain as far apart as ever when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal.

title: Kursk Becomes First Region to Appoint Ukraine War Veterans’ Rights Ombudsman
description: The southwestern Kursk region has become the first in Russia to appoint an ombudsman tasked with ensuring the rights of veterans who fought in the war against Ukraine, Governor Alexander Khinshtein announced Monday. “Essentially, we’re the first region where such a position is being introduced on a systematic basis,” Khinshtein said during a weekly regional government meeting.
content:
The southwestern Kursk region has become the first in Russia to appoint an ombudsman tasked with ensuring the rights of veterans who fought in the war against Ukraine, Governor Alexander Khinshtein announced Monday.
“Essentially, we’re the first region where such a position is being introduced on a systematic basis,” Khinshtein said during a weekly regional government meeting.
Maxim Kalutskhikh, a retired army colonel born in the Kursk region, will fill the newly created post.
Kalutskikh fought in Ukraine between 2022 and 2023 and currently serves as deputy chairman of the Kursk region’s veterans association. He graduated from the Ryazan Guards Higher Airborne Command School and has also served in an elite unit within Russia’s FSB security service.
Governor Khinshtein previously said the veterans’ rights ombudsman will help families with filling out government paperwork and applying for benefits, as well as in any other “situation where someone hits a dead end.”
In other regions, human rights ombudspeople currently handle complaints from veterans and their families.
Difficulties faced by veterans are often related to military medical board decisions, payment issues, confirmation of kinship with deceased service members and mistaken AWOL classifications, according to the exiled news outlet Govorit Nemoskva.

title: FM Lavrov Arrives in Tehran for Talks With Iranian Leadership
description: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov arrived in Tehran on Monday to hold a series of meetings with top Iranian officials as Moscow seeks to position itself as a mediator in the war between Iran and the United States.
content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov arrived in Tehran on Monday to hold a series of meetings with top Iranian officials as Moscow seeks to position itself as a mediator in the war between Iran and the United States.
Lavrov will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian before holding “confidential and thorough” talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement.
“Discussions will cover the situation in the Persian Gulf and ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful U.S. and Israeli aggression against Iran,” the ministry said.
The bilateral agenda will also focus on energy, transport and economic projects, it added.
Russia and Iran signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2025 that includes provisions for countering shared threats. That pact stops short of mutual defense obligations, unlike the security agreement Russia has signed with North Korea.
Moscow is one of Tehran’s closest partners and has repeatedly condemned the U.S.-Israeli war against the Islamic republic.
President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian earlier this month that Russia is ready to play a mediating role in ending the Middle East war.
Lavrov’s visit on Monday follows U.S. President Donald Trump’s claims that Russia is “doing very little, if anything” to help Iran in the war with the U.S. and Israel.
U.S. officials have minimized concerns over Russian-Iranian military ties in the wake of reports as early as March alleging that Moscow is providing Tehran with intelligence to help it strike American military forces in the Middle East.

title: Putin Approves Major Government Cabinet Reshuffle
description: President Vladimir Putin on Monday approved a major reshuffle of top government officials, coming weeks after Russia held parliamentary elections that handed the ruling United Russia party its largest-ever majority.
content:
President Vladimir Putin on Monday approved a major reshuffle of top government officials, coming weeks after Russia held parliamentary elections that handed the ruling United Russia party its largest-ever majority.
The proposed personnel changes would replace nearly half of Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin’s deputy prime ministers, according to independent journalist Farida Rustamova.
Rustamova said Dmitry Grigorenko’s removal from the post of chief of government staff was unexpected given his role as Mishustin’s “right-hand man” and his position being among “the most important in the government.”
Mishustin’s spokesman later said Grigorenko himself had requested to be transferred to another post. Mishustin nominated First Deputy Finance Minister Irina Okladnikova to replace Grigorenko. If lawmakers approve her candidacy, she will become the first woman to ever hold the position of chief of government staff.
In other notable changes, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov will go on to serve as a deputy prime minister in addition to remaining in his role at the Finance Ministry, a post he has held since 2011. Siluanov previously held a dual position as deputy prime minister from 2018 to 2020 under former Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev.
Russian political analysts described the reshuffle as “a major strengthening of the fiscal leadership” as officials focus on increasing state budget revenues. The lower-house State Duma must now approve the nominations.
Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin was nominated to become deputy prime minister tasked with overseeing the development of Russia’s transportation sector, among other things. The vacancy was left open after Vitaly Savelyev resigned following his election to the State Duma in late September.
Dmitry Yadrov, head of Russia’s civil aviation agency Rosaviatsia, was tapped to succeed Nikitin as transportation minister.
Primorye region Governor Oleg Kozhemyako was also nominated to serve as deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to Russia’s Far Eastern Federal District. He will replace Yury Trutnev, who sources told the Vedomosti newspaper could be appointed to another Kremlin post.
The reshuffle follows State Duma elections last month, which renewed the ranks of parliament and came as Russian officials scramble to find new sources of economic growth amid strained government finances, increasingly burdensome taxes and high interest rates.
State Duma leadership was reportedly alerted over the weekend to hold last-minute meetings on Monday to approve the cabinet nominations and schedule confirmation votes. Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin later announced that votes on the nominations will take place on Wednesday.

title: Russia and Ukraine Should Focus on Peace Talks, Rubio Says
description: Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending the war between them, U.S.
content:
Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending the war between them, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during his visit to Uzbekistan on Monday.
"We see nothing good coming from this war," Rubio said. "We see a lot of downside to it, including the very real risk of escalation and spread of this thing... into another country because of a failed sabotage attack, because of drones that are hit with electronic warfare and they wander into a neighboring country."
Rubio landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet top officials of the C5+1 grouping, which brings together the United States and the post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
U.S. President Donald Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November.
Rubio on Monday also appeared to confirm reports that the United States, Russia and China are in talks to hold a trilateral summit of leaders to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. According to those reports, the floated summit would exclude Ukraine.
"There's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear. He'd like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end," he said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov earlier confirmed that a "hypothetical" trilateral summit was under discussion.
Trump has so far failed to broker an end to the war in Ukraine despite a frenzy of U.S. diplomatic efforts since he returned to the White House in January 2025. While Washington has been a strong backer of Kyiv over the years, Trump has grown increasingly critical of Ukraine and has gone so far as to suggest that President Volodymyr Zelensky should step down from office.
On Sunday, Trump slammed Zelensky for not signing a peace deal with Russia earlier.
"He doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," the president wrote on Truth Social. "He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles."

title: Trump Needs More Time to Assess Impact of Russian Sanctions, Rubio Says
description: The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, U.S.
content:
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russia n exports, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia -related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlie r.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November's midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russia n goods and penalties on countries buying Russia n oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russia n energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important U.S. partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russia n oil.
Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russia n President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia ," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia ."
Rubio also defended a separate U.S. agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed b y s hipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

title: Ukraine Dismisses Russia’s Latest Claimed Territorial Advances as ‘An Illusion’
description: Ukraine on Saturday rejected Russia's claim to have captured more than 1,800 square kilometers (695 square miles) of Ukrainian territory and nearly 100 settlements, including the eastern town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
content:
Ukraine on Saturday rejected Russia 's claim to have captured more than 1,800 square kilometers (695 square miles) of Ukrainian territory and nearly 100 settlements, including the eastern town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
On Friday, the chief of Russia 's General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, told President Vladimir Putin that Russia n forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements and made significant territorial gains since last month.
Ukraine's General Staff spokesman, Andriy Kovaliov, dismissed the claims.
"In fact, through their active operations, the Ukrainian Defense Forces have liberated more territory since the beginning of the fall than the enemy has managed to capture," he said in an emailed statement.
"The Russia n military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its political leadership and domestic audience," Kovaliov added.
Russia 's advances along the front line have slowed this year. Still, its forces have been bearing down on the so-called "fortress belt" cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the capture of which would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donetsk region.
Kovaliov also rejected Gerasimov's claims that Russia n troops had reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk and were advancing in the suburbs of Sloviansk.
He said Dobropillia, southwest of the two cities, remained under Ukrainian control despite sustained Russia n attacks.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield claims.
With many front lines largely static across a deadly "kill zone," both sides have intensified their air campaigns in recent months.
Russia fired hundreds of ballistic missiles over the summer and early fall, and it is widely expected to target critical infrastructure, including heating and power sites, into the winter.
Ukraine, which has a far smaller missile arsenal, has launched hundreds of long-range drone attacks on Russia n oil refineries, ships and commercial sites.

title: Trump Signs Order Exempting Russia From New Sanctions Legislation
description: President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related U.S. sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.
content:
President Donald Trump waived key Russia -related U.S. sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.
In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump said the waiver was in the national interest of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming to Moscow while publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Weeks before U.S. midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russia n crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Trump's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until he or other White House officials determine that "further action is appropriate." He had signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," the order reads.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russia n oil, have raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
The law allows the president to waive sanctions simply by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest.
U.S. Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, blasted Trump for the waiver, saying he was handing a gift to Russia n President Vladimir Putin.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.
Putin's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called Trump's waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that the legislation could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the U.S. to a halt.
Trump has also faced criticism from Democratic lawmakers and some Republicans over ‌a recent diesel deal with Russia in which he agreed to lift sanctions on Russia n exports while Russia agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices.

title: To the West, Rich Russians Can Plead Powerlessness. Everyone Else Must Prove Their Courage
description: Opinion | More than a century ago, the French writer Anatole France mocked the “majestic equality” of the law, which forbade rich and poor alike from sleeping under bridges, begging in the streets and stealing bread.
content:
More than a century ago, the French writer Anatole France mocked the “majestic equality” of the law, which forbade rich and poor alike from sleeping under bridges, begging in the streets and stealing bread. They might have been equal before the law, but hardly equal in their ability to navigate it.
The EU — and, ironically, France itself — has now provided a modern variation on his joke.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a Russian passport has come with a growing list of restrictions in Europe, from banking and visas to asylum procedures. But not everyone is affected equally by those barriers. Russia’s wealthiest and best-connected individuals and organizations have resources and years to contest measures imposed on them and, in doing so, to make courts and governments look beyond the passport and ask who they are and how much influence they had over Putin’s regime. Russians with far less money, access and time struggle to get beyond the word “Russian” in Europe at all.
But the inequality goes deeper than who has heavyweight lobbyists or can afford better lawyers. It lies in the radically different degrees of political agency expected from different Russians. Those closest to the Kremlin spend years explaining why their proximity to power gave them little say over Putin’s decisions and left them unable to stop the war. Those much further from the regime face the opposite expectation. With fewer resources and far more to lose, they are still expected to prove that they protested, spoke out or otherwise did all they could to bring Putin down.
Few cases expose this inequality as clearly as those of Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. Both Russian billionaires were sanctioned shortly after the full-scale invasion over what the EU described as their ties to President Vladimir Putin and Russian decision-makers. In the years that followed, their listings were repeatedly challenged in court and contested politically .
Slovakia had long pushed for Usmanov’s removal. But the stakes changed when France — one of the EU’s largest and most influential member states — took up the demand, citing unspecified national-security grounds. Paris did not confirm reports linking the French position to negotiations with Azerbaijan over detained French nationals, but its demand put the renewal of the wider sanctions regime at risk. Extending the measures required unanimity; even one government could hold up sanctions on thousands over the fate of a single billionaire.
Once France had opened that door, Luxembourg followed. It argued that if Usmanov was removed, Fridman should be too — while the latter was pursuing a multibillion-dollar arbitration claim against Luxembourg over assets frozen under the sanctions regime. On Sept. 22, the compromise was struck. Fridman and Usmanov came off the list, while sanctions on more than 3,000 other individuals and entities were renewed for another three years, setting an uncomfortable precedent in which individual names could become bargaining chips in negotiations over the wider sanctions regime.
To be clear, there is nothing wrong with contesting sanctions. If the grounds for listing someone no longer hold, there should be a way to challenge them. Nor does this outcome prove that Fridman and Usmanov simply bought their way off the list. What it does show is what money and access give you: the ability to keep institutions listening.
And listen, they did. For years, lawyers picked apart evidence down to photographs, meeting records and emails; journalists interviewed them and investigated their connections. Their relationship with the Kremlin was scrutinized, weighed and reweighed, until questions about two Russian billionaires were resolved at the highest political level in Europe. And all that attention gave them space to make a paradoxical argument: despite standing near the top of the Russian system and prospering within it, they had little say over the man at its centre.
Fridman said it plainly after he was sanctioned in 2022: Western policymakers misunderstood Russia if they imagined oligarchs could simply tell Putin to stop the war. The removal of his personal sanctions four years later does not mean the EU accepted that argument; the decision came through political compromise.
But that brings us to the much bigger question: if one of Russia’s billionaires can say that even he has little ability to influence Putin, how exactly are Russians with no access to power supposed to do so?
For years, every Russian has nevertheless been expected to protest and challenge the regime with whatever means they have. Western nationality-based sanctions rested, at least in part, on an assumption: make the costs of the Kremlin’s policies felt, and discontent from below will eventually translate into pressure on the regime. But authoritarianism breaks that logic. Economic pain does not readily become protest when people have little room to organise and much to fear, while elites are often better shielded from the consequences.
In principle, the EU itself recognized this problem. Its sanctions were supposed to target “the Kremlin and its accomplices” while minimising the consequences for “ordinary Russians.” The Anti-Corruption Foundation pushed the same logic further, compiling a list of thousands of officials, businesspeople, propagandists and others it argued should face personal sanctions for enabling Putin’s regime and the war. Instead of spreading the costs across society and hoping they traveled upwards, the idea was to target those who sustained the system.
Yet Europe is increasingly doing the reverse. Restrictions tied to Russian nationality have accumulated, even as some of the individually sanctioned elite have found their way off the list. Those far from the Kremlin are still expected to bear the costs and resist; some of those sanctioned for their ties to it have managed to escape them. That inversion is difficult to reconcile not only with the EU’s stated commitment to “human dignity, freedom, democracy, the rule of law and human rights,” but with the purpose for which these measures were introduced in the first place: supporting Ukraine and weakening the system waging war against it.
For most Russians, the consequences cut deeply into everyday life. In the EU, a Russian passport can determine something as basic as whether you can cross a border, visit your family or keep a bank account — often leaving little room for personal circumstances.
Asylum makes the contradiction even sharper, because here the system is explicitly supposed to look at the individual . But under the EU’s new asylum rules, nationality helps determine how much time you get to make your case. Applicants from countries with an EU-wide recognition rate of 20% or lower can have their claims fast-tracked. Sometimes, those applying at the border can also be placed in a procedure that must normally be completed within 12 weeks. Russia is among the countries whose recognition rate falls below the 20% mark.
That does not mean every Russian asylum seeker will have their claim handled this way, let alone rejected. Each case still has to be examined individually. But where the procedure applies, the timetable shrinks. An applicant has weeks to reconstruct years of their life: protests they attended, organisations they worked with, statements they made, threats they received and reasons they cannot return — and provide evidence for all of it. If they fail to convince the authorities that the risk they face is sufficiently personal and serious, they can be denied protection and ultimately returned to Russia — potentially to the repression, prosecution or imprisonment they fled in the first place.
Formally, every Russian in Europe is judged as an individual. In practice, not everyone has the same chance to be seen as one. For some, it stretches over years; for others, it is measured in weeks.
That is the majestic inequality running through Europe’s policies towards Russians: the oligarch can afford to make Europe understand his powerlessness; the asylum seeker has to make Europe believe in their courage.

title: Russia Looks to Africa for Gas Buyers as Gazprom Struggles to Replace European Market
description: Russia is seeking new gas markets in Africa as state energy giant Gazprom struggles to replace the European customers it lost following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
content:
Russia is seeking new gas markets in Africa as state energy giant Gazprom struggles to replace the European customers it lost following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilyov said Friday that Russia was ready to supply gas to African countries, as well as explore for deposits and develop any reserves it finds.
Speaking at Russian Energy Week, Tsivilyov said Russian companies could also offer a full range of energy infrastructure services.
“Our country can offer a comprehensive solution: modernize existing hydropower plants, build solar and thermal power plants, lay power lines, supply substations and transformers, and create power system management and dispatch centers,” he said , according to the state-run TASS news agency.
He added that Moscow views Africa as a “long-term market.”
Gazprom badly needs new customers after losing more than half its gas exports to countries outside the former Soviet Union since 2022.
The company is expected to export 77 billion cubic meters of pipeline gas this year, down from 185 billion in 2021 and around 200 billion annually in the late 2010s, according to Economic Development Ministry estimates .
The ministry forecasts that exports will fall to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028, after the EU’s ban on Russian gas imports takes effect, a level last seen in the second half of the 1980s.
President Vladimir Putin’s efforts to secure a new gas deal with China that would bring annual supplies to 100 billion cubic meters have so far failed to produce an agreement.
His Aug. 31 meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek yielded no breakthrough, the South China Morning Post reported , citing people familiar with the talks.
Beijing wants to pay roughly the same price as Russian households — about $50 per 1,000 cubic meters — or, at most, the domestic rate for Russian industrial consumers of around $120-$130, the sources said.
Moscow, however, wants to use the price China pays for gas supplied through the existing Power of Siberia pipeline as a starting point, one source told the newspaper.
That price, at $250-$260 per 1,000 cubic meters, is already about 40% below Gazprom’s contract price of $420 for other customers outside the former Soviet Union.
Talks over the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which Putin has renamed Power of Baikal, are currently on hold because of the pricing dispute, the newspaper’s sources said.

title: Russian Firms Stand to Gain Most From Trump’s Diesel Deal, Analysts Say
description: U.S.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow could do more for Russian oil companies than for the American consumers he wants to help, analysts say.
While Russian firms stand to benefit from looser export restrictions, the promised shipments may do little to bring down U.S. fuel prices.
The agreement has drawn scathing criticism from Ukraine and its European allies, as well as scrutiny from lawmakers at home. But does it make economic sense?
Trump announced that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons thereafter.
The deal comes as U.S. diesel prices have risen to $6.179 per gallon, up nearly 70% year-on-year, amid the turmoil that has gripped the global oil market since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Reduced refinery output has sharply cut global diesel exports , which totaled about 172.2 million metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, down 10% from the same period last year.
Higher prices are hurting Americans, including the truckers and farmers who are part of Trump’s traditional support base. With just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections, 73% said they disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, according to poll aggregator Silver Bulletin .
Additional Russian supplies are not intended to directly ease a U.S. diesel shortage because the country already produces roughly a quarter more diesel than it consumes. But U.S. fuel prices are shaped by global markets. The more other countries are willing to pay for diesel, the more domestic consumers must pay in turn.
More Russian diesel on the global market could therefore help lower American prices by narrowing the gap between supply and demand, regardless of whether it is shipped directly to the U.S.
Encouraging Russia and Middle Eastern producers to increase fuel supplies is the most straightforward way for Washington to bring prices down.
That’s because U.S. refineries are already operating at close to full capacity , while restricting exports to force domestic fuel prices lower could create other problems, including storage constraints.
Like the U.S., Russia is a net exporter of diesel, meaning it produces more than it consumes and sells the surplus abroad.
That has not changed despite Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian refineries in recent months. While the attacks have caused sporadic gasoline shortages, Russia’s pre-war diesel output was more than double domestic demand, compared with a surplus of just 15-20% for gasoline.
Russia has therefore continued to export diesel, though in smaller volumes. Shipments totaled about 427,000 metric tons in September, compared with roughly 3 million metric tons a month before Ukraine intensified its strikes, Reuters reported .
These figures only cover shipments to the limited number of countries, mostly in Central Asia, exempted from restrictions Russia imposed in July to keep its domestic market supplied.
Other estimates are higher. Kpler put September shipments at 584,000 metric tons.
Energy analyst and former Gazprom Neft executive Sergei Vakulenko, citing shipping data, said Russia exported at least 1.6 million metric tons of diesel by sea between July and September, despite a broad export ban that exempted supplies to Mongolia and Central Asia.
Vakulenko, now based in Germany with the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said Russian authorities had made little effort to stop these “grey” shipments because the country lacked the storage capacity to hold the surplus.
This means that Russia could supply the 500,000 metric tons Trump requested for November without causing domestic shortages simply by legalizing existing grey exports, he said.
Moscow partially lifted its diesel export ban from Oct. 10 following the agreement with Trump.
Supplying 1 million metric tons of diesel a month during the winter is also realistic, especially as domestic demand falls after the autumn harvest season, Vakulenko added.
U.S.-based energy analyst Tatiana Mitrova also said the volumes Trump requested from Russia “would have gone to the global market anyway without any additional effort.”
The volumes Trump announced may be realistic, but they could be too small to bring prices down significantly.
For example, 500,000 metric tons of Russian diesel equals roughly 4% of monthly U.S. consumption or 0.4% of monthly global consumption . It would cover about 13% of the estimated monthly global diesel shortfall of 4 million metric tons.
Russian supplies could have a greater impact if exports returned to levels seen before Ukraine intensified its attacks. But Kyiv has yet to agree to halt its strikes, and Moscow would need to repair its damaged refineries and restore lost capacity.
“The volumes under discussion are too small, all else being equal, to noticeably affect global prices, especially before the midterm elections,” Vakulenko said.
Without an effective energy truce, the diesel deal will largely amount to “appearances rather than a real increase in Russian diesel supplies to the global market,” he said.
The deal could provide “temporary relief to a global market facing a significant diesel deficit,” but Russia’s constrained refinery capacity limits how much additional supply it can deliver, analytics firm Kpler said in a note .
Shipping Russian oil products through the Baltic and Black seas poses another challenge, as Ukrainian drone attacks also disrupt those routes, Kpler added.
Moscow-based analyst Kirill Rodionov said Russian companies stand to reap the most benefits from the deal, as it would allow them to officially export more diesel at higher prices.
Those exports would do little to lower U.S. fuel prices, but would allow the Trump administration to claim at least a partial foreign policy success, he said.

title: Russian Courts Paralyzed by Yandex Cloud Outages After Drone Attacks – Vyorstka
description: Russian arbitration courts have been forced to postpone hearings and freeze legal filings following widespread system failures caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex data centers, exiled outlet Vyorstka reported Friday.
content:
Russian arbitration courts have been forced to postpone hearings and freeze legal filings following widespread system failures caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex data centers, exiled outlet Vyorstka reported Friday.
The technical disruptions reportedly began on Oct. 8 after a Ukrainian drone attack damaged the first of three Yandex data centers in Russia.
According to Vyorstka, the outages disabled online video hearings, froze official audio recordings and prevented judges from opening or downloading case files submitted by the parties.
Judges were reportedly forced to put cases on hold, declare trial breaks or leave bankruptcy filings frozen.
Court rulings directly cited server failures at Yandex Cloud as the reason for legal proceedings.
“Difficulties operating the ‘Electronic Justice’ software package are observed on Oct. 14 due to a massive failure in the Yandex Cloud main data center,” states one judicial order by a regional court shared by the outlet.
Similar outages were recorded across at least nine Russian regions, Vyorstka reported.
PravoTech, the software provider behind Russia’s arbitration court databases, acknowledged the service degradation in an Oct. 8 post.
On Monday, it said basic search features had been restored, but warned that services were still slow due to the cloud provider’s ongoing issues.
The court system failure reflects a wider wave of digital disruptions across Russia following Ukrainian drone attacks on three of Yandex’s six data centers. Search navigation, online banking, food delivery and major retail chains using Yandex Cloud services were still affected.
Key Yandex services did not appear to be fully restored as of Friday evening, as the Kremlin sought to play down the attacks’ effects.

title: St. Petersburg Bans Migrant Workers From Gym, Hair Salon and Retail Work
description: St.
content:
St. Petersburg authorities have banned foreign citizens with work patents from employment in retail, healthcare, beauty salons and fitness centers, local media reported Thursday.
Governor Alexander Beglov’s decree expands on existing restrictions, which last year banned migrant patent holders — a temporary low-skilled work visa — from driving taxis and delivering food.
Employers have been given until Dec. 15 to bring their staffing into compliance.
The decision aims to combat “shadow employment” and reduce economic reliance on low-skilled foreign labor, according to local outlet Fontanka.
According to St. Petersburg authorities, it will also facilitate “a transparent, regulated labor market where jobs are generated for Russian citizens, including young people and students.”
The restrictions do not apply to highly qualified specialists, foreigners with work permits or citizens of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan.
Citizens of other visa-free countries eligible to obtain a work patent in Russia include Azerbaijan, Moldova, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Dozens of other Russian regions, as well as occupied Ukrainian territories, have introduced similar targeted bans on foreign labor.
The measures were accompanied by a broader federal push to restrict foreign labor following the March 2024 Crocus City Hall terrorist attack, after which Russian lawmakers passed dozens of migration restrictions primarily impacting Central Asian workers.

title: Putin Vows Retribution for Attacks on Russian Data Centers While Downplaying Damage to Refineries
description: President Vladimir Putin warned Thursday that Russia is actively retaliating in response to recent Ukrainian attacks on its data centers, while simultaneously brushing off recent drone attacks on oil refineries. “They took the first step and we began to answer.
content:
President Vladimir Putin warned Thursday that Russia is actively retaliating in response to recent Ukrainian attacks on its data centers, while simultaneously brushing off recent drone attacks on oil refineries.
“They took the first step and we began to answer. Now they’re squealing over energy, as well as other facilities, including data centers. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it,” Putin said via video link at a business forum.
“Before taking this step, they should have thought carefully about the consequences,” he told the Delovaya Rossiya association.
His first public comments acknowledging drone attacks targeting Yandex and Sberbank data centers this month contradict the Russian Defense Ministry’s own reports that it began striking Ukrainian data centers last month.
At the same forum, Putin downplayed the impact of recent Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, including a fire at Rosneft’s Ryazan refinery on Thursday.
“They hit here and there. Nothing particularly significant, but nevertheless they persist,” the Russian leader said of the refinery attacks.
Putin also admitted that Russian security services failed to anticipate attacks targeting commercial logistics hubs like Wildberries and Ozon.
“They’re constantly taking steps that, frankly, we probably should have foreseen, but we thought they wouldn’t think of doing it. They thought of it,” he said, responding to Wildberries co-founder Tatiana Kim.

title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Energy Plant in Russia’s Largest Oil-Producing Region
description: A suspected Ukrainian drone attack sparked a fire at an industrial facility in western Siberia’s Khanty-Mansi autonomous district on Friday, local authorities said, in what appeared to be the first strike on energy infrastructure in Russia’s largest oil-producing region.
content:
A suspected Ukrainian drone attack sparked a fire at an industrial facility in western Siberia’s Khanty-Mansi autonomous district on Friday, local authorities said, in what appeared to be the first strike on energy infrastructure in Russia’s largest oil-producing region.
Governor Ruslan Kukharuk said an “industrial facility in the Surgut district” caught fire following the attack. The extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Residents identified the facility as the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant, according to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ . Eyewitness footage shared by the channel showed a large fire sending thick black smoke into the sky.
The plant, owned by Gazprom Pererabotka, is Russia’s largest facility for processing a mixture of crude oil and gas condensate, with a design capacity of 12 million metric tons per year. It produces gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, liquefied petroleum gas and stabilized gas condensate.
Surgut lies around 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Kukharuk had earlier warned of a drone threat in the region. Russia’s civil aviation authority imposed flight restrictions at airports in Surgut and Kogalym .
The Khanty-Mansi autonomous district, also known as Yugra, accounts for around 40% of Russia’s oil production. Authorities issued the region’s first drone alert on Sept. 9.
Days before that alert, regional officials began preparing measures to assist residents affected by potential strikes. The regional social development department proposed adding drone attacks to a list of emergencies that qualify victims for hot meals, food packages, clothing and other essential supplies.
Friday’s attack came after Ukraine said it was resuming strikes on Russian energy infrastructure following an “energy ceasefire” declared by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had failed to observe Trump’s energy ceasefire and had killed more than 100 civilians over the previous week.
On Thursday, Ukrainian forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery, Russia’s third-largest by processing capacity.
