title: Jailed Election Expert Kynev Denied Crutches After Leg Broken During Arrest, Journalist Says
description: Russian political scientist and election expert Alexander Kynev is unable to walk after being denied crutches at a Moscow detention center, a journalist who received a letter from him said.
content:
Russian political scientist and election expert Alexander Kynev is unable to walk after being denied crutches at a Moscow detention center, a journalist who received a letter from him said.
Kynev, who was arrested in late September on drug charges, has been transferred to Moscow’s Pre-Trial Detention Center No. 4, known as “Medved” (“Bear”), journalist Gleb Yarovoy said . His leg was reportedly broken during his arrest.
“He writes that he is still in a cast and has about three more weeks to ‘walk’ around in it. Except he can’t walk,” Yarovoy wrote.
Kynev also said he was being held in quarantine and receiving no information about the outside world, according to Yarovoy.
Moscow’s Perovsky District Court ordered Kynev into pre-trial detention on Sept. 25 on charges of attempting to sell a large quantity of drugs. He denies wrongdoing and faces between 10 and 20 years in prison if convicted.
The legal news Telegram channel Slovo Zashchite reported that Kynev suffered two fractures to his shinbone after being beaten during his arrest and was taken to the hospital at Moscow’s Matrosskaya Tishina detention center. His lawyer, Mikhail Biryukov, previously said he could neither confirm nor deny that account.
The Medved detention center, in Moscow’s Yuzhnoye Medvedkovo district, previously held opposition politician Ilya Yashin while he was under investigation for spreading “false information” about the Russian military, the investigative outlet Agentstvo noted .
Other former inmates include police rights activist Vladimir Vorontsov, former monk Nikolai Romanov and Andrei Bykov, the former head of the Federal Penitentiary Service’s research institute.
Yelena Masyuk, a former member of the presidential human rights council, previously documented allegations of extortion and abuse at the facility, including beatings by fellow inmates and cases in which prisoners were driven to suicide.
Kynev remained in Russia and had regularly commented on the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections before his arrest.
He estimated that turnout would have been around 40% and the ruling United Russia party would have won no more than 35% of the vote without electoral fraud. He also warned that the party’s record haul of 349 seats could backfire.
A specialist in Russian regional politics and elections, Kynev previously taught at the Higher School of Economics and headed independent election monitor Golos’ analytical department.
The Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent” in February 2026, accusing him of spreading false information about government policies and the electoral system, as well as cooperating with an organization designated “undesirable.”

title: Novaya Gazeta Editor-in-Chief Detained in Moscow
description: Russian law enforcement officers on Thursday raided the Moscow apartment of Sergei Sokolov, the editor-in-chief of independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, before taking him in for questioning and subsequently releasing him.
content:
Russian law enforcement officers on Thursday raided the Moscow apartment of Sergei Sokolov, the editor-in-chief of independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, before taking him in for questioning and subsequently releasing him.
Novaya Gazeta said contact with Sokolov was initially lost at around noon Moscow time before he was scheduled to lead an editorial planning meeting.
The publication said Sokolov was being transported to the Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, for questioning and that a lawyer was on their way to assist him.
Sokolov was later released on Thursday evening after law enforcement questioned him, reportedly in connection with the case against Novaya Gazeta managing editor Oleg Roldugin.
The raid on Sokolov’s apartment was conducted as part of an ongoing criminal investigation opened earlier this spring, law enforcement sources told the RBC outlet.
Meanwhile, sources told the state-run news agency TASS that the investigation centered around the illegal use of personal information.
Investigators charged Roldugin with the same crime earlier this year in April.
Roldugin, a veteran investigative journalist known for reporting on alleged corruption among top Russian officials, denies that he had illegally obtained and published personal information.
Baza, a Telegram news channel with links to Russia’s security services, reported that Roldugin was suspected of acting either, in coordination with, or under Sokolov’s instructions.
The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Russian law enforcement to immediately release Roldugin and stop what it described as the targeted prosecution of Novaya Gazeta.
Novaya Gazeta ceased print publication shortly after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine due to the draconian censorship laws that the government introduced as part of a broader crackdown on the press. The newspaper has continued to publish articles and videos online.

title: Russia’s Growing State Sector Nears Limit for Sustained Growth, Economist Warns
description: Russia’s expanding state sector is approaching a size that could undermine sustained economic growth, a senior economist warned, as the government prepares further tax increases to help finance rising military spending.
content:
Russia’s expanding state sector is approaching a size that could undermine sustained economic growth, a senior economist warned, as the government prepares further tax increases to help finance rising military spending.
Alexander Isakov, head of Sberbank’s Center for Macroeconomic Research and chief economist at state development bank VEB.RF, said Russia’s consolidated budget now amounts to 39% of gross domestic product, up from 32-33% in 2018-2019.
“International comparisons and our own policy experience suggest that Russia is approaching the upper limit for the size of the state sector compatible with strong, sustained growth,” Isakov told RBC in an interview published Thursday.
He warned against allowing public spending to reach 40% of GDP, saying crossing that threshold would hurt businesses and investment while weakening the government’s ability to collect taxes.
The Finance Ministry forecasts spending across Russia’s budget system at 38% of GDP in 2027. The Economic Development Ministry expects the economy to grow by 1.4% next year, with investment rising just 0.2%.
Isakov said companies were postponing investment because of uncertainty over taxes and broader economic risks. That, in turn, reduces demand and the government’s potential tax base, he said, stressing that businesses need a stable tax system to plan and expand.
His warning comes amid growing concern among business leaders about the state’s role in the economy.
A survey by the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Economic Forecasting found that 35.1% of senior executives wanted the government to reduce its economic role, the highest share in 25 years. Nearly two-thirds, or 63.9%, wanted lower taxes.
The government has increased the tax burden over the past two years. Corporate income tax rose from 20% to 25% in 2025, while the standard value-added tax rate increased from 20% to 22% this year.
Changes to small-business taxation have also stripped hundreds of thousands of entrepreneurs of access to the simplified tax regime.
Further increases are planned for next year, including a windfall tax on cement, fertilizer and gold producers, a rise in the top personal income tax rate on passive income, including bank deposit interest, to 22%, and a 22% VAT on purchases from foreign online stores.
The measures are expected to raise 1.5 trillion rubles ($18 billion) in 2027.
Even so, the Finance Ministry forecasts a federal budget deficit of 5.5 trillion rubles ($66 billion) next year, equivalent to 2.2% of GDP. That is up from an earlier projection of 3.2 trillion rubles ($38.4 billion).
The wider deficit reflects a planned 6% increase in spending to 48.8 trillion rubles ($585.6 billion), with roughly one in every three rubles allocated to defense.
Spending under the “national defense” budget category is set to rise from 12.9 trillion rubles ($154.8 billion) this year to 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.2 billion) in 2027. Total defense spending over the three years from 2027 through 2029 is projected to reach 50 trillion rubles ($600 billion).

title: Kremlin ‘Fully Agrees’ With Trump’s Zelensky Criticism
description: The Kremlin expressed “full” agreement Friday with U.S.
content:
The Kremlin expressed “full” agreement Friday with U.S. President Donald Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over stalled peace efforts.
“The fact that Zelensky doesn’t want to take responsibility and enter a peaceful settlement process is unambiguous,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“Here, we fully agree with President Trump’s point of view,” Peskov said.
Trump sharply criticized Zelensky in an interview with the Newsmax outlet, saying he believes Russia and Ukraine will end up reaching a ceasefire after the Ukrainian leader steps down.
“He doesn’t want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t,” Trump said of Zelensky and the conflict running for more than four and a half years.
Trump noted that both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky would like to see the war end, “but I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.
Sources close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg last month that Putin expects Russian forces to take full control of the Donetsk region by late February 2027.
At a summit in Brussels on Friday, European leaders pushed back against the growing rift between Washington and Kyiv, offering unconditional backing to Zelensky as winter approaches.
Despite their public backing, European officials reportedly plan to privately urge Zelensky to tone down his public criticism of Trump.

title: Putin Hands Control of 5 Western Firms to Ukraine War Veteran
description: President Vladimir Putin signed a decree Thursday placing the Russian assets of five major Western manufacturing companies under the temporary management of a little-known firm owned by an ex-official who fought in Ukraine.
content:
President Vladimir Putin signed a decree Thursday placing the Russian assets of five major Western manufacturing companies under the temporary management of a little-known firm owned by an ex-official who fought in Ukraine.
The targeted European and U.S. assets include French flooring giant Tarkett, Belgian hygiene manufacturer Ontex Ru, German plastic packager Menshen, corrugated producer Kappa Rus and metal packaging producer Eviosys, a subsidiary of the U.S. Sonoco Products Company.
Their combined 2025 revenue exceeds 53 billion rubles ($633.2 million), with Tarkett accounting for 19.3 billion rubles, Kappa Rus 16.5 billion rubles, Ontex Ru 10.3 billion rubles, and Eviosys and Menshen 6.1 billion rubles and 1.4 billion rubles, respectively.
Putin’s decree hands management rights to Tsentr Kapital Management Company, a Moscow entity established in February 2026, according to corporate registry data cited by RBC.
Tsentr Kapital is owned by 47-year-old Marat Mirkhaidarov, the former deputy governor and chief of staff of Far East Russia’s Zabaikalsky region.
Mirkhaidarov volunteered to serve in Ukraine with Chechnya’s Akhmat unit in early 2024, according to exiled media reports.
“I’m a patriot, I served in the special military operation [in Ukraine]. I have combat awards,” Mirkhaidarov told the Agentstvo outlet on Friday, expressing caution about his and his family’s safety over the news.
Mirkhaidarov stepped down from his regional administration post in March 2025, citing the need for medical rehabilitation after sustaining injuries during a delivery mission near the frontline.
Putin signed an order in 2023 granting the state the authority to place foreign assets under its temporary management. The regime strips foreign owners of operational control over their Russian subsidiaries while preserving nominal legal title.
Moscow has described the asset seizures as a response to “hostile actions” taken by “unfriendly” foreign governments.
On Friday, the Kremlin said the latest transfers represent a continued policy “trend” targeting countries that froze more than 210 billion euros in Russian reserves in Europe.
“Their origin was one of the factors taken into account when making the decision,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“We’re talking about those countries that take part in illegally holding Russian money, Russian assets. These are countries that take part in the illegal expropriation of Russian companies’ property,” Peskov said.

title: Putin Praises Russia’s Stock Market as Shares Slide and Growth Target Slips Away
description: President Vladimir Putin said Russia’s stock market was stable and functioning reliably on Thursday, despite steep losses and officials’ acknowledgment that a national target for expanding the market is out of reach.
content:
President Vladimir Putin said Russia’s stock market was stable and functioning reliably on Thursday, despite steep losses and officials’ acknowledgment that a national target for expanding the market is out of reach.
Speaking at a meeting with the Delovaya Rossiya business association, Putin acknowledged that the market had fallen short of the government’s ambitions but said it was strengthening, Interfax reported.
His comments came after officials acknowledged that Russia would not be able to meet his goal of raising stock market capitalization to 66% of gross domestic product by 2030.
The benchmark MOEX Index has fallen 13.6% this year and 37% since the end of 2021. Earlier this year, it posted a record 19 consecutive weeks of declines.
At around 2,400 points, the index is back near levels seen in early 2019. Consumer prices have risen 71% since then.
Russian stocks were the worst-performing domestic investment category over the first nine months of 2026, the preceding 12 months and the period since the start of 2022, according to Central Bank calculations .
Even including reinvested dividends, Russian equities lost 11.3% in January-September and 10.5% since the start of 2022, the bank calculated. Losses were substantially greater after accounting for inflation.
The stock market’s value relative to GDP has nearly halved during more than four years of war, according to calculations by rating agency Expert RA and the Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting.
Economist Viktor Tunev estimated the ratio at about 20% this summer, saying stock market capitalization was plumbing new lows relative to the size of the economy.
Several of Russia’s largest listed companies have suffered particularly steep declines.
Shares in state-controlled lender VTB hit a record low this year and now trade at roughly one-twelfth of their price at the bank’s 2007 initial public offering, which was heavily marketed to ordinary Russians.
Gazprom shares fell in July to their lowest level since November 2008, during the global financial crisis.
During that crisis, the government allocated 175 billion rubles ($2.1 billion) from the National Wealth Fund to buy shares and bonds in major Russian companies.
Sberbank, Russia’s most valuable listed company, now has a market capitalization only slightly larger than that of Italian luxury carmaker Ferrari.
Economist Vladislav Inozemtsev has pointed to sharp market rallies whenever hopes of peace emerge. The continuing war, however, has left Russian equities largely cut off from foreign investment, with Russian retail investors accounting for about two-thirds of trading turnover.
Authorities have sought to attract household savings by improving the terms of individual investment accounts and introducing a long-term savings program with limited government matching contributions.
But retail investors cannot replace foreign institutional funds in large share offerings, Expert RA has warned .
A growing wave of state takeovers, including of publicly traded companies, has also undermined investor confidence. Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina and Finance Minister Anton Siluanov have repeatedly stressed that trust is essential to a stable market.
Companies have meanwhile faced successive tax increases as the government seeks to finance a budget swollen by military spending.
Authorities imposed an additional mineral extraction tax on Gazprom in 2022, followed by a windfall profits tax and an export duty linked to the ruble’s exchange rate in 2023. The corporate profit tax rose from 20% to 25% in 2025.
Another windfall tax, targeting nonferrous metals producers, is set to follow next year.
Individual investors also face higher taxes. Starting next year, income from securities trading will be included in the general personal income tax base and taxed at rates of 13% to 22%, depending on total income. Currently, it is taxed separately at 13% or 15%.

title: Russia Repels 644 Ukrainian Drones as Trump Calls Attacks on Russian Refineries ‘Disgrace’
description: Russia’s Defense Ministry said Friday that 644 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 26 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight, as U.S.
content:
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Friday that 644 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 26 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight, as U.S. President Donald Trump called Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries a “disgrace.”
Vladimir region Governor Alexander Avdeyev said air defenses repelled an attack aimed at municipal heating infrastructure serving the regional capital. According to Avdeyev, there were “minor” damages.
Unverified reporting by monitoring channels that shared video of an explosion against the dark sky claimed it targeted a data center owned by tech giant Yandex in Vladimir, which was previously damaged in last weekend’s strike.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defenses shot down 94 Ukrainian drones on approach to the capital between Thursday evening and Friday morning.
Nearly 160 flights were delayed or canceled across Moscow’s four main airports, with Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo bearing the brunt.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian attack on the eastern city of Kharkiv killed three people and injured five.
Russian strikes also left 370,000 residents in Ukraine’s northwestern Volyn region —which is near the Polish border — without electricity. Polish and NATO fighter jets were scrambled to safeguard Polish airspace.
Rolling blackouts were also introduced in Kyiv during Russian attacks, said private energy provider DTEK on X.
Trump blindsided Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities. Facing U.S. midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced, and criticized his willingness to strike deals with Moscow.
“All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet, after Ukraine hit a refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital.
For Russia's part, President Vladimir Putin played down the effect of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused “nothing particularly significant.”

title: From Wildberries to Yandex, Ukraine Is Turning Russian Business Giants' Dominance Into a Liability
description: Opinion | That the main events in Russia last week were once again shaped by Ukraine says a great deal about who is really setting the geopolitical agenda.
content:
That the main events in Russia last week were once again shaped by Ukraine says a great deal about who is really setting the geopolitical agenda. Those events were U.S. President Donald Trump’s rather sudden announcement of an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine and Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex’s most important data center.
Perhaps the Kremlin never agreed to the ceasefire in the first place because it has started to think that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries are not the worst thing that could happen.
Of course, taking a hit to the wallet hurts and having ordinary people cursing Putin and his war while they queue for petrol isn’t ideal. But in recent days people have become far angrier after discovering that they cannot call a taxi, order a delivery or even access their own money.
When Ukraine struck a Yandex data center in the town of Sasovo in the Ryazan region on the night of Oct. 7-8, it shut down two of the company’s three supercomputers, Chervonenkis and Lyapunov, which are used to train neural networks including YandexGPT and Alice AI. The company said it could not give a timeframe for when service would be restored.
A day later, a strike on Yandex’s largest data center, situated in the Kaluga region, disabled the company’s final, third supercomputer, Galushkin.
Then, a strike hit the data center in the Energetik district of the Vladimir region on Oct. 10, taking the ru-central1-a availability zone offline. The Yandex Cloud platform was switched to emergency mode, while the remaining IT infrastructure was deemed “unstable.”
Alice smart speakers were not the only thing that went down. The ru-central1-b availability zone of the Yandex Cloud platform, which stores the data of numerous large firms, including Yandex itself, was taken offline.
Yandex Go taxi services stopped working not only in Russia but in neighboring countries and even in some that do not border Russia at all. In Belgrade , for example, 32 of the city’s 33 taxi fleets operate through Yandex Go. Russian emigrants, accustomed to calling taxis through the app and pleased that they could even pay for the ride using a Russian bank card, discovered that the Serbs had not been so wrong after all to continue calling taxis by phone and paying in cash.
In Russia itself, almost every popular service began malfunctioning — from T-Bank to mobile operators, from Russian media websites to railway ticket-booking services. Never mind those services: Yandex Pay stopped working.
The problems are much more serious for those who stored their data in Yandex’s cloud. And many did. That included private users who feared losing access to Google Cloud and other foreign cloud-storage services, as well as almost the entire business sector, which the authorities had simply ordered to move all its data onto domestic servers.
Conveniently enough, the Russian authorities had forced Yandex to shut down its service center in “unfriendly” Finland. Now the company is frantically moving data onto third-party servers in Kazakhstan and Belarus. But Russian providers do not have much spare capacity to offer, while Kazakhstan is already concerned with moving its own services off Yandex servers and onto domestic ones. Everyone else will get whatever is left over.
Businesses do not currently even understand which of their databases have survived and can be restored from backups, which will be restored by Yandex and which have been lost forever. Accordingly, calculating the losses is also difficult , and it is unlikely to be done quickly .
The most pressing question, of course, is when everything will be fixed. Work to restore the services that had gone down began soon after the first attack and, as of Monday , some things had started working while others remained offline.
The main problems are with cloud services: Yandex Cloud Console and the API are available, Compute is partially available, IAM is available, while most other functions are restricted.
The company really is working around the clock to restore access. The state has promised assistance and perhaps the situation will get so dire that the ban on using foreign “unfriendly” facilities is lifted. It has reached the point of absurdity: Yandex support is operating through WhatsApp, while drivers are being advised to use Google Maps .
But as with the attacks on oil refineries, this is a developing situation. There were no attacks on the night from Sunday into Monday, but that does not mean they will not resume. Nor is there any guarantee that it will stop with Yandex’s data centers — of which it has two left. Rostelecom, for example, has 29 data centers. Because they are so sensitive, they may be better protected or out of the range of Ukrainian drones. But as the attacks on Yandex have shown, the way data centers are interconnected means that disruptions can affect the most unexpected areas.
Experts say that even this is not the main problem — the main problem is chips. The destroyed Yandex supercomputers used thousands of advanced Nvidia chips, which are under such strict export controls that it is nigh-on impossible to import them. Replenishing lost compute will take years. Without new chips, the company’s electronic brain will resemble that of an Alzheimer’s patient: it remembers this, forgets that, and everything else is jumbled up in its head. The Russian internet will be set back by at least 10-15 years, with all the consequences that would entail.
But I would point to an even more important issue. Many people were surprised by Ukraine’s choice of targets when they began smashing Wildberries warehouses. But after the attacks on Yandex’s data center, it became clear that Kyiv was striking at what it calculated to be the Achilles’ heel of the Russian economy.
Look at how Russia’s ecosystem of businesses is constructed. There is Wildberries — and several other, much smaller online marketplaces. For technology, there is Yandex — and several much smaller platforms. You can keep going: Aeroflot — and several smaller airlines; Sberbank — and several smaller banks.
Do you see the pattern? The Kremlin chooses an “anchor” representative for a given sector to which it gives maximum possible advantages, even arranging for state institutions to conduct most of their work through it. Several secondary players are allowed to exist to keep up some semblance of competition and to act as a reserve and to serve particular interests, both state and non-state.
This is not even a classic oligopoly. It is an exact replica of the hierarchical system of Putin’s rule, where nothing but a scorched field exists beyond the Kremlin’s inner circle. The system was assembled according to its creators’ own idea of how a properly organized state should work and what makes it easy to govern. It turns out that such a system is also an extremely convenient target if you want to disrupt the operation of entire sectors.
Perhaps that is precisely why, as of midday Monday, Russia had still not formulated a response to Trump’s energy truce. Both Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov came out with incoherent responses. Because it was stated quite clearly: the proposal concerns stopping strikes only on oil refineries. As for other targets in Russia, as Trump put it quite plainly: “do whatever you want.”
So perhaps right now they are sitting in the Kremlin trying to work out what will happen to the Russian internet if Ukraine continues striking data centers. Perhaps they have even got as far as wondering what will happen if they find a way to strike the banking system. Air travel? Any other sector organized according to this same hierarchical model?
Or perhaps they are not thinking about any of this at all yet. Perhaps they are too busy stamping on problems that keep springing up or trying to persuade Trump to give Russia something else useful.
Those problems, however, are not going anywhere because the main problem is the minds of those who govern Russia. Covering a building in protective netting won’t fix that. It isn’t a problem Trump can solve, either.

title: EU Weighs Schengen Visa Restrictions for Russians Amid Sabotage Fears
description: EU officials are weighing tighter visa restrictions for Russians amid growing fears of hybrid attacks and sabotage across the bloc.
content:
EU officials are weighing tighter visa restrictions for Russians amid growing fears of hybrid attacks and sabotage across the bloc.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola on Thursday called on Brussels to press ahead with targeted restrictions while stepping up support for Ukraine.
“We must also increase pressure on Russia, notably by making progress on targeted visa restrictions,” Metsola said at a press conference following a summit of EU leaders.
The EU executive is expected to propose “planning” targeted visa restrictions in early 2027, according to the news outlet Rapporteur. The plans are being spearheaded by Poland, Sweden and Estonia, according to Politico Europe.
The EU Council working group on visa policy met Wednesday to discuss issuing Limited Territorial Validity (LTV) visas to Russian applicants that would restrict travelers to the borders of the issuing state rather than allow access to the wider Schengen zone.
The outcome of those talks was not made public.
Germany has proposed requiring member states that still issue visas for nonessential travel to switch to LTV visas, Rapporteur reported. Ireland, which holds the EU Council’s rotating presidency, reportedly warned that the measure could fail to prevent security threats from spreading across the bloc.
The proposal follows an alleged drone plot in Germany in August involving a Russian passport holder who reportedly entered the Schengen zone on an Italian tourist visa.
Tourism industry experts told the Russian Union of the Tourism Industry that LTV visas could complicate trips spanning several European countries, lengthen visa processing times and reduce visa availability.
Meanwhile, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said he planned to propose a complete halt to issuing tourist visas for Russian citizens at the ongoing European Council summit.
“We fear that Russia will attempt to organize acts of sabotage in Europe. Why then are we letting Russians come here as tourists and allowing them to move freely?” Orpo said last week.

title: Russia to Ban Direct Person-to-Person Crypto Trades in July 2027
description: Russian citizens will not be allowed to buy or sell cryptocurrency directly without state-regulated intermediaries starting next summer, according to official guidance from Russia’s Central Bank.
content:
Russian citizens will not be allowed to buy or sell cryptocurrency directly without state-regulated intermediaries starting next summer, according to official guidance from Russia’s Central Bank.
The regulator wrote in an FAQ that peer-to-peer crypto transactions between individual buyers and sellers will be removed from the list of legal operations after July 1, 2027.
Media outlets that first reported on the looming ban noted that individuals may attempt to bypass it by disguising direct crypto sales as personal gifts or debt repayments.
Under a law President Vladimir Putin signed over the summer, cryptocurrencies may be bought and sold only through institutions regulated by the Central Bank.
These intermediaries include exchanges, brokers, asset managers and digital depositories.
Retail investors will be limited to purchases of 300,000 rubles ($3,690) a year through each intermediary.
The Central Bank has already begun building an official registry of authorized crypto operators, which currently includes 12 entities like the state lenders Sberbank and VTB.
The July 1, 2027, deadline is also set for cryptocurrency exchanges and digital depositories to obtain the required licenses.
The law prohibits cryptocurrency payments inside Russia but not cross-border settlements.

title: Russia Builds Major New Drone Attack Base in 6 Weeks, Satellite Images Show
description: Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defense experts and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.
content:
Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defense experts and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.
The site in what was an empty field in Russia's southwestern Rostov region on Aug. 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Wednesday, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed.
The construction coincides with a surge in the use of Russian jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, which is struggling to intercept the faster weapons that can travel at speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour.
With the full-scale war well into its fifth year, Kyiv expects Russia to further escalate jet drone and missile attacks this winter.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, Russia's newest types of jet-powered drone.
He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine.
"The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly," Monnik said.
The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be "probably a matter of weeks before [it is] fully operational, if not earlier."
The construction of the facility coincides with worsening relations between Russia and the NATO military alliance.
European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave.
Monnik said the combination of industrial production of jet-powered drones, their increasing sophistication and the relative lack of comprehensive counter-drone defenses in many NATO countries were a challenge for the West.
"This ability to rapidly field an ability to launch large-scale attacks using UAS [unmanned aerial systems] poses a strategic vulnerability for NATO countries," he said.
Monnik said the facility may have the potential to fire 100 jet-powered drones or more in 24 hours, although Russia normally fires them in small numbers throughout the day. It would also depend on factors like available supplies and objectives.
Rob Jordan, program director at the London-based RUSI think tank, said the concrete pads and two possible takeoff rails shown in the imagery looked consistent with launch tracks for Russian Geran drones.
"This level of construction in this short a time is impressive," he said. "This shows the relative faith Russia is putting in its deep strike capability — possibly to the detriment of its conventional land forces."
Russia's Defense Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the facility and on its jet-powered drone program more broadly.
Military analysts say Russia has shifted its drone production capabilities to jet-powered models as Ukraine has struggled to counter them.
Russia increased its use of jet-powered drones roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data reported by Reuters last month. Kyiv and the surrounding region were targeted most heavily, the data showed.
The jet drones pose a problem because they are too fast for the interceptor drones designed by Ukraine to cheaply intercept their slower, piston-powered predecessors. Kyiv is now scrambling to devise a solution.
Overhead imagery of the new facility taken on Aug. 31 pictured a few vehicles in a field but no sign of construction. Imagery taken the following morning showed that work had begun.
The site, which occupies an area of around 0.9 square kilometers, lies about 3.5 kilometers from Russia's Millerovo air base, home to the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
According to DroneSec, the new launch site likely sits within the air defense "bubble" provided by systems at the airbase, making Ukrainian attempts to target the new facility more difficult.
Of the eight launch platforms, two already had rails on them, a Reuters analysis showed. Rails were being constructed on two other pads as well, while other construction work was visible from space over the course of three days this week.

title: Russian Activist Fined Over ‘Party of Crooks and Thieves’ T-Shirt
description: A court in the Russian city of Kostroma has fined an activist for displaying “extremist symbols” over a photograph of him wearing a T-shirt with a slogan mocking the ruling United Russia party, the RusNews news outlet reported.
content:
A court in the Russian city of Kostroma has fined an activist for displaying “extremist symbols” over a photograph of him wearing a T-shirt with a slogan mocking the ruling United Russia party, the RusNews news outlet reported .
Andrei Tarasov, a former parliamentary candidate for the liberal Yabloko party, was fined 1,000 rubles ($12) by Kostroma’s Sverdlovsky District Court. The T-shirt bore the words “I’m against the party of crooks and thieves” alongside an image of a person kicking a bear, United Russia’s symbol.
An expert enlisted by the Interior Ministry deemed the slogan extremist on the grounds that it was attributed to the late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny.
The expert’s assessment said the phrase “delegitimized the ruling party in the eyes of voters” and “serves as a marker of opposition affiliation.”
The case followed a complaint by Communist Party member Sergei Shpotin, who ran for governor of the Kostroma region in 2025.
Shpotin complained that his fellow party members were being “dragged through the courts” while “this new liberal gets away with absolutely everything.”
The phrase “party of crooks and thieves” has long been used to describe United Russia. Opposition politician Boris Nemtsov used it during a Radio Liberty broadcast in 2010, and Navalny later popularized it on his LiveJournal blog.
The slogan was widely adopted by opposition groups and individual voters during the 2011 parliamentary election campaign.
Banners, flags and stickers reading “Down with the party of crooks and thieves” became a familiar sight at mass protests in 2011-2012, held against the backdrop of Vladimir Putin’s planned return to the presidency.
A June 2012 poll by the independent Levada Center found that 42% of respondents agreed with the description of United Russia as the “party of crooks and thieves.”

title: Japan Denies Spying Claims After Russia Arrests Journalist
description: Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday denied Russia’s allegations of espionage after the FSB security service arrested a Japanese journalist. “There is no such fact,” Takaichi told reporters when asked about Moscow’s claims that the reporter was acting on behalf of Japanese intelligence.
content:
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday denied Russia’s allegations of espionage after the FSB security service arrested a Japanese journalist.
“There is no such fact,” Takaichi told reporters when asked about Moscow’s claims that the reporter was acting on behalf of Japanese intelligence.
She said details remain sparse surrounding the arrest of Yuki Imai, a correspondent for the northern Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun, in Far East Russia’s Sakhalin region.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Wednesday that Japan had not been able to contact the individual and did not know about the arrest until the official announcement from Moscow.
The FSB accused Imai of collecting and storing information on Russia’s defense capabilities for intelligence purposes that it said could be used against Russian security.
Russia’s Ambassador in Tokyo Nikolai Nozdrev, who was summoned by Japan’s foreign ministry to lodge its protest, hit back Thursday with his own accusations that Japan enlists reporters into intelligence gathering.
Nozdrev said it was “unacceptable that Japanese special services recruit private persons, including Japanese journalists accredited in Russia, for ‘collaboration’ through the collection of classified information.”
Takaichi said Tokyo intended to focus on “the protection of Japanese nationals.” The Hokkaido Shimbun said the reporter’s safety was its top priority.
The case adds to long-running tensions between Russia and Japan, which have yet to sign a formal World War II peace treaty due to a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories.
Imai's arrest comes days after Japanese law enforcement in Osaka apprehended a 28-year-old Russian national linked to the international ransomware group Qilin and extradited him to Germany to face cybercrime charges.

title: Russia’s Oil and Gas Revenues Forecast to Rise 10% Year-on-Year in October to $12Bln
description: Russian federal budget revenue from oil and gas taxes, which account for about a fifth of total government income, is expected to increase by 10% year-on-year in October to reach 1 trillion rubles ($11.97 billion), according to a Reuters calculation.
content:
Russian federal budget revenue from oil and gas taxes, which account for about a fifth of total government income, is expected to increase by 10% year-on-year in October to reach 1 trillion rubles ($11.97 billion), according to a Reuters calculation.
Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer and exporter after the United States and Saudi Arabia, relies ​heavily on oil and gas sales, which ​help finance its war in Ukraine.
Oil and gas tax revenue is expected to more than double this month from September largely due to quarterly payments of the additional profit-based tax on oil production. Excluding the tax, October revenue is expected to exceed September levels by about 164 billion rubles, or 36%.
Reuters calculations are based on oil and gas production data, refining throughput and supplies on domestic and international markets.
Global oil prices have soared as the conflict in the Middle East disrupts supplies. However, the positive effect of higher oil prices will be partly offset by an estimated 5% decline in production in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period of 2025.
Russia's 2026 budget assumes oil and gas revenue of 8.918 trillion rubles out of total revenue of 40.283 trillion rubles.
According to the Reuters estimate, total oil and gas revenue in January-October 2026 is expected to reach 6.45 trillion rubles, down 14% from the same period a year earlier.

title: Ukraine Says Missile Strike Destroyed 6 Russian Warplanes at Voronezh Airfield
description: Ukraine’s Navy said Thursday that it destroyed six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers in an overnight missile strike on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in southwestern Russia’s Voronezh region.
content:
Ukraine’s Navy said Thursday that it destroyed six Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers in an overnight missile strike on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in southwestern Russia’s Voronezh region.
The Navy said the attack was carried out using its Neptune coastal missile system. It also reported damage to equipment supporting flight operations, a fire and secondary explosions.
Ukrainian monitoring channels published satellite images purportedly showing damage to an aircraft parking area. The reported destruction of the six warplanes could not be independently verified.
Last night, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an airfield in the Voronezh region. Four Su-34 aircraft were destroyed and two more Su-34s were hit. The Russians used them to terrorize our people. These very warplanes were ready to launch new attacks on Ukraine and were loaded with aerial bombs. Our Long Neptune missile was used to strike the target. I thank the warriors of the Ukrainian Navy for their precision! Our long-range sanctions also reached a site in the Oryol region used to store and launch attack drones. A target was also hit in the Black Sea. These are our justified responses to all of Russia’s terror against Ukraine. Russia is dragging out the war, so our long-range operations will continue.
Russian authorities did not acknowledge a strike on the airfield.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defenses intercepted 33 drones and “several jet-powered aerial targets.” Falling debris damaged outbuildings at several private homes and a car in the regional capital, Voronezh, he said.
Residents of Borisoglebsk reported explosions and a large fire, with smoke visible from several parts of the city.
The military airfield lies about 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) east of Borisoglebsk.
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided glide bombs at Ukrainian positions and populated areas. The Su-34M is an upgraded version of the aircraft.
In September, Ukraine’s military said it had destroyed a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet near the Millerovo airfield in the Rostov region and a Ka-27 helicopter near the Yeysk airfield in the Krasnodar region.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces had previously reported striking four aircraft at the Shagol airfield in the Chelyabinsk region: two Su-57 fighters, a Su-34 and another Sukhoi aircraft of an unidentified model. Those targets were about 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

title: Russian Ministers Join Board of Key Trade Payments Firm A7
description: Three of Russia's most senior government officials have joined the board of Russian payments firm A7, underscoring its growing role in sustaining trade with China and other partners as Western sanctions disrupt traditional banking channels.
content:
Three of Russia 's most senior government officials have joined the board of Russia n payments firm A7, underscoring its growing role in sustaining trade with China and other partners as Western sanctions disrupt traditional banking channels.
Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilyov and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov have joined A7's board, the government's press office said on Thursday.
The appointments highlight the increasing importance of A7, which was created in 2024 by defense sector-focused lender PSB, as Russia n companies seek alternative ways to settle cross-border transactions.
Traditional banks have struggled to process many Russia -linked payments because of Western sanctions, particularly for trade with China, Russia 's largest trading partner.
A7, itself targeted by multiple Western sanctions, estimates that alternative channels now account for up to 80% of payments in Russia 's foreign trade.
The U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on A7 on Oct. 1, saying it had built a global network of affiliated companies "to disguise payments linked to sanctioned sectors and persons as ordinary commercial activity."
A7 uses the A7A5 ruble-backed stablecoin for settlements. The token was launched in Kyrgyzstan in 2025 and is backed by ruble deposits held at PSB Bank.
PSB estimates turnover in the stablecoin has reached $140 billion.

title: Russian Business Investment Stalls in Third Quarter as Profits Fall, Uncertainty Persists
description: Russian businesses continued to scale back investment in the third quarter as falling profits, weak demand and economic uncertainty weighed on spending plans, a Central Bank survey of 11,500 companies showed.
content:
Russian businesses continued to scale back investment in the third quarter as falling profits, weak demand and economic uncertainty weighed on spending plans, a Central Bank survey of 11,500 companies showed.
The balance between companies reporting an increase in investment and those reporting a decline turned negative, according to the survey . It was also negative in the first quarter, when fixed capital investment plunged 14.3% year on year, its steepest fall since 2009 and during the pandemic in 2020.
The Economic Development Ministry forecasts investment will fall 5.4% this year, following a 9.9% decline in the first half.
A shortage of internal funds was cited as an obstacle to investment by 26.7% of respondents, followed by uncertainty about Russia’s economic situation at 25.8% and insufficient demand at 20.8%.
“There isn’t enough money or demand,” economist Dmitry Polevoy said .
Russian companies recorded combined profits of 13 trillion rubles ($154.7 billion) in the first seven months of the year, down 15.7% from a year earlier and the weakest result for the period since 2020. One in three companies was loss-making.
An increase in corporate profit tax that took effect in 2025 has added to the pressure on businesses’ finances. Companies’ own funds account for more than half of fixed capital investment, making them its largest source of financing, according to data from state statistics agency Rosstat.
Economic uncertainty, which businesses ranked as their biggest investment obstacle three months earlier, remains another major constraint.
Unpredictable tax increases, rising military spending, Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, e-commerce warehouses and data centers, asset seizures, criminal prosecutions of business owners and tighter regulation have clouded the outlook for new projects.
“This is normal, pragmatic behavior for a businessperson or investor: if you don’t know what tomorrow will bring, you would rather do nothing at all, rather than invest,” said Igor Nikolayev, chief researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Economics .
Vladimir Potanin, the main owner of metals producer Nornickel, has also warned that uncertainty over taxation makes investment planning difficult. Nornickel is among the companies facing a tax on windfall profits.
“If businesspeople don’t understand the rules governing how their income will be taken, it is extremely difficult for them to plan investment,” Potanin said .
Investment trends varied considerably across industries, the central bank said, with logistics and retail recording notable increases.
Some of that spending may reflect efforts to repair damage from Ukrainian drone attacks. Economic officials have said restoring “temporarily lost capacity” would affect investment activity.
The Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Economic Forecasting has noted investment in areas “linked to minimizing war damage.” In core industries, however, “the situation, by contrast, points to a continued pause in investment,” it said.
Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov has acknowledged that his ministry’s forecast for investment to return to growth in 2028 and regain its 2025 level in 2029 is “largely a target scenario.”
Without “additional decisions,” even those figures “will be difficult to achieve,” he said .
With fixed capital investment falling at such a pace, “the economy will not grow,” Nikolayev said.

title: Kazakhstan Arrests Russian Rapper Navai on Drug Smuggling Charges
description: A court in Kazakhstan has reportedly placed popular Russian hip-hop artist Navai in pre-trial detention after border authorities arrested him on suspicion of drug smuggling.
content:
A court in Kazakhstan has reportedly placed popular Russian hip-hop artist Navai in pre-trial detention after border authorities arrested him on suspicion of drug smuggling.
Navai Bakirov, 31, was detained on Tuesday at a border checkpoint while attempting to cross into Kazakhstan from neighboring Kyrgyzstan.
The Korday District Court ordered Bakirov to be placed in pre-trial detention for two months, Telegram news channel Baza reported on Thursday.
According to the report, Bakirov had allegedly admitted during police questioning to purchasing the drugs in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek, where he performed on Monday.
Baza, which is purported to have links to Russia’s security services, claimed Kazakh border guards uncovered 2.5 grams of marijuana in Bakirov’s vehicle after being alerted by a sniffer dog.
Bakirov’s arrest led to the cancellation of his concert in Astana on Wednesday. His show in Chisinau, Moldova, was rescheduled from this Friday to Dec. 8.
The Samara native rose to prominence across the post-Soviet space as part of the hit-making duo HammAli & Navai before launching a solo career.
Bakirov’s legal trouble in Central Asia comes nearly one month after he resolved a separate civil dispute in Moscow by compensating the city for damages caused when he crashed his Ferrari in central Moscow in May.

title: Starlink Functionality Restored Fully for Ukrainian Military, Source Says
description: Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality has been fully restored, a source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Thursday, a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.
content:
Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality has been fully restored, a source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Thursday, a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.
The source said the Defense Ministry would continue to seek clarification on the reasons for Wednesday's disruption of the military-grade version of SpaceX's internet service, which affected drone missions across the frontl ine.
“As of now, Starshield’s work in motion has resumed and continues, we record this in reports from units,” the Ukrinform news agency quoted its Defense Ministry source as saying.
Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that the functioning of Starlink’s military-grade service Starshield had been interrupted when terminals were moving at high speed, hampering Ukrainian drones for attack missions and air defense.
The reasons for the difficulties were not immediately clear but followed a souring of relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, after Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions on Russian diesel and called for Zelensky to be replaced.
Zelensky has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their U.S. counterparts that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday, Zelensky said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he dismissed the idea that the failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault.
“It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT.
Trump said on Tuesday that the U.S. was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. E SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, which operates Starlink, said the U.S. government controlled the system's speeds.
Separately, Zelensky said that, for the second night running, Ukraine had received no warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.

title: Kremlin Says Russia Restarts Diesel Exports After Deal With Trump
description: The Kremlin said on Thursday that Russian diesel had begun to reach global markets following an agreement with U.S.
content:
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Russian diesel had begun to reach global markets following an agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, while Moscow partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from Oct. 10 following the agreement.
"The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call.
LSEG data showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk.
According to the shipping data, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on Tuesday and was heading towards Morocco.
Under the terms announced by Trump last Friday, Russia agreed to immediately release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel onto global markets, followed by an additional 500,000 metric tons in November.
The initial 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) is less than a day's supply for the U.S. transportation sector alone, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued a license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The deal has sparked pushback from European and Ukrainian officials, who argued that unlocking Russian energy revenues directly fuels the Kremlin’s war effort.
Russia has rejected European criticism of the diesel deal as "cynical," given that Europe continues to buy some Russia n oil and liquefied natural gas.
Peskov's comments came a day after Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the diesel supply deal with the U.S. would boost Russia’s economy and include direct exports to the U.S. market.
“Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy,” Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum in Moscow, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
“In accordance with the agreements, supplies will go to world markets, as well as the U.S. directly,” he said .
He added that Russia aims to restore monthly diesel exports to 3.5 million metric tons by the end of 2026, bringing its share of the global market above 10%.

title: Moscow Court Places Prominent Economist Under House Arrest in Bribery Case
description: A Moscow judge has placed prominent establishment economist Sergei Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest on bribery charges, the RBC news outlet reported Thursday, citing law enforcement sources.
content:
A Moscow judge has placed prominent establishment economist Sergei Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest on bribery charges, the RBC news outlet reported Thursday, citing law enforcement sources.
Sinelnikov-Murylev, 66, is a senior researcher at the Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy and the former president of the Economic Development Ministry’s Russian Academy of Foreign Trade.
He received state awards and a presidential commendation in 2018 for contributing to Russia’s 2018-24 national development strategy. He also joined the government’s expert council in December 2022.
The Zamoskvoretsky District Court reportedly granted the investigation’s request to place Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest for two months.
The 66-year-old economist faces up to 15 years in prison if found guilty of receiving a large-scale bribe.
Specific details on the alleged bribe amount or the involved parties have not been disclosed . The Interfax news agency reported that the case material is available on the court’s website.
This is Sinelniov-Murylev’s second criminal prosecution in recent years. He was arrested in April 2023, and in March 2025 convicted of large-scale embezzlement and abuse of power, receiving a suspended prison sentence of five and a half years.
Sinelnikov-Murylev served as president, or rector, of the Russian Academy of Foreign Trade from 2007 to 2024, continuing there as chief researcher while also holding senior research roles at the Gaidar Institute.
According to RBC, Sinelnikov-Murylev in 2017 ranked third among Russia’s wealthiest university rectors with an annual income of 53.4 million rubles ($638,700 at the current exchange rate). He attributed the earnings primarily to research and teaching activities at the time.

title: FSB Arrests Swede in Pskov Region Over Border Crossing and Sabotage Allegations
description: Russia’s FSB security service said Thursday it has arrested a Swedish citizen in the northwestern Pskov region on allegations of illegally crossing the border to carry out sabotage attacks against military facilities.
content:
Russia’s FSB security service said Thursday it has arrested a Swedish citizen in the northwestern Pskov region on allegations of illegally crossing the border to carry out sabotage attacks against military facilities.
An FSB video published by the state-run news agency TASS showed the man identifying himself through an interpreter as 35-year-old Freddy Michael Stålkrantz Lindholm.
In a statement on its website, the FSB said it had detained Lindholm in the Sebezhsky district near the border with Latvia and Belarus. It did not indicate from which country he crossed into Russia.
The FSB claimed he crossed into Russian territory under the guise of enlisting in the Russian military, with the alleged intent of committing “sabotage and terrorist acts at military facilities.”
The FSB said Lindholm served as a contracted service member in Ukraine from February to June this year as a squad commander operating drones.
In the interrogation video, Lindholm said he had signed a military contract with the Aidar battalion, which Russia has banned as a terrorist organization.
He also said he signed the contract in the western Ukrainian city of Ternopil, where he underwent training to operate reconnaissance drones and later instructed other recruits.
The FSB reported that Lindholm was charged with illegally crossing the state border and added that he also faces charges of participating in a terrorist organization and mercenary activities.
The Swedish Foreign Ministry said it was aware of media reports about the detention, but was not currently involved in the case. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

title: Ukrainian Drones Spark Fire at Ryazan Refinery as Zelensky Vows to Resume Attacks
description: Ukrainian drone attacks set fire to a Rosneft oil refinery in the Ryazan region overnight, officials said Thursday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in response to Moscow’s continued strikes.
content:
Ukrainian drone attacks set fire to a Rosneft oil refinery in the Ryazan region overnight, officials said Thursday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in response to Moscow’s continued strikes.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the region had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
“The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene,” he said.
Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday that Ukraine had paused attacks on Russian refineries for three days to comply with U.S. President Donald Trump’s surprise announcement of an “energy ceasefire.”
He said Kyiv was now resuming the attacks because Moscow continued to hit the Ukrainian power grid and fuel depots over the same period.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told FT.
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, Zelensky said he could only agree if in return he was given more U.S.-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
The Kremlin said Thursday that Moscow did not perceive that Kyiv had ever complied with the ceasefire and said that the fact that it had struck another Russian refinery was "nothing new."
"The Ukrainian regime in Kyiv continues to strike these facilities, thereby, of course, coming into serious contradiction with the peace efforts of the United States and of the American negotiators who are indeed making very vigorous efforts to somehow initiate the peace process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"But so far, these vigorous attempts have been thwarted by the unwillingness of the Kyiv regime — and of Zelensky personally — to make peace," he said.
The Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery supplies fuel for Moscow and accounts for 5% of Russia’s total crude refining capacity.
The plant previously suspended operations following drone attacks in May, July and September.
On Wednesday, 24 hours before the confirmed attack, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak claimed Ukrainian forces had hit refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions. At the time, Ukrainian officials dismissed Novak’s claims as false.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. Ukraine’s air force said 580 Russian drones attacked the country overnight, of which 536 were shot down.
Three people were killed and six wounded in an attack on critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes in central Ukraine’s Kirovohrad region, said the local governor.

title: Government Says It Helped Yandex Migrate Systems After Data Center Attacks
description: Russia’s Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said Wednesday that his office helped tech giant Yandex migrate core systems to external backup servers following last week’s Ukrainian drone attacks. “The ministry assisted Yandex in providing additional sites for relocating key systems,” Shadayev told the business news outlet RBC.
content:
Russia’s Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said Wednesday that his office helped tech giant Yandex migrate core systems to external backup servers following last week’s Ukrainian drone attacks.
“The ministry assisted Yandex in providing additional sites for relocating key systems,” Shadayev told the business news outlet RBC.
Yandex maintained that it has “for many years” developed distributed infrastructure and backup capacities at independent sites.
Ukrainian drone attacks, which Shadayev referred to as “ unprecedented ,” damaged three of Yandex’s six data centers last week. The outages disrupted search, navigation, food delivery and banking services while also affecting corporate clients on Yandex Cloud, including retail giants like Lenta and Magnit.
Key Yandex services like Pay and Cloud did not appear to be fully restored as of Wednesday evening.
Meanwhile, a top executive of state telecom operator Rostelecom stepped up calls for the construction of geographically isolated, decentralized backup data centers to avoid vulnerabilities exposed by the attacks on Yandex.
“Everyone understands today that we need a so-called ‘doomsday’ site, a backup facility where you can always restore your services if something happens,” said senior vice president Valery Yermakov.
President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday convened a cybersecurity meeting with Shadayev, state security officials and top executives, including Sberbank CEO Herman Gref, whose bank’s own data center was hit by drones overnight Wednesday.
Peskov claimed the meeting was not in response to recent “situational” attacks, though Putin urged officials to bolster national digital defenses against growing security threats.

title: Nord Stream May Have Been Lawful Target, Argue Lawyers for Ukrainian Accused of Bombing
description: Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
content:
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia 's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure " may have been a lawful target .
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia 's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia 's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a " Russia n weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russia n natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia 's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia 's invasion.
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russia n gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

title: Fire Spreads at Rostov Oil Terminal After Drone Attack
description: Another storage tank exploded at an oil terminal in Russia’s southern city of Rostov-on-Don late Tuesday, as a fire sparked by a drone attack continued to burn for a fourth day, monitoring channels reported.
content:
Another storage tank exploded at an oil terminal in Russia’s southern city of Rostov-on-Don late Tuesday, as a fire sparked by a drone attack continued to burn for a fourth day, monitoring channels reported.
The blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery’s terminal has spread to eight of its 12 storage tanks, the independent news outlet Astra reported . The Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ said another tank exploded late Tuesday.
Footage from the site showed tanks engulfed in flames beneath columns of black smoke. The local Telegram channel Rostov Glavny reported a bright flash on the city’s left bank at 11:50 p.m. Tuesday.
Drones struck the terminal, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov’s Zheleznodorozhny district overnight on Oct. 10. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at the site.
Authorities had not announced that the blaze had been extinguished as of Wednesday morning.
The terminal’s storage tanks have a combined capacity of 60,000 cubic meters. The facility can handle 3.5 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, loading sea and river tankers for export. It has also been used to supply fuel to the Russian military.
Separately, Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said the region came under a large-scale drone attack overnight Wednesday. More than 160 drones were shot down over the city of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and eight districts, he said, without providing information on casualties or damage on the ground.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had ordered his military to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries from Oct. 11 at U.S. President Donald Trump’s request as part of an “energy ceasefire.”
Moscow has yet to confirm that it is observing the arrangement. The strike that sparked the terminal fire preceded the announced halt.

title: Russia Announces Visas for Citizens of Montenegro in Reciprocal Move
description: Russia will introduce visa requirements for citizens of Montenegro in retaliation to Podgorica’s decision to end its bilateral visa-free travel agreement with Moscow as it seeks to join the EU in 2028. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova confirmed that Montenegro’s foreign ministry notified Moscow of its intent to cancel the 2008 mutual travel agreement on Sept. 28. “In practice, this means that starting Nov. 1, our citizens will only be able to enter and remain in Montenegro with visas.
content:
Russia will introduce visa requirements for citizens of Montenegro in retaliation to Podgorica’s decision to end its bilateral visa-free travel agreement with Moscow as it seeks to join the EU in 2028.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova confirmed that Montenegro’s foreign ministry notified Moscow of its intent to cancel the 2008 mutual travel agreement on Sept. 28.
“In practice, this means that starting Nov. 1, our citizens will only be able to enter and remain in Montenegro with visas. Accordingly, citizens of Montenegro will also have to obtain visas for trips to Russia,” Zakharova said.
Montenegro announced in July that it would end visa-free access for citizens of Russia, Belarus, China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey to align with EU standards.
Zakharova argued the decision would curb Russian tourism, harm local businesses and degrade Montenegro’s investment climate.
Montenegro has for years remained one of the few European countries to offer visa-free entry to Russians for up to 30 days and absorbed a large wave of anti-war Russian emigres after the invasion of Ukraine.
Local media reported earlier this year that two-thirds of registered Russian residents had left Montenegro in anticipation of the new visa rules.
“It’s pointless for Montenegro to expect Brussels to compensate them for their inevitable losses,” Zakharova said.
She warned that EU accession would require prospective members among the Balkan nations to adopt a “confrontational anti-Russian course” that would go against their national interests.
The subject of tightening border controls recently drew the attention of the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, who was detained and deported from Montenegro on claims that he was seeking to film a documentary portraying EU integration as an externally imposed process.
Russian-Montenegrin relations have been strained since 2016, when Podgorica accused Russia of plotting a failed coup with Serbian ultranationalists. The Kremlin denied that claim.
Ties worsened further after Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and aligned with EU sanctions over Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Montenegro has also banned Russian state media and expelled Russian diplomats for espionage, prompting Moscow to add the country to its list of “unfriendly” states.

title: Putin Convenes Top Russian Officials to Discuss Cybersecurity
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin will discuss cybersecurity with top officials on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, describing it as an increasingly pressing issue but denying the meeting was prompted by a spate of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian data centers.
content:
Russia n President Vladimir Putin will discuss cybersecurity with top officials on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, describing it as an increasingly pressing issue but denying the meeting was prompted by a spate of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia n data centers.
"Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits and advantages, boosting efficiency. But at the same time, of course, attempts by various states to weaponize these new technologies... pose threats to entire sectors of any country's economy," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Naturally, we are no exception, and we must be prepared for these challenges. That is why the president is holding this meeting today."
Peskov said the meeting was not connected with Ukrainian drone strikes in the past week on four Russia n data centers — three belonging to tech group Yandex and one to Sberbank.
"No, this is a much more systemic meeting. It is not connected to those specific, isolated attacks," he said.
The participants will include government ministers, top security officials, the head of Sberbank and Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina, Peskov added.
