title: Russian Supreme Court Bans Ingush Sufi Muslim Order as ‘Extremist’
description: Russia’s Supreme Court on Wednesday outlawed the Batal Hajji brotherhood, a closed Sufi Muslim order originating from the North Caucasus republic of Ingushetia.  The court granted a request from state prosecutors to designate the order as an “extremist” organization for “providing material support for bandit insurgents of the North Caucasus.”  The Prosecutor General’s Office said Batal Hajji members were linked to numerous attacks on Russian police and military in the North Caucasus and orchestrated the deadly 2009 Nevsky Express train bombing claimed by Chechen rebel leader Doku Umarov.   The prosecutor also said that Batal Hajji affiliates aided the deadly March 2024 attack on the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow and the assassination of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov the same year by selling weapons and ammunition to the perpetrators.
content:
Russia’s Supreme Court on Wednesday outlawed the Batal Hajji brotherhood , a closed Sufi Muslim order originating from the North Caucasus republic of Ingushetia.
The court granted a request from state prosecutors to designate the order as an “extremist” organization for “providing material support for bandit insurgents of the North Caucasus.”
The Prosecutor General’s Office said Batal Hajji members were linked to numerous attacks on Russian police and military in the North Caucasus and orchestrated the deadly 2009 Nevsky Express train bombing claimed by Chechen rebel leader Doku Umarov.
The prosecutor also said that Batal Hajji affiliates aided the deadly March 2024 attack on the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow and the assassination of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov the same year by selling weapons and ammunition to the perpetrators.
“More than 100 members of the order have been convicted of the illicit trafficking of means for committing acts of terror. Leaders and members of the community organized illegal channels to supply foreign-made firearms from abroad,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement published Wednesday.
Russian authorities designated the brotherhood’s so-called “military wing” a “terrorist” organization in 2023.
The Batal Hajji brotherhood was founded in the 19th century by Ingush Sheikh Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, a pupil of the Chechen Muslim mystic Kunta-Hajji (Kunta Kishiev).
Membership in the closed order, which numbers around 20,000 members, is passed down strictly by birthright.
The order’s members held a handful of key government roles and a near monopoly on Ingushetia’s construction industry in the 1990s and early 2000s before a clash with the republic’s new Kremlin-appointed leadership led to their fall from power.
Around 100 of its members allegedly joined the Russian military in 2022 as part of the Batal Hajji Rapid Response Unit, a part of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov's Akhmat military unit within the Russian army, according to the exiled news website Meduza.

title: Latvia Formally Blacklists Russian Journalist Leonid Ragozin
description: Latvian authorities have formally declared Riga-based Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, local media reported, and Ragozin himself confirmed on Wednesday.
content:
Latvian authorities have formally declared Riga-based Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, local media reported, and Ragozin himself confirmed on Wednesday.
Latvian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Līga Jermacāne told the outlet Delfi that an unidentified Russian national was added to the persona non grata list last Wednesday. Foreign Ministry adviser Toms Sadovskis said the basis for the decision will be withheld for “national security” reasons.
On Wednesday, Ragozin confirmed that he was notified of his expulsion the day before.
Ragozin claimed he was blacklisted in retaliation for his critical reporting and commentary on Western policy and far-right political networks.
He argued that Latvia intentionally declared him persona non grata to prevent him from appealing his expulsion in Latvian courts.
“For me it is a huge personal tragedy. I am being evicted from my only beloved home, deprived of my circle of friendship and support,” Ragozin posted on X.
In a Meduza interview published Tuesday, Ragozin said he was outside Latvia and expressed concerns that returning to Russia could put him at risk of imprisonment.
Ragozin is a former producer for the BBC Russian Service and editor at Russian Newsweek. His freelance commentary has appeared in recent editions of Al Jazeera, Jacobin and The American Conservative.
Ragozin drew public ire for comments he made on a far-left podcast where he argued that the Kremlin felt compelled to use “brute force” in response to Western encroachment on its sphere of influence.
In Wednesday’s X post, Ragozin said, “I condemn the Russian aggression and support Ukraine’s sovereignty.”
“But I’ll continue to criticize Western countries for mishandling this conflict,” he wrote.
In an August column for The American Conservative, Ragozin argued that ordinary Russians perceive greater threats from Western nations than from their own government.
Latvia has declared more than 150 Russian cultural figures, state journalists and commentators personae non grata since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Russia Fumes as Top Gymnasts Blocked From World Championships in Netherlands
description: Russia has accused Dutch authorities of denying visas to three of Russia’s leading female gymnasts for the World Championships in Rotterdam, which kick off this weekend, and jeopardizing their qualification path for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
content:
Russia has accused Dutch authorities of denying visas to three of Russia’s leading female gymnasts for the World Championships in Rotterdam, which kick off this weekend, and jeopardizing their qualification path for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova, Tokyo 2020 team Olympic champion Viktoria Listunova and 2026 European silver medalist Anna Kalmykova have all reportedly been refused visas, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said Tuesday, citing the Dutch Embassy in Moscow.
The refusal notices apparently expressed diplomatic concerns, stating that “one or several Schengen member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
“We view the actions of the Dutch authorities as a deliberate elimination of the strongest gymnasts from competition for world medals and Olympic quotas,” the Russian Gymnastics Federation said.
The Dutch foreign and sports ministries declined to comment on individual visa applications, but clarified to local media that the refusals were unrelated to athletic performance.
The three denied athletes have faced scrutiny from Ukrainian sports authorities over their ties to the Russian military and public displays supporting the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Melnikova represents the military-affiliated CSKA sports club and has previously posted social media photographs featuring the pro-war “Z” symbol.
Listunova took part in a March 2022 pro-war rally with President Vladimir Putin and was previously denied neutral status by World Gymnastics over pro-military social media posts.
Kalmykova holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia’s Ambassador to the Netherlands Vladimir Tarabrin said he personally visited the Dutch Foreign Ministry to demand visas, but was presented with “utterly unconvincing arguments that defy any reasonable criticism.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov said the Russian Olympic Committee will lobby to strip the Rotterdam championship of its official Olympic qualifying status.
The Oct. 17-25 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam serve as the opening team qualifier for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Out of 61 members of the Russian delegation, 47 were granted Dutch visas, including five male and three female gymnasts.
World Gymnastics and European Gymnastics lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts after the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its ban on the countries’ Olympic committees in July.

title: Russia Arrests Japanese Journalist on Suspicion of Spying
description: Russia said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage and accused Tokyo of using media correspondents to gather intelligence, marking a new low in bilateral relations that have deteriorated sharply in recent months.
content:
Russia said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage and accused Tokyo of using media correspondents to gather intelligence, marking a new low in bilateral relations that have deteriorated sharply in recent months.
Russia's Foreign Ministry identified the journalist as Yuki Imai and the FSB security agency said he worked for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, which is a regional newspaper for Japan's northern island.
He was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region the day before he planned to leave the country, the FSB said without specifying the date. It accused him of collecting and storing information on Russia's defense capabilities for intelligence purposes that it said could be used against Russian security.
The Hokkaido Shimbun did not confirm the journalist's identity, saying only that it was still confirming details and that the reporter's safety was its top priority.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Tokyo had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the national.
Kihara stopped short of condemning Moscow, saying only that Tokyo would take appropriate action.

A senior official of the Japanese Foreign Ministry later summoned the Russian ambassador to Japan and lodged a protest for detaining the Japanese national and unilaterally issuing statements regarding the matter without providing an explanation to Tokyo, the ministry said in a statement.
The director-general of the Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Bureau, Kimitake Nakamura, also asked the ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev, to set up an opportunity swiftly to meet the detained journalist, the ministry said.
In a Russian state TV video report, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying.
The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months.
It is the most high-profile detainment of a foreign journalist since the 2023 detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich.
Gershkovich, who says his arrest was a carefully planned FSB sting, was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
The case adds to long-running tensions between Russia and Japan, which have yet to sign a formal World War II peace treaty due to a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories.
Those tensions heightened when Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine, with Russia regarding Japan as an "unfriendly" country. But business ties remain with Japan a purchaser of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Then in August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands, causing an uproar in Japan. On Tuesday, a delegation from a Chinese province visited the same island, in what appeared to signal closer coordination between Moscow and Beijing in their criticism of Tokyo.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Tuesday that Japan had refused to consider Moscow's concerns about what she called Tokyo's "remilitarization." She criticized Japan's alleged use of accredited journalists in Russia to gather information that could undermine Russian security.
"We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said.
Asked whether improving relations between Russia and the U.S. and Japan's purchases of LNG from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Kihara said: "It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia.
"From Japan's perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighboring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues."

title: Ukraine Accuses SpaceX of Crippling Drone Missions as Ties With U.S. Worsen
description: Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
content:
Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russia n missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since U.S. President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russia n diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelensky.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russia n refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The U.S. president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russia n bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you ​playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man." SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its onetime ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russia n oil refineries.
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russia n missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia 's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russia n attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
" Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russia n refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russia n missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia , and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia 's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia .
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia 's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

title: Russia’s Krasnodar Region Raises Alert as Oil Washes Ashore on Black Sea Coast
description: Authorities in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region have raised the alert level in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk over an oil spill after fuel oil washed ashore and satellite images showed pollution spreading along the Black Sea coast.
content:
Authorities in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region have raised the alert level in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk over an oil spill after fuel oil washed ashore and satellite images showed pollution spreading along the Black Sea coast.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev issued an order warning of a potential emergency in the two cities. He attributed the spill to “accidents” involving vessels targeted by Ukrainian naval drones on Oct. 6.
The order calls for increased environmental monitoring and surveillance of potential industrial hazards. It also recommends that the regional branch of Russia’s Marine Rescue Service take measures to prevent oil from reaching the shoreline.
Fuel oil has already been found along roughly 500 meters of coastline near Novorossiysk, the city’s chief rescue official, Alexei Oderov, said .
Local residents have also reported pollution on the shore. Olga Kotlyar, head of the Abrau-Dyurso rural district, appealed for volunteers to help municipal workers clean up a beach.
Birds with reported chemical burns from petroleum products have been found in Gelendzhik and the nearby resort village of Arkhipo-Osipovka.
The satellite monitoring project Transparent World earlier reported that an image taken overnight on Oct. 10 showed a large oil slick between Arkhipo-Osipovka and Novorossiysk.
Over the following two days, the slick broke into smaller patches and spread as far as Anapa, the project said. It also identified oil traces near Novorossiysk Bay and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s offshore loading facilities.
Transparent World linked the pollution to the Oct. 6 naval drone attack on the tanker Aframax Rio off Sochi. The vessel can carry up to 100,000 metric tons of oil, though its cargo at the time of the attack has not been independently confirmed.
The Mash Telegram channel, citing unnamed sources, reported that the tanker was fully loaded.
The attack triggered a major fire that blanketed Sochi in black smoke. The blaze was extinguished the following day.
Authorities closed beaches in Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius after the attack, but reopened them on Oct. 8, saying tests had found no oil contamination in local waters.
Russia’s consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said seawater samples from all districts of Sochi met sanitary standards.

title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Sberbank Data Center After Yandex Attacks
description: Ukrainian drones targeted a major data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in the Saratov region overnight, First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin said Wednesday, as attacks on Moscow disrupted more than 500 flights.
content:
Ukrainian drones targeted a major data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in the Saratov region overnight, First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin said Wednesday, as attacks on Moscow disrupted more than 500 flights.
Vedyakhin said all banking systems and online services continued to operate normally and no employees were injured in the attack in the Volga River city of Balakovo, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
Users across Russia nevertheless reported disruptions to Sberbank and its GigaChat artificial intelligence service, as well as several other major online platforms, according to outage tracker Detector404. The reports did not establish a link between the disruptions and the drone attacks.
NASA’s satellite fire-monitoring system showed multiple fires in Balakovo.
Saratov region Governor Roman Busargin said “all infrastructure facilities” were operating normally, without identifying Sberbank’s data center as a target. He said one woman was killed and several homes were damaged in the drone strikes.
The attack on Sberbank follows three consecutive Ukrainian drone strikes that disabled half of tech giant Yandex’s data centers. Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites.
“You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?” Ukraine’s Fire Point arms company said in a social media post Wednesday morning.
Sberbank began construction of the 55,000-square-meter (592,000-square-foot) facility in 2021, promoting the 122.2 billion ruble ($1.4 billion) project as one of Europe’s largest data centers, with completion expected in 2030.
Sberbank and its main domestic rival, Yandex, are leading Russian developers of artificial intelligence, with their respective GigaChat and YandexGPT models. State media reported in 2024 that Sberbank’s Balakovo center would host Russia’s biggest supercomputer, which was scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems destroyed 902 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions and annexed Crimea between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “most” of the 493 Ukrainian drones flying toward the region were neutralized, 180 of them on direct approach to the capital.
The attacks on Moscow prompted civil aviation authority Rosaviatsia to restrict arrivals and departures at all four Moscow airports after 10 p.m. Tuesday, in the second prolonged shutdown of Moscow’s airports in less than a week.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities and a data center with ground-launched missiles and long-range strike drones overnight.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak later accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions Wednesday, saying Kyiv was showing no signs of moving toward an energy ceasefire announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn denied those statements, telling reporters that Ukraine struck a data center and another unnamed target but not refineries.

title: Lukashenko Denies Belarus Breached Latvian Border as Experts Claim Intelligence Operation
description: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko on Tuesday claimed Latvia staged a security breach on its border last week after a previously unknown group took responsibility for the raid.
content:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko on Tuesday claimed Latvia staged a security breach on its border last week after a previously unknown group took responsibility for the raid.
Experts told Latvian media that the group, Chyornye Rusy (Black Rus), could be a front for Belarusian and Russian intelligence services.
Last Tuesday, Latvian authorities reported that masked and armed individuals attempted to force a group of 20 irregular migrants to push through the border between Belarus and Latvia into Latvian territory. The intruders damaged electrical equipment and stole surveillance cameras before retreating back into Belarusian territory.
Lukashenko dismissed the claims as a fabrication designed for Latvia to secure EU funding.
“We have absolutely nothing to do with this,” he said during a military readiness meeting, according to Belarusian state news agency Belta.
“Operations involving entry into the territory of a neighboring state are impossible without the agreement of the president. Such things were not coordinated with me, which means they were not conducted,” he added.
On Wednesday, Black Rus released a video claiming responsibility for the cross-border raid in which one of its members promised further incursions into NATO territory.
Latvia’s state security service launched proceedings into the creation of a criminal organization aimed at committing grave acts against peace and national security, according to Latvia’s LSM public service media organization.
Jānis Sārts, director of the Riga-based NATO Strategic Communications Center of Excellence, described the group’s video release as an “information operation directly linked to both the Belarusian and Russian authorities.”
“These types of groups cannot exist in Belarus and Russia independently,” Sārts told LSM.
Exiled Belarusian military journalist Dmitry Khalko described Black Rus as a “proxy” akin to the masked Russian soldiers who seized control of Ukraine’s Crimea in 2014.
“If necessary, the group can be blamed for certain events, border sabotage and so on,” Khalko told LSM. “Now they have a fig leaf to cover themselves with and say it’s not us, we don’t know anything.”

title: Forced Underground, Russia’s Feminists Find New Ways to Keep Working
description: Oksana, a feminist campaigner from the Chelyabinsk region in the Ural Mountains, expected life for Russian women “to get worse and worse” after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.  Since then, Chelyabinsk’s once-vibrant feminist community has slowly been driven underground, retreating from street activism to a feminist reading club.
content:
Oksana, a feminist campaigner from the Chelyabinsk region in the Ural Mountains, expected life for Russian women “to get worse and worse” after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.
Since then, Chelyabinsk’s once-vibrant feminist community has slowly been driven underground, retreating from street activism to a feminist reading club. Meanwhile, local authorities have pushed for new restrictions on reproductive rights.
Yet what Oksana has seen among the women around her has given her reason to hope.
“There are fewer men in Russia: some were killed, some are physically or psychologically disabled. But instead of falling at the feet of their ‘defenders,’ our women are finding mutual solidarity and moving toward greater independence,” Oksana told The Moscow Times.
“I see women of different ages…promoting an idea that having a man in the house just for the sake of it is no longer needed,” she said, asking to use a pseudonym for safety reasons. “If this isn't feminist ideology, then what is?”
As the Kremlin has pushed for “traditional values” and moved to choke off avenues for activism, the country’s feminist activists have learned to adapt.
Activists who spoke to The Moscow Times described how their work has shifted toward practical assistance for vulnerable women while seeking new allies among men and women who have never considered themselves feminists.
“Russian women are not ready to give up their independence and principles,” said Oksana.
“[These attitudes] extend beyond the family to a more global level. I think that at some point, it will spill over into politics as well. I hope so,” she said.
The Kremlin’s promotion of conservative Christian values and all-reaching crackdown on dissent since the invasion of Ukraine have turned Russia’s many women’s rights advocates into a prime target.
While some women’s rights groups shut down due to a lack of funding or pressure from authorities, activists continue to work inside the country. Though their work is carried out away from public view, they say it is more hands-on than ever.
“In addition to standing up to right-leaning conservative politics, the feminist community in Russia has taken on a significant part of the social function of the state,” said Marta, an activist who also asked to use a pseudonym for her safety.
Marta and her fellow activists now do “less online activism and more offline activity” — a change she attributes to wartime censorship laws and “a much greater demand for practical support.”
“People’s needs aren’t about information or knowledge, but rather money, medication and logistics, such as driving a woman to another region to help her access an abortion,” Marta said.
In addition to helping women access safe abortions, activists also assist survivors of domestic and reproductive violence as well as refugees, migrants and homeless women, she said.
Though Russia still has some of the world’s most liberal abortion laws at the national level, authorities have been gradually limiting women’s right to safe abortion through government decrees, ministry orders and regional legislation, according to a recent study by the Feminist Anti-War Resistance group.
Laws against “coercion” into abortion, a liability for attempting to induce a woman to end a pregnancy by using anything from verbal persuasion to material dependency, have been introduced in at least 32 Russian regions since 2023.
Abortions in private clinics are banned in at least 19 regions, while the procedure is only available in 40% of private medical facilities in 25 other regions, according to statistics published last week by the Russian Orthodox Church.
For Arina, an activist from a Siberian region, the prospect of further restrictions has affected her decisions about her own life.
“I made a decision not to interact with the male sex at all, because I would have no choice if something happened,” she said, referring to an unplanned pregnancy. “Bringing a new life into a state with such an economic situation and people in power is also somewhat irresponsible.”
The Moscow Patriarchate’s campaign to inch Russia closer toward a nationwide abortion ban has found support among conservative business figures and lawmakers.
Natalia Moskvitina, the longtime head of the pro-life movement Women for Life, became the latest addition to the list of high-profile conservative lobbyists when she was elected to represent the northern Vologda region in the State Duma in September.
“This is a real threat to women's safety and freedom,” said Arina, who asked to use a pseudonym.
“Many men already view women as objects and prey rather than as individuals. Now, a woman who champions the narrative that a woman’s body does not belong to her…is in the State Duma,” she said.
Moskvitina won her seat in a vote marred by widespread falsification and amid a viral campaign by the Alliance of Women's Initiatives of Russia that called on United Russia to withdraw her candidacy.
Activists warn that Moskvitina’s arrival in the Duma could ramp up efforts to introduce a federal law against “coercion” into abortion, which they fear would criminalize publishing information about reproductive choices.
“If she is allowed to realize her ambitions [in Duma], we will not only see a very serious attack on what is left of women’s reproductive rights, but it will also be a very strong blow to feminist activists,” said Marta, who took part in the campaign against Moskvitina’s candidacy.
“She will try in every possible way to hinder our activities…She considers us her enemies, so we are forced to do the same,” she added.
Activists interviewed by The Moscow Times said that building new alliances has become an important part of their efforts to resist the government’s encroachment on women’s rights.
“Previously, we worked primarily with women and queer people. Now, we have made a tactical decision to share feminist knowledge with men as well,” said feminist activist and rights defender Dasha Yakovleva. “There are many allies among them who need it.”
Building a diverse community of allies goes hand-in-hand with protecting women and queer people in Russia, Yakovleva said.
Another activist, who requested anonymity, said she and her colleagues were also “engaging with women who hadn't encountered feminism previously, or who would describe themselves as ‘I'm not a feminist, but’.”
“We are slowly but surely guiding them toward adopting a feminist perspective,” the activist said.
While Russia’s political opposition remains divided and riven with internecine conflict, feminist activists continue to work directly with communities across the country, delivering practical help alongside their advocacy.
For activists like Yakovleva, feminism offers a way to connect those immediate needs with bigger-picture questions about the problems facing Russian society.
“Feminism makes it possible to incorporate and combine a decolonial agenda, a critique of capitalism and [existing] social and political roles to address structural problems in a more systemic way,” activist Yakovleva said.
“For me, feminism is a very good response to a time of multiple crises — including in a global context because Russia’s export of traditionalism extends far beyond its borders.”

title: Russian Court Hands Exiled YouTuber Michael Nacke Combined 14-Year Sentence
description: A Moscow court has sentenced exiled journalist and YouTuber Michael Nacke to five years in prison in absentia on charges of calling for actions against Russia’s national security, bringing his combined sentence to 14 years.
content:
A Moscow court has sentenced exiled journalist and YouTuber Michael Nacke to five years in prison in absentia on charges of calling for actions against Russia’s national security, bringing his combined sentence to 14 years.
Nacke, 32, is a prominent critic of the Kremlin whose Russian-language YouTube channel covers Russia’s war against Ukraine. He was previously sentenced in absentia to 11 years in prison in 2023 for spreading what authorities called “false information” about the Russian military.
The latest conviction stems from a video Nacke published in 2024 that investigators said contained calls for activities “directed against state security,” the Moscow Prosecutor’s Office said .
Moscow’s Basmanny District Court said the video was published on May 7, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported . That day, Nacke uploaded a video titled “Now Putin Can Be Eliminated. The Day Putin Ceased to Be President.”
The court partially combined the new sentence with his earlier prison term, ordering him to serve a total of 14 years in a general-security penal colony. It also barred him from administering websites for five years.
Nacke worked at the Ekho Moskvy radio station from 2015 to 2020, hosting several programs on politics and public affairs. He moved to Georgia in June 2021 and later relocated to Lithuania.
Russian authorities designated him a “foreign agent” in 2022 and have placed him on an international wanted list.
His YouTube channel ranked second in journalist Dmitry Kolezev’s ranking of the largest Russian-language channels covering politics and public affairs in September 2026, drawing more than 80.4 million views. Only Mikhail Khodorkovsky’s channel received more views that month.
Nacke’s channel has consistently placed among the ranking’s top three in recent months.

title: Bulgaria Summons Russian Ambassador After Drone Attack Sinks Ship, Leaving 11 Missing
description: Eleven sailors were missing at sea on Tuesday from a ship sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria, possibly the second deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area in a week, prompting Bulgaria to summon Russia's ambassador.
content:
Eleven sailors were missing at sea on Tuesday from a ship sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria, possibly the second deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area in a week, prompting Bulgaria to summon Russia's ambassador.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation."
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incidents.
"This is absolutely unacceptable — another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
The attacks were also condemned by Ukraine and the EU.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. "Those responsible should be held accountable."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X on Tuesday that the strike "once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives."
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage," he said.
Speaking with von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte by telephone on Tuesday, Radev urged their support to bolster his country's maritime and airspace surveillance, the Bulgarian government said in a statement.
NATO will continue to adjust its military presence on its eastern flank "as needed," Rutte said.
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets. President Iliana Iotova identified the vessel as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and said a search and rescue operation was ongoing.
Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — were rescued and none seriously injured.
A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued.
After meeting Radev in Sofia, Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova said she had no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, the Bulgarian government said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.

title: Oil-Covered Birds Found Along Russia’s Black Sea Coast After Tanker Fire
description: Seabirds covered in oil have been found along Russia’s Black Sea coast following a fire aboard a tanker linked to the country’s so-called shadow fleet, a wildlife rehabilitation center said Monday.
content:
Seabirds covered in oil have been found along Russia’s Black Sea coast following a fire aboard a tanker linked to the country’s so-called shadow fleet, a wildlife rehabilitation center said Monday.
The center in the coastal resort of Anapa said it had begun receiving oil-coated birds from coastal towns and appealed for additional volunteers to help treat and feed them.
The reports came after the Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio caught fire in an attack off the coast of Sochi on Oct. 6. The 247-meter (810-foot) tanker has been linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
The blaze was extinguished on Oct. 7 and the vessel was then towed to Novorossiysk, about 200 kilometers (124 miles) northwest of Sochi. Workers started pumping oil out of the damaged tanker Monday, according to local reports .
Sochi authorities denied reports of oil-covered birds, saying beach inspections had found no traces of petroleum products.
Satellite images, however, showed an expanding oil slick in the days after the fire. A radar image from Saturday showed the slick stretching northwest toward Novorossiysk.
Independent environmentalist Zhora Kavanosyan said Novorossiysk’s chief rescuer Alexei Oderov had confirmed that petroleum products had washed ashore but that he described the scale of the contamination as “nothing catastrophic.”
Meanwhile, Russian transportation and maritime rescue authorities said Tuesday that inspections along the Krasnodar region’s Black Sea coast had found no oil spills.
The latest reports come nearly two years after a major oil spill in December 2024, when two Russian tankers released thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil into the Black Sea after being damaged in a storm in the Kerch Strait. The spill polluted beaches around Anapa and prompted authorities to declare a federal emergency.

title: Plague Research Isn't the Problem. But Russia Still Has Questions to Answer.
description: Opinion | The death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, at an anti-plague institute in Siberia continues to raise questions about what happened and what Moscow is being upfront about.
content:
The death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, at an anti-plague institute in Siberia continues to raise questions about what happened and what Moscow is being upfront about. Russian authorities have announced that the monitoring of her contacts is complete and no dangerous pathogens were detected. They also stated that testing of Shipilova’s clinical samples found no microorganisms associated with her work.
Still, the World Health Organization has requested more information about which tests were performed, the circumstances of her illness and the suspected cause of death. Nonetheless, the WHO's preliminary assessment is that the health risk is low for Russia overall and very low for the European region as a whole. Plague is treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed promptly and well-established infection control measures can limit its spread.
Continuing public concern, however, reflects distrust of Russia’s statements. Plague and other diseases were weaponized by the U.S.S.R. and the United States assesses that Russia still maintains an offensive biological weapons program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.
By itself, the existence of the laboratory is not suspicious, as there are good reasons to study plague that have nothing to do with weapons. The Irkutsk research institute was established in 1934 to address the natural spread of the disease, which is found in marmots and ground squirrels in Siberia, just as it is also found in prairie dogs in the western U.S.
It is the intent behind research into potentially fatal bacteria and viruses that matters and is central to assessing compliance with the Biological Weapons Convention. This is why a commitment to transparency is important, well beyond the details of a potential laboratory accident.
Without research on dangerous pathogens, we would lack many of the diagnostic tests, vaccines and treatments that we have available to protect us from them. Understanding how pathogens cause disease and finding better ways to prevent and treat infections can lead to lifesaving interventions.
But this work inherently carries risks that institutions must manage actively. Incidents like the one in Irkutsk often prompt calls for stronger international biosafety norms. The WHO and other organizations already provide guidance about assessing biological risks and carrying out laboratory work safely. The challenge is turning that guidance into sustained institutional practice: safeguards appropriate for the work, competent and supported personnel, accessible medical care and systems that identify problems and ensure they are corrected. Whatever their country, laboratories should be able to demonstrate these commitments.
What does a commitment to transparency look like? A laboratory should have a public record that explains the kind of work it does, why that work is important for the public to support and how it protects its workers and the surrounding community.
The Irkutsk Institute does describe its public health mission, including surveillance, diagnostic development and epidemic response. But descriptions of an institution’s mission can’t substitute for explanations when something goes wrong. While it is expected that some details like private medical information would not be disclosed, a commitment to transparency would include explaining the evidence that supports its conclusion that Shipilova’s death was unrelated to her work, what pathogens were tested for, what the results showed and what remains unknown.
Research institutions should also demonstrate their commitment to safety. It is often assumed that the presence of a high-containment laboratory raises the risk to the surrounding area. But these facilities can have engineered controls, specialized air-handling systems, waste decontamination systems and redundant safeguards that substantially reduce risks to the laboratory workers, as well as the broader community.
Safety goes beyond the engineering systems of the lab. Safety begins with assessing the hazards of the specific work being performed and establishing safeguards appropriate to those hazards. Safety is also about timely maintenance of equipment and the availability of adequate personal protective equipment like respirators. The people who are working with dangerous pathogens need to have the right training to be able to perform their work safely and demonstrate competence in the procedures they are carrying out. There also needs to be adequate oversight to ensure that the work is valuable and done safely.
Finally, a laboratory needs to demonstrate its support for the people who work in it. Accidents happen. Tubes break, animals bite and needlestick injuries still occur. Multiple and redundant safeguards should be in place to reduce the likelihood that any accident leads to infection or puts others at risk.
One of the most important safeguards is a culture in which laboratory workers can report problems and get help. Workers who become ill should have access to medical advice even if they do not recall any accident that could have led to an infection and clinicians should receive relevant information about their work. Workers should know that reporting is expected and that seeking help will not invite automatic blame. No one should fear their institution more than they fear disease.
This kind of culture takes care and effort to build. In the U.S., institutions working with regulated pathogens called “select agents” must immediately report occupational exposures, as well as releases beyond primary containment, to federal authorities. For laboratories themselves, reporting incidents and near misses can also reveal problems before someone is harmed.
The public needs to understand what such transparent reporting means. A record of “zero incidents” is not, by itself, evidence of a safe and well-run laboratory that has appropriate oversight. It could reflect work performed safely, or it could be an indication that there are problems that no one feels able to report.
Institutional leaders must provide the resources and oversight needed to work safely and ensure that workers have the authority to stop work when conditions are unsafe. We should expect an oversight system that is committed to the value of the work as well as the protection of the workers. How committed a research institution is can be demonstrated by how it trains, protects, equips and treats its laboratory workers — and how it responds when those protections fall short. This kind of system has parallels in other industries. For example, in aviation, safety depends on consistent monitoring rather than waiting for a catastrophic accident.
The tragic death of Darya Shipilova may have had nothing to do with the plague or with her work. The available information does not resolve those questions.
But uncertainty about her death should not prevent us from stating what research institutions and the systems that oversee them require: a commitment to transparency, a commitment to safety and a commitment to protecting the people who carry out the work.

title: Germany Detains Fourth Person Over Starlink Fire That Poland Blames on Moscow
description: Police have detained two more people in connection with a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month that Warsaw blames on Russia, private broadcaster RMF FM reported on Tuesday, citing anonymous sources, bringing the total to four.
content:
Police have detained two more people in connection with a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month that Warsaw blames on Russia, private broadcaster RMF FM reported on Tuesday, citing anonymous sources, bringing the total to four.
Earlier on Tuesday RMF said that German police had detained a woman in Berlin in the case. It then reported the detention of a fourth person, without providing any further details.
Poland said on Monday that two Turkish men had been detained in Germany on suspicion of being responsible for the blaze.
The blaze at the Starlink station in central Poland in September engulfed its power system and backup generator. Poland said at the time it believed the fire was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military, and blamed Russia.
"We have no doubt that Russian services are behind this act of sabotage, and it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning to individuals linked to the criminal underworld," Polish Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak told a news conference.
RMF reported that the detained woman in Germany may have acted as a driver and that Polish prosecutors would now assess the extent of her involvement and decide whether there were grounds to seek her extradition.
It did not give the woman's nationality or any other details.
The German Interior Ministry was not immediately available for comment. Poland's National Prosecutor's Office also had no immediate comment.
A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Criminal Police said the agency coordinated the exchange of information between Polish and German authorities in connection with the detention of three individuals.
Officials from several European Union countries have warned for months that Russia has been mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine.
Moscow says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.

title: Yandex Waives Cloud and Software Fees After Ukrainian Drone Attacks on Data Centers
description: Russian tech giant Yandex has waived fees for its cloud computing and virtual office suite through the end of October as engineers work to restore services damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers. “We understand that right now it’s important for you to focus on your own tasks, so we’re taking on the costs of cloud and collaboration tools ourselves,” Yandex B2B Tech said in a statement Tuesday.
content:
Russian tech giant Yandex has waived fees for its cloud computing and virtual office suite through the end of October as engineers work to restore services damaged in Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers.
“We understand that right now it’s important for you to focus on your own tasks, so we’re taking on the costs of cloud and collaboration tools ourselves,” Yandex B2B Tech said in a statement Tuesday.
Yandex Cloud, a cloud computing platform with more than 64,000 corporate clients, said subscribers will not be billed for usage between Oct. 8-31.
Yandex 360, a software suite that provides email, document editing, cloud storage and video conferencing, said fees would be waived for subscribers on personal plans.
The digital wallet application Yandex Pay said it would waive late fees or interest payments incurred during the downtime and increase interest rates on customers’ savings accounts to 20% this week.
The announcements follow three drone attacks on Yandex data centers in four days, which took three of the company’s six data centers offline.
Yandex Cloud, 360 and Pay all said they had partially restored operations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing Tuesday that it remained premature to estimate the financial losses from attacks on Yandex data centers.
“The company is strong and powerful. Yes, it’s currently facing difficulties and of course this issue is being discussed in the government, but the company is urgently taking measures to deal with the aftermath of this attack,” he said.
Yandex stock dropped 77 billion rubles ($918.5 million) over two days of trading on the Moscow Exchange, marking a 5.4% fall in market capitalization.

title: Ukraine Holds Off Refinery Attacks for Second Day After Trump Ceasefire Claim
description: Ukrainian forces appeared to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries during an overnight drone attack Tuesday, the second day since U.S.
content:
Ukrainian forces appeared to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries during an overnight drone attack Tuesday, the second day since U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire.”
Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries, or the energy sector in general, for the two days since the American President announced an energy ceasefire, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
However, Zelensky said, “Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine.”
The Kremlin said Monday that talks regarding a potential energy ceasefire were continuing.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “a majority” of the 417 Ukrainian drones launched toward the capital region had been “neutralized,” 65 of them directly on approach to the capital.
The air raid alerts caused flight delays and cancellations for around 150 flights at four Moscow airports, including around 100 at Vnukovo airport.
Ukrainian drones damaged industrial zones at the chemical hub of Nevinnomysk in the Stavropol region, according to the regional governor.
Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev said two men were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks over the past 24 hours.
A school building was damaged in the Kaluga region.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it carried out strikes against a Ukrainian missile and drone production workshop in Kyiv, a logistics center in Ternivka and other non-refinery targets.

title: French Navy Boards Russia-Linked Tanker in Indian Ocean
description: The French navy intercepted and boarded an oil tanker linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Indian Ocean, President Emmanuel Macron announced Monday.
content:
The French navy intercepted and boarded an oil tanker linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Indian Ocean, President Emmanuel Macron announced Monday.
The French joint staff said naval inspectors boarded the vessel to verify its nationality after doubts arose over its claimed Benin registration. The operation took place around 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island, an overseas territory of France.
Macron said the ship — the DF Peak — was suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illicit fuel transportation. The vessel is under U.S., EU, U.K. and Ukrainian sanctions.
The tanker was being escorted to Réunion for further checks, said armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin.
The DF Peak is at least the sixth shadow-fleet tanker French authorities have detained over the past year, according to the exiled outlet The Insider.
La France est déterminée à lutter contre la flotte fantôme, partout dans le monde. Ce matin, à plus de 450 nautiques au sud de La Réunion, notre Marine nationale a arraisonné le pétrolier DF Peak, suspecté de naviguer sous un faux pavillon et impliqué dans des activités illicites de transport de carburants. Cette action, conduite conformément au droit international de la mer, témoigne de notre détermination à faire respecter le droit et à lutter contre tous les trafics illicites, où qu’ils se produisent.
President Vladimir Putin has previously condemned European seizures of Russia-linked tankers as “piracy and robbery” and threatened retaliation.
Built in South Korea in 2006, DF Peak previously operated as the NS Captain and later as the Kaliningrad under Russia’s state shipping giant Sovcomflot.
Maritime database records cited by The Insider and Mediazona claim the DF Peak dropped its Russian flag in June 2025 to register under Benin and is currently registered to Hong Kong Ding Feng Shipping.
Russia's embassy in France said on Tuesday that France's seizure of the DF Peak was a blatant violation of international law, the state RIA news agency reported.

title: Trump’s Russian Diesel Debacle Risks Backfiring
description: Opinion | President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 9 that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel has roiled transatlantic relations.
content:
President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 9 that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel has roiled transatlantic relations. Such abrupt and dizzying shifts have been a consistent feature of Trump’s war diplomacy.
To assess its significance, we must distinguish the genuinely new from the wearily familiar. Since there is less to this policy than meets the eye, it is unlikely to have any real impact on the course of the war. Its few novel aspects will merely compound failure with ignominy.
This latest initiative resembles earlier Trumpian forays in three ways.
First, it restores Trump’s natural preference for Russia. Despite taking occasional steps that displeased Moscow, such as sanctioning its two biggest oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, Trump always returns to his default setting of rewarding Russia and pressuring Ukraine. Since the fighting can only stop if Moscow is decisively constrained from achieving its war aims, such a policy pursues the opposite of what is needed to end the war. It thus cannot succeed in its strategic goal.
Second, Trump’s main goal is to restore economic ties with Russia and, above all, to make new energy deals. Moscow has repeatedly dangled the carrots of huge investment proposals to American negotiators. While Trump’s latest move concerns energy trade, not investment, even this is not new. From March to June this year, the U.S. granted a temporary license allowing Russia to ship crude and oil products to mitigate the supply shock caused by the war with Iran.
Third, in importing Russian fuel without a quid pro quo, the White House is not striking a deal but making a unilateral concession to Moscow that weakens its negotiating position. Again, this is not new. In 2025, America abandoned earlier positions, notably by dropping the demand on Russia for an immediate ceasefire and the threat of new sanctions. In doing so, it surrendered its leverage and put its own objectives further out of reach. Now, it is repeating this error.
So what is new and consequential about the diesel deal? First, it is driven not by the prospect of lucrative deals for those around the White House, but by the urgent political need to reduce domestic fuel prices before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
Unlike the temporary waiver in March, which allowed more Russian oil onto the world market, the new volumes will be shipped specifically to the U.S. For this reason, it may be found illegal. A bipartisan group of senators has already declared that the trade would violate the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports and has called for the administration to “immediately reverse course.” The trade also cuts directly across the Lindsey Graham Act, passed with overwhelming congressional support last month, which included provisions to punish major importers of Russian oil.
Second, even in its own terms, the deal may fail. The modest volumes are too small to have any significant effect on prices at the pump and will likely arrive too late for the midterms.
Moreover, Russia may not even be able to deliver them. While it could make use of the temporary waiver Washington granted earlier this year to sell more oil products, Ukrainian attacks on its refineries caused exports to collapse in June. Russia imposed an export ban in July to stem and secure its own supply, but has now lifted it to export to the U.S. But its ability to do so will depend on the perilous security of its energy infrastructure.
All this lays bare the central contradiction in Trump’s position. On the one hand, he attributes the global fuel shortage to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian facilities when his own war against Iran is primarily responsible for the worldwide fuel deficit. On the other hand, he claims that supplies from Russia can meet the shortages that its absence from the market has created.
Third, America has reportedly threatened to cut off Ukraine’s access to intelligence and the PURL program if it continues to target Russian refineries. We have been here before, too. Washington suspended such support for brief periods several times in 2025, most severely in March, and issued similar threats last November to try to compel Zelensky to accept the administration’s 28-point peace plan . These cut-offs lasted only a few days, but hindered Ukraine’s operations.
What is new is the prospect of a longer, perhaps permanent, cut-off from all assistance that would be harmful to Kyiv, but not fatal. Ukraine has developed its own long-range strike weapons and Europe can provide some intelligence. The most serious consequence would be the loss of critically needed Patriot interceptors, 95% of which are obtained for Ukraine through PURL.
But America’s defense industry would suffer too. It would lose not only billions of dollars in weapons sales paid by Europe and delivered to Ukraine, but potentially also Kyiv’s cooperation as a unique and valuable source of technology and data. These losses would far outweigh any impact of a small, brief fall in domestic fuel prices.
In short, much about the diesel deal is a repeat of past efforts. Since it shares their flaws, it will share their failure.
But it adds contradictions of its own: trivial volumes of fuel that may not even arrive and are likely illegal if they do; threats that, if carried out, would hurt America’s national security.
Fresh absurdities appear every day. In its dealings with Russia, the administration has reportedly tried to offer assets , frozen in Europe, that it does not control; has proposed reviving the Nord Stream gas pipeline, a move that would require Europe’s consent; and has announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that neither country was aware of. This is a policy approaching total incoherence.
It was said of the Bourbon dynasty that it learned nothing and forgot nothing. History may record of this White House that, on its Russia policy at least, it learned nothing and understood nothing. Other countries have learned, to their cost, the lessons that await. When policy is driven by venal ineptitude rather than a judicious understanding of the national interest, the result is a masterclass in strategic failure.

title: Rostov Oil Terminal Burns for Third Day After Reported Ukrainian Drone Attack
description: A fire at an oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Rostov-on-Don continued to burn for a third day Monday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack over the weekend, according to independent media and Ukrainian monitoring channels.
content:
A fire at an oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Rostov-on-Don continued to burn for a third day Monday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack over the weekend, according to independent media and Ukrainian monitoring channels.
Footage published by Astra and Exilenova+ showed flames and thick smoke rising from the terminal’s fuel storage tanks. The facility, owned by the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, has a total storage capacity of 60,000 cubic meters and can handle 3.5 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, according to publicly available data.
Authorities had not announced that the fire had been extinguished as of midday Monday.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova said preliminary information indicated that seven of the terminal’s 12 tanks had burned and another showed signs of fire damage. Footage it published showed blackened tanks alongside others still engulfed in flames. The reported extent of the damage could not be independently confirmed.
The local Telegram channel Rostov Glavny also published footage of the blaze, saying the city had been shrouded in smoke for a second day. Its post suggested that reeds might be burning, citing rumors, but Astra’s analysis placed the fire at the oil terminal.
The facility, formerly known as Yug Rusi, was reportedly struck overnight into Saturday in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at the site.
The terminal transfers petroleum products onto sea and river tankers for export and has reportedly been used to supply fuel to the Russian military.
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said air defenses had shot down more than 100 drones over the region that night. He reported several fires following strikes and said six people had been injured, but did not mention damage to the terminal.
Ukraine had not publicly claimed responsibility for an attack on the facility.
The overnight attacks also damaged a railway drawbridge on the line between Rostov-on-Don and nearby Bataysk, causing lengthy delays to dozens of trains, according to Russian Railways.
Slyusar said two vessels were also damaged in the nearby city of Azov.

title: Tula’s ‘Model Police Officer’ Arrested Over $2K Bribe – Reports
description: An award-winning police officer in central Russia’s Tula region has been arrested on suspicion of extorting a 200,000-ruble ($2,400) bribe, the news outlet Ostorozhno Novosti reported Monday.
content:
An award-winning police officer in central Russia’s Tula region has been arrested on suspicion of extorting a 200,000-ruble ($2,400) bribe, the news outlet Ostorozhno Novosti reported Monday.
The officer, identified as Yekaterina F., 30, is a deputy supervisor of local district police officers who has served for at least nine years. She reportedly won the regional stage of an Interior Ministry competition honoring district officers in both 2023 and 2024.
Investigators allege that she demanded the money from a local resident in exchange for blocking a criminal fraud case against his son involving a forged driver’s license.
The man reported the extortion attempt to law enforcement before handing over the money, Ostorozhno Novosti reported.
The officer faces up to 12 years in prison if convicted of taking a large bribe through extortion. A Tula judge ordered to place her in pre-trial detention for one month and 29 days.
Regional authorities praised her in 2024 as a model police officer and a trusted figure in her community.
“Service is not easy for a woman. But I really like my work because I love helping people,” she said at the time.

title: Ukraine’s Strikes on Yandex Data Centers, Explained
description: A wave of attacks against the Russian internet giant Yandex has sent shockwaves across the country in recent days and caused major disruptions to daily life.
content:
A wave of attacks against the Russian internet giant Yandex has sent shockwaves across the country in recent days and caused major disruptions to daily life.
Yandex, often referred to as “Russia’s Google,” provides a range of digital services used by millions of Russians every day. Russian-language media reported widespread outages across the company’s products over the weekend, with people unable to access certain websites and applications.
The attacks, which Kyiv says are a retaliation for Russia’s strikes against similar targets, represent a new phase in Ukraine’s air campaign against Russia. Ukraine has increasingly sought to undermine Russia’s economy by striking infrastructure vital to some of its largest businesses in recent months, but this is the first time that targeting their data centers has become part of that strategy .
On Oct. 9, Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, announced that two of its data centers had been struck by drones, one in the city of Sasovo southeast of Moscow and the other in the Kaluga region southwest of the capital. A third facility in the suburbs of Vladimir east of Moscow would be hit before the weekend was through.
Serious damage was reported at all three locations . In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said that operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility, meanwhile, was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company.
“Yandex teams are working around the clock to ensure our services remain operational and to help those affected by the incident,” the company said after the two initial strikes. “This is our top priority right now, but unfortunately, it’s not easy.”
The effects of the attacks were not limited to the data centers they targeted. Nine people were injured in the Kaluga region, while about 1,600 customers were left without electricity in the Vladimir region, the heads of each region said. Neither explicitly mentioned the Yandex facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that the attacks were retaliation for Russia’s own strikes against its data centers. Indeed, last month, Moscow struck such facilities in the Kyiv region, causing temporary internet outages for roughly 100,000 households.
Moscow claimed that the data centers it struck were used by Ukrainian military intelligence bodies.
To understand the impact these attacks are having on regular Russians’ lives, consider what would happen if Google suddenly went offline.
Gone would be access to the company’s flagship internet browser, but also to its many other essential services: maps, payment, email and its virtual workspace, to name a few.
Like Google, Yandex is a company whose tendrils have stretched to nearly every corner of the Russian technology market since its founding in the 1990s. However, in Russia, its monopoly over digital services is arguably even larger.
While apps like Yandex Maps and Yandex Pay might be expected offerings of Russia’s largest technology company for people in the West, something like the widely used taxi and food delivery app Yandex Go rolls the function of Uber and DoorDash into one. In Russia, they’re all managed by the same company.
What’s more, Yandex offers a cloud computing service that provides digital infrastructure for some of Russia’s largest companies. According to the Yandex Cloud website , the platform has more than 64,000 customers.
As with any other major player in the technology industry, data centers form the backbone of all of these operations.
Understandably, after some of them were hit, people quickly began flagging issues. Russian-language media reported over the weekend that many Yandex apps had gone down temporarily but had been restored. Others were still experiencing interruptions or complete outages on Monday.
Yandex itself urged some users to switch to alternative platforms during the outages. Taxi drivers told the exiled outlet Vyorstka that they received a notification from Yandex advising them to switch to Google Maps or Waze while the company was fixing its servers.
Separately, the websites of other companies that use Yandex’s cloud services were reportedly impacted, including grocery giant Magnit, fast-food chain Vkusno i Tochka and household appliance retailer M.Video, the Kommersant newspaper reported , citing publicly available outage data.
Yandex’s operations outside of Russia also appear to have been affected. According to The Times of Central Asia, users in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have reported difficulties accessing the company’s apps. Similar outages were noted in the Armenian capital Yerevan, forcing users to book their taxis with a local competitor, which was in turn strained by the surge in traffic.
Particularly disruptive for Russians was the attacks’ effect on digital financial services . Yandex is so integrated into everyday payments that when its digital wallet application, Yandex Pay, went down, it warranted its own explanation from company leadership.
“All your money is safe,” Dima Pirogov, CEO of Yandex’s FinTech Division, said in a statement posted to the company’s social media platforms on Sunday. “The money itself isn’t stored in the data center. That’s where the servers that power our services are located.”
“We can’t yet give you a precise timeline for restoration,” Pirogov added, “but we promise: we won’t stop until the service is restored.”
President Vladimir Putin has so far not commented on the attacks. That’s not unusual — Putin is rarely the first one to telegraph the Kremlin’s reaction to such developments.
Some hints have emerged, however, that the Kremlin is taking the situation seriously.
On Monday, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told a State Duma committee that his office was working with the Defense Ministry on measures to protect data centers, a sign that officials are worried about the effect of further attacks.
“The scale of the attacks — which we were all monitoring in real time — was unprecedented,” Shadayev said, adding that “the entire industry is now helping to resolve” the chaos they caused.
As two major questions vex Yandex — how to restore service completely and how to repair damaged infrastructure — the company could be grappling with the fallout from the attacks for a while.
According to a source who spoke to Kommersant, delivering replacement equipment to the damaged facilities could take as long as six months.

title: EU Adopts Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Defense Firms and Executives
description: EU foreign ministers on Monday formally adopted the bloc’s largest-ever expansion of its Russia sanctions blacklist, targeting nearly 1,600 people and companies linked to the country’s military-industrial complex.
content:
EU foreign ministers on Monday formally adopted the bloc’s largest-ever expansion of its Russia sanctions blacklist, targeting nearly 1,600 people and companies linked to the country’s military-industrial complex.
The measures, initially agreed by EU envoys last week, add 826 Russian companies and 743 executives to the blacklist.
“Over half address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The companies supply components for Russian missiles, drones and aircraft, including explosives, ammunition, semiconductors and computers, according to the EU.
The bloc said they represent the “core” of the Russian military industry, employing more than a quarter-million people and generating an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.3 billion).
The EU also sanctioned 74 State Duma lawmakers and three members of Russia’s Central Election Commission over their involvement in parliamentary elections held in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
Separately, three people and four entities in North Korea were sanctioned over Pyongyang’s growing military and economic cooperation with Moscow.
Those listed face EU asset freezes, while EU citizens and companies are barred from making funds available to them. Sanctioned individuals also face travel bans across the 27-member bloc.
The latest additions bring the total number of people and entities under EU sanctions over Russia’s war in Ukraine to nearly 4,600.
