title: Abramovich Aides Backdated Documents to Hide Assets and Avoid Taxes, Report Says
description: Aides to Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich, including employees of accounting firm Deloitte Cyprus, allegedly backdated more than 1,000 documents to conceal assets and help his businesses avoid taxes, according to an investigation published Monday.
content:
Aides to Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich, including employees of accounting firm Deloitte Cyprus, allegedly backdated more than 1,000 documents to conceal assets and help his businesses avoid taxes, according to an investigation published Monday.
The Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism examined corporate records from the Cyprus Confidential leak, a collection of more than 500,000 documents that includes internal correspondence.
The investigation describes an alleged scheme spanning at least 1999 to 2013, in which documents for more than 100 companies linked to Abramovich were backdated, sometimes by as much as five years. Deloitte Cyprus signed off on financial statements based on those records, the report said.
Abramovich and his longtime aide Eugene Tenenbaum deny wrongdoing.
The investigation identified Tenenbaum and Demetris Ioannides, the former chairman of Deloitte Cyprus, as central figures in the alleged arrangements. Ioannides later founded Meritservus, which served as Abramovich’s main financial adviser for nearly two decades.
One case involved Kravin Investments, a Cyprus-registered company that received about $3 billion from the sale of shares in Russian oil producer Sibneft in May 2003 and retained roughly $2 billion.
The money generated interest that should have been subject to tax in Cyprus, according to the investigation.
In correspondence from 2005, Ioannides said Kravin’s financial statements for 2003 and 2004 needed to be amended. Documents were subsequently produced showing that Kravin was merely holding the money on behalf of Kelvedon Worldwide, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands.
Those documents were dated 2003 despite having been created at least two years later, the investigation said. The arrangement removed the $2 billion from Kravin’s balance sheet, along with the associated tax liability.
Another case concerned the transfer of $98 million out of Cyprus-based companies holding Sibneft shares in 2000.
Backdated consultancy agreements purported to show that an intermediary had earned the money by advising on share purchases and would pass 99.9% of it to Abramovich as an agency commission, the report said. The share transactions had taken place a year earlier.
The leaked records included 50 promissory notes, with repayment applications bearing Abramovich’s signature.
The journalists also examined records relating to about $650 million in property and luxury assets, including the Fyning Hill estate in England’s West Sussex, a London penthouse, a French chateau, aircraft, helicopters, yachts and cars.
Those assets disappeared from the accounts of Cyprus-based Amiscan Investments after documents were produced suggesting they had been transferred to another company in early 2003, according to the investigation.
The report also raised questions about evidence presented during a 2008 legal dispute involving Abramovich and his former Sibneft-Yugra business partner, Shalva Chigirinsky.
Tenenbaum told the High Court of England and Wales that he had not known the details of the disputed transactions before spring 2004. The leaked correspondence, however, indicated that he had approved agreements in 2003, including the transfer of Sibneft-Yugra shares to an Abramovich-owned company, the investigation said.
Some documents submitted to support Abramovich’s position also appeared to have been backdated, according to the report. The court ultimately declined to hear the merits of Chigirinsky’s claim, which exceeded $5 billion.
Deloitte Cyprus said it complied with applicable laws and could no longer access the decades-old correspondence.

title: Russia Weighs Drone Defenses for Data Centers After ‘Unprecedented’ Yandex Attacks
description: Russia is working on measures to protect data centers from drone attacks after a series of “unprecedented” strikes on tech giant Yandex’s facilities, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said Monday. “Yandex faced an unprecedented attack.
content:
Russia is working on measures to protect data centers from drone attacks after a series of “unprecedented” strikes on tech giant Yandex’s facilities, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said Monday.
“Yandex faced an unprecedented attack. The Digital Development Ministry, together with the Defense Ministry, is working on the issue of protecting these facilities,” Shadayev told a State Duma committee, according to Interfax.
He did not specify what protective measures were under consideration.
His comments follow drone attacks on three Yandex data centers in four days that have caused server outages that triggered service disruptions for users. The strikes hit facilities in the Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir regions between Thursday and Sunday.
The disruptions affected Yandex’s ride-hailing, food delivery and payment services, as well as companies that rely on Yandex Cloud, including online retailer Wildberries and fast-food chain Vkusno i Tochka.
Industry analysts told the Kommersant newspaper that replacing damaged server equipment could take up to six months.
Shadayev said backup systems and the distribution of computing capacity across multiple sites had helped services continue operating despite the scale of the attacks, adding that companies across the industry were helping address the disruptions.
Russian IT companies and mobile operators had begun buying mobile data centers even before this month’s attacks, the BBC’s Russian service reported . The outlet linked one supplier to a senior Federal Security Service (FSB) officer.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the targeted attacks as retaliation to Russia’s recent missile strikes against Ukrainian server facilities in Kyiv.
Russia has conducted a strike campaign against Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Last month, the exiled news outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that a large stake in Yandex was controlled by people linked to Bank Rossiya and President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle following the sale of the company’s Russian business in 2024.

title: Russia Plans Rehab Centers for Ukraine War Amputees
description: Russia plans to open rehabilitation centers in all eight of its federal districts for soldiers who lost limbs in the war in Ukraine, the Vedomosti business daily reported Monday, citing the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland foundation.
content:
Russia plans to open rehabilitation centers in all eight of its federal districts for soldiers who lost limbs in the war in Ukraine, the Vedomosti business daily reported Monday, citing the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland foundation.
The foundation did not give a timetable for opening the facilities. The first center is already operating at a Russian State Social University site in the Moscow region and has served 650 veterans.
Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova, who has been reported to be President Vladimir Putin’s cousin, said the center teaches former soldiers how to use prosthetic limbs in everyday life.
One participant told Vedomosti that veterans learn to walk with prostheses and take part in adaptive sports. But some arrive without a finished prosthesis or with one that no longer works, he said.
The man, who was mobilized in 2022 and lost his entire right leg at the front, said he now uses ropes to secure his broken prosthesis to his body so he can practice walking.
He said all 28 men at the center had lost a leg. He also told the newspaper that he does not tell people outside his military circle that he lost his leg in the war, saying instead that he lost it in a motorcycle accident.
“What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas,” he said.
The planned network comes as Russian officials report growing demand for prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation among soldiers returning from Ukraine.
Deputy Prime Minister Tatyana Golikova previously said the government planned to establish 10 prosthetic and orthopedic rehabilitation centers under the Federal Medical and Biological Agency by 2028, with funding already allocated in the budget.
In March 2025, Denis Kovlen, the Defense Ministry’s chief medical rehabilitation specialist, said Russia needed another 25 to 30 centers to provide prostheses and rehabilitation for people who had lost limbs in combat.
The number of Ukraine war veterans needing prosthetic limbs had tripled since 2022, he said, without providing an absolute figure.
Russia’s Social Fund reported that the number of people registered as having disabilities exceeded 11.1 million by early 2025, reversing a decline before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies estimated that at least 376,000 Russian troops had suffered severe wounds resulting in disability by early January 2025. It put the total number wounded at 611,000.

title: Zelensky Accuses Russia of Breaking Energy Ceasefire as Kremlin Says Talks Ongoing
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia on Monday of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by U.S.
content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia on Monday of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, urging Washington to ensure Moscow abides by the agreement as the Kremlin said contacts over a possible truce were ongoing.
Russia attacked gas production facilities belonging to Ukraine’s state oil and gas company Naftogaz in the Kharkiv region overnight, causing a fire and damaging critical equipment, the company said Monday.
Ukrainian drone attacks, meanwhile, appeared to spare Russian oil refineries overnight after Trump made the surprise announcement that the ceasefire had taken immediate effect.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday that contacts over a possible energy ceasefire were continuing. He declined to say whether it would apply only to oil refineries, saying further information would be released in due course.
“There were Russian violations of the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump,” Zelensky told a security conference in Warsaw via video link.
Zelensky said he had learned about the agreement through the media and was awaiting details of the terms discussed by Washington and Moscow.
“This energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect it,” he said.
The Kremlin has not formally confirmed that it agreed to a ceasefire. Sources close to the Russian government told Bloomberg that Moscow remained skeptical that Washington could deliver a binding agreement on terms favorable to Russia.
Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said employees were working to repair the damage from the overnight attack.
“Our employees are doing everything possible to repair the damage as quickly as possible and prevent risks to the stable operation of the energy system,” he said on Telegram.
Zelensky also said in his nightly video address Sunday that Russian forces had struck a combined heat and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, that evening. A Ukrainian official said the attack took place after Trump’s ceasefire announcement.
“The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders,” Zelensky said in the address.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 37 drones were destroyed as they approached the capital between Sunday evening and Monday morning.
Local authorities and independent media reported no new strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has repeatedly targeted in recent months.
Russian attacks on other targets continued Monday. The Defense Ministry said its forces struck a cargo vessel carrying military supplies near the Ukrainian port of Odesa. Local officials said Russian shelling and air attacks injured at least 12 people in Kharkiv that morning.
In Russia’s southern Rostov region, firefighters continued battling a blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery following a drone attack Saturday, the exiled news outlet Astra reported .
Authorities in the southwestern Belgorod region said one civilian was killed and three others were injured Sunday evening.
Separately, Peskov rejected Zelensky’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire to allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections, saying Moscow wanted an overall peace deal instead.
“Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday.
Peskov said Putin and other Russian officials had repeatedly stated that they did not want a temporary ceasefire and were prepared to work toward long-term peace.
Russia has long pressed Ukraine to hold elections and says that its failure to do so makes Zelensky an illegitimate leader. Elections in wartime are prohibited by Ukrainian law.

title: Russian Rocket Engine Executive Arrested in $59M Defense Contract Case
description: A senior executive at a Russian rocket engine maker has been arrested in connection with the alleged theft of more than 5 billion rubles ($59.5 million) under state defense contracts, the Kommersant newspaper reported, citing two sources familiar with the case.
content:
A senior executive at a Russian rocket engine maker has been arrested in connection with the alleged theft of more than 5 billion rubles ($59.5 million) under state defense contracts, the Kommersant newspaper reported , citing two sources familiar with the case.
Vladimir Koltsov, deputy director of the Voronezh-based Chemical Automatics Design Bureau, or KBKhA, faces charges of exceeding his authority over construction contracts and concealing delays from management, the newspaper said.
KBKhA is part of Russia’s state space corporation Roscosmos. Koltsov, who oversees infrastructure and capital construction, has been held in pretrial detention since mid-September and faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted.
Investigators allege that KBKhA paid contractors Nagval Stroytekh and Garant-Stroy more than 5 billion rubles ($59.5 million) in advances between 2021 and 2024.
The contracts covered facilities to manufacture spherical pressure vessels for rockets and spacecraft, as well as a consolidated production facility for liquid-fueled engines used in Soyuz launch vehicles.
The contractors completed work worth just 535 million rubles ($6.4 million) before KBKhA unilaterally terminated the contracts, Kommersant reported. Investigators allege that the companies used the remaining funds at their own discretion.
Koltsov is accused of giving management false information about construction progress and concealing missed deadlines to avoid disciplinary action and make it appear that he was fulfilling his duties.
He declined to answer questions when interrogated as a suspect, invoking his constitutional right not to testify against himself or close relatives, the newspaper said.
Sergei Gutenko, chief executive of Nagval Stroytekh, was previously detained in the same case. He was placed on an international wanted list and ordered held in custody in absentia in November 2025.
Gutenko was detained in Thailand in February and deported to Russia. He has admitted guilt on fraud charges, according to Kommersant.
His case is being heard by Voronezh’s Sovetsky District Court, with the next hearing scheduled for Oct. 14.
KBKhA develops and manufactures liquid-fueled rocket engines for space launch vehicles and ballistic missiles. It merged with the Voronezh Mechanical Plant in 2019 as part of plans to establish a rocket engine manufacturing center in the city.

title: Trump Says Russia and Ukraine Reached ‘Energy Ceasefire'
description: Updated to include U.S.
content:
Updated to include U.S. President Donald Trump’s comments.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire," hours after Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy had pushed back against U.S. pressure for a unilateral end to strikes on Russian refineries.
In a social media post, Trump said the energy ceasefire would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate further.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire, if Russia was.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelensky said that Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
On Saturday, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for raising U.S. diesel prices and said Zelensky had "better damn well stop," adding that Ukraine should replace him as leader because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.
The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of next month's midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
Zelensky on Sunday repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries only as part of a mutual de-escalation of the conflict, which would require Moscow to cease its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.
Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees," Zelensky said.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelensky said, without alluding specifically to Trump's remarks. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so."
On Saturday, Zelensky responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, which he said would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine.
Analysts said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.
The diesel deal was also criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.
On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Putin.
"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher, referring to Ukraine's prohibition on elections under martial law for security reasons.
"In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.
Zelensky said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defense packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.
On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession.

title: Russia’s Yandex Says Data Center in Vladimir Shut Down After Drone Attack
description: Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday that its infrastructure had been damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data center in the Vladimir region.
content:
Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Sunday that its infrastructure had been damaged in a drone attack, resulting in the complete shutdown of its data center in the Vladimir region.
No one was injured in the attack, but some of Yandex's services are currently unavailable to users, the company said.
This is the third major data ​centre to have been taken out of action in the last few days.
On Friday, Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called "Russia's Google," said its data center in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down Yandex's data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI ​model are housed.

title: Russian Attack on Ukrainian City Kills 20, a Day After Trump Eases Diesel Sanctions on Moscow
description: Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after United States President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
author_name: Sergiy Chalyi and Max Hunder for Reuters
content:
Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russia n attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after United States President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russia n diesel in a major setback for Kyiv.
"Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House.
Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russia n bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.
A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.
"Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears.
Eighteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the front line.
It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russia n strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, 80 miles east of Kyiv.
A senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, said Russia had hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday.
Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed.
"If (the Russia ns) have money, they’ll be able to carry on fighting us," said Nataliia Malysheva, a 49-year-old local resident whose parents died in hospital after being pulled from the rubble.
"How many lives have been lost here, how many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?"
"Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelensky said.
A missile attack on Saturday afternoon also hit a restaurant, wounding seven people in Kyiv.
Russia n drones flew over Kyiv throughout the day, part of a vast new wave of bombardment of the capital, the heaviest since the early days of the war.
Russia ’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russia n diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the U.S. conflict with Iran .
Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war .
Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russia n oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid.
On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week.
The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions .
Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelensky said had caught Kyiv by surprise.
The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.
Russia n President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of ‌peace ⁠talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.
U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russia n state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.
Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russia n-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, the Russia n-installed governor said on Saturday.
Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

title: Germany Sticks to Russia Sanctions After Trump Diesel Announcement
description: Germany said on Saturday it would maintain sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine following United States President Donald Trump's announcement that his administration had temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel.
content:
Germany said on Saturday it would maintain sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine following United States President Donald Trump's announcement that his administration had temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russia n fuel.
"The federal government has taken note of the U.S. decision relating to Russia n diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
He said Germany's position remained clear: "The federal government remains committed to the decisions on sanctions against Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions."
He said Germany's support for Ukraine was unchanged and diplomatic efforts to reach a solution would continue.
Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. He said his administration temporarily lifted U.S. sanctions on Russia n fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine.
Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, have risen to near record levels, posing a risk for Trump's fellow Republicans ahead of the November 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who visited Kyiv last weekend, has said repeatedly that Germany, Ukraine's largest European donor, would not reduce its support for the Kyiv government.

title: Rosatom Says it Wins Tribunal Ruling in Finnish Nuclear Plant Dispute
description: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said on Saturday that an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal had ruled in its favour in a long-running dispute with Finnish utility Fennovoima over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
content:
Russia 's state nuclear corporation Rosatom said on Saturday that an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal had ruled in its favour in a long-running dispute with Finnish utility Fennovoima over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
Rosatom said the tribunal found that Fennovoima had unlawfully terminated the contract for the construction of the planned plant in northern Finland in 2022.
The parties have been locked in legal disputes since Fennovoima scrapped the 7 billion euro ($7.8 billion) project in May 2022, citing significant delays and political risks shortly after Russia launched its conflict in Ukraine.
Rosatom said the tribunal found that the project was making good progress when it was terminated.
"Today's victory is important, but not final. We will continue to prove that we are right regarding the Finnish project in courts of various instances," Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said in a statement.
Fennovoima did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The contract to build the 1.2 gigawatt plant was signed in 2013 with Fennovoima, a consortium in which Finnish stakeholders including Fortum, Outokumpu and SSAB originally controlled two thirds through a joint venture, and the Russia n side held one third.
After the project's termination, Fennovoima wound down its operations and is primarily engaged in legal proceedings.

title: Putin Downplayed Immediate Ukraine Talks Resumption in Phone Call With Trump, Kremlin Says
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin told U.S.
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday that Kyiv had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of trilateral Ukraine peace talks after it had hit Moscow with drones during last month's election, the Kremlin said.
Trump has so far unsuccessfully tried to broker a peace deal to end the war in Ukraine, which started with Russia's invasion in February 2022.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Russia's war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will keep working toward a settlement to end the conflict.
Putin had said that Moscow had been ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after last month's Russian parliamentary elections, but Ukraine launched attacks on Moscow and hit polling stations, putting the peace process in jeopardy, according to him.
"By launching a massive drone attack on Moscow, other cities and polling stations, as well as on specific individuals involved in organizing the election, on the main voting day, the Kyiv regime effectively disrupted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process," Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said about the call with Trump.
"And now, as the president said, we will consider when those negotiations can be resumed," he added, referring to trilateral negotiations involving the U.S., Russia and Ukraine.
Ushakov also said Putin and Trump discussed major economic initiatives during the phone call, including potential supplies of Russian fuel.
Trump said earlier on Friday after the call with Putin that Russia had agreed to immediately supply diesel to U.S. and global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month, although analysts said the amounts would likely not reduce prices greatly.

title: Fear and Distrust Are the Real Russian Plague
description: Opinion | Modern disease outbreaks differ from historical ones for reasons that go beyond vaccines, better treatments and improved hygiene.
content:
Modern disease outbreaks differ from historical ones for reasons that go beyond vaccines, better treatments and improved hygiene.
Sure, that all helps. But these scientific advances went hand in hand with social transformations that made experts and public health authorities more credible than a local leader or a healer who believed eating the organs of the deceased could save people from the plague.
Trust in science and institutions, sometimes reinforced by figures like a Catholic priest promoting vaccination, allowed technological advances to spark broad societal progress that reached far beyond the educated classes. For years, Western democracies championed the building of trust between citizens and authorities.
Where that trust breaks down, ancient instincts can take over despite the availability of modern medical equipment and treatments.
And there are few words that awaken those instincts like “plague,” especially when it appears alongside the word “Russia” in 2026.
So why is this apparently isolated suspected case resonating with people far from the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk?
There is nothing particularly Russian about laboratory-acquired infections, one possible explanation that has been raised in this case. Even if we set aside the contentious debate over the origins of Covid-19 and focus only on plague, a researcher in the United States died from a laboratory-acquired infection in 2009.
The publicly available database of laboratory-acquired infections maintained by ABSA International, the biosafety association, is impressively long and mostly limited to lab personnel. Researchers are human beings who can make mistakes. Those studying dangerous pathogens risk, first and foremost, their own lives in pursuit of medical progress (or for military purposes, but we should not presume that is the case here).
What is different between Russia and the U.S. is what happens after a suspected laboratory infection. Here there is something distinctly Russian or, better yet, something distinctly Russia-in-2026.
A prolonged political crisis inevitably brings a crisis of trust. In 2014, Russian authorities denied state-sponsored doping at the Sochi Olympics and the presence of Russian troops in Crimea and the Donbas.
The state’s undercounting of Covid-19 deaths in 2020-2021 was followed by the approval of vaccines before large-scale clinical trials were complete, which resulted in the approval of one vaccine that does not work at all and another with adverse effects .
After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, official sources appeared to inhabit a parallel reality, denying responsibility for civilian deaths, concealing mobilization plans and withholding the scale of military losses.
It’s no surprise that official assurances about the suspected plague case in eastern Siberia have been met with doubt, both locally and internationally.
World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has said the organization lacks the information needed for a full risk assessment. He has also sought clarification about reports of a second employee with unexplained pneumonia, whose existence is denied Russian authorities deny.
His concern is more than a matter of curiosity. A lack of transparency undermines the foundational rules that allow the WHO to help countries combat disease. The WHO’s 2024 manual for plague surveillance, diagnosis, prevention and control treats communication as an integral part of outbreak control , not an add-on.
Under the International Health Regulations, countries must notify the WHO within 24 hours of assessing an event of potential international concern. Suspected pneumonic plague must always be assessed using the regulations’ decision instrument , and a suspected case outside a known endemic area should be reported without waiting for lab confirmation .
These requirements provide a starting point for protecting communities. Effective public health measures also depend on communicating risks, addressing misinformation and involving communities in the response.
None of these measures are possible without transparency and a willingness to address the concerns of local populations. Without reliable information, people may become extremely worried, creating conditions for unrest or a witch hunt. Or they may become recklessly complacent . In both cases, societal turbulence might become more dangerous than the disease itself.
There is also nothing particularly Russian about studying infectious agents for both civilian and military purposes. Many powerful countries have explored this path, says Natalia Rapoport, a professor emerita in the University of Utah’s biomedical engineering department.
The daughter of the prominent Soviet pathologist Yakov Rapoport , she recounts his memoirs of performing an autopsy on Abram Berlin, a victim of a lab-related plague outbreak in Moscow in 1939.
She explains how fear of the plague becamed intertwined with fear of repression. Her father feared arrest, which eventually came more than a decade later. When he was taken to the plague hospital, he called her mother and said: “Don’t worry, it’s not what we were afraid of. It is just the plague.”
The plague is not just a bacterium. It is also a social phenomenon. And h ow much devastation and fear it brings depends on how well our society functions, not just a group of prepared experts.

title: Montenegro Expels Founder of Russian Pro-War Blog Rybar for 'Security Reasons'
description: Montenegro expelled Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Russian pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, and three other Russian nationals on Friday after detaining them in an operation targeting suspected Russian influence activities, police and the country’s National Security Agency said.
content:
Montenegro expelled Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Russian pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, and three other Russian nationals on Friday after detaining them in an operation targeting suspected Russian influence activities, police and the country’s National Security Agency said.
The agencies said the four could no longer remain in Montenegro “for reasons of national and internal security of the state.” Their statement identified the Russians only by their initials, but a police source confirmed their identities to Reuters.
Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defense Ministry press officer, was detained in the Adriatic resort town of Risan along with others including his wife, Rybar creative director Valeria Zvinchuk, local media reported.
Security sources told Vijesti that police and the National Security Agency (ANB) carried out the operation to counter “hybrid activities” by Russian information networks.
Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed the arrests earlier Friday, saying Montenegro had faced warnings of attempts to destabilize the country as it pursues European Union membership.
“Montenegro is protecting its interests and no one will endanger our European future,” Spajić wrote on X.
Intelligence agencies had monitored the group for several days after its arrival in Montenegro to film material about the Balkan country’s alignment with EU visa policies, the Russian news outlet Readovka reported .
Authorities suspected the material was intended to undermine Montenegro’s tourism industry, economy and national interests, according to the report.
Rybar said before the expulsion announcement that its team had entered Montenegro legally and planned to film at a local monastery.
The Russian Embassy in Podgorica said it had demanded clarification on the reasons for the arrests.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, said that Russia may need to "top up" its prisoner exchange fund with European and U.S. citizens in order to free its own citizens being held in Europe following Zvinchuk ’ s detention.
"Now, it is quite likely that we will have to replenish the exchange fund with European and American idiots in order to get our own people out. There’s no other way: when in Rome, do as the Romans do…," said Medvedev.
Rybar has about 1.5 million Telegram subscribers and publishes daily military analysis of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Zvinchuk is subject to Western sanctions. It also operates a broader network of websites and social media channels.
In October 2024, the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification of 19 individuals involved in managing Rybar-led social media channels, saying they had promoted Russia's political interests in the U.S. ahead of the 2024 presidential elections.

title: In Russian-Occupied Oleshky, Civilians Struggle to Survive as Hunger Deepens
description: Lyudmila often has to call her sister about 40 times before the line connects.
content:
Lyudmila often has to call her sister about 40 times before the line connects. When she finally gets through, she can barely make out what her sister is saying.
"I hear occasional words, sometimes they're incomplete. The main thing is that I hear her voice," Lyudmila, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, told The Moscow Times.
A refugee now living in Europe, Lyudmila comes from a village on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. Her sister lives across the river in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, where relentless bombardment has plunged the town into a deepening humanitarian crisis.
Conditions in Oleshky have continued to deteriorate since late 2025. Roads leading in and out of the town are heavily mined and badly damaged, leaving its 2,000 remaining residents, including an estimated 50 children, largely cut off from food, water, gas, electricity and medicine, residents and volunteers told The Moscow Times.
"She says everything is destroyed, houses are often burning and strikes land nearby every five to 10 minutes," Lyudmila told The Moscow Times.
With a pre-war population of 24,000, Oleshky served as a satellite town to Kherson city over the Dnipro River. It became a frontline town after Russian forces retreated across the Dnipro in late 2022.
Today, Russian forces use positions on the occupied bank to strike Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv targets Russian forces on the other side of the river in response, defense analyst Konrad Muzyka said.
Months of bombardment have destroyed much of the town’s infrastructure, according to a representative of a Russian organization that evacuates civilians from frontline areas.
"Everything has been smashed by drones. Residential buildings without damage can be counted on one hand. It's practically impossible to get in or out," the representative told The Moscow Times, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.
There have been no food deliveries by road since June, when a delivery driver hit a mine and died.
"For the past two months, people have been eating grass," said a resident who escaped the town on foot on Wednesday.
"Food can only be bought in Radensk," he told The Moscow Times, referring to a small settlement 23 kilometers (14 miles) away.
Every few days, Lyudmila's sister makes that journey by foot to buy food while her husband, who is recovering from a shrapnel wound sustained in a drone strike, waits anxiously at home.
"By the time she gets back, her legs are completely swollen," Lyudmila said.
"To blow up on a mine or die of hunger? People from Oleshky are forced to choose between two deaths," Ukraine's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said in a post last week.
Drone footage shared by Lubinets earlier this week showed about two dozen of Oleshky's remaining residents trying to flee the city on electric bikes, bicycles and even on foot.
Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the Oleshky city military administration, said 12 people who fled the town last month had reached Ukrainian-controlled territory. Other evacuees remain in nearby towns in Russian-occupied southern Ukraine.
Ukraine blames Moscow for the deepening crisis in what Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described as a Russian "siege."
The Kremlin has acknowledged the situation in the town as "critical," but accused Kyiv of preventing civilians from leaving.
With Moscow prohibiting humanitarian bodies and international organizations from working in Ukraine's occupied territories, evacuating civilians is left to small volunteer groups. The groups often undertake days-long journeys through Russia and Belarus to repatriate people.
"We work wherever access is possible, but in Oleshky, it's the hardest," the volunteer, who was last in the town over a month ago, said.
Ukraine’s military used drones to deliver another batch of food and medicine to Oleshky on Sunday following an initial operation in late September. The latest delivery consisted of nearly 400 packages weighing almost 4 metric tons, Sybiha said.
Neither Lyudmila’s sister nor the resident who escaped on Wednesday received any of the aid, they said.
"Where they sent it and to whom is unknown. No one in their area received anything," Lyudmila said.
After the first delivery on Sept. 27, Hasanenko accused Russian forces of taking some of the supplies.
It is difficult to establish how many people have been killed in Oleshky. By the end of June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine recorded at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and neighboring Hola Prystan in 2026.
Separately, Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-appointed governor of the occupied Kherson region, said Wednesday that 68 people had been killed across the entire region so far this year.
Efforts to arrange a safe evacuation from Oleshky have yet to produce a breakthrough, Ukraine’s human rights commissioner’s office said Thursday. It said talks with Russia were ongoing and that Kyiv had offered a localized ceasefire, a safe evacuation route and arrangements to receive residents in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
On the ground, people who spoke to The Moscow Times were reluctant to discuss military activity in detail. The man who escaped Oleshky said some people in the town blame Kyiv for the constant drone attacks.
"Ukrainian drones show no mercy, even to civilians," he said.
Others, like Lyudmila's sister, blame Moscow for occupying the town, and then turning it into a wasteland.
"The Russians came and created this crisis. Now, my sister and her husband are waiting for Ukraine to save them," she said.

title: Why I Left Russia the Same Day I Was Released From Detention
description: Opinion | On Dec. 8, 2025, I walked out of a courthouse in St.
content:
On Dec. 8, 2025, I walked out of a courthouse in St. Petersburg after spending almost five month s in pre-trial detention. The court gave me a fine rather than a prison sentence. That same morning, I was still in custody. I h ad been accused of financing extremist activity over donations of around $40 to Alexei Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation.
The first thing I did was go with my closest relatives and lawyers to a nearby café. We discussed the most practical things: how to pay the fine, how to collect my belongings from the detention centre, what would happen if the prosecution appealed. The lawyers explained that the prosecution could file its appeal on the final day of the statutory deadline. Until then, I was still forbidden to leave the area and, if there was an appeal, the restrictions could remain in place until the city court issued its decision.
I thought I was finally going home. I wanted to see my wife, hug my children, lie down in a normal bed. I had imagined that evening many times during my months of detention.
But on the way home, my family told me that I could not stay in Russia. They believed the prosecution would almost certainly seek an actual prison sentence. It turned out that there were already people ready to organise my departure. At first, I understood that to mean I had at least a day or two. Then everything sped up. We managed to pick the children up from school and have lunch when the coordinator told me that I needed to leave as quickly as possible.
About half an hour later, it became clear that the driver was already ready.
At that moment, my parents called me. Then my older son, who was in Georgia. Everyone congratulated me on my release, told me to relax and finally enjoy some time with my family. I could not tell them that in a few hours I would be leaving again. The fewer people who knew the route, the safer it seemed.
My younger son sat beside me, listened to those conversations and cried. He already knew that I would be leaving in a couple of hours.
I was asked whether I understood that, by leaving now, I might never be able to return to Russia. I said yes.
I very much wanted to stay. More than anything, I wanted to spend at least one night at home with my wife and children. But the fear of ending up behind bars again was stronger. I explained to the children: it was better for us to live apart for a while longer but be able to talk at any time and see each other on video than for me to end up back in prison for several years.
I understood something else as well: I was leaving while my undertaking not to leave the area was still in force. That decision was not without risk either. But I compared that risk with another one — that the prosecution would appeal the verdict and I would be taken back into custody.
The main issue became time. At first, it seemed to me that I might have to cross the border illegally or semi-legally. Then I learned that the crossing would be ordinary, using my passport. Paradoxically, that was exactly what convinced me that I had to leave immediately. St opping me would be easy if an alert was put out. A few hours after the court hearing, it might not yet be there. A few days later, the likelihood seemed much higher.
I did not know how quickly information moved between agencies. And it was precisely that uncertainty that determined my decision.
I took a small backpack containing a laptop, chargers, one book, a couple of changes of underwear, toiletries, documents and cash. Almost nothing else, so that I could remain highly mobile and support the cover story that had been proposed to me.
We hugged, my wife and children and I, and I walked to the first point on the route. On the way, I checked whether anyone was following me. I was almost certain there was no surveillance: hardly anyone could have expected a person to voluntarily leave his family on the very first day after his release. But I still kept looking back.
At the agreed location, a man was waiting for me with a clean phone containing none of my personal data: a SIM card unassigned to me, a VPN and secure messenger apps. It came with the coordinator’s contacts and instructions already included.
A taxi was ordered for me to the next point. I did not have any bank cards, only cash. On the way, it turned out that the driver did not have change for large banknotes, so we stopped at a hypermarket to get some smaller denominations. For some reason, I remember that small detail very clearly. When you are trying not to leave any digital traces anywhere, an ordinary problem with getting change suddenly becomes part of the operation.
It was almost midnight when I got into another car that was supposed to take me further. The coordinator asked me to make contact with him every two or three hours.
The driver thought I was a businessman from Minsk. I decided not to undermine that story. He offered me a pillow from the boot. I lay down on the back seat and tried to sleep. I could not. The day kept replaying in my head over and over. That morning, I had been in a cell. Now I was driving along a highway at night, not knowing what would happen at the border or what information about me might already have appeared in any databases.
At around six in the morning, we crossed the Russian-Belarusian border. My passport was scanned like it would be at an airport. The few minutes of waiting to see if my documents had been flagged felt very long. Then the officer gave a signal. I could go.
Relief washed over me. Almost immediately, another thought crossed my mind: there is no way back now.
In Minsk, the driver dropped me off at the bus station and I bought a ticket for a bus to Vilnius. Next to me was a man with the same combination of citizenships as me: Russian and Israeli. He had travelled that route many times and explained to me how the border checks worked. At the Belarusian border, I stood in the queue behind him, listened to the questions he was asked and watched how he answered them.
When it was my turn, I first handed over my Israeli passport. When asked how I had entered Belarus, I said that I had arrived by car from Russia that morning. They then asked for my Russian passport. The officer looked at the stamps, asked questions and eventually let me through.
I wrote to the coordinator: “I think that’s it. I’m free.”
But the bus then waited for the other passengers for about another half an hour. The barrier did not open and I was still feeling nervous. Formally, the check was already behind me, but I was still waiting for the final movement forward.
Everything about the process on the Lithuanian side was easier. The border guard asked where I was going. I explained that someone was meeting me in Vilnius.
I was taken to a hotel in Vilnius. Just over a day earlier, I had been in a cell. I collapsed onto the bed and, for the first time in many months, fell asleep on a normal mattress.
The next day, I hardly went anywhere. I restored access to services and changed my passwords — my old phone was still with the investigators. I bought a sweater. At the supermarket, I bought a pile of fruit that I had missed while in pretrial detention.
But even in Vilnius, I still did not tell anyone where I was for several days. My lawyers, family and closest friends had agreed to observe a “period of silence” until it became clear whether there would be an appeal. My parents believed that I was still in St. Petersburg. When my name accidentally appeared in a local housing-search chat and a journalist asked my family whether this meant I was abroad, we had to get the post deleted urgently.
After prison, I began to see my formal status differently. The court’s decision mattered enormously. I had been released but had no answer to the question of what would happen the next day if the prosecution lodged an appeal, if new information entered a database or if another agency made its own decision.
No one ordered me to leave Russia that same night. No one forced me to take a clean phone, use cash, check whether I was being followed, or conceal from my parents where I was. I made all of those decisions myself.
That, for me, was the main change. When the consequences cannot be reliably predicted, people begin to restrict their own behaviour in advance. Not because someone has already issued a new order, but because the cost of a mistake seems too high.
The court released me on December 8, but I only felt safe once I was on the other side of the border.

title: Sberbank Warns of Rising Overdue Loans as Russian Companies Struggle
description: Russian companies are increasingly struggling to repay their debts as prolonged high interest rates and slowing economic growth weaken their finances, the country’s largest lender Sberbank said.
content:
Russian companies are increasingly struggling to repay their debts as prolonged high interest rates and slowing economic growth weaken their finances, the country’s largest lender Sberbank said.
Chief Financial Officer Taras Skvortsov said the state-controlled bank continued to see deteriorating loan quality and rising overdue debt among corporate borrowers.
“For several months, we have seen a steady trend of more loans becoming overdue and a deterioration in corporate clients’ financial condition,” Skvortsov told Interfax.
The warning points to growing pressure on Russia’s banking sector as businesses struggle with high borrowing costs and weak growth. The Economic Development Ministry estimates that gross domestic product expanded 0.6% in January-August and forecasts the same pace for the full year.
Skvortsov said the difficulties affected several sectors, including individual residential development projects, retail, commercial property and online marketplaces.
He said the deterioration was driven by a broader trend linked to persistently high interest rates and slowing growth, rather than problems at a few large clients.
Russian companies’ combined profits minus losses fell to their lowest level since the pandemic in the first seven months of the year. One in three companies reported a loss.
Sberbank CEO German Gref has previously warned that difficulties in the wider economy eventually feed through to banks.
Property developers face particular pressure. Sberbank and other creditors are working to rescue Samolet, one of Russia’s largest developers.
Ildar Khusainov, head of real estate agency Etazhi, estimates that about 30% of developers are struggling financially.
The coal industry is in its second consecutive year of losses, while steelmakers and forestry companies also face a crisis.
Ukrainian drone attacks on online retailers’ warehouses have put further pressure on loans to both marketplace operators and merchants selling through their platforms. Wildberries borrowed primarily from VTB, while Sberbank has received thousands of applications to restructure loans.
Sberbank is due to publish its financial results under international accounting standards in late October. Skvortsov warned that its cost of risk would rise in the second half of the year, meaning the bank would set aside more money to cover potential loan losses.
VTB First Deputy CEO Dmitry Pyanov expects banks to make substantial provisions for loan losses over the next three years.
At the end of June, Sberbank reported 2.6 trillion rubles ($30.7 billion) in overdue loans, including 1.6 trillion rubles ($18.9 billion) more than 90 days past due.
Overdue loan figures alone do not fully capture borrowers’ financial difficulties. Restructuring can allow troubled loans to remain outside that category despite a deterioration in borrowers’ ability to repay.
Pyanov has described restructuring as a way to avert default. The Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting, a think tank close to the Kremlin, has said banks also use it to mask problems.
Including troubled restructured debt, the Central Bank classified 11.6% of banks’ corporate loans, totaling 11.7 trillion rubles ($138.1 billion), as problem loans at the end of July.
That amount rose by 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion) during the month, which the regulator attributed to risky loan restructurings for property borrowers and worsening conditions at some industrial companies.
The think tank said an improvement in the banking sector would depend on a revival in economic activity that allowed borrowers to resume servicing troubled, restructured debt.
But economic forecasts point to several more years of sluggish growth.
The OECD expects Russia’s economy to expand 0.5% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. The World Bank forecasts growth of 0.6% this year and 0.7%-0.8% over the following two years.
The Bank of Finland forecasts growth of 1% in 2026 and 0.5% annually in 2027 and 2028.

title: All 4 Moscow Airports Restrict Flights Amid Drone Attack
description: All four airports serving Moscow imposed temporary flight restrictions Friday afternoon amid a drone attack, Russia’s aviation regulator said, as new figures showed flight cancellations nationwide had doubled in the first nine months of 2026. The restrictions at Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky took effect at about 3:40 p.m. local time, Rosaviatsia said.
content:
All four airports serving Moscow imposed temporary flight restrictions Friday afternoon amid a drone attack, Russia’s aviation regulator said, as new figures showed flight cancellations nationwide had doubled in the first nine months of 2026.
The restrictions at Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky took effect at about 3:40 p.m. local time, Rosaviatsia said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defenses had destroyed 15 drones approaching the capital.
Residents in several southern Moscow districts reported explosions and air defense activity, the independent outlet Astra reported .
Vnukovo was the worst affected, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24. More than 40% of its flights were delayed, with an average delay of 102 minutes, while another 10% were canceled.
Separately, authorities in the Yaroslavl region northeast of Moscow said small reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine had been shot down Friday. The regional security ministry said efforts to destroy the objects were continuing.
The afternoon restrictions followed overnight closures at Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky because of drone threats. Those restrictions were lifted by 7 a.m., though Zhukovsky subsequently suspended operations twice more.
More than 150 flights were delayed overnight.
The disruptions came as the Kommersant newspaper reported that flight cancellations in Russia doubled between January and September compared with the same period last year, citing insurer AlfaStrakhovanie.
The insurer linked the deterioration to airport restrictions imposed because of Ukrainian drone threats. Emergency flight restrictions have been imposed almost daily in southern and central Russia since late April, the newspaper said.
More than 7.6 million passengers waited over three hours to depart in the first nine months of 2026, 2.5 times the number a year earlier.
AlfaStrakhovanie tracks 30 major Russian airlines and about 60 foreign carriers accounting for roughly 97% of passenger traffic in Russia.
The number of flights delayed by more than an hour rose 70% to 128,000. Delays of at least two hours doubled to 77,000, while those lasting at least three hours rose 2.2-fold to 51,000.
Some 36,000 flights were delayed by four hours or more, 2.4 times the number a year earlier. The share departing within 15 minutes of their scheduled time fell from 57% to 52%.
Separate Transportation Ministry figures showed that 118,100 flights departed more than two hours late between January and August, up 20.3% year on year. Those figures cover a broader range of aviation, including small aircraft, cargo, charter and government flights.
Sources at four regional airports told Kommersant they wanted faster notification when emergency restrictions were lifted. Gelendzhik airport said timely Defense Ministry updates were particularly important for assisting passengers and clearing aircraft left on the apron during closures.
Rosaviatsia also cited weather and aircraft malfunctions as causes of delays and cancellations.
Industry sources have previously told Kommersant that frequent airport closures allow airlines to obscure problems with the condition of their fleets.
The Transportation Ministry said the share of delays attributed to technical problems fell from 12.7% to 10.1% year on year. Industry sources linked the decline to airlines operating fewer aircraft.
According to Kommersant, airlines had not brought 20% of their aircraft into service for the peak travel season. Among the top 10 carriers, excluding Aeroflot, roughly a third of their fleets were idle.

title: St. Petersburg Court Fines Yabloko Leader $12 for Writing Peace Slogans on Ballot
description: A St.
content:
A St. Petersburg judge on Friday fined Yabloko party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov 1,000 rubles ($11.80) for writing anti-war slogans on his ballots during last month’s State Duma elections.
Rybakov had written four party slogans on his ballots while voting at a polling station on Sept. 20: “For Peace,” “For Freedom,” “For a Life Without Fear” and “For a Ceasefire Agreement.”
Police accused him of “ignoring society’s interests, showing disrespect and breaking public order.”
The Vyborgsky District Court found Rybakov guilty of disorderly conduct.
Rybakov and his defense urged the court to drop all charges, maintaining that spoiling a ballot is a legally recognized form of political expression.
Rybakov and his lawyers sought dismissal of the case, arguing that spoiling a ballot was a lawful form of political expression.
“I expressed my civic stance that I couldn’t vote because there was no one to vote for… Over 900,000 voters did the exact same thing by invalidating their ballots,” Rybakov said during an earlier hearing.
Rybakov was not present for Friday’s verdict, which was briefly interrupted by an evacuation order.
Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party, was the only registered political party campaigning for peace in the 2026 State Duma elections.
Ryabkov's case came amid mounting pressure on the party. Three prominent Yabloko members have received prison sentences in the past four months, most recently Yelena Perepelitsa on Thursday.
Yabloko candidates were widely barred from contesting the Sept. 18-20 elections, in which the ruling United Russia party secured a record majority in the State Duma.
Besides being struck from the party-list ballot, Yabloko’s candidates running for seats in the lower house faced interference from the authorities, police detentions and disqualification in single-member constituencies where they could still run.
Yabloko was also barred from almost all regional legislative elections. The northwestern Novgorod region was the only region where Yabloko cleared the 5% vote threshold needed to win seats in the regional legislature.

title: Rosneft Recruits Anti-Aircraft Gun Crews to Defend Samara Refinery Against Ukrainian Drones – Vyorstka
description: State oil giant Rosneft has advertised jobs for anti-aircraft gun and armored vehicle crews to defend a refinery in the southern city of Samara against Ukrainian drones, the exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported Friday.
content:
State oil giant Rosneft has advertised jobs for anti-aircraft gun and armored vehicle crews to defend a refinery in the southern city of Samara against Ukrainian drones, the exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported Friday.
The listings on Russian recruitment website HeadHunter sought personnel to operate Soviet-era anti-aircraft guns and infantry fighting vehicles at the address of Rosneft’s Kuibyshev refinery, the outlet reported.
The Kuibyshev refinery, on the Volga River, has been repeatedly targeted since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Applicants’ duties included intercepting aerial targets and keeping armored vehicles stationed at the refinery ready for combat, Vyorstka reported.
The advertised monthly compensation totaled 249,000 rubles ($2,938), including salary, regional governor bonuses and military reserve pay. Applicants were also offered hostel accommodation, three meals a day and mandatory health and life insurance.
The listings were removed and archived shortly after publication, with HeadHunter indicating that the employer was no longer accepting applications, Vyorstka said.
Russia’s top business lobby told President Vladimir Putin in May that recruiting reservists to guard major companies was difficult because they were regularly rotated to other facilities.
Russian businesses spent more than 441 million rubles ($5.3 million) on anti-drone protection in the first half of 2026, a more than sixfold increase compared to the previous year.
In August, President Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing the state to place strategically important facilities under temporary administration if their operators were deemed to have failed to protect them adequately from Ukrainian attacks or repair damage quickly.
The measure covers industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities considered important to national security and economic stability.
Putin later said the decree had “nothing to do with any plans for nationalization” of private property.

title: Russia’s Central Bank Says Putin’s Stock Market Target Is Out of Reach
description: Russia’s Central Bank sees no realistic path to meeting President Vladimir Putin’s target for expanding the stock market by 2030, a senior official said, as falling share prices and limited investor demand push the goal further out of reach.
content:
Russia’s Central Bank sees no realistic path to meeting President Vladimir Putin’s target for expanding the stock market by 2030, a senior official said, as falling share prices and limited investor demand push the goal further out of reach.
The Central Bank and Finance Ministry are reassessing what level of market capitalization Russia can achieve, Interfax cited First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin as saying Thursday.
Putin ordered Russia to double its stock market capitalization to at least 66% of gross domestic product by 2030 in a decree issued in May 2024, shortly after beginning another presidential term.
“Our calculations simply do not get us to 66%,” Chistyukhin said.
The assessment underscores the difficulties of expanding a market that has lost access to much of its foreign investor base since Russia invaded Ukraine and now relies heavily on individual investors.
Market capitalization, the combined value of listed companies, has fallen by about a third since Putin issued the decree.
“We are moving very quickly, but unfortunately in the opposite direction,” Sergei Shvetsov, chairman of the Moscow Exchange’s supervisory board, said previously.
According to Central Bank calculations , the MOEX stock index has been among the worst-performing financial instruments both since the start of the war and this year. Investors have lost 10.5% since the beginning of 2022, even after accounting for dividends.
Rating agency Expert RA estimated that stock market capitalization had fallen from 47% of GDP to 23%, meaning it would now need to roughly triple to meet Putin’s target.
The Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting, a think tank close to the Kremlin, projects that capitalization will reach 40% of GDP by 2030 in its optimistic scenario. Its pessimistic forecast puts the figure at 28.8%, below the level when Putin signed the decree.
Market capitalization can grow through rising share prices or new listings. Chistyukhin warned that the measures under consideration might still be insufficient to reach the target.
Meeting it would require enormous share offerings, he said, raising questions about whether investors could absorb them.
Since the invasion, funds belonging to investors from countries Moscow designates as “unfriendly” have been frozen in special accounts. Individual investors now account for about two-thirds of share trading on the Moscow Exchange.
Chistyukhin cited the roughly 30 billion ruble ($354 million) initial public offering by state housing finance company Dom.RF, the largest in recent years, as a deal individual investors had been able to absorb.
Offerings of 300 billion rubles ($3.54 billion) or 500 billion rubles ($5.9 billion) would pose a much greater challenge, he said.
Expert RA has also warned that individual investors cannot replace foreign funds in large deals worth 50 billion rubles ($590 million) or more.
Sberbank CEO German Gref and Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina have both identified investor confidence as essential to increasing stock market valuations.
Repeated tax increases, nationalizations and the seizure of shares bought on the exchange have raised concerns about the security of investments.
Gref said Sberbank, Russia’s most valuable publicly traded company, had long tracked the performance of its most successful investors. Those who took a cautious approach and favored bank deposits consistently came out ahead.
“Over a 10-year horizon, a five-year horizon and a three-year horizon, conservative investors won every time,” he said.

title: Nearly Half of Russian Companies Plan to Skip Year-End Bonuses, Survey Finds
description: Nearly half of Russian companies do not plan to pay employees annual bonuses for 2026, a survey showed, as businesses face financial pressure from rising taxes, high borrowing costs and weak demand.
content:
Nearly half of Russian companies do not plan to pay employees annual bonuses for 2026, a survey showed, as businesses face financial pressure from rising taxes, high borrowing costs and weak demand.
The survey of 1,076 organizations across Russia, conducted by accounting service Aktion Bukhgalteriya and reported by Forbes , found that 46.9% did not intend to pay year-end bonuses. Another 20.4% had postponed a decision indefinitely, while 10.4% planned to reward only some employees.
Just 22.3% said they would definitely pay bonuses to all staff.
The findings point to growing pressure on employee compensation as companies contend with higher operating costs and customers increasingly fall behind on payments, business experts said.
Annual financial results were the main factor determining bonus decisions for 56.9% of respondents. Another 23% said the decision rested with the owner or parent company, while 8.8% cited the tax burden and social insurance contributions payable on bonuses.
Rising taxes and costs are driving the trend, Yekaterina Avdeyeva, chair of the coordinating council at the Center for Business Protection NGO, told Forbes.
Russia raised its corporate income tax rate from 20% to 25% on Jan. 1, 2025, followed by an increase in value-added tax to 22% in 2026. The annual revenue threshold at which businesses using the simplified tax system must pay VAT was also cut from 60 million rubles ($708,000) to 20 million rubles ($236,000).
Borrowing costs are adding to the strain, with the Central Bank’s key interest rate at 14%.
For many industries, typical profit margins make borrowing at rates of 10% to 15% economically unviable, Avdeyeva said. Bank deposits offering returns of 13% to 19% can generate comparable income without the risks of running a business, she added.
Companies also face weak demand and increasingly late payments from customers and business partners, she said.
The pressure is likely to widen the gap between bonus payments at large and small businesses, Alla Starchenko, a leading expert at Aktion Bukhgalteriya, told Forbes.
Large companies have financial reserves, established performance targets and formal incentive programs that will allow them to keep paying bonuses, she said.
Small businesses, where decisions often depend on a single owner and current revenue, will increasingly forgo bonuses or limit them to a few key employees, Starchenko added.
Further tax increases are now the main risk facing businesses, Avdeyeva said. Forgoing bonuses could become routine as companies try to stay afloat, though the practice could also hurt productivity, she added.

title: Ukraine Drones Hit Second Yandex Data Center in Two Days
description: Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Friday that several modules at its data center in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been completely disabled by a drone attack, the second in two days. “Part of Yandex data center infrastructure in Kaluga was damaged in a drone attack.
content:
Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Friday that several modules at its data center in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been completely disabled by a drone attack, the second in two days.
“Part of Yandex data center infrastructure in Kaluga was damaged in a drone attack. Several data center modules are completely disabled,” Yandex told Interfax, warning that some of its services may experience disruptions.
Kaluga region Governor Vladislav Shapsha southwest of Moscow said nine people were injured and infrastructure was damaged by Ukrainian drones. He did not comment on the Yandex data center attack.
The strike comes a day after a Ukrainian drone hit another Yandex data center in the Ryazan region southeast of the capital, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed.
Yandex, whose apps have become an indispensable part of many Russia ns' lives, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to keep its services going.
"Our teams are working day and night to do everything possible to keep services running and to help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one," the company said in a statement Friday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described the targeted attacks as retaliation to Russia’s recent missile strikes against Ukrainian server facilities in Kyiv.
“We always respond symmetrically,” Zelensky told reporters Thursday.
Russia has conducted a strike campaign against Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
In the Tver region north of Moscow, a drone reportedly struck an experimental plant described as a major chemical producer of liquid fuel for Russia’s Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles.
Tver region Governor Vitaly Korolyov confirmed a drone attack on an unidentified factory, saying its employees had been evacuated in advance.
In the southwestern Belgorod region, Ukrainian shelling of a residential home killed a husband and wife and injured four others, including a 10-year-old child.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 505 Ukrainian drones overnight.
On Friday morning, reports indicated that Ukrainian also attacked a Lukoil refinery in the northern republic of Komi.
Both Russia and Ukraine have expanded drone attacks this year on economic targets, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, e-commerce warehouses and, most recently, data centers.

title: Former German Chancellor Schroeder Celebrates Putin's Birthday at President's Home
description: Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder helped celebrate Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday at the leader's home, the Kremlin said on Thursday.
content:
Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder helped celebrate Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday at the leader's home, the Kremlin said on Thursday.
Pictures posted on Telegram showed Schroeder and Putin smiling broadly and shaking hands, with an old-style stove and a Russian samovar used to boil water for tea in the background.
"Vladimir Putin found out from the morning news the day before that Gerhard Schroeder was in Moscow and had come on business for the company Globus," the Kremlin said on Telegram.
"The president invited his old friend to his home. Gerhard Schroeder was with Vladimir Putin when the head of state celebrated his birthday yesterday."
Schroeder, who served as chancellor from 1998 to 2005, recently joined the supervisory board of Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus. He visited one of its Moscow stores on Wednesday and was greeted with applause from employees, Russian TV footage showed.
Schroeder has faced criticism, notably in Germany, over his links to Russian business and Putin, ties that have persisted despite Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent waves of Western sanctions.
Putin suggested in May that Schroeder could represent European countries in peace talks to settle the conflict.
European foreign ministers rejected the notion of any such role for Schroeder.
