title: Oil Slick Expands Near Sochi After Tanker Fire, Greenpeace Says
description: An oil slick in the Black Sea near Russia’s resort city of Sochi has expanded following a fire aboard a tanker attacked by sea drones earlier this week, Greenpeace said Friday, a day after authorities reopened beaches and reported no oil contamination.
content:
An oil slick in the Black Sea near Russia’s resort city of Sochi has expanded following a fire aboard a tanker attacked by sea drones earlier this week, Greenpeace said Friday, a day after authorities reopened beaches and reported no oil contamination.
The slick grew from 8 to 25 square kilometers over three days, the environmental group said , citing satellite images from Planet Labs.
Greenpeace said the slick extended along the route taken by the Aframax Rio after the attack. Around midday Wednesday, the tanker was near Lazarevskoye, about 50 kilometers from the site of the fire. By Thursday, it was near Tuapse. Environmentalists believe the vessel may be under tow to Novorossiysk.
Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius closed their beaches on Tuesday after the Liberian-flagged tanker caught fire following an attack attributed to Ukrainian sea drones.
Authorities reopened the beaches Thursday, saying tests found no oil contamination.
Sochi’s administration said seawater samples taken across the city met sanitary standards, according to consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor. Satellite monitoring also found no oil slicks, it added.
Sirius administration head Dmitry Plishkin said tests found no traces of oil in seawater and air pollution levels remained within permitted limits.
The tanker was attacked on the evening of Oct. 6. The fire sent thick black smoke over Sochi. Russia’s Transportation Ministry said burning oil prevented rescue vessels from approaching the ship. The flames were extinguished on Wednesday.
All 23 crew members, who were Indian nationals, were rescued.
The amount of oil aboard the tanker has not been disclosed. The Mash Telegram news channel, citing unidentified sources, reported that the vessel was fully loaded.
The tanker continued to drift along the coast after the fire. Its operator, Executive Ship Management, said Wednesday that officials and two senior crew members had started inspecting the vessel to assess its condition.
Built in 2004, the Aframax Rio is 247 meters long and 42 meters wide, with a deadweight capacity of 107,100 metric tons.
According to the investigative outlet The Insider, the tanker has called at Russian Black Sea ports and is under Ukrainian sanctions. Kyiv has linked it to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” a network of tankers used to transport oil and circumvent sanctions.

title: Moscow Region Man Killed in Ukrainian Drone Attack

content:

A 37-year-old woman also sustained injuries during the attack.

Civil aviation authorities temporarily suspended arrivals and departures at Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky airports to ensure flight safety during the air raid alert.

title: Russia Says Checks Following Siberian Plague Lab Death Are Complete
description: Russia said on Thursday it had completed health checks on all the contacts of a deceased lab worker at a plague research facility in Siberia, signaling a desire to draw a line under the affair.
content:
Russia said on Thursday it had completed health checks on all the contacts of a deceased lab worker at a plague research facility in Siberia, signaling a desire to draw a line under the affair.
Statements from the state health watchdog and the regional governor said monitoring of all the dead woman's contacts had concluded, and reiterated that no dangerous pathogens had been found in nearly 5,000 samples.
"Amidst intense media scrutiny, the specialists thoroughly investigated the situation. It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion," Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said.
Yet despite pressure from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United States, Russian authorities have yet to state definitively whether the death of 28-year-old lab worker Darya Shipilova on Oct. 2 could have been caused by plague.
They have previously stated that she died from pneumonia but that the origin of the pneumonia had yet to be determined. They have also said she was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body.
On Wednesday, senior WHO official Maria Van Kerkhove said the global body wanted more information from Russia on what laboratory tests had been conducted, which pathogens were evaluated and that "if this individual didn't die from plague, then how did she die?"
Russia says it has provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures.
Global health officials — as well as the world's media — have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the Covid-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China.
However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined.
The lung infection can have a variety of causes other than plague, including other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as Covid or flu.

title: Russian Liberal Politician Jailed for 4 Years Over Donation to Navalny Group
description: Elena Perepelitsa, a member of Russia's liberal Yabloko party which opposes the war in Ukraine, has been sentenced to four years in a penal colony for donating money to an "extremist" organization, state news agency TASS reported on Thursday.
content:
Elena Perepelitsa, a member of Russia's liberal Yabloko party which opposes the war in Ukraine, has been sentenced to four years in a penal colony for donating money to an "extremist" organization, state news agency TASS reported on Thursday.
She was the third Yabloko member to be jailed in less than four months as authorities step up pressure on the opposition party, which was largely barred from contesting September's parliamentary election.
Perepelitsa was found guilty of donating money to the late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, which is designated in Russia as a "foreign agent" and outlawed as an extremist organization.
In a post on Telegram, Yabloko confirmed the verdict and shared Perepelitsa's statement to the court in which she denied knowingly financing extremist activity.
Since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022, Russia's use of extremist designations and strict wartime censorship laws have prompted many opposition figures and activists to flee the country, while those who remain risk prosecution for expressing anti-war views and other dissent.
Yabloko's deputy leader Maxim Kruglov was convicted in June of spreading lies about the Russian army and jailed for seven years.
In August, the party's deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg was sentenced to just over 11 years in a penal colony for discrediting Russia's Armed Forces and spreading false information about them, after condemning the war in Ukraine.

title: How ‘Digital Oblivion’ Is Helping Russia Rewrite the Past
description: The disappearance of independent journalism, firsthand accounts and historical archives from the internet is helping Russia and other authoritarian states rewrite history and shape collective memory, researchers warn.
content:
The disappearance of independent journalism, firsthand accounts and historical archives from the internet is helping Russia and other authoritarian states rewrite history and shape collective memory, researchers warn.
From altered reporting on the Beslan school siege to vanishing articles documenting anti-government protests, the loss of online records — a process that researchers call “digital oblivion” — is contributing to public “amnesia” about key events that autocrats find unhelpful.
As artificial intelligence becomes a gateway to news and information, the researchers warn that gaps in the historical record combined with a flood of propaganda can shape the answers people receive about the past.
“Digital tools are used to consolidate what would have otherwise been a more painstaking process,” Steven Feldstein, a researcher with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said at a recent panel at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York.
Autocratic leaders who have long relied on violence, intimidation and legal harassment to consolidate power have added powerful digital tactics to their toolkit. These can make independent accounts of key events harder to find, unsafe to publish or impossible to verify.
Digital oblivion can involve a government’s or a company’s deliberate removal of a website or archive, or can be the quiet disappearance or blocking of online photos, blogs or social media posts. Records can also become inaccessible through broken links and obsolete media formats, even when the cause is unclear.
The erasure can be ad hoc or systematic. It is more expansive than old-school censorship.
“Contemporary autocratic politics is all about a ‘glorious past.’ The thing that needs to happen is the ‘past’ needs to be cleaned up,” said panelist M. Gessen, co-founder of Kronika, an initiative to preserve independent journalism.
Documentation of large-scale anti-Putin protests in Moscow in 2015 has become difficult to find online, as has material tracing the development of Russia’s LGBTQ+ movement, Gessen said.
In some cases, reporting remains available while passages challenging the official account disappear.
A Russian translation of “The School,” journalist C.J. Chivers’ account of the 2004 Beslan hostage crisis for Esquire, was heavily edited around the tragedy’s 20th anniversary, according to a 2025 analysis by Mediazona using the Wayback Machine.
The translation had been preserved on the website of Pravila Zhizni, the magazine that replaced Russian Esquire after it lost its license in 2022.
Mediazona’s analysis found that parts of the online article changed, including a passage describing how most of the deaths occurred after Russian troops stormed the school. The article’s conclusion that the siege had shaken faith in the Russian government and its ability to protect the Russian people also disappeared.
An investigation by Citizen Lab , a Canada-based research group, documented extensive blocking of content on Ukraine, Belarus and LGBTQ+ issues, as well as accounts belonging to independent media and users opposing Putin or supporting Ukraine, on Russian social network VKontakte.
At times, ordinary people have voluntarily become tools of digital oblivion, the panelists said.
Gessen cited the example of a Belarusian woman who deleted photos documenting her participation in anti-government protests following President Alexander Lukashenko’s disputed 2020 re-election in order to protect herself.
China’s restrictions on information about the June 4, 1989, Tiananmen massacre mark an early success story for digital oblivion. Online censorship makes accounts of the military’s crackdown on the student-led protests difficult to find on the Chinese internet, while documentation of subsequent protests in Hong Kong has also been heavily restricted.
The panelists said similar pressures on the public record can emerge in democracies.
Gessen recalled the case of a U.S. scientist who removed language about climate change from existing research and inserted language acceptable to the Trump administration to safeguard funding from the National Institutes of Health.
Panelists also pointed to the Trump administration’s removal of information from government websites and changes that have made studies and reports harder to find online.
AI is accelerating the impact of these disappearances, the researchers warned. Digital oblivion regularly leads to large language models being trained on faulty and incomplete sources, or censored information. Decisions by AI companies about which material to use and how to present it can then influence what people know and understand about a historical event.
“AI companies have become increasingly opaque in how they are training their models,” Sarah Myers West, co-director of the AI Now Institute and an expert on technology policymaking, said at the panel, titled “Digital Oblivion: How Autocrats Engineer Forgetting.”
A flood of low-quality, AI-generated content often called “AI slop” can create further noise, making reliable accounts harder to find.
Pro-Kremlin information operations have demonstrated how large volumes of misleading content can influence AI responses.
NewsGuard, a company that analyzes misinformation, said in a March 2025 report that the pro-Kremlin disinformation network Pravda was flooding search results and material retrieved by AI chatbots with false claims and propaganda.
A separate NewsGuard analysis showed a video produced by Russian influence operation Storm-1516 was provided by an AI chatbot as evidence that Ukrainian soldiers had burned an effigy of U.S. President Donald Trump and promoted other false claims about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
A November 2025 analysis by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue identified roughly 900 political websites that have linked to Pravda network articles, with the majority citing them as credible sources.
The institute said the network had published more than 6 million articles since its launch in 2014 and was publishing new content every few seconds.
Efforts to preserve that record are growing, such as in librarians’ work to save data and archives, citizens protesting data-center construction and communities rejecting Flock cameras.
In Russia, activists are working to safeguard the history of the LGBTQ+ movement as state restrictions threaten both its participants and its archives.
Readers can also reduce their exposure to manipulated narratives by consulting original reporting and verifying information through multiple reliable sources, rather than through the framework, and lack of context, of an AI platform, panelists said.
But preserving access to reliable information also requires action from governments as AI infrastructure becomes increasingly embedded in institutions, schools and systems, they argued.
“They need to have real incentives to train their models on facts,” said Gessen.

title: U.K. Expands Sanctions to Cover 90% of Russian Oil Output, Shadow Fleet and Finance Networks
description: Britain on Thursday announced sanctions targeting 38 Russian energy companies, shadow fleet oil tankers and financial networks that allegedly fuel Russia’s war effort. “The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences,” the Foreign Office said in a statement.
content:
Britain on Thursday announced sanctions targeting 38 Russian energy companies, shadow fleet oil tankers and financial networks that allegedly fuel Russia’s war effort.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences,” the Foreign Office said in a statement.
London added 17 entities and individuals supplying high-priority goods to Russia, including importers of machine tools and electronics key to the country’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities.
One of the sanctioned individuals is Dutch national Alexander Jan Hendrik Tattersall, who is allegedly associated with the sanctioned Turkish trader Redwing Metal.
Britain sanctioned two Russian energy producers, saying the restrictions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity.
An additional 12 tankers were also sanctioned, expanding the total number of targeted shadow fleet vessels to more than 600.
Targeting Russia’s alternative payment systems and crypto exchanges used to bypass Western sanctions, Britain designated five financial entities, including one registered in Canada and three in Kyrgyzstan.
The financial measures follow the U.S. Treasury’s recent crackdown on Russia’s A7 shadow banking network, which the U.S. claimed to have processed through sub-agents more than $17 billion in global transactions between January 2025 and June 2026.
The Foreign Office claimed two of the newly sanctioned payment platforms directly facilitated transactions for the A7 platform.

title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Yandex Data Center, Industrial Facilities Across Russia
description: A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at a data center owned by Russian tech giant Yandex in the Ryazan region overnight, the company said Thursday, suspending the site’s operations and triggering service disruptions.
content:
A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at a data center owned by Russian tech giant Yandex in the Ryazan region overnight, the company said Thursday, suspending the site’s operations and triggering service disruptions.
The attack marks the first confirmed strike against Russian data infrastructure since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, weeks after Moscow launched attacks against Ukrainian data centers.
Yandex confirmed that operations at the facility in the town of Sasovo were fully suspended while emergency teams worked to contain the damage, according to a statement circulated in the media. Governor Pavel Malkov said the roof of a Sasovo district company, which he did not name, caught fire.
NASA’s fire monitoring service FIRMS showed a fire in Sasovo early Thursday morning.
Outage tracking platform Downdetector recorded more than 1,300 user reports of disruptions affecting Yandex Cloud, Yandex Documents and Yandex Tables, while core consumer tools like search and taxi services remained online.
Yandex shares dropped more than 3.4% during Thursday morning trading on the Moscow Exchange.
A fire also broke out at an industrial site in Russia’s town of Salavat in the republic of Bashkortostan after drone debris fell on it, local authorities reported on Thursday.
There are no casualties, and the enterprise continues operations, they added.
Ukrainian forces struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemicals complex in central Russia’s Bashkortostan region, Kyiv’s military said on Thursday.
In a statement, the General Staff said the attack had sparked a fire.
On Thursday afternoon, eyewitnesses told the exiled outlet Astra that Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s largest oil refinery in the Omsk region of western Siberia.
Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed a Ukrainian drone attack on the Omsk region without specifying the targets. Civil aviation authorities suspended inbound and outbound flights during the afternoon air raid alert.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 399 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight.
The Sasovo attack comes after Russian forces have, since late September, hit at least eight major data centers across Kyiv, causing widespread internet blackouts in Ukraine. Russia claimed the data centers processed military intelligence for Ukrainian forces.

title: Lithuania Deploys Army to Kaliningrad Border After Belarus-Latvia Breach
description: Lithuania is deploying troops to reinforce its border with Russian exclave Kaliningrad, officials announced late Wednesday, citing concerns over potential military mobilization in Russia and renewed hybrid threats.
content:
Lithuania is deploying troops to reinforce its border with Russian exclave Kaliningrad, officials announced late Wednesday, citing concerns over potential military mobilization in Russia and renewed hybrid threats.
The decision follows a high-profile security breach on the border between Latvia and Belarus this week, said Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas.
Defense Minister Robertas Kauna confirmed the deployment of border security, saying it was a “preventive” step in response to “signals of a possible increase in aggressive foreigners due to possible mobilization in Russia.”
Kaunas said around 100 soldiers would help guard the Lithuanian-Russian border over the next two weeks, according to the Elta news agency.
“The order is being executed immediately,” Kaunas wrote on Facebook
Katelynas and Lithuania’s border security service stressed that the situation along the Kaliningrad border remains calm, with zero illegal border crossings from neighboring Belarus over five consecutive days.
On Tuesday, Latvian authorities reported that masked and armed individuals escorted a group of 20 irregular migrants to push through the Belarus border into Latvian territory. The masked operatives damaged electrical equipment and stole border surveillance cameras before retreating back into Belarusian territory.
Also this week, the Kremlin warned that Lithuania’s preliminary parliamentary vote to lift a constitutional ban on hosting foreign nuclear weapons marked a dangerous escalation of regional tensions.

title: Russian Bomb Kills 33 at Bus Stop in Kramatorsk
description: A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said on Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow.
content:
A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said on Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow.
Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a bus stop.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus.
“For them (the Russians), a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Moscow's forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine's “fortress belt,” local officials say, the backbone of its defenses in the Donetsk region.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow's battlefield gains in the region has significantly slowed this year.
Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying “we have no right to risk” citizens' lives.
Thursday's attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air attack across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country's power grid.
Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defenses.

title: Regions Calling: In Irkutsk, Locals Ask 'What Plague?'
description: Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments beyond the Russian capital from The Moscow Times.
content:
Hello and welcome to Regions Calling , your guide to developments beyond the Russian capital from The Moscow Times.
The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region soared to global headlines after local bloggers circulated unconfirmed reports and the head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia named “plague” as the suspected cause.
We spoke with residents of both regions about how the health scare is affecting their everyday lives. We also asked an independent health policy expert to weigh in on Moscow’s handling of the possible outbreak and what risks it poses to the rest of the world.
But first, a look at the latest news from the regions:
Authorities in the Krasnodar region closed beaches in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and surrounding areas on Tuesday after an oil tanker caught fire offshore following a reported drone attack. Ecologists have already warned that the incident could have potentially catastrophic environmental consequences, including water contamination and the release of large volumes of hazardous substances into the air.
Meanwhile, Yevgeny Naumov, the mayor of the region’s capital Krasnodar, preemptively resigned on Monday after four years in office plagued by controversy. In January, Naumov signed off on plans to build an Orthodox Church on the grounds of a riverside park despite protests from residents. Since November 2025, more than 30,000 people have signed a petition demanding his resignation.
A string of deadly bear attacks on humans has continued across Siberia and the Far East over the past few weeks. In the latest confirmed incident, a 55-year-old man was killed by a bear that entered a trailer parked on the premises of a local company in the eastern part of the Irkutsk region. At least 20 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since April. In response, lawmakers are reportedly considering lifting hunting quotas, establishing regional population limits and giving local authorities extra powers to control bear numbers. Authorities in the Krasnoyarsk region said Monday that they have already culled more than 850 bears “as part of the population control measures.” Read more about reasons behind the attacks in the previous edition of Regions Calling .
A military court in the Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia on charges of organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization. Khankhalaeva called the verdict “high praise” and proof that she and fellow members of pro-independence group Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia “are doing the right thing” in comments to The Moscow Times.
The former head of Dagestan Sergei Melikov was appointed as a senator from the western Bryansk region in Russia’s upper-house Federation Council last week. Melikov, who had headed Dagestan since 2020, resigned from the post in May following public backlash over his handling of deadly floods in the mountainous republic.
“There are no conversations on the streets, no bustle, no fear, no lines at the pharmacies like there were during Covid,” a woman from Irkutsk, the capital of the Siberian region of the same name, tells The Moscow Times.
“There was panic for maybe the first few hours after the news broke. Then memes began to appear online and everyone calmed down,” she adds. “ There are so many things going on at once: the fuel crises , the bear invasion , now the plague. People here treat these things as background noise.”
Irkutsk , a region roughly the size of Turkey with a population of 2.3 million people, made international headlines after a 28-year-old employee of a local plague research institute died at a hospital in the Irkutsk suburb of Shelekhov last week.
The highly urbanized industrial region was until now best known for the UNESCO-enscribed Lake Baikal , the world’s largest freshwater lake by volume — that is, before the latest global plague-induced scare.
But for most locals, who say they found out about the possible plague case from social media, little has changed.
“Life goes on as usual in Irkutsk,” another local told The Moscow Times on Wednesday. “Today I met a doctor on the street and asked them about the outbreak. She said that there was one case, but now everything is calm.”
News that the lab worker, Daria Shipilova, may have died from plague first surfaced in since-deleted posts on local anonymous Telegram channels in the early hours of Oct. 2, local independent news outlet Irkutsk Blog reported .
A handful of news outlets soon picked up the rumor and added more unverified details.
The exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) cited an anonymous source who said the victim was hospitalized after arriving from Thailand, while local TV channel NTS was the first to speculate that the woman got infected after accidentally breaking a test tube containing live bacteria.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev confirmed that the head of state health and safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had arrived in the region because of “a suspected case of a highly dangerous infection.”
“All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness and laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev said on Oct. 2.
Rospotrebnadzor also avoided the word “plague” in its first statement on the matter published Sunday, saying Shipilova died from a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The first — and only — Russian official to use the word “plague” was Alexei Tsydenov, the head of the republic of Buryatia , which borders the Irkutsk region to the east and south.
“The woman who died — possibly from the plague — in the Irkutsk region had not traveled to Buryatia. There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the area bordering Mongolia,” Tsydenov said .
Vadim Palko, a journalist at Irkutsk Blog, said he believes that Tsydenov’s statement was more of a calculated attempt to distance himself from unwelcome news that likely upset the Kremlin than a heartfelt urge to reveal the truth to the public.
“He tried, first of all, to protect himself by signaling that all the problems are coming from Irkutsk,” Palko said, adding that Tsydenov’s reaction was likely prompted by rumors that the lab worker allegedly traveled to a “plague hotspot in Buryatia.”
The atmosphere in Buryatia, meanwhile, has been largely similar to that in Irkutsk.
“I found out about the plague from Instagram, from friends who sent me funny reels about it,” said a resident of Buryatia’s capital Ulan-Ude.
“I haven’t been taking any precautionary measures…But now that you have asked, I am thinking maybe I should have? But, actually, what should be done in case of a plague outbreak?” she told The Moscow Times.
This lack of “effective and trusted communication” with the public could prove Moscow’s biggest misstep in handling the plague scare, said Judyth Twigg, a professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University and an expert on Russia’s health system.
The World Health Organization recorded 3,847 suspected human plague cases and 423 deaths across 10 countries between 2019 and 2025. The majority were recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, but some were also reported in the rural parts of the western United States.
“Residents [of the Irkutsk region] should have received practical guidance…with regular updates, even when the update is that there are no new cases,” Twigg told The Moscow Times.
“It’s what health authorities elsewhere do with plague cases as a matter of routine course, and none of it would have required Russia to concede anything embarrassing beyond the possibility of a laboratory accident,” she added.
Twigg said the measures Russia has reportedly taken appeared operationally sound, including the rapid identification and observation of contacts, isolation measures, precautions scaled to a dangerous pathogen and on-site oversight by specialists.
Today, plague “is not a plausible mass threat to any society with a functioning public health system,” she said, a take echoed by other health science professionals.
“Even though the plague pathogen Yersinia pestis is dangerous and actually causes a very severe and tricky disease, events of the past are not expected to repeat today,” said science journalist Irina Yakutenko, referencing the 14th-century plague pandemic known as the Black Death.
“Beyond the pathogen itself, certain conditions are needed for it to spread: people, rats and fleas who are all constantly in contact with each other,” added Yakutenko.
Rospotrebnadzor announced Wednesday that it has concluded a series of “preventive and anti-epidemic measures” in the Irkutsk region, which reportedly included medical observations of more than 90% of contacts and 5,000 laboratory tests that failed to reveal any dangerous pathogens.
“There are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region,” the health watchdog said.
Meanwhile, the lack of transparency surrounding the incident has already fueled conspiracies that the Irkutsk plague research lab could be part of a state-sponsored bioweapons program.
“Russia's history…provides plenty of reason to ask hard questions. In this case, though, there’s nothing in the public record supporting the conclusion that this civilian surveillance institute was doing something exotic,” Twigg said.
“Transparency would be Moscow's cheapest and most effective rebuttal, but the system isn’t designed to supply transparency.”
Residents of Oshurkovo, a village on the left bank of the Selenga River in the republic of Buryatia , put up scarecrows to protest the planned opening of a controversial apatite ore mining site.
“Even the pumpkin knows that apatites equal the death of Baikal. Do you?” says the banner attached to the scarecrow.
State environmental watchdog Rosprirodnadzor greenlit the Russian Copper Company ’s mining project earlier this year despite residents and scientists voicing concerns about the threat it poses to Lake Baikal, which is fed by the Selenga.

title: EU Lifts Belarus-Related Sanctions on Russian Billionaire Gutseriev – RFE/RL
description: The European Union has removed Russian billionaire Mikhail Gutseriev and Belarusian businessman Viktor Shevtsov from its Belarus sanctions list following successful court challenges, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Belarusian service reported Wednesday.
content:
The European Union has removed Russian billionaire Mikhail Gutseriev and Belarusian businessman Viktor Shevtsov from its Belarus sanctions list following successful court challenges, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Belarusian service reported Wednesday.
Both men had been sanctioned over alleged support for President Alexander Lukashenko’s government. Their removal follows rulings that the EU Council had failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify keeping the restrictions in place.
Gutseriev remains subject to separate EU sanctions linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine. He was added to that list on July 23, with the EU Council citing his involvement in industries that generate substantial revenue for the Russian government and investment projects that support it.
Shevtsov is not subject to any other EU sanctions, RFE/RL reported.
Gutseriev initially failed to overturn the Belarus sanctions. The EU’s General Court rejected his challenge in September 2023, and the Court of Justice dismissed his appeal in May 2025.
But the General Court annulled his 2024 sanctions renewals in October 2025, followed by the February 2025 renewal on May 13 this year.
The court found that the EU Council had not provided sufficient evidence that Gutseriev continued to support Lukashenko’s government or benefit from his ties to it.
The EU first sanctioned Gutseriev on June 21, 2021, describing him as a longtime friend of Lukashenko. It cited his investments in Belarus, including the Nezhinsky mining and processing complex, and his attendance at Lukashenko’s September 2020 inauguration.
Gutseriev founded the Safmar group, whose interests span oil production, coal, real estate, retail and media. Forbes estimates his net worth at $7.7 billion.
The decision follows the EU’s removal of Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list in September after pressure from France and Luxembourg.
Bloomberg reported that Luxembourg pushed for Fridman’s removal after he filed a $16 billion arbitration claim over frozen assets. France sought to lift sanctions on Usmanov as part of negotiations with Azerbaijan to secure the release of French nationals held there.

title: U.S. and Russia Explore Nord Stream Restart, Sources Say
description: Top Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S.
content:
Top Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a U.S. investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.
The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump, the people said.
Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable U.S. investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.
“Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (U.S. International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies,” a White House official said when asked about the pipeline discussions.
There had been “no Nord Stream discussions recently,” the official told Reuters.
Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with U.S. Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential U.S.-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.
It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restart of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.
A U.S. official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The Nord Stream gas pipelines are sanctioned by the U.S. and the EU, making any restart illegal.
Trump could waive or soften U.S. sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.
Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros rebuilding their military to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Nord Stream and Russian gas were sanctioned in Europe and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines required government approval and this was not desired.
Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.
Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.
Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using U.S. talks to push for business deals instead.
Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.
Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.
“This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly,” said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who was in charge ​of German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.
“Americans and Russians will share the profits,” he said.
While Germany's coalition government is opposed to restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.
Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.
But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a U.S. investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.
The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.
The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence, should Gazprom sell its stake, said another person.
Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating “prosperity agreements” to encourage peace and give “leaders ... something to look forward to.”
While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.
Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, said one person with knowledge of the government's thinking.
Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, which are owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, said two other people familiar with the matter.
Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while U.S. authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.
“On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States,” said a White House official.
Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Ye Earned $20M From Canceled St. Petersburg Gigs, Kommersant Reports
description: Controversial American rapper Ye earned approximately $20 million from two canceled concerts in St.
content:
Controversial American rapper Ye earned approximately $20 million from two canceled concerts in St. Petersburg and is unlikely to return the funds, the business newspaper Kommersant reported Thursday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Originally scheduled for Oct. 10-11 at Gazprom Arena, Ye’s shows were canceled late last month following weeks of venue disputes and backlash from conservative Russian politicians over his past public support of Nazism.
One source told Kommersant that Ye’s $20 million performance fee includes budget allocations for his staff. Another said Ye is unlikely to return the money because his contracts typically do not contain these types of clauses.
State media previously estimated Ye’s performance fee, excluding the musician’s rider and other expenses, at 1 billion rubles ($11.7 million).
Say Agency, the Moscow-based event organizer, announced it would begin refunding tickets next Monday, Oct. 12.
The first court hearings of at least nine civil lawsuits against Say Agency and ticket operator Intickets are scheduled to begin early next month.
Russian law enforcement agencies have launched a preliminary investigation into Say Agency over possible fraud, Kommersant reported.
Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, previously visited Moscow in 2024 to celebrate the birthday of fashion designer and collaborator Gosha Rubchinskiy. Rumors of a performance at Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium circulated at the time.
The rapper has drawn controversy in recent years for his antisemitic remarks. He has previously voiced admiration for Adolf Hitler, and in May 2025, he released a song called “Heil Hitler.”
Ye has faced concert cancellations and performance bans in several European countries this year following his comments.
Ye apologized for his remarks in January, attributing them to his undiagnosed brain injury and untreated bipolar disorder.

title: Denmark Says Russia Has Conducted Sabotage Attacks Against Its Defense Firms
description: Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
content:
Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, Josefine Christensen, lead analyst at the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," Christensen said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western [military alliance] NATO from supporting Ukraine," she said.
Moscow maintains political control over operations, but operational boldness is growing, she said. Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russia n Embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
Christensen cited a Russia n Defense Ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," Christensen said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defense intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including at Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation.

title: Years After His Death, Vladimir Zhirinovsky Lives Rent-Free in Russians’ Heads
description: In late September, President Vladimir Putin took a moment at a meeting with parliamentary party leaders to remember a familiar face missing from this year’s State Duma elections: Vladimir Zhirinovsky. “I would like to say that we certainly miss him, especially under the current circumstances.
content:
In late September, President Vladimir Putin took a moment at a meeting with parliamentary party leaders to remember a familiar face missing from this year’s State Duma elections: Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
“I would like to say that we certainly miss him, especially under the current circumstances. It is a pity that he is gone,” Putin said at the Sept. 28 meeting.
More than four years after his death in 2022 at age 75, Zhirinovsky continues to hold a place in Russia’s popular consciousness, from TikTok to the Kremlin.
His party still campaigns on his image, social media users recast his speeches as prophecies and polling suggests that Russians remember him more fondly than they viewed him during his lifetime.
Meanwhile, the once-fringe nationalist rhetoric he championed has become more prominent in mainstream Russian politics since the invasion of Ukraine.
“Rest in peace, Uncle Vova; you always knew everything,” reads one comment on his official Instagram page .
A fixture in Russian politics for decades, Zhirinovsky led the right-wing populist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) from its inception in 1992 and ran no fewer than six failed presidential campaigns.
As a lawmaker, he was better known for his provocative, outlandish speeches and clashes with fellow politicians than for his legislative work.
Among his more notorious statements were calls to use nuclear weapons against other countries and demands to seize Alaska from the U.S., along with numerous abusive comments toward women.
His persona nevertheless became a source of comic relief for many Russians and the inspiration for countless memes , Instagram reels and musical mixes .
Since his death, that trend has only grown. Social media users create AI videos that cast him as an honest politician and a near-prophet, often contrasting him against depictions of corrupt, greedy officials.
A March 2025 survey by state pollster VTsIOM found that 66% of respondents said they had trusted Zhirinovsky, up from 60% in a survey conducted shortly after his death. During his lifetime, trust in Zhirinovsky had usually fluctuated within 15-30%.
As during his lifetime, it can be difficult to tell where the admiration ends and irony begins.
Following reports that an employee at a Siberian anti-plague institute had fallen ill and died last week, excerpts from Zhirinovsky’s speeches about plague resurfaced on social media.
“Zhirinovsky even predicted the plague in Russia,” says the author of one post.
“He just ran his mouth a lot,” came a reply in the comments.
Yet the idea that Zhirinovsky foresaw events others failed to anticipate has become central to his posthumous popularity. Collections of his predictions that appear to have come true regularly circulate online.
One of the most widely cited examples comes from a State Duma speech in late 2021, when he appeared to anticipate Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
“At 4 a.m. on Feb. 22, you'll feel [our new policy],” Zhirinovsky said. “I’d like 2022 to be peaceful. But I love the truth, for 70 years I've said the truth. It won’t be peaceful. It will be a year when Russia once again becomes great.”
Russian troops invaded Ukraine on Feb. 24, two days after the date he had named.
Some of his statements from the 2000s have also been interpreted as forecasts of Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Many more predictions, including claims that the 2024 U.S. presidential election would be canceled and that NATO would collapse, would not come true.
VTsIOM head Valery Fedorov told the RBC news website that Zhirinovsky’s public image has evolved since his death from that of a scandal-prone politician to a symbol of “patriotism and strategic foresight,” a change he linked to the upheavals of recent years that he said have challenged Russians’ worldview.
“In times of fundamental shifts in the very foundations of how we see the world, radical critics of the old order often turn out to be the greatest realists,” Fedorov said. “Zhirinovsky, who fiercely and relentlessly stripped away the illusions surrounding the rulers and ideologues of the ‘unipolar world,’ proved to be a true herald of a new era of ‘warring kingdoms’.”
Exiled political analyst Abbas Gallyamov, a former Putin speechwriter, offered a different explanation.
“Of course, part of it is that people tend to think more kindly of someone after their death than during their lifetime,” Gallyamov told The Moscow Times.
“But the main reason is that Russia now has a kind of political vacuum: people are dissatisfied with the leaders they have, and no new ones are in sight,” he said. “That applies to the gray mass of officials like [State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav] Volodin, to opposition figures and to Putin himself.”
Zhirinovsky’s image has helped fill that vacuum, Gallyamov said.
“In terms of showmanship, no one comes close to him,” Gallyamov said. “Living standards are falling, there’s no gasoline, and none of the politicians are responding to people’s concerns. That’s when you start wistfully remembering the colorful, charismatic Zhirinovsky.”
Putin and ordinary Russians alike associate Zhirinovsky with the 2000s, a period they now recall with nostalgia amid the war in Ukraine and the economic malaise that has stemmed from it, Gallyamov said.
He also argued that Zhirinovsky helped build a constituency for the nationalist rhetoric that Putin later adopted as his own, then yielded his political niche to the president without putting up a fight.
As for the now 74-year-old Putin, remembering Zhirinovsky may also offer reassurance about his own mortality , Gallyamov suggested.
“The president is aging,” Gallyamov said. “He finds the thought of death unpleasant, but takes comfort in the idea that the ‘right people’ are remembered and loved even after they die.”

title: EU Approves Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Citizens and Entities
description: The European Union has agreed to blacklist more than 1,600 people and entities in the single largest expansion of its sanctions regime against Russia since the beginning of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, diplomats said Wednesday.
content:
The European Union has agreed to blacklist more than 1,600 people and entities in the single largest expansion of its sanctions regime against Russia since the beginning of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, diplomats said Wednesday.
The new listings target 743 individuals and 826 entities primarily linked to Russia’s defense industry, according to Euronews.
More than half are concentrated on missile production, Reuters reported Tuesday.
The 22nd package also targets 77 political figures and election officials in connection with last month’s parliamentary elections held in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Several other Russia-related listings were approved under the EU’s separate North Korea sanctions framework.
The sanctions entail travel bans, asset freezes and prohibitions on receiving EU funding.
EU foreign ministers will formally approve the expanded sanctions list in Luxembourg on Monday, per Reuters, AFP and Euronews. The bloc last approved its 21st sanctions package in July.
The agreement will bring the total number of people and entities under EU sanctions over the war to nearly 4,650.
The agreement follows backlash over the recent removal of oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, concessions made to prevent all other EU listings from lapsing. Usmanov’s removal was linked to the release of a French prisoner in Azerbaijan.
EU officials are reportedly also considering moving toward qualified majority voting for future sanctions to prevent vetoes by single members.

title: Afraid of Mobilization, Many Russians Are Preparing for the Worst. The West Should Help.
description: Opinion | I recently returned from Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where conversations with old Russian friends and newer arrivals in the city who weren’t even of military age in 2022 left me with an unsettling sense of déjà vu.
content:
I recently returned from Tashkent, Uzbekistan, where conversations with old Russian friends and newer arrivals in the city who weren’t even of military age in 2022 left me with an unsettling sense of déjà vu.
One Russian software CEO, who was on a business trip, told me he had sent a dozen male employees of military age on “extended vacation” to Armenia for a few months. Several of my contacts who fled Russia in 2022, but had since returned, are now preparing to leave again or have already gone back to Georgia or Turkey.
“My plan is simple: wait it out outside Russia until it’s safe to return,” said 29-year-old Ruslan, who featured in my recently published book, “ Leaving Russia . ”
When the partial mobilization was announced in September 2022, Ruslan fled Moscow with his pregnant fiancée and their Labrador, Smeliy, driving almost 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) to Georgia in their battered Renault Duster. They struggled to settle in Tbilisi and, in 2024, returned home after a year in Serbia, convinced it was safe to do so.
“This time, I’m leaving on my own for a while,” explained Ruslan, who flew back to Georgia last month. “I never imagined I’d have to go through this all over again.”
There are growing signs of a new wave of Russian emigration, with people already leaving ahead of the State Duma elections on Sept. 18-20. Meduza reported that rumors of post-election mobilization sent Russian arrivals and housing demand surging in Georgia, Armenia and Serbia. Serbian realtors described long lines for apartments, with demand at its highest level since early 2024. Some clients were already booking accommodation for late September.
There is also mounting evidence that Russia is preparing to expand its military manpower, but it may not need another headline-grabbing mobilization order to do so.
Unlike in 2022, the Kremlin now has quieter ways to replenish and expand its ranks: sustained recruitment, conscription, pressure on potential recruits and coercive mobilization in occupied Ukraine. In June, authorities in the Penza region conducted raids to detain local men and pressure them into signing military contracts.
Russia needs more soldiers. Western estimates put Russian casualties at more than 30,000 a month , a staggering toll from the army’s attritional meat-grinder tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent into infantry assaults despite heavy losses.
But replacing battlefield losses is only part of the problem. Modern warfare demands increasingly specialized skills, from drone operators and engineers to programmers and technicians capable of operating sophisticated weapons.
The Kremlin knows it. Russia is already offering university students vast financial incentives to join drone units as operators and engineers. The message is unmistakable: the next generation of Russia’s military will need brains as well as bodies.
If volunteers and mercenaries from North Korea and Nepal are no longer enough, the new draft is likely to target the country's educated youth. That puts the country’s universities at the heart of a new manpower drive. With more than 2 million men in higher education, they represent a vast pool of young people with precisely the skills the military increasingly needs.
Moscow is increasingly treating lecture halls as a recruitment pool. The military is offering university students substantial financial incentives to join drone units as operators and engineers. There have been unconfirmed reports of universities being given recruitment quotas and students, particularly those who failed exams or are in debt, being pressured to enlist.
According to the independent Russian student magazine Groza , 269 Russian universities and colleges are now actively promoting military contracts, effectively turning campuses into recruitment centers.
The offer is hard to ignore, with large payments, academic leave and free tuition after service. In some cases, however, the pressure goes further, with students threatened with academic penalties or expulsion if they refuse.
But signing up does not guarantee a safe distance from the battlefield. Groza reports that drone recruits can be reassigned to combat units, with no guarantee that their contracts will end after a year.
None of this proves that a new mobilization is imminent. But it points to a broader anxiety that has been building for months: requests for emigration assistance have surged, while online searches for mobilization, property in Yerevan and ways to leave Russia have risen sharply.
Unlike four and a half years ago, when emigration was triggered by a sudden shock, in 2026 it is being driven by accumulated risk. Years of war, tighter internet controls, economic decline, the erosion of familiar services, drone attacks and shrinking opportunities have worn people down. Whispers of another mobilization have added to the pressure.
Another reason Russians I spoke to are preparing for the worst is that they no longer trust official assurances. Before the election, the Kremlin promised no new tax rises. Days later, it unveiled new taxes and levies to help fund military spending. The lesson was simple: promises made before the vote can disappear after it.
That loss of trust matters because another mobilization would now hit a population already primed to leave.
The first, in September 2022, came after a series of battlefield defeats. The Kremlin called up 300,000 reservists, triggering a historic exodus of an estimated 1 million Russians. Nearly five years into the war, a second mobilization could turn that exodus into a brain drain on steroids.
Another wave of engineers, programmers, scientists and entrepreneurs leaving would drain the very skills Russia needs to sustain its economy, drive innovation and expand its military-industrial base.
The problem is that the West has been making that escape harder. Since 2022, the European Union has suspended its visa facilitation agreement with Russia and, in 2025, tightened the rules further, effectively ending multiple-entry visas for most Russian citizens.
At the same time, a rise in Russian-linked hybrid attacks across Europe has deepened suspicion of Russian nationals, blurring the distinction between those fleeing the Kremlin and the state they are trying to escape. Dissidents and anti-war activists are finding it harder to secure humanitarian visas, while some exiles have had bank accounts frozen or closed under financial compliance rules.
Even routine travel can now become a bureaucratic ordeal. My Russian wife’s relatives applied for tourist visas to visit us in Ireland in March. The process once took six weeks, but they are still waiting.
The contrast is striking. As ordinary Russians face ever tighter barriers to entering the West, the EU has shockingly just agreed to remove two of Russia’s richest billionaires, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, from its sanctions list. The bloc renewed sanctions on thousands of others, but the contrast will not be lost on Russians watching from inside the country.
If Putin orders another mobilization, the West should be ready with practical escape routes for the Russians he is trying to conscript. That means accelerated visas, workable banking arrangements, recognition of qualifications and help establishing themselves abroad.
This is not simply a humanitarian obligation. It is also a strategic opportunity.
Every engineer who escapes the draft is one fewer engineer Putin can put to work on the war and potentially one more who can help rebuild Russia when the war is over.
Putin wants to conscript Russia’s future. The West should help it escape.

title: Latvia Moves to Expel Russian Journalist Leonid Ragozin, Delfi Reports
description: Latvian authorities have launched proceedings to declare Riga-based Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, Delfi reported Tuesday.
content:
Latvian authorities have launched proceedings to declare Riga-based Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, Delfi reported Tuesday.
While Ragozin was not identified by name, Foreign Minister Baiba Braže announced blacklisting proceedings against a Russian citizen based on new information from “competent authorities” and discussions with the prime minister.
Sources familiar with the matter told Delfi that the move targets Ragozin, who has resided in Latvia since around the time of Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. There was no indication when the decision would be made.
Ragozin drew public ire for comments he made on a podcast hosted by Aaron Maté of fringe far-left outlet The Grayzone, which has been accused of taking a pro-Russian slant.
He argued that Russia was compelled to respond to the West with “brute force,” saying, “ [Russia] always consider themselves as the underdogs and as the side that is being under constant pressure from the West, encroaching on its sphere of influence, on its strategic interests. It compels them to respond to hybrid actions, to clandestine actions, to sort of invisible actions that change the landscape in the former Soviet Union.”
Late last month, Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava urged the foreign ministry to declare Ragozin a persona non grata due to “opinions that are in blatant contradiction to the interests of the Latvian state.”
“His actions can be regarded as ones aimed at steering Western public opinion in a direction favorable to Russia,” Dombrava wrote on Sept. 30.
Ragozin is a former producer for the BBC Russian Service and editor at Russian Newsweek. His freelance commentary has appeared in recent editions of Al Jazeera, Jacobin and The American Conservative.
In an August column for The American Conservative, Ragozin argued that ordinary Russians perceive greater threats from Western nations than from their own government.
On Wednesday, Ragozin thanked supporters while criticizing those reacting to the news of the proceedings to declare him persona non grata with “sadistic glee.”
Latvia has declared dozens of Russian cultural figures, state journalists and commentators personae non gratae since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Russian Who Swam to Lithuania to Seek Asylum Gets 6 Years in Russian Prison After Return
description: A Russian man who swam across the Neman River to Lithuania seeking asylum was sentenced to six years in prison after Lithuanian authorities returned him to Russia, media reported.
content:
A Russian man who swam across the Neman River to Lithuania seeking asylum was sentenced to six years in prison after Lithuanian authorities returned him to Russia, media reported.
The Baltic Fleet Military Court on Sept. 30 found Igor Odintsov guilty of publicly calling for terrorism, the regional news outlet Russky Zapad reported . He will serve his sentence in a high-security penal colony.
The court found that Odintsov had posted messages on a messaging app that portrayed the “ideology and practice of terrorism as correct and deserving of support and emulation.”
Investigators also said he held “radical views,” opposed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and had a “negative attitude” toward the Russian authorities.
The Lithuanian news outlet Lrytas identified Odintsov, 68, as the Kaliningrad region resident who swam across the Neman on Sept. 17 and sought asylum, saying he faced persecution in Russia over his social media posts.
Lithuanian authorities detained him at around 1:50 p.m. local time and returned him to Russia through the Panemune border crossing at 7 p.m. that same day.
Odintsov fled to Lithuania on the day he was due to appear in a Russian court over the case.
Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service said at the time that it had received no information about threats against him, any special status he held or arrangements for his admission to the European Union. It said he did not fall into a category of vulnerable people and decided to return him to Russia.
The border service now says it has “doubts” about whether Odintsov’s statement could be considered a request for protection, saying it “was not expressed clearly and understandably.”
Sigitas Šamborskis, chairman of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad, said he knew Odintsov and called the Lithuanian authorities’ decision to expel him a “betrayal.”

title: Rosatom Takes Full Control of Transport Conglomerate Delo Group in $900M Buyout
description: Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom has completed its acquisition of founder Sergei Shishkarev’s remaining 51% stake in transport conglomerate Delo, both parties announced Wednesday.
content:
Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom has completed its acquisition of founder Sergei Shishkarev’s remaining 51% stake in transport conglomerate Delo, both parties announced Wednesday.
Neither party disclosed the amount Rosatom paid, though Shishkarev has valued his stake in Delo at 77 billion rubles ($900.3 million).
“From this moment, we begin the final consolidation of all Rosatom logistics assets, which will result in the creation of the largest national logistics company,” Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev said in a statement.
Likhachev said the deal brought Rosatom’s market share in Russia’s container handling market to 50% and rail container transport to 44%.
He boasted that Rosatom’s logistics arm operates in all Russian maritime basins, owns the country’s largest container fleet and owns port facilities in major cities.
In his statement, Shishkarev cited “insurmountable disagreements” leading to the buyout seven years after Rosatom first bought a stake in Delo in 2019 as part of plans to capitalize on Arctic shipping routes.
Shishkarev, who founded Delo 33 years ago, vowed to remain in the logistics sector and pledged to pay a “significant portion” of the buyout money toward state security.
Russia’s federal budget unveiled recently showed record corporate donations of 471.5 billion rubles ($5.5 billion) in 2026 to help offset surging wartime military spending.
Likhachev said Rosatom’s strategic goal was to “strengthen our country’s transport sovereignty, ensure sustainable international transport and develop the Northern Sea Route, and with it, the Trans-Arctic transport corridor.”

title: Kremlin Says France's Test Nuclear Launch Is Part of 'Dead End' Anti-Russia Strategy
description: The Kremlin said on Wednesday that France's test launch of a nuclear-capable missile showed that Europe was building its defense identity around confrontation with Russia, describing the strategy as a "dead end."
content:
The Kremlin said on Wednesday that France's test launch of a nuclear-capable missile showed that Europe was building its defense identity around confrontation with Russia , describing the strategy as a "dead end."
On Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the test of the submarine-launched ballistic missile off the coast of Brittany as a message "sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received," without mentioning Russia directly.
The launch came amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine, European security and nuclear deterrence. Russia has recently renewed warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself and the exclave of Kaliningrad.
Asked about the test launch, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia had received France's message and said it was an example of what he called Europe's obsession with militarization.
"They are building their identity in the field of defense and security on the basis of confrontation with the Russia n Federation. This is a dead end path. As history shows, it leads to nothing good," he said.
He said Russia remained on alert, but open to dialogue. "We believe that any problems should be resolved not through demonstrative missile launches, but through dialogue," he said.

title: Northern Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Offers 1M-Ruble Bounty for Downed Drones
description: Authorities in northwestern Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets autonomous district have established a reward of 1 million rubles ($11,700) for reservists who successfully shoot down enemy drones.
content:
Authorities in northwestern Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets autonomous district have established a reward of 1 million rubles ($11,700) for reservists who successfully shoot down enemy drones.
It is the highest publicly recorded bounty offered by any Russian region for downing Ukrainian drones, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
Other regions offer significantly lower rewards, ranging from 20,000 rubles to 200,000 rubles.
Reservists operating in Yamal’s mobile firing squads will qualify for an equal share of the bounty if the intercepted drone does not cause damage to local infrastructure, according to a regional decree cited by the agency.
Previously, a one-time reward of 1 million rubles was reportedly awarded to a serviceman in the republic of Chechnya last December.
Located around 2,200 kilometers (1,367 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the natural gas-rich Yamalo-Nenets was struck by Ukrainian drones for the first time in early September.

title: Second Prison Guard Dead After Failed Inmate Escape Attempt in North Caucasus
description: A Russian prisoner who was extradited from Georgia last month was shot dead after attempting to escape a transport train in the North Caucasus last week, killing two prison guards and injuring two others.
content:
A Russian prisoner who was extradited from Georgia last month was shot dead after attempting to escape a transport train in the North Caucasus last week, killing two prison guards and injuring two others.
The Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) on Wednesday confirmed the second officer died in a hospital from wounds sustained last Friday, Oct. 2, during the incident at a station in the republic of Kabardino-Balkaria.
One guard died at the scene near the Murtazovo station en route from the republic of North Ossetia-Alania to the Krasnodar region.
FSIN said it shot and killed the inmate on the spot.
The surviving officers who contained the situation will receive state honors, while the families of the two deceased guards will receive financial support, FSIN said.
The deceased inmate was reportedly identified as 43-year-old Dmitry Pushkaryov, who was extradited from Georgia to Russia on Sept. 24 alongside another suspect.
Pushkaryov was said to face drug trafficking charges, with Russian authorities claiming he helped create a narcotics lab on a dairy farm in Far East Russia and managed an online drugs marketplace before fleeing abroad.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, has opened a criminal probe into weapons theft, assault on law enforcement officers and disrupting the operation of a penal institution.

title: U.S. Embassy Urges Citizens to Leave Russia Over Siberian Plague Suspicions
description: The U.S.
content:
The U.S. Embassy in Moscow issued a health alert on Tuesday over the death of a plague lab worker in the Irkutsk region, urging Americans to leave Russia and those in the affected area to follow local health guidance.
The death of an Irkutsk anti-plague institute employee last week has fueled fears of a possible outbreak, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that she had the disease.
U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio urged Russia to share more information, while President Donald Trump said he planned to address the matter in a call with President Vladimir Putin.
“U.S. citizens in the area should follow the guidance of local health authorities, avoid affected facilities, and seek medical care promptly if they develop fever or respiratory symptoms,” the U.S. Embassy in Moscow said in a statement.
It emphasized that the U.S. government has “limited ability to help U.S. citizens in Russia, especially outside of Moscow,” citing reports of hospital quarantines following the death.
The embassy reiterated that U.S. citizens are advised to depart Russia and not travel due to security concerns. The U.S. State Department’s Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Russia has been in place since January 2022, on the eve of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The State Department has sent a formal diplomatic demarche to the Russian government requesting clarification, a source close to the matter told AFP.
The World Health Organization said no cases have been recorded within Irkutsk, but Director-General Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for “timely, complete and transparent information sharing.”
Russian authorities have denied any active public health crisis, insisting the situation is under control. The Kremlin urged the public to ignore online rumors and rely only on updates from Russia’s consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Speaking to the press on Wednesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused the media of disseminating false information about the case, saying Russia informed the WHO about the death of a laboratory worker at a Siberian plague research institute last week in line with established procedures.
Peskov was commenting on an ABC News report that the United States had lodged a formal diplomatic complaint over Russia's handling of the reported death, urging Moscow to provide greater transparency about the incident.
Peskov said much of the reporting surrounding the incident was false and that people should rely on information released by state health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
In response to Trump’s offers of assistance, Rospotrebnadzor offered to aid the U.S. with its own domestic health challenges, citing rising measles cases and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.

title: Kim Jong Un Wishes Putin ‘Victory and Glory’ on His 74th Birthday
description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un wished President Vladimir Putin “victory and glory” on his 74th birthday Wednesday, pledging to deepen ties as Pyongyang continues to support Russia’s war in Ukraine. “My dearest friend, Comrade Vladimir Putin, please accept my most heartfelt and warm congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of your birthday,” Kim wrote in a telegram published by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency.
content:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un wished President Vladimir Putin “victory and glory” on his 74th birthday Wednesday, pledging to deepen ties as Pyongyang continues to support Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“My dearest friend, Comrade Vladimir Putin, please accept my most heartfelt and warm congratulations and best wishes on the occasion of your birthday,” Kim wrote in a telegram published by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency.
Kim praised Putin’s “outstanding and skillful leadership,” saying Russia had strengthened its standing as a world power over the past two decades. He also claimed that Putin enjoyed the Russian people’s “great trust and support.”
Russia would “certainly achieve victory in its just and sacred war” and defend its sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity, Kim said.
The North Korean leader pledged to keep expanding the countries’ comprehensive strategic partnership, describing Russia as a “brotherly” nation.
Moscow has deepened cooperation with Pyongyang since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to South Korean military intelligence, North Korea has supplied Russia with more than 12 million artillery rounds and ballistic missiles. It has also sent around 13,000 troops to Russia’s Kursk region, of whom about 2,300 have been killed, the intelligence service estimates.
Bloomberg Economics estimates that North Korea has earned over $14 billion from military support for Russia since 2022, including $849 million from sending troops.
Ukrainian officials have warned that Pyongyang plans to expand its military presence in Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said North Korea intends to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 troops. Ukrainian intelligence previously reported plans to send a missile unit with six launchers and around 120 missiles to southern Russia’s Voronezh region.
Kyiv has also said North Korea supplied Russia with 40 KN-23 and KN-24 short-range ballistic missiles in 2026. Zelensky said in late July that Russian forces were already using them to strike Ukraine.
