title: Sochi Closes Beaches After Drone Attack Sets Oil Tanker Ablaze
description: Authorities in Russia’s Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius closed beaches after a tanker caught fire offshore following a reported attack by naval drones, officials said Tuesday.
content:
Authorities in Russia’s Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius closed beaches after a tanker caught fire offshore following a reported attack by naval drones, officials said Tuesday.
Sochi Mayor Andrei Proshunin said the city’s beaches and waterfront promenades would remain closed until further notice. The decision followed a meeting with security officials, emergency responders and public health and weather agencies.
“I ask residents and visitors to Sochi not to put themselves at risk and to wait for an official decision on reopening,” Proshunin wrote on Telegram.
Sirius officials also closed all beaches and urged residents to limit their time outdoors and keep windows shut where possible.
“We are continuously monitoring water and air quality together with Roshydromet,” Sirius administration head Dmitry Plishkin said , referring to Russia’s weather and environmental monitoring agency.
The fire broke out around 6 p.m. Tuesday, sending thick black smoke over Sochi. Preliminary reports identified the vessel as the Aframax Rio, which may have been carrying between 95,000 and 100,000 metric tons of oil, according to open-source information cited by the independent news outlet Astra.
Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin said the oil-laden tanker had been attacked by unmanned boats. He added that all 23 crew members, who are Indian nationals, were rescued.
“Oil is currently burning in the Black Sea,” the Transportation Ministry said Tuesday night. “Firefighting can begin once the intensity of the fire decreases enough for rescue vessels to safely approach the tanker.”
On Wednesday, Russia’s Transportation Ministry said firefighters had extinguished the blaze and a joint task force with other ministries was beginning cleanup operations.
The ministry maintained that the fire on board the Aframax Rio did not cause an oil spill.
The Telegram news channel Mash reported that the Liberian-flagged vessel had been sailing from Novorossiysk to India and was almost fully loaded.
While local Telegram channels initially placed the tanker in international waters, the Ukrainian monitoring channel Crimean Wind said satellite imagery showed it drifting in Russian territorial waters about 11 kilometers (7 miles) off Sochi.
The news website Fontanka reported that an Emergency Situations Ministry vehicle had arrived at Sochi’s port and beach entrances had been cordoned off. A burning smell was noticeable near the port, though people continued to stroll along the waterfront, the outlet said.
Residents elsewhere in the city also reported a strong smell, with one saying it was noticeable even inside a car.
According to shipping records , the Aframax Rio regularly transported oil from the Russian ports of Ust-Luga, Novorossiysk and Taman to India, Singapore and Saudi Arabia between 2024 and 2026.

title: Russia Drops Criminal Case Against Children’s Hospice Founder Lida Moniava
description: Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against Lida Moniava, a prominent advocate for critically ill children’s care, after finding no grounds for prosecution, her supporters said Tuesday, citing her lawyer.
content:
Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against Lida Moniava, a prominent advocate for critically ill children’s care, after finding no grounds for prosecution, her supporters said Tuesday, citing her lawyer.
Moniava was arrested on Sept. 2 and charged with spreading “false information” about Russia’s military over a social media post about Ukrainian civilians killed in Russian attacks. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Her support group said lawyer Mikhail Biryukov had confirmed the decision and that an official notice closing the case had been sent by mail.
“This is a miracle. But it didn’t happen on its own. You made it happen,” the group wrote, thanking those who attended her court hearing, wrote letters in her defense and publicly supported her.
The group gave special thanks to hospice patients who came to court, some of whom were in wheelchairs or using ventilators.
Moniava is the founder of the Moscow-based charity Lighthouse, which operates hospices for seriously ill children and young adults in the Russian capital and surrounding region.
Her case had prompted an outpouring of support from families whose children had received care from the charity.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moniava created a foundation that provided shelter, medical supplies and food to people fleeing from the war. That foundation suspended operations in 2025 due to the dwindling number of refugees arriving in Moscow and the Moscow region.
Following her Sept. 2 arrest, Moniava announced that she was stepping down as Lighthouse’s director and leaving its board but said she intended to stay in Russia.
However, on Wednesday, Biryukov said Moniava would remain Lighthouse’s director.
“If there’s no verdict and no judicial investigation, and the case is closed, that means there’s no reason for her to step down as director,” Biryukov told RBC.
The dismissal of her case marks a rare outcome in Russia’s crackdown on anti-war speech. In a February 2025 report, rights group OVD-Info said it knew of just over 20 instances in which anti-war criminal cases had been dropped at various stages since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: At Least 24 Killed in Ukraine, Zelensky Condemns One of Russia's Most 'Vile Strikes'
description: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, killing at least 24 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.
content:
Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, killing at least 24 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.
The heaviest death toll was in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-story residential building. At least 18 people, including four children, were killed there, local officials said.
Zelensky said the strike coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday.
"Today, as a birthday 'gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky," Zelensky said, adding that six more people were also killed in Kyiv, Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack.
In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight — many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions — and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes."
In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed.
Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 people alive as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said.
"There's a lot of destruction, especially in the town center," said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — a sharp increase from recent weeks when, on average, air defenses took down 50% to 60%.
Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defenses struggling to cope with their speed.
The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Zelensky said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot [missile interception] systems that can and must protect people's lives."
Ukraine received a new 1.2 billion euro ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defense needs, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
The U.S.-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles but tight global supplies have been drained by the Iran war as well as the Ukraine conflict.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defense company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv.
Last week Zelensky said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an interview with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow.
Zelensky said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
In the Reuters interview, Zelensky said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's deep underground metro stations.
Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night.
"The metro is better because we live on the ninth floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the ninth floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters.
Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles as well as the drones had targeted Kyiv.
Overnight air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app.

title: Putin Orders Priority Rail Transit for Russian Grain – Kommersant
description: President Vladimir Putin has ordered Russian Railways to give priority to export grain shipments across the national rail network as Ukrainian drone attacks cut off southern shipping hubs,  the Kommersant newspaper reported Tuesday.
content:
President Vladimir Putin has ordered Russian Railways to give priority to export grain shipments across the national rail network as Ukrainian drone attacks cut off southern shipping hubs, the Kommersant newspaper reported Tuesday.
Standard Russian Railways rules generally prioritize domestic freight and transit shipments over export goods. Now, grain trains can leapfrog other export commodities like coal on congested rail routes leading to Baltic and Arctic ports.
“Regarding commercial shipping in the Black Sea, the president indeed instructed the Agriculture Ministry together with other agencies to work out alternative delivery routes for domestic grain to world markets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the publication.
Grain has been moved into the third-highest priority category on Russia’s railway system, which is reserved for cargo transported under direct presidential orders.
The shift in priorities follows a 465% year-on-year surge in daily rail deliveries of agricultural goods to northwestern Russia in September, according to sources cited by Kommersant.
Companies are actively repurposing their fertilizer, coal and other cargo terminals at Baltic and Arctic ports to handle grain exports.
Russia’s overall agricultural exports slumped, with total grain exports for September falling nearly fourfold year-on-year to 1.7 million metric tons. Outbound shipments from Russia’s primary Black Sea grain hub of Novorossiysk plunged tenfold.
Despite the workarounds, market analysts warn that Baltic and Arctic ports lack the storage capacity and specialized infrastructure of southern terminals to handle larger long-term volumes.
Agricultural consultancy SovEcon recently slashed its forecast for Russia’s 2026/27 grain exports from 49.4 million metric tons to 44.7 million metric tons amid expectations that normal commercial operations in the Black Sea will remain disrupted until at least 2027.

title: Are Russian Gray Ops the New War on Terror?
description: Opinion | This article was adapted from the Threatologist newsletter.
content:
This article was adapted from the Threatologist newsletter .
Russia is menacing Europe. It is testing reactions and resolve, spreading instability and chipping away at the principles of collective defense. The only appropriate response is to acknowledge the seriousness of the threat and ramp up preparedness and defense spending — and to show Russia that the West will not shy away from confrontation.
This, at least, is the narrative that dominates the media and security landscape. There is strong justification for it: there is ample evidence of Russia pushing the boundaries and engaging in nefarious activities, and Russia has long held a low — and, until the war in Ukraine, entirely justifiable — opinion of the West’s resolve. But to what degree does the nature of the threat align with the perception?
Browse through any serious newspaper and it likely won’t be long before you encounter a headline warning of the threat that Russia poses to Western security. Over the last two weeks, the Estonian foreign minister has cautioned that Russia is escalating a campaign of sabotage and arson; the German chancellor has spoken about preparing for Russian hybrid attacks and the Danish intelligence services have claimed that Russia could be readying a limited military operation against a NATO country. Pick a different week and the details will change, but the underlying message will likely remain the same.
This rhetoric has a long history. For some commentators, there has always been a threat from the East and the transition from the U.S.S.R. to the Russian Federation meant little more than a change of clothes. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was, therefore, little more than a vindication of long-held beliefs. Historian Mark Smith penned an entire book on what he termed “The Russia Anxiety,” which he characterized as “an historic syndrome that alternates between three sets of symptoms: fear of Russia, disregard of Russia and contempt for Russia.”
Over the years, Russia has provided ample material to fuel these concerns : from a British perspective, the poisonings of Alexander Litvinenko in 2006 and Sergei and Yulia Skripal in 2018 stand out as two of the most egregious examples. Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the number of nefarious incidents linked to Russia has proliferated, from an arson attack on a London warehouse involving the Wagner private military company to damage to undersea cables allegedly inflicted by the shadow fleet.
Much of this activity is bracketed under the label “gray zone” or “hybrid” operations (the different terms and the problems with how they are defined are a topic I’ll tackle later). These refer to hostile acts that seek to cause damage and spread instability but fall short of the threshold that would necessitate a military response. Since this threshold is by design not clearly demarcated, such activities test where they are and how far back they can be pushed. Hybrid operations are also marked by challenges of attribution, which can further complicate responses. Although there are reasonable doubts about whether it holds in the age of Trump, NATO’s Article 5 is the bedrock of Western collective security. Hybrid operations seek to remain below the threshold at which it can be invoked while at the same time further undermining confidence that it ever will be.
NATO’s Article 5 has been invoked precisely once in the history of the organization: After the terrorist attacks on the United States on Sept. 11, 2001. The response to those events is relevant in other ways too. The West transformed its security architecture in the wake of those attacks. It launched ruinous wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. It increased security at airports and most other places where people gather. It forced schools and universities to identify and report potential extremists. It policed thought as well as behavior. It created entire new security institutions.
However, questions were asked about whether this corresponded to the scale of the actual threat. Between 2001 and 2011, U.S. expenditure on domestic security alone increased by approximately $1 trillion and similar hikes were seen elsewhere. The total number of people killed globally by Muslim extremists operating outside war zones, by contrast, averaged 200-300 per year over that same period. The definitional parameters can be tweaked to produce different figures, but it is indisputable that in statistical terms terrorism was never a primary threat to Western lives. Certainly no jihadist groups ever seriously threatened to bring down a Western state or defeat its military. Yet the impact of terrorism on Western security postures was transformative.
The process of exaggeration, inflation, and securitization gave rise to a cottage industry of “critical terrorism” scholars who devoted entire journals, books, and conferences to challenging the shortcomings of Western counterterrorism approaches. Occasionally, parts of this community would smear other academics or lambast the sources of research funding while hypocritically submitting funding bids to the very same sources. But they also raised valid concerns about whether the response to terrorism corresponded to the actual threat it posed. A single person with a knife and a grudge could be transformed into a global menace by invoking the specter of jihadism. A small group could become a “threat to our way of life” without being able to secure control over territory as small as their own apartment.
There are lessons that we can draw from both the Global War on Terror and the responses to it. One of the flaws of the critical terrorism crowd was that it had very little to say about terrorism itself. Scan through its core journals and you’ll find that articles dealing with actual political violence are a relative rarity; its focus instead was on challenging the discourses around terrorism and the way that this was used to justify policy responses. The group also demonstrated only limited understanding of the state apparatuses that were tasked with challenging it. One of its doyens, Richard Jackson, once charged that “Policymakers are, for the most part, uninterested in evidence-based policy, or in the rigorous evaluation of counterterrorism policy, or in listening to reasonable, evidence-based suggestions about how to more effectively, and more ethically, respond to acts of terrorism”. This was always untrue and, ironically enough, an entirely unsubstantiated claim. Critical assessments of the West’s current security posture should not fall into the same trap of simply dismissing concerns about the threat posed by Russia and the motives of those who draw attention to it.
At the same time, we can recognize that two things can be true simultaneously: we can acknowledge that Russia is engaging in activities that give rise to genuine security concerns while also recognizing that the nature of the threat that it poses is being exaggerated and/or misunderstood .
The first part of this is uncontroversial: Russia has invaded its neighbor, so the threat that it poses is not purely abstract or theoretical, its potential to inflict harm far exceeds that of terrorists and there are numerous deleterious activities that can plausibly be linked to it.
The second part, however, is defensible even in the face of this. By bundling together very different types of activity and treating everything from a bin fire to an explosive-laden drone attack on an aircraft as the same thing, we lose sight of which activities pose a genuine security threat and which are merely a nuisance.
The cynical among you will rightly point out that this heightened rhetoric serves the interests of a security community that desires ever-more resources. Both state apparatuses and the think tank community that supports them benefit from heightened perceptions of threat, just as they did in the case of terrorism. But it is equally true that, among the same community, there are people who genuinely want to understand the nature of the threat and design responses to it. They are poorly served by discussions that cast Russia as a ubiquitous, all-powerful bogeyman — a narrative that benefits the Russian security apparatus more than it does its Western counterparts.

title: Russia Investigates Contaminated Dog Vaccine Linked to Mass Pet Deaths
description: Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the use of forged quality certificates during the distribution of a popular canine vaccine blamed for the deaths of dozens of dogs over the summer, the Prosecutor General’s Office said Tuesday.
content:
Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the use of forged quality certificates during the distribution of a popular canine vaccine blamed for the deaths of dozens of dogs over the summer, the Prosecutor General’s Office said Tuesday.
Inspectors discovered a falsified certificate uploaded to the state electronic database for a batch of the vaccine, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement, without identifying the maker or the medication by name.
Law enforcement sources told Interfax that the investigation targeted Moscow-based pharmaceutical company Vetbiochim, which produces the widely used Multican-8 vaccine.
At least 169 dogs have reportedly died since August across Russia, primarily in the Yaroslavl region, after receiving doses of Multican-8. Authorities revealed that samples from a batch of Multican-8 contained live Aujeszky’s disease virus, which is almost universally fatal to domestic dogs.
Vetbiochim recalled several batches of Multican-8 in late August following initial reports of illness and deaths from pet owners.
In comments to the RBC news outlet on Tuesday, Vetbiochim said it was fully cooperating with law enforcement and providing all requested documentation.
“We’re not avoiding responsibility, and we’re not hiding from the public or the investigation,” Vetbiochim said.
The company said it had launched an internal audit to determine how the contaminated batch and falsified documentation were released into circulation.
“We want an objective investigation to identify those responsible and to ensure they face proper consequences. We’ll do everything we can to make that happen,” Vetbiochim said.

title: Kremlin Launches Preparations for Putin’s Annual ‘Direct Line’ Call-In Show
description: The Kremlin said Tuesday that it had launched preparations for President Vladimir Putin’s annual press conference and “Direct Line” call-in show. “We’re preparing in the same way as last year and previous years, in a combined format,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing, confirming his previous comments made on Sunday. “It will be both a Direct Line and an annual major press conference of the head of state,” Peskov said.
content:
The Kremlin said Tuesday that it had launched preparations for President Vladimir Putin’s annual press conference and “Direct Line” call-in show.
“We’re preparing in the same way as last year and previous years, in a combined format,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing, confirming his previous comments made on Sunday.
“It will be both a Direct Line and an annual major press conference of the head of state,” Peskov said.
Putin’s call-in show and end-of-year press conference have been combined since they were merged due to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.
Peskov did not name the exact date for this year’s event. Last year’s was held on Dec. 19, 2025.
On Sunday, Peskov said a “matured” neural network developed by state lender Sberbank would help the Kremlin field a much larger volume of public requests prior to the event. The Kremlin claimed that more than 3 million queries were submitted to last year’s show.
First launched in 2001, Putin’s call-in program aims to cast the Russian leader as a “problem-solver-in-chief,” as he personally addresses the complaints of ordinary citizens that regional and local officials are accused of ignoring.

title: Russians in ICE Detention Plan Hunger Strike to Protest Poor Conditions
description: More than 50 detainees, including Russian citizens, are planning to launch a hunger strike this week to protest what they have described as unbearably harsh conditions at one of the largest U.S. immigration detention centers, according to three people familiar with the matter.
content:
More than 50 detainees, including Russian citizens, are planning to launch a hunger strike this week to protest what they have described as unbearably harsh conditions at one of the largest U.S. immigration detention centers, according to three people familiar with the matter.
The detainees are located at the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center in Folkston, Georgia, that was expanded last year under a $47-million contract with the Department of Homeland Security.
A document written by detainees dated Sept. 14 and seen by The Moscow Times describes a range of issues. Among them: a lack of adequate medical and dental care, problems communicating with people on the outside, disparaging attitudes from staff and poor living conditions at the facility, part of which is a converted former prison .
Detainees complain of having limited time outdoors, being unable to sleep, mold on ceilings and mattresses and poor ventilation. One of the document’s authors said that he had not had a dental cleaning in his nearly two-year stay at the facility.
The document, originally written in Cyrillic, was authored by two Russian-speaking detainees and signed by 14 of them in total . The wife of one man who signed the document said it was submitted as a formal complaint to multiple federal oversight bodies.
“​​According to my husband, the most serious problems include food, the inability to sleep and rest properly, difficulties obtaining necessary medical care and the overall conditions of long-term detention,” said another Russian woman whose husband is detained in the facility.
The two women gave similar accounts of the center’s conditions and recent developments, as relayed by their husbands, in separate text exchanges with The Moscow Times. Both requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation.
The women said that detainees and their family members on the outside have previously tried to raise the issues with staff, including through formal complaints. The first woman said little had changed — until an inspection was announced for Oct. 6.
After that, “conditions inside the facility, according to my husband and other detainees, began to noticeably change,” she said. “In particular, the food and some living conditions improved.”
Detainees are skeptical that those changes will last, however.
The hunger strike, a drastic form of protest that puts a participant’s health at risk, was initially scheduled to begin Tuesday, the day of the inspection. The first woman said that some people had already begun refusing food on Monday.
She said the goal is to “disrupt this show, draw the inspectors’ attention to real, everyday problems, and demonstrate that people have serious grievances against the facility.”
Both women said their husbands told them that staff had gathered the would-be participants last week after learning of the planned hunger strike and tried to persuade them to call it off.
“[The women’s husbands] say they were warned of the consequences if they continued, including possible separation and isolation,” the second woman said.
Neither ICE nor GEO Group, the private contractor managing the Folkston D. Ray ICE Processing Center, responded to a request for comment.
On its website, GEO Group states that the facility provides basic services including “around-the-clock access to medical care,” “dietitian-approved meals” and in-person and virtual visitation. It also says that the center is accredited by the American Correctional Association.
Hundreds of Russians have fled to the U.S. to seek political asylum in recent years. A growing number of them have wound up in ICE facilities under the administrations of Presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, at times facing prolonged detention while their asylum applications are processed. Some have been forcibly deported back to Russia.
The planned hunger strike will involve detainees of several nationalities. The Moscow Times could not establish how many Russian citizens are planning to participate.

title: Kremlin Warns Lithuania Lifting Nuclear Arms Ban Risks Escalation
description: The Kremlin on Tuesday warned that a preliminary decision by NATO member Lithuania to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear arms on its territory could lead to a new round of escalation in the region.
content:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned that a preliminary decision by NATO member Lithuania to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear arms on its territory could lead to a new round of escalation in the region.
Lithuania's parliament on Tuesday voted in favor of removing the ban, in the first of two ballots required for the change.
Asked by reporters how Russia viewed that development, as well as a proposal floated this month by U.S. President Donald Trump to build an American military base in the Baltic country, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said:
“If the military infrastructure of what is, in effect, NATO's leading country (the U.S.) is moving closer to our borders, then, of course, this cannot be perceived as anything other than a step towards escalating tensions.”
He added: “The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring state. Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent; on the contrary, they will, much to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions.”
Lithuania, a ​member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and close Moscow ally Belarus. The U.S. has ​kept an armored battalion of almost ​1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning ‌the ⁠troops arrive and leave every few months.
The legal overhaul of the nuclear arms ban, which requires a two-thirds majority in two parliamentary votes to go into effect, is set to remove prohibitions put in place more than three decades ago after Lithuania broke away from the Soviet Union.

title: Russia Holds Major Nuclear Accident Drill at Beloyarsk Plant
description: More than 1,000 people began a two-day emergency exercise at Russia’s Beloyarsk nuclear power plant on Tuesday, testing how staff and emergency services would respond to simultaneous accidents at two reactors.
content:
More than 1,000 people began a two-day emergency exercise at Russia’s Beloyarsk nuclear power plant on Tuesday, testing how staff and emergency services would respond to simultaneous accidents at two reactors.
The exercise in the Sverdlovsk region, which organizers said is the largest in Russia’s nuclear industry this year, will simulate a natural disaster compounded by failures in reactor safety systems.
The plant’s reactors will continue operating normally throughout the exercise, its communications department said.
Emergency crews will extend the drill to the nearby town of Zarechny on Wednesday to rehearse the response to a simulated nuclear accident.
Crews in protective equipment will use fire engines and military vehicles to clear debris, extinguish simulated fires and set up decontamination facilities. They will also practice sheltering and evacuating residents.
Plant management has asked residents to remain calm during the exercise, which may include sirens and loudspeaker announcements.
The drill is part of an annual program in which different Russian nuclear plants take turns hosting large exercises. Plant officials said the scenario combines highly unlikely events to test emergency preparedness.
Russian federal regulations require nuclear plant operators to hold exercises involving specialist support teams and emergency services at least once a year.
International Atomic Energy Agency safety standards also call for regular drills to test coordination between plant staff and outside agencies. The agency’s guidance includes exercises involving emergencies at multiple reactors on the same site.
Participants at the Beloyarsk drill include plant employees, specialists from nuclear plant operator Rosenergoatom and state nuclear corporation Rosatom, rescuers, police, medical workers and local officials.
Military radiation, chemical and biological defense units are also taking part, along with observers from Belarus and Kazakhstan.
Beloyarsk supplies about 16% of the Sverdlovsk region’s electricity. Its two operating units use BN-600 and BN-800 fast-neutron reactors, which began operating in 1980 and 2015, respectively.
The exercise comes amid reported drone strikes on Russian nuclear infrastructure, though its announced scenario centers on a natural disaster and equipment failures.
Rosatom said drones struck cooling towers at the Kursk II nuclear power plant twice this year, hitting unit 2, which is under construction, on July 6 and unit 1 on Sept. 17. The company said neither incident affected plant operations or radiation levels.

title: Head of Russian Military’s Patriot Park Arrested in Bribery Probe
description: Law enforcement authorities have detained the head of Russia’s military theme park, Patriot Park, on bribery charges, media outlets reported and the Defense Ministry confirmed on Monday evening.
content:
Law enforcement authorities have detained the head of Russia’s military theme park, Patriot Park, on bribery charges, media outlets reported and the Defense Ministry confirmed on Monday evening.
Investigators have accused Patriot Park general director Igor Vasilyev of accepting 80 million rubles ($931,000) in bribes, according to the Fontanka news website.
A Moscow court is expected to rule to place Vasilyev in pre-trial detention later on Tuesday.
Russia’s Defense Ministry told state media it was fully assisting military investigators.
Vasilyev, who served as governor of the Kirov region from 2016 to 2022, was appointed as general director of Patriot Park in March this year.
His arrest follows a recent series of detentions targeting executives and military supervisors connected to Patriot Park.
Two of Vasilyev’s deputies were arrested last Friday on an alleged fake contract scheme totaling 100 million rubles ($1.1 million).
On Wednesday, a military court reportedly accused Major General Sergei Nikitushkin, who heads a Defense Ministry department that oversees Patriot Park, of accepting bribes.
Vasilyev’s predecessor, Vyacheslav Akhmedov, was sentenced to five years in prison last year for fraud related to construction at the theme park.
Akhmedov’s and Vasilyev’s deputy, Vitaly Melimuk, was arrested for allegedly accepting a bribe from a private contractor earlier in April.
The broader purge began in April 2024 with the high-profile arrest of Deputy Defense Minister Timur Ivanov. Since then, investigators have targeted several deputy ministers and multiple generals on charges of bribery, embezzlement and forming criminal organizations.
Vasilyev is identified as at least the 12th defendant in cases surrounding Patriot Park, a pet project of the country’s military establishment designed to showcase Russian hardware and boost national pride.

title: Irkutsk Maternity Hospital Screens Patients for Plague After Lab Worker’s Death
description: A maternity hospital in Siberia’s Irkutsk region has started screening pregnant patients for possible plague exposure and restricting visitors following the death of a local anti-plague institute employee, the independent outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) reported Monday.
content:
A maternity hospital in Siberia’s Irkutsk region has started screening pregnant patients for possible plague exposure and restricting visitors following the death of a local anti-plague institute employee, the independent outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) reported Monday.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, died last week after being hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Her death has fueled fears of a possible plague outbreak, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that she had the disease.
Blogger Ulyana Gavryunina told the outlet that staff at the Irkutsk City Perinatal Center gave her a “Checklist for Suspected Plague” when she arrived for an examination on Oct. 5. The questionnaire asked about symptoms and contact with sick people or recent arrivals from abroad.
Gavryunina said the center has barred entry to everyone except pregnant patients since Friday and that staff checked her temperature and asked her to show her tongue when she arrived.
Staff reportedly cited unconfirmed information about an unidentified infection as the reason for the restrictions. The center also introduced a mask requirement and temporarily barred partners from attending births, she added.
Unconfirmed reports have suggested Shipilova contracted plague during a work trip to the neighboring republic of Buryatia or after accidentally breaking a test tube containing the plague bacterium in a laboratory. Neither account has been officially confirmed.
The Shelekhov hospital was subsequently placed under quarantine and 189 people who had been in contact with Shipilova were placed under medical observation, according to earlier reports.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday urged Russians to disregard rumors of a possible plague outbreak and rely on statements from the consumer protection and public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
The agency said the Irkutsk region’s public health situation remained “stable” following an investigation.
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have stepped up precautions amid the reports. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is also monitoring information about the suspected case.
The World Health Organization said Tuesday that Russian authorities had identified Shipilova’s contacts and that none were showing symptoms. It said it had requested more information from Russia about her death.
Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which circulates among small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization, people can become infected through flea bites or contact with infected animals or tissues.
The most common form, bubonic plague, causes painful, swollen lymph nodes and rarely spreads between people. Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets during close contact.
Both forms can be treated with antibiotics, though early treatment is critical.

title: 2 Killed in Massive Ukrainian Drone Attack on Moscow
description: A massive Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region overnight killed two people and ignited a fire at a major fuel depot overnight, authorities said, and media reported Tuesday.
content:
A massive Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region overnight killed two people and ignited a fire at a major fuel depot overnight, authorities said, and media reported Tuesday.
A 20-year-old man was killed in the village of Radumlya north of Moscow, while rescuers recovered the body of a 71-year-old man from under the rubble of a destroyed home in Barybino to the south.
Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov confirmed the fatalities and said that nine people were injured in the attack. Forty-seven private homes and four apartment buildings were damaged across seven municipalities, Vorobyov said, ordering local authorities to speed up reconstruction efforts.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “a majority” of the 650 drones launched toward the Russian capital had been intercepted, 105 of them on their immediate approach to Moscow. He reported dozens more interceptions in rapid succession on Tuesday morning.
The exiled outlet Astra reported that video of one of the attacks showed a fire at the Moscow region’s largest fuel storage hub: the Volodarskaya line production and dispatch station. The Moscow Times could not independently verify the report.
The Transneft-owned facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products per year and directly supplies fuel to Moscow’s main airports: Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Vnukovo. According to Astra, the Volodarskaya station has not been a previous target of Ukrainian attacks.
Severe delays and flight cancellations were reported at Sheremetyevo International Airport during the overnight air raid alerts.
The attack follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s weekend pledge to target Russian energy infrastructure in response to Moscow’s intensified air campaign against Ukrainian cities.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 868 Ukrainian drones over dozens of Russian regions overnight.
It said its forces conducted retaliatory strikes against cargo ships and port infrastructure in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports of Chornomorsk and Izmail, as well as digital data centers across several major Ukrainian cities.
On Sunday, the Russian Defense Ministry said it would intensify strikes on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine in response to Zelensky’s pledge.

title: Moscow Court Jails Ex-Sochi Mayor for 15 Years in Prison in Corruption Case
description: A Moscow judge has sentenced the former mayor of the Black Sea resort city of Sochi to 15 years in maximum-security prison for corruption, state media reported Monday, citing the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office.  Alexei Kopaygorodsky, 41, served as mayor from September 2019 until May 2024, when he abruptly resigned, citing a transition to a federal post.
content:
A Moscow judge has sentenced the former mayor of the Black Sea resort city of Sochi to 15 years in maximum-security prison for corruption, state media reported Monday, citing the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office.
Alexei Kopaygorodsky, 41, served as mayor from September 2019 until May 2024, when he abruptly resigned, citing a transition to a federal post. After the transfer failed to materialize, Kopaygorodsky joined a volunteer army battalion fighting in Ukraine.
He was arrested in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine in September 2024 and transferred to Moscow, where prosecutors sought 21 years in prison for him and 16 years for his wife.
The Meshchansky District Court found Kopaygorodsky guilty of receiving large-scale bribes, embezzling municipal property and laundering criminal proceeds, according to Interfax.
His wife Yanina Kopaygorodskaya was sentenced to 10 years in prison for serving as an accomplice, while her assistant Alexander Pasunko was fined 190,000 rubles ($2,200).
Kopaygorodsky and his wife were also ordered to pay fines of half a billion rubles ($5.9 million) each.
In addition, the former mayor was stripped of his state medal, banned from holding public management roles for 14.5 years and will face three additional years after his prison term.
Prosecutors accused Kopaygorodsky of embezzling two municipal land plots and concealing their origin, as well as accepting more than 319 million rubles ($3.7 million) in bribes from business leaders and developers in exchange for favors and protection in 2022-24.
Kopaygorodskaya was also accused of threatening one witness in order to receive false testimony and bribing another witness through Pasunko with half a million rubles ($5,900) while under house arrest.
Earlier in January, a Sochi court seized the family’s assets worth more than 1.6 billion rubles ($18.8 million).
Kopaygorodsky is among at least 10 current and former deputy governors who have faced criminal prosecution since Veniamin Kondratyev became Krasnodar region governor in 2015.

title: Kremlin Downplays Estonia’s Troop Shift to Border, Plays Up Russia’s Intelligence Capabilities
description: The Kremlin on Monday said Russia’s intelligence services were capable of monitoring military movements along the country’s borders, brushing aside reports that Estonia is shifting troops closer to the Russian border. “There should be no doubt that our Defense Ministry and other relevant services possess the necessary intelligence to properly monitor and assess the situation around our borders,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
content:
The Kremlin on Monday said Russia’s intelligence services were capable of monitoring military movements along the country’s borders, brushing aside reports that Estonia is shifting troops closer to the Russian border.
“There should be no doubt that our Defense Ministry and other relevant services possess the necessary intelligence to properly monitor and assess the situation around our borders,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
His comments come in response to the Financial Times detailing Estonia’s strategic pivot toward an “active defense” posture after observing Russia’s military tactics in Ukraine.
Under the updated doctrine, the Baltic nation of 1.3 million is moving primary combat units from northern Estonia’s Tapa to Jõhvi — 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with the Leningrad region.
Estonia is also constructing new facilities in the border city of Narva to house up to 1,000 troops during a crisis.
Instead of a doctrine involving efforts to “harry” invading Russian forces until the arrival of NATO reinforcements, Estonian military planners are now opting to “fight over every inch of territory.” The country is also acquiring drones and ballistic missiles capable of striking up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) inside Russian territory.
Estonia, a former Soviet republic that has long had strained relations with Moscow, has been at the forefront of countering Russian security threats and has strongly backed Ukraine since Putin ordered the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The FT report comes amid escalating rhetoric between European officials and Russia.
Martin Jaeger, the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, said Monday that Germany faces a real risk of entering a “violent conflict” with Russia as Moscow expands its “shadow war” of hybrid attacks across Europe.
Jaeger warned that in the short term Russia could engage in “low-intensity military activities, particularly in the Baltic states.”

title: Russia Sentences ‘Masyanya’ Creator to 4 Years in Absentia Over Anti-War Cartoon
description: A St.
content:
A St. Petersburg court has sentenced Oleg Kuvaev, creator of the animated series “Masyanya,” to four years and one month in prison in absentia over an episode that investigators said urged Russian soldiers to surrender or desert.
The city’s Nevsky District Court found Kuvaev guilty of publicly calling for actions against state security and failing to comply with obligations imposed on people designated as “foreign agents,” the city courts’ press service said .
The court also barred him from publishing online or administering websites for four years. Kuvaev has lived in Israel since 2006.
Investigators said Kuvaev’s 2023 episode “Idoliada,” the 169th installment of “Masyanya,” contained calls for Russian servicemen to surrender, desert and disobey their commanders.
The episode also promoted “I Want to Live,” a Ukrainian project that helps Russian soldiers surrender, according to investigators.
Case materials cited by the courts’ press service described the cartoon as expressing “ideological hatred and hostility” toward Russia’s government and officials, as well as opposition to the invasion, which Moscow calls a “special military operation.” Investigators argued that its verbal appeals were directed against Russian state security.
Those allegations placed the cartoon’s political message at the center of the criminal case. According to the exiled news outlet Mediazona, the court questioned Justice Ministry expert Vladislav Ivanov and two viewers, Nikita Sotnikov and Nikita Grishchenko.
The viewers objected to the episode’s portrayal of the Russian military, saying it mocked the Armed Forces and could lead audiences to side with Ukraine, Mediazona reported.
The criminal case was opened three years ago. Russian authorities designated Kuvaev a “foreign agent” in December 2023.
Kuvaev has continued to produce anti-war work from abroad, including an AI-generated animated video parodying the Soviet song “May There Always Be Sunshine” released in November 2025.
The video depicted rag dolls dressed as Soviet schoolchildren, wearing red Young Pioneer neckerchiefs, flying on missiles above ruined cities and sheltering from bombardment. Its lyrics replaced the original song’s wish for peace with wishes for perpetual war and slaughter.
Kuvaev presented the video as “new Russian children’s songs.”
He has also said he hopes Russia will break up and its ethnic republics will become independent, contrasting that position with what he described as the views of the Russian opposition.
Responding to the verdict, Kuvaev dismissed the proceedings.
“There is really nothing to say,” he said in comments reported by the Astra Telegram channel . “Except perhaps: ‘I regret and express concern about the state of sanity in the rotten empire’.”

title: Soviet TV Hypnotist Anatoly Kashpirovsky Dies at 87
description: Anatoly Kashpirovsky, the Soviet-era hypnotist whose televised “healing sessions” drew enormous audiences in the late 1980s, died on Saturday in Moscow at the age of 87. “Anatoly Mikhailovich passed away from advanced cancer that had spread to his lungs and brain,” Kashpirovsky’s nephew Yury Mamayev told state media. “There was multiple organ failure, meaning that the affected organs simply stopped functioning as a result of the cancer,” the TASS news agency quoted Mamayev as saying.  A representative said earlier that Kashpirovsky suffered “sudden” cardiac arrest following a sharp drop in blood pressure.
content:
Anatoly Kashpirovsky, the Soviet-era hypnotist whose televised “healing sessions” drew enormous audiences in the late 1980s, died on Saturday in Moscow at the age of 87.
“Anatoly Mikhailovich passed away from advanced cancer that had spread to his lungs and brain,” Kashpirovsky’s nephew Yury Mamayev told state media.
“There was multiple organ failure, meaning that the affected organs simply stopped functioning as a result of the cancer,” the TASS news agency quoted Mamayev as saying.
A representative said earlier that Kashpirovsky suffered “sudden” cardiac arrest following a sharp drop in blood pressure.
Born in Soviet Ukraine in 1939, Kashpirovsky graduated from the Vinnitsa Medical Institute in 1962 and spent 25 years working as a psychiatrist in a regional psychiatric hospital.
He became a household name in the 1980s as public interest in the occult grew across the country during Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s perestroika reforms.
Soviet Central Television started airing his six-part program, “Health Sessions of Psychotherapist Anatoly Kashpirovsky,” in October 1989. Its audience was estimated at more than 200 million people.
Following the Soviet collapse, Kashpirovsky entered politics, winning a seat in Russia’s first State Duma in 1993 on the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR)’s ticket.
In June 1995, he took part in negotiations during the Budyonnovsk hospital hostage crisis , convincing Chechen rebel warlord Shamil Basayev to release some of the 1,500 hostages but failing to persuade him to surrender.
Later in life, Kashpirovsky clashed with health regulators over allegations that he was practicing folk medicine illegally. While the Russian Academy of Sciences dismissed his methods as “absolute pseudoscience,” Kashpirovsky defended his medical credentials and won multiple defamation lawsuits.
He maintained a loyal following, touring and hosting “healing sessions” on YouTube until March this year.
His funeral will be held on Thursday, Oct. 8, at Moscow’s Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, on the anniversary of his six-part television program’s premiere.

title: The Kremlin’s Election Fraud Works Because Thousands Are Complicit
description: Opinion | The ruling United Russia party predictably won the parliamentary elections held on Sept. 18-20, receiving 58% of the votes and 349 of the 450 seats in the lower-house state Duma.  Russian officials declared that this result demonstrated popular support for Putin’s regime and its war, or, as Putin himself put it, rallying “in the face of historic challenges” in a year when the war has come to many Russians’ doorsteps.
content:
The ruling United Russia party predictably won the parliamentary elections held on Sept. 18-20, receiving 58% of the votes and 349 of the 450 seats in the lower-house state Duma.
Russian officials declared that this result demonstrated popular support for Putin’s regime and its war, or, as Putin himself put it, rallying “in the face of historic challenges” in a year when the war has come to many Russians’ doorsteps. However, for any independent observer, the declared results of these elections inevitably raise doubts.
Even before the final result was announced, many journalists and political analysts got to work on exposing the falsehood of the state’s claims. For example, Novaya Gazeta Europe used statistical analysis (the Shpilkin method ) to estimate the scale of electoral fraud and concluded that United Russia’s “real result” was around 34%.
Such calculations are not undisputed, however; experts continue to debate their methodologies. In particular, Leonid Volkov, one of the leaders of the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), argues that the number of added votes can be estimated when there is a “clearly defined core of verifiably honest polling stations.” Yet the scale of fraud in this election was so great that such a core has been effectively eliminated.
I believe it is important to draw attention to two aspects that have been overshadowed in these discussions.
First, knowing exactly what was inside the ballot boxes does not give us the real result. The elections were not competitive: not only were opposition forces in exile unable to participate, but even Yabloko, a long-standing sparring partner for United Russia that had received between 2 and 4% of the vote for the past 20 years, was removed from the ballot.
Furthermore, there is extensive evidence of the use of “administrative resources,” a euphemism for putting pressure on groups of voters, such as military personnel or state employees, to vote for United Russia.
Finally, the entire state apparatus worked in support of the ruling party, affecting the electoral process at every stage through the media, electoral commissions, the police, and the courts.
The second aspect to consider is the actual techniques of electoral malpractice. There have been reasonable doubts about the fairness of Russian elections expressed repeatedly throughout the quarter-century of Putin’s rule. What matters, however, is exactly how elections are falsified.
Over the past decade, statistical analysis has revealed the so-called Churov Saw: statistically unlikely spikes in graphs of voting results at round numbers: 60, 65, 70% and so on. These statistical anomalies not only prove the fact of the fraud but also indicate who committed it. Apparently perfect numbers mean that members of certain election commissions simply wrote the made-up figures into the final results tables, and that there were no independent observers to prevent them from doing so.
This, however, was not always the case. In the 2000s and the early 2010s, more primitive techniques were widely used: stuffing stacks of completed ballots into ballot boxes; voting under the names of people who had died or moved away; “carousel voting,” in which groups of voters traveled from one polling station to another to cast their votes multiple times; and manipulation, including pressure on voters, often elderly or ill, during home voting, where a portable ballot box is brought to the homes of voters who cannot come to a polling station. It was this home voting that secured a first-round victory for the Kremlin-backed Sergei Sobyanin in the 2013 Moscow mayoral election, preventing Alexei Navalny from going head-to-head with him in the second round.
These methods of electoral fraud were more expensive and complicated to organize, as well as more scandalous when exposed. Obviously, numerous videos of ballot stuffing or carousel voting leave ordinary citizens with far less room for doubt than statistical calculations that are not only difficult to understand, but also open to being challenged by experts. The fact that the authorities were forced to use these unsophisticated techniques meant that they had not yet gained complete control over the voting process.
This control was secured through the destruction of the election-monitoring movement, which had existed in Russia since the early 2000s but grew considerably after the decline of the 2011-2012 street protests, when numerous protesters became election observers. Golos, the largest election-monitoring organization, was among the first targeted under the “foreign agent” legislation in 2013, when the Justice Ministry treated the 7,700-euro Sakharov Prize — which the organization had refused to accept — as foreign funding.
The organization came under increasing pressure and eventually ceased its work because of the repression: in 2025, one of its co-chairmen, Grigory Melkonyants, was sentenced to five years in prison. At the same time, opportunities for election monitoring were increasingly restricted: the introduction of three-day voting made continuous observation of ballot boxes physically impossible, further restrictions limited who could be an observer — the list goes on.
The relatively small number of independent observers who nevertheless worked during the 2026 election faced unprecedented obstacles. In St. Petersburg, for example, more than 250 of the 430 observers appointed by Yabloko were unable to even begin observing the election.
Finally, even political analysts have become subject to repression. Just a few days after the election, prominent political scientist Alexander Kynev, a former head of Golos' analytical department, was brutally arrested on charges of allegedly distributing drugs.
Securing control over election commissions not only makes electoral fraud easier. It also corrupts tens, if not hundreds, of thousands of their members who either participate in electoral fraud or, at the very least, turn a blind eye to it. Russia has almost 50,000 election commissions, each of which consists of between three and 16 members. Since many polling stations in Russia are established in schools, a lot of those commissions are made up of teachers who are responsible for the education of future Russian citizens and voters. As the regime makes them legal and moral accomplices in its crimes, corruption inevitably seeps into the younger generations.
Thus, there is little point in trying to calculate the ruling party’s real result. When opposition candidates and observers are barred from participation, such a result simply does not exist.
It seems quite likely to me that, if Russia ever has fair democratic elections again, all this fabricated popular support for United Russia will disappear overnight.
What will not disappear, however, is the damage its supposed victories have inflicted. Unfortunately, statistics can hardly address the moral question of how so many people are made complicit in rigging, manipulation, coercion or worse — and even more people are completely desensitized to it. This is the deeper problem we need to address.

title: Russia’s Currency Buying Spree Set to Pressure Ruble as Oil Revenues Rise
description: Russia’s Finance Ministry plans to increase its daily foreign currency purchases more than sixfold this month, adding pressure on the ruble, though analysts said that rising oil revenues and exporters’ tax payments could cushion the impact.
content:
Russia’s Finance Ministry plans to increase its daily foreign currency purchases more than sixfold this month, adding pressure on the ruble, though analysts said that rising oil revenues and exporters’ tax payments could cushion the impact.
The ministry said it would buy 279.4 billion rubles ($3.30 billion) worth of foreign currency between Oct. 7 and Nov. 6 under Russia’s fiscal rule, equivalent to 12.7 billion rubles ($149.9 million) a day.
After accounting for the Central Bank’s daily foreign currency sales of 600 million rubles ($7.1 million) to offset earlier spending from the National Wealth Fund, net purchases will total 12.1 billion rubles ($142.8 million) a day. That compares with current net purchases of 1.9 billion rubles ($22.4 million).
The increase highlights the competing effects of higher oil prices on the ruble. Stronger energy revenues prompt the government to buy more foreign currency under the fiscal rule, which puts pressure on the Russian currency. But they also give exporters more foreign earnings to sell domestically, something that could support the ruble.
Economist Yegor Susin estimated that the increased purchases could weaken the ruble’s average monthly exchange rate by 2 to 3 rubles (2.4 to 3.5 U.S. cents) per dollar. Yaroslav Kabakov, director of strategy at brokerage Finam, described the ministry’s increased purchases as the main factor favoring a weaker ruble.
The yuan rose 1.1% on the Moscow Exchange after the announcement, climbing from 12.59 rubles ($0.1486) to 12.73 rubles ($0.1502).
The planned purchases reflect a rise in the oil price used to calculate Russia’s energy taxes, which averaged $92.10 a barrel in September, up from $67.10 in August.
Russia’s mineral extraction tax is calculated using the previous month’s average oil price, meaning September’s increase will boost October tax receipts. The Finance Ministry expects oil and gas revenues to exceed the baseline set under the fiscal rule by almost 290 billion rubles ($3.42 billion).
Gazprombank analysts said the ministry’s plans appeared to suggest it did not expect oil prices to fall sharply.
The support for the ruble from higher export earnings will take longer to materialize. According to Central Bank estimates, oil export revenues reach the domestic currency market with a lag of 1.5 to two months, meaning September’s higher prices will begin influencing the exchange rate only from late October.
Oil companies could nevertheless step up foreign currency sales sooner to meet tax payments. They have accumulated more than $200 billion abroad, and October brings a quarterly payment of Russia’s tax on additional income from hydrocarbon production.
Analysts at Tverdye Tsifry estimated that October oil and gas budget revenues could approach 1 trillion rubles ($11.8 billion), even after substantial payments under the fuel subsidy mechanism that compensates producers for supplying the domestic market.
Susin said meeting those tax obligations would require companies to increase sales of foreign currency earnings, potentially supporting the ruble. By November, revenues from oil sold at $80 to $100 a barrel should also be reaching the market, he said.
Analysts at Vector Capital said exporters’ foreign currency earnings remained high and should soften the pressure from the ministry’s purchases. They did not expect a sharp depreciation, though they also saw little reason for the ruble to strengthen.
Still, the timing of those competing flows could produce volatility. Yuri Kravchenko, head of money market analysis at Veles Capital, said the gaps between changes in oil prices, the receipt and sale of export earnings, and government currency operations could cause sizable swings in either direction.

title: Ovechkin to Launch His Own Beer Brand in Russia
description: Washington Capitals star Alexander Ovechkin plans to launch his own beer brand in Russia with a producer owned by Arnest, a group that has rapidly expanded by buying the Russian businesses of departing Western companies.
content:
Washington Capitals star Alexander Ovechkin plans to launch his own beer brand in Russia with a producer owned by Arnest, a group that has rapidly expanded by buying the Russian businesses of departing Western companies.
The OVI range will be produced by Bochkarev Breweries and is expected to go on sale before the end of 2026, the Kommersant newspaper reported Monday. It will include a classic lager, a lower-alcohol lager and an alcohol-free beer, priced at about 100 rubles ($1.18) per can.
The venture brings together one of Russia’s best-known athletes, whose support for President Vladimir Putin has drawn renewed criticism abroad, and a company that has become a major beneficiary of the Western corporate exodus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“I have long wanted to create my own beer, one that I would enjoy drinking myself,” Ovechkin said in comments supplied to Kommersant by the brewer’s press office. He said he preferred pale beers with a clean, balanced taste.
Bochkarev Breweries belongs to businessman Alexei Sagal’s Arnest group. Its brewing business was built around Heineken’s Russian assets, which Arnest acquired in 2023 for a symbolic 1 euro.
The company produces brands including Bochkarev, Okhota and Krusovice and ranks third in Russia by beer production volume.
Arnest’s expansion has extended well beyond brewing. In 2022, it bought aluminum packaging plants from Ball Corporation. It subsequently acquired Oriflame’s Russian assets, Heineken’s Russian business and Unilever’s operations in the country. In 2026, it bought Avon’s Russian business and agreed to acquire Reckitt’s assets.
Alexei Dyumin, a former Putin bodyguard who now serves as secretary of Russia’s State Council, reportedly helped Sagal lobby for the Heineken and Unilever deals. The Bell has also reported ties between Sagal and Denis Manturov, who headed Russia’s Industry and Trade Ministry for many years.
Sagal has attributed his success to approaching Western companies directly.
For Ovechkin, the beer venture follows a fresh controversy over his political activities in Russia while playing for a U.S. team.
In September, he appeared in a campaign video for the ruling United Russia party ahead of Russia’s State Duma elections. Asked about his decision afterward, he said: “I’m Russian and I support my country.”
The video drew criticism in the the West. Latvia barred Ovechkin from entering the country, while the Ukrainian Canadian Congress called on Canada’s government to impose sanctions on him. U.S. Republican Representative Joe Wilson urged the NHL’s leadership to review Ovechkin’s participation in the political advertisement.
Ovechkin has publicly supported Putin since at least 2017, when he founded the Putin Team movement. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he said he supported peace and wanted the fighting to end as soon as possible.
He has played for the Capitals since 2005. In April 2025, he broke Wayne Gretzky’s record for NHL regular-season goals, finishing the 2025-26 season with 929.

title: Krasnodar Mayor Resigns After Contentious Tenure
description: Yevgeny Naumov, the mayor of the southern Russian city of Krasnodar, announced his early resignation on Monday.
content:
Yevgeny Naumov, the mayor of the southern Russian city of Krasnodar, announced his early resignation on Monday.
Naumov, whose five-year term was set to expire in November 2027, did not explain the reason behind his departure.
The Krasnodar City Duma accepted Naumov’s resignation and appointed First Deputy Mayor Dmitry Vasilyev as acting head of the city.
The City Duma will select the city's next mayor from a shortlist presented by Governor Veniamin Kondratyev.
Kondratyev initiated a new selection process for mayoral candidates last month.
Born in Krasnodar in 1980, Naumov spent his career within the municipal and regional administration. Local lawmakers elected him mayor in November 2022.
Naumov’s four-year tenure was marked by local protests and controversies over infrastructure and urban planning decisions.
In January, he signed off on plans to build an Orthodox Church on the grounds of a riverside park despite opposition from residents. Since November 2025, more than 30,000 people have signed a petition demanding his resignation.
A local court began hearing a lawsuit against Naumov’s administration over the construction project.
Media reports say that residents objected to a general infrastructure plan adopted by the city under Naumov’s leadership, with some 27,000 residents commenting on the plan, sparking mass protests.
Complaints against Naumov’s administration have also piled up due to the administration’s failure to manage winter weather emergencies and stalled transit projects.

title: Officials Seek to Reassure Public After Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute Worker’s Death
description: Russian health authorities maintain that the health situation in Siberia’s Irkutsk region remains stable amid concerns surrounding the death of a lab worker at a local anti-plague facility, state media reported Sunday.
content:
Russian health authorities maintain that the health situation in Siberia’s Irkutsk region remains stable amid concerns surrounding the death of a lab worker at a local anti-plague facility, state media reported Sunday.
The female employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was hospitalized last Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died on Thursday.
The lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” according to a statement from consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor cited by Interfax.
Media reports have described the suspected infection as pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs and can spread between humans through respiratory droplets.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, initially claimed the employee had died of the plague, before modifying his statement with the word “maybe.”
Rospotrebnadzor said that laboratory analysis of material from the patient did not reveal any microorganisms associated with her work handling dangerous pathogens.
Earlier reports claimed the lab worker may have broken a test tube containing live bacteria.
According to Interfax, the institute’s special commission and Rospotrebnadzor concluded that no emergency or security breach had occurred. The watchdog noted that no other infectious disease complaints had been registered among institute employees over the preceding 10 days.
Rospotrebnadzor said all close contacts were placed under medical observation with daily laboratory testing, which detected two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus, but no other infections.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev said in a video published Monday that family members and close relatives under quarantine could be discharged next week.
Local media reported that, contrary to earlier reports, area hospitals continued to operate on standard schedules aside from localized precautions.
The Kremlin on Monday referred all questions about the issue to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the situation.
"We're watching and monitoring it closely," Rubio told reporters before leaving for a trip to Europe. "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it."
Rubio, citing what Russia has released about the death, said it seemed there was a worker in the lab who was infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.
"There's very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia , obviously,” he said. "But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads."
A European Commission spokesperson said Monday that Europe was also “very closely” monitoring the situation.
“We are aware of the reports concerning the laboratory incident in Russia, seemingly involving a pathogen-causing plague,” the spokesperson said.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, the location of the ​first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the ​small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas. It is rare for Russia ns ⁠to fall ill with plague, however, though cases in other parts of the world — notably Africa — occur ​every year.

title: Putin Says Chinese Cars Are Cheap. Yet Russian Buyers Pay a Hefty Premium.
description: At last week’s meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, President Vladimir Putin praised Chinese cars and predicted that “we will all soon be driving” them. “Whether that’s good or bad, I don’t know, but they’re inexpensive and good quality,” he said.
content:
At last week’s meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, President Vladimir Putin praised Chinese cars and predicted that “we will all soon be driving” them.
“Whether that’s good or bad, I don’t know, but they’re inexpensive and good quality,” he said.
While Chinese manufacturers have filled much of the gap left by Western brands, higher import charges and local assembly costs mean Russian buyers pay more for the vehicles, while further increases in recycling fees will add to prices next year.
Higher recycling fees imposed in 2024 and 2025 have reduced imports of new cars from China. Chinese manufacturers increasingly supply the market through assembly plants in Russia and Belarus, sometimes selling their models under local brands, according to the analytics agency Avtostat.
A Chinese-Belarusian joint venture assembles Geely models and sells them under the Belgee brand. In Russia, factories owned by AGR assemble Chery models under the Tenet name. AGR, a Russian holding company linked to the owners of dealership group Avilon, operates former Western car plants.
Chinese brands account for more than 40% of Russia’s new-car market, excluding vehicles sold under local names, according to Oleg Moseyev, an auto industry analyst and former president of the Russian Automobile Dealers Association (ROAD).
Lada’s share fell to 25% in the first half of the year, a level its manufacturer, AvtoVAZ, has described as a “critical threshold.”
At the start of the year, the average passenger car cost about $23,000 in China and $45,000 in Russia, according to GlobalData.
Avtostat CEO Sergei Tselikov wrote in February that passenger cars cost roughly twice as much in Russia as in China. Local assembly from imported kits also produces this price gap, he said.
Importers pay other charges and incur local production expenses when they bring in kits, which carry no recycling fee, Tselikov said.
Surveys and reports have also documented quality complaints from private motorists and taxi drivers who drive Chinese models.
Russian consumers retain an attachment to established foreign brands, and the average driver would still choose one if given the opportunity, Tselikov said.
An automotive expert said Russian buyers had little alternative to Chinese manufacturers.
“Without the Chinese, we would have faced shortages and technological decline,” the expert said . “As it is, given the progress Chinese manufacturers have made, we are driving modern cars. We just pay twice the price.”
The cost of importing a budget model illustrates how the charges accumulate.
ROAD CEO Alexei Podshchekoldin used the Jetta VA3 sedan as an example a year ago. At the time, the car cost less than 900,000 rubles ($10,620) in China, but official importers sold it in Russia for 2.56 million rubles ($30,208).
Customs duties and other import charges accounted for 1.03 million rubles ($12,154) of the price, including a recycling fee of 667,400 rubles ($7,875) and 20% value-added tax.
Shipping added 350,000 rubles ($4,130), the distributor’s margin totaled 160,000 rubles ($1,888) and the dealer received 120,000 rubles ($1,416), or about 5% of the final price.
Since that calculation, the recycling fee has risen above 800,000 rubles ($9,440) and VAT has increased to 22%. Other costs have also climbed. A scheduled increase of 10% to 20% in recycling fees at the start of next year will add to those expenses.
The Geely Cityray compact crossover was the most popular new-car model imported into Russia in September, according to Avtostat.
Prices in China start at 85,500 yuan, equivalent to about 1.06 million rubles ($12,508). In Russia, unofficial dealers charge at least 1.8 million rubles ($21,240), and authorized dealerships list prices starting at 2.5 million rubles ($29,500). Promotional offers sometimes reduce the authorized dealer price to about 2 million rubles ($23,600).
For the Jetour G700, a hybrid SUV showcased at the 2026 Beijing auto show, prices in China start at 329,000 yuan, or about 4.08 million rubles ($48,144). The model combines a long driving range and off-road capabilities with a luxury interior.
An unofficial importer bringing the vehicle into Russia for an individual buyer charges at least 7.8 million rubles ($92,040).
“We make very little on it,” a dealer offering the vehicle said. “The price difference is because the recycling fee for the engine and electric motor, with a combined output of 750 horsepower, will be about 3.6 million rubles ($42,480) even for personal use.”
Importing it through a company would push the price well above 8 million rubles ($94,400), the dealer added.
Some customers choose Chinese brands for political reasons, according to another dealer. They include officials who buy luxury vehicles from China to avoid supporting manufacturers in countries Moscow considers “unfriendly.”
“Of course, they buy luxury cars,” the dealer said. “But at least they can’t be accused of supporting the auto industry of ‘unfriendly’ countries.”
