title: Dozens Detained at Moscow Communist Party Rally
description: Moscow police detained around 60 people on Sunday during a Communist Party rally commemorating the 1993 constitutional crisis, after the event spiraled into a protest against alleged fraud during last month’s parliamentary elections.
content:
Moscow police detained around 60 people on Sunday during a Communist Party rally commemorating the 1993 constitutional crisis, after the event spiraled into a protest against alleged fraud during last month’s parliamentary elections.
An estimated 2,000 people gathered for an annual memorial honoring those killed during an Oct. 4, 1993, standoff when President Boris Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the Supreme Soviet parliament building to dissolve opposition to his administration.
Eyewitnesses told the Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti that police officers charged into the crowd after chants of slogans like “Down with the Tsar!” “Freedom for political prisoners!” and “For fair elections!” broke out against the ruling United Russia party.
United Russia won a record number of seats in the State Duma during the country’s first wartime parliamentary elections last month. The Communist Party — the largest Kremlin-approved systemic opposition faction — won fewer seats than in previous elections.
The Communist Party said 65 “mostly young people” were detained at the tail end of the rally on Sunday afternoon.
“Efforts are underway to release the detainees and provide them with the necessary help,” the party said in a statement on its Telegram channel.

title: Russia Says It Hit Kyiv Bridge, 2 Vessels in Black Sea
description: Russia hit on Sunday the Northern bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv, targeting a route used to transport troops and military cargo, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
content:
Russia hit on Sunday the Northern bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv, targeting a route used to transport troops and military cargo, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry also said it hit two dry cargo vessels carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa in the northwestern Black Sea.
In an earlier statement, the ministry said that Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel east of Odesa overnight, as well as a Nova Poshta logistics center in Chornomorsk and a data center in Odesa.
On Sunday, Russia promised to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Reuters that Kyiv would step up attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The ministry said air defense forces had intercepted and destroyed 559 Ukrainian drones between 8 p.m Moscow time (5 p.m. GMT) on Saturday and 8 a.m. Moscow time (5 a.m. GMT) on Sunday over multiple Russian regions and above the Azov and Black seas.
Reuters could not independently verify the claims made by either side of the conflict.

title: OPEC+ Agrees to Keep November Oil Output Targets Steady
description: OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.  Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday.
content:
OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
“The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota,” said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
“Consequently, the oil market remains tight.”
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Even so, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members’ 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven hold their next meeting on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group called the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee (JMMC), which does not decide policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.

title: Germany's Merz Arrives in Kyiv to the Sound of Sirens and Explosions
description: The sound of air raid sirens and explosions rang out in Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived for a visit to show support for President Volodymyr Zelensky amid escalating Russian attacks.
content:
The sound of air raid sirens and explosions rang out in Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived for a visit to show support for President Volodymyr Zelensky amid escalating Russian attacks.
Merz will announce a package of measures including the release of 1 billion euros ($1.13 billion) in military aid and 350 million euros for repairs in the energy sector, German government officials said. A deal for joint production of various kinds of drones is also due to be finalised.
“I traveled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said, adding that Russian forces were bombing towns, residential buildings and heating plants. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us.”
“I will tell President Zelensky today: 'You can continue to count on our help,'” Merz said.
Four air raid alerts were heard in Kyiv on Sunday morning, and explosions and air defense systems also sounded across the city.
One of the Russian strikes hit the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, damaging its roadway, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. He said the strike had also damaged a hot water supply system in the area.
Russia has been attacking Kyiv's bridges since last week in an effort to disrupt links between the capital's two banks and logistics routes between central and eastern Ukraine.
The German chancellor is accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and an economic delegation including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense, Quantum Systems and other companies.
Merz is also expected to press the Ukrainian government for progress on reforms requested by EU partners, including in the fight against corruption.
Zelensky said on Wednesday, after speaking to Merz by phone, that Ukraine would soon finalize a deal with Germany for the production of drones, missiles and related software.
A key focus of the agreement is expected to be the rapid production of anti-jet drones, which Quantum, a German defense-technology company, has successfully tested. Since the summer, Russia has used dozens of high-speed jet attack drones daily to target civilian and military infrastructure.
In April, Quantum and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones announced the creation of Quantum WIY Industries, a joint venture to produce the Strila interceptor drone and related air-defense technologies.
The deal also involves the joint development and production of weapons with a range of more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) that Ukraine can use to launch attacks deep inside Russia.
On Thursday, Merz said Germany would not be intimidated by the rising number of hybrid attacks by Russia on European states.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Saturday that Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in Ukraine in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months. It warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against staying in or traveling to Ukraine.
Zelensky told Reuters on Saturday his country's armed forces would double down on their attacks on oil refineries in Russia in response to Moscow's “new doctrine” of escalating attacks on civilian infrastructure, which he said was aimed at forcing residents of Kyiv and other cities to flee.

title: Ukraine Will Hit Russian Refineries in Response to Moscow's ‘New Doctrine’ of Airstrikes
description: Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.

content:

“The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs once again warns foreign nationals, including diplomatic mission staff, against staying in Ukraine or travelling to its territory.”
“Responsibility for any adverse consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning,” the ministry said.
Russia has recently escalated strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital, hitting a bridge across the Dnipro river in an air attack on Saturday. The intensifying campaign has upended life for the capital's 3 million residents ahead of the bitter winter months.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that Ukraine was paying the price for its own attacks on Russia and would continue to do so as Moscow's forces systematically strike different targets there.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on the other side's grain vessels in the Black Sea in recent months, while Russian oil refineries and other enterprises continue to come under Ukrainian shelling and Ukrainian drones kill civilians in Russian border regions.
Both sides deny targeting civilians or civilian infrastructure.

description: The Trump administration’s talks with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the New York Times reported on Saturday.
content:

The White House, the U.S. Treasury Department and Lukoil didn't respond to requests for comment outside regular business hours.
The group pursuing the deal includes U.S. investor and billionaire Todd Boehly, two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Kushner or Witkoff's family, and an arm of the U.S. government, the newspaper said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the deal during a Sept. 5 meeting with Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin, the NYT said citing people familiar with the meeting. Putin proposed completing the deal as a way to show Russians they could do business with the United States, one of the people said.

title: Ex-Deputy Governor Who Planned to Fight in Ukraine Gets 14 Years for Military Supplies Theft
description: A Russian court sentenced a former deputy governor of the southern Krasnodar region to 14 years in prison for abuse of authority and organizing the theft of supplies intended for troops fighting in Ukraine, the regional courts’ press service said.
content:
A Russian court sentenced a former deputy governor of the southern Krasnodar region to 14 years in prison for abuse of authority and organizing the theft of supplies intended for troops fighting in Ukraine, the regional courts’ press service said .
Vlasov resigned as deputy governor of Krasnodar in September 2025 and announced plans to join the Kuban brigade fighting in Ukraine. He was arrested the following day.
Vlasov, who also headed the Kuban Cossack Host, was fined 1 million rubles ($11,900) and barred from holding managerial or administrative positions in state or local government for three years.
His adviser, Alexander Starodubtsev, received six years for fraud, the same fine and a two-and-a-half-year employment ban. Both men will serve their sentences in general-regime penal colonies.
The verdict has yet to take legal effect.
The Sovetsky District Court in Krasnodar found that the Cossack organization received a 100 million ruble ($1.19 million) government subsidy in August 2022 to buy supplies for BARS-1, BARS-11, BARS-16 and other units fighting in Ukraine.
It bought uniforms, protective gear and other equipment worth 57.75 million rubles ($687,225) between August and December that year but failed to deliver them by the deadline.
Acting on Vlasov’s instructions, Starodubtsev stole goods worth about 2.31 million rubles ($27,489) with the intention of selling them through an online classifieds website, the court found.
Belts, gloves, raincoats, boots and socks were advertised on Avito, the local outlet Za Krasnodar reported in September. Investigators recovered stolen goods from Starodubtsev’s home, it said.
In early 2023, Starodubtsev also took goods worth 347,868 rubles ($4,140) that had been incorrectly recorded as delivered. He kept them at home awaiting buyers until law enforcement officers seized them, according to the court statement reported by Kubanskie Novosti.
Vlasov instructed employees of the Cossack organization and representatives of military units to falsify delivery records to conceal the theft, the court found.
One BARS member testified that, at Vlasov’s instruction, he signed a delivery document for about 20 million rubles ($238,000) worth of goods despite receiving none of them, according to case materials published by Za Krasnodar.
The witness, whose testimony was read out in court because he was in the combat zone, said shortages of uniforms, drones and other equipment prevented units from fully carrying out combat tasks.
Kommersant reported in August that commanders and military representatives also described receiving fewer supplies than records showed. The organization’s former chief accountant testified that she handled paperwork without monitoring deliveries.
Vlasov became deputy governor of Krasnodar in September 2020 and took over the Kuban Cossack Host in 2021.

title: Lukashenko Vows Belarus’ Full Support for Putin on Ukraine
description: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko reaffirmed his alignment with Russia over its war in Ukraine on Friday, despite highlighting nuances in his own perspective on the conflict.
content:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko reaffirmed his alignment with Russia over its war in Ukraine on Friday, despite highlighting nuances in his own perspective on the conflict.
His comments follow Belarus’ efforts to improve ties with the United States after years of isolation and Western sanctions. U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has reopened a dialogue with Minsk, easing some sanctions in exchange for prisoner releases.
“I told [Russian] President [Vladimir] Putin openly: I have my own understanding of certain aspects of the conflict in Ukraine, but we’ll always remain committed to our common course,” Lukashenko said, according to the state news agency Belta.
“If you, the Russian leadership, make a decision, we’ll always be with you despite our particular ways of understanding what’s happening there. We’ve never been traitors,” Lukashenko added.
He spoke at a gathering of the governing body of the Eurasian Economic Union, a Russian-led bloc, which includes Armenia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan alongside Belarus.
Twice this year, the president of Kazakhstan has proposed freezing the conflict to restart diplomatic talks.
Lukashenko said that he, like Putin, knows the situation on the front lines in Ukraine, which he claimed allows them both to maintain “more refined approaches” to the war.
Belarus allowed Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Lukashenko has said that Belarusian troops would not be sent directly into the war. At the same time, he has intensified military preparations with the deployment of Russia’s nuclear-capable Oreshnik hypersonic ballistic missile system and announced a “targeted mobilization” of Belarusian forces.
Belarus has also sought to have U.S. sanctions lifted since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year. The Biden administration had introduced many of the sanctions in response to the 2020 election crackdown in Belarus and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Nearly 200 People Under Observation After Irkutsk Lab Worker Dies From Plague
description: Health authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk region have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation after a laboratory worker died from plague, according to media reports and a statement by a regional leader Friday.
content:
Health authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk region have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation after a laboratory worker died from plague, according to media reports and a statement by a regional leader Friday.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, confirmed that the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague. Irkutsk officials had previously described the illness only as a “particularly dangerous infection.”
Citing information from Russia’s consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor and Buryatia’s government, Tsydenov said the woman had not visited his republic and that her infection was unrelated to the region.
“There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in areas bordering Mongolia,” he wrote on social media.
The woman was identified as Daria Sh., a 27- or 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, by the exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) and pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV .
She reportedly told medical staff that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples for testing.
She was hospitalized Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia in Shelekhov, a town near the regional capital of Irkutsk. She was placed on a ventilator and died Thursday, according to the reports.
The Shelekhov district hospital was placed under quarantine pending an assessment by a special commission.
At least 197 people who may have had contact with her were reportedly placed under medical isolation , including more than 100 in hospital wards.
Authorities canceled planned public events in Irkutsk, while law enforcement reportedly opened a criminal investigation into potential health safety violations resulting in death.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev urged the public to remain calm after meeting with Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova to coordinate emergency containment measures.
“All identified contact persons have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness, and their laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev wrote on Telegram on Friday. He did not mention the reports of the laboratory worker’s death.
Media reports have described the suspected infection as pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs and can spread between humans through respiratory droplets. Tsydenov’s statement did not specify the form of plague.

title: Ex-German Chancellor Schroeder Joins Board of German Chain in Russia
description: Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder has joined the supervisory board of Hyperglobus, the Russian arm of the German superstore chain Globus, business media reported Friday.
content:
Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder has joined the supervisory board of Hyperglobus, the Russian arm of the German superstore chain Globus, business media reported Friday.
The appointment comes as Western retailers face the risk of state asset seizures, which President Vladimir Putin defended as a response to the EU freezing its state funds.
Hyperglobus owner Thomas Bruch praised Schroeder as an “ideal addition” who would help maintain a “dialogue-oriented approach” in Russia, according to a statement published by Kommersant.
Schroeder was quoted emphasizing the importance of maintaining economic ties and investing in Russia’s food sector. He will be responsible for supporting the strategic development of the business, RBC cited the company as saying.
Schroeder’s appointment marks a strategic move to safeguard the company from state seizures, according to Kommersant.
Putin has previously proposed Schroeder as the EU’s representative in potential talks with Russia. Brussels and Berlin have rejected the candidacy of Schroeder, who is Putin’s longtime personal acquaintance and who has previously headed the boards of Russian state energy giants Rosneft and Nord Stream.
Russian authorities recently took control of the domestic operations of German wholesaler Metro Cash & Carry, Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailers Auchan and Leroy Merlin (renamed to Leman Pro in Russia), as well as two French logistics companies.
On Thursday, Putin defended the asset seizures as a “symmetrical response” to Western freezes of Russian state assets abroad. He noted that control could eventually be returned under “favorable conditions.”

German media reported recently that Globus expanded its Russia footprint with tens of millions of euros in investments and new large-format stores around Moscow.
Globus Holding said it had fully spun off its Russian superstores and that they are legally and operationally independent. It said questions should be directed to Hyperglobus.

title: Russia Jails Indigenous Buryat Activist 20 Years in Absentia
description: A military court in Russia’s Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia for organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization, Buryatia’s Interior Ministry announced Friday.  Khankhalaeva, 53, is a U.S.-based opera singer and the founder of Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia, an exiled movement advocating for the Siberian republic of Buryatia’s independence from Russia.  Russian authorities claimed Khankhalaeva was guilty of “engaging in active anti-state activities” aimed at Buryatia’s secession, as well as inciting “social and ethnic discord.” Buryatia is a resource-rich region of around 970,000 people that shares a border of over 1,000 kilometers with Mongolia.
content:
A military court in Russia’s Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia for organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization, Buryatia’s Interior Ministry announced Friday.
Khankhalaeva, 53, is a U.S.-based opera singer and the founder of Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia, an exiled movement advocating for the Siberian republic of Buryatia’s independence from Russia.
Russian authorities claimed Khankhalaeva was guilty of “engaging in active anti-state activities” aimed at Buryatia’s secession, as well as inciting “social and ethnic discord.”
Buryatia is a resource-rich region of around 970,000 people that shares a border of over 1,000 kilometers with Mongolia. Nearly one in three of its residents identify as Buryat, a Mongolic ethnic group indigenous to the region.
Although the Chita military court sentenced Khankhalaeva in August, the ruling had not been made public until now.
Khankhalaeva said she also found out about her sentencing from the news.
“I am on Russia’s list of extremists and terrorists, so I have been trying to find out if there is a case against me, but this information seems to be classified,” she told The Moscow Times.
Khankhalaeva called the case against her “high praise” for her and her movement’s work, adding that it “means that everything we are saying is the truth.”
“Of course, this [sentencing] won’t affect my activist work. On the contrary, to me it is proof that we are doing the right thing,” said Khankhalaeva.
The activist noted that she had “expected some kind of a reaction” from Russian authorities” after the movement held its second Congress of Supporters of Buryatia’s Independence in the U.S. last month.
“By the fifth year of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, there are more and more supporters of the independence of Buryatia,” she added.
Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia was among the 172 ethnic, Indigenous rights and decolonial groups and media outlets designated as “terrorist” organizations by Russia in 2024.
Earlier that year, the pro-independence movement was also added to Russia’s growing list of “extremist” organizations over its ties with the non-existent “Anti-Russian Separatist Movement.”
Khankhalaeva has denied the accusations against her, stressing that Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia “never called for violence” and “advocates for achieving our goals strictly with non-violent means.”

title: U.S. Blacklists Russia’s A7 Payment Platform Over Alleged Sanctions Evasion
description: The U.S.
content:
The U.S. Treasury Department has expanded sanctions against Russia-backed cross-border payments platform A7, prohibiting all transactions and labeling it a “transnational criminal organization” for allegedly helping Iran and cybercriminals process illicit global transactions.
“Today’s action targeting A7 continues Treasury’s unprecedented efforts to isolate Iran and its financial enablers,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement Thursday.
The Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) alleged that A7 had built a massive global network of front companies and “sub-agents” to bypass Western banking restrictions.
They claimed the A7 network “created pathways” for Iran’s central bank, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as well as oil and weapons smuggling networks, to use its shadow banking channels to move illicit funds.
The Treasury also alleged that the A7 network “catered” to cybercriminals.
Treasury officials claimed A7 sub-agents processed more than $17 billion in global transactions between January 2025 and June 2026.
A7 was accused of using fake trade documents, import-export records and misleading goods descriptions through sub-agents to “disguise” illegal payments as normal business transactions.
Moscow-based A7 defended its business model and denied involvement with sanctioned Iranian entities in a statement.
“A7 categorically rejects any allegations that it has worked with Iran or terrorist organizations,” the company said.
The company said it was servicing “legitimate import and export operations involving consumer goods and commodities.”
A7 added that it was providing “uninterrupted payment settlements for the Russian market, which has been subject to unlawful restrictive measures.”
A7, set up in 2024 by the defense sector-focused bank Promsvyazbank, has become the leader in Russia’s cross-border payments market as the country seeks to develop alternative payment systems with its main trading partners.
Ilan Shor, a Moldovan businessman who was sentenced in Moldova to 15 years in prison for money laundering, owns 51% of the company. Shor fled Moldova first to Israel and then to Russia.
An investigation by The Washington Post reported that Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) worked closely with Shor and helped finance his political activities.
The United States sanctioned Shor and his wife, Russian singer Jasmin, in 2022 for activities Washington said were aimed at destabilizing Moldova. Shor is also under European Union and British sanctions.
Last year, the U.S. sanctioned individual A7 entities for issuing a ruble-backed digital token called A7A5 and using it to bypass financial restrictions.

title: Navigating Identity: A New Bookshop Reflects a Changing Pushkin House
description: Pushkin House in London has opened a new bookshop designed by Alexander Brodsky, the renowned Russian architect known for projects including the Joseph Brodsky museum in St.
content:
Pushkin House in London has opened a new bookshop designed by Alexander Brodsky, the renowned Russian architect known for projects including the Joseph Brodsky museum in St. Petersburg.
Founded by Russian émigrés in Bloomsbury in 1954, Pushkin House describes itself as a space that “explores and debates” Russian cultures and identities through exhibitions, seminars, lectures and other cultural events.
The renovation comes amid a broader reassessment of the center’s role since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As its audiences have changed, Pushkin House has expanded its programming to include more Ukrainian and other post-Soviet voices, while examining the hierarchies that have long shaped how Russian culture is presented.
Brodsky, whose work is held in collections including New York’s Museum of Modern Art and London’s Tate Modern, had always insisted that the renovated space should be a working bookstore rather than an art installation, Pushkin House Executive Director Elena Sudakova said.
“His vision as an artist is therefore very much a representation of changes that have been happening here since 2022, a year that has truly catalyzed our programming shift towards reassessment and re-evaluation of cultural thinking that we are a part of,” Sudakova told The Moscow Times. “The open plan of Brodsky’s ground floor bookshop invites visitors to partake in this process.”
Brodsky has a long connection with Pushkin House. In 2017, he created a pavilion in Bloomsbury Square, “Beyond 101 KM: Further Everywhere,” dedicated to 20th-century poets exiled from Soviet cities.
“In hindsight, that pavilion was prophetic,” Sudakova said.
She also recalled early conversations between Brodsky and her predecessor, Clem Cecil, about creating an imaginary bedroom for Russian national poet Alexander Pushkin in the building.
“Brodsky has always insisted that this building is a house and that it must behave like one,” she said.
That bedroom has yet to materialize. But two weeks before the interview, Brodsky tested the building’s domestic potential himself, spending the night there while finishing his sculptures without telling the staff, Sudakova said.
Since 2022, Pushkin House’s audiences “have become broader, more diverse, and, in many ways, more invested in the life of the House,” she said.
Creating opportunities for communication and cultural exchange has become a central part of its work.
“Ukrainians have arrived in Britain in significant numbers, alongside Russians leaving the country in the context of war and repression. These are not simply demographic shifts for Pushkin House; they have changed the people who walk through our doors,” Sudakova said.
Visitors include established émigré families and their descendants, recent arrivals from Russia and Ukraine, people from across the wider post-Soviet region, British enthusiasts of Russian culture, students and cultural professionals, she said. Others are Londoners encountering these cultures for the first time.
In the first months of the full-scale war, Pushkin House overhauled its program to provide a platform for Ukrainian artists and anti-war voices. It also used its street-facing billboards to display anti-war works by Russian artists.
“These gestures were deliberately visible — a way of acknowledging the complexity and discomfort of our position rather than retreating from it,” Sudakova said.
In the years that followed, staff began to reflect more deeply on the center’s blind spots and how it was perceived by others.
Sudakova said Pushkin House moved toward a coherent institutional program that includes more active engagement by its audience.
“Our thinking around decolonization has emerged from this process: not as a rejection of Russian culture, but as an attempt to loosen its inherited hierarchies and open it to a wider field of voices, experiences and histories,” she said.
Few institutions like Pushkin House exist in Europe today.
Many Russian state-backed cultural centers across the continent closed after 2022. Those that stayed open , including the Russian Houses in Brussels and Vienna, host programming that reflects official Russian narratives.
Anti-war migrants have meanwhile established several independent cultural centers, but they primarily serve Russian-speaking émigrés rather than for residents of the host countries.
Amsterdam’s Pegasus bookstore is among the independent institutions that worked with Russian culture before the invasion of Ukraine.
A representative for the bookstore said it had never applied for Russian government grants and had long considered “shared values” when deciding which organizations, writers and translators to work with.
“Thus, we already thought carefully about who we are supporting, how we can help to correct imbalances and who we would like to give a voice to,” the representative told The Moscow Times. “After 2022, we did not need to change our strategy because we were always critical when weighing the literature and writers to publish.”
Demand for Russian-language books has nevertheless increased significantly as people who left Russia following the invasion settled abroad. Pegasus has expanded its selection of books published outside Russia known as tamizdat .
Staff said they had also become more vigilant about checking whether authors had expressed support for the war.
“We definitely notice that the local attitude toward Russian culture and literature has changed,” Pegasus said. “Very few translations from Russian are being published. Fortunately, the lacuna of Ukrainian literature is filled in its place. … This is because the paradigm is changing: since 2022, the Netherlands is finally more aware of its Russocentrism.”
At Pushkin House, contemporary fiction in translation is the most popular category among English-speaking book buyers. Readers seek works from Ukraine, the South Caucasus, Central Asia and the Baltic states as well as from Russia.
Bestsellers include Soviet-era dissident literature such as Vasily Grossman’s “Life and Fate,” émigré writing from different generations and books by women from across the post-Soviet world, including Latvian author Nora Ikstena’s “Soviet Milk.”
Russian-language bestsellers include Maria Stepanova’s “Focus,” Alexei Navalny’s memoir “Patriot” and Anton Dolin’s “Bad Russians.” All three are published outside Russia as tamizdat , as their authors are banned in Russia or address subjects that are off-limits there.
“Russian-speaking readers naturally want to understand current events and reflect on the present, but this does not mean that their reading is limited to politics or the war. They continue to buy both classics and contemporary fiction," Sudakova said.
That balance between past and present runs through nearly every aspect of Pushkin House’s work, she said.
Brodsky’s renovation has also uncovered part of the building’s buried heritage — 18th-century sandstone and marble floors dating to architect Henry Flitcroft’s design in the mid-1740s, long concealed beneath layers of 20th-century cement.
“There is wonderful poetry in this: a Russian architect illuminating British classical heritage,” Sudakova said.

title: Russia Will Consider Partial Lifting of Diesel Export Ban in Case of Overproduction, Novak Says
description: Russia said on Friday it would consider a partial lifting of diesel export restrictions in case of overproduction, raising the prospect of a possible reprieve for global fuel markets strained by war and supply shortages.
content:
Russia said on Friday it would consider a partial lifting of diesel export restrictions in case of overproduction, raising the prospect of a possible reprieve for global fuel markets strained by war and supply shortages.
Speaking in the upper chamber of the Russian parliament, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak also said that the domestic diesel market is currently balanced.
Russia this week extended its ban on diesel exports for fuel producers until the end of October, adding further strain on the global energy market.
Russia was the world's second-largest diesel exporter after the United States before it started to limit overseas sales this summer to meet the demand of the domestic market, supplies to which were dented by Ukrainian attacks on refineries.
Global fuel shortages and sharp price increases have been in focus, especially in the U.S., where diesel prices have shot to records over $6.50 a gallon as the wars in Iran and Ukraine constrain deliveries of fuel, a political risk for U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
"Today, the diesel market is balanced and supplies are sufficient. Although we extended the diesel export ban into October just a few days ago, we will continue to monitor the situation and, if diesel production exceeds domestic demand, we will consider partially reopening exports," Novak said.
President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that Russia will not supply its diesel to global energy markets until sanctions against Moscow are lifted.
Novak said that the situation with Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure has remained "tense."
He said Russia thwarted attacks on four refineries overnight, while the authorities were assessing the damage at one of the plants.
Novak also said that the damage caused by repeated raids on refineries has been significantly lower thanks to protection measures.
"This allows us to restore damaged equipment and bring facilities back into operation more quickly after repairs," he said.

title: Here's How Russia Plans to Pay for the Ukraine War in 2027
description: Russia plans to raise defense spending to a post-Soviet high next year while cutting civilian programs and increasing taxes, signaling that the Kremlin is bracing for a prolonged war in Ukraine despite saying it is ready for peace talks.
content:
Russia plans to raise defense spending to a post-Soviet high next year while cutting civilian programs and increasing taxes, signaling that the Kremlin is bracing for a prolonged war in Ukraine despite saying it is ready for peace talks.
The draft 2027 budget unveiled Thursday allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.2 billion) to defense, 26% more than was earmarked for that year in the previous budget and 375% above the pre-war level of 2021.
Defense would account for roughly a third of federal spending next year, setting a post-Soviet record in nominal ruble terms.
Analysts say that Russia still has the resources to keep fighting, but that households, businesses and public services will bear more of the cost.
Economist Boris Grozovsky said Russia’s wartime economy still has a “considerable” financial cushion.
“But the message is clear: everyone will pay for the war, as much as they can. Wherever a little more money appears, the government will come for it, while handing out as little as possible itself,” he wrote in an analysis published by the exiled outlet IStories.
The published defense allocation does not capture the full cost of the war. Russia has released only planned military spending rather than actual outlays since 2022, while classified budget items make the overall bill difficult to establish.
Soaring war costs have put increasing pressure on state finances. The federal budget deficit reached 5.65 trillion rubles ($67.8 billion), or 2.6% of gross domestic product, in 2025.
The government projects a shortfall of 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.6 billion), or 3.2% of GDP, for 2026 before it narrows to 5.4 trillion rubles ($64.8 billion), or 2.2%, in 2027.
In a forecast published before the draft budget was unveiled, economists at Russia’s largest lender Sberbank put next year’s deficit at 2.7% of GDP, questioning whether the government could deliver the spending restraint and higher non-oil and gas revenues needed to meet its earlier target.
This deficit is high by recent Russian standards, but it is still manageable and remains lower than in many European countries, such as France ( 5.4% of GDP ) and Britain ( 4.3% of GDP ).
The projected deficit does not in itself point to an imminent fiscal crisis, but containing it while increasing military spending is becoming more difficult.
The government plans to borrow 6.1 trillion rubles ($73.2 billion) next year, up from 5 trillion rubles ($60 billion) in 2026, to help finance the deficit.
Yet debt servicing is projected to reach 4.6 trillion rubles ($55.2 billion) in 2027, or 9.4% of total federal spending. Those costs remain high because the Central Bank has kept interest rates elevated to contain stubborn inflation that has been fueled by heavy government spending.
To help close the gap, Moscow is also cutting civilian spending and planning another round of tax increases for a third consecutive year.
The draft reduces allocations for healthcare by 5.5%, education by 5.4% and social programs by 6% compared with the amounts previously budgeted for 2027 .
Some of Russia's national projects, government programs targeting priorities like healthcare and infrastructure, will also face cuts going forward.
Funding for the Long and Active Life project, which supports health initiatives, would fall by about 20%, from 181.1 billion rubles ($2.17 billion) in 2026 to 145.9 billion rubles ($1.75 billion) next year.
The allocation for the federal cancer program would drop from 44.9 billion rubles ($538.8 million) to 3.9 billion rubles ($46.8 million).
The proposed tax measures are expected to raise an additional 1.5 trillion rubles ($18 billion).
They include a 22% value-added tax on purchases from foreign online retailers and a customs fee of 100 rubles, or about $1.20, on each parcel worth less than 200 euros.
Tax rates on income from sources including deposit interest, dividends and property sales would rise from a range of 13% to 15% to a range of 13% to 22%. The Finance Ministry has also proposed a one-time windfall tax on mining and metals companies.
The changes to taxes on passive income are expected to raise the most revenue, up to 700 billion rubles ($8.4 billion), followed by levies on online purchases , which would bring in another 500 billion rubles ($6 billion).
Analyst Alexandra Prokopenko said the budget showed defense spending growing faster than overall expenditure, squeezing the funds available for other purposes.
In an analysis for Carnegie Politika , she warned that the government may soon be approaching the limits of how much additional revenue it can raise through taxes to fund the war.
That could increase pressure on the Central Bank to support the wartime economy by cutting interest rates to reduce borrowing costs for the government and businesses, as well as increase debt restructuring for struggling companies, she said.

title: Fire Sweeps Historic St. Petersburg Mansion
description: A major fire swept through a 19th-century landmark in central St.
content:
A major fire swept through a 19th-century landmark in central St. Petersburg on Thursday evening, destroying large sections of an empty historic mansion that is undergoing a multi-million-dollar renovation process to turn it into luxury apartments.
The blaze broke out shortly after 8 p.m. at the Miller Mansion in central St. Petersburg, across from St. Isaac's Cathedral, one of the city’s most iconic landmarks. By Friday morning, the mansion was completely burned out .
Emergency services raised the alarm to a 3-alarm fire as flames spread across 2,000 square meters (21,500 square feet) of the main building and reached the roof of an adjoining structure.
A major fire swept through a 19th-century landmark in central St. Petersburg on Thursday evening, destroying large sections of a historic mansion. Read more: https://t.co/9tziMuz8AE pic.twitter.com/nMxq1vApF4
Authorities reported no injuries or deaths. Firefighters brought the flames under control overnight.
Investigators suspect welding work being conducted inside without proper safety precautions set off the fire.
The St. Petersburg branch of Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said the building’s old wooden floorboards, interior partitions and concealed wall cavities allowed the fire to travel rapidly between floors.
“We always consider every lead, starting with aliens,” spokesman Andrei Litovka told reporters late on Thursday.
Originally built in the late 18th century and redesigned in 1880 with Italian Renaissance-style facades, the protected heritage building had been scheduled for a major overhaul.
Earlier this year, a local developer secured a 768 million ruble ($9.2 million) loan to restore the site and convert it into a luxury residential development. The project was due to be completed in 2027.

title: Ukrainian Drones Target Volgograd, Krasnodar Industrial Sites
description: Ukrainian drone attacks targeted industrial facilities in southern Russia’s Volgograd and Krasnodar regions, officials and media reported Friday.
content:
Ukrainian drone attacks targeted industrial facilities in southern Russia’s Volgograd and Krasnodar regions, officials and media reported Friday.
Volgograd region Governor Andrei Bocharov said a “mass” drone attack targeted “industrial infrastructure” and damaged an apartment building, injuring one person.
The exiled outlet Astra reported that eyewitness footage showed a large glow from a fire in Volgograd's Krasnoarmeiskyi district, home to both the Volgograd oil refinery — Lukoil’s largest in southern Russia — and the Kaustik chemical plant.
Authorities in the Krasnodar region said an “enterprise” was slightly damaged by drone debris in the Black Sea town of Tuapse, which hosts an oil refinery and port facilities that include a grain terminal.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 646 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russia.
President Vladimir Putin recently admitted that Ukrainian refinery attacks have inflicted costs equivalent to 1% of Russia’s GDP.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched more than 100 attack drones overnight, nearly 50 of which were jet-powered, as he called on Western allies to tighten sanctions on Russia’s supply chains for foreign components.
Russian air strikes killed one and injured two in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, and forced the closure of the Southern Bridge and Paton Bridge across the Dnipro River, with partial restrictions on the Metro Bridge.

title: Russian Businesses to Pay $5.7Bln in ‘Voluntary’ Budget Contributions – The Bell
description: Russia expects to receive 471.7 billion rubles ($5.7 billion) in voluntary contributions from businesses this year as it seeks to plug a widening budget deficit amid record war spending, The Bell reported, citing documents accompanying the government’s three-year budget bill.
content:
Russia expects to receive 471.7 billion rubles ($5.7 billion) in voluntary contributions from businesses this year as it seeks to plug a widening budget deficit amid record war spending, The Bell reported , citing documents accompanying the government’s three-year budget bill.
The Finance Ministry documents do not identify the contributors or disclose how much each paid.
The payments come amid a wave of nationalizations affecting hundreds of companies worth more than 7 trillion rubles ($84 billion), with some business owners who lost their assets also facing criminal cases.
Contributions surged after President Vladimir Putin’s annual meeting with business leaders in March, when he asked billionaires on the Forbes list to contribute toward the war effort.
At the time, the federal budget deficit had reached nearly 6 trillion rubles ($72 billion), exceeding the government’s original full-year target of 3.7 trillion rubles ($44.4 billion). The Finance Ministry now expects the deficit to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.6 billion) by year-end.
Budget receipts from nongovernmental organizations stood at 15.6 billion rubles ($187.2 million) before the meeting, then rose to 159.7 billion rubles ($1.9 billion) over the following month. By mid-August, they had reached 383.7 billion rubles ($4.6 billion).
Billionaires Suleiman Kerimov, Vladimir Potanin and Oleg Deripaska offered at the March meeting to contribute personal funds to the budget, according to a source cited by business publication Ekspert.
They proposed paying a combined 460 billion rubles ($5.5 billion) if the Kremlin dropped plans to impose a windfall tax on their businesses, the source said.
The government nevertheless plans to introduce the tax in 2027. Companies subject to it will include Potanin’s Nornickel, Deripaska’s Rusal and gold producer Polyus, associated with Kerimov. The Finance Ministry expects to collect 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion) annually from those companies over the next three years.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, said in August that businesses were helping support the budget through contributions drawn from personal wealth and family funds, describing the payments as entirely voluntary.
Shokhin said businesses wanted to ensure that donations were not accompanied by a higher tax burden. Companies’ financial capacity needed to be balanced against the government’s need for budget support, he said.
The draft budget for 2027 through 2029 includes a total of 3.7 trillion rubles ($44.4 billion) in revenue from additional taxes.
Alongside higher taxes on large companies, the government plans to raise the top personal income tax rate on passive income, including interest on bank deposits, to 22%.

title: 7 Reported Killed in Explosion at Ammunition Plant Near Moscow
description: Seven people were killed in an explosion at a chemical plant in Russia’s Moscow region, the Telegram news channel Shot reported, as emergency crews responded to a fire at the facility.
content:
Seven people were killed in an explosion at a chemical plant in Russia’s Moscow region, the Telegram news channel Shot reported , as emergency crews responded to a fire at the facility.
The blast hit the Krasnozavodsk Chemical Plant, which produces ammunition and pyrotechnics, according to publicly available information. Authorities had not commented on the incident, and the reported death toll remained unconfirmed.
Shot reported that the seven people were inside workshop No. 4, which collapsed completely. Survivors said more workers had been inside, the channel reported, adding that rescue operations were continuing.
The Telegram channel Mash, citing local residents, reported three powerful explosions that shook nearby homes before a fire broke out. More than 40 workers were at the plant at the time, and an evacuation was underway, it said.
The Telegram channel 112, which has close ties to Russian law enforcement agencies, also reported an explosion and said emergency services were heading to the site.
Footage filmed by witnesses showed flames and a column of smoke rising above the plant.
Preliminary reports pointed to a technical cause for the explosion. No aerial attacks had been reported in the area.
The plant was previously targeted in a Ukrainian attack on July 7, 2025. Ukraine’s military said at the time that the facility produced thermobaric warheads for Shahed-type drones, known in Russia as Geran drones.
Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, part of its National Security and Defense Council, said the plant also produced explosives, gunpowder and components for ammunition and missile systems. It described the facility as part of the supply chain for Russian artillery shells, multiple-launch rocket systems and ballistic missiles.

title: Putin Says World Is Living Through a Dangerous Moment, Warns West Not to Escalate
description: President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
content:
President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday the world was living through a dangerous moment and warned the West not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russia n exclave of Kaliningrad, which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Locked in a war in Ukraine which he said Russia had no choice but to launch in order to safeguard its own security, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
But he reiterated that Moscow would resort to all weapons in its arsenal, including nuclear ones, if its most westerly territory — Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania — was threatened.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russia n Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russia n Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda ," Putin told the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow.
Putin said Russia realized it would be facing "an enemy [NATO] twice our size."
"And we will have to make use of our competitive advantages in this struggle. Yes, of course, France and Britain are nuclear powers — we understand that perfectly well and are fully aware of it," he said. "But no one else possesses the kind of weapons that Russia has today. That is our competitive advantage."
Putin's comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia , warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia 's Baltic exclave.
Russia 's warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russia n territory that is slightly bigger than the U.S. state of Connecticut. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by emphasising that it was a defensive alliance and that nuclear threats were not helpful.
Relations, already dire since Putin's decision to send troops into Ukraine in 2022, have worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios.
"We must realize that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return," he said.
"At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state," Putin said.
"Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome," he added.
Putin, who said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was worked out first, ruled out the idea of stopping Russia n strikes on Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea area, while conceding that Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries across Russia had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP).
He said Russia was now responding to Ukraine in kind.
But while he cast Western help to Kyiv when it came to launching deep strikes inside Russia as a future threat, he said Moscow was not planning to attack arms factories in Europe which supplied Ukraine "tomorrow."

title: Legendary Striker Artyom Dzyuba Indicates Likely Retirement at 38
description: Artyom Dzyuba, Russia's all-time leading scorer and former national football team captain, said Thursday that his professional playing career was likely over.
content:
Artyom Dzyuba, Russia's all-time leading scorer and former national football team captain, said Thursday that his professional playing career was likely over.
The 38-year-old striker has been without a club since departing Russian Premier League side FC Akron Tolyatti at the end of the 2025-26 season in May.
“My career is over. That’s it, guys,” Dzyuba told reporters, according to a video published by the outlet RB Sport.
He stopped short of issuing an official retirement statement, saying he could still play at the Fonbet Russian Cup, which started in July and runs through June 2027.
A product of Spartak Moscow’s youth academy, Dzyuba enjoyed a long career across Russian football.
In March 2025, while playing for newly promoted Akron Tolyatti, the Samara-based club founded in 2018, Dzyuba secured his place in Russian football history by scoring his 234th career goal.
Dzyuba racked up 264 total club and international goals over his professional career.
His club career saw him win four Russian Premier League titles, three Russian Super Cups and four Russian Cups. All but one were with Zenit St. Petersburg.
On the international stage, Dzyuba scored 31 goals in 56 caps for Russia, tying Alexander Kerzhakov as the top scorer in the history of the Russian national team.
Dzyuba rose to national prominence during Russia’s home 2018 FIFA World Cup, where he converted a game-tying penalty against Spain. Russia won 4-3 after a penalty shootout and reached the quarterfinals for the first time since 1970.

title: Kremlin Regrets U.S. Still Links Economic Ties to Peace in Ukraine
description: Russia believes it could already be working with the United States on mutually beneficial economic projects, the Kremlin said Thursday, calling it unfortunate that Washington was linking progress on such initiatives to a settlement of the conflict in Ukraine. “Regretfully, as before, the Americans link this entire process, despite the obvious benefit, to the Ukrainian settlement,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing. “They say that first comes the settlement, and only then the implementation of projects.
content:
Russia believes it could already be working with the United States on mutually beneficial economic projects, the Kremlin said Thursday, calling it unfortunate that Washington was linking progress on such initiatives to a settlement of the conflict in Ukraine.
“Regretfully, as before, the Americans link this entire process, despite the obvious benefit, to the Ukrainian settlement,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“They say that first comes the settlement, and only then the implementation of projects. We believe we don’t have to wait, we could work for our mutual benefit right now,” Peskov said.
His comments follow a visit to Washington by President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev on Monday.
A U.S. official said Dmitriev held “constructive” talks on ending the war in Ukraine and possible U.S.-Russia energy initiatives in the postwar period. Reuters reported that Dmitriev met with representatives of the U.S. Treasury and Energy departments.
Peskov said Dmitriev had briefed Putin on the outcome of his contacts with U.S. officials, adding that dialogue between Moscow and Washington was continuing.
Earlier in September, the Kremlin said U.S. President Donald Trump urged Putin in a call to end the war in order to open up “impressive and large-scale” U.S.-Russian trade prospects. Putin was said to have responded with an “objective and thorough analysis” of the battlefield situation and his views about achieving the war’s objectives.
Putin continues to demand the complete withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the unoccupied parts of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region as a condition for peace, a stance rejected by Kyiv.
Dmitriev told Reuters in June that he had remained in contact with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during a pause in their visits to Russia. He took part in all the negotiators’ meetings with Putin, including those held in early September.
On Wednesday, Peskov dismissed press reports that the Kremlin was discussing the release of political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions.

title: Russian Orthodox Church Denies That Troops Lost Medieval Warrior Prince’s Relics in Ukraine
description: The Russian Orthodox Church has denied reports that Russian troops abandoned fragments of the remains of St.
content:
The Russian Orthodox Church has denied reports that Russian troops abandoned fragments of the remains of St. Dmitry Donskoy while retreating near the eastern Ukrainian city of Lyman.
The pro-war Telegram channel Alex Parker reported that Russian forces may have lost the relics during a withdrawal in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Another Telegram channel, Kremlin Tabakerka, claimed that a site where officers had gathered for a prayer service came under fire, forcing them to leave the relics behind and retreat.
Neither channel’s account was accompanied by confirmation from Russian military officials.
“This is a fabrication, and it is being spread, one can assume, with anti-church intentions,” Vakhtang Kipshidze, deputy head of the church’s department for relations with society and the media, told the state-run RIA Novosti news agency.
Dmitry Donskoy, a medieval Russian prince, defeated the forces of Mongol commander Mamai at the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380. The Russian Orthodox Church canonized him in 1988.
Restorers opened his sarcophagus in the Moscow Kremlin’s Archangel Cathedral in July. The church subsequently announced the discovery of his relics and proposed sending some of them to Russian forces fighting in Ukraine.
President Vladimir Putin visited the remains to pray before fragments were sent to the front.
Small pieces were separated from the remains and placed in specially prepared reliquaries for transport to the front line, said journalist Ksenia Luchenko, who writes about the Orthodox Church .
Relics of other Orthodox saints, including St. Nicholas, Sts. Peter and Fevronia of Murom, St. Luke of Crimea and St. Matrona of Moscow, have previously been taken to the front, along with religious icons, according to Luchenko.
The reports emerged amid a Ukrainian counteroffensive in the Donetsk region, where Ukrainian forces have reportedly eliminated a Russian-held salient near Lyman and threatened to encircle Russian units advancing toward Sloviansk.
Military consultancy Rochan Consulting estimated that Ukrainian forces had recaptured 240 square kilometers of territory.
Andriy Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, said his forces had captured 250 Russian soldiers during the operation, which Ukraine calls “Vivaldi.”
“The Russians surrendered in entire units, along with officers, pilots and artillerymen,” Biletsky said.

title: Jailed Gulag Historian in Stable But Precarious Condition After Suspected Stroke, Source Says
description: Jailed gulag historian Yury Dmitriev is in stable condition after a suspected stroke, but concerns remain over his access to adequate medical care, a person familiar with his case told The Moscow Times on Thursday.
content:
Jailed gulag historian Yury Dmitriev is in stable condition after a suspected stroke, but concerns remain over his access to adequate medical care, a person familiar with his case told The Moscow Times on Thursday.
Dmitriev, 70, is serving a 15-year sentence that his supporters see as retribution for his work uncovering Soviet-era atrocities as the head of human rights group Memorial’s branch in the republic of Karelia.
He was transferred to a prison hospital in the republic of Mordovia on Friday after experiencing “loss of coordination and severe weakness” that left him unable to stand, prompting his supporters to warn that his life could be at risk if he is not moved to a civilian hospital immediately.
Dmitriev is now conscious, moving around and has written a short note to his family, the source familiar with his case said, speaking on condition of anonymity for safety reasons . However, he is also experiencing problems with the left side of his body, including difficulty moving his left hand.
While prison medics told Dmitriev that he had suffered a medical episode, he believes he had a stroke, the source said.
“The prison hospital does not have the medical equipment necessary to understand the seriousness of the situation and whether it has stopped or is still in progress,” the source said.
Dmitriev’s lawyer has submitted a written request to prison officials seeking proper medical care for him, the source said.
The lawyer was denied access to Dmitriev over the weekend, with prison hospital staff confirming only that he was at the facility and “alive.” Staff later told the lawyer by phone that his condition was “stable” without providing further details.
People corresponding with Dmitriev have reported a decline in his health since 2025, and his allies have repeatedly warned that securing his release is a matter of life and death.
His support group said he had been placed in solitary confinement three times over the past four months for alleged infractions including performing morning exercises improperly and sitting on his bed before lights out.
As the head of Memorial’s Karelia branch, Dmitriev spent decades locating and exhuming mass graves of people killed under Soviet dictator Josef Stalin's rule in the northwestern Russian republic that borders Finland.
He was arrested in 2016 on child pornography charges and acquitted in 2018, but the acquittal was overturned. He was subsequently convicted of sexually assaulting his adopted daughter, and his sentence was increased to 15 years in 2021. He denies wrongdoing.
Memorial, a co-recipient of the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize, has designated Dmitriev a political prisoner and says his prosecution appears linked to his work “preserving the memory of political repressions.”
The group says that he has “not had a single full medical checkup” since his initial arrest in 2016.

title: Russian Military Court Orders Senior Training Official Held in Custody
description: A Moscow military court has ordered a senior Russian general responsible for military training facilities and equipment held in pre-trial detention in a criminal case whose details have not been disclosed, the Kommersant newspaper reported.
content:
A Moscow military court has ordered a senior Russian general responsible for military training facilities and equipment held in pre-trial detention in a criminal case whose details have not been disclosed, the Kommersant newspaper reported .
The 235th Garrison Military Court issued the ruling against Major General Sergei Nikitushkin on Wednesday evening, the newspaper said. The charges against him were not immediately known.
Nikitushkin heads the department responsible for training facilities and equipment within the Russian Armed Forces’ Main Directorate of Combat Training.
The directorate oversees troop training, develops training infrastructure and supplies equipment used to prepare soldiers for combat.
Nikitushkin, 51, served in Russia’s war on Ukraine and was promoted to major general by President Vladimir Putin in December 2024. The Baza Telegram channel reported that he had worked on modernizing tank training grounds in Russia.
He previously complained of insufficient funding to buy simulators for training troops to operate armored vehicles, communications equipment, drones and night-vision devices. He said the war in Ukraine had demonstrated the importance of such equipment in preparing soldiers for future combat.
The directorate also oversees Patriot Park, a military exhibition complex near Moscow that has been implicated in embezzlement cases involving several senior officers.
Those convicted include former Deputy Defense Minister Pavel Popov, whose prison sentence was reduced to 10 years, and Major General Vladimir Shesterov, a former deputy head of the Defense Ministry’s innovation development directorate, who received six years.
Putin appointed Colonel General Rustam Muradov to lead the Main Directorate of Combat Training in June.

title: Russia Expels ‘Group’ of Hungarian Diplomats in Tit-for-Tat Move
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday it would expel an unspecified number of Hungarian diplomats in a tit-for-tat move.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday it would expel an unspecified number of Hungarian diplomats in a tit-for-tat move.
The move comes after Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on Sept. 8 that Budapest was expelling 10 Russian diplomats for activities incompatible with their status. The wording is often used as a euphemism for spying.
Moscow, which had vowed to retaliate, said it had summoned Hungary’s chargé d’affaires Gábor Gergics to lodge a “decisive protest” over the “groundless and openly unfriendly” expulsion.
Staffers from Hungary’s Embassy in Moscow, as well as its consulates in St. Petersburg and Kazan, have been declared personae non gratae as a reciprocal measure, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Thursday.
They were given two weeks to leave Russia.
The Hungarian Foreign Ministry said in a statement it acknowledged Russia's decision, adding: “Hungary is not interested in an escalation of diplomatic tension.”
Hungary’s former Prime Minister, Viktor Orbán, who in April was voted out of office after 16 years in power, had maintained close ties with Russia and President Vladimir Putin following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Since taking office in May, Orbán’s successor Péter Magyar has sought to mend ties with the EU and Ukraine that were tense under his predecessor.

title: Government Submits 3-Year Budget to State Duma as 2026 Deficit Set to Reach $88Bln
description: The Russian government on Wednesday submitted its three-year draft federal budget for 2027-29 to the State Duma, with this year’s deficit nearly doubling from previous projections, amid soaring war spending.
content:
The Russian government on Wednesday submitted its three-year draft federal budget for 2027-29 to the State Duma, with this year’s deficit nearly doubling from previous projections, amid soaring war spending.
Russia’s 2026 budget deficit will reach a record 7.345 trillion rubles ($88 billion), up from the previous forecast of 3.785 trillion rubles ($45 billion). The new projection represents 3.2% of GDP compared to the previous target of 1.6%.
Deficits are also expected to reach 5.443 trillion rubles (2.2% of GDP) in 2027, 5.12 trillion rubles (1.9% of GDP) in 2028 and 5.245 trillion rubles (1.9% of GDP) in 2029.
Combined budget deficits over the three years between 2027 and 2029 will total nearly 16 trillion rubles ($192 billion).
Russia is drawing up a three-year budget in an attempt to improve long-term planning, but it has had to revise its figures sharply upwards each year and has repeatedly missed its annual deficit targets.
President Vladimir Putin said last month that the size of the budget deficit poses no “critical” risk for the Russian economy, and that it will be managed. Analysts consider a budget deficit of up to 4-5% of GDP to be manageable.
“The draft budget is balanced, which is an important condition for maintaining macroeconomic stability and reducing inflation,” the government said in a statement on Wednesday.
Nominal GDP is forecast to rise by 1.4% and reach 248.3 trillion rubles ($2.98 trillion) in 2027. By 2029, it will rise by 2.4% and reach 281.7 trillion rubles ($3.38 trillion).
The budget targets an annual inflation rate of 4% and sets a baseline oil price of $50 per barrel.
Russia's budget situation has gradually deteriorated throughout the four and a half years since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, as the country has had to tap its fiscal reserve fund, increase borrowing and raise taxes to keep up with growing military spending.
Earlier reports said 2027 defense spending would rise by 27% to a record 17.1 trillion rubles ($210 billion), representing more than a third of total federal spending. Exiled outlet Vyorstka reported that only 2.3 trillion rubles ($28 billion) are itemized in public documents, while the remainder are classified as “top secret.”
A record 34.9% of total budget spending will remain classified in 2027, according to the outlet.
The State Duma will hold its first of three readings of the draft budget bill on Oct. 29, Budget Committee chairman Andrei Makarov said Thursday.
