title: Russian Pro-War Writers Say State Has Failed Them
description: Russian writers who back Moscow’s war in Ukraine have complained that they lack state backing and struggle to reach a broad readership, the Ostorozhno Novosti news outlet reported.
content:
Russian writers who back Moscow’s war in Ukraine have complained that they lack state backing and struggle to reach a broad readership, the Ostorozhno Novosti news outlet reported .
Poets and authors at a literary roundtable in St. Petersburg accused the authorities of failing to promote their work and restricting their access to schools and literary events.
Poet Alexander Pelevin said Russia had failed to launch a “special cultural operation” since the war began, using a phrase that echoes Moscow’s official term for its invasion of Ukraine.
He said Russian authors had produced a body of “magnificent poetry” during the war, but the state had failed to help distribute it and had marginalized writers who describe themselves as patriotic.
Pelevin also acknowledged that patriotic poetry was in decline, saying it was difficult to keep writing about the capture of yet another small village.
Another pro-war poet, Ukraine war veteran Axel Kobokki, blamed the failure to launch a cultural campaign on the image of patriotism promoted by the state, adding that Russians had little trust in people aligned with the authorities.
Participants also argued that liberal public figures built credibility by defending people facing state persecution, while patriotic figures lacked comparable successes.
One participant alleged that school extracurricular reading lists included books only from certain publishers of pro-war authors, describing the arrangement as a way to siphon off money.
Another claimed that orders to keep patriotic writers out of schools came from the highest levels of government. Participants also complained that writers serving at the front were not granted leave to attend literary events.
The exiled investigative outlet Vyorstka previously reported that Russian publishers had released at least 259 books about the war since 2022, with most getting print runs of between 1,000 and 3,000 copies.
Book industry representatives told Vyorstka that publishers had little interest in pro-war literature because of weak reader demand. Poor sales meant the books were often sent to publicly funded institutions like schools, universities and libraries, they said.

title: Russian Exports to Turkey Fall 40% Amid Ukrainian Strikes on Southern Ports
description: Russian exports to Turkey fell about 40% in August to their lowest monthly value since 2022, as Ukrainian attacks on southern Russian ports disrupted shipments, the Vedomosti newspaper reported, citing Turkish trade data and industry officials.
content:
Russian exports to Turkey fell about 40% in August to their lowest monthly value since 2022, as Ukrainian attacks on southern Russian ports disrupted shipments, the Vedomosti newspaper reported , citing Turkish trade data and industry officials.
Shipments to Turkey, Russia’s third-largest trading partner, totaled $1.93 billion, down from $3.23 billion in July, according to figures from the Turkish Statistical Institute reviewed by Vedomosti.
The decline highlights the growing disruption to Russian trade through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, with exporters turning to longer, more expensive routes to reach the Turkish market.
Before August, monthly exports to Turkey had fallen below $3 billion only once this year, reaching $2.49 billion in February before recovering to $4.42 billion in April.
Andrei Gnidchenko, a leading expert at the Kremlin-linked Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting, attributed the decline to reduced or halted shipments of coal, iron and steel, copper, motor fuels and grain.
The Russian Grain Union said no grain was shipped to Turkey in August. Russian coal shipments to the country fell to 1.5 million metric tons from 2.1 million in July, according to commodity pricing agency Argus.
Yulia Shlenskaya, head of customs and logistics operator KVT Service, told Vedomosti that cargo flows through southern Russian ports had dwindled to almost nothing. Some shipments to Turkey were rerouted in September through the Caucasus or ports in northwestern Russia, increasing transit distances and costs, she said.
Ukraine began striking Russian ports on the Black Sea and Sea of Azov in July. The attacks destroyed terminals handling grain, food products, vegetable oil and petroleum, and damaged more than 100 vessels, according to the report.
Shipping in the Sea of Azov halted completely on July 11, Vedomosti said. Russia subsequently struck Ukrainian port infrastructure and foreign vessels, also bringing operations at the port of Odesa to a standstill.
Turkey’s Foreign Ministry has urged both countries to take urgent steps to ensure safe shipping.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Sept. 19 that he had sent Moscow and Kyiv a draft memorandum proposing an end to the attacks. The Kremlin confirmed receiving the document but said no substantive negotiations were underway.
Ukraine has also proposed a Black Sea ceasefire to allow grain exports to resume, but Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said Russia had rejected every proposed version of an agreement.

title: Zabaikalsky Region Offers Bounties for Bears as Human Encounters Rise
description: Authorities in Russia’s Far East Zabaikalsky region have introduced a bounty for bear culling in the region to curb the sharp rise in dangerous encounters with humans.  The regional ministry of natural resources on Thursday offered a reward of 15,000 rubles ($180) for every bear hunted.
content:
Authorities in Russia’s Far East Zabaikalsky region have introduced a bounty for bear culling in the region to curb the sharp rise in dangerous encounters with humans.
The regional ministry of natural resources on Thursday offered a reward of 15,000 rubles ($180) for every bear hunted.
More than 100 bear sightings have been recorded in the Zabaikalsky region so far, with 35 taking place directly inside human settlements. Hunters have culled 70 bears across the region as part of its campaign to regulate the animal’s population.
The Zabaikalsky region introduced a high-alert status on Tuesday, with officials urging residents to avoid forests for foraging, fishing or recreation.
“The main goal of these measures is to protect human life and health and reduce the risk of dangerous encounters with wild animals,” the ministry said in a statement.
At least 22 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia in 2026. Experts attribute the spate of killings to climate change, with a lack of berries forcing bears to look for food elsewhere, as well as people leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears.
Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said Wednesday the government was drafting measures to manage the brown bear population, which has doubled over the last three decades to 308,000.
Lifting hunting quotas and setting regional population limits, as well as giving local authorities extra powers to control bear numbers, were among the proposals.

title: Russia’s Finance Ministry Fails to Sell Bonds as Borrowing Plans Weigh on Market
description: Russia’s Finance Ministry failed to sell government bonds at an auction on Wednesday, its first unsuccessful placement since July, as plans for heavier borrowing and higher military spending weighed on the debt market.
content:
Russia’s Finance Ministry failed to sell government bonds at an auction on Wednesday, its first unsuccessful placement since July, as plans for heavier borrowing and higher military spending weighed on the debt market.
The ministry said the auction of federal loan bonds, known as OFZs, maturing in 2030 had failed because no bids were submitted at acceptable prices.
The failed sale comes as the government prepares to borrow more to cover a widening budget deficit. Analysts said the increased supply of bonds was putting pressure on prices and driving up the government’s borrowing costs.
Wednesday’s auction was the last scheduled sale of the quarter, during which the ministry raised 1.264 trillion rubles ($15.29 billion) for the budget. It sold two bond issues totaling 150 billion rubles ($1.82 billion) last week and raised 139.6 billion rubles ($1.69 billion) the week before.
The ministry last experienced a failed auction in July, when a market selloff forced it to suspend government debt sales.
Raiffeisenbank analysts said the bond market had been disappointed by substantial changes to the government’s budget plans for this year and next.
According to Reuters, Russia plans to increase military spending by about a third next year to 17.1 trillion rubles ($206.91 billion). Together with spending on other security agencies, that would account for more than 40% of the budget.
The Finance Ministry has raised its deficit forecast for this year to 7.3 trillion rubles ($88.33 billion), from an initial 3.6 trillion rubles ($43.56 billion), and plans to borrow an additional 1 trillion rubles ($12.1 billion) to help cover the shortfall.
It plans to sell 7.7 trillion rubles ($93.17 billion) in bonds next year to finance the deficit and meet spending needs.
Those borrowing plans are placing substantial pressure on government bonds, Raiffeisenbank analysts said. The Moscow Exchange’s OFZ price index has fallen back toward its summer lows, to around 111.2 points, while yields on long-term government debt have approached 17%.
As market conditions deteriorate, Central Bank lending to commercial banks has increasingly helped finance government borrowing.
In early September, the Finance Ministry sold nearly 1 trillion rubles ($12.1 billion) in floating-rate bonds to banks in a single placement. The same day, banks borrowed almost the same amount from the Central Bank.
Economist Vladislav Inozemtsev described the arrangement as a coordinated operation in which the Central Bank lent to banks, the banks lent to the government, and the government bonds were then pledged as collateral for the Central Bank loans.
He characterized it as effectively financing government spending through money creation.
The Finance Ministry will probably have to return to that approach if the next two or three auctions also fail, analysts at Vector Capital said .

title: Vatican Envoy Discusses Humanitarian Issues, Visits POWs in Russia, Foreign Ministry Says
description: Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
content:
Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
Zuppi's three days of talks coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end the four-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were "beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive."
The Foreign Ministry said Zuppi met Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov and other Russian officials and discussed prospects for a settlement as well as humanitarian issues, including prisoner of war exchanges and displaced children.
The statement said Zuppi, head of the Italian bishops ​conference, also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv's military used drones last weekend to deliver food and medicine to civilians.
The Foreign Ministry statement said Ukraine was blocking all attempts to provide supplies to the town's residents. Ukrainian officials say Russian forces are preventing them from leaving the town.
The ministry statement said Zuppi was permitted to visit prisoners of war and "was personally able to talk with Ukrainians and see for himself that Russia strictly follows all the relevant humanitarian standards."
It said the visit "confirmed the constructive and regular nature of the Russian-Vatican dialogue and the willingness of both sides to continue cooperating on humanitarian issues."
Zuppi last ​visited ⁠Moscow in October 2024 to discuss prospects for ending the war launched by Russia's 2022 invasion of ⁠its ​neighbor.
Zuppi has also ​held talks in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr ​Zelensky.

title: Russian Regions Turn to Residents and Businesses to Fund Bomb Shelters
description: Authorities in several Russian regions are turning to residents and businesses to pay for bomb shelters and protection against drone attacks, local media reported, as the country restores its civil defense infrastructure amid the war in Ukraine.
content:
Authorities in several Russian regions are turning to residents and businesses to pay for bomb shelters and protection against drone attacks, local media reported, as the country restores its civil defense infrastructure amid the war in Ukraine.
Building owners in St. Petersburg have received orders to equip shelters, while apartment residents in Yekaterinburg have been asked to approve charges for converting underground parking facilities. In Omsk, parents of kindergarten children have been asked to contribute toward supplies for a basement shelter.
The measures would shift some preparation costs to households and businesses as Russia works to restore more than 20,000 protective facilities across 82 regions, a program the Emergency Situations Ministry estimates will require about 155 billion rubles ($1.88 billion).
In St. Petersburg, owners of buildings containing civil defense facilities have received notices requiring them to prepare the shelters, BFM news website reported . The St. Petersburg Pharmaceutical Factory was ordered to put an underground facility near the Nevskaya Ratusha complex in order. Similar instructions have been sent to municipal authorities.
The requirements apply both to apartment buildings with existing shelter facilities and to those without them, Nikolai Pitirimov, co-chairman of the board of the St. Petersburg Clean Technologies Cluster for the Urban Environment, told BFM.
Buildings must provide at least temporary shelter, with the responsibility falling on homeowners’ associations, he said.
In Yekaterinburg, residents of one district received notices asking them to vote on equipping shelters in underground parking facilities, local news outlet E1 reported .
The Akademichesky property management company said a one-time charge of 841 rubles ($10.18) per person registered as living in an apartment would appear as a separate item on utility bills. The company said the amount was set by a governor’s decree.
In Omsk, about 2,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, parents at one kindergarten were asked to contribute 200 rubles ($2.42) per child for benches and emergency water supplies in a basement being converted into a shelter, the local outlet Gorod55 reported , citing residents.
City authorities said parents had only been advised to help provide supplies and prepare the basement as their means allowed.
Emergency Situations Minister Alexander Kurenkov said in February that his ministry was restoring more than 20,000 civil defense facilities nationwide.
Russian authorities began a large-scale reconstruction and modernization program for Soviet-era shelters in late May 2025. At the time, Kurenkov said restoring the civil defense system had become increasingly urgent because of the war in Ukraine.

title: Russia Draws Up Measures to Control Bear Population After Spate of Deadly Attacks
description: The Russian government said on Wednesday it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiraled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks.
content:
The Russian government said on Wednesday it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiraled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks.
In the latest attack, reported by state media, a 23-year-old man out gathering berries was killed by a bear this week in Kamchatka, in Russia's far east.
Last week, a Russian woman in Siberia was fatally mauled by a bear in her garden, amid a nationwide spate of killings that experts blame on climate change and human incompetence.
"It is clear that as the population grows, so too does the number of problems. Systemic measures are needed to ensure that humans and animals can coexist safely and to maintain the necessary balance," said Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev.
"In this regard, the Russian government is currently preparing a series of priority measures," he said.
The government said it would look at lifting hunting quotas on brown bears, would establish regional population limits, give local authorities extra powers to control their numbers, and identify regions that need more financing to tackle the problem.
The population of brown bears has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000, in part due to shorter and milder winters. At least 22 people have been killed by bears across Russia, the world's largest country, since this spring, the RIA state news agency said.
Experts cited in Russian media have said bears have been forced to look further afield for food this year because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on in September.
People are also guilty of leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and of ignoring safety rules, experts say.
Investigators in Krasnoyarsk in Siberia — home to nearly 27,000 bears, according to environment ministry data — said last week that they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of negligence that led to the deaths of seven people in September alone.
The federal environment ministry has sought to play down the spate of attacks, saying that around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually in recent years, but that social media and smartphones are making such attacks seem more widespread.

title: St. Petersburg Plans Officials’ Pay Raises Amid Budget Cuts
description: St.
content:
St. Petersburg plans to raise officials’ base salaries by up to 5% annually over the next three years while proposing sharp cuts to this year’s spending on education, health care and infrastructure, the RBC news website reported Wednesday.
The pay increases are included in the city’s draft budget for 2027 and its spending plans for 2028 and 2029. The city government approved the document on Sept. 29 and submitted it to the Legislative Assembly.
The plans would increase pay for lawmakers, deputy governors, city government members and other officials as the authorities seek to curb borrowing and narrow the budget deficit. Payments to Russian troops fighting in Ukraine and their families would also rise.
The Legislative Assembly speaker’s monthly base salary would increase from about 149,100 rubles ($1,804) to 168,800 rubles ($2,042) by 2029. Base salaries for deputy speakers and deputy governors would reach 159,400 rubles ($1,929), while those for city government members would reach 154,700 rubles ($1,872).
Officials’ total pay is higher because it includes allowances, bonuses and other supplementary payments.
Separately, the city administration has proposed cutting its 2026 budget by 70.2 billion rubles ($849.4 million), from 1.651 trillion rubles ($19.98 billion) to about 1.58 trillion rubles ($19.12 billion).
The largest reduction, 36.7 billion rubles ($444.1 million), would fall on spending classified under the economy. Transport spending would be cut by 9 billion rubles ($108.9 million), with another 10.8 billion rubles ($130.7 million) removed from construction of the Shirotnaya high-speed highway.
Education spending would fall by 15.5 billion rubles ($187.6 million), while the health care committee’s budget would be reduced by 8.5 billion rubles ($102.9 million).
Housing and utilities spending would be cut by about 6.8 billion rubles ($82.3 million). Spending on improvements to public spaces would fall by 2.3 billion rubles ($27.8 million), and road repairs would lose 1.9 billion rubles ($23 million).
Meanwhile, payments to troops fighting in Ukraine and their families would increase by 6.4 billion rubles ($77.4 million).
The city administration attributed the proposed spending cuts to high borrowing costs, a planned cooling of the economy and efforts to reduce borrowing.
It said the revisions would narrow the 2026 budget deficit by about 80 billion rubles ($968 million), from 189 billion rubles ($2.29 billion) to 108.8 billion rubles ($1.32 billion).
The draft budget projects a deficit of 103.4 billion rubles ($1.25 billion) in 2027.

title: Yabloko Leader Demands Investigation After Political Analyst Was Reportedly Tortured During Arrest
description: Yabloko party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov said Wednesday that he formally asked Russian law enforcement authorities to investigate reports that independent political analyst Alexander Kynev was beaten and tortured following his arrest in Moscow last week.
content:
Yabloko party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov said Wednesday that he formally asked Russian law enforcement authorities to investigate reports that independent political analyst Alexander Kynev was beaten and tortured following his arrest in Moscow last week.
Rights groups have said that Kynev was hospitalized at a medical facility inside a Moscow detention center for bone fractures and other injuries after his arrest on drug charges. Officials have not commented on those allegations.
“I believe those responsible should not only be named and punished, but immediately dismissed from law enforcement agencies,” Rybakov wrote in a post on Telegram. “Regardless of how state security agencies feel about the detainee, torture and violence are categorically unacceptable.”
Exiled Russian political commentator Ekaterina Shulmman, who knows Kynev personally, claimed on Tuesday that police officers broke one of his legs and electrocuted him in what she described as an attempt to make him confess to treason charges. She did not say where she had received that information.
Kynev’s attorney later denied Shulmann’s claim, stating he was unaware of any evidence that his client was tortured or faced allegations of treason. The drug charges Kynev currently faces, and which he has denied, carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
News of Kynev’s arrest came the same day that Russian election authorities announced the final results of this month’s parliamentary elections, which handed the ruling United Russia party an unprecedented supermajority in the lower-house State Duma.
Independent experts have described the elections as the least competitive in Russia’s modern history. Voters were left with virtually no real opposition option after Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party and the only registered political force campaigning for peace, was struck from the party-list ballot by the Russian Supreme Court in August.
Kynev, who wrote regular opinion columns for The Moscow Times before it was designated an “undesirable” organization in 2024, chose to remain in Russia despite his public criticism of the government and the invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Kynev a “foreign agent” in February. Over the years, he has worked for a number of independent political organizations, including the now-disbanded election observer Golos.
Separately, Rybakov was himself briefly detained on Tuesday and charged with disorderly conduct for spoiling his ballot during the Sept. 20 elections at a St. Petersburg polling station.

title: Russia's War Veterans Pose a Threat to the Kremlin. So Putin Is Bringing Them Onside.
description: Opinion | The first session of Russia’s State Duma after the 2026 parliamentary elections opened with a 20-second standing ovation for the newly elected “participants in the special military operation.” Veterans of the war in Ukraine now comprise just over 10% of the lower chamber of parliament.
content:
The first session of Russia’s State Duma after the 2026 parliamentary elections opened with a 20-second standing ovation for the newly elected “participants in the special military operation.”
Veterans of the war in Ukraine now comprise just over 10% of the lower chamber of parliament. The Central Electoral Commission chief Ella Pamfilova declared that the new veteran members will “set a certain tone” for the new State Duma. That tone will be one of further militarization of Russian politics and society. It is also a reflection of the emergence of a new political constituency produced by the war against Ukraine.
Like the wider process surrounding the vote, the number of veterans entering parliament was managed at the top. United Russia initially announced after voting had ended that 86 veterans from the party had been elected. This statement was quickly removed from state media and later revised to say that 49 United Russia veterans would take up their seats.
On Sept. 25, Pamfilova confirmed the final number of veterans across all parties at 46, which broadly aligns with the 40-50 projected by Kremlin insiders back in May. These shifting figures suggest that veterans’ representation in parliament was a matter of managed political allocation rather than one left entirely to the electoral process.
The latest election is part of a broader reshaping of Russia’s political system. In February 2024, Putin personally announced an ambitious new state project — the Time of Heroes program — designed to equip patriotic veterans for future service in senior government roles and top positions in state-linked companies.
Out of 83 participants admitted in the first cohort, reportedly selected from 44,000 applicants , three went on to become heads of Russian regions and at least eleven secured jobs in the Presidential Administration.
For Putin, the initiative addressed the need for a new “ genuine ” Russian elite, distinct from the bureaucratic and business elites who had “lined their pockets in the 1990s.” Drawn from contract soldiers and mobilized servicemen who fought in Ukraine, this new generation would become the force to whom “Russia can one day be entrusted,” Putin claimed.
Beyond the program itself, the Kremlin has also eased the path for veterans to run in elections at all levels, leading to more than 1,600 veteran candidates registering for municipal and regional elections in 2025. The latest Duma elections mark the latest step in the project to systematically integrate former combatants into Russia’s political system.
To encourage participation in its primaries, United Russia gave veterans from some regions a 25% bonus to their vote totals, alongside simplifying requirements for submitting documents and conducting their campaigns.
Some of the newly elected United Russia deputies have been accused of war crimes in Ukraine. One of them is Nursultan Mussagaleyev, a decorated “Hero of Russia” who is suspected of killing civilians in the Kyiv suburb of Bucha.
Another, Adam Delimkhanov, commanded Chechen forces during the assault on Mariupol, which effectively destroyed the city.
Vladislav Golovin, the new chairman of the State Duma Youth Policy Committee, is another participant in the devastating siege of Mariupol. Ukrainian authorities have accused him of war crimes against civilians and of involvement in the military training of Ukrainian children.
Golovin, 29, is also head of Yunarmiya, a youth military-patriotic movement run by the Defense Ministry, and was among the top five candidates on United Russia’s federal electoral list.
Yet the Kremlin’s veteran category extends beyond those who fought at the front. The professional perks available to former combatants have made veteran status attractive to career politicians and technocrats looking to advance their careers.
As a result, the “veteran” category encompasses a diverse mix of former military personnel and officials or managers who, in some cases, have spent only limited periods near the front to acquire veteran credentials.
The former mayor of the southern city of Krasnodar, Yevgeny Pervyshov, for example, secured the governorship of Tambov region after signing up to fight in 2022 and entering the Time of Heroes program. The drone regiment in which he served is known for recruiting high numbers of United Russia members and is mostly involved in drone operations far from the front line.
This mixing of former combatants with ordinary officials goes beyond mere career opportunism. Rather, it should be read both as a way of inculcating patriotism and as a deliberate effort by the Kremlin to prevent the emergence of a distinct veteran bloc within Russia’s political structures.
The late Wagner leader Yevgeny Prigozhin’s mutiny exposed the risks posed by organized combatants who are critical of the Kremlin’s conduct of the war. Capable of turning their networks and battlefield experience against the regime, they could cause a problem for Russia’s leadership, especially if it does not carefully manage the process of demobilization once the fighting subsides.
By bringing this group into the political system on its own terms, the authorities are thus seeking to manage a hardline constituency that could otherwise acquire a distinct political voice.
The war has reshaped every facet of the Russian system. Its economy, industry and judiciary are increasingly geared towards sustaining Putin’s militarized political course. The new Duma provides the latest confirmation of this trend.
For the Kremlin, the systematic and tightly managed integration of veterans into state structures could help renew an ageing government bureaucracy by embedding some of the regime’s most loyal supporters within its institutions. It also demonstrates to the wider population that frontline service presents a viable route to social and political advancement.
For veterans, it offers a degree of recognition and suggests that they have an important role to play in civilian life — a sharp contrast with the lack of institutional support afforded to veterans of the Afghan and Chechen wars. Representatives of both groups found themselves on the margins of society without adequate possibilities for rehabilitation. In the case of the Afgantsy , many found their way into organised crime.
The Kremlin’s initiative to appoint loyal veterans to positions of responsibility in the system is still only in its early stages. The cohort that has entered the Duma will provide the first real chance to test the effectiveness of its approach.
There are already grumblings from some veteran groups that some of the new Duma deputies are “ fake ” veterans. The Russian authorities know that pro-war groups present a far greater threat than the anti-war community because they are more difficult to control and cannot be accused of lacking patriotism. Taking more steps beyond increasing the role of veterans in parliament may be required to keep them under control.

title: Moscow Sends Nuclear Warning to NATO as Tensions Rise in the Baltic
description: Russia has warned NATO that it is willing to resort to the use of nuclear weapons if the Western military alliance tries to enforce a blockade of the Kaliningrad region, a Russian exclave bordering the Baltic Sea.
content:
Russia has warned NATO that it is willing to resort to the use of nuclear weapons if the Western military alliance tries to enforce a blockade of the Kaliningrad region, a Russia n exclave bordering the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Russia accused the alliance of a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
The document said this included the possibility of " Russia n strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
" Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note said.
The warning underscores Moscow's concerns about what it sees as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized region wedged between Poland and Lithuania.
In a written response seen by Reuters, NATO said it was a defensive alliance committed to countering threats to its members. "None of NATO's exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russia n Federation," it said.
"We call upon the Russia n Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russia n Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," the response added.
In addition to the private warning, Russia n embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described these as diplomatic reminders to "hotheads in Europe."
Russia's relations with European governments have dramatically worsened this year. European officials have increasingly accused Russia of stepping up a so-called "hybrid" war against the bloc through acts of sabotage.
The Kremlin has dismissed those allegations, as well as warnings from some European officials that Russia is preparing for a possible military attack against NATO.
"I would say that the Russia n letter is only another Russia n attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible," a NATO diplomat told Reuters. "[It] reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine."
But a senior European Defense official said it was the first time since the Cold War that Russia is "threatening us like this. So, this is serious."

title: Garry Kasparov and Ilya Ponomaryov Targeted in Alleged Assassination Plot in U.S., Report Says
description: A Russian intelligence network planned to assassinate exiled opposition figures Garry Kasparov and Ilya Ponomaryov in the United States this summer, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported Tuesday.
content:
A Russian intelligence network planned to assassinate exiled opposition figures Garry Kasparov and Ilya Ponomaryov in the United States this summer, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported Tuesday.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Justice Department unsealed an indictment charging five men over alleged plots involving surveillance, recruitment and targeted killings against two opposition figures, who were not identified by name.
El Mundo said it had obtained information that the alleged plot organizers were in contact with people assigned to track and kill Kasparov and Ponomaryov around the time when both were alerted to the assassination threat.
Ponomaryov declined to confirm or deny whether he had been tipped off, but told The Moscow Times that the allegations mark “a new level of escalation” by Russia.
“America was previously considered safe, especially compared to the EU, Turkey and Ukraine. The Kremlin is now destroying that framework as well, which had been in place since World War II,” he said.
According to El Mundo, a recruited operative had allegedly taken photos and videos of the Washington house and office linked to Ponomaryov, whom the U.S. Justice Department indictment identifies only as “Victim-1.” The operative refused to carry out the assassination, according to the indictment.
Kasparov, a chess grandmaster, was reportedly provided special protection for the first time since he moved to New York in 2013. El Mundo did not indicate whether Ponomaryov, who lives between Kyiv and Washington, was offered the same protection.
The Spanish newspaper reported that Vladimir Kara-Murza, another exiled anti-Kremlin figure who was released from Russian prison in 2024 in a landmark East-West prisoner swap, is also viewed as a potential target of assassination.
Two of the indicted Russian nationals also reportedly targeted Ivan Tyutrin, who founded the Free Russia Forum conference in Lithuania with Kasparov, as well as Bashkir independence activist Ruslan Gabbasov, who previously discovered a tracking device inside his car in Lithuania.
Kasparov wrote in a Substack post that he and Tyutrin were not told they were explicit targets.
"We were, however, warned by security services in Lithuania and the U.S. that our lives were in danger and that we should take precautions," he wrote.
"But I will not stop and I will not hide... I will continue to do everything I can to rally the free world against Putin's murderous dictatorship," added Kasparov, whom Russia has placed on its lists of "foreign agents" and "terrorists and extremists."
The Kremlin and the Russian Embassy in Washington have not commented on the U.S. allegations, though Moscow has previously denied carrying out targeted killings abroad.

title: Kremlin Denies Talks on Freeing Political Prisoners for U.S. Sanctions Relief
description: The Kremlin on Wednesday dismissed press reports that it was discussing the release of political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions.
content:
The Kremlin on Wednesday dismissed press reports that it was discussing the release of political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions.
Earlier, The Atlantic reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had “signed on” to White House special envoy John Coale’s initiative to pull back sanctions gradually if Moscow would agree to free Russian political prisoners.
Coale has spearheaded a similar arrangement with neighboring Belarus, a close Russian ally, where President Alexander Lukashenko has pardoned hundreds of prisoners for sanctions relief.
The White House envoy is now reportedly hoping to turn that strategy toward Moscow in order to break the deadlock in U.S.-Russian relations and “help advance the cause of peace.”
However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists on Wednesday that U.S. and Russian officials have not discussed the idea.
“In this formulation, the issue was not discussed and could not be discussed because we categorically deny the existence of any political prisoners,” Peskov said during a daily briefing.
Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights group Memorial currently recognizes 1,826 people as political prisoners in Russia.
Peskov described the framing of The Atlantic’s report as “completely inappropriate.”
The spokesman did acknowledge, however, that Russian and U.S. intelligence services remain in regular contact regarding prisoner exchanges.
Russia and the U.S. have carried out two prisoner swaps since Trump took office in January 2025.
Earlier this week, the White House nominated Coale to serve as its special envoy for hostage affairs.
Coale, a lawyer who previously represented Americans released during the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, was officially appointed to the Belarus role in November, though he had negotiated prisoner releases before that as deputy Ukraine envoy.

title: Ex-Dagestan Head Sergei Melikov Appointed Senator From Bryansk Region
description: Sergei Melikov, the former head of the republic of Dagestan, has been appointed as a senator from the western Bryansk region in Russia’s upper-house Federation Council.  Melikov, a member of the ruling United Russia party, replaced Vadim Dengin, a member of the far-right Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) who ran for the lower-house State Duma in this month’s elections.
content:
Sergei Melikov, the former head of the republic of Dagestan, has been appointed as a senator from the western Bryansk region in Russia’s upper-house Federation Council.
Melikov, a member of the ruling United Russia party, replaced Vadim Dengin, a member of the far-right Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) who ran for the lower-house State Duma in this month’s elections.
Melikov previously served as a Federation Council senator from the southern Stavropol region between 2019 and 2020 before President Vladimir Putin appointed him as regional head of Dagestan.
Russia’s Federation Council is an unelected assembly of regional representatives and presidential appointees. Bryansk region Governor Yegor Kovalchuk signed a decree appointing Melikov as senator.
Melikov, a former high-ranking military officer who served in the First Chechen War, resigned from his post in Dagestan in May following deadly floods that decimated the mountainous region.
Though appointed to stabilize one of Russia’s most complex regions, Melikov struggled to address Dagestan’s chronic infrastructure issues, with frequent power outages and poor road conditions plaguing the republic.

title: Government Extends Diesel Export Ban Until End of October
description: Russia has extended its ban on diesel exports for fuel producers until Oct. 31, the government said on Wednesday, adding further strain to a global energy market already rattled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
content:
Russia has extended its ban on diesel exports for fuel producers until Oct. 31, the government said on Wednesday, adding further strain to a global energy market already rattled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
"The decision was taken to maintain stability in the domestic fuel market, particularly given the elevated demand for motor fuel during the harvest season," a government press release read.
Since the summer, Russia has repeatedly imposed curbs on gasoline and diesel exports to rein in rising fuel prices and tackle shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries.
Ukraine's military claimed last week that it knocked out more than 45% of Russia's refining capacity.
A growing number of Russian regions have recently seen the reintroduction of fuel rationing measures to combat shortages of gasoline and diesel. Industry analysts previously warned that supplies will remain tight across much of the country until peak demand subsides in the fall.
The average price of gasoline in Russia has climbed 21% since the start of the year, with a single-week increase pushing the national average to 78.51 rubles per liter ($3.39 per gallon) as of Sept. 14.
A separate diesel export ban for non-producers remains in effect through January. An export ban on jet fuel also remains active through November, alongside a total ban on gasoline exports in place through January.
Also on Wednesday, Russia's Federal Anti-Monopoly Service said it was investigating 58 cases of suspected price gouging by independent gas station chains across the country amid the recent fuel shortages.

title: Bodies of Missing Crew Members Found After Fishing Boat Fire Near Kamchatka
description: Police investigators said Wednesday that they recovered the remains of four missing crew members of a Russian fishing vessel that caught fire near the Far Eastern Kamchatka peninsula.
content:
Police investigators said Wednesday that they recovered the remains of four missing crew members of a Russian fishing vessel that caught fire near the Far Eastern Kamchatka peninsula.
The fire erupted Friday evening while the vessel Triumf was sailing in the Pacific Ocean off the eastern coast of Kamchatka.
A total of 29 crew members were on board, and a rescue operation successfully brought 25 sailors to safety. Seven of the injured crew members received medical treatment in the regional capital of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky.
The four remaining sailors were initially listed as missing at sea before they were discovered during an inspection of the charred vessel.
Investigators said they will carry out forensic examinations to identify the remains. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Russia’s Crude Exports Rise as Diesel Ban Limits Gains From Higher Oil Prices
description: Russia’s crude oil exports rose to their highest level in more than a month, while higher prices pushed the estimated value of shipments close to its highest since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.
content:
Russia’s crude oil exports rose to their highest level in more than a month, while higher prices pushed the estimated value of shipments close to its highest since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.
Crude shipments averaged 3.71 million barrels a day in the four weeks through Sept. 27, the most since early August, according to vessel-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. In the final week of that period, exports reached 3.99 million barrels a day.
The increase could help Moscow fund its rising military spending, but it comes with a costly trade-off. Ukrainian drone strikes have disrupted Russian refineries, leaving more crude available for export, while restrictions on diesel and gasoline shipments have cut sales of more valuable fuels.
The estimated value of crude shipped from Russian ports in the week to Sept. 27 reached $2.75 billion, up $180 million from the previous week, according to Bloomberg.
Its four-week average, which smooths out fluctuations in weekly shipments, rose by $290 million to $2.39 billion, the highest since the second half of May.
The figures estimate the value of crude shipments, not the Russian government’s oil tax revenue.
Tensions in the Middle East have kept Brent crude above $100 a barrel and strengthened demand for Russian oil, meaning Russian grades have recently sold at a premium instead of their customary discount.
In mid-September, Urals crude shipped from Russia’s western ports traded above $110 a barrel, while the ESPO grade exported from the Far East topped $120, Reuters reported, citing traders. Brent futures reached $108 to $109 a barrel at the time and approached that range again last week.
Those prices are well above the $59 a barrel assumed for Urals in Russia’s budget. Moscow has allocated 12.9 trillion rubles ($153.5 billion) to national defense this year. A Finance Ministry draft budget would raise that to 17.1 trillion rubles ($203.5 billion) next year, equivalent to 6.9% of gross domestic product and 35% of federal spending.
Yet Russia is missing out on exports of refined fuels as a wave of Ukrainian strikes strains its refineries and contributes to shortages at home.
Diesel exports stood at about 1 million barrels a day before the summer attacks, according to Bloomberg. The ban on diesel shipments is expected to be extended through the end of October, even as diesel prices in European and Asian markets exceed $200 a barrel.
Combined Russian exports of crude oil and petroleum products have fallen to about 28 million metric tons a month, their lowest level since the pandemic, according to Raiffeisenbank analysts.
“The rise in oil prices expected for September is unlikely to make up much of that shortfall,” the analysts wrote. “Non-oil and gas exports are also declining.”

title: Something Strange Is Happening With Russian Romantasy
description: Opinion | If the mysterious Russian soul is traditionally supposed to be understood by reading imperishable Russian literature, perhaps the best way to understand the feelings of Russian women in wartime is to read popular romantic fiction.
content:
If the mysterious Russian soul is traditionally supposed to be understood by reading imperishable Russian literature, perhaps the best way to understand the feelings of Russian women in wartime is to read popular romantic fiction.
The Russian romance novel changes along with society. It was only after the collapse of the Soviet Union that the genre burst onto Russian bookshelves and then quickly blended with the workplace novel, detective fiction, the eternal Cinderella story and specifically Russian traditions.
Later, it was joined by the enormous industry of popadanki : modern women who find themselves transported into another time or world, where they have the chance to begin life again using the knowledge and experience acquired in their previous lives.
At first, the central fantasy of the popadanka consisted largely of precisely that fantasy. The heroine finds herself in a world whose rules are stacked against her, but makes a place for herself through her knowledge, character or luck. Part of the appeal lay in the high-status man — a king, prince, duke, mage, werewolf, dragon or vampire — who nearly always appeared.
But recently, Russian-language online literature has seen the particularly noticeable emergence of a more specific variety of this man: a general, commander-in-chief, head of the secret service, investigator or inquisitor — a person whose power extends not only over the heroine but over the surrounding society as well.
A typical extract would go something like this:
General Ratmirov entered the room without removing his black uniform. Tall and broad-shouldered, with a silver scar at his temple and the cold gray eyes of a man accustomed to giving orders, he silenced even the old clock on the mantelpiece with a single glance. His cruelty was legendary: enemies of the Empire whispered his name, subordinates snapped to attention, and traitors, people said, he could sense before they even managed to sell themselves to foreign intelligence.
Only little Lidochka was unafraid of him. She quietly placed a homemade blueberry pie on the table, adjusted her lace collar and looked at the general with that special feminine gaze that made something ache painfully in the hero’s chest for the first time in twenty years of service. Lidochka knew that beneath the icy armor of the stern security man lay a tormented soul. All it needed was patience, tenderness and true love. And today, she was also planning to tell him that she was expecting their fourth child.
If you look at what the world looks like for real Russian women today, what you will find is depressing. Russian women are losing control over their bodies and their way of life. I do not know whether Rosstat can be trusted, but even it cannot manage to put an attractive gloss on the situation.
Russian women are certainly well established in the workplace and some have even made it into management positions. But they earn noticeably less than men and shoulder most of the unpaid second shift of domestic labor at home. They have made far less progress toward political power: women remain few in number in the State Duma and their share has barely changed in recent years.
At the same time, the Russian state is intruding ever more actively into women’s reproductive lives. Abortion formally remains legal, but there are fewer places where it can be obtained as administrative restrictions pile up in some regions. Russia is not unique in this — one need only look at the United States after the Dobbs vs. Jackson Women's Health Organization case that concluded Americans had no constitutional right to an abortion . But a comparison with Europe, where women make up close to half of those in power, shows that recent reforms more often expand reproductive autonomy rather than restrict it. Correlation does not prove causation, but the contrast is striking.
Even within the Russian opposition, women remain a minority. Men still noticeably outnumber women on the register of “foreign agents,” although the number of women is growing. Perhaps women genuinely have less desire to enter politics, or perhaps the state considers fighting against women beneath its dignity. In any case, the overall picture is visible even without official data: a woman bears a great deal of responsibility for her own life, but has noticeably less right to decide exactly how she should live it.
Romance fiction is a poor tool for measuring public opinion. You cannot count the generals on book covers and conclude that they is exactly the kind of man Russian women want.
But popular fiction and sales charts are still useful mirrors of what fantasies are culturally permissible. It shows what writers and readers enjoy fantasizing about, what conflicts seem recognizable to them and what kinds of resolution bring emotional satisfaction.
Researchers of romance fiction have long drawn attention to this duality: the genre provides a temporary escape from everyday life while simultaneously reproducing (and, yes, sometimes subverting) familiar scripts of love, sex and the distribution of power between men and women.
As noted above, the male love interest in the recent incarnations of the popadanka story has most often belonged to a hero from the security or coercive apparatus.
This has already become such a recognizable trend that books are sold in entire themed series. On the self-publishing site Litnet, for example, there are collections called “A Popadanka for the General” and “After Divorcing the Dragon General.”
Their blurbs repeat what is practically a ready-made formula: “powerful general,” “stern dragon general,” “commander-in-chief of the imperial army,” themes of protection, submission, forced marriage, the heroine’s dependence on the hero and the obligatory transformation of conflict into mutual love.
In one book, the heroine is literally bought by a general, after which he provides her and her child with a roof over their heads. The subsequent plot is supposed to transform a relationship of ownership and dependence into a romantic one.
The shift is also visible in our still-small pilot sample, although 20 of the most popular books per year is not enough for a serious statistical conclusion: in 2016, we did not find a single security-service hero among the top 20, whereas among the current top 20 for 2026 there were four — and that is based only on the blurb, which may not mention the male protagonist’s profession.
It seems to us that the real percentage of “sexy inquisitors” among this year’s leading romantic heroes is much higher. At least, among all the women’s erotic fiction we forced ourselves to read while preparing this article, there simply were no other kinds of male leads.
But perhaps fate was simply having a laugh at our expense.
In any case, the growing erotic appeal of men from the security apparatus should be regarded not as a proven trend but as a hypothesis that needs to be tested on a larger sample. But the very appearance of entire commercial “litmob” collaborative writing efforts centered on the figure of the general demonstrates at least one thing: the publishing ecosystem considers this image comprehensible and attractive to female readers.
And this is where things get really interesting.
What distinguishes the general from an ordinary alpha male is not that he is stronger or rougher. His power is institutional. He controls more than his own body, money or castle. Behind him stand the army, the law, the state, the right to give orders and legitimate violence. The heroine enters into a relationship not simply with a strong man, but with a man who embodies the system of power. In effect, she marries the state.
Psychologically, this fantasy has a perfectly understandable structure. If the outside world is perceived as dangerous and difficult to control, the attractiveness of a man capable of providing resources and protection increases. Experimental studies have shown that even a brief reminder of resource scarcity can shift women’s preferences toward signs that a man can provide more to her offspring. Other studies link a woman’s own control over resources with changes in how important she considers a partner’s economic qualities.
Benevolent sexism also plays a role. This is a model where a man should protect, provide for and take care of a woman who, in return, accepts a more dependent and traditional role. Paradoxically, some women may prefer such a man even when they simultaneously perceive his behavior as patronizing and restrictive.
In a series of five studies, the attractiveness of such a partner was explained primarily by the fact that he signaled a willingness to protect, provide and invest in the relationship. Such a man is especially attractive to women with a stronger need to feel secure in a relationship.
Departures from this pattern of behavior — choosing a different model of relationships — are condemned by society, and most likely, under present conditions, departing from this model may simply be unsafe for a woman. Thus, even despite potentially disagreeing with this model, women decide it is safer to agree with the person posing a threat than to defend their own interests.
The romance novel takes this construction to its ideal form. The general is frightening, but the heroine is not afraid. He is rough, but she alone sees his vulnerable soul. He may command thousands of people, but before her he gradually lays down his weapons and becomes a tender and playful partner.
The world remains hierarchical and dangerous. The heroine is given no opportunity to change its rules. Instead, she receives a personal exemption from those rules.
This is perhaps the most important detail. The female protagonist does not defeat the system. Instead, she integrates herself into it and becomes the beloved woman of the man who runs the system, like President Vladimir Putin’s reported partner Alina Kabaeva.
Hence the inevitable motif of healing the powerful hero, whose cruelty is reframed through his pain. If he is cold, it means he once suffered. If he trusts no one, it is because he was betrayed. If he is capable of violence, it means the harsh world forced him to become that way.
The heroine’s task is not to demand that he cease to be dangerous, but to discover that he is not a danger to her specifically because he loves her. And human history — including in contemporary Russia — knows many examples of women making such a choice.
Choosing a powerful, high-testosterone male as a protector threatens the woman herself with unpleasant consequences. Not only do Russian men have economic and political power over women, but physical power as well. That is why the situation regarding violence against women in Russia is alarming. In 2024, 963 Russian women were killed by their partners or other family members and journalists have founds that courts are often lenient toward Ukraine war veterans accused of domestic violence. But as we’d say in Russia, the naive feminine rowan trees stubbornly keep trying to move closer to the masculine oak!
It is also interesting to compare this Russian romantasy with its English-language counterparts. There, too, the male heroes are far from gentle and psychologically healthy. English-language romance is experiencing its own boom in dominant, dark and sometimes downright monstrous men. In 2025, the U.S. market grew especially rapidly thanks to the romantasy genre. In contemporary dark romance, it is easy to encounter a billionaire, mafioso, cowboy, athlete, biker, vampire, demon or faerie lord. Recent research on the genre itself likewise emphasizes its fascination with power imbalances, morally ambiguous heroes and the exploration of dangerous fantasies within the safe space of fiction.
The distinction, therefore, is not between a domineering Russian man and an egalitarian Western man. Both can be domineering, but the source of their power differs. The typical English-language alpha hero is a free agent. The billionaire is powerful because he created or inherited his own economic empire. The cowboy owns land and a horse. The mafioso exists in outright defiance of the state. The vampire, mage or faerie lord possesses innate supernatural power. Even when such a man is dangerous and despotic, his erotic capital is usually built around his personal autonomy: he is so strong, rich or talented that he makes his own rules.
The masculine general represents a different kind of fantasy. His power does not merely belong to him, but to the system. His epaulettes, rank, subordinates, access to force and ability to decide other people’s fates become part of his sexual appeal.
While English-language fantasy lionizes the man who cannot be controlled, its Russian counterpart focusses on how he could command the world around him.
That is precisely why General Ratmirov seems to me more frightening and more interesting than just another literary cliché. Perhaps he is a miniature model of a much larger social shift. When a woman’s own economic, political and bodily autonomy becomes less secure, fantasy may offer another form of adaptation: find the strongest man within the existing system and turn his power into your protection.
Then the final pie, lace collar and fourth pregnancy begin to look somewhat different. This is not simply bad literature. It is a very compact model of a social contract: he gets power over the world, while she gets power over his heart; he protects her from the world, while she agrees to live and feel secure in a world whose structure he has no intention of changing.
And what are we supposed to do about that? Perhaps we should simply leave them alone and watch what happens next.

title: Ye Shows in St. Petersburg Officially Canceled After Weeks of Conflicting Reports
description: Two St.
content:
Two St. Petersburg concerts by controversial rapper Ye scheduled for next month have been officially canceled following weeks of conflicting statements from venue management and local promoters.
An Instagram account affiliated with the U.S. touring agency Access Opera confirmed the cancellation Tuesday, directing ticket holders to seek refunds from the Russian promoter Say Agency.
The shows, originally scheduled for Oct. 10 and 11 at Gazprom Arena, triggered immediate backlash from conservative Russian politicians due to Ye’s past public support of Nazism, which constitutes a criminal offense under Russian law.
Gazprom Arena claimed it had never signed a contract with Say Agency and could not host the Ye shows. Local media reported at the time that the sudden cancellation followed a phone call “from above,” suggesting the Kremlin may have directly intervened.
Say Agency later insisted the Ye concerts would still take place. However, the promoter has since retracted those statements and said it will release an official announcement about the status of the shows on Wednesday.
Despite the cancellation, a Turkish agency that organized Ye’s performance in Istanbul in May listed a tentative July 10, 2027, date for a Moscow show on its website.
Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium had said it would be open to hosting Ye’s concert following Gazprom Arena’s withdrawal.
Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, previously visited Moscow in 2024 to celebrate the birthday of fashion designer and collaborator Gosha Rubchinskiy. Rumors of a performance at Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium circulated at the time.

title: Ksenia Maximova Went From Top Model to Anti-War Activist to London Councillor. Now She’s Wanted By Russia.
description: Ksenia Maximova was ranked among the world’s 50 most successful models in the 2000s, but today is better known as a prominent figure in Russia’s anti-war movement in London.  Since 2022, Maximova has worked to support Ukraine, help anti-war Russian emigres and refugees in Britain and collaborated with the Russian Anti-War Committee.
content:
Ksenia Maximova was ranked among the world’s 50 most successful models in the 2000s, but today is better known as a prominent figure in Russia’s anti-war movement in London.
Since 2022, Maximova has worked to support Ukraine, help anti-war Russian emigres and refugees in Britain and collaborated with the Russian Anti-War Committee. More recently, she became a rare Russian-born figure to enter British politics after she was elected as a Liberal Democrat councillor in London.
On Monday, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) opened a criminal case against her, accusing her of participating in a “terrorist organization” and claiming that the Russian Democratic Society, which she co-founded, collected money and other assistance “in the interests of the Kyiv regime.”
Maximova, 40, was also placed on Russia’s wanted list and added to its register of “terrorists and extremists.”
In an interview with The Moscow Times, Maximova discussed entering British politics as a Russian immigrant, her work supporting Ukraine and why she is considering running for Parliament.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
The Moscow Times: Does being added to the list of ‘terrorists and extremists’ affect your political career?
Ksenia Maximova: I’d say it’s more no than yes. Everyone in the U.K. has been incredibly supportive. Sometimes it even feels like a bit too much, to be honest, given how many messages my colleagues have been sending me. There’s an expression: ‘Wear it as a badge of honor,’ but I’d rather have a different kind of badge of honor.
First, I was put on a wanted list, then I was designated a ‘terrorist and extremist.’ Technically, it should have happened in the opposite order: first the charges, then the designation and then the wanted list. It’s also possible that at some point I’ll end up on an Interpol list and that could cause some problems when crossing borders. The biggest problem is that I still have family in Russia, and that’s what worries me.
MT: How much did you expect to be directly targeted?
KM : Honestly, I expected it. There’s even a joke that if you’re still not designated as a ‘foreign agent,’ an ‘undesirable organization’ or an ‘extremist,’ maybe you’re actually working for the FSB and someone is protecting you.
MT: When you became a municipal councillor, it was seen in exiled media as a success story — an example of someone from Russia getting involved in Western politics and integrating into society. How did it feel from your perspective?
KM: For me, it was a logical next step. At some point, I realized that if I wanted to work on Russia-related issues, it made sense to do it from within British politics. Constantly trying to push things from the outside wasn’t very effective. I also wanted firsthand experience of Western politics — to understand how it works and what it’s like to be part of a Western political party.
It’s actually been a real eye-opener. My first experience was with the Russian anti-war opposition, but so much of it seemed to be about undermining each other and fighting among themselves — this constant territorial behavior, arguing over who has the right to what and who controls what.
Then I joined the Liberal Democrats, and I don’t know if every party is like this, but people immediately started helping me. They explained how everything worked, supported me and kept checking in to make sure I understood what I was doing. It was a real shock to the system. I thought: ’This is what political participation can actually look like.’ I’ve been trying to bring some of that back into the Russian opposition movement — to foster more of a culture of mutual support. [The Russian Democratic Society] has always worked that way, thankfully, and it still does. But I’d like to see more of that across the Russian anti-war movement as a whole.
Also, there are already quite a few municipal councillors with Russian roots. I’m definitely not the first. Sometimes I even felt a little awkward about how much attention it got: ‘Oh, a Russian municipal councillor!’ There have been others before me, there are some now and there will be more.
MT: How do you balance your work as a municipal councillor with your work in the Russian anti-war movement?
KM: I clearly need to find a way to streamline things — that’s what I’m thinking about now, as I don’t have enough time.
As for my work as a municipal councillor, you could say we inherited our district at the worst possible time. We were elected in May and then we had an absolutely brutal drought all summer. I was visiting Kyiv and my constituents were messaging me saying: ‘All our parks are on fire.’ And I had to deal with it. Then we were told that the local council didn’t budget any money for firefighters or for maintaining water levels in the ponds. Everything dried up and the animals were dying.
An enormous number of requests keep coming in. The economy is doing badly across the country, people are struggling financially and a lot of people are losing their homes, so I also have to deal with social housing cases. Those are considered some of the most difficult cases. I was actually used to this from my human rights work, because every now and then random people would somehow get hold of my contact details — both Russians and Ukrainians. Imagine, a completely random person you’ve never met or even heard of lands in your inbox and says: ‘I’m a refugee,’ or ‘I’m about to be deported,’ or ‘I’m having problems with my visa.’ And you just try to figure it out and help however you can. It’s basically the same thing here, except now the British have been added to the mix.
I originally decided to run for the municipal council because it seemed like the natural path toward eventually running for Parliament. I’m still figuring things out, but I’ve now submitted an application to become a parliamentary candidate. The next step is to sit down, learn our policies and take the tests I need to qualify.
As for my anti-war work, I suppose you could say it’s broader in scope. There’s a diaspora organization, a committee in the British Parliament and an interparliamentary alliance on Russia that I’m currently putting together. Much of this is really about [shaping] Western policy toward Russia. I also work as a Russia expert — we produce reports and analysis and then use them for advocacy, whether that means pushing for sanctions or finding ways to support Ukraine.
MT: Speaking of supporting Ukraine, could you tell more about your trips there?
KM: I’ve been spending a lot of time there lately. I stayed for about a month and a half on my last trip. I’m a British citizen, so I can travel there freely, although there are obviously limits on how long I can stay.
It’s simply easier for me to do my work from there because so many experts, journalists, politicians, decisionmakers, stakeholders, foundations and NGOs are concentrated in Kyiv. When you’re working on Russia- and Ukraine-related issues from the West, you have to chase people around and seek out the relatively small number of people who are actually working on these issues.
I also wrote a post saying that Ukrainians don’t necessarily hate Russians who are anti-war and doing something useful for Ukraine — and I got absolutely slaughtered on social media for it. A lot of people assume that Ukrainians simply hate all Russians, full stop. But that’s not what I’ve experienced. I’ve had no problems staying there, and I can continue my advocacy work on Russia from Kyiv without any issues.
Obviously, there are airstrikes, and lately they’ve become even more intense. It’s hard to get used to. Everyone is chronically sleep-deprived. Nobody goes to shelters anymore, because otherwise you’d basically be living there.
I feel a little strange in Europe after coming back from Ukraine. You return and realize that, broadly speaking, people are preparing for war, but at the same time, there’s still very little readiness to take concrete action or, for that matter, allocate a budget for it. People who haven’t experienced this firsthand still seem to operate at a much slower pace. You want to do something, but you don’t know where to start. The Russian anti-war community has been sounding the alarm in the West for years. I’ve realized that there’s a particular nuance here. Even though I grew up in the West from my teenage years onward, I did grow up in Russia before that. When you spend part of your life in Russia, you’re left with this feeling that you always need to be prepared, ‘just in case.’ It’s this underlying state of alertness that you carry with you and the West simply doesn't have that. Several generations of people in the West have grown up completely at ease and now getting them to see things differently is incredibly difficult.
As for our reports on Russia, it’s not that the [West] doesn’t want to listen, we actually get commissioned to produce them. But the whole system and institutional structure simply isn’t set up to respond quickly to changes.
MT: You said you’re considering running for Parliament. Could you tell us more about your plans and what it’s like building a political career as an immigrant, starting at the local level?
KM: I had absolutely no problems. I joined the party and about six months later decided to run for office. People actually encouraged me to do it and explained how the process worked. Not once did anyone suggest that the fact that I’m Russian might be an issue.
I found that voters actually really wanted to talk about international politics. People are anxious and don’t understand what’s going on. During the campaign, I had a few doorstep conversations where I asked people about their concerns and they said things like: ‘Can you get rid of Trump?’ or ‘Can you bring down petrol prices?’
There was one time when someone asked me how I felt about the war in Ukraine. It was January and I had just come back from Kyiv, so I replied: ‘I’ve just been freezing in Ukraine along with everyone else, so I hope that answers your question.’ That was basically it. I was actually surprised. I had expected that at some point someone might make an issue of [my nationality]. I even told our team that maybe we should make it clear that I work with Ukraine and support it. But in the end, nothing happened at all.
As for the Parliament, I think I need to weigh the pros and cons and consider how much I’d actually be able to do, and how effective I could be, particularly in continuing my human rights work and work on Russia. MPs are being pulled in so many different directions right now — they have international issues, national issues and then all the local issues in the constituencies they represent.
On the other hand, if you’re an MP, you’re a British politician and you have a certain level of influence. I think our party, the Liberal Democrats, could do quite well at the next election because Labour and the Conservatives are unpopular, while the Greens haven’t really managed to push their agenda through. [Nigel] Farage has also weakened, although he could still regain some strength. So we’re basically the centrists, with a relatively conservative economic position but liberal values. People are tired of all the extremes, and I think we certainly have a chance.
So, I’m also interested to see what happens at the next election.

title: At Least 6 Crew Members Confirmed Dead After Military Plane Crashes in Amur Region
description: Six crew members on board a Russian military aircraft that crashed in the Far Eastern Amur region were killed, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
content:
Six crew members on board a Russian military aircraft that crashed in the Far Eastern Amur region were killed, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The Tu-95 strategic bomber went down in a remote area during a routine training exercise, the Interfax news agency cited a military spokesperson as saying. It was not carrying any weapons on board at the time of the crash.
One crew member survived the crash and was hospitalized, the Defense Ministry said. Air Force officials were dispatched to the crash site to conduct an investigation.
Unverified reports from Telegram news with ties to Russian law enforcement and security services claimed the bomber plane may have crashed as the result of an engine fire and explosion.
Officials have not commented on the possible cause of the crash.
The Tu-95 was reportedly stationed at the Ukrainka air base, one of Russia’s largest long-range Air Force bases. Reports said the plane crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo, which is located 30 kilometers (18.5 miles) north of the Ukrainka base.

title: Russia Tightens Cash Outflow Limits to Neighboring Countries
description: President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order on Tuesday tightening restrictions on taking cash from Russia to neighboring countries.
content:
President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order on Tuesday tightening restrictions on taking cash from Russia to neighboring countries.
Individuals are now prohibited from taking more than 1 million rubles ($11,900) in cash to Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are members of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union.
Individuals had previously been allowed to move the ruble equivalent of $100,000 under an order signed by Putin in March.
In addition, businesses are banned from removing any amount of cash from the country , according to the newspaper Kommersant.
Individual violators of the new restrictions face total confiscation of any sums exceeding 1 million rubles, while businesses caught attempting to transfer funds will be forced to surrender the entire cash amount.
Exceptions apply to travelers passing through government-designated international airports, official diplomatic missions and individuals who provide bank authorization statements.
The new restrictions take effect immediately.
Russia previously banned individuals from taking more than $10,000 in foreign currency out of the country in March 2022 following the launch of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Russian Summer Air Travel Fell Amid Surge in Daily Drone Attacks
description: Russian airlines recorded a 7% drop in passenger traffic during the summer travel season, as a surge of daily Ukrainian drone attacks disrupted operations at dozens of airports across the country, the Interfax news agency reported Tuesday.
content:
Russian airlines recorded a 7% drop in passenger traffic during the summer travel season, as a surge of daily Ukrainian drone attacks disrupted operations at dozens of airports across the country, the Interfax news agency reported Tuesday.
Dmitry Yadrov, who heads the civilian aviation agency Rosaviatsia, said in a meeting with Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin that Russian airlines transported 39.5 million passengers between May and August.
That is reportedly down from around 42.6 million passengers who were transported over the same period last year.
The drop comes amid near-daily disruptions at Russian airports due to Ukrainian attacks.
Earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned foreign airlines and insurance companies that Ukrainian drones made Russian airspace dangerous. In response, Rosaviatsia vowed it would work to prevent any disruption to civil aviation.
“Despite all the challenges we faced, primarily those related to restrictions on the use of airspace, the industry as a whole — airlines, airports, air navigation — operated normally, reliably and safely,” Yadrov told Mishustin on Tuesday.
Russia’s Economic Development Ministry projects passenger traffic to reach 108.5 million in 2026, down 0.3% year-on-year, according to Interfax. The ministry cites “systemic constraints,” including difficulties maintaining foreign aircraft and prolonged airport closures in southern Russia, as the main causes for the expected decrease.
Aviation experts warn that demand for air travel could fall even further as the government is weighing whether to introduce new passenger fees to offset rising aircraft leasing costs and jet fuel prices.
According to the newspaper Kommersant, those proposed surcharges could raise between 68 billion rubles and 84 billion rubles ($807 million and $997 million) annually.
