title: Russians Prepare for an Election With Less Choice Than Ever
description: In the hit 2007 Russian political satire “Election Day,” a group of radio executives is sent to a provincial region as it elects its new governor.
content:
In the hit 2007 Russian political satire “Election Day,” a group of radio executives is sent to a provincial region as it elects its new governor. Their task is to manufacture a candidate, win over voters and make sure the right person gets elected.
One song from the film’s soundtrack, sung by punk rocker Sergei Shnurov, would become a national catchphrase: “Elections! Elections! All the candidates are motherf***ers!”
But what was once political comedy now feels like a glimpse into a different era. Elections at that time may have been cynical and manipulated, but they still involved a semblance of genuine competition.
Nearly two decades later, as Russia prepares to elect a new State Duma for the first time since invading Ukraine, the question is how much of that competition remains.
When Russians head to the polls on Sept. 18-20, they will elect 450 lawmakers in the lower-house State Duma as well as regional legislators and governors across the country’s 11 time zones.
Among the major political parties contesting seats in the Duma — Russia’s most important election this year — are the ruling, pro-Kremlin United Russia party, the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), A Just Russia, New People and Yabloko.
Experts say these parties’ platforms are broadly similar and largely back the Kremlin’s policies. The only exception is Yabloko, which is campaigning on an anti-war platform but was barred from the State Duma’s party-list vote, the nationwide contest in which voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate.
United Russia, which currently holds 321 of 450 seats in the State Duma, is widely expected to win a majority of the vote. Even so, experts say that the elections remain an important gauge of public sentiment.
The election will also be held in the four partially occupied regions of Ukraine that Moscow claims to have annexed and where fighting continues.
Voting will be spread over three days, while 33 regions will offer electronic voting — two measures that critics say could make it easier to manipulate the results.
Experts differ on how and when exactly Russia’s elections lost their competitiveness, but they agree that the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 marked a major turning point.
Political scientists now describe Russia as an electoral authoritarian system: an autocracy that continues to hold elections while tightly controlling the conditions under which they take place.
“You can't openly call for an end to the war and you can't openly challenge [President Vladimir] Putin's legitimacy,” said Ora John Reuter, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and expert on Russia’s electoral politics.
“Beyond that, the candidates and parties that are running have a little bit of freedom to debate other policy issues within those constraints,” he told The Moscow Times.
Exiled political commentator Ekaterina Schulmann said that by 2011, the authorities were already shaping the composition of successive Dumas by “the desired degree” and that they “did not differ significantly from one another.”
For the Kremlin, United Russia “must always have a constitutional majority,” while the other parties must know their place and “not interfere with the smooth and energetic legislative process — essentially the rubber-stamping of bills sent over from various branches of the executive government,” Schulmann explained .
It would be wrong to believe that “there were some remnants of freedom before, which have only now been completely stamped out,” she added.
But the range of political alternatives available to voters has narrowed sharply, even by formal measures, experts say.
“Over the past 10 years, the number of legally registered political parties has dropped from 75 to 17,” said Vadim Ternovoy, an expert with the Election Atlas project.
For the first time since 2012, “only parties that are exempt from collecting voter signatures were able to nominate candidate lists for the State Duma elections,” he said. Under Russian law, parties must collect 200,000 voter signatures to appear on the ballot unless they are already represented in the State Duma or have won seats in at least one regional legislature.
The number of candidates in elections at all levels has fallen by around 20% since 2022, Ternovoy said. This figure refers to those who put themselves forward, rather than those who were ultimately registered — which suggests that even the willingness to participate in elections is declining.
Experts linked the decline in interest to the growing imbalance between the risks and benefits of being in politics. Repression has affected not only civil society activists and anti-war Yabloko candidates, but also members of the Communist Party and LDPR in some regions, Ternovoy said.
Even prominent United Russia members have complained of pressure from within their own party during primaries and some have faced criminal charges, he added.
“As a result, many people who might take part in elections with a realistic chance of doing well simply choose not to run. This leaves voters with fewer opportunities to hear different views and make their own voices heard,” he said.
The erosion of Russia’s political and electoral system began in the mid-2000s as the Kremlin tightened its grip on the media and moved against oligarchs who had amassed political influence. But at times, this decline slowed, and some reforms briefly opened space for political competition.
Direct gubernatorial elections were abolished between 2004 and 2012, though this restriction remains in some regions. Direct mayoral elections have also been scrapped in regional capitals and major cities, while regulations governing political parties have been tightened.
More recent measures include rules barring “foreign agents” from running for office and greater restrictions on independent election observers.
The independent election watchdog Golos, which had documented election violations since 2000, was forced to close last year after its co-chair was jailed in what supporters called an attempt to silence the group.
These restrictions were “in fact a response to growing public demand for greater political participation and accountability from the authorities,” Ternovoy said, pointing to late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny’s attempt to mount a presidential campaign in 2018, as well as mass protests over the exclusion of opposition candidates from the 2019 Moscow City Duma elections .
The fate of Yabloko, the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform, is perhaps most illustrative of the 2026 campaign’s limitations.
In its decision to bar Yabloko from the party-list vote to the State Duma, a court cited alleged violations involving foreign funding, campaign materials distributed through restricted foreign platforms and copyright rules. The party denies wrongdoing.
Yabloko still has registered candidates running in single-member districts, a defined geographic area that elects one lawmaker to the State Duma, as well as in regional legislative elections.
In total, at least 36 opposition candidates were barred from the State Duma and regional legislative elections, according to the exiled outlet Vyorstka. More than half of those cases involved Yabloko candidates, Vyorstka said.
Seventeen of these candidates were disqualified over online posts mentioning Navalny, who is on Russia’s federal list of “extremists and terrorists.” Seven others were barred for sharing links to Facebook and Instagram, which are banned in Russia, or for displaying the platforms’ logos.
Nikolai Bondarenko, a prominent Saratov politician running for the State Duma with the Communist Party, was disqualified after being fined 1,000 rubles ($12) over a photo of Navalny posted in 2024 on a Telegram channel bearing his name. Bondarenko denied having a connection to the channel.
Boris Nadezhdin, whose anti-war presidential campaign in 2024 drew long lines of supporters before the authorities disqualified him, is another would-be candidate this year.
He was barred from running for the State Duma as an independent after being fined for displaying alleged “extremist” symbols in a photo of Navalny, briefly detained and designated a “foreign agent.” He left Russia in August.
Amid these restrictions, the public’s interest — and even interest from candidates themselves — appears limited.
While televised debates are formally part of the election campaign, Putin has never participated in one and many United Russia candidates have followed suit.
In Ryazan, the state broadcaster Rossia 1 spent two consecutive days unsuccessfully trying to assemble State Duma candidates in its studio. Both times, the presenter ended the program shortly after the introduction because no one had shown up.
Sixty-six percent of Russians do not know when the State Duma elections would be held, while 28% said they do not plan to vote, according to a survey published in June by the independent pollster Levada Center.
Among those who do not plan to vote, 41% said their vote would make no difference, while 24% do not believe the elections will be fair.
Yet Ternovoy said the initial registration of anti-war party Yabloko — even without any particularly recognizable party leaders — nonetheless triggered “a largely spontaneous mobilization of part of the anti-war electorate.”
And when Yabloko was barred from the party-list vote in the Duma, Election Atlas documented an 80-fold surge in interest in the party across social media.
Ternovoy compared this to Nadezhdin’s brief 2024 presidential campaign, which coincided with a decline in support for the war in opinion polls.
“Had Yabloko remained on the ballot [for the State Duma party list], it would, under the law, have been entitled to free airtime on the country’s largest television and radio stations starting in late August ... which could have had a significant impact on public opinion,” he added.
He pointed to Election Atlas’ monitoring of social media, which last month showed that people were more concerned with the growing restrictions on political competition than with what officials including Putin were up to.
“To me, this looks like an important shift in public opinion and, quite possibly, the main outcome” of these elections, he said.

title: Putin Casts Parliamentary Election as Barometer of Support for War, Urges Russians to Vote
description: President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday framed participation in an upcoming parliamentary election as a barometer of support for Russia's war in Ukraine and urged Russians to vote.
content:
President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday framed participation in an upcoming parliamentary election as a barometer of support for Russia's war in Ukraine and urged Russians to vote.
Russia holds a three-day parliamentary election starting on Friday to choose the composition of its 450-seat lower house of parliament, the State Duma, which has a track record of faithfully approving the Kremlin's initiatives.
It is the first parliamentary election since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and comes at a time when opinion polls show some Russians have become more anxious about how the conflict affects them, as the economy is under strain, and as most anti-war candidates have been excluded from the ballot.
The political system is tightly controlled and the ruling United Russia party, backed by Putin, is widely expected to retain its dominance.
In a televised address to the nation ahead of the vote, Putin referred to the war in Ukraine and to Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine, saying that casting a vote would help secure Russia's victory and demonstrate national resolve in the face of external pressure.
"Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us, or in undermining our statehood and our socio-political system," Putin said.
He said the vote would serve as a collective response to those seeking to weaken Russia, hinder its development, and deprive it of its sovereignty and right to determine its own future.

title: Krasnoyarsk Woman Killed by Bear Amid Rise in Attacks
description: A bear killed a 66-year-old woman in the Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk, law enforcement authorities said Wednesday, marking the latest fatal encounter amid a reported rise in bear attacks across Russia this year.
content:
A bear killed a 66-year-old woman in the Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk, law enforcement authorities said Wednesday, marking the latest fatal encounter amid a reported rise in bear attacks across Russia this year.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, said the woman was found dead in the remote village of Verkhny Kebezh, around 3,400 kilometers (2,100 miles) east of Moscow.
Investigators released images showing a rural wooden house and its yard, which appeared to be the woman’s home.
News of the deadly attack came after officials on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East said they shot and killed a bear that wandered onto the grounds of a school in the village of Palana.
Russia has recorded around 20 bear attacks since the start of the year, experts say, though it is not clear how many of them have been fatal. Bears are confirmed to have killed at least five people in Siberia over the past month alone, state media reported .
Russia’s Natural Resources and Environment Ministry has dismissed reports of an uptick in bear attacks this year, noting that the annual figure tends to hover between 20 and 30. In 2014, Russia saw a record 166 bear attacks.
It blamed the recent public anxiety over bear encounters on videos spreading across social media.
The ministry also said Russia’s brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990 and now stands at 307,000.

title: Drone Downed in Lithuania Was Russian and Likely Aimed at Ukraine, President Nausėda Says
description: A drone that was shot down by a NATO fighter jet in the skies above Lithuania for the first time was likely directed at Ukraine and veered off course, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday. “Most likely, it was a Russian drone intended for Ukraine that was diverted from its course by Ukrainian electronic warfare measures and entered our territory, where it was shot down,” Nausėda told reporters after a state defense council meeting.
content:
A drone that was shot down by a NATO fighter jet in the skies above Lithuania for the first time was likely directed at Ukraine and veered off course, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Wednesday.
“Most likely, it was a Russian drone intended for Ukraine that was diverted from its course by Ukrainian electronic warfare measures and entered our territory, where it was shot down,” Nausėda told reporters after a state defense council meeting.
Nausėda identified the drone as a Gerbera, a low-cost plywood long-range aerial drone used by Russia. Gerberas are often employed as decoys to overwhelm air defenses, but they can also carry explosives.
An Italian fighter jet that is part of NATO’s Baltic air policing mission intercepted the unmanned aircraft over central Lithuania early Tuesday.
Russia has not commented on the incident.
Suspected Russian drones have previously been shot down over Poland, Romania, Latvia and Estonia, all of which are NATO and EU members.
Lithuania’s public broadcaster LRT, citing government officials, reported that the drone entered the country from Belarus and crossed 100 kilometers (62 miles) of territory before it was shot down.
Belarus is not formally involved in Russia’s war against Ukraine, but it has allowed Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for military operations.
Nausėda said the Lithuanian army is analyzing the drone’s electronics to determine its targeting. He said Lithuania needs to have the means to intercept drones, but questioned the efficiency of using fighter jets to do so.
The president also said that the security situation in Lithuania and across NATO countries more broadly remains unchanged, but warned that “incidents, provocation, sabotage acts, including false-flag operations” are still possible.

title: Syzran and Saratov Oil Refineries Halt Operations After Drone Attacks, Sources Say
description: Two Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the cities of Syzran and Saratov have suspended processing following Ukrainian drone attacks over the past week, three industry sources told Reuters on Wednesday.
content:
Two Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the cities of Syzran and Saratov have suspended processing following Ukrainian drone attacks over the past week, three industry sources told Reuters on Wednesday.
The sources said the Syzran plant paused operations on Tuesday, while the Saratov refinery halted work last Friday. Both facilities have repeatedly come under attack since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
At the Syzran refinery, sources said the main CDU-6 crude distillation unit was damaged in a drone strike. The unit, which accounts for 71% of the plant's processing capacity, could take at least a month to repair, they added.
The refinery's second crude distillation unit, accounting for the other 29% of production capacity, was already undergoing maintenance after an attack in July.
Sources said the Saratov refinery has been shut down for several weeks following earlier strikes and was on the verge of restarting operations when it was attacked late last week.
Both refineries have a combined processing capacity of 290,000 barrels of oil per day.
Ukraine has been carrying out a far-reaching drone strike campaign against Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure since the spring, saying its goal is to raise the costs of the war for the Kremlin.
The near-nightly attacks have led to nationwide fuel shortages since June, prompting authorities to introduce rationing measures in some parts of Russia and across annexed Crimea.
U.S. President Donald Trump has recently blamed Ukraine's strikes for the surging cost of diesel across the globe and called on both Moscow and Kyiv to halt their attacks on energy infrastructure. However, neither side of the conflict has indicated that it's ready to agree to Trump's ceasefire request.

title: Belousov Awards Warship Captain for ‘Skillfully and Decisively’ Firing Flares at Danish Helicopter
description: Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday that Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded a ship captain for his “skillful and decisive actions” after firing signal flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea earlier this week.
content:
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday that Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded a ship captain for his “skillful and decisive actions” after firing signal flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea earlier this week.
The captain, who was not identified by name, received Russia’s medal “For Courage” following an incident during which his ship, the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny, “prevented a provocation by a Danish helicopter” in international waters by launching two signal flares at the aircraft.
In a statement, Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that the Danish helicopter failed to respond to the Soobrazitelny’s radio calls when it was detected in the southwestern Baltic Sea on Monday. The helicopter left the vicinity of the Russian ship after the flares were fired, it added.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus accused the crew of the Soobrazitelny of making no attempt to contact the helicopter, which he said narrowly avoided the flare signals that were launched in its direction.
Bruus said the helicopter was following its usual route to photograph the corvette as part of a routine operation that it has done several times before.
Russia has “increased their willingness to take risks in terms of how far they are prepared to go,” Bruus said in comments to Reuters.
Russia’s Ambassador to Copenhagen Vladimir Barbin, who was summoned over the incident, in turn accused Danish military aircraft of “dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships,” creating the risk of collision. Barbin claimed Denmark has rejected Moscow’s proposals to sign a maritime and airspace agreement that could help prevent future incidents.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen blamed Russia for seeking to “sow fear and discord” over Monday’s close encounter, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it part of “a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe.”
The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out of the Baltic Sea for commercial and military shipping. They are also a major artery for global oil shipments, including from Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of oil tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

title: Belarus Frees 25 More Political Prisoners in Return for U.S. Sanctions Relief
description: Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, an envoy for U.S.
content:
Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, an envoy for U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
The deal was part of lengthy negotiations in which Washington is urging Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to free hundreds of people, including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers in exchange for sanctions relief and an easing of his international isolation.
Trump's envoy, John Coale, told reporters in the Belarusian capital Minsk: "We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies."
The figure of 25 was much lower than the 250 that Coale persuaded Lukashenko to release when he last visited Minsk in March.
Coale said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues to pave the way for another prisoner release and the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve U.S.-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future. We are not finished!" he posted later on X.
Belarusian human rights group Viasna said a new round of prisoner pardons had started, with relatives of some detainees being told they could pick up their loved ones from prison on Wednesday morning.
Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the former Soviet state still holds more than 900 political prisoners, even after Coale negotiated the release of hundreds since the middle of last year.
Among the most frequent charges against them are "extremist" activity, conspiring to seize power, incitement to hatred or insulting the president.
At Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the people in question were political prisoners and rejected assertions by rights groups and the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
The two companies to be removed from U.S. sanctions are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Sanctions against them have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get U.S. banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's efforts since last year have led to the release, among many others, of Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales Bialiatski and leading opposition figures. His diplomacy has earned gratitude from many Belarusians, while also raising concerns.
"We should use every opportunity to save lives. But we should not confuse releases with political change. Repression continues, and Lukashenko continues supporting Russia 's war," exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said in comments to Reuters on Tuesday.
"The purpose should be to empty the prisons, not to rehabilitate the dictatorship."

title: Russian General Who Oversaw Capture of Ukraine’s Kostiantynivka Dies
description: A military commander who President Vladimir Putin recently awarded Russia’s highest state honor for the capture of the eastern Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka has died, Russian and Ukrainian military officials said Wednesday.
content:
A military commander who President Vladimir Putin recently awarded Russia’s highest state honor for the capture of the eastern Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka has died, Russian and Ukrainian military officials said Wednesday.
Major General Apti Alaudinov, who serves as serves as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s ideological arm and commander of the Akhmat special forces, said Major General Anton Grunis “passed on to another world” in a short post on Telegram.
“He left us as a hero who carried out his sacred duty,” Alaudinov said without specifying when Grunis died or the circumstances of his death.
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander, Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, later claimed that Grunis was “eliminated” in a nighttime raid in the eastern Donetsk region on Sept. 12.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify the claim.
Grunis commanded the Russian Armed Forces’ 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade, which has played a key role in Russia’s offensive in the Donetsk region.
In July, Grunis personally briefed Putin on the capture of Kostiantynivka, one of four heavily fortified cities that make up Ukraine's so-called “fortress belt” in Donetsk. Earlier, Grunis boasted that his troops had “sliced up the city like a pie” by outflanking Ukrainian defense lines along local reservoirs.
Ukraine has denied claims that Russia fully captured Kostiantynivka. According to the U.S.-based Institute for the Study of War, Russian forces control parts of the city, but Ukrainian forces continue to carry out counteroffensives in the area.
Putin awarded Grunis the Hero of Russia medal in August.
In 2023, the Russian president had praised him as a commander “with a Lithuanian surname, born in Kazan, who fights brilliantly.”

title: I’m Proud That We Published the Syutkins’ Columns
description: Opinion | Pavel Syutkin, a longtime Moscow Times columnist and historian of Russian cuisine, was sentenced in Moscow yesterday to six years in prison.
content:
Pavel Syutkin, a longtime Moscow Times columnist and historian of Russian cuisine, was sentenced in Moscow yesterday to six years in prison. His “crime” is all too common in Putin’s Russia: spreading what the authorities call “fake news” about the Russian military.
For years, Pavel and his wife, Olga, had written a weekly column that highlighted the richness of Russian cuisine for The Moscow Times. They continued to write it even after we were forced into exile in the Netherlands in 2022.
I must confess that after our move to Amsterdam, I regularly suggested to our editor-in-chief that we stop publishing the Syutkins’ columns. As a Russian, I assumed that after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, no one would want to read about Russian cuisine, much less cook it. But our American editor showed me the readership figures, which proved that these columns remained very popular. Fortunately, The Moscow Times is a serious publication, so the final decision about editorial content rests with the editor, not the publisher. Today, I am proud that we published the Syutkins’ columns. And I'm sending them both my support.
Syutkin, one of the leading advocates of Russian cuisine both at home and abroad, never hid his opposition to the war or to Putin. He was arrested in October 2025. He was also added to the state financial monitoring agency Rosfinmonitoring’s list of “terrorists and extremists,” which effectively amounts to a civil execution. Inclusion on the list freezes a person’s bank accounts and severely restricts access to money, effectively depriving them of all legal means to support themselves. It is impossible to challenge this designation in court.
If Russia were a normal country, Pavel Syutkin would receive state honors and recognition for promoting Russian culture around the world. At one time, Russia seemed to be that kind of country. In 2015, after the annexation of Crimea and the outbreak of war in eastern Ukraine, Syutkin represented Russia as an official ambassador at the World Expo in Milan. But 11 years later, he was sentenced to six years in prison, nearly as long as some sentences handed down to convicted killers in Russia.
Syutkin was imprisoned simply because he dared to express his opposition to the war — a freedom that is still guaranteed by the Russian Constitution. The Nobel Peace Prize-winning human rights organization Memorial has designated him as a political prisoner.
Syutkin is now the fourth journalist connected to publications where I have worked to be arrested. All of them are innocent.
Ivan Safronov, my former colleague at Vedomosti, was sentenced to 22 years for “treason.”
Another former Vedomosti colleague, Sergei Mingazov, died as a result of the Putin regime’s cruelty. Sergei, who had cancer, was also accused of spreading “fake news” about the military’s actions in Ukraine. The judge refused to suspend or postpone his trial. Deprived of adequate medical treatment, he died before the court delivered its verdict.
Evan Gershkovich, a former Moscow Times journalist, was luckier. In 2024, he and 15 other prisoners held in Russia were exchanged for eight Russians imprisoned in several countries, including intelligence operatives and a convicted assassin.
This list is by no means exhaustive and will continue to grow. The Moscow Times made its choice long ago. We will continue to serve our readers by reporting the truth and exposing misinformation, even as the Putin regime seeks to intimidate us and obstruct our work.

title: Yabloko Leader Slams Exiled Opposition’s Voting Strategy
description: Nikolai Rybakov, the chairman of the liberal opposition party Yabloko, has criticized the tactical voting strategy promoted by exiled opposition figures Yulia Navalnaya and Maxim Katz ahead of this weekend’s parliamentary elections.
content:
Nikolai Rybakov, the chairman of the liberal opposition party Yabloko, has criticized the tactical voting strategy promoted by exiled opposition figures Yulia Navalnaya and Maxim Katz ahead of this weekend’s parliamentary elections.
In a video released on Monday, Navalnaya and Katz said they had joined forces and agreed to endorse a joint slate of candidates running for the lower-house State Duma in single-seat constituencies. For party-list candidates, they urged Russian voters to back anyone running from a political party other than the ruling United Russia party.
Speaking to a crowd of supporters in St. Petersburg on Tuesday evening, Rybakov balked at the idea of voting for candidates in nominally opposition parties that he said have backed the war against Ukraine, as well as repressive political measures against anti-war Russians.
“These people put my comrades in prison for 11 years, and now you want us to support them in the elections?” Rybakov said , referring to the political prosecutions of Yabloko members in recent years.
“[Navalnaya and Katz] are proposing to dance to their tune again and vote for the very people who led to the death of people in Russia and Ukraine,” he said in a video shared by the outlet Varlamov News.
Rybakov accused Navalnaya and Katz of “manipulating [voters] from abroad” and told supporters that following their voting strategy “will end in the deaths of people and prison terms.”
Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party, was disqualified from the party-list vote after the Russian Supreme Court ruled in August that it had engaged in copyright violations during political campaigning and had broken campaign finance laws.
More than 100 Yabloko candidates, who are all running on a pro-peace platform, are still allowed to compete in single-member constituencies, but they appear unlikely to win any seats in parliament.
Under Russian election law, half of the State Duma’s 450 seats are distributed among the list of political parties that receive more than 5% of the votes. The remaining 225 seats are given to the winners of elections in single-member constituencies.
Under Rybakov’s leadership, Yabloko has urged supporters to spoil party-list ballots and vote for the remaining single-district candidates when three-day voting begins this Friday.
Four other systemic opposition parties are participating in the State Duma elections: the Communist Party, the ultra-nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR), New People and the left-leaning A Just Russia party. Each party broadly supports the war against Ukraine and tends to vote in line with United Russia on key issues.

title: United States Charges 5 People in Alleged Russian-Backed Murder Plots
description: The U.S.
content:
The U.S. Department of Justice has charged five people in connection with alleged Russia n plots involving surveillance, recruitment and targeted killings, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday.
The five people allegedly worked for Russia n intelligence services to "conduct attacks and murders around the world, including in the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment , adding that the individuals were still at large .
The DOJ said Russia n national Yuri Khrameev, 63; his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22; were charged with an alleged conspiracy to finance terrorism.
Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters the plots included "efforts to murder a Russia n dissident who investigators believed was located in the Washington, D.C., area."
According to the Justice Department, the network allegedly recruited multiple people in the United States to provide surveillance on Russia n dissidents, including one living in the U.S. and one in Lithuania.
One recruit was allegedly offered $40,000 to "eliminate" or "disappear" a person residing in the U.S., according to the Justice Department. Last year, another U.S. recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania, it said.
The Russia n embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia has previously denied conducting such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States.

title: Russia Resumes Postal Service to North Korea After 6 Years
description: Russia’s national postal service has resumed regular mail deliveries to North Korea following a six-year hiatus due to the Covid-19 pandemic, news agencies reported Tuesday.
content:
Russia’s national postal service has resumed regular mail deliveries to North Korea following a six-year hiatus due to the Covid-19 pandemic, news agencies reported Tuesday.
Russian Post restarted package deliveries to North Korea in June 2025 and has now expanded the service to letters, postcards, printed material and specialized materials for the visually impaired.
Mail weighing up to 20 kilograms (44 pounds) will reach recipients in North Korea within 15 days, according to Interfax.
The deliveries will first be flown to Far Eastern Russia’s Vladivostok, then transported to Pyongyang by a partner North Korean airline.
Last year, Russian Post said Russians frequently send clothing, footwear, documents, books and non-perishable food items like tea, coffee, grains, dried fruits, nuts and canned goods to North Korea.
Russian Post CEO Mikhail Volkov has described North Korea as an “important strategic partner.”
The full restoration of mail services with North Korea comes after Russian Post resumed mail and package deliveries to the United States this summer following a suspension after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Former Russian Coal Assets of Ukrainian Billionaire Akhmetov Change Hands
description: The former Russian coal assets of Ukrainian billionaire Rinat Akhmetov have been transferred to the Russian Industrial Company (RPK), the Kommersant newspaper reported Tuesday, citing data from the SPARK corporate database.
content:
The former Russian coal assets of Ukrainian billionaire Rinat Akhmetov have been transferred to the Russian Industrial Company (RPK), the Kommersant newspaper reported Tuesday, citing data from the SPARK corporate database.
RPK CEO Felix Nakhshunov has ties to the Roskhim industrial group, which is headed by Igor Rotenberg, the son of billionaire and longtime Putin friend Arkady Rotenberg.
Roskhim has emerged as a major beneficiary of the Kremlin’s redistribution of industrial assets since Russia invaded Ukraine, acquiring several companies that were seized by the state from their previous owners.
Secured debts and promissory notes belonging to the Obukhovskaya Mine Management Company and Donskoy Anthracite were transferred to RPK, according to Kommersant. Both companies operate in southern Russia’s Rostov region and specialize in mining and processing anthracite coal. Their combined reserves are estimated at 97.3 million metric tons.
Akhmetov acquired the businesses through his DTEK energy group for $39 million in 2012. After the start of the war in Ukraine, the assets were transferred to Russia’s state-controlled Sberbank to settle outstanding debts.
The associated claims and shares later passed to Cyprus-based Valleyton Investments. In 2024, Putin authorized their acquisition by a Russian company called Best Solution.
Best Solution’s financial statements valued the two coal producers’ promissory-note liabilities at 2.75 billion rubles ($32.7 million). Sberbank held additional claims worth about $400 million.
RPK was established in May 2026, and its ownership has not been disclosed.
Nakhshunov previously headed Radamant and RH-Resource, two limited-liability companies that were part of Roskhim. He also holds a stake in Keser, a contractor for the Roskhim-owned Berezniki Soda Plant.
His brother, Maxim Nakhshunov, has served since 2024 as executive director of Metafrax Chemicals, which is managed by Roskhim.
Roskhim said the Nakhshunov brothers’ transactions were their private business and that the group had no involvement in them. An unidentified source told Kommersant that the newly acquired assets could be prepared for resale.
The Financial Times has described the Rotenberg brothers as driving a wave of nationalizations in Russia that began after the invasion of Ukraine.
During the war, Roskhim has taken control of several industrial companies seized by the state, including Bashkir Soda Company, Kuchuksulfat, Metafrax Chemicals, Volzhsky Orgsintez and the Dalnegorsk Mining and Processing Plant.
In 2026, Roskhim also acquired a 55% stake in the Petersburg Oil Terminal and management rights over Transbunker, Russia’s largest marine-fuel supplier.

title: ‘My Case Is Unquestionably Political’: Culinary Historian Pavel Syutkin on His Prosecution
description: Opinion | Russian culinary historian Pavel Syutkin was sentenced Tuesday to six years in prison over social media posts about alleged Russian atrocities in Bucha, Ukraine, during the opening weeks of Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
content:
Russian culinary historian Pavel Syutkin was sentenced Tuesday to six years in prison over social media posts about alleged Russian atrocities in Bucha, Ukraine, during the opening weeks of Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
In an April letter translated and republished below, Syutkin, a longtime food columnist for The Moscow Times, describes the criminal case against him in his own words.
The letter was originally published here .
My case is unquestionably political. There’s not much to prove in cases like this. They are punishing me for my words and for openly opposing the war. I have never tried to hide my position. Moreover, after months in prison, I have become even more convinced that many Russians feel the same.
The investigators are outraged that I published political commentary on a channel devoted to culinary history, thereby sowing doubts about Putin’s most peaceful policy in history among an audience with no formal political training. For many years, I have answered such arguments as follows:
“The very idea that ordinary people might have opinions of their own in Russia today clearly borders on criminality. Well, all of us, cooks, doctors, scientists and drivers, are what you call the people. Under the Constitution, all power in the country belongs to them. No matter how ridiculous that may sound today.”
In any case, I am a historian, not a cook. I have the right to share my thoughts with my readers, whoever they may be. I also have the right to analyze my country’s past and present.
My cellmates have criminal case files running to 20 or even 80 volumes. Mine consists of just one. “Well, maybe we’ll split them into one and a half,” the investigator clarified. Most of it consists of two expert assessments, one psychological and one linguistic. The first is straightforward: my mental health is sound enough to send me to Mars. But the second is a rather comical document.
I should explain that my starting position is simple. I do not admit guilt of any kind. I do confirm that I wrote everything the investigators cite about Putin and his war. The logic is obvious: Russian citizens have the right to express their opinions, including publicly, on matters of public importance. The Constitution guarantees that right. There are no untouchable figures in our country. Even the president, as a public official, may be criticized, especially when there is plenty to criticize him for.
The actions taken against me by the investigators and the Federal Security Service violate Russian law as well as Russia’s international obligations. Even amid the current drive to isolate the country from the civilized world, Russia has not withdrawn from the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The covenant affirms everyone’s right to freedom of expression. It also prohibits discrimination on the grounds of political opinion. The slogan used by Soviet dissidents in the 1970s therefore suits my case perfectly: “Observe your own Constitution!”
The investigators’ main objective is to prove that Syutkin P. P., “who harbored hatred and contempt for the state structure of the Russian Federation, as well as for its domestic and foreign policies, and who is a staunch opponent of the special military operation being conducted by the Russian Armed Forces on the territory of Ukraine, formed the criminal intent to publicly disseminate knowingly false information under the guise of reliable reports.” That is a quotation from the indictment.
The investigators have therefore placed their main hopes in the expert assessment, or, as it’s called in the case, the “comprehensive psychological and linguistic study.” It was conducted by Tatyana Troitskaya, a well-known “in-house” expert in political cases. The public knows her for the numerous “expert assessments” she has produced in the trials of political prisoners.
The assessment itself reads like some kind of comedy sketch. One of my posts, featuring a collage of portraits of Putin, Stalin and Hitler, received close scrutiny from Troitskaya. The portraits, she discovered, appeared against a “blood-red background.” From this, she concluded that “the author considers Putin’s policies bloody.” How my particular shade of “blood red” differs from the red used in the Soviet and Russian flags remains a mystery. Nor does the presence of portraits of Putin and Hitler in the same image show that the author, meaning me, equates the two.
In fact, drawing historical parallels appears to have been my principal sin in the expert’s eyes. The words “Kyiv was bombed” forced an analogy with the actions of Nazi Germany. My comparison of the tragedy in Bucha with Babyn Yar prompted the expert to produce several pages of historical research intended to prove me wrong. Her main argument, however, was a statement from the Russian Defense Ministry claiming that nothing had happened in Bucha and that, if anything had happened, Ukrainian fascists had killed everyone. My cellmate later joked: “Could I bring in a letter from the housing office saying I never committed a crime? Or perhaps one from the local clinic?”
Troitskaya’s masterpiece was her conclusion about what the author might have been thinking when he wrote a post. Take my joking remark, “When we finally defeat the fascists, there may still be some food left.” According to the expert, it “referred to the final victory over Putin and his regime.” That, she emphasized, was how “the author’s opinion may be interpreted.”
Troitskaya justifies these paradoxical conclusions by stating that she “uses a working hypothesis” under which “the views expressed in the published materials effectively coincide with the author’s own views and positions.” In other words, the expert is attempting to answer the question of what the author might have been thinking when he published a particular post. Troitskaya’s method for identifying a “hidden meaning” supposedly encoded in the material, to use the words from the methodology section of her own assessment, is simply an anti-scientific invention. Naturally, it appears in none of the methods used by Russia’s leading state forensic institutions, including the Justice Ministry’s Federal Center for Forensic Examination, the Interior Ministry’s Forensic Science Center and the Investigative Committee.
One particularly absurd example of this approach concerns a post cited as evidence of my guilt: “A terrible morning for Putin today. He woke up to the news that Ukraine had won.” In her introduction, Troitskaya writes that her analysis aims to “establish the meaning of the statement based on, among other things, the context of the message.” Unfortunately, she did not even bother to establish the context of this particular post. I published it on May 15, 2023, the morning after Ukrainian performers won the Eurovision Song Contest, which was watched by millions of Russians. It had nothing whatsoever to do with discrediting Putin or his war.
Another episode in my “criminal” activity involved using the word “war” to describe current events. “We are conducting a special military operation,” the expert and the investigators insisted. This did not stop Russian propagandists from repeatedly claiming that they were carrying on the glorious legacy of their grandfathers, who defeated fascism.
At the same time, I understand perfectly well that these arguments of ours will have no effect. “Russian courts have no authority to make independent decisions in political cases,” I said at one hearing. They merely rubber-stamp the materials handed to them by the investigators and the FSB.
I am certain that we will see this in my trial.

title: MFA Repeats Warning for Foreign Embassies in Kyiv to Evacuate After Train Strike Near Poland
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday once again urged foreign embassies in Kyiv to evacuate following a Russian strike on a passenger train near the Polish border shortly after European diplomats used the same rail track.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday once again urged foreign embassies in Kyiv to evacuate following a Russian strike on a passenger train near the Polish border shortly after European diplomats used the same rail track.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the warning, first issued this spring, “remains relevant” despite occasional diplomatic requests to grant Western “political tourists” safe passage into Ukraine.
“Western politicians and diplomats should make a sober assessment of the existing risks,” Zakharova said in response to a question about Sunday’s attack on a passenger train around 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
The rail track that was attacked had been used minutes earlier by another train carrying a group including former British prime minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt.
Zakharova accused the politicians of “blatantly ignoring” the warnings of their own governments against visiting Ukraine.
She argued that Ukrainian railway stations and transportation infrastructure used for military purposes were legitimate targets and accused President Volodymyr Zelensky of treating Western visitors as “human shields.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its attacks on Sunday targeted infrastructure used to move military cargo from Europe to Ukraine.
Ukraine operates several border crossings with Poland, through which a significant proportion of the military and humanitarian aid from its Western allies is delivered to the country.

title: Culinary Historian Pavel Syutkin Sentenced to 6 Years in Prison Over Bucha Posts
description: A Moscow judge on Tuesday sentenced culinary historian and former Moscow Times columnist Pavel Syutkin to six years in prison on charges of spreading “fake news” about the Russian military.
content:
A Moscow judge on Tuesday sentenced culinary historian and former Moscow Times columnist Pavel Syutkin to six years in prison on charges of spreading “fake news” about the Russian military.
State prosecutors sought an eight-year prison sentence for Syutkin over Telegram posts about alleged atrocities committed against civilians in the Kyiv suburb of Bucha during the opening weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Russia denies committing war crimes in Bucha.
A judge at Moscow’s Zyuzinsky District Court found Syutkin guilty of spreading “false information” about the Russian Armed Forces, the court’s press service said in a statement on Telegram.
In addition to the six-year prison term, the court banned Syutkin from managing websites for four years.
Syutkin’s attorney Yevgeniya Grigoryeva told the state-run news agency TASS that the defense plans to appeal the ruling, which she said will likely be heard in the Moscow City Court.
The trial was held behind closed doors. Ahead of the verdict, Syutkin told reporters the secrecy was maintained due to an FSB witness in the case.
“But that’s just the formal pretext. I think the real reason is that the court itself feels some discomfort about handing down a sentence in this kind of political case,” Syutkin told reporters in a video shared by the Mediazona outlet.
“This verdict is honestly a certain mark of quality for the work I’ve been doing, an effort… aimed at reviving civil society in our country,” Syutkin said in another video, followed by applause from those who went to hear the verdict in court.
Syutkin was arrested last October and added to the Russian financial monitoring agency Rosfinmonitoring’s list of “terrorists and extremists,” a move that froze his bank accounts.
The Nobel Peace Prize-winning human rights organization Memorial has designated Syutkin a political prisoner.
He has published several books on the history of Russian and Soviet cuisine and hosted programs on national television and radio devoted to the history of food. In 2015, Syutkin represented Russia as an official ambassador at the World Expo in Milan.
Syutkin and his wife, Olga, wrote a weekly cooking column for The Moscow Times until Russian authorities banned the news outlet as “undesirable” in July 2024.

title: U.S. Seeks Release of Belarusian Funds as Trump Envoy Meets Lukashenko in Minsk
description: The White House is seeking the release of Belarusian funds that are frozen in U.S. banks, Trump’s special envoy to Belarus John Coale told President Alexander Lukashenko during a meeting in Minsk on Tuesday.
content:
The White House is seeking the release of Belarusian funds that are frozen in U.S. banks, Trump’s special envoy to Belarus John Coale told President Alexander Lukashenko during a meeting in Minsk on Tuesday.
Lukashenko said last week that up to $ 44 million belonging to Belarus was “stuck at Citibank” and called for its return. He claimed the funds were payment for shipments of Belarusian potash, an ingredient used in fertilizers.
“Return the money! This is a disgrace for the United States. Then we will agree on more serious things,” state media quoted Lukashenko as saying in an interview.
On Tuesday, Coale said that Citibank must release the funds and promised the Belarusian president to resolve the issue.
Lukashenko told Coale, who has visited Minsk multiple times since being appointed special envoy, that his government remains open to discussing “any issues” with the United States on the condition that “we both strictly abide by our agreements.”
Belarus has sought to have U.S. sanctions lifted since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year. The Biden administration had introduced many of the sanctions in response to the 2020 election crackdown in Belarus and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.S. has negotiated the release of hundreds of Belarusian political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief since Coale initiated talks with Minsk last year. Tuesday marked Coale’s first visit to Belarus in six months.
At the latest meeting, which Belarusian state media said lasted around three hours, Coale told Lukashenko that Trump “fully supports everything we’re doing.”
Before traveling to Belarus, the American envoy met with Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys in Vilnius and freed Nobel laureate Ales Bialiatski in Washington to discuss regional security and ongoing prisoner releases.
Rights groups estimate that more than 900 political prisoners remain behind bars in Belarus, while UN experts reported Tuesday that “systematic” human rights violations exist across the country’s entire judicial process.
“Oh, for heaven’s sake, take them,” Lukashenko told reporters last week, expressing frustration that U.S.-Belarusian talks are “stuck” on the issue of releasing political prisoners.

title: World Taekwondo Lifts Ban on Hosting Competitions in Russia
description: Taekwondo’s global governing body has decided to allow Russia to host international competitions, the Russian Taekwondo Union said Tuesday.
content:
Taekwondo’s global governing body has decided to allow Russia to host international competitions, the Russian Taekwondo Union said Tuesday.
World Taekwondo initially suspended Russian and Belarusian athletes and canceled all Russia-based events in March 2022 after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Junior and senior taekwondo athletes from both countries were allowed to return in January, even before the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its ban on their national-level Olympic committees later this summer.
World Taekwondo has not publicly confirmed the Russian federation’s announcement. Its 2026 and 2027 schedules do not list any events being held in Russia.
“This year’s calendar is already set, so we should look toward 2027,” a Russian Taekwondo Union source told the state-run TASS news agency.
Earlier this month, the International Equestrian Federation (FEI) announced it would once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia starting Oct. 5.
The FEI said it would continue to support Ukraine through a relief fund that it established in 2022 “to help address some of the urgent needs of the country’s equestrian community.”
Other international federations, including aquatics, motorsport, modern pentathlon, wrestling and gymnastics, have also eased restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes.

title: Denmark Summons Russian Ambassador After Frigate Fires Flares Toward Military Helicopter
description: Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador after accusing a Russian frigate of firing flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters on Monday, narrowly missing the aircraft.
content:
Denmark has summoned Russia's ambassador after accusing a Russian frigate of firing flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters on Monday, narrowly missing the aircraft.
The Fennec military helicopter was on a routine mission to photograph the Russian frigate, Danish military officials said in a statement late Monday. One of the flares — pyrotechnics usually used as a warning signal at sea — passed close to the helicopter.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was serious but not surprising, describing it as part of a pattern in which Russia has intensified its so-called hybrid campaign against the European Union and NATO.
" Russia wants to sow fear and discord. Our answer is to stand closer together and strengthen the defense of Denmark and Europe," Frederiksen said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called the incident "unacceptable" and said it could have endangered people's lives.
"Denmark is working to ensure that all shipping can pass peacefully through Danish waters, but Russia is gradually moving the line for what it considers acceptable behavior," Rasmussen said in a statement.
He said he had summoned Russia 's ambassador to Denmark for a meeting.
The Russia n Embassy in Copenhagen did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out of the Baltic Sea for commercial and military shipping. They are also a major artery for global oil shipments, including from Russia 's so-called "shadow fleet" of oil tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

title: Ukrainian Attack Kills One in Belgorod, Hits Commercial and Industrial Sites Across Russia
description: Overnight Ukrainian drone and missile strikes across southern Russia killed one person and struck commercial and industrial sites, regional officials said Tuesday.
content:
Overnight Ukrainian drone and missile strikes across southern Russia killed one person and struck commercial and industrial sites , regional officials said Tuesday.
Acting Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev confirmed one death in an attack near the border with Ukraine. He also said that a woman who was hospitalized for her injuries following strikes earlier this month had died.
In the nearby Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar said an Ozon warehouse was among several sites damaged during a missile attack on the port city of Taganrog.
Ozon confirmed that it suspended operations at the facility, where it said a fire broke out. No one was hurt, the company said.
Federal investigators launched a criminal probe into terrorism over the attacks on Taganrog, citing damage to Ozon and other residential and agricultural buildings.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said an “industrial facility” was damaged in overnight strikes. Unconfirmed reports said that a fire broke out at the Syzran Oil Refinery.
NASA’s fire monitoring service FIRMS showed an active fire Tuesday morning on the southwestern outskirts of Syzran, where the refinery, which has been attacked multiple times this year, is located.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
In Ukraine, officials said one person was killed in Russia n attacks on Kyiv. Separate attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia also killed one person.
Two gas stations in Kyiv were damaged in the overnight strikes , the state energy company Naftogaz said.
The attacks targeting energy infrastructure in both Russia and Ukraine came despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump earlier in the week that the two warring sides allegedly agreed to pause such attacks.
Trump has sought to blame the surging cost of diesel in the United States on Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries. While those attacks have put pressure on fuel prices both inside Russia and globally, so too has the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran led to major disruptions in energy markets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday that Trump ’ s suggestion for a ceasefire on energy sites, which has been repeatedly floated over the past year, was a “ very good idea ” but alone would not bring down global fuel costs.

title: Ukraine Wants Specifics From Partners on Halting Strikes, Zelensky Says
description: Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russia if its partners ensure that Moscow will refrain from hitting Ukrainian energy facilities, infrastructure and food supply routes, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday.
content:
Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russia if its partners ensure that Moscow will refrain from hitting Ukrainian energy facilities, infrastructure and food supply routes, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday.
Zelensky's comments, posted on Telegram, appeared to amount to a denial that Ukraine had formally endorsed U.S. President Donald Trump's statement that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
Zelensky said Ukraine was not convinced that Russia was willing to abide by any agreement.
"Ukraine is not certain that Russia is willing to stick to any agreement," he wrote. "The war must be brought to an end. And a de-escalatory step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step toward peace. We expect specifics from our partners."
Ukraine was willing to sign on to an agreement to refrain from strikes on infrastructure, he said, but any such accord had to be "reliable, long-term, and actually have a real impact on people's lives."
In his statement, Trump said the two sides had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" he wrote.

title: Russian Convoy Resupplies Syrian Coastal Facilities for First Time Since Moscow-Damascus Deal
description: A convoy of Russian naval and cargo vessels delivered supplies last week to Syrian coastal facilities long used by Moscow’s military, two sources familiar with the operation said, in the first such mission since Damascus and Moscow agreed last month on the future of Russia’s military presence in the country.
content:
A convoy of Russian naval and cargo vessels delivered supplies last week to Syrian coastal facilities long used by Moscow’s military, two sources familiar with the operation said, in the first such mission since Damascus and Moscow agreed last month on the future of Russia’s military presence in the country.
The operation offers an early indication that Moscow is continuing to resupply facilities at Tartus port and the Khmeimim airbase under the new deal, which provides for civilian facilities used by Russia to be transferred to Syrian control and military sites to be turned into joint training centers.
Russian forces are to remain at the bases under the agreement. Russia has used Khmeimim and Tartus to project power across the Mediterranean, Middle East and Africa. Tartus provides Moscow with its only naval repair and replenishment facility in the Mediterranean.
Moscow has supplied both sites in recent months but last week's was the first since the Aug. 9 agreement was announced.
The four-vessel convoy arrived at the Mediterranean port of Tartus on Sept. 7, according to movements tracked by Reuters and maritime intelligence firm SynMax.
Satellite imagery verified by Reuters showed the Russian Ro-Ro cargo ship Sparta and navy replenishment oiler Akademik Pashin docked on Sept. 8 in Tartus at piers 3 and 4, respectively.
A Reuters reporter saw the two vessels docked there on Sept. 9, while Russian tanker General Skobelev remained offshore. A surveillance balloon was seen flying over the port during the unloading operation.
A Syrian military source and a Russian-Syrian businessman familiar with the operation said Sparta unloaded supplies including ammunition destined for Khmeimim and Tartus. Reuters could not independently confirm the contents of the shipment or their intended recipients.
SynMax identified the fourth vessel in the convoy as Admiral Levchenko, a Russian Udaloy-class destroyer.
Syria’s General Authority of Ports and Customs and Russia's embassy in Damascus did not respond to requests for comment.
The vessels stopped transmitting their signal shortly after crossing Strait of Gibraltar towards the Mediterranean. Reuters tracked the group via satellite imagery as it continued east and ultimately reached the Syrian coast.
Sparta has long been used in Russian military logistics in Syria and is under U.S. sanctions. General Skobelev is also under Western sanctions over transporting Russian oil.
Damascus and Moscow reached the agreement over Khmeimim and Tartus after 18 months of negotiations following the December 2024 overthrow of former President Bashar al-Assad, a close Russian ally.

title: Russia’s Opposition Wants You to Vote Against United Russia. That’s Where Its Strategy Ends.
description: Opinion | Russia’s parliamentary elections are days away, and the opposition has finally settled on its voting tactics.
content:
Russia’s parliamentary elections are days away, and the opposition has finally settled on its voting tactics. Yulia Navalnaya and Maxim Katz have agreed to endorse a joint slate of candidates in single-seat constituencies. For the party-list vote, they are urging Russians to back any Kremlin-approved party with a chance of clearing the 5% threshold, so long as it isn’t United Russia.
Ilya Yashin is calling on people to go to the polls at noon on Sept. 20 and vote against United Russia too. The liberal Yabloko party, whose federal list was thrown out , wants voters to spoil their party-list ballots and support its remaining single-district candidates. The Anti-War Committee has left the choice to voters, urging them to judge candidates above all by where they stand on the war.
According to the logic of protest voting, United Russia stands for Putin’s policies, and so every vote withheld from it makes it clearer that support for said policies is collapsing. A poor result would also expose the Kremlin’s weakness to the public and to the elites inside the system. Governors, officials, lawmakers from other parties and business elites would see that the center of power can no longer deliver the numbers it used to. They would start acting on their own and bargaining more aggressively. The belief that the regime is unshakeable would start to crack.
Authoritarian regimes really do rest on their own people believing the center is strong, so this could theoretically work. The trouble is that the weakness has to become common knowledge first. If United Russia actually gets 38% of the vote but is awarded 58% by election officials, how does the public find out about the 38%? How do regional elites, senior officials or the heads of the approved opposition parties find out? You need a parallel count, a vast network of observers, polling-station records collected and verified, a way to penetrate the black box of electronic voting and the means to spread an alternative result across the country. In today's Russia, that work has become virtually impossible.
Nor will the Kremlin-approved parties supply this missing knowledge. Even if the Communists, the LDPR or New People get more votes than the official count records, their leaders will be thinking about their own position inside the system — seats, committee posts, financing, relations with the presidential administration and access to regional power. Picking a fight with the Kremlin is far more costly than a few lost percentage points. The authorities don’t even need to transfer votes from one party to another. They just need everyone to accept the official result and refrain from challenging it.
Then comes the problem of interpreting the results. While the opposition calls a vote for the Communists or New People a “vote against Putin,” those parties’ leaders call it support for their own platform. The Kremlin will count it as a vote for the loyal parties that accept the existing order. If Navalnaya’s and Katz’s supporters follow their call and vote for New People, the official statistics will record those votes as support for New People. The party will gain seats, funding and political weight, while the organizers of the protest vote are left arguing that some share of those votes was really theirs.
That raises the main question: What happens on Sept. 21?
Suppose millions really do vote against United Russia, and its real result comes in far below what the Kremlin needs. How will the public learn this if the Central Election Commission announces something else?
Even if the fraud can be proved, what then? Will the opposition call on people to defend their votes? If so, how? What is a voter supposed to do when it turns out that his vote, along with millions of others, has vanished from the official count? Will there be concrete demands and organized protests? Or will it end with statements denouncing falsification and a few YouTube streams?
The Navalnaya-Katz appeal puts it plainly: We’ll do our part, drop in the ballots the authorities don’t want and then see what they do. The organizers themselves don’t know what comes next. Maybe the public suddenly recognizes that the authorities represent no one, or maybe it doesn’t.
For a campaign run by political consultants, this structure makes sense. There’s a task, a date, an audience, a set of tools and a measurable result. The campaign ends, the team conducts a postmortem and eventually moves on to the next project.
But politics is much more far-reaching and continuous than that; one action ends and sets up the next. Success opens new possibilities, while failure forces you to look at your mistakes and change course. Tasks change, and so do the tactics, resources and ways of working with people. A political leader has to know what he or she will do under each likely outcome. United Russia unexpectedly underperforms — what then? The results are rewritten wholesale — what then? A few opposition-endorsed candidates make it into the State Duma — what then? The whole thing flops — what does that teach you, and how does your strategy change?
The Russian opposition’s love of elections points to a deeper problem in how it thinks about politics. Elections are treated as the central democratic ritual, so a democratic opposition apparently has to make them its priority no matter what. The result is a kind of cargo cult . The procedure is formally there, but its political content is long gone. The authorities set the date, write the rules, admit some candidates and bar others, control the information space and announce the final number. The opposition pours enormous effort into finding the best way to operate within boundaries built by someone else. The Kremlin acts, the opposition reacts. The initiative is always on the Kremlin’s side.
Tied to this is the idea of “safe” protest by Russians inside Russia. The opposition understandably wants to limit the risks for people living under repression. But political action is only safe for as long as the authorities are willing to put up with it. As soon as a protest becomes genuinely visible and genuinely threatening, the risk to the protesters goes up. Making safety the main criterion confines the struggle to the forms the regime finds most convenient.
The opposition tailors its proposals to whatever its audience already feels ready to do. It offers people a simple, one-off and safe act that requires almost no commitment. You can see the environment at work here. Opposition leaders have become media personalities living in a world of views, subscribers, likes, reposts and donations. Successful bloggers only have to understand what their audiences like and what they will watch. Political leaders have to be able to argue with their audiences, change their minds, make demands of them and raise their capacity for responsibility and collective action. When a politician starts living by the rules of the media, politics itself becomes another convenient product: clear, safe, emotionally appealing and undemanding.
The reaction to the Navalnaya-Katz alliance shows the other side of this. Two well-known figures recorded a video together, and thousands of viewers immediately felt hope rekindled: At last they've agreed, now something will happen. Politics is treated like a service again. We sit in front of a screen, and the good politicians are supposed to work things out, come up with the right plan and tell us where to go and which button to press. The individual remains a spectator, even when he sincerely believes he’s participating. But a mass audience alone does not a political force make.
For much of that audience, opposition unity is when several well-known talking heads have put their public feuding on hold to record a joint video and agree on a shared appeal. However, genuine political unity means a mass organization with membership, local branches, internal procedures, feedback, a division of duties, elections and rotation of leadership, as well as a path for ordinary members to take on more responsibility and move up. That kind of structure turns millions of scattered supporters into a political actor that can exist without the latest video, the latest campaign or the decisions of a few media personalities. As long as unity means coordination among popular bloggers, it’s merely unity at the top with nothing underneath.
The Russian opposition’s main problem is not that it recommends the wrong box on the ballot. The problem starts when election campaigns are self-contained episodes with nothing accumulating in between them. A million people came to the polls — what connects that million the next day? Discontent turned out to be bigger than expected — which organization captures that energy and turns it into the next action?
The real measure of these elections will be whether protest politics emerges from them larger, more organized and more politically significant than before. If nothing changes politically, in Russia or in exile, the argument over which box to check on the ballot will stay as relevant as the medieval dispute over how many angels can fit on the head of a pin.

title: Kremlin-Linked Businessman Helped Pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s Wedding – ProPublica
description: Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin, helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year, ProPublica reported Monday, citing financial records and three sources familiar with the matter.
content:
Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin, helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year, ProPublica reported Monday, citing financial records and three sources familiar with the matter.
The payments included around $100,000 to rent a private island and $70,000 for a fireworks display on the first day of the three-day wedding of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s son, according to the report.
The funds were paid through IB Challenger, a Dubai-based firm used by Kremlev to run operations for the International Boxing Association (IBA), which he heads, after moving them from Switzerland following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The IBA told ProPublica it incurred no wedding expenses itself, while declining to comment on IB Challenger’s payments.
Kremlev is under Ukrainian sanctions due to his ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin through Alexei Rubezhny, head of the Kremlin leader’s personal security service.
National security experts told ProPublica that a member of Putin’s circle gaining intimate access to Trump’s family by financially backing his son’s wedding raises serious concerns.
“If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something,” said Frank Montoya Jr., a retired career FBI official who held senior counterintelligence roles.
“This should be unthinkable for the son of the president. End of story,” Montoya Jr. added.
Kremlev’s press office said the he met Trump Jr. “a couple of years ago” and the two men have since maintained a “friendly relationship.”
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. also described Kremlev as his “personal friend” who he had met through a mutual friend in the hunting world. He did not dispute Kremlev’s wedding payments.

title: Rublev’s ‘Trinity’ Icon Removed From Display After Climate Control Failure – RBC
description: Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century masterpiece “Trinity,” one of Russia’s most sacred icons, has been removed from public view following a climate control failure at the Trinity Lavra of St.
content:
Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century masterpiece “Trinity,” one of Russia’s most sacred icons, has been removed from public view following a climate control failure at the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius outside Moscow, the news outlet RBC reported Monday, citing a source in the Russian Orthodox Church and an art conservator.
President Vladimir Putin ordered the icon to be transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church in 2023, defying warnings from art experts at the Tretyakov Gallery — where it had been housed since 1929 — who cautioned that relocating the fragile relic could cause irreversible damage.
The Church confirmed on Sunday that the icon was taken out of its specialized climate-controlled display case into a Tretyakov-compliant inspection room on the monastery grounds for a “routine inspection” of its condition.
“The icon will continue to be studied and treated in the Lavra’s restoration workshops, while the display case is being repaired,” art historian Ksenia Korobeynikova wrote on Telegram.
The exiled news outlet Echo, citing an anonymous source, reported Saturday that the sealed protective glass case housing the “Trinity” broke some time ago, leaving internal humidity levels at around 80%, which is above the safe range of 50-55%.
A specialized technician flown in from Germany reportedly repaired the case, but the unit failed again shortly after their departure.
Museum experts have said that the high humidity causes the antique wood that the “Trinity” was painted on to swell and warp.
“The icon is curling up into a tube,” Echo quoted its source as saying.
