title: Former Rosnano Executive Jailed 9 Years for Embezzlement
description: A judge in Moscow has sentenced Andrei Kushanryov, a former senior executive at the state nanotechnology corporation Rosnano, to nine years in prison after finding him guilty of embezzling billions of rubles meant for the development of a high-tech memory chip.
content:
A judge in Moscow has sentenced Andrei Kushanryov, a former senior executive at the state nanotechnology corporation Rosnano, to nine years in prison after finding him guilty of embezzling billions of rubles meant for the development of a high-tech memory chip.
State prosecutors had accused Kushnaryov of conspiring with former Rosnano deputy board chairman Yury Udaltsov and others to misappropriate public funds between 2013 and 2021, when he served as investment managing director at the state corporation and CEO of its subsidiary Crocus Nanoeletronics.
Udaltsov reportedly fled from Russia to Germany in 2015 and remains wanted.
Prosecutors said the funds were allocated to launch Russian production of MRAM chips in partnership with France’s Crocus Technology. Investigators had alleged that more than 7.5 billion rubles ($89.2 million) went missing from a total budget of nearly 12 billion rubles.
“Kushnaryov and the others never intended to develop new nanotechnology projects and knew full well that the project would never actually be carried out,” Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said in a statement.
Kushnaryov, who pleaded not guilty , was ordered to pay a fine of 76 million rubles ($904,000) and barred from holding senior corporate roles for two and a half years.
A judge at the Gagarinsky District Court also granted Rosnano’s lawsuit against Kushnaryov for 7.5 billion rubles in damages.
The ruling is the latest in a legal crackdown against former executives of Rosnano, which former Kremlin adviser and veteran reformer Anatoly Chubais headed for over a decade.

title: Regions Calling: Russia’s Indigenous Activists Assemble in Berlin
description: Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
content:
Hello and welcome to Regions Calling , your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
MT’s special correspondent Leyla Latypova traveled to Berlin last week for the Indigenous Vision forum, which brought together some of the leading Indigenous voices from Russia and allies from the U.S., Europe, Central Asia and Oceania.
For this week’s edition, Latypova spoke with conference organizers and attendees to understand where Russia’s Indigenous rights movement sits on the global political stage.
BERLIN — Dozens of Indigenous activists from Russia and allies from around the world gathered in Germany’s capital last week for the second annual Indigenous Vision Forum.
Organized by a consortium of NGOs led by exiled and diaspora activists from Russia’s ethnic republics and Indigenous communities, the first forum was held in July 2025 under an umbrella theme of “centering Indigenous voices, resilience and knowledge.”
This year’s topic, “navigating the future,” reflects the transformation that Russia’s Indigenous opposition has undergone since 2022. What began as a grassroots movement united by anti-war sentiment at the start of the invasion of Ukraine has since evolved into a political force aiming to shape global discourse and policies on Russia.
“This was a natural transformation,” said Sargylana Kondakova of the Free Yakutia Foundation, an exiled anti-war group from the republic of Sakha that co-organized the event.
“We understand that if we won’t speak on the international stage, if we won’t enlist the support of our allies, then everything could end very tragically for our peoples,” she added.
Kondakova, who rose to prominence in 2022 with a video condemning the invasion of Ukraine that she filmed on the streets of Melbourne, is reluctant to call herself a politician. Yet she said she realizes that everything Indigenous campaigners from Russia do is political.
“Our future also depends on who we are negotiating with, where we speak, what we say and how we say it,” she said.
Since last year’s forum, Indigenous activists from Russia have appeared at the UN, the OSCE and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), where they gained five out of 15 seats in the body’s Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces.
In a likely nod to these achievements, the forum’s inaugural panel tried to locate where the West stands on the discourse surrounding the decolonization of Russia.
Mariia Mezentseva-Fedorenko, a Ukrainian MP and chairwoman of Kyiv’s delegation to PACE, kicked off the event with a speech highlighting Ukraine’s efforts to codify the notions of “decolonization” and “oppressed nations” of Russia in international law.
Mezentseva-Fedorenko — who spoke via videoconference from Kharkiv, where air raid sirens wailed as she spoke — is among a growing number of Ukrainian foreign policy figures who believe Russia’s Indigenous communities could hold the key to ensuring Europe’s long-term political security.
“I'm here out of solidarity, both personal and Ukrainian,” said Tetiana Katrych from the Ukrainian NGO Decolonization. “The same empire colonized us…We are just at different stages of leaving it.”
Katrych believes that a Ukrainian victory in the war can’t guarantee that Russia won’t attack its neighbor again, meaning “stable peace for both Ukraine and Europe can be achieved only when the empire ceases to exist in its current form.”
“We want to cooperate with the republics and Indigenous peoples to ensure stable peace,” said Katrych.
Events in Germany, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party won a historic victory in Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt state election, hung over nearly every discussion at the forum.
Activists warned that the global rise of the far-right risks pushing the fight for Indigenous rights to the margins of international policymaking and further threatens vulnerable groups who fled Russia for the West but remained outspoken about their causes in exile.
Indigenous activists said they are also forced to face off with mainstream Russian opposition movements and politicians, who they accuse of trying to “co-opt and hijack the decolonial agenda.”
“Seeking policy change and publicity for Indigenous people [of Russia] on international platforms is about Indigenous people currently inside the country. This is a foundation for the future, although the results of these efforts will not be immediately noticeable,” said Seseg Jigjitova of Nomads Indigenous Collective, a German NGO that co-organized the forum.
Jigjitova said every discussion at the forum — whether about Indigenous political prisoners in Russia or the revitalization of the Indigenous Māori language in New Zealand — “appealed to all Indigenous peoples, including those inside Russia.”
As Russia is home to more than 180 ethnic groups, the country’s Indigenous rights movement likewise boasts a rich ethnic and political diversity.
While some prominent figures belong to nations numbering fewer than 2,000 people, others number in the millions and have ethnic homelands in Russia’s republics that were once nearly equal players in the federation or attempted to secede from it altogether.
As well as its diversity, the Indigenous rights movement’s growing visibility since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has also exposed its divisions.
The sources of these divisions range from left-right political lines to differing understandings of who should be considered Indigenous in Russia to varying degrees of support for economic and political independence of the republics to backing cooperation with mainstream opposition groups .
The Berlin forum further shed light on these cracks, with a handful of high-profile Indigenous figures notably absent. Kondakova said this was because organizers were limited to about 100 attendees.
“We couldn’t even invite some of our allies,” said Kondakova.
“There are [Indigenous] organizations whose political views we don’t share and have debates or even conflicts with them, but that’s normal. We still have contact, we talk, we don’t label anyone as enemies and don’t ban them from our platforms],” Kondakova told The Moscow Times. “That’s already a good thing, since we are striving to build democracy [in Russia].”
Forum co-organizer Batlay Matenov, a member of the PACE Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces, saw it somewhat differently.
He said he “actually did send out invitations” to his fellow PACE Platform members, none of whom were present at the event.
“Some people didn't reply, and there were others I decided not to invite,” he said.
Matenov, the only Indigenous activist at the event who currently holds public office, described his time on the PACE Platform as “tough” and “difficult.”
“If a politician promises you something, you 100% won’t see it followed through, or maybe you will, but in three years or something like that,” he said. “I actually became a little disillusioned with politics.”

title: Russian Orthodox Church Sends Bones of Medieval Warrior Prince to Ukraine Front to Boost Troop Morale
description: Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russian Orthodox Church's latest show of support for the war.
content:
Bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russia n prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols have been sent to the front in Ukraine to raise army morale in the Russia n Orthodox Church's latest show of support for the war.
The sarcophagus of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389 and is revered by Russia n nationalists for defeating the Mongol Golden Horde at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was uncovered this summer during restoration work at Moscow's Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin.
Putin personally inspected what experts said were the prince's well-preserved remains in August, hailing them as "an absolutely unique and marvellous discovery" that reinforced the foundations of Russia n history.
The Russia n Orthodox Church, which has backed Putin throughout the conflict, said it had dispatched a fragment of Donskoy's right hand to Donetsk, one of four Ukrainian regions Russia claims to have annexed in 2022.
Referring to Donskoy as "the holy commander," the Moscow Patriarchate of the Russia n Orthodox Church said part of his remains had been sent to the front to stand invisibly shoulder-to-shoulder with Russia n troops.
"A fragment of the Grand Prince's right hand — the very same right hand with which he wielded his sword on Kulikovo Field — has been sent to the front to strengthen the soldiers' spirits," it said in a statement.
The relic, held in a small ornate casket beneath toughened glass, will be shown to Russia n combat units along the front line, it said.
Donskoy, whose name was given to a Soviet tank column funded by the church in World War II, was declared a saint by the Russia n Orthodox Church in 1988.

title: Rosneft’s Ryazan Oil Refinery Shuts Down After Drone Attack, Industry Sources Say
description: The Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery has been forced to suspend operations following a Ukrainian drone strike on the facility last weekend, two industry sources told Reuters on Thursday.
content:
The Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery has been forced to suspend operations following a Ukrainian drone strike on the facility last weekend, two industry sources told Reuters on Thursday.
The sources said the oil refinery's main unit, CDU-6, as well as another primary unit, CDU-4, were shut down after the attack.
CDU-6, which caught fire in the attack, can process 8 million metric tons of oil per year, or around 160,000 barrels per day, the sources said, accounting for almost half of the plant's capacity. CDU-4 can process 4 million tons of oil per year.
Another primary unit, CDU-3, has been under maintenance since mid-May.
The sources said repairs to the damaged units could take up to several weeks.
The Ryazan oil refinery, which supplies Moscow with fuel, was also attacked by drones in May and July. Following the July attack, the facility suspended operations for around two or three weeks, the industry sources said.
Ukraine began ramping up its attacks against Russian oil refineries and supply lines this spring in a bid to deprive the Kremlin of windfalls from surging oil prices. Drone strikes have halted or scaled back production at facilities that account for large shares of Russia's gasoline output.

title: Moscow Outlines Major Suburban Metro Expansion Project by 2035
description: Authorities in Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region have unveiled major plans to extend the Russian capital’s metro network deep into its outer suburbs over the next decade.
content:
Authorities in Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region have unveiled major plans to extend the Russian capital’s metro network deep into its outer suburbs over the next decade.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announced Wednesday that around 30 new metro stations will open in the next five years, followed by an additional 35 stations by 2035 — twelve of which will be built in the Moscow region.
“The quality of life will improve for 2 million Moscow residents and 3.7 million residents of the Moscow region,” Sobyanin said, noting that the Moscow metropolitan area is home to roughly 20 million people.
On Telegram, Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov published a video showing the scale of the planned expansion into the suburban districts of Krasnogorsk, Khimki, Mytishchi, Balashikha, Odintsovo and Leninsky.
Those metro stations will serve approximately 600,000 daily commuters, Vorobyov said, cutting travel times into central Moscow by up to an hour. The governor said construction of the new lines is expected to begin after 2028.
The transit expansion marks the latest phase in the rapid development of Moscow’s metro system under Sobyanin, who has served as mayor for nearly 16 years.

title: Voronezh Woman Killed and Caspian Seaport Hit in Ukrainian Drone Strikes
description: A Ukrainian drone attack in the southern Voronezh region killed a woman, local authorities said, as other strikes across the country damaged infrastructure and wounded dozens of people.
content:
A Ukrainian drone attack in the southern Voronezh region killed a woman, local authorities said, as other strikes across the country damaged infrastructure and wounded dozens of people.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said a woman identified only as having been born in 1983 was killed when a drone crashed into a house in the town of Borisoglebsk. Two others were injured, he said.
In a separate seaborne drone attack on the Black Sea city of Sochi, 28 people were injured , emergency officials said.
Further to the east, in the North Caucasus republic of Dagestan, acting regional head Fyodor Shchukin said Ukrainian strikes sparked fires at a seaport and a theater in the capital city of Makhachkala. He said both fires were quickly put out.
Unverified reports said the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port, Russia’s only deep-water port on the Caspian Sea, was hit in the attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed his military struck a seaport in Dagestan. He said several sites were also hit in the Moscow, Astrakhan, Bryansk and Voronezh regions.
Meanwhile, in the southwestern Belgorod region, authorities said Ukrainian strikes over the past 24 hours had killed a man and wounded 13 others.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 448 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.

title: FSB Arrests Former British Embassy Guard Accused of Gathering Intel for Ukraine
description: Russia’s FSB security service said Thursday that it arrested a former guard at the British Embassy in Moscow for allegedly gathering sensitive information on British diplomats on behalf of Ukraine.
content:
Russia’s FSB security service said Thursday that it arrested a former guard at the British Embassy in Moscow for allegedly gathering sensitive information on British diplomats on behalf of Ukraine.
The agency alleged that Ukrainian intelligence services planned to use the information to carry out a false-flag attack targeting British diplomatic personnel.
According to the FSB, Ukraine intended to frame Russia for the operation to “draw the United Kingdom into a direct military conflict with Russia” and secure increased military aid from London.
Russian authorities said the former guard, who has not been named, collected sensitive data, including diplomats’ personal details, photos, home addresses, vehicles used, itineraries, security systems and internal embassy schedules.
The FSB said the former guard was placed in pre-trial detention and faces treason charges, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison for men. The maximum sentence for women is 20 years in prison.
A spokesperson for the British embassy told The Moscow Times that the mission does not comment on “security matters.”
“It is common that Russian state actors seek to drive wedges between Ukraine and its international partners through disinformation,” the spokesperson said.
Russia’s FSB has regularly announced the arrests of people accused of working on behalf of Ukraine since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Individuals facing these accusations are often charged with treason.

title: Moscow Region Imposes Quarantine Near Over Lumpy Skin Disease in Cattle
description: Authorities in the Moscow region have introduced a quarantine after lumpy skin disease was detected in cattle in several towns and villages about 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Moscow, according to a document on the regional government's website on Wednesday.
content:
Authorities in the Moscow region have introduced a quarantine after lumpy skin disease was detected in cattle in several towns and villages about 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Moscow, according to a document on the regional government's website on Wednesday.
Lumpy skin disease is a viral infection mainly spread by biting insects that affects cattle. It causes fever and painful skin lumps, weakens animals and reduces milk output. The disease does not infect humans.
The disease, which is widespread in North Africa, was detected in several European countries last year. Authorities in France ordered infected cows culled, sparking protests from farm unions.
The Moscow regional government's order banned the transport of cattle, cattle products, including milk, and feed to and from the quarantined area. It also banned agricultural fairs there.
Earlier this week, authorities in the Irkutsk region near Lake Baikal in Siberia imposed a lumpy skin disease quarantine in two settlements and said infected animals would have to be culled.
An outbreak of cattle diseases officially identified as pasteurellosis or rabies in Siberia in spring led to the mass culling of livestock and sparked rare protests by local farmers.

title: Drones Hit Russia's Gas Hinterland in Northern Siberia for the First Time
description: An industrial facility caught fire in Novy Urengoy, a gas-producing city in northern Russia, following a drone attack, regional Governor Dmitry Artyukhov said on Wednesday, in the first such attack on the country's natural gas hinterland.
content:
An industrial facility caught fire in Novy Urengoy, a gas-producing city in northern Russia, following a drone attack, regional Governor Dmitry Artyukhov said on Wednesday, in the first such attack on the country's natural gas hinterland.
Artyukhov did not identify the facility involved.
"Most importantly, there were no fatalities or injuries. The extent and nature of the damage are being determined," he said on the Telegram messaging app.
State-run energy company Gazprom did not reply to a request for comment about the attack on the region, some 3,000 kilometers (1,800 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Novy Urengoy is Russia's unofficial gas capital, located in the Yamal-Nenets autonomous district in northwestern Siberia.
Gazprom used to export gas from Yamal as far as western Europe until the ties broke down following the start of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022.
It estimated the region's gas resources at 26.5 trillion cubic meters as of 2020, enough to cover global demand for more than six years.

title: Russia and Vietnam Sign Strategic Oil Reserve Deal
description: Russia and Vietnam signed a framework agreement Wednesday to cooperate on establishing a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam, as the two countries moved to deepen energy ties during President To Lam’s visit to Moscow.
content:
Russia and Vietnam signed a framework agreement Wednesday to cooperate on establishing a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam, as the two countries moved to deepen energy ties during President To Lam’s visit to Moscow.
Following talks with To Lam, President Vladimir Putin also said Russia was working to introduce visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens “in the near future,” though he gave no timetable.
Vietnam’s Deputy Foreign Minister Le Thi Thu Hang previously said Hanoi expected a “breakthrough” in Russian-Vietnamese oil, gas and nuclear power cooperation.
To Lam, who last visited Moscow in May 2025 to attend the Victory Day parade on Red Square and sign a strategic partnership agreement with Russia, held a joint press briefing with Putin after talks between Vietnamese and Russian officials.
In addition, Putin and To Lam presided over the formal launch of a joint infectious disease research laboratory via video link.
During his three-day state visit to Moscow, which began Monday, To Lam has so far met with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev and upper-house Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matvienko.
To Lam also met with Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, Russian war veterans and members of the Vietnamese diaspora at the embassy in Moscow, where he emphasized Vietnam’s transition toward diversified international integration.
Russia remains Vietnam’s top arms supplier and is involved in nuclear power and South China Sea gas projects, including in waters also claimed by China, though Hanoi has been diversifying its military sourcing.

title: Prosecutors Seek 8-Year Prison Sentence for Culinary Historian Pavel Syutkin
description: State prosecutors in Moscow have asked a judge to sentence culinary historian and former columnist for The Moscow Times, Pavel Syutkin, to eight years in prison for spreading “false information” about the Russian military, the civil rights group For Human Rights said Wednesday.
content:
State prosecutors in Moscow have asked a judge to sentence culinary historian and former columnist for The Moscow Times, Pavel Syutkin, to eight years in prison for spreading “false information” about the Russian military, the civil rights group For Human Rights said Wednesday.
Syutkin was arrested last October over Telegram posts about alleged atrocities committed against civilians in the Kyiv suburb of Bucha during the opening weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Russia continues to deny committing war crimes in Bucha, alleging the visual evidence was staged by Ukraine. That claim has been repeatedly debunked by independent fact-checking organizations.
Closing arguments in Syutkin’s trial were heard behind closed doors at the Zyuzinsky District Court, according to exiled news outlet Mediazona. A verdict is expected next Tuesday.
Syutkin maintains his innocence. “My case is clearly political,” he wrote in April. “There’s really nothing to prove in cases like this. You get punished for what you say and for openly opposing the war.”
Syutkin has published several books on the history of Russian and Soviet cuisine and hosted programs on national television and radio devoted to the history of food. In 2015, Syutkin represented Russia as an official ambassador at the World Expo in Milan.
Syutkin and his wife wrote a weekly cooking column for The Moscow Times until Russian authorities banned the news outlet as “undesirable” in July 2024.

title: Leader of Yabloko’s Sverdlovsk Region Branch Left Russia, Reports Say
description: The head of the Sverdlovsk regional chapter of the liberal Yabloko party has left Russia amid a growing number of arrests of other party members, local media reported Wednesday, just weeks before parliamentary elections are scheduled to be held.
content:
The head of the Sverdlovsk regional chapter of the liberal Yabloko party has left Russia amid a growing number of arrests of other party members , local media reported Wednesday, just weeks before parliamentary elections are scheduled to be held.
Regional party chairman Maxim Petlin has not been seen in the capital city Yekaterinburg for “several months,” anonymous sources told the news outlet 66.ru. It was not immediately clear when he left Russia or where he is currently located.
Petlin later told the newspaper Kommersant that his lawyer advised him not to comment on reports of his departure “for the safety of my family and myself.”
In June, the politician withdrew his candidacy in this month’s State Duma elections due to reported pressure from law enforcement authorities, including short-term detentions and police searches at his home.
Yabloko is Russia’s oldest liberal party and is the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform. Several of its candidates have been disqualified from running in next week’s elections over various violations.
On Monday, Sverdlovsk region police arrested at least six Yabloko members running for federal or regional office in connection with public displays of “extremist” symbols. The charges disqualify them from the upcoming elections.
Yabloko’s Sverdlovsk regional chapter said Wednesday that Petlin was in communication with one of its arrested members.
Candidates of the party campaigning in single-member districts are still allowed to run for office after Russia’s Supreme Court last month ruled to cancel the registration of Yabloko’s federal slate of candidates for the State Duma.

title: Russians Aboard Ship Seized by Norway Have Returned Home, Foreign Ministry Says
description: A group of Russians who were on board a ship seized by Norway last week have returned home, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday, as it accused authorities in Oslo of trying to push Russia out of the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
content:
A group of Russians who were on board a ship seized by Norway last week have returned home , Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday, as it accused authorities in Oslo of trying to push Russia out of the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
The 69 Russian passengers and crew members were stuck for several days after a Norwegian court on Wednesday ordered the seizure of the Professor Molchanov, which operates as a cruise ship, at the request of the Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz.
Norwegian authorities said Tuesday that they had helped the group of Russians return home. Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova credited Oslo’s “logistical support” in their return, as well as the help of Russian diplomats.
“As far as we know, practically everyone has already returned home,” Zakharova said.
But the legal and diplomatic standoff over the seized vessel is “far from being resolved,” she warned, adding that Russia plans to appeal the arrest of the Professor Molchanov.
Russia argues that holding the ship violates the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which allows equal economic access to the archipelago while giving Norway sovereignty over the territory.
Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland. The Svalbard Treaty also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia, to settle there without a visa.
“We’re convinced that the Norwegian authorities’ actions belie the desire to complicate as much as possible the activities of Russian operators on Svalbard… and gradually move toward reducing Russia’s presence on the archipelago,” Zakharova said.
The Professor Molchanov is being held in the town of Barentsburg, a Russian-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago.
Barentsburg is one of two Russian settlements in the Svalbard archipelago, which together have a population of 392, according to the Norwegian government.
The court-ordered vessel seizure was made on behalf of Naftogaz, which is seeking to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation award for assets Russia took when it annexed Crimea in 2014.

title: EU Court Rejects Abramovich’s Latest Challenge to Sanctions
description: The European Union’s General Court on Wednesday rejected Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s latest attempt to overturn sanctions that freeze his assets and bar him from entering or traveling through the bloc.
content:
The European Union’s General Court on Wednesday rejected Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich’s latest attempt to overturn sanctions that freeze his assets and bar him from entering or traveling through the bloc.
Abramovich had challenged the EU Council’s decisions to renew the measures and sought damages. The court upheld the decisions and ruled that the criteria used to impose the sanctions were proportionate.
It was the third time the EU court had rejected a challenge from Abramovich, following rulings in December 2023 and September 2025.
Abramovich argued that he had been sanctioned because of his public profile. The court rejected that claim, saying the restrictions were based on his stakes in major Russian companies.
Abramovich is the majority shareholder in Evraz, one of Russia’s leading steel and mining groups. He also owns shares in Norilsk Nickel, a major producer of palladium and nickel. The court said both companies operate in sectors that provide substantial revenue to the Russian government.
British authorities have linked Evraz to Russia’s military-industrial complex since Moscow invaded Ukraine. When sanctioning Abramovich in March 2022, Britain said the company could have supplied steel to the Russian military for use in tank production.
Britain sanctioned Evraz itself in May 2022, saying the company produced 28% of Russia’s railway wheels and 97% of its rails. It said Russia used rail infrastructure to transport troops and military supplies to the front.
The Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project reported in 2022 that an Evraz subsidiary had supplied $1.4 million worth of steel to Russian tank manufacturer Uralvagonzavod under a 2018 contract.
Evraz has denied supplying products to the Russian military.
The total value of Abramovich’s assets frozen in the EU has not been disclosed. Forbes estimated that France had frozen $340 million worth of his property on the French Riviera and the Caribbean island of St. Barts. Portuguese authorities have also frozen a villa belonging to him in the Algarve valued at about 10 million euros.

title: Vostok Oil’s First Tanker Cannot Conceal Rosneft’s Empty Promises
description: Opinion | Bukhta Sever, the Arctic oil terminal built for Rosneft’s massive Vostok Oil project, has sent out its first export cargo.
content:
Bukhta Sever, the Arctic oil terminal built for Rosneft’s massive Vostok Oil project, has sent out its first export cargo. Or is about to.
The shuttle tanker Valentin Pikul spent 84 days waiting beside the port’s only loading berth. Now full, it is preparing to head for China along the Northern Sea Route. A sister ship, the Akademik Gubkin, is on its way to the terminal.
The two 120,000-ton tankers were built in sections in South Korea to Samsung’s AST69K design. The sections were then shipped to the Zvezda yard in Russia’s Far East and welded together.
Rosneft says it will need at least 40 tankers to carry oil from Bukhta Sever, plus more than 10 support vessels, some of them ice-class. Most of this fleet exists only on paper.
The loading ceremony for the Valentin Pikul followed a familiar script. Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin reported another triumph to President Vladimir Putin, and the numbers grew more impressive as he spoke. Sechin even called the tankers Arc7 vessels, despite shipping registers identifying them as Arc6.
That was the modest part of the performance.
Sechin promised that Vostok Oil would ship about 30 million metric tons of crude during the second half of 2027. Later, if the market cooperates, output could rise to 100 million tons a year.
Thirty million tons in six months works out at roughly 164,000 tons a day. Bukhta Sever would have to load the equivalent of about two Aframax tankers every day, without a break.
Rosneft does not have the ships, and they cannot simply be hired elsewhere because there is no large reserve of ice-capable tankers waiting for work on the world market.
Then there is the route itself. Shipping through the eastern part of the Northern Sea Route is possible for only a few months each year, with heavy icebreaker support. Keeping two tankers a day moving through those waters would strain a mature transport system with a full fleet behind it. Vostok Oil has neither.
Sechin has been reciting some version of this promise for years. In November 2020, he told Putin that the project would reach annual shipments of 30 million tons in 2024. Construction at many of its sites had scarcely started.
Nothing close to 30 million tons was shipped in 2024. The date has since moved to 2027, while the promised rate has doubled: Rosneft now proposes to move the same amount in half the time.
It will not happen. Vostok Oil is unlikely to export 30 million tons during all of 2027, let alone its final six months. The production forecasts are no more convincing than the shipping plan.
Today, Vostok Oil has two main production clusters: Payakha and Vankor. The East Taimyr licenses once bundled into the project have quietly dropped away after disappointing results.
Rosneft still calls Vostok Oil “a new world-class oil province,” claiming a resource base of more than 7 billion tons of premium low-sulfur crude.
The careful wording matters. In Russian petroleum classification, “resources” are a long way from reserves ready for commercial development. The term includes oil that may be present but has yet to be confirmed by adequate exploration drilling.
None of the independent oil specialists interviewed for this article believes that Vostok Oil has 7 billion tons of proven oil.
The Payakha cluster contains two discovered fields, Payakha and West Irkinskoye. Their potentially recoverable reserves have been put at around 1.5 billion tons. Even that figure is shaky. The oil falls into the C1 and C2 categories, either preliminarily appraised or still insufficiently explored. As more wells are drilled, estimates of this kind often shrink by 30% to 50%.
Payakha would be immensely difficult to develop even if the oil is there. The fields sit near the mouth of the Yenisei River amid swamps that are almost impassable in summer. Winter replaces the mud with the brutal conditions of the High Arctic.
The deposits lie more than four kilometers down, trapped in geologically complex formations. Getting the oil out will require hydraulic fracturing. That means bringing in entire fracking fleets, each made up of dozens of trucks carrying heavy equipment, across terrain that barely supports ordinary transport.
The cost of every barrel will be enormous.
Vankor cannot fill the gap. Its five fields — Vankorskoye , Suzunskoye , Lodochnoye , Tagulskoye and Ichemminskoye — have recoverable reserves estimated at about half a billion tons. They have also been producing for years.
The cluster reached its peak in 2017 at around 20 million tons. Water now accounts for as much as 84% of the fluid brought up from its wells. At this stage, Vankor cannot supply much more than 7 million to 8 million tons of oil a year.
Why drag it into Vostok Oil at all? Vankor already has a perfectly serviceable route south into Transneft’s national pipeline network.
Rosneft is nevertheless building a new 790-kilometer pipeline in the other direction, north to the Arctic coast. There is too little oil at Vankor to justify it. The pipeline’s real value is presentational: adding an established producing cluster helps inflate Vostok Oil’s numbers.
Sechin gave Putin a preview of Vostok Oil’s methods in August 2020. During a Kremlin meeting, he produced a bottle of dark liquid and announced that it contained “premium oil” from West Irkinskoye Well No. 31. The crude, he said, was better than Middle Eastern grades.
Documents from the drilling operation make the gift rather hard to explain.
Testing at Well No. 31 produced just two samples. There was so little oil in the sampling chambers that the laboratory combined them into one, according to a report on core and reservoir fluids from West Irkinskoye wells No. 31 and No. 32.
The combined sample came to about 140 cubic centimeters — less than a glass. Seventy percent was water. Only 30% was oil.
And all of that oil was still at the Tyumen Petroleum Research Center when Sechin met Putin, the records show. Whatever was inside the Kremlin bottle, it did not come from the sample Sechin claimed to be presenting.
That episode captures Vostok Oil rather well. A tiny amount of actual oil had been turned into a bottle for television and a story about a vast new province.
Around 4 trillion rubles have already gone into the project. Independent specialists still see no realistic path to the production figures Sechin keeps promising.
Foreign oil traders appear to have reached the same conclusion. Western and Chinese companies resisted Rosneft’s efforts to bring them in. The company eventually persuaded Trafigura of Singapore to take a stake. A consortium of Vitol and Mercantile & Maritime also joined.
They had seen the project up close and wanted no part of it. Strip away the talk of a new oil province, and Vostok Oil is a staggeringly costly development with uncertain reserves and a transport plan that depends on dozens of ships that have not been built.
The Valentin Pikul is finally loaded. After trillions of rubles, Rosneft has managed to fill one tanker.
Sechin would like Putin to see the beginning of a 100-million-ton oil giant. For now, Bukhta Sever has one berth. One tanker has been filled; everything beyond it remains a promise.

title: Kabardino-Balkaria Avalanche Deathtoll Climbs to 13 as Rescue Efforts Continue
description: At least 13 people are now confirmed to have died after an avalanche struck a group of climbers in the North Caucasus republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, Russian emergency services said Wednesday.
content:
At least 13 people are now confirmed to have died after an avalanche struck a group of climbers in the North Caucasus republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, Russian emergency services said Wednesday.
The avalanche swept down Mount Mizhirgi, one of the highest peaks in the North Caucasus, at around 5 p.m. local time on Sunday, hitting a group of 33 climbers. Ten climbers had made their own way down the mountain by Monday morning.
Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said 12 bodies had been lowered to the Bezengi base camp on Tuesday evening, with the fate of five climbers still unknown. By Wednesday morning, the ministry said rescuers found the body of the 13th climber.
Russia’s National Guard said some of its servicemen were among the dead. It also denied reports that the victims included members of its elite Vityaz formation, which specializes in high-risk law enforcement operations.
One of those killed was a professional climber involved in training “representatives of law enforcement agencies,” Alexander Yakovenko, a member of the Russian Mountaineering Federation, told the newspaper Kommersant.
Search and rescue efforts have been hampered by difficult terrain and a high risk of further avalanches, officials said.

title: 4 Killed in Ukrainian Attack on Novorossiysk
description: Four people including a child were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the southern Krasnodar region, local officials said Wednesday.
content:
Four people including a child were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the southern Krasnodar region, local officials said Wednesday.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said another 29 people were wounded in the attack, which took place in Novorossiysk, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone strikes and a major outlet for Russia n oil, petroleum products and grain exports.
Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said drone debris fell on the premises of a number of businesses and close to a residential building.
In Anapa, another town in the Krasnodar region, three homes and a kindergarten were damaged by falling drone debris, but no one was injured, Kondratyev said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it intercepted 596 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.
Airports in more than a dozen regions introduced temporary flight restrictions amid the cross-country drone attacks.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian drone attack on a border crossing with neighboring Moldova killed two people and injured at least three others.
Passenger and vehicle traffic was temporarily halted across the border after the attack, which caused a major fire, officials said.

title: Germany Says It Is Closing a Russian Cultural Center. That Might Not Be So Simple.
description: BERLIN — On a rainy Friday evening in Germany’s capital, hundreds of people gathered to protest the government’s announcement that it was terminating the lease of the Russian House, a Russian cultural center owned and operated by Moscow.  Demonstrators called on the government to reverse its decision, end its “russophobia” and stop what they called its constant “aggression” toward Russia. “It’s the only place left for cultural exchange,” a protester told The Moscow Times, declining to give their name.
content:
BERLIN — On a rainy Friday evening in Germany’s capital, hundreds of people gathered to protest the government’s announcement that it was terminating the lease of the Russian House, a Russian cultural center owned and operated by Moscow.
Demonstrators called on the government to reverse its decision, end its “russophobia” and stop what they called its constant “aggression” toward Russia.
“It’s the only place left for cultural exchange,” a protester told The Moscow Times, declining to give their name.
Down the street, a dozen or so supporters of Russia’s liberal opposition chanted slogans like “Russia without Putin” and held signs up with phrases like “The Kremlin shouldn’t have an address in Berlin.”
A bit further away, roughly 100 pro-Ukraine activists held up boxes that symbolized suitcases and bore slogans like “Suitcase, train station, Moscow,” and spoke about their efforts to close the Russian House dating back to 2022.
The flurry of demonstrations came after Germany said it would shutter the Russian House after it officially blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August.
But closing it, or the bookstore on its premises — places many demonstrators viewed as places of cultural enrichment — may not prove as simple or straightforward as the government’s announcement made it seem.
Several protesters told The Moscow Times that the decision to close the Russian House was politically motivated and “regrettable.”
Shortly after Berlin announced its closure, the Russian government said that it would move to shut down Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers — a decision many demonstrators told The Moscow Times was a “different matter.”
Located in Berlin-Mitte, what is now the Russian House opened in East Berlin in 1984 as the House of Soviet Science and Culture, and only later became the Russian House after the Soviet collapse. The seven-story, 30,000-square-meter building has been the subject of fierce debate since at least the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to its website, the Russian House aims to “familiarize German visitors with important aspects and events in Russian culture and science,” as well as to support Russians in Germany “in preserving and developing their national and cultural identity.”
Organizers say the institution attracts around 200,000 visitors per year to its programming of Russian language courses, film screenings, cultural events, concerts and more.
In July, Director Pavel Izvolskiy told the newspaper nd that the Russian House’s mission was to build bridges between Germans and Russians, a mission it has followed since 1984.
It is operated and owned by Rossotrudnichestvo, the Russian government agency responsible for cultural exchange and foreign aid.
The European Union sanctioned Rossotrudnichestvo in 2022, calling it “the main state agency projecting the Kremlin’s soft power and hybrid influence, including the promotion of the so-called ‘Russkiy Mir’ concept,” and accusing it of organizing “international events aimed at consolidating a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian.”
Izvolskiy told nd that Rossotrudnichestvo is not the center’s operator, but “merely ensures” its operation.
But in June 2025, a Munich administrative court ruled that the Russian House was indeed subject to the sanctions placed on Rossotrudnichestvo, meaning that it would only be able to disburse funds for "maintenance operations.” Its German bank account was frozen, meaning all bank transactions must be approved by the German Bundesbank.
After the announcement was made, German media pointed out that closing the Russian House would not be as simple as the government made it seem.
Firstly, it is governed by a 2011-2012 intergovernmental treaty on cultural information centers. That treaty is automatically renewed unless terminated, with the current version ending on June 7, 2027.
According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, the German government has until Dec. 6 to cancel the agreement.
Furthermore, the building remains the property of the Russian Federation. While the land belongs to Germany, the two governments signed a 2013 agreement which granted Russia its use for 99 years.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin wrote on X last week that the German government had ordered all Russian staff of the Russian House and the Russian consulate in Bonn to leave the country “as quickly as possible.”
However, a source connected to the Russian House told The Moscow Times that there “aren’t actually that many staff members who had moved there [solely for work],” and that many of the staff members have European passports.
One of the main controversies surrounding the Russian House stems from its 2022 screening of a documentary about the murder of Jews in Belarus which allegedly depicted Ukrainians as Nazis.
Another charge leveled at the Russian House is that the bookstore inside its premises sold bars of soap in the shape of Russian tanks.
“It's time we recognized that this isn't about mutual cultural exchange, but rather Russian war propaganda in Germany,” Green Party MP Robin Wagener, the politician who made that claim, told Deutsche Welle.
Moreover, France in July accused the Russian House of espionage, saying it was “used as a cover by Russian intelligence services.”
“Its energy consumption is significantly higher than what you would expect from a cultural institution,” said Roderich Kiesewetter, a German MP from the center-right Christian Democratic Union party.
MnogoKnig, the bookstore inside the Russian House facing Friedrichstrasse, has also been accused of being an instrument of Russia’s propaganda apparatus for selling soaps and other products that evoke Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Yet the Latvia-based bookstore chain sells books in Russian, Ukrainian, English and other languages, including books banned in Russia such as slain Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny’s “ Patriot ” and journalist Elena Kostyuchenko’s “ I Love Russia .”
The store made headlines last week after Latvia’s State Security Service raided four of the chain’s locations in Riga over alleged violations of EU sanctions.
“German newspapers accused [MnogoKnig] of selling coloring books featuring a T-34 tank, claiming this was Russian propaganda. But this is so far from the truth,” a source close to the Russian House told The Moscow Times, speaking on condition of anonymity. They added that the store also sells books that are banned in Russia.
“As far as propaganda goes, I think if the leadership in Moscow knew about this, they’d be more likely to scold the Russian House in Berlin for not being ‘Z’ enough,” they said, referring to a symbol widely used by pro-war Russians.

title: Trump Presses Putin for Swift End to Ukraine War in ‘Confidential’ Call
description: U.S.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump urged Russia’s Vladimir Putin during an hour-long phone call to end the war against Ukraine in order to open up “impressive” U.S.-Russian trade prospects, the Kremlin said Tuesday.
“Donald Trump clearly conveyed the idea that an early end to the conflict would be desirable,” Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov told reporters.
Trump was said to have pitched the idea, which Ushakov claimed Putin supports, as a way to “immediately open impressive and large-scale prospects for the full restoration” of U.S.-Russian relations.
Ushakov added that Trump emphasized the “enormous benefits” of developing U.S.-Russian trade and economic ties.
“Donald Trump is interested in achieving a breakthrough during his presidency,” he said.
The White House did not immediately confirm that Putin and Trump spoke by phone.
Putin continues to demand the complete withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the unoccupied parts of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region as a condition for peace, a stance rejected by Kyiv.
Ushakov said Putin provided Trump with an “objective and thorough analysis” of the current battlefield situation and his views about achieving the war’s objectives.
Tuesday’s phone call followed visits to Moscow and Kyiv by Trump’s special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Ushakov said both presidents viewed the diplomatic outreach positively, while Putin continued to praise Trump’s mediation efforts.
According to Ushakov, the latest phone call outlined “specific measures” the U.S. could take to accelerate an end to the war.
“You understand yourselves that [the call] was confidential, so I will hardly be able to share many important details and nuances,” he said.

title: Russian Postal Workers to Arm Themselves With Anti-Drone Weapons
description: The Russian government has authorized federal postal service employees to carry anti-drone weapons as Ukraine ramps up its attacks across the country. “Special technical means of countering unmanned aerial, underwater and surface vessels and vehicles, autonomous land vehicles and other automated unmanned systems” have been added to an official list of weapons, ammunition and special gear.
content:
The Russian government has authorized federal postal service employees to carry anti-drone weapons as Ukraine ramps up its attacks across the country.
“Special technical means of countering unmanned aerial, underwater and surface vessels and vehicles, autonomous land vehicles and other automated unmanned systems” have been added to an official list of weapons, ammunition and special gear.
A 2005 government decree already allows postal employees to carry 9mm pistols, as well as stun guns and body armor. These weapons are typically given to security staff transporting cash.
The expanded decree signed by Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin last Thursday does not specify which Russian Post workers will receive the anti-drone weapons.
The expansion follows a surge in Ukrainian drone strikes targeting Russian infrastructure over the summer, including oil refineries and the warehouses and logistics hubs of major online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.
The attacks reportedly led to a 560% increase in the commercial procurement of anti-drone defense systems in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
Last month, President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order allowing the state seizure of critical infrastructure facilities if they are deemed to be poorly protected against Ukrainian strikes and other threats.
Putin has since maintained that the order has “nothing to do with any plans for nationalization” of private property.

title: Georgy Matyukhin, Russia’s First Central Bank Chief, Dies at 91
description: The first governor of Russia’s Central Bank after the fall of the Soviet Union, Georgy Matyukhin, has died at the age of 91. Russia’s Central Bank announced Tuesday that Matyukhin passed away on Saturday, one day ahead of his 92nd birthday.
content:
The first governor of Russia’s Central Bank after the fall of the Soviet Union, Georgy Matyukhin, has died at the age of 91.
Russia’s Central Bank announced Tuesday that Matyukhin passed away on Saturday, one day ahead of his 92nd birthday.
The regulator praised Matyukhin as an “active and responsible leader” who was appointed to lead the State Bank of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic “during a critical turning point” in 1990.
“He oversaw the formation of the Bank of Russia under new conditions, leading it until 1992,” the Central Bank said in a statement.
Matyukhin played a key role in the development of modern Russia’s financial sector during severe currency shortages and soaring inflation.
Russian business media described one of his main achievements as the establishment of Russia’s two-tiered banking system, with separated central monetary authority from commercial banking operations.
Matyukhin is also remembered for personally signing the 5,000-ruble banknote, a gesture that no subsequent Central Bank governor has since repeated.
Born in the Altai region city of Barnaul on Sept. 6, 1934, Matyukhin initially trained as a geologist before graduating from the Moscow State Institute of International Relations in 1961.
He then worked within the KGB’s foreign intelligence division before being stationed under diplomatic cover in Uruguay, from where he was eventually expelled alongside a group of Soviet spies.

title: Hungary Expels 10 Russian Diplomats for ‘Unacceptable Activities’
description: Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats on Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their diplomatic status.
content:
Hungary expelled 10 Russia n diplomats on Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their diplomatic status.
Those kicked out "were engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban said in an emailed statement on Tuesday.
Hungary has "called on the individuals in question to leave" the country, Orban said. She added that the action "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia."
"Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules," Orban said, without giving details of what the mission staffers had allegedly done.
Russia 's Foreign Ministry said it would retaliate for the expulsion of its diplomats.
"The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the state-run news agency TASS.
Hungary's former prime minister, Viktor Orban, who in April was voted out of office after 16 years in power, had maintained close ties with Russia and President Vladimir Putin following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Since taking office in May, Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, has sought to mend ties with the EU and Ukraine that were tense under his predecessor.

title: Finland Completes Construction of Russian Border Fence
description: Finland has completed construction on a 200-kilometer (124-mile) fence along its eastern border with Russia, three years after the project began, the Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported Monday.
content:
Finland has completed construction on a 200-kilometer (124-mile) fence along its eastern border with Russia, three years after the project began, the Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported Monday.
Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen presented the completed fence near a shuttered border crossing, saying the barrier addresses heightened security risks following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and could be extended further.
“What we particularly need is EU funding for eastern member states so that projects like this can be financed,” Rantanen said.
The new fence cost 356 million euros ($413 million), with an estimated 2-3 million euros for annual maintenance, according to Finnish border authorities.
The barbed wire fence spans Finland’s southeastern border with Russia and parts of its eastern flank. It features patrol roads, loudspeakers, night lighting and surveillance cameras.
Russia and Finland share a 1,340-kilometer (833-mile) border, the longest of any EU or NATO member.
Similar fences have been erected in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland on their borders with Belarus to stem migrants from crossing.
Finland shut its eastern border crossings with Russia indefinitely in December 2023 following an influx of asylum seekers. Helsinki claimed the influx was a so-called “hybrid attack” in retaliation for Finland joining NATO in April 2023.
The Kremlin has rejected those accusations.
Over the summer, Russia closed five railway border checkpoints with Finland without disclosing the reasons or when they might reopen.
The Finnish government last week proposed an extension of its Border Security Act until Dec. 31, 2028 — a temporary one-year law that allows border guards to turn away asylum seekers under certain circumstances.

title: FSB Arrests Moldovan Suspected of Shooting Air Force General
description: Russia’s FSB security service said Tuesday that it arrested a Moldovan man who is suspected of shooting a Russian Aerospace Forces general on behalf of Ukraine last week.
content:
Russia’s FSB security service said Tuesday that it arrested a Moldovan man who is suspected of shooting a Russian Aerospace Forces general on behalf of Ukraine last week.
The FSB said its agents in the southern Astrakhan region arrested the man, identified as 21-year-old Nicolae Cociu. Investigators claim that Cociu shot a Russian serviceman near the Saratov region city of Engels last Thursday.
While authorities did not identify the Russian serviceman by name, pro-Kremlin media reported last week that Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, who heads a strategic bomber division at Engels-2 airbase, was shot and wounded in the Saratov region.
In an official statement, the Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, confirmed the armed attack against the officer, who was hospitalized after receiving six gunshot wounds.
The shooting occurred days after Ukraine pressed criminal charges against Varpakhovich in absentia for allegedly ordering a fatal missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv in July 2024.
On Tuesday, the FSB claimed Ukrainian security services recruited Cociu while he was living in Moldova in 2025. Investigators alleged that he traveled to Kyiv in spring 2026, where he agreed to carry out the contract killing for $70,000 and underwent weapons and explosives training before entering Russia through its border with Estonia.
In an interrogation video published by state-run news agencies, Cociu confessed that he was recruited through a job advertisement on Instagram. “I was sent to Russia with the task of killing a Russian general,” Cociu, his face blurred, said on camera.
A second video showed Cociu providing detailed testimony and showing investigators how he discarded evidence and fled the crime scene.
Cociu was charged with attempted murder and illegal arms trafficking, charges that carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. The Investigative Committee said it plans to petition a judge to place Cociu in pre-trial detention.

title: 4 Killed in Ukrainian Drone Attacks on Russian Regions and Crimea
description: At least four people were killed and 18 others were injured overnight in Ukrainian drone attacks across Russia and annexed Crimea, officials said Tuesday.
content:
At least four people were killed and 18 others were injured overnight in Ukrainian drone attacks across Russia and annexed Crimea, officials said Tuesday.
A 39-year-old man was killed in an attack on a gas station in the Bryansk region town of Starodub, 35 kilometers (21 miles) north of the Ukrainian border, acting Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said . Three others were wounded, he added.
In the nearby Belgorod region, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said one person was killed in a border district as a result of a “targeted” hit. Four others were injured across the region, where Shuvayev said Ukraine carried out 112 attacks in the past 24 hours.
Unverified reports said that Ukrainian drones targeted a Rosneft-operated oil refinery in the southern Saratov region.
Saratov region Governor Roman Busargin confirmed only damage to residential homes and that 10 people, including three children, were injured.
Crimea’s Kremlin-installed leader Sergei Aksyonov reported two deaths and one injury from a drone strike near the city of Simferopol.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 384 Ukrainian drones across Russia and Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, at least three people were killed in Kyiv after Russia resumed its strikes on the Ukrainian capital following a three-day ceasefire that coincided with renewed talks to end the war.

title: Russia Orders Closures of German Consulate and Cultural Centers in Tit-for-Tat Move
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Monday it was shuttering the German consulate in St.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Monday it was shuttering the German consulate in St. Petersburg and German cultural centers across the country.
The closures were announced in retaliation for Germany’s decision last week to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin after its government blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.
Moscow gave diplomats and employees at the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg until Sept. 18 to cease operations and leave Russia.
Staff at Germany’s Goethe-Institut cultural center branches in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg were given until this Sunday.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s ambassador in Moscow to inform him about the retaliatory decisions.
“It was the German authorities who once again provoked a new spiral of escalation in bilateral relations. Full responsibility for the consequences lies entirely with the German government,” the Russian ministry said in a statement.
President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow for the early August incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
On Sunday, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed Berlin’s accusations against Moscow amounted to “an effective declaration of war against us.”
Lavrov said last week that Moscow would respond to the closure of its cultural center in Berlin by closing the Goethe-Institut cultural centers across Russia.
Russia’s first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

title: Moscow Police General and Gas Station Executives Arrested in Fuel Theft Scheme
description: Law enforcement authorities in the Moscow region have arrested a police general, two senior officers and several corporate executives at a local gas station network accused of stealing fuel designated for police vehicles, Russia’s Interior Ministry said Monday.
content:
Law enforcement authorities in the Moscow region have arrested a police general, two senior officers and several corporate executives at a local gas station network accused of stealing fuel designated for police vehicles, Russia’s Interior Ministry said Monday.
Major General Sergei Malkov, who managed logistics as deputy head of the Moscow region ’s Interior Ministry branch, allegedly oversaw the criminal scheme alongside Igor Martyshov, board chairman of EuroTrans, a major gas station operator.
Malkov and two of his subordinates, Colonel Alexei Suyarov and Lieutenant Colonel Anna Levina, were fired from the Interior Ministry following their arrests. Investigators have asked a judge to place them in pre-trial detention.
Interior Ministry spokeswoman Irina Volk said three other EuroTrans executives have been placed in pre-trial detention. All seven individuals face charges of large-scale embezzlement, which carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
The arrests come after antitrust authorities in June accused EuroTrans, which operates 57 gas stations in and around Moscow, of price gouging as Ukrainian drone strikes against oil refineries triggered widespread fuel shortages.
Following the news of the arrests, EuroTrans shares dropped 6% on the Moscow Exchange, according to Interfax.
Russian gasoline production plummeted to roughly 70% of domestic consumption levels by late August following months of oil refinery attacks, Reuters reported.

title: Communist Bondarenko Barred From Running in State Duma Elections
description: The Central Election Commission on Monday barred Communist Party candidate Nikolai Bondarenko from running in Russia’s upcoming parliamentary elections following his recent conviction for displaying “extremist” symbols.
content:
The Central Election Commission on Monday barred Communist Party candidate Nikolai Bondarenko from running in Russia’s upcoming parliamentary elections following his recent conviction for displaying “extremist” symbols.
Bondarenko, a former Saratov regional lawmaker and popular YouTuber with more than 2 million subscribers, was detained and fined last month over an old social media post featuring a photo of the late opposition activist Alexei Navalny.
His defense team argued that the account that made the post does not belong to Bondarenko. A judge rejected an appeal against the ruling and fine last week.
On Monday, election officials, citing the “extremism” charge, voted to remove Bondarenko from the ballot in this month’s State Duma elections.
Russian election laws prohibit anyone convicted of an “extremism” offense from running for office for a year.
In a statement, the Communist Party accused officials of blocking Bondarenko’s election bid because they are “afraid.”
Bondarenko rose to national fame through his fiery, unfiltered attacks against Russia’s deeply unpopular 2018 pension reforms.
During his tenure in the Saratov regional assembly from 2017 to 2021, he built a large social media following through theatrical political stunts, including a viral experiment where he tried to survive on a monthly pension of 3,500 rubles ($52).
His populist rhetoric, savvy use of social media and diatribes against the ruling United Russia party earned him high praise from Navalny, who once dubbed Bondarenko his “favorite” regional lawmaker.
Bondarenko was stripped of his seat in the Saratov regional assembly in 2022 after state prosecutors claimed he failed to declare ad revenues and user donations generated through his popular YouTube channel.
His disqualification from the upcoming State Duma election follows a series of similar cases in which potential candidates have faced charges that effectively bar them from office.
On Monday, the chairman of the liberal Yabloko party in Yekaterinburg was also detained and charged over displaying “extremist” symbols in old social media posts, the newspaper Kommersant reported .

title: Russia and North Korea Open First Road Bridge Across Shared Border
description: Russia and North Korea opened the first road bridge linking the two countries on Monday, coming after months of construction delays.
content:
Russia and North Korea opened the first road bridge linking the two countries on Monday, coming after months of construction delays.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song presided over a ceremony via video link to mark the official launch of traffic along th e two-lane bridge, which stretches one kilometer (0.6 miles) over the Tumen River.
Mishustin hailed bilateral relations as being at an “unprecedentedly high level of comprehensive strategic partnership,” adding that the bridge, which cost 9 billion rubles ($104 million), would boost trade and tourism.
A rail bridge, built in the 1950s, already connects the two countries.
The new road bridge is named after Yakov Novichenko, a Soviet officer who saved North Korean founder Kim Il Sung by shielding him from a grenade explosion in Pyongyang in 1946.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed the formal construction agreement during a 2024 summit in Pyongyang.
Work on the bridge began in April 2025. North Korea completed its section ahead of a planned June 19, 2026 deadline, while construction delays on the Russian side pushed the opening back by several months.
According to news agency Interfax, the bridge and its newly constructed border checkpoint, which connects the Far East Primorye region with North Korea, are designed to process up to 300 vehicles and 2,300 people daily.
Some observers have said that the bridge will provide Russia and North Korea an additional route through which they can discreetly move military cargo and personnel.
In 2025, North Korea’s shipments of rocket artillery, shells and short-range ballistic missiles to Russia were estimated to be between $7 billion and $13.8 billion, according to the Institute for National Security Strategy, a government-funded research institute in South Korea.
Russia and North Korea have deepened military ties since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, the two countries signed a mutual defense treaty that requires them to provide military support if either is attacked.

content:
At least six people were killed in a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks targeting Russia’s Belgorod and Perm regions and annexed Crimea overnight, officials said Monday.
A man and woman were killed when a drone struck their car in the Belgorod region near the border with Ukraine, according to the local emergency headquarters.
On Monday morning, officials in Belgorod said a man was killed in a separate drone attack in the border town of Grayvoron.
In the Perm region, 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of Ukraine, one person was killed and four were injured after a drone hit an apartment building, Governor Dmitry Mahonin said .
Unverified reports said smoke was seen rising over an industrial area in Perm that houses at least two defense facilities, including a gunpowder plant and a rocket engine manufacturing facility.
Meanwhile, in annexed Crimea, a 15-year-old girl and a man were killed in an overnight attack in the port city of Sevastopol. Kremlin-installed authorities said shrapnel-laden drones damaged windows in eight apartment buildings and a kindergarten.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 306 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning.

title: Avalanche in Kabardino-Balkaria Kills 11 Climbers
description: At least 11 people were killed and six others injured after an avalanche struck a group of climbers in Russia's Kabardino-Balkaria region in the North Caucasus, local emergency services said.
content:
At least 11 people were killed and six others injured after an avalanche struck a group of climbers in Russia 's Kabardino-Balkaria region in the North Caucasus, local emergency services said.
The avalanche swept down Mount Mizhirgi, one of the highest peaks in Russia 's North Caucasus, at around 5 p.m. local time on Sunday, hitting a group of 33 climbers.
As of 9 a.m. local time on Monday, 10 climbers had made their own way down the mountain, while the fate of six others remained unknown, emergency services said.
More than 50 emergency workers were involved in the search and rescue operation, but efforts were being hampered by difficult terrain and a high risk of further avalanches, they said.

title: U.S. Envoys Make First Kyiv Visit Amid Ukraine Peace Push
description: U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
content:
U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia 's war against Ukraine.
Kushner and Witkoff travelled from Moscow, where they held three hours of talks with Russia n President Vladimir Putin on Saturday but did not appear to secure a breakthrough in the conflict.
Previous rounds of U.S.-mediated peace talks encouraged by U.S. President Donald Trump, who campaigned on a promise to quickly end the war, have yielded few results. He suggested on Friday that the U.S. had a fresh proposal, though he did not elaborate.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described Saturday's meeting as "highly useful," while a White House official told Reuters that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
The two envoys met Zelensky and other top Ukrainian officials in central Kyiv.
Zelensky, who believes Washington will be key to any peace deal, has said a window of opportunity to make peace exists before the U.S. begins focusing on its next presidential election.
After the first round of talks between Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators that lasted about three hours, the U.S. envoys said that they were looking forward to making more progress.
"Substantive, important, and we are very encouraged,” Witkoff told reporters after the talks, which also included a working lunch.
Zelensky said that more talks, which would also include European representatives, were planned later on Sunday. British, French and German national security advisers were in Kyiv on Sunday.
"Security guarantees are needed. A dignified post-war peace is needed. Our proposals have been drawn up," Zelensky said as his negotiating team was preparing to meet U.S. envoys.
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Moscow several times in their roles as peace envoys. But Sunday is their first visit to Kyiv in their capacity as U.S. negotiators.
Ukraine's leadership has long sought their visit, and on the streets of Kyiv, which has been heavily bombarded in recent weeks, some residents were hopeful.
"The issue can be solved in the blink of an eye. We want peace. I've fought myself, so I know what war is like. We need peace, because there's no other way," said military veteran Stepan Yermak.
In previous talks, the sides have remained far apart on key issues, including the future of the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas. Russia has demanded Ukraine's withdrawal from an entrenched belt of towns that it still controls there, but Kyiv has refused, reasoning that it can still hold on.
For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and the U.S. are crucial to deterring Russia from invading again.
"We need an agreement that will never be broken," said Svitlana Kurylenko, a 19-year-old cafe worker.
"Just leave Ukraine alone and let people live in peace."
Though the front lines of the ground war remain largely static, both Russia n and Ukrainian forces have intensified long-range air strikes in recent months.
Russia has pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones for the past two weeks, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
The Kremlin has said it would pause strikes on Kyiv until Monday, while Zelensky has said Ukraine would also halt strikes on Moscow.
There was no let-up in fighting along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front, however, and Russia bombarded other Ukrainian cities on Saturday.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russia n refineries, oil terminals and the warehouses of online retailers in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war.
Ukraine said on Sunday it had struck the Ryazan oil refinery, around 480 kilometers (300 miles) inside Russia , overnight, causing a fire.

title: Moscow Not Ruling Out Trilateral Meeting of Russian, U.S. and Chinese Leaders, Agencies Report
description: Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Sunday that Moscow has not ruled out a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the U.S. and China, state news agency TASS reported.
content:
Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Sunday that Moscow has not ruled out a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the U.S. and China, state news agency TASS reported.
However, before moving on to the actual preparations, it is necessary to understand what the meeting's agenda would be, Ryabkov said.
"Here, the main question boils down to how the substance of the meeting will be formulated, and what we can expect as a result."
Earlier this month, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov raised the possibility of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.
On Sunday, Ushakov was quoted by Russia n news agencies as saying that while such a meeting of Russia n, U.S. and Chinese leaders "would not be without merit," its organization was the prerogative of the summit's hosts.
"If they are able to organize such a meeting – and this requires a certain amount of diplomatic preparation – then I think it could take place," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin also plans to set up bilateral meetings for Putin during the summit, including one with Xi Jinping, and, "if the opportunity arises," a meeting with Trump, Ushakov said.

content:

"All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov said, referring to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The German government said on Sept. 1 that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russia n cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia dismissed the German accusations as baseless, accusing Berlin of planting evidence to frame Russia for the attack.

content:
