The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.
He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict."
These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia 's smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.
A White House official told Reuters the talks had been "substantive" and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.
There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday.
"The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russia n-American projects were discussed in some detail," Ushakov said. "Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides."
Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted on X that the meeting had been an "important peacemaking visit." He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
The Russia n president praised Trump's efforts to end the war.

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.

title: Russian Figure Skater Valieva Has Neutral Status Revoked, Source Says
description: Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva will not be able to compete internationally this year, after the sport's governing body revoked her neutral athlete status, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Saturday.
content:
Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva will not be able to compete internationally this year, after the sport's governing body revoked her neutral athlete status, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Saturday.
She has received a letter informing her of the International Skating Union's (ISU) decision to revoke her neutral status, the source said.
The ISU declined to comment. Valieva's representatives were not immediately available for comment.
Russian athletes have been barred from competing under their national flag since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The ISU has established a pathway for select athletes to compete as individual neutral athletes subject to rigorous vetting, including a strict background check. Athletes can not be affiliated with the Russian military or security services, have participated in the war in Ukraine, or have "at any time since February 2022, actively and publicly supported that war."
Without neutral status, skaters cannot enter ISU events, earn world ranking points or compete for global titles.
According to an Associated Press source, Valieva's status was withdrawn over a "potential breach of criteria."
Valieva, 20, was 15 when she became the center of a global controversy at the 2022 Olympics, after a sample taken two months earlier tested positive for the banned substance trimetazidine.
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) imposed a four-year ban on Valieva in 2024, with the sanction backdated to when she tested positive for trimetazidine, which prevents angina attacks, at the Russian national championships in December 2021.
The failed test emerged after she helped Russia win team gold at the Olympics, a result which was later annulled, elevating the United States to the top of the podium.
Valieva returned to ice skating in February at the Russian Jumping Championships but remained ineligible for this year's Milano-Cortina Olympics.
The Ukrainian Figure Skating Federation (UFSF) last week urged the ISU to review its readmission of Russian and Belarusian competitors as individual neutral athletes, warning that its screening process failed to enforce basic neutrality rules.
It called on the ISU to institute stricter background audits, implement continuous compliance monitoring, and require all applicants to publicly condemn Russia’s war in Ukraine.

description: U.S. special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on Saturday for talks on how to end the war in Ukraine, where they were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
content:
U.S. special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on Saturday for talks on how to end the war in Ukraine, where they were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
A motorcade, carrying Witkoff, Kushner and Dmitriev, left Moscow's governmental airport and headed towards the city, a Reuters witness said. U.S. President Donald Trump suggested on Friday the U.S. had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year. He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be.
Dmitriev, who told Reuters in June that he had remained in contact with the U.S. negotiators during a pause in their visits to Russia, took part in all their previous meetings with Putin alongside Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov.
He also played a role in negotiating U.S. sanction waivers for Russian oil this year.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday the two men would fly to Ukraine on Sunday after visiting Moscow. In an X post on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia hit two Ukrainian airports ahead of U.S. envoys' visit to Kyiv.
Peskov said in a statement posted on the Kremlin's channel in the Max messaging app that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday, in connection with Witkoff and Kushner's visit to the Ukrainian capital.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported 53 Ukrainian drones in Russian airspace on Saturday, significantly fewer than the average seen in recent months. Moscow is celebrating its City Day on Saturday, with hundreds of thousands of people taking part in open-air festivities across the city.
A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the 4-1/2-year-old war, which is the deadliest in Europe since World War II.
A source close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of a possible trip by President Trump's envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” the source told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow's slow rate of progress. Ukraine refuses to surrender land that it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was “unshakeable.”
Since the last peace talks in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside the other's territory, while the war at sea has also escalated.
On the ground, the front lines have remained largely static, with Russia making only gradual gains in its attempt to take the whole of Ukraine's Donbas region.
Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to a summer of fuel shortages and rising prices for Russian motorists, while some 30 attacks on warehouses belonging mostly to Wildberries and Ozon, the country's largest online retailers, have affected the consumer economy.

description: Russia hit Ukraine's airports in the capital Kyiv and the nearby town of Boryspil ahead of visits to Moscow and Kyiv by U.S.
content:
Russia hit Ukraine's airports in the capital Kyiv and the nearby town of Boryspil ahead of visits to Moscow and Kyiv by U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.

title: Justice Ministry Designates Novaya Gazeta as ‘Foreign Agent’
description: Russia’s Justice Ministry on Friday designated the independent online news outlet Novaya Gazeta as a “foreign agent.” Authorities claimed Novaya Gazeta publicly opposed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, spread “false information” about elections and collaborated with other “foreign agents.” Hundreds of cultural figures, journalists, businesspeople, as well as news outlets and organizations, have been branded “foreign agents” since Russia introduced the label in 2012. Russia applies the designation to individuals it views as enemies of the state.
content:
Russia’s Justice Ministry on Friday designated the independent online news outlet Novaya Gazeta as a “foreign agent.”
Authorities claimed Novaya Gazeta publicly opposed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, spread “false information” about elections and collaborated with other “foreign agents.”
Hundreds of cultural figures, journalists, businesspeople, as well as news outlets and organizations, have been branded “foreign agents” since Russia introduced the label in 2012.
Russia applies the designation to individuals it views as enemies of the state. Those branded as “foreign agents” are required to include a lengthy disclaimer in all of their public appearances and statements, including posts on social media.
Authorities also expanded the registry of persons “affiliated with foreign agents” by adding more than 100 individuals connected to Novaya Gazeta. The list reportedly includes Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov.
Affiliated individuals are not subject to the same strict requirements, but are required to declare their status on all electoral campaign materials.
Novaya Gazeta ceased print publication shortly after the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine due to censorship laws that the government passed as part of a broader crackdown on the press.
The newspaper has continued to publish articles and videos online.
Novaya Gazeta’s former editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression.”
Also on Friday, Russia’s Justice Ministry added writer Felix Sandalov, poet Sergei Leibgrad, scientist Tatiana Tatarinova and the academic journal Historical Expertise to its list of more than 1,250 “foreign agents.”
All five entities and individuals were accused of systemically distributing materials produced by existing “foreign agents” or “undesirable” organizations and spreading “false information” about government policy.

title: The ECHR Has Abandoned Russians Who Are Victims of Their Own Government
description: Opinion | On September 3, the European Court of Human Rights adopted a decision that is unprecedented in the history of international justice as a whole: it struck out 879 remaining applications for cases against Russia, whose applicants included more than 1,500 people and organisations in total.
content:
On September 3, the European Court of Human Rights adopted a decision that is unprecedented in the history of international justice as a whole: it struck out 879 remaining applications for cases against Russia, whose applicants included more than 1,500 people and organisations in total.
In its decision in the case of Lebedeva and Others v. Russia , the Court announced that it would continue to examine only interstate and individual applications against Russia connected with the armed conflicts in Ukraine and Georgia. Everything else has been thrown in the bin. Among the applicants in these cases are residents of the Dagestani village of Vremenny, whose homes were destroyed during a 2014 counter-terrorism operation; victims of bombings during the Second Chechen War; relatives of those killed on the Kolskaya drilling platform in 2011; a man who was abducted and tortured several years ago by Kadyrovtsy; relatives of journalist and human rights defender Timur Kuashev, who was killed by Russian security services in 2014; and relatives of the Syrian El-Ismail, who was tortured and killed by Wagner PMC mercenaries in 2017. Many of them had waited decades for a decision from the Court. Today, their wait came to an end: they have been left alone with the Russian state.
On March 16, 2022, shortly after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe.
Russian authorities immediately ceased all cooperation with Strasbourg. They stopped responding to requests from the ECHR, presenting their position in court cases and corresponding on the implementation of the Court’s judgments. The Court received its last official letter from Russia on March 28, 2022, in which the authorities stated their intention not to implement its judgments from March 16, 2022 onward. In June 2022, that refusal was enshrined in law: Vladimir Putin signed legislation prohibiting the implementation in Russia of ECHR judgments that became final after March 15, 2022.
It is known that at that moment, voices inside the ECHR were already calling for the Court to stop examining any applications against Russia. At first, the Court did not support this position and confirmed in March 2022 that it would continue examining Russian cases concerning all facts that occurred before Sept. 16, 2022, the date on which the European Convention on Human Rights ceased to apply to Russia. The Court also confirmed that Russia remained obliged to cooperate with the Court and implement all of its judgments.
Since 2022, in addition to cases connected with the armed conflicts in Ukraine and Georgia, the ECHR had been dealing with a backlog of more than 15,000 Russian applications. The Court filtered some of them out, sometimes according to the principle that “when the forest is being felled, chips will fly.” In thousands of others, it issued standardised judgments, in which stories spanning many years were reduced to rows listing the violated articles of the Convention and the amounts of compensation.
Finally, more than 600 applications in landmark cases were examined in detail — among them, for example, Memorial’s cases concerning access to Soviet archives and slave labour in Moscow.
Now, four years later, when fewer than a thousand Russian applications remained and all of them were important and complex enough not to be dealt with under the simplified procedure, the supporters of the shredder inside the Court have nevertheless prevailed.
There can be no doubt that this mass dismissal — a massacre — of applications will go down in history as one of the most shameful decisions the ECHR has adopted in its entire existence. The issue is not even the number of applicants affected — relative to the total volume of cases against Russia, there really are not that many — but the principle itself.
The Court justified its decision on purely bureaucratic grounds. It concluded that, in view of Russia’s non-participation in the Council of Europe, there was no point “deployment of further significant judicial resources” to examining the remaining cases. It is true that the Convention allows the Court to discontinue proceedings in a case if "it is no longer justified to continue the examination of the application.” But the same provision contains an important qualification: the examination must continue “if respect for human rights requires it.”
It is obvious that convenience or the saving of resources alone cannot justify a refusal to administer justice, all the more so when the state in question has been expelled from the Council of Europe and refuses to cooperate with the ECHR or implement its judgments. In effect, today the ECHR has allowed itself to strike cases out if the defendant does not turn up in court and ignores the court’s other judgments. We as lawyers admit that it will not be easy for us to explain this logic to our clients. Even Russian judges have not yet thought of anything like this.
The fact that the Court has already examined, or will continue to examine, thousands of applications against Russia in no way justifies refusing to examine the remaining ones, particularly after so many years of waiting. We should recall that the earliest of the applications thrown out today was submitted to the Court in 2007 — 19 years ago! Moreover, this approach only aggravates the problem because it discriminates between applicants without any coherent justification. The right to access justice should not depend on how well a particular applicant’s story fits the Court’s current priorities.
Today’s decision is an enormous blow to the authority of the ECHR, the Council of Europe and the international human rights protection system as a whole.
First, the Court has let down the people who placed their trust in it. For years, they went through the Russian courts and gathered evidence in the hope that their case would receive an independent assessment in Strasbourg. Now, everyone who has already spent years seeking justice is being told to begin another round: find another suitable international body to protect their rights, understand its rules, prepare the application all over again and be forced to wait again, with no guarantees. Many applicants will discover that access to such bodies — for example, at the UN — is already closed to them because the relevant deadlines have expired.
Second, the Court’s decision is a gift both to the Kremlin and to other states that violate human rights.
For years, the Russian authorities tried to rid themselves of the ECHR’s inconvenient scrutiny: they disputed its findings, restricted the implementation of its judgments and then refused to implement them altogether. Now the ECHR has done the Russian state’s work for it. A huge number of the Kremlin’s human rights violations will receive no judicial assessment at all. No violations — no problems.
Other offending states also receive the message that if they ignore the Court for long enough, they can wait until it stops examining applications against them. Refusal to cooperate becomes a way to weaken judicial oversight, while non-implementation of court judgments becomes an argument against issuing new ones.
When the ECHR plays into the hands of violators in order to reduce its own workload, it is shooting itself in the foot. All the more so because the Court’s authority is already facing a serious and growing threat. One need only recall the recent Chișinău Declaration , in which Council of Europe member states openly put pressure on the Court in an attempt to change its case law to the detriment of human rights. As ECHR President Mattias Guyomar said just a few months ago, the role of the Court is to show that “human rights matter at all times, even during war, when lawlessness may seem to reign.” The Court could have proved that these were not empty words. For example, by supporting the creation of real mechanisms for paying compensation already awarded in cases against Russia.
Concrete proposals on this issue have long been on the table. In its submissions to the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, Memorial has repeatedly proposed ways of securing the payments already awarded. We propose creating a special fund within the Council of Europe system and mechanisms for recovering compensation from Russian state assets abroad. The fund should search for assets, initiate the necessary legal procedures and distribute the funds in a fair and equitable manner. States should create legal grounds for recovery within their jurisdictions. This is an unusual solution that requires political will, but it is legally sound.
Stopping the examination of applications is easier. It does not require legal courage, the search for new approaches or standing up to a state accustomed to getting its way through force and blackmail.
Meanwhile, Europe is creating a compensation mechanism for Ukraine and a special tribunal for the crime of aggression. But promises to hold Russia accountable are worthless if, at the same time, the ECHR denies hundreds of its victims judicial protection and the Council of Europe fails to secure implementation of judgments that have already been delivered. Against this background, the new institutions risk becoming mere decorations of justice. It is difficult to promise justice convincingly in the future while denying it today.

title: Zelensky Orders ‘Tangible Response’ Against Russia After Drone Strikes SBU HQ in Kyiv
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he has ordered the head of Ukraine’s SBU security service to carry out an “appropriate and tangible” response to a Russian drone strike against the agency’s headquarters in central Kyiv on Friday afternoon.
content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he has ordered the head of Ukraine’s SBU security service to carry out an “appropriate and tangible” response to a Russian drone strike against the agency’s headquarters in central Kyiv on Friday afternoon.
In a post on X, Zelensky wrote that a Russian drone took direct aim at the office of SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad.
Ukrainian media reported that Poklad was not in his office at the time of the attack, which took place at around 3:30 p.m. local time.
Heavy black smoke was seen rising in central Kyiv following the strike, which Ukraine’s foreign minister described as a major escalation of the war.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people were injured in the attack.
Zelensky said he spoke with Poklad and instructed him to prepare a response that “mirrors” the Russian strike. “Our military will support this response,” the Ukrainian president wrote.
The Kremlin did not immediately comment on the attack.
Ukraine’s SBU is a vast and secretive agency responsible for ambitious operations deep inside Russia.
It is also widely seen as a leading player in a campaign of covert assassinations of senior Russian military officials and other figures blamed by Ukraine for carrying out war crimes.

title: ‘It Still Causes Severe Stress’: Fear of Expulsion Upends Life for Some Russian Asylum Seekers in Europe
description: Between learning a notoriously difficult local language, studying for a professional certification in economics and volunteering to help Ukrainian refugees, Nikita Belov might seem like the exact kind of Russian asylum seeker who would be welcomed in Europe.
content:
Between learning a notoriously difficult local language, studying for a professional certification in economics and volunteering to help Ukrainian refugees, Nikita Belov might seem like the exact kind of Russian asylum seeker who would be welcomed in Europe.
But that didn’t stop authorities in Finland from nearly deporting him and his mother, Olga, last month. After being denied asylum and told that they faced little risk back home, the pair were “on the brink of deportation,” Belov, 25, said, before a court stepped in and ordered their case to be reconsidered.
Hundreds of Russians have landed in a similar situation in recent years. After fleeing to Europe to escape state repression, many of them manage to find a legal path to permanent residency — but others face a harsh reality when their asylum applications are rejected at their host country’s discretion.
In 2025, the EU reported that more than 10,000 Russians were ordered to leave the bloc’s member states . Advocates argue that high-profile cases like the Belovs’ show that some of the most vulnerable among them are slipping through the cracks.
Experts who spoke with The Moscow Times attributed the trend in rejected asylum applications to rising anti-immigration sentiment across Europe, which is pressuring governments to curb pathways to settlement .
“There is a strong wave of fighting illegal migration,” said Artyom Klyga, a lawyer based in Germany who works on cases of conscientious objectors and army deserters, some of the most at-risk asylum seekers from Russia. “It’s become a very popular topic for the political agenda, not only in Germany but in all of Europe.”
In the Belovs’ case, it’s unclear to what extent broader political trends were a factor. The evidence is largely circumstantial: In Finland, a right-wing government that came to power in 2023 has taken steps to curb illegal immigration and accelerated deportations, coinciding with sweeping new EU-wide migration rules designed to expedite the processing of asylum applications .
The Belovs’ lawyer told The Guardian that those changes in particular have created headaches since they came into effect this summer, adding that it’s now “even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing.” Back in Russia, they face likely persecution for speaking out against the war in Ukraine. Their case was only reconsidered after a large public outcry.
“It certainly left a deep mark,” Belov said in a phone interview with The Moscow Times, reflecting on his and his mother’s ordeal, which saw them detained briefly this spring. “It still causes severe stress, sometimes even panic attacks.”
“I don’t know how long it will take to recover from this considering the process is not yet over and a positive decision is not guaranteed,” he added.
Elsewhere, the stories of Russians facing asylum denials and expulsions cut across demographics and geography. Last year, Austria deported two men from the North Caucasus republic of Chechnya who were at risk of being conscripted back home. A few months later, Latvia ordered 841 Russian citizens to leave after they failed to undergo background checks and prove their proficiency in the local language.
One of the countries that has attracted the most attention is Germany, whose historically liberal immigration policies have made it one of the top destinations for migrants in recent decades.
During the initial months of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, German officials signaled that their country could serve as a safe haven for Russians fleeing conscription . The reality, however, has fallen far short of the rhetoric: a report by German media last year revealed that 95% of asylum applications from draft-eligible Russian men had been rejected since the war began.
In fact, Germany’s so-called “total protection rate” — the number of all positive decisions — for asylum seekers from Russia declined each year between 2022 and 2025, from 11.5% to 4.8%, according to government tallies shared with The Moscow Times. As of June, this year’s was only slightly higher at 5.1%.
Edith Avram, a spokesperson for Germany’s Federal Office for Migration and Refugees, said in an email that the asylum process is “conducted on an individual case-by-case basis.”
“The applicant’s country of origin and the reasons on which the application is based are important factors in the examination of an asylum application,” Avram said. “However, neither factor alone determines whether protection is granted or the application is rejected.”
Advocates complain that the system is mercurial, producing judgments that ignore the facts — and risks — of individual cases.
In one recent example, German immigration authorities came under scrutiny for denying an asylum request from Georgy Avaliani, a pacifist who reportedly fled the front line in Ukraine, underwent torture after being recaptured and then escaped again.
Media reported that the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees believed there was little risk of him being persecuted in Russia. In reality, deserters can face a harsh punishment of up to 10 years in prison. Klyga, who is advising Avaliani and his German lawyer , said that an appeal against the denial of his asylum request has been filed in a Berlin court.
Similarly, Said Abuyev, a 53-year-old Chechen man facing deportation from Germany, told The Moscow Times that he fears imprisonment or worse back home. He is a regime opponent who previously served four-and-a-half years in a brutal detention facility on charges of weapons possession and being part of an illegal armed group that he claims were fabricated .
When asked what awaits him in Russia, he replied: “I can’t say for sure, but it won’t end well.”
The Chechen government is notoriously repressive and operates with near impunity, meting out severe punishments to critics and regularly drawing accusations of human rights abuses. Abuyev’s case is one of many that have caught the attention of advocates who say Europe isn’t doing enough to shelter asylum seekers from the broader North Caucasus region.
The prevalence of extraditions and deportations to the North Caucasus grew so alarming that in 2024 human rights watchdog Amnesty International published a report on the issue, calling on EU members to immediately halt the expulsions. But according to Rosa Dunaeva, a Chechen activist based in Austria, little has changed.
“It’s double standards,” Dunaeva said. “They hand over Chechens to Russia without a full risk assessment.”
Across Europe, scores of similar cases are likely playing out far from public view. The asylum process is inherently sensitive — especially when a person faces criminal charges at home — and many applicants avoid media attention to keep from drawing further scrutiny from the Russian authorities.
Klyga said that he is aware of a particularly troubling case from this summer in which a Russian man fleeing conscription was deported from Lithuania to Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave between the Baltic country and Poland. The man has been outspoken about his opposition to the war and could face prison time. Klyga requested not to publish the man’s name because it could interfere with efforts to provide support to him.
Much of Europe’s hesitation in granting asylum to Russians stems from fears that migration could be used as a backdoor for covert Russian operations, analysts say. With Moscow increasingly accused of orchestrating acts of sabotage across the continent, restricting entry to Russians is seen by some governments as an easy political fix.
“There is this rising pressure on European policymakers to react to this and to do something about this, and one dimension of this debate is about what can be done with migration,” said Simon Papuashvili, program director for Eastern Europe and the Caucasus at the International Partnership for Human Rights, a Brussels-based NGO.
For now, Brussels looks poised to increase restrictions rather than ease them.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas just this week announced that the bloc is considering cutting off visas for former Russian combatants and tightening entry restrictions for tourists .
Her comments came shortly after Germany said Russia was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport last month. One of the suspects in that incident allegedly holds a Russian passport and obtained an Italian tourist visa, German media reported .
“If it is true,” Kallas said of the allegations, “it shows very clearly that visas are a tool of these people who are meaning harm to the European Union.”

title: Moscow Police Detain Yabloko Candidates Running in State Duma Elections
description: Russia’s liberal Yabloko party said Friday that law enforcement authorities in Moscow detained two of its members who are running for seats in the lower-house State Duma.
content:
Russia’s liberal Yabloko party said Friday that law enforcement authorities in Moscow detained two of its members who are running for seats in the lower-house State Duma.
The press service for Yabloko said Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno and Grigory Grishin were detained separately during the day and taken to local police stations.
Both politicians later said they were charged with publicly displaying “extremist” symbols, an administrative offense that has been used against other anti-Kremlin candidates this summer to disqualify them from upcoming elections.
Their detentions come after another Yabloko candidate, Artyom Snegovsky, was detained Tuesday and charged with “discrediting” the Russian military in social media posts. Snegovsky was later released from police custody.
While Russia’s Supreme Court ruled last month to cancel the registration of Yabloko’s federal slate of candidates for parliamentary races later in September, candidates running in single-member districts can still stand for election.
Under Russian election law, half of the State Duma’s 450 seats are distributed among the list of political parties that receive more than 5% of the votes. The remaining 225 seats are given to the winners of elections in single-member constituencies.
At least 19 Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts have so far been disqualified from running due to various violations , according to the exiled news outlet Vyorstka.
Yabloko is Russia’s oldest liberal party and is the only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform.

title: U.S. Special Envoys to Visit Russia and Ukraine This Weekend
description: U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are scheduled to visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend to revive negotiations aimed at ending the war, Russian and Western media reported Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
content:
U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are scheduled to visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend to revive negotiations aimed at ending the war, Russian and Western media reported Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
President Donald Trump later confirmed the trip, saying the two envoys would be “bringing with them a proposal to end the war.” Earlier in the day, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had declined to confirm or deny the report, telling journalists that officials would announce details “when these contacts take place.”
The last round of U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in February, shortly before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran.
Since then, the Kremlin has repeatedly signaled that Witkoff and Kushner could soon visit Moscow again. In June, Peskov said Witkoff and Kushner were “occupied with other matters right now” and vowed that talks would resume when “they become available.”
The two Americans last visited Russia in January, when they held four hours of late-night talks with President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. Putin said this week that “we enjoy working with” Witkoff and Kushner, and added that they were “always welcome” in Moscow.
A source told Reuters that a trip to Ukraine by the special envoys was still under discussion, with Sunday cited as a possible date. It would mark Witkoff’s and Kushner’s first visit to Kyiv since peace talks began under the Trump administration.
“The Russians don’t want them to visit Kyiv and are trying to make them change the plan,” the source was quoted as saying.
The Kyiv Independent, citing its own sources, reported that it was possible U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys may ultimately cancel their trip to Russia and Ukraine after Witkoff allegedly “started to get scared.”
According to those sources, the envoys were planning to arrive in Kyiv by plane despite airspace over the capital remaining closed. But those plans are now in doubt after “Russia did not commit” to pausing its strikes on Ukraine during the visit.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he expected Witkoff and Kushner to hold meetings in Moscow and Kyiv “in the coming days.”
“It is important that America remain actively engaged,” Zelensky said in his nightly video address.
Despite the latest efforts to reboot peace talks, which the Kremlin recently said were on a “deep pause,” a vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine. Both sides have ramped up their attacks in recent weeks, causing extensive damage to commercial and industrial infrastructure.
At the same time, Putin continues to demand that Ukraine give up more territory as a condition for peace, while Ukraine rejects terms that it considers tantamount to surrender.
On Thursday, Putin said there was a “chance” of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

title: The Tate Brothers Have a Russia Problem. They Could Be in Big Trouble.
description: Opinion | The manosphere darlings Andrew and Tristan Tate have been a menace on our feeds for years, earning their scandalous reputation over years of hard work spouting misogyny, trafficking women, having close ties with the Romanian mafia through their cage-fighting and webcam businesses, becoming the faces of modern-day social media misogyny, including being charged with human trafficking.
content:
The manosphere darlings Andrew and Tristan Tate have been a menace on our feeds for years, earning their scandalous reputation over years of hard work spouting misogyny, trafficking women, having close ties with the Romanian mafia through their cage-fighting and webcam businesses, becoming the faces of modern-day social media misogyny, including being charged with human trafficking .
They could now add another charge to their roster of infamy. In late August, Alicia Kearns, the British Conservative MP and former chair of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee, referred both brothers to Counter Terrorism Policing. The trigger was a 40-minute video the Tates published themselves, documenting a June trip to Russia in which the two rode a Soviet tank, threw grenades and fired a flamethrower on a military range. The question is whether they were required to register under the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme, the disclosure regime created by the National Security Act , under which failing to declare that you are acting for a specified foreign power carries up to five years.
No evidence has been produced that the brothers were paid or directed by Moscow. Their representative says the visit was "private and personal," that they received nothing from the Russian state and deliberately stayed away from the St. Petersburg forum that many people assume they visited.
But the possibility of these men acting in the Kremlin’s interests is part of a larger pattern. Rather like the looksmaxxing influencer Braden Eric Peters — better known online as Clavicular — they are a fantastic hotbed of propaganda darlings for the Kremlin due to their large audience reach and their simple needs and wants in return for posting content: money, attention and women.
The Tate brothers epitomize the evolution of how the manosphere has become useful to the Kremlin. It begins with a popular figure spouting seemingly innocuous Kremlin talking points. In a re-upload of an old interview, Andrew would argue the familiar line that NATO has always encroached on Russia following the collapse of the U.S.S.R. and the loss of Central European countries as the buffer states, adding: "when all these countries that were previously U.S.S.R. now now all join the EU, all join NATO, all put in anti-missile systems along their borders [...] we're the aggressive ones." One could only wonder if such discourse would go down well in the presence of his many Romanian friends.
What about his brother, Tristan? He has been doing much the same work, although largely overshadowed by the older Tate. In 2024, Dmitry Medvedev, ex-president of Russia and now a hawk reduced to barking like a rabies patient from his seat on the Security Council, posted that Russia could retaliate against NATO missiles with weapons of mass destruction aimed at Kyiv and NATO facilities, and that this meant World War III. Tristan replied: "We are relying on Russia to save the world." Other narratives spread by the brothers include Russia being a manufactured boogeyman held to account for the crimes of a U.S.S.R. that no longer exists, puzzlement over why Poland should be frightened of it, and, by February 2026, the position that Ukraine must join NATO because Russia would never attack NATO, which rather concedes what happens to countries outside it.
Then the double standard. In a 2023 interview , Andrew recalls his father's bafflement at the Taliban's refusal to be beaten by America: they didn't want pride flags; they wanted to be left alone to be their own people. Tate considers Russia part of that same tradition of resisting outside influence without appearing to notice that the argument works just as well one country to the west. Ukraine also wants to be left alone by Russia, and to be its own people too, but is denied the privilege of being an individual subject. You find the same asymmetry in almost every proponent of these talking points. When Russia resists NATO and the EU, it is because it wants to pursue its own path. When Ukraine resists Russia, there must be someone pulling the strings behind the scenes. As Andrew himself puts it: "so what is [war] for if its not for money and power?"
That’s a fair question, and one he could have answered had he read about how the men surrounding the Kremlin have profited from the war. Despite sanctions, Russian billionaires' combined wealth hit a record $696.5 billion in April 2026, an 11% rise in a year. The state has spent the war nationalizing some 200 companies for reasons ranging from their foreign ownership to the pretext that their 1990s privatization was improper. So: a fundamental double standard. Maybe one of the reasons why the war has persisted into its fifth year is simple to understand: profit.
Next, the influencer undertakes something akin to a christening: a pilgrimage to the Third Rome. In June, the brothers, frozen out of every decent public event in the West, flew to Moscow and were met at the airport by an ensemble of performers, one of the women offering them bread and salt , which Andrew chewed with his mouth open.
No alpha male trip, in which the men took selfies in Red Square and drank cocktails at a rooftop bar, would be complete without cosplaying as soldiers. While still a far cry from their father, Emory Tate, who wore a uniform for a living in the United States Air Force , the two enjoyed a day at the Russian equivalent of Six Flags, riding a T-80BV tank, throwing grenades from a trench and firing a flamethrower on a range in camouflage and Russian flag patches, while the officer running the course joked that whoever finished fastest would get a special medal from the Russian defense minister. Naturally, no propaganda trip is complete without Katyusha, much to our ears' regret.
Then comes the reckoning. The strong hand of the law quickly turned the Tates into simple, meek "betas" like the rest of us, as the brothers admitted in court that the Andrew and Tristan we see on our screens are mere characters. Their properties and luxury cars? Rentals. How surprising and disappointing!
But whatever characters their lawyers now say they were playing, the state has the bigger stick and always did. Instead of sitting in a Miami jail cell because of a tank ride, the brothers are there awaiting extradition on charges brought by women.
Where is Russia in all this? The Russia that met them at the airport with bread and salt? Nowhere to be found, just after Tenet Media , when the Justice Department alleged RT had funnelled nearly $10 million through shell companies to a Nashville firm paying American influencers to make videos, without telling them or their audiences where the money came from. The two RT employees indicted are now safely in Moscow. The company folded. And the influencers who suffered the reputational damage? They are picking up the pieces, as they should.
We've come in many ways to misunderstand the importance of free speech in a unilateral, absolutist manner. Many in Europe who, sometimes rightfully, point to more frivolous cases of prosecutions over social media posts, shiver at the mere mention of a return to a time when the UK government legally penalized pessimism, despair and anti-war sentiment under the Emergency Powers (Defense) Act 1939.
The arrest of the brothers has earned a similar response from their supporters. They think that the Tates’ referral to counter-terror investigators is merely another way to suppress their freedom to express their truth following the initial failure of Romanian authorities to prosecute the brothers due to procedural defects and their travel bans being lifted.
So I asked someone who lives inside that jurisdiction. Imogen Payter heads UK Friends of Ukraine and works across party lines. Saying NATO bears responsibility for the invasion is not in itself a criminal act, she told me. What moves something across that line is coordination with, direction from, funding by or material benefit from a hostile state. Which is why she thinks this story is worth watching. "The issue being raised isn't simply that they have expressed views sympathetic to Russia," she said, but the combination of the statements, the visit, the military-style activities and the unanswered question of the Russian state's involvement. "I certainly agree that the Tate brothers need investigating."
The ground has been moving for months. On July 8, the National Security (State Threats) Act became law, letting the Home Secretary designate bodies engaged in foreign power threat activity, modelled on terrorism proscription, with sentences of up to fourteen years. Days after Kearns wrote her letter, Germany blamed Russia for the Aug. 4 drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, closed Moscow's last consulate general in the country and evicted the Russian House from Berlin. Britain lined up behind Berlin.
Payter reads it the same way: not a government preparing to criminalize pro-Russian opinions, but "a growing recognition that Russia's information warfare is part of a broader campaign against European security."
This is new. For years the British instinct on all of this was a sort of tired shrug: unpleasant, yes, but people are allowed to be wrong in public, especially as the alternative looks worse. What has changed is not the tolerance for opinion, but the willingness to ask what sits underneath it.
That shift has a cost, and the people warning about it are not the Tates' defenders. Because material benefit includes information, Index on Censorship warned that journalists may not interview members of proscribed groups for legitimate purposes for fear of falling foul of the law. Independent reviewers of terrorism legislation said the same of foreign correspondents and NGO workers.
Which brings us to what I suspect the brothers failed to understand about the video they made themselves. The tank isn’t the problem. You can pay to ride a tank, and there are even places in Britain for exactly that. But it is unlikely that the full package, complete with jokes about medals from the defense minister, is something you can buy. And that access, unlike opinion, is precisely what this legislation was written to make visible.
None of which means charges. An intelligence journalist put it to me privately that the authorities have more obvious material to work with: the sex and trafficking charges. Whether the brothers did anything that violated Ukrainian sovereignty and international law is yet to be determined.
But the strongest defense against Russian influence, as Payter puts it, isn't censorship. It is transparency, scrutiny and making sure that people acting on behalf of hostile states cannot pass it off as ordinary political campaigning.

title: Air Tanzania Suspends Flights to Russia Following Zelensky’s Airspace Warning

content:

content:

Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 490 drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

title: Ukraine’s SBU Accuses Russian Volunteer Corps Commander of Plotting to Kill Opposition Figure
description: Ukraine’s SBU security service alleged Thursday that a commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, a unit of far-right Russians fighting alongside Ukrainian forces, was recruited by Moscow to assassinate a Russian opposition figure.
content:
Ukraine’s SBU security service alleged Thursday that a commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, a unit of far-right Russians fighting alongside Ukrainian forces, was recruited by Moscow to assassinate a Russian opposition figure.
In a statement, the SBU, without identifying the commander by name, claimed that the “individual” was in contact with Russia’s FSB security service and tasked with “preparing the assassination” of an opposition figure who was expected to arrive in Ukraine on Aug. 24, when the country celebrates its national day of independence.
The Ukrainian agency said the accused commander gave a confession and provided information that helped it identify other people said to have been involved in the assassination plot. It did not identify the targeted Russian opposition figure.
While the SBU did not explicitly name the Russian Volunteer Corps commander, a confession video attached to its statement appears to show Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of combat operations for the unit.
Kaplunov, who Ukrainian media previously reported was the target of the assassination plot, told Ukraine’s Radio NV that SBU officers “kidnapped” him and forced him to deliver a false confession under duress.
Denying any links to the FSB, Kaplunov accused the SBU of attempting to fabricate charges against senior officials within Ukraine’s HUR military intelligence agency.
In its own statement, the HUR, which directly oversees the Russian Volunteer Corps, warned that a “targeted disinformation campaign” was being carried out against it. It did not specify who was carrying out that alleged campaign.
The apparent infighting follows a shootout between SBU and HUR officers in Kyiv earlier this week.
Ukrainian law enforcement authorities launched a criminal investigation into the armed clash, while President Volodymyr Zelensky has demanded a public explanation for the “absolutely disgraceful situation” from both security agencies.

title: International Equestrian Federation Lifts Restrictions on Russian Riders
description: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russian riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia, the governing body has said.
content:
The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russia n riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia , the governing body has said.
Russia n and Belarusian riders have been barred from representing their countries under their national flags at FEI events since March 2022, though some have competed as neutral athletes.
The FEI said the decision followed the International Olympic Committee's move in July to provisionally lift its suspension of the Russia n Olympic Committee (ROC).
Russia 's equestrian federation said Wednesday that the FEI Council had approved the move after what it described as extensive negotiations between the national body and international officials.
Under the new rules, Russia can host FEI-sanctioned competitions from Oct. 5, subject to compliance with FEI regulations. The restrictions on Russia n national flags, anthems, colors, uniforms and other national identifiers will also be lifted.
"The FEI has also received written confirmation from the Russia n Equestrian Federation that it does not develop equestrian sport or operate equestrian clubs in the Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia regions, nor in Crimea and Sevastopol," an FEI spokesperson said in Wednesday's statement.
The FEI said it would continue to support Ukraine through a relief fund that it established in 2022 "to help address some of the urgent needs of the country's equestrian community."
Other international federations, including aquatics, motorsport, modern pentathlon, wrestling and gymnastics, have also eased restrictions on Russia n and Belarusian athletes.

title: Aerospace Forces General Reportedly Shot and Wounded in Saratov Region
description: A senior Russian Aerospace Forces officer was shot and wounded in the southern Saratov region, law enforcement authorities and Russian media reported Thursday.
content:
A senior Russian Aerospace Forces officer was shot and wounded in the southern Saratov region, law enforcement authorities and Russian media reported Thursday.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, said it opened a criminal probe into attempted murder and arms trafficking following “an attempt on the life of a serviceman” in the city of Engels.
“Cartridge casings and bullets from a firearm were recovered at the scene,” the Investigative Committee said in a statement.
The officer was airlifted to a military hospital in Moscow, law enforcement sources told the newspaper Kommersant.
While authorities did not immediately identify the officer, unverified reports claimed the victim to be Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, who heads a strategic bomber division at Engels-2 airbase.
Russia’s Defense Ministry has not commented on the shooting.
The reports, which The Moscow Times was unable to independently verify, claimed Varpakhovich was shot twice in the torso and the face by a gunman riding a motorcycle and wearing a helmet outside a private cottage.
The shooting occurred after Ukrainian law enforcement authorities pressed formal criminal charges against Varpakhovich in absentia on Monday.
Kyiv accuses Varpakhovich of ordering a fatal missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in the Ukrainian capital in July 2024.
Ukraine has not commented on the shooting in Engels on Thursday.
If confirmed, Varpakhovich would be the seventh Russian general to have been targeted in assassination attempts in nearly two years, according to analysis by the exiled news outlet Meduza.

title: Russian Government Seizes Control of Industrial Fan Producer Ventprom
description: A Sverdlovsk region judge has reportedly ordered the nationalization of Ventprom, Russia’s largest manufacturer of industrial ventilation equipment for mines, tunnels and metros.
content:
A Sverdlovsk region judge has reportedly ordered the nationalization of Ventprom, Russia’s largest manufacturer of industrial ventilation equipment for mines, tunnels and metros.
Yekaterinburg’s Leninsky District Court on Aug. 17 ruled to transfer a 100% stake in the Artyomovsky Machine Engineering Plant Ventprom to the state, according to the Interfax news agency.
“Nothing has changed for us except the shareholder,” a Ventprom spokesperson told Interfax on Thursday.
The government seized the strategic factory after branding its former owners and associates an “extremist organization,” the regional news outlet Vecherniye Vedomosti reported earlier.
The Sverdlovsk region’s deputy prosecutor filed a lawsuit against eight individuals and two foreign companies in connection with the “extremist” designation. They include former Ventprom executives Oleg, Igor and Olga Gorshkov, as well as companies registered in Britain and Germany.
Court records published by Vecherniye Vedomosti show Google and Russia’s communications watchdog Roskomnadzor as being among third parties listed in the court case.
Defense lawyers declined to discuss specifics of the case with the news outlet due to client confidentiality. Unverified reports claimed the “extremist” designation stemmed from a bank transfer that was made to a Ukrainian citizen, as well as to the fact that Gorshkov has lived outside of Russia since 2023.
Vecherniye Vedomosti said Google was likely drawn into litigation since one of the Ukrainians listed in the case, Viktor Litovchenko, is a popular blogger on YouTube, which the tech giant owns. Neither Litovchenko nor the second Ukrainian, Natalia Prushinskaya, reportedly held shares in Ventprom.
Ventprom, which supplies ventilation systems to the Moscow, St. Petersburg, Novosibirsk and Minsk metro networks, as well as to Lukoil, Alrosa and Rusal, reported more than 3 billion rubles (almost $35 million) in revenue last year.

title: Russia Can Manage Its Growing Deficit, Putin Says
description: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia's budget deficit, which grew by 40% in the first half of this year to reach 2.8% of GDP, poses no "critical" risk for the economy and remains manageable.
content:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia's budget deficit, which grew by 40% in the first half of this year to reach 2.8% of GDP, poses no "critical" risk for the economy and remains manageable.
"Considering that we have one of the lowest levels of national debt in the world, there is nothing critical here," the Kremlin leader said at the annual Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
The costs of Russia's war against Ukraine have gradually risen since Putin ordered the full-scale invasion in February 2022. In recent years, the government has had to raise taxes and increase borrowing to help finance the military.
Russia's official deficit target for this year is 1.6% of GDP.
The growing budget deficit and new inflation risks are major factors that Central Bank policymakers are weighing ahead of next week's key rate meeting. For months, businesses have pushed for the regulator to lower the key rate, which currently stands at 14%.
Analysts polled by Reuters this week said they expect Russia's Central Bank to hold the key rate.
At the Eastern Economic Forum on Thursday, Putin said it was important that high borrowing costs not hamper business investment too much, but added that it remains critical for monetary policy to address inflation risks.
Annual inflation in Russia stood at 6.3% as of Aug. 31, according to the Economic Development Ministry.
Countering claims by businesses that credit has become off-limits for some, Putin said the government has developed multiple loan programs to support firms even in the high-rate environment.

title: Norway Seizes Russian Ship to Enforce $4.2Bln Claim by Ukraine’s Naftogaz
description: Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.2 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets following the 2014 annexation of Crimea, officials said late on Wednesday.
content:
Norway has seized a Russia n ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.2 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets following the 2014 annexation of Crimea, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according to Covington, the U.S. law firm representing Naftogaz.
The Svalbard governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held i n Svalbard, adding: "The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel."
Russia 's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. "We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.
It was not immediately clear how many passengers and crew were on board .
Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea. A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.2 billion plus interest and legal costs.
" Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said.
Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland and is governed under a 1920 treaty that also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia , to settle there without a visa.
The ship arrived on Tuesday in Barentsburg, a Russia n-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago, with a party of Russia n scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.
Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda radio, said the vessel had docked without incident and the expedition members had headed ashore. News did not emerge until Wednesday evening that the ship had been seized.
"This seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Gorbunov wrote in a piece for Komsomolskaya Pravda.
"For the time being, the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg. It is completely unclear how long this ban will last," the journalist added.
Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russia n-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating the ship's arrival in Svalbard en route to Barentsburg, a Russia n mining settlement, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a Norwegian court for the vessel to be arrested there and subject to a compulsory sale.
The application was approved by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on Monday. In its ruling, it required the governor of Svalbard to enforce the order, supervise the vessel and ensure that it is not moved.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement measures across multiple jurisdictions, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom and Finland, where Russia n assets have been frozen. Russia is appealing the process, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russia n assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.

title: Russia Will Close Germany’s Goethe-Institut Cultural Centers, Lavrov Says
description: Russia will close Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Thursday, after German officials ordered the closure of the Russian cultural center in Berlin as retaliation for a drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle Airport that they blamed on Moscow.
content:
Russia will close Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Thursday, after German officials ordered the closure of the Russian cultural center in Berlin as retaliation for a drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle Airport that they blamed on Moscow.
Germany also ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn in response to what it said was an attempted attack at the airport. This week, President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow for the incident.
Lavrov said Russia would close the Goethe-Institut centers in the cities of Moscow, St Petersburg and Yekaterinburg as retaliation for the closure of the Russian cultural center in Berlin.
"Of course, they will be closed after our cultural center was kicked out," Lavrov said on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
The centers had stayed open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West," he added.
Russia 's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

title: Nearly 9K Ukrainian Drones Targeted Moscow in August, Mayor Says

content:

Russia’s Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin said that civil aviation authorities were working with the military to prevent “any significant disruption” to domestic air travel.

Moscow’s Simonovsky District Court is expected to rule on pre-trial detention measures, her attorney told the news outlet RBC.
The charge of spreading false information about the military carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Moniava is the founder of the Moscow-based charity “Lighthouse,” which operates hospices for seriously ill children and young adults in the Russian capital and surrounding region.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moniava created a foundation that provided shelter, medical supplies and food to people fleeing from the war. The organization also later helped Armenians fleeing from conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh, as well as Russians displaced from the Kursk and Belgorod regions.
That foundation suspended operations last September due to the dwindling number of refugees arriving in Moscow and the Moscow region.
Moniava was previously detained in January and in February. She was fined 45,000 rubles ($520) after being found guilty of “discrediting” the Russian military in posts on Telegram.
Despite facing pressure from the authorities, Moniava has refused to leave Russia.
“If I leave, critically ill children will end up in nursing homes and intensive care units for longer periods. Knowing that, I doubt I could live happily in some other country,” she wrote earlier this year.

title: ‘Complete Nonsense’: Putin Dismisses Mobilization Rumors
description: President Vladimir Putin has dismissed growing speculation that he plans to announce a new round of military mobilization following State Duma and regional elections later this month. “It’s complete nonsense.
content:
President Vladimir Putin has dismissed growing speculation that he plans to announce a new round of military mobilization following State Duma and regional elections later this month.
“It’s complete nonsense. It’s an information attack on Russia,” Putin told reporters late on Tuesday in his first remarks on the rumors.
As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has stalled in its fifth year, questions are once again mounting over whether Putin could resort to a politically costly mobilization to boost his military’s manpower.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected reports of an impending draft, characterizing them as a foreign disinformation campaign.
Last week, Ukrainian intelligence agencies warned that Russia was “drawing up plans” to mobilize 600,000 men this year and in 2027.
Putin declared a “partial” mobilization of 300,000 reservists in September 2022, a move that was similarly dismissed just days before it was announced. That call-up triggered a mass exodus of draft-eligible men from Russia.
Since then, the Kremlin has gradually made legal changes that some observers view as preparations for a fresh wave of mobilization.
The Russian military has moved to a digital draft registry with automatic travel bans, shifted to year-round draft processing , and now allows reservists to be deployed to guard “critical infrastructure” without being formally called up to serve.
However, some experts caution that another mass mobilization would encounter logistical hurdles and fail to address challenges on the front line. At the same time, observers point to the fact that Putin’s “partial” mobilization order remains in effect, suggesting Putin might not need to formally announce a new draft.

title: Russia Says It Won’t Let Ukraine Disrupt Air Travel After Zelensky Warning
description: Russian transportation authorities on Wednesday vowed to prevent any disruptions to domestic air travel after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned the day before that Kyiv's drone attacks were making Russian airspace too dangerous for flying.
content:
Russian transportation authorities on Wednesday vowed to prevent any disruptions to domestic air travel after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned the day before that Kyiv's drone attacks were making Russian airspace too dangerous for flying.
Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin said that civil aviation authorities are "constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have solutions for all of this," as quoted by the news agency Interfax.
"We are working in close contact with the Defense Ministry and the Russia n National Guard. And I believe that we will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation ," Nikitin added.
Following Zelensky's warning, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv had officially notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace is unsafe for commercial flights.
Those comments appeared to have an almost immediate impact on air travel inside Russia. On Wednesday, Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport showed 21 canceled flights and 235 delays, while Vnukovo airport saw 22 canceled flights and 94 delays, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Turkish carrier Pegasus Airlines said it had canceled some flights to Russia for "technical and operational" reasons but did not provide further information.
Vnukovo airport said Pegasus Airlines had canceled six arriving and six departing flights at the hub on Tuesday. The carrier said overnight flights into Wednesday would be impacted, but other ongoing flights were "operating as scheduled."
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300 kilometers (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were near-certain through 2026, including near Moscow and St Petersburg.
"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russia n territory," the alert said. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."

title: Germany Shutters Russian Consulate, Berlin Culture Center After Blaming Moscow for Airport Drone Attack
description: The German government said on Tuesday that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russian cultural center in Berlin.
content:
The German government said on Tuesday that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russia n cultural center in Berlin.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said intelligence findings indicated that individuals involved in the attack were acting on behalf of Russia n state agencies.
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the offenses and intelligence findings establish Russia n responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," he said.
Standing alongside Dobrindt, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany did not view Leipzig as an isolated incident.
"It fits into a broader pattern of Russia n hybrid operations in Europe," he said.
Wadephul said Germany's response would include closing Russia 's consulate general in Bonn and terminating its agreement with the Russia n House cultural center in Berlin.
"Germany remains secure, and Germany will defend itself against adversaries who seek to create insecurity," Wadephul said. "We will not allow Russia 's attacks to divide or intimidate us in our social cohesion."
Russia 's ambassador to Germany was summoned on Tuesday.
Responding to Germany's announcement, Russia n Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin's "anti- Russia n action," according to Interfax news agency. She did not elaborate.
The Russia n Embassy in Berlin had previously dismissed such accusations as "fabricated provocation" and as "a new wave of anti- Russia n hysteria in Germany."
"If such serious accusations are being made, they should be supported by evidence. To my knowledge, none has been presented," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Kyrgyzstan.
"It is clear that Germany is pursuing a path of further escalation," Peskov added.

title: How Russia Developed the First Killer AI Drone Despite Struggling in the AI Race
description: Opinion | On July 6 in Zaporozhzhia, a drone with no connection to its original operator determined targets on its own and delivered a lethal payload, killing three civilians.
content:
On July 6 in Zaporozhzhia, a drone with no connection to its original operator determined targets on its own and delivered a lethal payload, killing three civilians . The incident may be the first case of Russia deploying a drone that could target and detonate based entirely on determinations made by an onboard AI.
Russia has crossed this threshold in autonomous weaponry despite its position as a laggard in frontier models. By investing heavily in more narrow use cases than the generalized models that dominate headlines, Russia is carving out a niche as a leader in applying machine learning to acts of war.
Putin understood early on the importance of artificial intelligence, declaring in 2017 that “whoever leads in AI will rule the world.” He poured billions into the development of Russian AI, built partnerships between state institutions and tech firms and hosted international conferences.
But Russia’s foreign policy undermined the drive for AI leadership at every turn. The invasion of Crimea cut Russian academics off from the international community just as the AI revolution was beginning, and the full-scale invasion sent tech talent fleeing months before the launch of ChatGPT-3 set off the chatbot boom. Russia never came close to China or the United States in its ability to release the powerful language models that have become nearly synonymous with AI, with firms like Yandex relying on retrained versions of Alibaba’s Qwen and Sber’s GigaChat, Russia’s only foundational model, years behind the leaders in the sector.
Instead of competing on language models, Russia has focused extensively on how smaller, less generalized models can be applied to the battlefield. The result was an intense focus on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), a form of machine learning that breaks images into constituent features and, after millions of examples, can classify the patterns. GosNIIAS, the State Research Institute for Aviation Systems, launched Platform-GNS in 2023, a system for simplifying the training of CNNs, and made the system freely available to any qualifying enterprise within the Russian defense-industrial base. GosNIIAS supplemented the training platform with an extensive dataset of battlefield and target imagery that partners can use as training sets for their models. Freely sharing the foundations for model training creates a broad ecosystem for attempting new approaches to battlefield challenges.
Complementing the public-private partnership between GosNIIAS and drone makers, developers on the Habr forum publicly shared tutorials and guidelines for training CNNs for military and military-adjacent use cases. The field coalesced around an approach called You Only Look Once (YOLO), which is able to analyze the entirety of an image at once rather than feature-by-feature, yielding far more efficient training and classification. YOLO is freely available as a Python library and has been a favorite for detecting images in video since its launch in 2015. One Habr post shows how YOLO can make battlefield determinations based on under 20,000 images. These optimized image detection models require only a fraction of the power and memory to execute as CNNs, which in turn required only a fraction of the power and memory of language models.
To make any of that useful on the battlefield, however, the models needed to fit within the constraints of lightweight drones already constrained by the demands of power and computation for flying and maneuvering. The larger the model, the more power required and the more weight the drone must bear. The more power, the more heat generated and the more space and weight needed still. Russia has applied several engineering approaches to reduce the power and heat needed, such as activating the models only in the terminal stage of the flight and finding the appropriate balance between model compression and accuracy. But sufficiently efficient chips solve the constraints by executing more computational processes and holding more memory while requiring less power to do so.
At the time of writing, NVIDIA’s Jetson Orin Nano is the only chip with the required performance numbers and was the chip found in the drones in Zaporozhzhia. The United States, along with most Western countries, banned the sale of powerful chips to Russia shortly after the full-scale invasion. But Russia quickly found alternative imports. NVIDIA chips are readily available on secondary markets in Singapore, and a report by Kateryna Bondar at CSIS revealed that the majority of electronic components used in Russian drones are of Western origin. Russia blends these Western devices with ones from China, like the Leetop A603 motherboard used on the Zaporozhzhia drone. China’s chips are rapidly catching up as well, with the Beijing-based manufacturer Cambricon expected to produce chips on par with Jetson Orin Nano within the next one to two years.
The progress by Russian drone makers, researchers and developers on Habr all point to a far expanded use of fully autonomous lethal weaponry as the war progresses. The models will continue to advance both in accuracy and efficiency as they have over the past few years. The chips needed to mount the models will become more energy efficient, more performant and hold more memory. Soon, they will be developed by a Russian partner. Russia has little prospect of catching up on large language models. But in applying AI to lethal means, the Russian tech community is already changing the nature of the war.

title: Man Shot Dead After Attacking People at Moscow Church
description: An allegedly mentally ill man was shot and killed by a bystander outside a Moscow church after attacking people and badly injuring at least one paramedic with a shovel, Russian media reported Tuesday.
content:
An allegedly mentally ill man was shot and killed by a bystander outside a Moscow church after attacking people and badly injuring at least one paramedic with a shovel, Russian media reported Tuesday.
Eyewitnesses told state news agencies that the assailant began harassing churchgoers of the Church of the Holy Myrrh-Bearing Women at around 9:50 a.m. Moscow time in the southeastern Maryino district.
The 29-year-old initially fled to a nearby park when priests, who purportedly knew the man, called for a psychiatric emergency team, the Kommersant newspaper reported , adding that a regular ambulance arrived instead.
“A really young female medic was trying to help when he grabbed a shovel and started striking her on the head,” an eyewitness told the news agency TASS.
The medic was reportedly hospitalized in critical condition, while a woman who works at the church and a passerby who tried to defend her were also hurt.
Another bystander shot the man when another ambulance team and National Guard troops were sent to detain him, according to Kommersant.
The shooter was arrested. Law enforcement sources told TASS that the weapon, a non-lethal rubber bullet firearm, was legally owned.
Moscow police told the news outlet Podyom that they had not been informed about the incident.
Kommersant reported that the man began regularly attending church after running into financial trouble with his ad agency. He was at some point reportedly diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and placed on a registry at a local psychiatric facility.
Church staff said the man had received regular medication and was usually calm.
The publication reported that the man was suffering from depression over the past two weeks and, on the morning of the attack, asked for an ambulance after complaining of hallucinations and “voices in his head.”
The Moscow Times was unable to independently verify the reports.
