title: Why the Middle East Oil Shock Failed to Save Russia’s Budget
description: In the early weeks of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, observers were quick to declare Russia a major beneficiary of the conflict.
content:
In the early weeks of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, observers were quick to declare Russia a major beneficiary of the conflict. After all, the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted roughly a fifth of global oil supplies, forcing countries to scramble for alternative sources and turning attention toward Russian crude.
Six months into the war, however, Russia’s windfall looks surprisingly meager.
During the first seven months of the year, the federal budget collected 4.6 trillion rubles ($55.2 billion) in oil and gas taxes. While undoubtedly large, that figure represents only an extra 127.6 billion rubles ($1.52 billion) over original budget projections.
Compared to previous years, Russia still faces a shortfall. Energy revenues between January and July were down 20% compared to the same period last year, and down 35% compared to the 2022 windfall that preceded tighter Western sanctions.
Part of the reason revenues fell short of expectations is that global energy markets stabilized faster than predicted.
Iran’s initial closure of the Strait of Hormuz did boost the appeal of Russian crude, pushing the price of the flagship Urals blend from $56.60 a barrel in February up to $94.50 in March and $112.30 in April, according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
However, the scramble for oil soon lost urgency. Energy suppliers found workarounds to route cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz despite the effective closure, while alternative transit networks through the Gulf of Oman, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal helped stabilize supply lines.
At the same time, China slashed its imports of crude oil and drew from its huge stockpiles, which removed an enormous amount of pressure from global markets.
Some countries also switched to using alternative energy sources like coal.
As market panic subsided, the price premium on Russian crude narrowed, with Urals dropping back to $63 per barrel in June and $60 in July.
A relatively strong ruble also played a role in Russia’s lackluster windfall.
Russia sells its oil in foreign currencies and assesses energy taxes based on dollar-denominated benchmarks. When the ruble strengthens alongside high global oil prices, each dollar earned converts into fewer rubles for the domestic treasury.
Russia’s 2026 budget was built on an assumed exchange rate of 92.2 rubles to the dollar. Instead, the actual average rate over the first seven months was much stronger, at 76.5 rubles to the dollar.
Because a stronger ruble yields fewer domestic rubles per foreign dollar earned, higher dollar sales still failed to generate the total ruble revenue the government had budgeted.
Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries and supply lines this spring and summer are also likely to have made a dent in energy revenues.
As Russia’s Central Bank acknowledged in a recent report , damage to refineries and transportation infrastructure led to a drop in petroleum product output and reduced demand in raw crude.
Looking ahead, analysts expect Russia’s full-year energy profits to remain subdued. Moscow-based analyst Kirill Rodionov argues that even with ongoing attacks between Iran and the U.S., oil prices are unlikely to return to the spring peak of around $110 per barrel.
“At best, the budget’s oil and gas revenues will break even with last year,” Rodionov said. “Under the most likely scenario, they will fall below 2025 levels.”
Analyst Pavel Ryabov goes further, warning that 2026 energy revenues could sink to levels not seen since 2020. With war spending having already driven the government deficit to 6.5 trillion rubles ($78 billion) — nearly double the full-year target — Moscow will have to lean far more aggressively on the non-energy domestic sector.
“The budget is becoming less dependent on oil and gas,” Ryabov said , “and increasingly dependent on the state’s ability to squeeze tax revenue out of the domestic economy.”

title: 7 Injured in Krasnoyarsk Region School Attack
description: A seventh-grade student attacked staff and classmates at a school in the Krasnoyarsk region town of Kansk, injuring seven people on the first day back to school on Tuesday.
content:
A seventh-grade student attacked staff and classmates at a school in the Krasnoyarsk region town of Kansk, injuring seven people on the first day back to school on Tuesday.
Five children and two adults were treated at a local hospital and discharged for outpatient care, the regional health ministry told the RBC news outlet.
Regional investigators confirmed they launched a criminal probe into the “incident,” saying they were establishing the circumstances and determining the motives behind the “crime committed by the minor.”
The attack occurred at School No. 2 in Kansk, which is located 230 kilometers (143 miles) east of Krasnoyarsk and 3,350 kilometers (2,082 miles) from Moscow.
Unverified reporting by Telegram news channels with links to Russia’s security services claimed that the 13-year-old student discharged pepper spray and drew a knife. One of the teachers was reportedly stabbed in the back, while all seven victims sustained burns to the face and eyes.
“Her eyes were wild,” one of the eyewitnesses was quoted as saying, describing the girl’s frantic behavior before the assault.
Another student’s mother reportedly tackled and pushed the attacker into the hallway. One of the Telegram news channels claimed the girl had been bullied at school.
The Moscow Times was unable to independently verify these reports.
Russia saw an uptick in attacks at schools and universities in the 2025-26 academic year.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, opened eight criminal probes into school attacks committed by teenagers in the first half of 2026, the agency’s chief, Alexander Bastrykin, said in June.

title: Bomb Threats Force Evacuations at Russian Schools
description: A wave of false bomb threats triggered mass evacuations at schools, kindergartens, hospitals and museums across at least nine Russian regions, local officials and media reported Tuesday.
content:
A wave of false bomb threats triggered mass evacuations at schools, kindergartens, hospitals and museums across at least nine Russian regions, local officials and media reported Tuesday.
In the Leningrad region, Governor Alexander Drozdenko said “a dozen” schools, kindergartens and hospitals responded to bomb scares. The hoaxes came amid Day of Knowledge celebrations that mark the start of the new school year every Sept. 1.
“We can’t ignore these threats, even though we understand the enemy’s goal to… ruin the holiday for children and adults,” Drozdenko wrote on Telegram, likely a reference to Ukraine.
St. Petersburg and Leningrad region police told the Fontanka news outlet that “more than 100 institutions” received false threats.
In Moscow, at least four museums, including the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, evacuated visitors or temporarily closed for what they called “technical reasons.”
A government building in the Far Eastern Zabaikalsky region and a number of hospitals in the central republic of Tatarstan were also reportedly evacuated .
Fake bomb threats were also reported across the Ural Mountains, the Yamal-Nenets autonomous district, the Orenburg region and the Krasnoyarsk region.
Mass bomb threats, which the Kremlin referred to as “telephone terrorism,” have periodically plagued Russian cities in the years before and since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Russian Ambassador to U.K. Ends His Tenure
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday confirmed the end of Ambassador Andrei Kelin’s posting to Britain as it sought to downplay speculation over whether Moscow was downgrading diplomatic representation in London amid tensions over support for Ukraine. “Andrei Vladimirovich Kelin has wrapped up his planned tenure as ambassador,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said during a weekly press briefing.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday confirmed the end of Ambassador Andrei Kelin’s posting to Britain as it sought to downplay speculation over whether Moscow was downgrading diplomatic representation in London amid tensions over support for Ukraine.
“Andrei Vladimirovich Kelin has wrapped up his planned tenure as ambassador,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said during a weekly press briefing.
She said President Vladimir Putin would appoint Kelin’s replacement “in due course,” saying the process is “moving along at its own pace following the set procedures.”
Zakharova urged against “politicizing” Kelin’s exit, but noted that his tenure comes during an “extremely difficult period” in bilateral ties.
“He worked hard to protect our country’s interests and keep the lines of communication open. That was despite Britain’s efforts to completely dismantle bilateral relations,” she told reporters.
Kelin’s tenure between November 2019 and July 2026 spanned the Covid-19 pandemic, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and a ban on Russian diplomats from entering the British parliament.
Russia’s chargé d’affaires now heads the diplomatic mission until the appointment of a new ambassador.
Kelin’s departure after more than seven years in the post prompted media speculation — denied by the embassy — that Moscow was downgrading diplomatic relations with Britain.
Britain is a leading ally of Ukraine and provides it with weapons including missiles and drones. Russia warned Britain last month that it would face unspecified “consequences” for supplying drones that were used by Ukraine to attack Russian territory.

title: Ukrainian Drone Attack Sparks Fire at Ust-Luga Port
description: A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at northwestern Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major hub for oil exports, local authorities said early Tuesday.
content:
A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at northwestern Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major hub for oil exports, local authorities said early Tuesday.
Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defense units intercepted 52 drones during a four-hour assault over the region.
“Damage and fire were recorded in the Ust-Luga port area as a result of the drone attack,” he wrote on Telegram, adding later that there were no casualties.
By around 9:30 a.m. Moscow time, Drozdenko said the fire was extinguished.
Ust-Luga, Russia’s largest shipping terminal on the Baltic Sea and second-largest nationwide behind Novorossiysk, was previously attacked by Ukrainian drones and caught fire on Aug. 14.
According to Reuters, Ust-Luga handles 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Last year, more than 32.8 million metric tons of refined products were exported through the port.
Elsewhere, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said at least 21 drones were intercepted on approach to the capital overnight Tuesday.
In the southwestern Belgorod region, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev reported one death and 16 injuries following shelling and drone strikes over the past 24 hours.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 516 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed at least 12 people in Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, local officials said .

title: Bessent Reportedly Tells Russian Finance Minister No Economic Lifelines Until Ukraine War Ends
description: U.S.
content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov on Monday that Washington will not grant Russia economic relief or negotiate side agreements until Moscow ends its war against Ukraine, a source told Reuters.
The meeting between Bessent and Siluanov took place on the sidelines of a G20 summit of finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina. The United States currently holds the rotating G20 presidency.
Siluanov's unexpected visit, his first in-person attendance at a G20 event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, drew immediate criticism from European officials.
"Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a signal I find troubling," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters.
Klingbeil said he would have preferred a clear U.S. stance denying Siluanov a regular guest platform.
Earlier, a U.S. official told Reuters that the focus of the Bessent-Siluanov meeting was President Donald Trump's peace plan for Ukraine. Russia 's Finance Ministry said the two officials discussed economic cooperation within the G20 framework.
However, when Siluanov tried to discuss areas of mutual interest, the source said Bessent interrupted him, emphasizing that "nothing is possible until the war is over."
Asked about Siluanov's attendance, White House spokesman Kush Desai told AFP that the Trump administration has been working with Russia to push for a peace deal that "would stop the endless bloodshed that the president has really condemned."
"The president and the administration will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to, to further that," Desai said. "That's what we're working on here at the G20."
Includes reporting from AFP and Reuters.

title: Russia’s Economic Doomsayers Were Wrong. So Were the Optimists.
description: Opinion | A review of the predictions made by experts from 2022 to 2026 shows, first, that nobody produced an accurate forecast.
content:
A review of the predictions made by experts from 2022 to 2026 shows, first, that nobody produced an accurate forecast. And second, that the mistakes of loyalist analysts were no greater than those of their colleagues who do not depend on the Putin regime.
By many indications, Russia’s period of stagnation that has existed almost since the middle of 2024 is now coming to an end. Understandably, experts are trying to predict what will come next.
It seems plausible to suppose that those who, over the years of the war, more accurately predicted the zigzags of the Russian economy will manage better this time too. So let us familiarize ourselves with how they fared up to now.
Within weeks of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, economic experts split into two main camps: the “Collapse Party” and the “Stagnation Party.”
There is a third group, the “Triumph Party,” which is too small to be worth discussing. Among those constantly present in the public sphere, the most with his permanent forecast that Russia stands on the threshold of “colossal economic growth” — usually 10-15% a year. There’s no point entertaining his ridiculous predictions, so we should focus on the debate between collapse and stagnation.
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the West cut it off from SWIFT, seized any reserves it could get hold of, fairly quickly curtailed purchases of gas and oil and, to the extent it could, blocked supplies to Russia of numerous intermediate products and goods on which its national economy depended.
The Russian economy should have collapsed if it clung to its pre-war assumptions. If it adapted rapidly to the new circumstances, it could instead get away with stagnation.
In March 2022, most economists were in the Collapse Party. Knowledgeable people did not spare the public a catalogue of the economic horrors to come.
Sergei Guriev warned that the war would cause the largest economic decline since the early 1990s and that the Kremlin wouldn’t direct any women to the task of softening the shock, using it to fund the military instead.
Oleg Itskhoki warned that despite Russia’s huge size, large population and army, it had a weak economy that was greatly exposed to the outside world. Isolation would be “catastrophic for everyone.” Konstantin Sonin even warned that Russians could expect key industries like food production to be nationalized.
Most international economic organizations believed Russia would collapse. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development , the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Goldman Sachs predicted a 10% fall in Russian GDP in 2022. Goldman Sachs predicted the same amount. Barclays predicted 12.4%. The Institute of International Finance predicted 15%. The most cautious of all was Bloomberg Economics under Alexander Isakov, who predicted a 9% contraction.
Those predictions seem generous compared to some of the most dire . Yevgeny Kogan warned of a 15-18% fall in GDP, while Oleg Derepaska suggested the crisis could be three times worse than in 1998.
Russia’s two leading state analytical services presented the public with their expectations in March 2022. They too painted them in gloomy colours, though didn’t go so far as to predict a collapse.
The Central Bank, after surveying 35 loyalist experts and averaging their forecasts, reported that inflation in the first year of the war was expected to be 20% (in reality , it hit 12%), while GDP was expected to fall by 8% (in reality, it fell by only 1.4%). The government-adjacent Centre for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting (CMASF) believed that the economy would decline by 6.6%. For the following year, 2023, both agencies predicted that the decline would slow and Russia would gradually stagnate.
Two experts stood out quite noticeably from this consensus.
First, Dmitry Nekrasov pointed out that many Ukrainians and opposition-minded Russians were in a bubble with a distorted view of the real conditions of the Russian economy. Second, Andrei Klepach suggested that after an initial panic, the ruble would strengthen against the dollar as Russian energy exports continued, adapting to the new reality. The danger, he thought, was that household incomes could fall by 4-7% if the government didn’t enact support measures against surging inflation.
Perhaps Nekrasov is insufficiently academic for a professional economist and Klepach is too much of a regime loyalist for one to sympathize with when he was fired after his recent warnings of a social and economic crisis were leaked. But thanks to their impartiality and knowledge of their subject, their approach to what was happening in the Russian economy proved the most promising.
By the end of 2022, most analysts no longer doubted that Russia’s economy wouldn’t collapse any time soon. The “stagnation party” was gaining members. The evolution of Vladislav Inozemtsev’s assessments is characteristic of this. His initial assumptions that the Russian economy was heading toward “dying by winter” were replaced at the beginning of 2023 with expectations of slow decline.
Since I myself engage in economic commentary, I will also say something about my own evolution.
In March 2022, of all the forecasts, I considered the CMASF report predicting a gradual decline to be the most convincing prediction.
I assumed then that this scenario was achievable only if military operations were suspended and at least some sanctions were relaxed. But in reality, neither of those things happened and the Russian economy adjusted to the new reality even earlier than CMASF expected.
By autumn 2022, it appeared that Putin’s economic advisors had quite some talent at helping the economy cope. There was a surprise for us analysts: Putinomics flourished in 2023-24, with early signs emerging in mid-2022.
Over just those two years, GDP grew by a full 9%, while monetary incomes adjusted for inflation rose by as much as 15%. Could anyone who wasn’t a pro-Kremlin sycophant have predicted this?
Even while this uptick was taking place, experts continued their pessimistic assessments. In four scenarios, CMASF even predicted a decline of between 2% and 6% for 2023. The Central Bank, which was less close to the authorities, was kinder and placed GDP fluctuations in a range from -1% to +1%.
Nekrasov believed there would be neither noticeable growth nor decline in 2023. Klepach expected “recovery growth” to begin only in the second half of the year. But his subordinates at the VEB Institute had already announced in March 2023 the “resumption of economic growth” and apparently became the first professionals to do so.
Overall, nobody properly predicted this strange two-year flourishing. Nor could anyone explain its scale, either. It began and persisted just as unexpectedly as it ended. Much remained unclear. Explaining all these fluctuations solely through jumps in Elvira Nabiullina’s interest rate somehow seems far too simple.
We should now turn our attention to the most pressing current issue. How close are we now to a crisis and how will unfold?
Whether we like it or not, among analysts it is simply impossible to find anyone who, during this war, flawlessly foresaw every successive turn in the Russian economy. There are only those who have demonstrated conscientiousness and competence.
The recent arguments about Russia’s decline made by one such expert, Klepach, look all the more weighty because his previous forecasts were more complimentary than most others, despite the tendency of assessments from within Russia to be overly rosy.
The trend among both former camps is toward greater pessimism. That consensus, like all consensuses, is not necessarily correct. Nor does it necessarily reflect the latest shifts in Russia. Pressure on the analysts who remain there is growing rapidly, so much so that they are silent about that pressure itself. So I simply hope that, since we now know much more about Russia than we did at the beginning of 2022, we will make fewer serious mistakes this time. All anyone can really promise is that there will be no fewer surprises.

title: European Forces Intercept Russian ‘Shadow Fleet’ Tanker in Mediterranean
description: A European naval mission boarded a Russia-linked oil tanker suspected of sailing under a false flag in the Mediterranean over the weekend, the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said Monday.
content:
A European naval mission boarded a Russia-linked oil tanker suspected of sailing under a false flag in the Mediterranean over the weekend, the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said Monday.
Personnel operating under the Mediterranean naval initiative Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI boarded the MV SUN on Sunday for “flag verification,” Kallas wrote in a post on X.
“This is the sixth suspected shadow fleet vessel boarded by our EU operations in recent months,” she said, referring to vessels with opaque ownership used to bypass Western sanctions against Russia.
She said EU defense ministers plan to discuss “actions against the shadow fleet” at their meeting in Ireland on Tuesday.
In July, the EU adopted a mechanism allowing member states to confiscate and sell Russian oil carried aboard shadow fleet vessels attempting to evade the bloc’s sanctions.
President Vladimir Putin this month vowed to retaliate in kind if European countries carried out plans to seize Russian commercial vessels.
Putin, who previously said the Russian Defense Ministry had received instructions to prepare a response, has slammed previous interceptions of Russia-linked vessels as “piracy.”
EUNAVFOR MED Irini is an EU naval mission first ​launched in 2020 to enforce a UN arms embargo on Libya. EU governments have since broadened its scope, authorizing ​it to conduct verification boardings.
The EU has sanctioned around 600 ships suspected of being part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” network.

title: Russia Reports Hottest July on Record
description: Russia experienced its hottest July on record this summer, the country’s national meteorological service, Rosgidromet, said Monday.
content:
Russia experienced its hottest July on record this summer, the country’s national meteorological service, Rosgidromet, said Monday.
Nationwide average temperatures in July surpassed the previous record set in 2010, when the average temperature exceeded the norm by 7.8 degrees Celsius.
“July was the hottest in our country for the entire period of instrumental observations since 1891,” Rosgidromet chief Yury Simonov said at a press conference.
He did not say how much warmer on average this year’s record-setting July was, according to the Interfax news agency.
Simonov noted that regional temperatures exceeded seasonal norms by 4 C in northern Siberia, the southern Urals and the Far East republic of Sakha.
Simonov attributed the historic heat to a stationary high-pressure system that trapped warm air over northern Russia and prevented cooler air with rain from moving in from the west.
“This is a very strong anomaly for such northern parts of the country,” Simonov said.
While vast parts of Russia sweltered, Simonov said residents of Moscow largely saw cooler weather as the capital recorded an average summer temperature of just 0.9 C above the norm.
Russia is warming 2.5 times faster than the rest of the world, fueling more extreme weather events across the country.

title: Putin Arrives in Kyrgyzstan for SCO Summit
description: BISHKEK, Kyrgyzstan — President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Monday to attend an annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), as well as a series of bilateral meetings with the leaders of China, India and other nations.
content:
BISHKEK, Kyrgyzstan — President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Monday to attend an annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), as well as a series of bilateral meetings with the leaders of China, India and other nations.
A Moscow Times reporter observed a heavy police presence and traffic jams in the capital Bishkek ahead of the Russian president’s arrival.
Putin will first meet Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss the long-delayed Power of Siberia 2 natural gas pipeline project, followed by a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Those first two meetings, as well as a third with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, are part of the Russian leader’s nine bilateral talks with foreign leaders that will extend through Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Putin will join other heads of state at the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games, a biennial cultural and athletic event featuring traditional Central Asian sports such as horseback archery, falconry and mounted wrestling.
On the sidelines of the SCO summit, Putin will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian for the first time since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February 2026.
Putin will also discuss Black Sea security and the war in Ukraine with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. In addition, he will meet with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan to discuss Yerevan’s growing pivot toward the EU and the arrests of Armenia’s pro-Russian opposition figures.
Putin traveled to Bishkek with a “ compact ” seven-member delegation that includes Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, presidential aides Maxim Oreshkin and Yury Ushakov, as well as Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, SCO coordinator Bakhtiyor Khakimov and Russian Ambassador to Kyrgyzstan Sergei Vakulov.
The 10-member SCO bloc was founded in 2001 by Russia and China to counter Western influence across Eurasia. Its other members include India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus and four Central Asian republics.
Following the SCO’s final session and press conference in Bishkek, Putin is scheduled to fly directly to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum.

title: Indonesia Investigating Reports of Citizens Recruited Into Russian Military
description: Indonesian authorities are verifying Ukrainian claims that at least eight of its citizens have been recruited to fight alongside Russian forces in Ukraine, media reported Monday.
content:
Indonesian authorities are verifying Ukrainian claims that at least eight of its citizens have been recruited to fight alongside Russian forces in Ukraine, media reported Monday.
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) last week published scans of seven e-visa applications and one migration card it said belonged to Indonesian men who had allegedly enlisted in the Russian military.
“Indonesia, the world’s largest Muslim country with a population of over 280 million, has joined the list of countries that the Kremlin has turned into yet another source of cheap manpower for the war,” SZRU said in a statement Thursday.
According to the Jakarta Globe, Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Yvonne Mewengkang said officials were cross-checking the information with its diplomatic missions and other ministries.
“Further confirmation is required regarding the individuals’ identities, citizenships, recruitment process, and the nature of their involvement,” she was quoted as saying.
Yvonne said Indonesian authorities would also look into whether the recruits fell victim to fraudulent job postings or human trafficking, in which case Jakarta would take steps to protect the eight men identified by Ukraine.
If confirmed to be voluntary recruitment, the men could have their citizenship revoked under Indonesian law.
Ukraine’s SZRU said Russia has similar recruitment schemes involving promises of high pay, non-combat assignments and expedited Russian citizenship with citizens of Nepal, Cuba, Kenya and India.
Indonesia, Southeast Asia's largest economy, maintains a neutral foreign policy, refusing to take sides in the Ukraine war. Yvonne stressed that the actions of individual citizens do not reflect Indonesia’s foreign policy or its neutral stance on the conflict.
The Kremlin said last week that Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto will be the main foreign guest at Russia's Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Sept. 1-4. Prabowo visited Moscow for talks with President Vladimir Putin in July 2024.
Jakarta has maintained billion-dollar trade ties with Moscow, but major arms imports have stalled in recent years following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Drone Hits High-Rise Apartment Building in Yekaterinburg as Ukraine Targets Wildberries Hub
description: A drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the city of Yekaterinburg as Ukraine targeted a logistics hub owned by online retailer Wildberries, local officials and Russian media reported on Monday afternoon.
content:
A drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the city of Yekaterinburg as Ukraine targeted a logistics hub owned by online retailer Wildberries, local officials and Russian media reported on Monday afternoon.
Sverdlovsk region Governor Denis Pasler said four people were injured in the air attack. Artyom Zhoga, who serves as President Vladimir Putin’s representative to the Urals Federal District, confirmed several apartments were damaged.
Independent media cited Yekaterinburg residents as saying that several fires erupted throughout the city as a result of the drone barrage. Photos on social media showed damage to the upper floors of a high-rise apartment building.
Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, told Russian media that employees at its logistics hub in Yekaterinburg were evacuated, but said the facility, which has been targeted before, was not damaged.
The attack on Yekaterinburg followed earlier drone strikes throughout Russia. The Defense Ministry said Monday morning that it intercepted 239 Ukrainian drones across the country and in annexed Crimea overnight.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said at least six drones were intercepted on approach to the capital. Officials reported multiple injuries in the Bryansk and Kursk regions, while falling drone debris sparked a wildfire in the Rostov region.
Airports across the country introduced temporary flight restrictions amid the attacks.

title: Investigators Drop Murder Charges Against St. Petersburg Businessman Ilya Traber
description: Investigators have dropped all charges against St.
content:
Investigators have dropped all charges against St. Petersburg businessman Ilya Traber over the 2020 contract killing of a local politician and business rival, Russian media reported Monday.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top investigative body, “terminated the criminal prosecution” after finding Traber had no involvement in the killing, his attorney Igor Sochiyants told the state-run TASS news agency.
“The murder charges against him have been dropped,” Sochiyants was quoted as saying.
Traber, 75, now has the legal right to seek state compensation for his unlawful detention, according to the St. Petersburg outlet Fontanka.
The exoneration follows Traber’s release from Moscow’s Lefortovo pre-trial detention center due to health concerns last Thursday. Fontanka, without citing sources, reported that Traber has since been holding a “series of meetings” with government officials and business figures.
Russian authorities have not publicly commented on Traber’s release or exoneration.
Traber was arrested on June 17 and charged with ordering the October 2020 murder of Alexander Petrov outside his home near the Leningrad region town of Vyborg.
The Kremlin has previously confirmed Traber’s ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin during his early political career.
Traber, who had built a shipping and port empire in northwestern Russia during the 1990s, reportedly surrendered ownership stakes in at least four major companies during his two months in detention.

title: 2 Killed in Ukrainian Attack on Belgorod, Authorities Say
description: A Ukrainian missile attack on the city of Belgorod in western Russia killed two people and injured 16 others, acting regional Governor Alexander Shuvaev said Sunday.
content:
A Ukrainian missile attack on the city of Belgorod in western Russia killed two people and injured 16 others, acting regional Governor Alexander Shuvaev said Sunday.
Shuvaev said a man and a 16-year-old were killed in a strike on a “commercial facility” in the city. He said seven warehouses were also set ablaze during the attack but did not specify where.
The online retailer Ozon said that its warehouse in the city was hit. The company said it evacuated employees from the facility, but added that there were casualties and suspended operations as a result.
Ozon did not say whether any of its employees were killed.
Videos shared on social media showed multiple fires burning across the city, including one reportedly near a television tower. One of the strikes reportedly hit the Belgorod thermal power plant, where a fire broke out, the local news outlet Pepel reported .
Ukraine began attacking Ozon warehouses last week after more than a month of strikes against facilities owned by its biggest competitor, Wildberries. Officials in Kyiv have accused Wildberries of supplying the Russian military with drone parts and other equipment.
The Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent Ukrainian drone and missile attacks since the 2022 invasion.

title: Russia Claims Strike on Ukrainian Shipment Terminal
description: Russian forces struck a transhipment terminal in the southern Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv on Aug. 29, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Telegram.
content:
Russian forces struck a transhipment terminal in the southern Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv on Aug. 29, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Telegram.
The attack caused a temporary power outage that shut down the port city's public transport network. Refuelling vessels and unloading points for fuel and lubricants were also hit, the ministry said.
Across the border in Russia, three people have been killed and nine injured in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian Belgorod region, according to local authorities. Three of the injured are in serious condition, the authorities said.
In Kyiv, Russian missiles struck logistics warehouses Moscow claimed contained components for Ukraine's domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles, which Kyiv uses to strike oil terminals and logistics hubs in Russia.
The Moscow Times could not immediately confirm that the affected facility was related to Flamingo manufacturing. Local authorities said at least 37 people were killed in a secondary explosion caused by the blast.
Russian authorities also claimed to have struck a site handling shipments of military hardware from Kyiv's allies in the town of Kalinivka. The supply of weapons from the West to Kyiv was established as one of Russia's so-called red lines even before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, though that line has been crossed repeatedly since February 2022.
Russia warned on Aug. 27 that it could strike British military targets inside and outside Ukraine in response to Ukraine's alleged use of British weapons to hit targets in Russia.
The Russia n Defense Ministry also said on Saturday that Russia n troops had captured the village of Khrapivshchyna in Ukraine's Sumy region, as well as the villages of Novoandriivka and Rubizhne in the Donetsk region.

title: Russian Military Conducts Mobile ICBM Test
description: Russia’s Defense Ministry announced Friday that it conducted a successful combat training launch of a mobile, solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missile from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the northwestern Arkhangelsk region.
content:
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced Friday that it conducted a successful combat training launch of a mobile, solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missile from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the northwestern Arkhangelsk region.
The Strategic Missile Forces deployed a mobile launcher battery to a remote area before firing the missile across the country to the Kura test site on the Kamchatka Peninsula, located more than 6,700 kilometers (4,160 miles) to the east.
Video released by the Defense Ministry showed the missile launch from a forested location.
The military said the goal of the launch was to confirm the “tactical, technical and flight characteristics of the missile system.”
“All assigned tasks were completed in full,” the ministry said, adding that the ICBM maintained a “flawless trajectory.”
It did not identify the missile used in the launch. The Defense Ministry reportedly launched the RS-24 Yars system from Plesetsk to Kura as part of wide-ranging missile forces exercises in mid-May.
The latest launch comes less than a week after unverified reports claimed that Ukrainian drones targeted Plesetsk, Russia’s only military spaceport.

title: Moscow Court Jails Ex-Ukrainian Presidential Aide Oleksiy Arestovych 11 Years in Absentia
description: A judge in Moscow on Friday sentenced Oleksiy Arestovych, a former adviser to the Ukrainian president’s office, to 11 years in prison in absentia after finding him guilty of spreading false information about the Russian military and publicly calling for terrorism.
content:
A judge in Moscow on Friday sentenced Oleksiy Arestovych, a former adviser to the Ukrainian president’s office, to 11 years in prison in absentia after finding him guilty of spreading false information about the Russian military and publicly calling for terrorism.
Russian investigators accused Arestovych of publishing false statements about a deadly Russian missile strike on a railway statio n in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk in April 2022.
Prosecutors also accused Arestovych of calling on Ukrainians to sabotage railway lines used to resupply Russian troops in a March 2022 video.
A judge from the Second Western District Military Court delivered the guilty verdict against Arestovych following a closed-door trial.
In addition to the 11-year prison sentence, t he judge also banned Arestovych from managing websites for four years.
Prosecutors had requested a sentence of 15 years in prison for Arestovych, according to the exiled news outlet Mediazona.
“What a sophisticated cover-up operation,” Arestovych wrote on Telegram in response to the court ruling.
Arestovych served as an adviser to the head of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s office until January 2023, when he resigned after claiming a Ukrainian air defense missile caused a deadly strike on an apartment in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro.
He has since recast himself as a critic of the Ukrainian government and amassed an online following on his YouTube channel. Arestovych now lives outside of Ukraine. Zelensky sanctioned him last year.
Russia added Arestovych to its list of “terrorists and extremists” in May 2023 and placed him on its wanted list in October 2023. Moscow’s Basmanny District Court placed Arestovych in pre-trial detention in absentia in February 2024.

title: Sverdlovsk Region Court Bars Yabloko From Regional Assembly Race
description: A judge in the Sverdlovsk region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the court said Friday.
content:
A judge in the Sverdlovsk region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the court said Friday.
The regional ban follows Russia’s Supreme Court ruling last week to reject Yabloko’s final appeal against a nationwide ban barring its candidate list from the State Duma elections next month.
The Sverdlovsk Regional Court ruled in favor of a lawsuit filed by the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), which accused Yabloko of a range of violations that include those cited in the Supreme Court ruling.
LDPR claimed Yabloko committed copyright infringement, overspent its funds and shared content on banned platforms like Instagram and Facebook. Konstantin Kiselyov, who leads Yabloko’s Sverdlovsk region list of candidates, argued that the same accusations can be leveled against the other parties running in the elections, including LDPR.
“Each party and their leaders are on these banned social networks. I come across official state agencies there, and they can’t live without them,” Kommersant quoted Kiselyov as saying in court.
Yaroslav Shcherbakov, another Yabloko member in the Sverdlovsk region, also accused LDPR of openly calling for the elimination of its political competitor.
Yabloko’s Yekaterinburg branch said it would appeal the ruling.
The Sverdlovsk region is the fifth in Russia where Yabloko has had its list of candidates barred from running in the regional assembly races in September, either through court rulings or rejections by local election commissions.
Yabloko faces the risk of being stripped of its official registration due to legal requirements to field candidates in at least 20% of regional assembly elections or 10% of gubernatorial races every seven years, according to exiled journalist Farida Rustamova.

title: Access Restored to Wikipedia in Russia After Overnight Outage
description: Russian users reported widespread outages of Wikipedia early Friday before access was restored later in the day, independent monitoring groups said.
content:
Russian users reported widespread outages of Wikipedia early Friday before access was restored later in the day, independent monitoring groups said.
Issues with opening the online encyclopedia began shortly after midnight Moscow time. Monitoring services S boy and D owndetector tracked a spike in outage reports across major cities like Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk.
Users reported that Wikipedia remained accessible when using VPNs.
Network testing data from OONI Explorer, the world’s largest open dataset on internet censorship, reportedly showed access anomaly rates for Wikipedia’s Russian-language version briefly hit 100% early Friday, while hitting 75% for the English-language version.
Access began to be restored and disruption rates dropped significantly by 10 a.m. Moscow time. The tech platform Habr reported that Wikipedia was inaccessible in Russia for eight hours.
Russia’s communications watchdog Roskomnadzor has not commented on the outage.
Roskomnadzor has fined Wikipedia multiple times over its refusal to delete articles related to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russian officials have pushed for a domestic alternative to Wikipedia to combat what they claimed to be its Western bias. Those efforts have failed so far.
Fears that authorities may try to block Wikipedia in Russia have grown amid an ongoing wartime crackdown on dissent.
Wikipedia’s Russian-language version continues operating despite the closure of its operator, the Wikimedia Foundation’s Russian division.

title: Kremlin Says Ukraine Peace Talks on ‘Deep Pause’
description: Peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine are on a “deep pause” as Russian troops press their offensive in eastern Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Friday. “We’re pressing forward with the special military operation and our troops are making gains on the frontlines,” Peskov told reporters. “As for peace talks, that topic is currently on a deep pause,” he added.
content:
Peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine are on a “deep pause” as Russian troops press their offensive in eastern Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Friday.
“We’re pressing forward with the special military operation and our troops are making gains on the frontlines,” Peskov told reporters.
“As for peace talks, that topic is currently on a deep pause,” he added.
Peskov’s comments mark a departure from previous remarks this summer in which he confirmed that Russia was maintaining dialogue with U.S. negotiators.
Earlier on Friday, The New York Times reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow this week with the aim of pushing the Kremlin to pursue a peace deal with Ukraine.
Peskov’s public dismissal of diplomacy also comes on the back of a senior Vatican diplomatic envoy meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov this week to call for peace in Ukraine.
In Friday’s comments, Peskov said the Russian military was “intentionally destroying the Kyiv regime’s military and military-adjacent infrastructure.”
“Our forces know what they’re doing and how to do it,” he said, one day after the chief of Russia’s General Staff claimed Russian troops were inching closer to the heavily fortified Donetsk region city of Slovyansk.
President Vladimir Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.
“The Ukrainian side knows our demands full well. They just don’t want to discuss them peacefully,” Peskov said.

title: Calls to Rebury a Siberian Mummy Unearth Decades of Distorted History
description: Millions of tourists flock to southern Siberia’s republic of Altai each year, drawn by its dramatic mountain ranges steeped in the legends of the indigenous Altai people.
content:
Millions of tourists flock to southern Siberia’s republic of Altai each year, drawn by its dramatic mountain ranges steeped in the legends of the indigenous Altai people.
One of the region’s most famous tales centers on the “ Altai Princess ” — a permafrost-preserved mummy discovered on the Ukok Plateau in 1993 by a team of Novosibirsk archeologists led by Natalya Polosmak.
The finding was hailed at the time as an international sensation. Dated to the 5th century BC, the 25-year-old woman’s waxen skin is covered in vibrant indigo tattoos, and she was buried in a wooden chamber alongside six horses, dressed in silk, wool and felt.
But more than three decades later, local shamans are calling for the mummy to be reburied. They claim the remains had “ stood guard at the gates of the underworld, ” and that disturbing her opened a Pandora’s box of natural disasters and political conflict, including the war in Ukraine.
According to Dr. Maria Ochir-Goryaeva, an archaeologist specializing in Eurasian nomads of the Scythian era, the label “ princess ” and the myths surrounding the mummy were conjured up by the Russian team that unearthed her.
“ In her grave, there were no signs of either royal power or shamanism, ” Ochir-Goryaeva, who now lives in Germany, told The Moscow Times. “ She was certainly an aristocrat, a prominent figure... in this regard, Altaians are right: this mummy is the cultural heritage of the repubic of Altai. ”
An Oirat (Kalmyk) from the republic of Kalmykia in southern Russia, Ochir-Goryaeva has spent over four decades leading digs in the lower Volga steppe. For her, the controversy around the Altai Princess highlights how regional inequality distorts Russian archaeology, privileging central institutions, romanticizing history and stripping local communities of their heritage.
Though the Ukok Plateau is rich with archaeological sites, Polosmak — the lead Novosibirsk archaeologist — and her team targeted burial mounds with permafrost beneath them. Ochir-Goryaeva argues that this selective focus on frozen graves can help sensationalize discoveries.
“ Archeologists can find fur coats, pants, dresses and so on, which gives the impression of an unusually wealthy culture, ” Ochir-Goryaeva said. “ In reality, people in these mountains lived poorly, ” isolated in their respective valleys.
She contrasts those kinds of high-profile expeditions with the work that local archaeologists do every day: operating on thin budgets and trying to save sites threatened by urban construction rather than hunting for spectacular finds.
“ All my life in Kalmykia, I worked in ‘rescue archeology,’ saving anything in a construction zone ” before it disappeared, Ochir-Goryaeva said, noting that local excavators are usually more mindful of the environmental damage caused by digging up the steppe.
Immediately after the Altai Princess was discovered, her mummy was flown from the republic of Altai to Novosibirsk, around 700 kilometers (435 miles) away. Archaeologists argued the National Museum in Gorno-Altaysk lacked the facilities to preserve her.
Ochir-Goryaeva views the move as part of a legacy of colonial archaeology in Russia, where local heritage is claimed, packaged and carted off to faraway urban centers.
Although the mummy was finally returned to Altai in 2012 after the National Museum was renovated, Ochir-Goryaeva said that returning artifacts to indigenous lands remains rare in Russia, where “ extraordinary finds are almost always taken from the regions to the capital. ”
In Altai, the initial loss of the mummy fueled deep-seated grievances over the state exploitation of indigenous lands. In 1997, Altai’s regional parliament, the El Kurultai, introduced a temporary moratorium on archaeological digs to stop outside treasure hunting.
Though the ban was lifted in 2010, local mistrust has only deepened as Moscow has tightened its political grip on the republic. Over the past decade, the Kremlin eliminated direct mayoral elections, appointed outside executives to run the region and backed large land buyouts by state corporations like Sberbank.
Recent local protests over land rights have reignited calls from local activists to rebury the Altai Princess.
Ochir-Goryaeva views reburial as impractical — “W e can ’ t put something back into permafrost, especially when it is melting on a global scale ” — though she would support scaling back digs altogether.
“ Digging a burial mound creates waste heaps. Earth and dust are everywhere, ” Ochir-Goryaeva said. “ We drive by car every day, constantly back and forth, and it destroys the steppe that has very little fertile soil. ”
“There is enough material and available methods now to know everything about the ancient population. You don’t need to stir up the ground to do this,” she said.

title: Lukashenko to Meet Putin on Saturday
description: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko will hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Russia this weekend, the Kremlin said Friday. “The talks are planned for Saturday,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Interfax news agency.
content:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko will hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Russia this weekend, the Kremlin said Friday.
“The talks are planned for Saturday,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Interfax news agency.
Lukashenko arrived in Russia on Thursday, with his office saying he and Putin will discuss “key areas of bilateral cooperation” and “pressing regional and international issues, as well as security matters.”
Lukashenko is also scheduled to discuss Russian-Belarusian trade and economic cooperation with Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. The Belarusian president hosted Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov on Tuesday in Minsk, where the sides discussed growing bilateral trade in the first half of 2026.
Belarus remains heavily reliant on Russia both economically and politically, and the country currently hosts a portion of Russia’s tactical nuclear weapons.
Russia used Belarusian territory as a launching pad during the start of its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Minsk has so far avoided direct involvement in the conflict, even as the two nations continue to deepen their military and economic ties.
Lukashenko issued a public message on Monday congratulating the people of Ukraine on their Independence Day and expressing confidence that Minsk and Kyiv would eventually restore cooperation “despite geopolitical upheavals.”
On Tuesday, Lukashenko ordered a snap combat readiness inspection of the Belarusian military.

title: Ukrainian Drone Attack Kills One, Sparks Fire at Yaroslavl Oil Refinery
description: A Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and sparked a fire at one of Russia’s largest oil refineries in the city of Yaroslavl, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said Friday.
content:
A Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and sparked a fire at one of Russia’s largest oil refineries in the city of Yaroslavl, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said Friday.
Yaroslavl region Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said one civilian was killed and 27 others were injured after falling drone debris hit an intercity bus.
He claimed that 67 Ukrainian drones were downed over the region, but that drone debris fell on residential areas, commercial properties and “industrial infrastructure.”
Ukraine’s military said it struck the Slavneft-Yanos refinery, which it said provides fuel and lubricants for the Russian military. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later confirmed the attack and added that Ukraine’s SBU security service had struck a Tu-95MS missile-carrying aircraft in the Saratov region city of Engels.
Independent reports said that Ukrainian drones had already attacked Slavneft-Yanos at least seven times this year before Friday’s attack.
In the Moscow region town of Pavlovsky Posad, a drone slammed into a Magnit grocery store, blowing out windows at a neighboring clinic. Governor Andrei Vorobyov said the clinic remained open despite the damage.
Separate Ukrainian attacks in the southwestern Belgorod region killed two people and injured nine others over the last 24 hours, according to the local governor.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 512 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

title: St. Petersburg Businessman Ilya Traber Released From Detention – Fontanka
description: Russian investigators have released Ilya Traber, a prominent St.
content:
Russian investigators have released Ilya Traber, a prominent St. Petersburg businessman with alleged ties to President Vladimir Putin, from pre-trial detention, the news outlet Fontanka reported Friday.
The investigation reportedly justified the decision to release Traber based on a “sharp decline” in his health. The businessman, however, still faces charges of organized murder and arms trafficking.
Traber, 75, was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention in mid-June. He and his longtime business partner, Vladimir Danilenko, are accused of hiring two men to carry out the 2020 contract killing of businessman and politician Alexander Petrov.
Traber first drew public scrutiny for his ties to the Russian president during Putin’s early political career.
In 2011, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that Traber had met with the Kremlin leader in the 1990s to discuss an oil terminal project. At the time, Putin was working in the St. Petersburg mayor’s office.
Years later, Peskov said Putin knew Traber but could not confirm if the two were on friendly terms.
Traber, who had built a shipping and port empire in northwestern Russia during the 1990s, has reportedly surrendered ownership stakes in at least four major companies during his two months in detention.
There has been no official confirmation of Traber’s release from law enforcement agencies.
According to Fontanka, he walked out of Moscow’s Lefortovo prison on Thursday evening and was traveling back to St. Petersburg.

title: Car Bomb Kills Military Officer in St. Petersburg
description: A Russian military official has been killed in a car explosion in St.
content:
A Russian military official has been killed in a car explosion in St. Petersburg, investigators said Thursday, with local media identifying his rank as lieutenant colonel.
The blast occurred around 10 a.m. local time near a supermarket in the Shushary neighborhood, the news outlet Fontanka reported.
Investigators later confirmed the military official’s death but described the incident only as a “vehicle fire,” not an explosion. They also said his wife, who was also inside the car at the time of the blast, was receiving medical treatment.
The Investigation Committee, Russia ’s top investigative body, said it launched a criminal probe into the incident.
The exiled news outlet Agentstvo said pro-war Telegram channels identified the victim as 43-year-old Sergei Sechkov. The outlet said it confirmed Sechkov’s death with his father in brief online comments.
Officials have not revealed the officer’s identity.
Russia has accused Ukraine of carrying out several assassinations of military officers since the full-scale invasion. Ukrainian sources have claimed responsibility for some of the attacks while denying involvement in others.
Ukraine has not commented on the car explosion in St. Petersburg.
Later on Friday, Fontanka reported that Russian law enforcement identified a 24-year-old woman who was allegedly recruited by Ukrainian handlers online to plant a “powerful and complex” bomb under the military officer’s car on Wednesday night.
The woman was said to have boarded a flight to Turkey early Thursday morning and, by the time Russian authorities contacted Turkish law enforcement, had already flown to Moldova.
A Russia n military officer was last killed in a bomb attack in annexed Crimea earlier this month. Police arrested a woman suspected of assassinating him on behalf of Ukraine.

title: For Russians in Exile, Germany’s New Intelligence Hotline Is Worth Using
description: Opinion | The news that the German special services have opened a special direct line for residents and citizens of Russian, Chinese and Iranian origin fearing transnational repression from their states reminded me of how I myself became acquainted with German counterintelligence.
content:
The news that the German special services have opened a special direct line for residents and citizens of Russian, Chinese and Iranian origin fearing transnational repression from their states reminded me of how I myself became acquainted with German counterintelligence.
Immediately after moving to Berlin, I received what was practically an official letter inviting me to a meeting at one of the German security agencies.
Moreover, the department whose employees I was being invited to meet was precisely the one responsible for protecting the constitutional order.
This in itself made me smile. The department that imprisoned me in Russia has almost the same name: Service for the Protection of the Constitutional System and the Fight against Terrorism.
Having arrived at the appointed time, I went into an office where I met about six or seven people.
What immediately surprised me was that these were not at all the traditional stern, grey “bulldog faces” who look at you as if you’re definitely guilty. Sitting in front of me were fairly young people, around 30-40, clearly educated and intelligent-looking. They spoke to me quite kindly, asked what risks I saw for myself, whether I was under threat and how I ended up in a Russian prison.
The unexpected feeling for any person who has spent a long time dealing with the Russian law-enforcement system was not even the content of the conversation. These people did not see me as an enemy or a source of new shoulder straps. After the Russian experience, this is also something you have to get used to.
At the end of the conversation, they asked whether I thought I was currently at risk.
I said: “You know, according to the ponyatiya , if a deal has been made concerning a person, his previous sins are wiped clean. Therefore, I think the Kremlin does not yet perceive me as an enemy, as I have been exchanged.”
We were talking through an interpreter, who hesitated at this moment. It was clear that the word ponyatiya — a term originating in Russian prisons, describing a set of unwritten understandings — was difficult to translate. Or perhaps my interlocutors were struggling with the concept as a whole.
“Remember when the hero gets temporary invulnerability powers and starts flashing? Well, in my case, I am still flashing for now.”
They laughed, which greatly eased the atmosphere.
The main purpose of that meeting, as far as I understood, was to tell me they would help if I ever felt under threat.
Since then, I have not encountered any situations in which I would have considered such an approach really necessary. But I still have their contact details lying around somewhere.
I do not know whether every Russian who sought refuge in Germany had a meeting like this. Possibly not. But that is precisely why the news about the appearance of an official hotline initially surprised me a little. I already assumed that such mechanisms existed anyway.
In addition to the hotline, Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the BfV, issued a special brochure for people who, on German territory, encounter surveillance, pressure or threats from foreign states. Russia, China and Iran are notorious for carrying out this transnational repression.
The brochure lists different methods of such work. These can be career intelligence service employees operating under diplomatic cover, organizations connected with the state, surveillance and other forms of pressure on journalists and activists. But there is also a much more down-to-earth thing there — so-called gig-economy agents. That is, people who are hired for a simple one-off task with no need for a complex recruitment operation and the years of training that go into preparing a professional spy. Sometimes it is enough to pay someone for surveillance, a photograph, gathering information or another small assignment.
The purpose of the new helpline goes beyond helping the individual, as it has the dual benefit of helping German counterintelligence better understand the transnational networks operating in the country.
In fact, the German authorities are directly talking about the existence and even intensification of such work on the country’s territory. That is why the hotline has now been set up.
And here one more point is important. The hotline did not appear by itself.
Just eight days before, the German government approved a serious reform of legislation governing the intelligence services. The foreign intelligence service — the BND — will be granted the ability to store intercepted communications and metadata for longer, as well as to use artificial intelligence to analyse large volumes of information. The BfV domestic intelligence agency is receiving comparable surveillance capabilities. Security services have a reputation for intervening in national affairs, covertly or openly. But German agencies were strictly forbidden from doing this and forced to only observe and collect information. The new Intelligence Services Reform Act is set to finally change that, allowing the security services to step in if ordinary police measures are insufficient.
Germany as a whole is reconsidering its attitude towards espionage, sabotage, foreign interference and attempts to put pressure on people living on its territory. In my view, there are several fairly obvious reasons why this is happening now.
The first is that the scale of emigration has changed.
After 2022, an enormous number of opposition figures, journalists, human-rights defenders, activists, people who helped Ukraine or simply openly opposed the war left Russia for dozens of European cities.
The Russian authorities’ attitude towards these people did not change simply because they crossed the border. The tools of repression just went after them. Not long after this hotline was announced, news broke that a former member of the Pussy Riot performance art group said the FSB threatened her in 2023, saying they would kill her family if she refused to inform on dissident artists.
The second reason is that this kind of work has become easier and cheaper.
It is absolutely unnecessary to send a so-called illegal abroad with a 20-year-long cover story. The internet makes it much harder to maintain a false identity. Sabotage and intelligence gathering can be entrusted to a “ gig economy ” actor already in Europe who might be completely oblivious to the true reason why they have just been offered a small amount of money to follow unusual instructions.
The third reason is that the war sharply changed European countries’ attitude toward such malign activity.
The surveillance of a member of Russia’s exiled opposition is one thing. But when these gig-economy agents start conducting reconnaissance of military facilities, observing routes for aid to Ukraine and preparing to sabotage them, it stops looking like a collection of separate incidents. Each case adds up to a big problem for the state.
And finally, it seems that the German authorities are finally admitting that they previously simply did not see a significant part of what was happening.
The government acknowledges that the real number of episodes of transnational repression may be substantially greater than what appears in criminal statistics.
I think it is important in this context for me to address the Russian emigre community directly.
The concerns of the German intelligence services are not groundless. For recruiters, we are fertile ground.
When people flee their country, it is easy for them to become tired, burned out and disappointed. Some people fail to integrate and master the new local language. Some cannot find normal work for years. Many lose the social status they had become accustomed to. In Russia, they were journalists, politicians, teachers and entrepreneurs. But in exile, it suddenly turns out that nobody needs them and they have to start life practically from the beginning.
It is understandable that some people feel resentful, or even envious toward those who have turned out to be more successful in emigration.
Just look at our own community: how quick we are to throw accusations at each other, how often we try to explain our own problems by the fact that someone else received more money, attention or opportunities. Internal conflicts within the opposition have not diminished over recent years, but have only multiplied.
These people who have lost their bearings and hope are vulnerable; there may quite easily be those whom someone will one day approach and listen to very attentively. It is well established that intelligence operatives see a person on the verge of a breakdown as an opportunity. They make them feel understood and validated before directing them to direct their hatred to the country that gave them sanctuary.
Some will be offered money. Some will be offered the hope of returning to Russia with a promise that their previous sins will be forgotten. Others will be fueled by the simple desire to blame other people for their failures. In some cases, this could lead to people directly inside the opposition being compromised.
Russians are by no means the only wave of emigrants to have experienced this. It is an inherent part of life in exile, which the German authorities understand perfectly. And, what is much more unpleasant, the Russian authorities understand it perfectly as well.
Does all this mean that now it is necessary for us to restrict our contacts, close ourselves inside a circle of old friends and see an FSB agent lurking in every new acquaintance?
Of course not. Isolating ourselves in this way would be doing the work of the Russian intelligence services for them.
But it is still worth observing several simple rules.
First: there is no need to tell new acquaintances personal information — who lives where, who is meeting whom, where someone is planning to go, and so on — without good reason. Often it is not one enormous secret that turns out to be dangerous, but a dozen small things that can then be put together.
Second: practice normal digital hygiene. Enable two-factor authentication, keep devices updated, exercise caution with opening links and files and check who has access to your accounts. These are basic things that people talk about constantly. But be honest: do you personally follow them?
Third, don’t ignore strange events that keep happening. One call, message, or chance meeting most likely means nothing. But if such things begin to repeat, it is worth at least recording the evidence and noting down dates and circumstances. There is no need to conduct an investigation yourself. It is simply better to have the facts if they are ever needed.
Fourth, be careful with your personal information. Your home address, habitual route and information about your family absolutely do not have to be publicly available. When you first meet someone new, it is entirely reasonable to go to a public place and tell someone where you are, especially if you are making yourself vulnerable.
Of course, if a situation becomes an obvious attempt at pressure, a threat, or an offer to help in exchange for information, there is no need to start playing at being an intelligence officer yourself. That is precisely what people who professionally deal with such things exist for.
The meaning of all these rules is not to start suspecting the people around you.
Ordinary hygiene. We lock the door of the flat not because we consider every passer-by a thief.
But I think there is a final, very important psychological barrier to Berlin’s idea.
We Russians grew up in a country where going to law-enforcement agencies, and especially to the intelligence services, is in itself perceived as a risk.
You come for help and do not know whether, as a result, you yourself will become an object of attention.
For many Russians, this reaction is already practically reflexive. Better not to get involved.
My experience with officials in Germany was very different. Other people may have had different experiences, but I’m confident that it’s best to check with them if you have any concerns.
You simply have to remember that we are in a difficult situation. We are citizens of a state that unleashed a bloody war on its neighbors, and its opponents at the same time. Russia has shown for over a century that state borders are no obstacles to it persecuting its opponents. It would be naïve to think it wouldn’t.
Therefore, the very idea of the German authorities creating a clear direct channel for people who feel threatened seems to me entirely justified.
I wish that none of us ever has to use this telephone. Better still — that it will soon become unnecessary. All I have to say now is to take care of yourselves. The threats are real, but help is there.

title: Russia Expels Romanian Diplomat in Tit-for-Tat Move
description: Russia announced Thursday that it was declaring an employee of the Romanian embassy in Moscow persona non grata in retaliation for Bucharest expelling a Russian diplomat last month.
content:
Russia announced Thursday that it was declaring an employee of the Romanian embassy in Moscow persona non grata in retaliation for Bucharest expelling a Russian diplomat last month.
"Romania's Charge d'Affaires ... was handed a note from the ministry declaring an employee of the Romanian Embassy in Moscow persona non grata," Russia's foreign ministry said in a statement.
"This measure is a response to the Romanian side's earlier, unjustified decision to declare a member of staff at the Russian Embassy in Bucharest persona non grata," it added.
Romania ordered the Russian diplomat's expulsion following a series of airspace violations involving drones.
In May, Bucharest accused Moscow of launching a drone that crashed into an apartment building in the city of Galati, injuring two people. Russia rejected the allegations.
While dozens of drone incursions have been detected over Romanian territory since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the incident in Galati was the first time a residential building was hit.

title: TotalEnergies Exits Arctic LNG 2 Project
description: French energy company TotalEnergies said Thursday that it has completed its exit from a Russian gas project sanctioned in the West.
content:
French energy company TotalEnergies said Thursday that it has completed its exit from a Russian gas project sanctioned in the West.
CEO Patrick Pouyanne had announced in July a plan to transfer the company's 10% stake in the Arctic LNG 2 liquefied natural gas project to the majority shareholder, Novatek.
The firm had already taken a $4.1 billion write-down of its stake in the project in 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"TotalEnergies confirms that the transfer of its 10% interest in Arctic LNG 2 to NordLine [a Novatek subsidiary] has been completed. TotalEnergies is therefore no longer a shareholder," the company said in a statement.
It added that it still had the right to reimbursement of $1.3 billion in loans it provided to the project with other shareholders, while indicating that repayment was unlikely for now.
"Such reimbursement might be implemented in the future subject to applicable sanctions," TotalEnergies said.
Many Western companies quickly sold, suspended or scaled back their operations in Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has since made it difficult for firms to leave, requiring presidential authorization for sales. Pouyanne said in July that TotalEnergies had recently received approval for the Arctic LNG 2 stake transfer.
Novatek, which was founded in 1994, has been TotalEnergies' main partner in Russia. In 2013, they jointly launched the Yamal natural gas field in Siberia, from which they ship LNG to Europe.
TotalEnergies still holds a 19.4% stake in Novatek and a 20% stake in Yamal. The company says it cannot sell those stakes under the current sanctions regime against Russia.

title: Ex-Kremlin Loyalist Declared Mentally Fit to Stand Trial for Putin Criticism
description: A Moscow psychiatric facility has declared former Kremlin loyalist and blogger Ilya Remeslo mentally competent to stand trial on charges of spreading false information about the military, his attorney said Thursday. “Remeslo is sane.
content:
A Moscow psychiatric facility has declared former Kremlin loyalist and blogger Ilya Remeslo mentally competent to stand trial on charges of spreading false information about the military, his attorney said Thursday.
“Remeslo is sane. He did not and does not suffer from any mental illness,” attorney Sergei Badamshin wrote in a post on Telegram, citing an evaluation from the Serbsky State Scientific Center for Social and Forensic Psychiatry.
Serbsky’s conclusion comes about a month after Remeslo was transferred there from a pre-trial detention facility in Moscow.
He previously spent a month at a St. Petersburg psychiatric hospital this spring after publicly denouncing President Vladimir Putin for mishandling the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Remeslo later called his hospitalization involuntary and a form of retaliation by the authorities for his critical remarks.
On Wednesday, a judge at the Moscow City Court rejected Remeslo’s appeal against his criminal charges and upheld his pre-trial detention until Sept. 16.
“Russia will be free,” Remeslo said after the ruling, according to the exiled news outlet Mediazona.
That phrase was often used by the late opposition activist Alexei Navalny, whom Remeslo had actively campaigned against, including by filing police complaints.
Remeslo faces up to 10 years in prison if found guilty of spreading false information about the Russian military.

title: Russian Forces Inching Closer to Slovyansk in Eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk Region, Gerasimov Says
description: Russian forces have advanced toward the outskirts of Slovyansk within eastern Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt” of heavily fortified cities in the Donetsk region, Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Thursday.
content:
Russian forces have advanced toward the outskirts of Slovyansk within eastern Ukraine’s so-called “fortress belt” of heavily fortified cities in the Donetsk region, Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Thursday.
Speaking at an undisclosed location while inspecting troops from Russia’s “South” grouping of forces, Gerasimov said that Russian troops are positioned just 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the eastern outskirts of Slovyansk.
The general noted that Russian forces captured at least three villages to the northeast and southeast of the city over the summer, with active street fighting continuing in two other settlements.
Gerasimov added that Russian operations are currently advancing along a 160-kilometer (99-mile) front.
The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said earlier this week that Russian troops have intensified efforts to push toward Slovyansk from the east and southeast following unsuccessful assault attempts from the northeast.
Slovyansk and neighboring city of Kramatorsk represent Ukraine’s primary defensive strongholds in the region following the Russian capture of Kostiantynivka last month.
Kostiantynivka had served as the southern end of the “fortress belt,” while Slovyansk anchored the group of cities in the north.
In response to the offensive, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that he had appointed two prominent military commanders to lead defensive operations in the region.
Zelensky claimed in June that the Kremlin had ordered Russian forces to fully capture the Donetsk region by Dec. 31.
Russian President Vladimir Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.
