title: Death Toll From Fire at Amur Gas Chemical Complex Rises to 15
description: The Amur Gas Chemical Complex in Far East Russia said Thursday that the death toll from a fire that broke out at the facility earlier this week had risen to 15 people.
content:
The Amur Gas Chemical Complex in Far East Russia said Thursday that the death toll from a fire that broke out at the facility earlier this week had risen to 15 people.
The plant had initially said that seven people were killed in the blaze on Tuesday, including six Chinese nationals.
By Thursday, the death toll had risen to 15, among them 14 foreigners, AGCC said in a statement without providing details about their nationalities. The company said 39 workers remain hospitalized, including nine who were airlifted to Moscow.
The complex, which bills itself as one of the world's largest polyethylene and polypropylene producers, is a $10 billion joint venture between Russian petrochemical giant Sibur and China's state-owned oil and gas company Sinopec.
When the fire broke out this week, the complex was undergoing final testing ahead of its planned launch in early 2027.
AGCC said construction at the complex would continue, as would preparation for next year's launch.
The Investigative Committee, Russia's top investigative body, said it opened a probe into possible safety violations and was working to establish the cause of the fire.
The Amur Gas Chemical Complex is expected to produce 2.3 million metric tons of polyethylene and 400,000 tons of polypropylene per year.

title: Where Can Russian Athletes Compete After the IOC’s Provisional Ban Lift?
description: Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
content:
Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
The shift began in September 2025, when the International Paralympic Committee voted against maintaining its ban on Russian and Belarusian athletes, paving the way for them to compete at the 2026 Milano-Cortina Paralympic Games, where Russian competitors won eight gold medals.
By December, the IOC recommended that international federations lift their bans on Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
However, some individual governing bodies acted even earlier. The International Judo Federation became the first to restore full participation rights to senior Russian athletes in November of last year. World Taekwondo followed this January by approving the full return of both junior and senior athletes from Russia and Belarus.
Since then, eight additional Olympic sports federations have restored full participation rights to Russian athletes and teams, allowing the use of the Russian flag, national anthem and team uniforms.
Below is a list compiled by The Moscow Times detailing where and how Russian athletes can currently compete on the international stage:
Archery: On August 14, World Archery reinstated Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flag and bringing their status in line with Belarusian athletes, who were reinstated in May.
Aquatics : The World Aquatics Bureau lifted its ban on senior Russian and Belarusian athletes on April 13, 2026, two months after it lifted its ban on Junior athletes.
In its statement, World Aquatics President Husain Al Musallam said, “Over the last three years, World Aquatics and the AQIU have successfully helped ensure that conflict can be kept outside the sporting competition venues. We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”
Boxing : On July 30, World Boxing announced that it was restoring full participation rights to all Russian athletes.
" The Executive Committee accepted that Russian athletes would now take part in World Boxing competitions like boxers from any other national federation. However, World Boxing will strictly monitor the behaviour of Russian delegations during events as well as compliance with anti-doping protocols," the statement read.
World Boxing previously lifted its restrictions on Belarusian athletes on May 12.
Equestrian: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russian riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia, the governing body has said.
FEI had already approved a return to competition for junior athletes from Russia and Belarus on May 19, 2026, but did not change its stance that senior athletes should compete with neutral status at that time.
Fencing : The International Fencing Federation (FIE) reinstated Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2, 2026.
“The decision reflects the FIE’s commitment to the fundamental principles of the Olympic Charter, including non-discrimination, equal treatment and the universality of sport, as well as the objectives and principles set out in the FIE Statutes,” FIE’s statement read.
On July 28, Russian fencer Pavel Graudyn won gold in the Men's individual sabre at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, marking Russia's first gold at a major championship since the International Fencing Federation lifted its restrictions.
Field Hockey : On Sept. 17, the Russian Field Hockey Federation announced that it had received a letter from the International Hockey Federation (FIH) lifting all restrictions against its athletes and national teams.
Gymnastics : The Executive Committee of World Gymnastics released a statement on May 18, 2026, that it had decided to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts.
On July 28, 2026, European Gymnastics voted to bring itself in line with World Gymnastics in allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete with their national symbols.
Handball : On July 15, 2026, the International Handball Federation (IHF) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian teams and officials, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
“The IHF reiterates its longstanding commitment to the Ukraine Handball Federation and continues to stand in solidarity with Ukraine. It strongly condemns the ongoing war in Ukraine and its devastating consequences. It is the IHF’s sincere hope that the conflict will soon come to an end, paving the way for a return to peace, the restoration of normal sporting relations and the resumption of peaceful international cooperation,” the IHF statement said.
“At the same time, the IHF remains committed to safeguarding the values of sport, promoting dialogue within the international handball family, and ensuring that its decisions continue to reflect the recommendations of the IOC and the interests of the global handball community”
Judo : The International Judo Federation, calling sport the “last bridge for reconciliation and peace,” was the first to allow Russian and Belarusian senior athletes back, doing so on Nov. 27, 2025.
“Athletes have no responsibility for the decisions of governments or other national institutions, and it is our duty to protect the sport and our athletes,” the federation’s statement said.
“Sport must remain neutral, independent and free from political influence. Judo, rooted in the values of peace, unity and friendship, cannot allow itself to become a platform for geopolitical agendas. The decision to reinstate full national representation reflects the IJF’s confidence in its ethical safeguards, as well as in the strength and integrity of the sport,” it continued.
Modern Pentathlon : The International Union of Modern Pentathlon lifted its ban on Russian athletes on July 13, 2026, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
Taekwondo : The World Taekwondo Council allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes back into the fold on Jan. 31, 2026, at a meeting in the United Arab Emirates.
Triathlon : Mikhail Degtyarev, head of the Russian Olympic Committee and the Russian Minister of Sport, said on Aug. 21 that World Triathlon had granted Russian athletes full participation rights.
World Triathlon lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian junior athletes in April 2026, while senior athletes continue to compete as neutral athletes.
"This was made possible by the restoration of the Russian Olympic Committee's status. Earlier in April, World Triathlon already admitted Russian junior and para-athletes," Degtyarev said.
Volleyball : The International Volleyball Federation (FIVB) announced on July 8, 2026, that Russian teams and athletes would be restored to the World Ranking with the same World Ranking points they had at the time of the initial ban.
“The FIVB remains deeply concerned about the ongoing war in Ukraine and strongly condemns all forms of violence. We continue to hope for a peaceful resolution as soon as possible and remain committed to supporting the Ukrainian volleyball community through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment programme,” FIVB added.
Weightlifting : The International Weightlifting Federation decided on June 26, 2026, to reinstate Russian and Belarusian athletes.
“The IWF remains committed to promoting fair competition, safeguarding the integrity of the sport and ensuring that athletes have the opportunity to compete in an environment that respects the principles of neutrality, inclusion and excellence,” the decision read.
Wrestling : United World Wrestling announced on May 15, 2026, that Russian and Belarusian wrestlers would be able to compete without restrictions starting with immediate effect.
Baseball/Softball : On Jan. 19, 2026, the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes. However, senior athletes remain banned.
Chess : The International Chess Federation (FIDE) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian youth chess players on Dec. 14, 2025. Senior athletes may compete under a neutral designation.
Curling : World Curling announced on Jan. 30, 2026, that, following the IOC’s recommendation, Russian and Belarusian junior athletes would be able to compete in international competition. Senior athletes remain unable to compete.
Sailing : The Russian Sailing Federation published a statement on June 9, 2026, announcing that the World Sailing Federation had approved a return to competition for Russian junior athletes.
Ski Mountaineering : The International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.

title: Russian Spy Chief Says Meeting With CIA Director Was ‘Nothing Special’
description: Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), confirmed Thursday that he met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in Moscow earlier this week but otherwise sought to downplay the significance of the talks. “The meeting took place, and there’s nothing special about it,” Naryshkin told state media reporters two days after Ratcliffe’s rare and unannounced trip to Russia on Tuesday.
content:
Sergei Naryshkin, the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), confirmed Thursday that he met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in Moscow earlier this week but otherwise sought to downplay the significance of the talks.
“The meeting took place, and there’s nothing special about it,” Naryshkin told state media reporters two days after Ratcliffe’s rare and unannounced trip to Russia on Tuesday.
Ratcliffe’s flight marks the first visit to Russia by a CIA chief since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Naryshkin said he and Ratcliffe discussed “a range of issues that fall within the scope of our intelligence services” as part of a “standard working format,” but did not provide further details.
He described the work of intelligence agencies as “a delicate and special thing,” and noted that he meets with spy chiefs from other countries “almost every week, whether face-to-face or online.”
Sources previously told The Wall Street Journal that Ratcliffe was sent to Moscow to warn Russia against attacking any NATO member state. Neither Washington nor Moscow has confirmed the reporting.
U.S. President Donald Trump has also sought to temper expectations from Ratcliffe’s Russia trip by calling it “sort of semi-routine.” Like Naryshkin, Trump declined to address speculation surrounding the CIA director’s trip, noting only that “something may come out of it,” referring to Ukraine peace negotiations, which have stalled since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February.
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia and the United States remain in contact on talks to end the war in Ukraine. He previously said that Ratcliffe did not meet with President Vladimir Putin this week.
Peskov dismissed U.S. press reports that Russia could be planning to attack NATO and that Ratcliffe had sought to warn the Kremlin against such a move.
“There’s a lot of this kind of scaremongering being published right now. Naturally, it has zero basis in reality and does not reflect the intentions of the Russian Federation at all,” the spokesman said.
Ratcliffe and Naryshkin have maintained regular contact since he was appointed CIA chief in January 2025.

title: At Least 8 Russians Missing in Nepal Following Deadly Himalayan Flood
description: At least eight Russians are missing in Nepal after a catastrophic and deadly torrent of floods and mud swept through the border region with China, Russia’s Embassy in Kathmandu said Thursday.
content:
At least eight Russians are missing in Nepal after a catastrophic and deadly torrent of floods and mud swept through the border region with China, Russia’s Embassy in Kathmandu said Thursday.
In a statement, the embassy said it is coordinating with Nepalese authorities to establish the location of the missing Russians as search operations continue across the devastated valley.
Two Russian women survived the disaster by escaping up a mountain slope, embassy officials added, noting both survivors later contacted diplomatic personnel while awaiting transit clearance at a Nepalese-Chinese border checkpoint.
The disaster struck Wednesday when a massive collapse of rock and ice unleashed a wall of mud and water down a Himalayan river. Local authorities estimate nearly 1,500 people remain missing, including around 800 foreign tourists.
Nepalese police warned the death toll is expected to surpass 165, while Chinese authorities reported three fatalities on their side of the border.
Scientists at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an ice-and-rock avalanche originating in a high-altitude area likely blocked a tributary river before giving way and triggering the cascading flood.
The U.S. Geological Survey reported that the disaster generated a seismic event equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 glacier collapse, sending a massive flow of debris downstream.

title: Ukrainian Drones Attack Ozon Warehouses in Overnight Barrage
description: Ukrainian drones targeted warehouses belonging to Russia’s second-largest online retailer Ozon, as well as industrial infrastructure in the republic of Bashkortostan, the company and Russian media reported Thursday.
content:
Ukrainian drones targeted warehouses belonging to Russia’s second-largest online retailer Ozon, as well as industrial infrastructure in the republic of Bashkortostan, the company and Russian media reported Thursday.
Ozon said its logistics center in the regional capital of Ufa was “temporarily closed” for inspections after drones caused “minor damage” to the building. It said incoming seller shipments were being rerouted to other facilities.
Another Ozon location in the neighboring Orenburg region was evacuated due to emergency alerts, but later resumed operations after it appeared not to have been struck.
There were also unconfirmed reports of an explosion at the Bashkir Soda Company in the city of Sterlitamak following a suspected drone strike. Authorities have not commented on the reported attack.
Sterlitamak is located around 120 kilometers (75 miles) south of the regional capital Ufa and 1,200 kilometers east (750 miles) of the border with Ukraine.
Elsewhere, in the southwestern Belgorod region, authorities said one person was killed in a cross-border Ukrainian attack.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 267 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
The Defense Ministry also said it attacked Ukrainian steelworks in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, logistics centers in and around Kyiv, as well as three Ukrainian ports.

title: Russians Are Rushing for Cash. Should the Kremlin Be Worried?
description: As the Kremlin prepares to roll out its latest financial innovation — the digital ruble — Russians are increasingly turning to a more old-fashioned alternative: cash.
content:
As the Kremlin prepares to roll out its latest financial innovation — the digital ruble — Russians are increasingly turning to a more old-fashioned alternative: cash.
Households and businesses have added 2.1 trillion rubles ($25.3 billion) to their cash holdings so far this year. That marks the largest increase recorded since the start of the war, surpassing the 1.8 trillion rubles ($21.7 billion) added between January and August 2023.
Back then, cash demand was driven by Russians fleeing the country amid military mobilization, panic during the short-lived Wagner mutiny and, reportedly, off-the-books payments to mercenaries fighting in Ukraine.
According to projections by Sberbank, Russia’s largest lender, cash in circulation could rise by 3.8 trillion rubles ($45.8 billion) over the course of 2026, making it the largest annual increase on record.
Much like in 2023, several factors are driving the current rush to cash.
First is simple practicality. Withdrawals began rising in February, when Russia started routinely jamming mobile signals to counter Ukrainian drone attacks. The jamming inadvertently knocked out card payment terminals and mobile banking apps.
“When the internet was shut down across the city in the spring, cards simply didn’t work. Cash was the only way to buy groceries or pay for services,” said Artyom, a Moscow resident who, like others cited in this story, asked to use a pseudonym.
Svetlana, who lives in the southern Samara region, said she also encountered regular problems when trying to use her card to pay for groceries at the supermarket earlier this year. However, she added, the internet outages mostly stopped by the summer.
Public anxiety is also playing a role. Despite official assurances that personal savings will not be touched to fund the military, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov sparked alarm in June when he suggested that the 67 trillion rubles Russians hold in bank deposits were merely “enriching bankers” and should instead be put toward manufacturing or the war effort.
Dmitry Orlov, deputy chairman of Moscow-based Fora-Bank, said that high withdrawal rates reflect people hedging against both internet blackouts and “unsettling comments” from public officials about potentially freezing bank deposits.
At the same time, rumors of renewed military mobilization have led to a spike in people looking into the possibility of relocating abroad. Because Russian bank cards no longer work abroad, anyone planning to leave must withdraw cash to convert into euros or dollars.
Businesses are also driving the shift, though mostly to avoid taxes. In January, the government raised the value-added tax (VAT) from 20% to 22% and lowered the income threshold at which companies are required to pay it. Operating off the books helps smaller businesses stay under that threshold or cut costs by paying employees and suppliers under the table.
In Moscow and smaller regional towns alike, small shops, coffee stands, repairmen and hotels frequently ask for cash, often offering small discounts to avoid electronic payments, according to multiple Russians who spoke to The Moscow Times.
Taras Skvortsov, Sberbank’s Chief Financial Officer, said that the main driver of cash leaving the banking system is companies keeping cash in circulation for “grey-market” transactions rather than depositing it back into banks.
That trend expands Russia’s infamous informal economy — already estimated at around 11% of GDP — and fuels tax evasion, with tax-related offenses jumping 17% year-over-year in the first half of 2026.
It also squeezes the banking sector. When money stays out of bank vaults, banks have less capital available to lend to consumers or to buy the government bonds that fund Russia’s budget deficit and infrastructure projects. Skvortsov warned that these liquidity shortages may eventually force the Central Bank to step in with support measures.
While the absolute numbers look staggering, the percentage growth tells a more subtle story. Cash in circulation grew 11.7% between January and July — roughly matching 2023 rates, and well below the 22.4% spike seen during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Cash also still accounts for roughly 15% of Russia’s overall money supply (known to economists as M2, which combines physical currency with funds held in bank accounts) — a percentage that has remained largely stable.
“The recent trend of cash’s declining market share has reversed, but given normal seasonal fluctuations, nothing extreme is happening overall,” said Moscow-based economist Yegor Susin.
Janis Kluge, an economist at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, noted that alongside cash, “transferable” checking accounts have also grown. This suggests Russians are not panic-draining their bank accounts all at once, but are instead keeping their funds easily accessible as falling interest rates lower the appeal of holding money in savings accounts.
“Russian households and businesses are prioritizing liquid assets over locked savings accounts,” Kluge explained. “The primary driver behind both rising cash and checking balances is simply falling interest rates.”
Last month, the Russian Central Bank cut its key interest rate for the tenth consecutive time to 14%, down from 18% a year prior, thus giving Russians less incentive to deposit their money in savings accounts.

title: Trump Confirms CIA Director’s Moscow Trip, Calling It ‘Semi-Routine’
description: U.S.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump confirmed Wednesday that he had dispatched CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow the day before, expressing hope that the spy chief’s unannounced visit could help end the war in Ukraine.
“Something may come out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended,” Trump told conservative radio host Glenn Beck in a telephone interview.
His comments confirm reporting that Ratcliffe flew to Moscow, the first visit to Russia by a CIA chief since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, for a series of “meetings” on Tuesday.
The Kremlin also later confirmed Ratcliffe’s visit, saying he had arrived for “contacts between security services.” The Kremlin did not provide further details, but stressed that Ratcliffe did not meet with President Vladimir Putin.
Asked by Beck to address speculation surrounding the trip — ranging from warnings to the Kremlin against testing NATO resolve to discussions over Iranian sanctions — Trump responded: “None of the above.”
“I hate to disappoint people,” the president said, seeking to temper expectations by describing Ratcliffe’s trip as “sort of semi-routine.”
Sources later told The Wall Street Journal that the CIA director was sent to Moscow to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO amid concerns members of the Western military alliance are running low on munitions.
Trump has vowed to broker an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine, but has struggled to bring Moscow and Kyiv toward a compromise.
Russian officials have repeatedly said in recent months that they also expect U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to visit in an effort to mediate peace with Ukraine.
“We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump told Beck. “Frankly, they both [Russia and Ukraine] want to see it ended at this point.”

title: Moscow to Summon Romanian Envoy After Russian Diplomat Expelled Over Drone Incursions
description: Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced plans to summon Romania’s chargé d’affaires in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported Wednesday.
content:
Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced plans to summon Romania’s chargé d’affaires in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported Wednesday.
According to the ministry’s short statement, Liliana Burda was expected to be summoned on Thursday.
The Russian ministry did not publicly confirm plans to summon Burda or the reason for her planned summoning as of publication.
The move would come exactly one month after Moscow’s promise to retaliate after Bucharest in late July declared a Russian diplomat persona non grata over repeated drone incursions into Romanian airspace.
At the time, Romania’s foreign ministry also recalled its own ambassador to Russia for consultations.
The ministry summoned Russia’s Ambassador in Bucharest, Vladimir Lipayev, to show him fragments of a drone destroyed over Romanian territory.
“The Romanian side expressed its firm protest against these illegal and irresponsible actions and made clear where responsibility lies,” the ministry said on July 27, adding that Russia’s violation of Romanian airspace was “absolutely unacceptable and intolerable.”
The Romanian military shot down three drones said to be of Russian origin between July 24 and July 26.
Romania, which shares a border with Ukraine, has reported multiple breaches of its airspace since the 2022 Russian invasion.

title: NKHP Grain Export Terminal Says Repairs After Ukrainian Attack May Take 4 Months
description: Repair works at NKHP, one of three grain terminals at Russia's main Black Sea export port of Novorossiysk, could take up to four months following a Ukrainian attack, the company said on Wednesday.
content:
Repair works at NKHP, one of three grain terminals at Russia 's main Black Sea export port of Novorossiysk, could take up to four months following a Ukrainian attack, the company said on Wednesday.
A ttacks over recent months have halted almost all grain shipments through ports on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which used to account for 70% of all Russia n grain exports.
Ukraine hit Novorossiysk in a major drone attack on August 12 that put all three grain terminals out of operation.
The other export terminal, owned by Demetra, suffered less significant damage than NKHP, while the third, owned by Delo Group, was not damaged in the attack, though operations were suspended.
The owner of NKHP, Russia n state-owned United Grain Company, confirmed after the attack that the terminal had been damaged.
Reuters sources said the loading gallery was among the facilities affected. The final repair timeline has yet to be determined, according to a financial report published on Wednesday.
NKHP, with an annual capacity of 7.1 million metric tons, is one of the three largest terminals at the port of Novorossiysk with a combined annual capacity of over 20 million tons, while total seaborne exports stood at 52.7 million tons last season.
The Russia n government is considering scrapping its grain export duty as exports face disruption from drone attacks in the Black Sea. It is also discussing ways to redirect export flows through other ports, including Baltic, Caspian and Far Eastern routes.

title: Fire at Amur Gas Chemical Complex Kills 7 Workers, Injures Dozens More
description: At least seven workers were killed and dozens of others were injured after a fire broke out at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex (AGCC) in Russia’s Far East, the company said Tuesday.
content:
At least seven workers were killed and dozens of others were injured after a fire broke out at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex (AGCC) in Russia’s Far East, the company said Tuesday.
Located near the Amur region town of Svobodny, AGCC is a $10 billion joint venture between Russian petrochemical giant Sibur and China’s state-owned oil and gas company Sinopec. Designed to become one of the world's largest polymer manufacturing facilities, the complex was undergoing final testing ahead of its planned launch in early 2027.
In a statement on Tuesday, AGCC said the fire broke out in a support section of a pyrolysis unit. The company said primary equipment was not damaged.
Nineteen workers were initially hospitalized with moderate to severe injuries. Another 104 workers received treatment for minor cuts and bruises, the company said.
By Wednesday, AGCC said it recovered the bodies of six Chinese workers and one Russian. Nine Chinese contactors remain missing, it added.
Consumer protection authorities said local air quality monitoring detected no toxic chemical spikes in Svobodny. The Amur region’s government said the incident posed no threat to people living in nearby towns.
A commission has been formed to investigate the cause of the fire, AGCC said.

title: Russian Election Commission Registers 1.6K War Veterans as Candidates in Upcoming Races
description: Russian election authorities said Wednesday that they have registered nearly 1,600 Ukraine war veterans to run as candidates in federal, regional and local elections taking place next month.
content:
Russian election authorities said Wednesday that they have registered nearly 1,600 Ukraine war veterans to run as candidates in federal, regional and local elections taking place next month.
A total of 1,586 war veterans out of 1,668 who had filed for nomination were cleared to run, Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said.
At least 200 veterans have been nominated for seats in the 450-member State Duma, she added. One veteran is running for governor.
“I’m confident that our voters will show them total support and trust,” Pamfilova was quoted as saying at a press conference by the Interfax news agency.
In March 2025, reports indicated that the Kremlin planned to place up to 100 Ukraine war veterans into the State Duma this year in what was described as the “easiest” way to integrate them into government.
That number would account for more than one-fifth of the lower house of parliament’s seats.
Pamfilova called the veteran candidates “more than worthy” and said their election into public office would serve as “major proof of the renewal of our legislative body.”
President Vladimir Putin has hailed Ukraine war veterans as Russia’s “new elite.” Several state-backed programs have since worked to elevate thousands of them into government positions.
Pamfilova said 1,486 of the nominated veterans were backed by political parties, but did not specify which party had the most nominees. Another 100 are running as self-nominated independent candidates, she told reporters.
In the September 2024 elections, 308 war veterans representing United Russia won in local and regional races.
Pamfilova added that more than 2 million voters said they wanted to vote online during the September elections.

title: Pskov Court Bars Yabloko From Regional Assembly Race
description: A judge in the western Pskov region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the party said on Tuesday evening.
content:
A judge in the western Pskov region has disqualified the liberal Yabloko party’s list of candidates from the upcoming regional assembly elections, the party said on Tuesday evening.
The regional ban follows Russia’s Supreme Court ruling last week to reject Yabloko’s final appeal against a nationwide ban barring its candidate list from the State Duma elections next month.
Like the lawsuit that led to Yabloko’s federal ban, the Pskov region lawsuit was filed by the small nationalist party Rodina, which claimed Yabloko committed technical violations during its campaign registration.
The Pskov Regional Court ruled in favor of Rodina, effectively stripping Russia’s only registered party campaigning on a pro-peace platform from its final remaining stronghold.
Pskov was the last of three regions where Yabloko held seats in regional assemblies and had secured ballot access for next month’s elections, according to the outlet 7x7.
Regional election commissions previously rejected Yabloko’s registration in St. Petersburg and similarly removed its list of candidates in the republic of Karelia following another lawsuit filed by Rodina there.
Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party, said it will appeal the Pskov region ruling.
“The Pskov Yabloko team considers it illegal, unfounded and meant to unfairly eliminate political competitors,” the party chapter said in a post on Telegram.
Yabloko’s counter-lawsuit to pull Rodina’s list of candidates from the regional assembly race is scheduled to be heard on Thursday.
The Pskov chapter of Yabloko has long been the political base of Lev Shlosberg, a prominent anti-war politician who was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison last week under wartime censorship laws.

title: 3 Killed in Russia as Ukraine Sets Wildberries Warehouse and Oil Refinery Ablaze
description: At least three people were killed in drone attacks across Russia on Wednesday as Ukraine struck and set fire to a Wildberries warehouse in the central Tambov region, the second time the facility has been targeted since July, as well as an oil refinery further to the east.
content:
At least three people were killed in drone attacks across Russia on Wednesday as Ukraine struck and set fire to a Wildberries warehouse in the central Tambov region, the second time the facility has been targeted since July, as well as an oil refinery further to the east.
Tambov region Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said the blaze “completely” destroyed the Wildberries facility in the city of Kotovsk. One worker sustained a concussion from the blast wave, the governor said initially, only later to add that a second person was injured.
Wildberries said it safely evacuated all of its employees from the warehouse. It did not comment on the extent of the damage to the facility.
Videos and photos shared on social media showed a large column of black smoke rising from the warehouse and spreading across the morning sky in Kotovsk. The smoke cloud was also visible in NASA satellite images.
Local officials asked residents to avoid going outside over the next two days due to the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
The Wildberries warehouse in Kotovsk was previously struck on July 18, when Ukraine began its air campaign against the online retailer, which it accuses of helping supply the Russian military. Ukraine has also recently started attacking facilities belonging to Wildberries competitor Ozon.
In the neighboring Lipetsk region, a man and a 14-year-old were killed in a fire sparked by a falling drone. In the southwestern Belgorod region, a woman was killed in a drone attack, local authorities said.
Elsewhere, in the Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukraine said it struck and set fire to a Lukoil-operated oil refinery in the town of Kstovo. The facility has been attacked at least twice this year.
“The war must return to where it came from. Ukraine responds to Russian strikes, and we do so in a way that ensures the cost of the war for the aggressor inevitably rises,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote in a post on X.
Authorities in Nizhny Novgorod only confirmed that an industrial enterprise in the region was damaged in overnight attacks but did not provide further details.

title: Annexed Crimea Declares Regional Wildfire Emergency
description: Authorities in annexed Crimea declared a regional state of emergency on Tuesday as a wildfire that began last week following a Ukrainian drone attack continued to grow in size.
content:
Authorities in annexed Crimea declared a regional state of emergency on Tuesday as a wildfire that began last week following a Ukrainian drone attack continued to grow in size.
The blaze broke out last Wednesday in a forest nature reserve near the resort city of Yalta and expanded from just over 3 hectares (8 acres) to 50 hectares (124 acres) in the span of three days.
Emergency officials have not officially confirmed the cause of the fire, but reports citing NASA satellite imagery said it started on the night of a Ukrainian drone attack on Yalta.
The Interfax news agency reported that Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-installed head of Crimea, declared the wildfire a cause for a “regional natural emergency.”
The emergency zone boundaries have been set within the Yalta Mountain-Forest Nature Reserve. Police were advised to block roads leading into the nature reserve to keep people out of danger.
Emergency authorities said fire engines are unable to reach the fire’s epicenter due to cliffs and rocky terrain, while strong winds and hot weather are causing the flames to spread rapidly.
Crimea’s regional government said a “severe fire risk” remained in effect across the eastern and southern parts of the peninsula through Thursday.
Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, previously declared a state of emergency in late June after Ukrainian attacks knocked out major power stations and damaged the regional energy grid.

title: CIA Director Makes Rare Visit to Moscow
description: CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow on Tuesday aboard a U.S. military transport plane, Axios and CBS News reported, with sources familiar with the trip saying that the intelligence chief was slated to hold a series of “meetings” in the Russian capital.
content:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow on Tuesday aboard a U.S. military transport plane, Axios and CBS News reported, with sources familiar with the trip saying that the intelligence chief was slated to hold a series of “meetings” in the Russian capital.
News of the rare visit broke just hours after the Kremlin told journalists it had no information about a Boeing C-17 Globemaster landing at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport.
Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed the large U.S. military transport plane flew from Joint Base Andrews near Washington, D.C., stopping in Riga, Latvia, on Aug. 23 before continuing to Moscow on Tuesday.
U.S. officials have not officially commented on the visit. The U.S. Embassy in Moscow did not respond to a request for comment.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later confirmed the visit in remarks to The Washington Post, saying the purpose of Ratcliffe’s trip was for “contacts between security services,” not for a meeting with President Vladimir Putin. He did not provide further details.
An anonymous source told The Kyiv Independent that the United States asked Ukraine to halt its strikes on Moscow and St. Petersburg ahead of Ratcliffe’s trip. The source said Ukraine would be briefed on the American intelligence chief’s meetings in Russia.
The last time a CIA director visited Russia was in November 2021, just months before President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At that meeting, former Director William Burns met with Nikolai Patrushev, who was then serving as secretary of Russia’s Security Council.
Since his appointment in January 2025, Ratcliffe has maintained regular contact with his Russian counterpart, SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin.
Ratcliffe ’s visit marks the first known trip to Russia by a senior American official since U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with President Vladimir Putin in January to discuss Ukraine peace negotiations.
U.S. President Donald Trump has vowed to broker an end to Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine. However, the American president has struggled to bring Moscow and Kyiv toward a compromise, as both sides ramp up airstrikes deep inside each other’s territory this summer.
In July, sources told Politico that FBI Director Kash Patel was also planning a trip to Russia later this year.

title: Russia Steps Up Recruitment of Women for Ukraine War – Vot Tak
description: Russia is increasingly recruiting women for the war against Ukraine amid signs that its pool of potential male recruits is shrinking, according to an investigation by the Poland-based news outlet Vot Tak.
content:
Russia is increasingly recruiting women for the war against Ukraine amid signs that its pool of potential male recruits is shrinking, according to an investigation by the Poland-based news outlet Vot Tak.
At least 50 Russian women serving in the war have been killed, with the annual death toll rising the longer the war has gone on, the outlet found.
Vot Tak identified each of the 50 women and examined how Russia recruits women, what motivates them to enlist and how their roles have expanded from medical and support work to operating drones, firing sniper rifles and taking part in assaults.
Women have traditionally served mainly in civilian and support positions in the Russian military. In early 2022, 310,000 women worked in the armed forces, but only about 40,000 were service members. By March 2023, 1,100 women were deployed in Ukraine, according to then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, the only official figure released during the war.
Vot Tak found that women are now being recruited for a wider range of combat duties, including as drone operators, snipers, machine gunners and assault troops.
One of the women interviewed by Vot Tak was Yelizaveta Tsybina, a 24-year-old drone operator with the call sign “Bayana” who signed her fourth volunteer contract this summer. She is now based at a barracks in the southwestern Kursk region.
“They present it all beautifully and patriotically,” Tsybina told Vot Tak. “But when you arrive, the situation, the way you are treated and the work itself are completely different.”
She said that although she did not initially want to enlist after Russia invaded Ukraine, many of her friends did, and her boyfriend signed a contract in June 2024. A military enlistment office rejected Tsybina because she lacked medical training. Her boyfriend was killed that August.
She then trained as a drone operator and joined the St. George volunteer assault brigade, formed largely from former Wagner mercenaries and Russians who had fought in eastern Ukraine since 2014. A week after signing a six-month contract, she was sent on her first combat mission.
“I didn’t think I would survive my first contract,” she said.
In late 2024, Tsybina was deployed near Soledar in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, where she used drones for reconnaissance and later helped direct artillery fire. Her unit was subsequently sent to Chasiv Yar, where she said she dropped munitions on a dugout after seeing Ukrainian soldiers enter it.
Tsybina returned to her home region of Krasnoyarsk in May 2025 with a minor wound and concussion. Four months later, she was back in the military.
“It draws you in. Unfortunately, I can’t get out of it anymore,” she told Vot Tak. “When I return to civilian life, everything feels wrong — the environment, the routine, the people, the relationships. It feels as if I’m not where I belong.”
Tsybina has since signed three more fixed-term contracts with volunteer formations. She said she avoided signing with the Defense Ministry because its contracts are effectively impossible to terminate while the war continues.
“If I had the choice, I would choose not to start down this path,” she said. “I am afraid to say this openly, but disappointment with the Russian Armed Forces is the view of most Russian soldiers.”
Women can sign military contracts in any Russian region and are offered the same bonuses, salaries and benefits as men, according to Vot Tak. Advertisements generally seek Russian citizens aged 18 to 45 with at least a secondary education and no criminal record, though the criteria vary.
Like men’s contracts, women’s agreements with the Defense Ministry are automatically extended until the war ends.
Since late 2025, students have been targeted at universities in at least five cities, as well as the Ulyanovsk region , Vot Tak found. A college in Krasnoyarsk held a closed recruitment meeting attended only by women.
The recruitment drives are often short-lived. One in the Tomsk region lasted 10 days. A Telegram channel reopened recruitment in March 2026 and expanded it in June to drone, communications, logistics and supply roles. Two weeks after Vot Tak contacted the channel, a recruiter said applications had closed because of an “extremely large influx” of candidates.
Recruiters also made misleading promises, the outlet reported, including telling prospective recruits that contracts could be terminated after one year and that women would not be transferred to assault units or sent to the front. In practice, Defense Ministry contracts are extended indefinitely and women have served in frontline and assault roles.
Russia had initially tried to recruit women as medics and cooks early in the war. By 2023, volunteer formations were advertising for female snipers, drone operators, electronic warfare specialists and assault troops.
The Defense Ministry has also reportedly recruited female prisoners in exchange for expunging their convictions. More than 80 may have left Siberian prisons to work as medics in late 2024, Vot Tak reported, though the practice appears to have since been phased out.
Vot Tak said it identified 50 female service members killed since February 2022. The annual toll rose from five in 2022 to 15 in 2025. Twelve were killed in the first half of 2026 alone.
Most were between the ages of 31 and 49. The oldest, Irina Anisimova from the Saratov region, was 57 when her death was reported in October 2024. The youngest was 23-year-old Yana Koshkina, who volunteered in 2023 and was killed in a drone strike near Bakhmut while commanding a casualty evacuation team.
One of the first was Valentina Galatova, 27, who was killed during a combat mission in Mariupol on April 14, 2022.
Galatova first traveled to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine with humanitarian aid in 2014 and later settled in Donetsk with a commander from a Russia-backed formation. After he was killed in 2020, she joined his regiment.
Officially listed as a paramedic, Galatova worked as a political officer and therapist, her mother told Vot Tak. During the full-scale invasion, she joined assaults and died in mortar fire in Mariupol.
Women have also been implicated in abuses. Vot Tak previously reported that an assault platoon commander with the call sign “Witch” allegedly ordered subordinates to shoot five Ukrainian prisoners of war in May 2024. A female sniper called “Ripley” told a pro-Kremlin correspondent that she would be willing to shoot foreign fighters who try to surrender.
Some women now enlist as soon as they turn 18, while others try to flee after encountering withheld pay, violence by commanders or indefinite contracts, Vot Tak said.
Sofya, who asked that her name be changed, signed a Defense Ministry contract at 19 after graduating from medical college in 2023. Now 22, she trains soldiers in first aid and wants to leave.
She told Vot Tak that recruiters had promised her about 80,000 rubles ($967) a month but did not pay the agreed salary. She dismissed recruitment into drone units as another lure to send young people into Ukraine.
“I am disappointed in today’s army and want to leave as soon as possible,” she said. “Everyone is waiting for the war to end so they can get out — young people and older people alike.”
“At 22, I have no desire to die because of politicians’ wars.”

title: Senior Vatican Official Calls for Peace in Ukraine After Meeting With Lavrov in Moscow
description: A senior Vatican official called for an end to the war in Ukraine after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Moscow on Tuesday.
content:
A senior Vatican official called for an end to the war in Ukraine after meeting with Russia n Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Moscow on Tuesday.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, whose position at the Vatican is analogous to a foreign minister, said that as the war between Russia and Ukraine continues, it "creates new victims ... and renders future reconciliation ever more difficult."
"It is therefore urgent and necessary to end and to look beyond the conflict," Gallagher said, speaking alongside Lavrov at a joint press conference following their meeting.
He also said that he and Lavrov had discussed avenues toward peace in Ukraine and that the two had agreed to cooperate on humanitarian matters such as caring for children impacted by the war.
Gallagher, the Vatican's second-highest diplomatic official, last visited Moscow for talks with Lavrov in 2021, the year before President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Pope Leo has repeatedly called for an end to the conflict. In an appeal earlier this month, he lamented the "ever-growing number of civilian victims, including children," as a result of the war in Ukraine.
Gallagher said Tuesday that the Vatican would "continue to provide strong spiritual, diplomatic and humanitarian support by contributing to and offering a space for dialogue" to end the conflict.

title: St. Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena Cancels Ye Concerts
description: St.
content:
St. Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena has denied plans to host two October concerts for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, triggering a public dispute with the event’s promoter.
Say Agency, one of Russia’s top organizers for international music acts , insisted Monday that the performances remained scheduled for Oct. 10 and 11. Both the agency and Gazprom Arena initially promoted the shows last week.
However, the venue abruptly reversed its position on Monday, declaring that the concerts “ cannot take place ” because it was not organizing them and had not signed rental contracts. All promotional materials for the Ye performances were removed from Gazprom Arena’s website.
Local news outlet Fontanka reporte d that the sudden cancellation followed a phone call “from above,” suggesting that the Kremlin may have intervened. The outlet added that organizers launched ticket sales before receiving permits from the local authorities.
Despite Gazprom Arena’s withdrawal, Say Agency CEO Anna Subcheva said the two concerts would still take place and that formal contracts are expected by Thursday. Subcheva said Ye had already received a 1.5 billion ruble ($17.7 million) advance payment.
Ye previously visited Moscow in 2024 to celebrate the birthday of fashion designer and collaborator Gosha Rubchinskiy. Rumors of a performance at Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium circulated at the time.
The rapper has drawn controversy in recent years for his antisemitic remarks. He has previously voiced admiration for Adolf Hitler, and in May 2025, he released a song called “Heil Hitler.”
Some Russian officials and political figures criticized plans to host the Ye concerts in St. Petersburg given his past public displays of Nazi symbols, which is a criminal offense in Russia.
Moscow’s Luzhniki Stadium said it would be open to hosting Ye’s concert following Gazprom Arena’s withdrawal.

title: ‘Information Ducks’: Kremlin Dismisses Mobilization Rumors
description: The Kremlin on Tuesday dismissed growing speculation that President Vladimir Putin may announce another mobilization wave following next month’s parliamentary elections, calling reports about a possible new draft deliberate fabrications. “The Ukrainian authorities are spreading all of this,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in an interview with the broadcaster RTVI. “Their regime is trying to destabilize our country ideologically.”  “All of this amounts to ‘information ducks’” — fabrications — “deliberately dumped into the news cycle,” he added.
content:
The Kremlin on Tuesday dismissed growing speculation that President Vladimir Putin may announce another mobilization wave following next month ’s parliamentary elections, calling reports about a possible new draft deliberate fabrications.
“The Ukrainian authorities are spreading all of this,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in an interview with the broadcaster RTVI. “Their regime is trying to destabilize our country ideologically.”
“ All of this amounts to ‘information ducks’ ” — fabrications — “deliberately dumped into the news cycle,” he added.
Peskov, who often uses the word “duck” to describe something as being false, similarly dismissed draft rumors in September 2022, just days before Putin declared a “partial” mobilization of 300,000 reservists.
The spokesman’s remarks follow recent claims by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that Russia is planning to mobilize an additional 300,000 troops following the State Duma and regional elections in September.
Meanwhile, Western intelligence officials cited by The Wall Street Journal said the Russian military carried out mobilization readiness exercises in the Kaliningrad region last month.
Despite official denials, military analysts point to Russia ’s heavy battlefield losses and declining voluntary enlistment figures as signs that a new call-up may be unavoidable.
However, some experts also note that another mass mobilization would present serious logistical hurdles and might fail to address tactical challenges on the front line.

title: Deadly Ukrainian Strikes in Southern Russia Force Oil Refinery to Shut Down
description: At least two people were killed in a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks in southern Russia that targeted two oil refineries, forcing at least one facility to halt operations, regional officials said.
content:
At least two people were killed in a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks in southern Russia that targeted two oil refineries, forcing at least one facility to halt operations, regional officials said.
In the Krasnodar region, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev wrote in a post on Telegram that falling drone debris killed two people and injured two others during a strike on the Afipsky oil refinery, which sparked a fire at the facility.
Authorities in the neighboring Rostov region said that the Novoshakhtinsky refinery sustained damage and temporarily suspended processing operations following a separate attack. They did not provide further details.
Both refineries have previously been targeted in drone strikes.
Ukraine began intensifying its attacks against Russian oil refineries earlier this year, driving widespread fuel shortages across the country this summer.
The latest strikes follow an August 21 attack on the Perm oil refinery, which was forced to suspend operations after drone impacts ignited fires and damaged key technical processing units, industry sources told Reuters.

title: Ex-Pussy Riot Member Says She Helped the FSB Spy on Kremlin Critics
description: Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has revealed that she was coerced into working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, saying that she gathered information on anti-war activists and was involved in a failed assassination plot against an exiled Kremlin critic.
content:
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has revealed that she was coerced into working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, saying that she gathered information on anti-war activists and was involved in a failed assassination plot against an exiled Kremlin critic.
Flores said FSB officers coerced her into signing a cooperation agreement following a February 2023 raid on her Moscow apartment, threatening her with criminal prosecution over social media posts about alleged Russian war crimes in Ukraine alongside death threats against her relatives.
“They began recruiting me with all kinds of threats and abuse [including] threats to murder my family and that I’d never be able to prove who killed my mother,” she told the exiled news outlet Port in a video interview.
Operating under the codename “Harley,” Flores said she was assigned to build detailed profiles on Russian artists and political dissidents. Between early 2024 and June, she received monthly payments of 50,000 rubles ($600) from her security service handlers after an initial disbursement of 30,000 rubles ($360).
Flores detailed how she deliberately sabotaged her FSB assignments for over two years, faking personal feuds with targets like artists Philippenzo and Pavel Krisevich to delay their arrest by law enforcement authorities.
In mid-2025, Flores said she was ordered to lure her ex-boyfriend and former Pussy Riot member Pyotr Verzilov into a cafe in Serbia where undercover FSB agents planned to kidnap and kill him. The activist said she was offered 3 million rubles ($36,000) for her role in that assassination plot.
“That was the point of no return. Before, I thought I just needed to wait to get my passport back and flee. But then I realized how far they were willing to go,” Flores said in the interview with Port.
Refusing to help carry out the assassination plot against Verzilov, Flores stalled her handlers and sought help from human rights lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov. Exiled businessman Leonid Nevzlin subsequently helped her flee Russia earlier this month.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify any of the claims made by Flores.

title: Putin Signs Order Allowing Government to Seize Critical Infrastructure Following Attacks
description: President Vladimir Putin on Monday granted the government powers to take control of critically important infrastructure sites if they are deemed to be poorly protected against Ukrainian strikes and other threats.
content:
President Vladimir Putin on Monday granted the government powers to take control of critically important infrastructure sites if they are deemed to be poorly protected against Ukrainian strikes and other threats.
The special powers, set out in an executive order , allow the state to assume control over the physical, financial and legal assets of facilities that fail to maintain adequate security or are slow to make repairs following attacks.
Putin's order encompasses a wide array of sectors, including fuel, energy, industrial, communications, transportation and commercial logistics sites deemed essential to national security and economic stability.
The new powers come a week after the president instructed the government to help rebuild commercial warehouses that have been damaged in Ukrainian attacks.
Since the start of the summer, Ukraine has ramped up its attacks against Russian oil refineries and, increasingly, warehouses and logistics hubs belonging to major online retailers.
On Monday, Russia 's second-largest online retailer Ozon said four of its facilities in southern Russia were targeted in Ukrainian attacks.

title: Russia Is Betting on the MC-21 to Reverse Its Aviation Decline. It’s No Silver Bullet.
description: This article was first published by VPost.
content:
This article was first published by VPost.
It took 21 years for President Vladimir Putin to step aboard Russia’s new MC-21 passenger jet, the long-delayed plane that Moscow hopes will replace the aging Airbus and Boeing aircraft underpinning its commercial fleet.
But the plane Putin inspected at the Irkutsk Aviation Plant in July was markedly different from the aircraft that was originally envisioned. Western sanctions imposed after Russia invaded Ukraine forced manufacturer United Aircraft Corporation to replace its foreign-made engines, composite wing and other components with Russian alternatives.
The MC-21’s troubled development reflects the mounting pressure on Russian civil aviation after sanctions forced manufacturers to redesign aircraft using heavier and costlier domestic components, while airlines increasingly rely on aging Western-made planes kept flying through improvised supply chains.
Industry insiders say Russia has so far avoided a safety crisis, but warn that its fleet will continue to shrink — and that the MC-21 is unlikely to be produced quickly or cheaply enough to reverse the decline.
“Production of the MC-21 will be limited,” said Kirill Zhirikhin, who worked on tests of the aircraft’s capabilities at Russia’s Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI) from 2007 to 2022.
Russian officials have repeatedly promised Putin that airlines will receive dozens of domestically produced aircraft, including the MC-21, Tu-214 and Sukhoi Superjet, in the coming years.
“Under Russia’s wartime conditions, this is unimplementable. The announced targets would require some kind of ideal conditions,” Zhirikhin said.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the sanctions that followed it have strained the economy while redirecting money, industrial capacity and skilled labor toward the defense sector. For the aviation industry, shortages of qualified workers and broader economic pressures are now among the most acute problems, Zhirikhin said.
“There are very few qualified people. Only the loyalists stayed,” he said. “Aviation is an industry that needs to keep working continuously. A country cannot drop out of aircraft production for three years and then return and produce 50 or 100 planes a year. It’s physically impossible.”
The MC-21 was developed by the United Aircraft Corporation and is being produced at the Irkutsk Aviation Plant, which also manufactures Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jets.
During his visit, Putin walked past six MC-21 fuselages on the assembly line.
Irkutsk Aviation Plant head Andrei Soynov told the president that four planes would be completed by the end of 2026 and transferred to Aeroflot once the MC-21 had passed all certification requirements.
Zhirikhin said the United Aircraft Corporation had made considerable progress in developing the aircraft but argued that the MC-21 remained at least 15 years behind its foreign competitors.
“They might finish the MC-21 just to show it off and possibly deliver a few aircraft through transactions within the state-controlled industry,” he said. “But it will not become a mass-produced plane.”
The post-invasion version shown to Putin will not be able to fly nonstop from Moscow to Vladivostok as originally planned because Russian-made components have made the aircraft about six metric tons heavier.
In an exchange captured on camera, Putin told Sergei Chemezov, head of the state-owned defense and technology conglomerate Rostec, that the plane needed to be able to fly farther.
“We will work on it,” Chemezov replied , adding that a longer-range version remained under development.
In June, the Russian government raised the projected cost of the first 18 localized MC-21 aircraft by almost two-thirds. Their total cost increased to 96.1 billion rubles ($1.2 billion) from 58.3 billion rubles ($730 million).
The estimated cost per aircraft is now 5.34 billion rubles ($67 million), up from between 3.14 billion and 3.29 billion rubles ($39 million to $41 million) in 2023.
More than 400 foreign-owned aircraft, mostly Boeing and Airbus jets, remained in Russia after the invasion of Ukraine, when Western sanctions forced leasing companies to terminate their contracts.
The fleet’s future has raised long-term concerns as Russia is forced to cannibalize existing aircraft for spare parts and obtain components through channels designed to circumvent sanctions.
Major airlines have established their own maintenance centers, while Aeroflot has been authorized to service Airbus and Boeing engines independently.
About 20% of Russia’s fleet has been grounded in recent years, partly due to a global problem with Pratt & Whitney engines.
Open-source data show that reported malfunctions involving commercial and military aircraft increased after the invasion, reaching 300 in 2024.
Russia has nevertheless avoided major crashes involving its largest airlines. In one serious incident in 2023, a Ural Airlines Airbus A320 made an emergency landing in a field near the Siberian city of Novosibirsk.
News reports cannot provide a complete picture of the industry, said Andrei Menshenin, an independent Russian journalist who previously covered aviation for the St. Petersburg-based news outlet Fontanka.
“Inside airlines, dozens of incidents can happen that never become public,” Menshenin said. “There could be a system failure, for example, or an engine failure that keeps a plane on the ground.”
A pilot working for one of Russia’s largest airlines, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the industry had overcome its initial difficulties but now faced financial pressure that was being felt by passengers and staff.
“Aviation is fully safe,” the pilot said in a Telegram call from Russia, adding that airlines had continued flying “as before.”
Crews had expected malfunctions to become more frequent after the invasion, “but nothing like that happened” at his airline, he said.
“As the special military operation began, we feared: How would we fly? What would happen? Nobody knew,” he said, using Russia’s official term for its invasion. “There was uncertainty. What would happen next? What would happen if the planes were grounded? What would happen if Russian aviation couldn’t cope?”
The pilot dismissed reports that Russian crews had been forced to use paper maps and said Aeroflot continued to receive the necessary components and software updates despite sanctions.
Menshenin said critical aeronautical data, which aircraft should receive every 28 days, was most likely reaching Russia through Kazakhstan using improvised arrangements.
Investigations have also found that Russia imports aircraft components, including engines, through countries like India and China.
The pilot said crews remained cautious and that airlines could operate aircraft with certain repairs deferred under the Minimum Equipment List (MEL), which sets out the conditions under which an aircraft may fly with specific equipment inoperative.
“For example, one airline may have one or two minor deferred defects under the MEL, while another, such as S7, may have five MEL items requiring additional procedures before departure,” the pilot said.
Menshenin said safety standards were broadly similar across Russian airlines but were likely to deteriorate as the country became increasingly isolated, inevitably leading to more incidents.
“Russian aviation is becoming isolated and moving toward such ‘safety giants’ as North Korea and the Central African Republic,” Menshenin said. “We should expect incidents to increase. That doesn’t necessarily mean planes will crash, but pilots will be the last line of defense, with more responsibility on their shoulders.”
The closure of Western airspace after the invasion of Ukraine cost Aeroflot and S7 Airlines a large share of their international destinations. Both carriers have gradually rebuilt parts of their networks by focusing on Asia and neighboring countries.
Russian airlines are no longer thinking about a “great future” and are instead trying to solve practical problems, including how to keep operating as capacity declines, according to a source close to the Russian aviation market.
“The overall feeling in the industry is: We will fly, but the question is at what scale,” the source said on condition of anonymity.
Recent reports have said that foreign carriers now account for nearly half of Russia’s aviation market.
The aviation market source attributed that growth to Russia’s aircraft shortage and said the share of international flights operated by Russian airlines had plateaued.
The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity from a major international aviation hub, said that even if the MC-21 entered service with Aeroflot, it would not be commercially viable or resolve the industry’s long-term problems.
“Everyone has come to terms with the situation,” he said. “No one expects sanctions to be lifted. They need to work now, and everyone is working and trying to maintain safety while seizing the opportunities that remain.”
The source said the industry consensus was that Russian airlines remained safe, but that major carriers had little idea of what would come next.
Even if airlines transition to the MC-21, domestically produced aircraft are unlikely to improve the situation in the way Putin wants, the source said. They could instead push prices higher because they are less fuel-efficient.
“The Russian aviation industry understands that, at some point, bankruptcies will begin,” he said. “For various reasons, some airlines may not have aircraft, while others may receive Russian-made planes, but the economics won’t work.”
The source predicted that Russian aviation would continue to contract and become increasingly focused on domestic routes.
“The dilemma facing Russian aviation today is how to maintain connectivity within the country and with the friendly nations Russia still has,” he said.

title: Russia and Ukraine Release 20 Prisoners of War
description: Ukraine and Russia exchanged 10 prisoners of war each, officials in Kyiv and Belarusian state media announced Monday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling the swap a “special stage” of ongoing prisoner exchanges with Moscow.
content:
Ukraine and Russia exchanged 10 prisoners of war each, officials in Kyiv and Belarusian state media announced Monday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling the swap a “special stage” of ongoing prisoner exchanges with Moscow.
Belarusian state media reported that Minsk mediated the latest release of servicemen held in captivity. Russia ’s Defense Ministry did not immediately confirm the exchange.
On the Ukrainian side, t wo of the freed soldiers had been previously classified as missing in action since 2024 and eight since 2025, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said .
The group included soldiers and sailors from the Ukrainian armed forces and national guard who had been fighting in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
“Today, as part of a special stage of the exchange, we are bringing back 10 of our warriors — through Belarus,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It’s very important that we managed to bring them back.”
It was not immediately clear why Zelensky designated the swap on Monday as “special.”
The latest release of prisoners came less than a week after Russia and Ukraine each exchanged 103 servicemen following mediation from the United Arab Emirates.
At the time, Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said that another exchange was expected before the end of the month.
Both Russia and Ukraine have released hundreds of prisoners of war since the start of the year through mediation from the United States and the UAE.
Repatriations of fallen soldiers and prisoner-of-war exchanges remain among the few channels of direct communication between Moscow and Kyiv since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

title: Kremlin Says It’s Working to Minimize Impact of Ukrainian Attacks on Russian Grain Exports
description: The Kremlin said on Monday that measures were being taken to minimize the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's grain exports as global wheat importers brace for tighter supplies amid attacks on Black Sea grain infrastructure.
content:
The Kremlin said on Monday that measures were being taken to minimize the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia 's grain exports as global wheat importers brace for tighter supplies amid attacks on Black Sea grain infrastructure.
Tit-for-tat attacks by Russia and Ukraine, both major grain exporters, on ports and vessels in recent weeks have shuttered grain terminals and forced shippers to delay or cancel loadings for dozens of cargoes during the peak export season.
"Measures have been identified and will be further developed, ensuring that all grain intended for export is shipped on time and in full," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, without providing further details.
President Vladimir Putin acknowledged last week that Russia was experiencing problems with its agricultural exports, but said officials would work to resolve them. The Kremlin leader also promised that there would be no shortages on global markets.
Russia would have about 60 million metric tons of grain for export in the current season, Putin estimated. Russia n grain exports are expected to pick up to 2.2 million tons in August from 1.95 million in July, the Sovecon consultancy said.

title: Siberian Wildfires Reach 3.5M Acres Across Krasnoyarsk and Sakha Republic
description: Wildfires across Siberia continued to expand as blazes in the Krasnoyarsk region and the republic of Sakha grew to nearly 3.5 million acres, roughly the size of the U.S. state of Connecticut, forest fire authorities said Monday.
content:
Wildfires across Siberia continued to expand as blazes in the Krasnoyarsk region and the republic of Sakha grew to nearly 3.5 million acres, roughly the size of the U.S. state of Connecticut, forest fire authorities said Monday.
In the Krasnoyarsk region, 128 active wildfires were burning across 405,800 hectares (1 million acres), according to the regional forest fire center. S akha, Russia’s largest ethnic republic, had 36 active blazes covering 987,067 hectares (2.44 million acres) as of midnight Monday, federal authorities said .
Russia’s Aerial Forest Protection Service said more than 1.3 million hectares (3.3 million acres) of wildfires were burning across Russia.
Authorities have blamed the fires on summer heat and Siberian silk moth infestations, which have killed off vast swaths of trees and left behind highly flammable deadwood.
The Krasnoyarsk region declared a wildfire emergency on June 10, barring the public from entering woodlands, lighting campfires, burning trash or grass and conducting any other fire-hazardous work.
The spread is concentrated in four northern districts that cover around three-quarters of the Krasnoyarsk region’s territory, the Interfax news agency quoted the regional forest fire center as saying.
The EU’s Copernicus satellite monitoring unit said that wildfires in Krasnoyarsk, Sakha and the Yamalo-Nenets autonomous district have been burning with particularly high intensity since the end of July.
“[In] the Siberian Arctic, the peak emissions have been occurring slightly later than usual and at a time when the number of fires might be expected to decrease,” the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Services said Friday.

title: Russian Government Proposes Tax Relief for Wildberries and Sellers After Drone Attacks
description: The Russian government has drafted a financial assistance package for online retailer Wildberries and sellers who use the platform following weeks of Ukrainian attacks on the company’s warehouses and logistics centers, the Finance Ministry said Monday.
content:
The Russian government has drafted a financial assistance package for online retailer Wildberries and sellers who use the platform following weeks of Ukrainian attacks on the company’s warehouses and logistics centers, the Finance Ministry said Monday.
Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said the proposed measures include a deferral of taxes and insurance payments, as well as a freeze on tax audits , all with the aim of “easing administrative and financial pressure” on impacted businesses.
Under the draft proposal, sellers whose losses exceed 5% of annual revenue will receive a 12-month deferral on value-added tax (VAT), corporate tax and other liabilities due between August 2026 and July 2027.
Following the deferral period, Wildberries sellers will be allowed to settle their tax obligations in equal monthly installments over 12 months.
A matching deferral plan through July 28, 2027, followed by a one-year installment structure, would also be granted to Wildberries & Russ (RWB), the parent company of the e-commerce giant.
In addition, the government plans to freeze tax audits and procedural deadlines for both RWB and Wildberries sellers through the end of the year.
The relief measures have been submitted to the cabinet of ministers for final approval by Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
The proposal follows instructions from Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak last month directing federal agencies and the Central Bank to organize emergency support for Wildberries and businesses that sell goods on the platform.
Bloomberg reported in early August that the Russian government was weighing targeted state support, including debt restructuring and loan payment holidays.
Ukraine has struck more than two dozen facilities belonging to Wildberries since mid-July. Officials in Kyiv have accused Wildberries of supplying the Russian military with drone parts and other equipment.
Some estimates place total damages to the retailer’s properties and seller inventory at 878 billion rubles ($10.5 billion).
Last week, President Vladimir Putin ordered the government to help rebuild commercial warehouses that have been damaged in Ukrainian attacks.
Update: Mishustin approved the relief measures on Aug. 26, 2026.

title: At Least 3 Killed as Ukrainian Drones Target Ozon Hubs Across Southern Russia
description: Ukrainian strikes killed at least three teenagers in the Krasnodar region, Russian officials said Monday morning, coming as the country's second-largest retailer Ozon reported that four of its logistics centers across southern Russia were targeted in the overnight attacks.
content:
Ukrainian strikes killed at least three teenagers in the Krasnodar region, Russian officials said Monday morning, coming as the country's second-largest retailer Ozon reported that four of its logistics centers across southern Russia were targeted in the overnight attacks.
Russian human rights chief Maria Lvova-Belova said another six children were hospitalized for injuries they sustained during the deadly attack in Krasnodar. Earlier, local officials said drone debris fell onto a "private children's center."
Ozon said a large fire broke out at its logistics hub in the town of Enem in the Krasnodar region as a result of a drone attack. It also reported a fire at one of its facilities in the republic of Dagestan following drone strikes.
"According to preliminary information, several people were injured," the online retailer said , referring to the attack in Dagestan.
Multiple videos shared on social media showed multiple drones flying into the warehouse in Dagestan early Monday morning before bursting into fireballs. Men with automatic rifles could be seen trying to shoot down the drones as they flew toward the facility.
Ozon also said workers were evacuated from its warehouses in the nearby republic of Adygeya and the Stavropol region, though neither facility was damaged, it added.
Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 28% on the Moscow Exchange following news of the attacks, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by more than 13%.
Ukraine began attacking Ozon warehouses this weekend after more than a month of strikes against facilities owned by its biggest competitor Wildberries. Officials in Kyiv have accused Wildberries of supplying the Russian military with drone parts and other equipment
Ozon suspended operations at its logistics center in the Samara region after it was hit by Ukrainian drones on Saturday.
