title: Russian Supreme Court Removes Taliban From List of Terrorist Organizations
description: Russia’s Supreme Court on Thursday formally removed the Taliban from the country’s list of banned terrorist organizations, a symbolic move underscoring Moscow’s warming ties with Afghanistan’s de facto rulers. “The previously established ban on the Taliban’s activities... has been suspended,” Supreme Court Judge Oleg Nefedov was quoted as saying by the state-run news agency TASS. “The decision enters into legal force immediately.” Thursday’s ruling, which was made during a closed-door hearing, follows a request last month from the Prosecutor General’s Office to remove the Taliban from its list of terrorist organizations.
content:
Russia’s Supreme Court on Thursday formally removed the Taliban from the country’s list of banned terrorist organizations, a symbolic move underscoring Moscow’s warming ties with Afghanistan’s de facto rulers.
“The previously established ban on the Taliban’s activities... has been suspended,” Supreme Court Judge Oleg Nefedov was quoted as saying by the state-run news agency TASS. “The decision enters into legal force immediately.”
Thursday’s ruling, which was made during a closed-door hearing, follows a request last month from the Prosecutor General’s Office to remove the Taliban from its list of terrorist organizations.
While the move does not amount to formal diplomatic recognition, it clears a legal obstacle for Russian officials engaging with the Taliban at official events and is widely seen as a step toward normalization.
The Taliban authorities praised the move as a “significant development in relations between Afghanistan and Russia" in a foreign ministry statement.
“With this decision, the only remaining obstacle to further political and economic cooperation between the two countries has been removed,” Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said in a meeting with Moscow's Ambassador to Kabul Dmitry Zhirnov, according to the statement.
Representatives of the Taliban have made several high-level visits to Russia in recent years, including participation in Russia’s flagship economic forum in St. Petersburg in 2022 and 2024. They also met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in October 2023.
Russia first banned the Taliban as a terrorist organization in 2003 over its alleged support for Islamist insurgents in the North Caucasus. However, since the militant group seized control of Afghanistan in August 2021, the Kremlin has strengthened ties with the country’s de facto rulers.
Russia is not alone in shifting its posture. Kazakhstan removed the Taliban from its terrorist list last year, and China has deepened economic ties, becoming the first country to appoint a new ambassador to Afghanistan in 2023.
Still, no country has formally recognized the Taliban government, which remains diplomatically isolated despite growing regional engagement.

title: Putin's Demands Mean Trump Can Never Truly End the War. Here's Why.
description: Opinion | After talks with President Vladimir Putin, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said he was optimistic about soon striking a peace deal that would give Russia five Ukrainian territories and block Kyiv’s NATO aspirations.
content:
After talks with President Vladimir Putin, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said he was optimistic about soon striking a peace deal that would give Russia five Ukrainian territories and block Kyiv’s NATO aspirations. Both he and President Donald Trump are wrong.
Trump’s attempts to end Russia’s three-year, full-scale war against Ukraine will fail because they ignore Putin’s demand to “eliminate the root causes” of the war. A few days ago, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov described those causes as “ the Nazi government, represented by Zelensky and his associates” who were on a mission to “exterminate everything Russian.”
In reality, this amounts to Russia’s denial of Ukraine as a sovereign actor, questioning the democratic legitimacy of President Volodymyr Zelensky and depicting Ukraine as an artificial and U.S. puppet state.
The Trump administration’s approach to peace talks has ignored Russia’s repeated requests for these “root causes” to be resolved before any ceasefire, let alone agreement, can be reached. Trump’s growing frustration with Russia’s foot-dragging is rooted in an unwillingness to understand that Russia will only end its war if Ukraine capitulates by agreeing to jettison its identity, sovereignty and independence and become Little Russia.
As this is unlikely, a successful outcome to Trump’s peace talks will likely be illusory.
On April 1, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said the Trump administration is attempting “some kind of scheme” to reach a ceasefire before moving on to “other models and schemes” to end the war. Because this does not address the “root causes” of the war, Russia will not agree to U.S. peace proposals.
Understanding what the Kremlin means by this requires us to appreciate that Putin has held a long-term inability to accept Ukraine as a state fully independent of Russia and a Ukrainian identity distinct from Russian. Putin’s obsession throughout his quarter of a century of direct and indirect rule has been to transform Ukraine through soft and hard power into a puppet state resembling that of President Alexander Lukashenko’s Belarus.
Herein lies the crux of the Trump administration’s difficulties reconciling the Kremlin’s goal of evisceration with that of Ukraine’s defence of its identity, sovereignty and independence.
Contrary to what Trump believes, the Kremlin’s demands to resolve these “roots” lie not in NATO enlargement per se, but in the supposed loss of Ukraine to Putin’s Russian World and the Russian Orthodox Church’s Holy Rus.
Russia has laid claim to Crimea and the port of Sevastopol since the start of the post-Soviet era. Most Russian politicians, even those who claimed to be opposed to Putin’s authoritarian regime, supported Moscow’s goal of “reuniting” with these regions.
Even the pro-Western, democratic President Boris Yeltsin took the entire decade of the 1990s to sign a treaty recognizing Russia’s border with Ukraine. The obstacle, after all, was not Ukraine — President Leonid Kuchma could never been described as anti-Russian. It was Russia.
In 1990, Russian nationalist dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn called for the Soviet Union to be replaced with a Russian Union of the three eastern Slavic states. Like Putin in his 2008 speech to the NATO-Russia Council, Solzhenitsyn had a history of questioning Ukrainian sovereignty over its southeastern regions.
In 2014, Putin referred to Ukraine’s southeast using the tsarist term of “New Russia,” describing the region as “historically Russian lands” that were wrongly included inside Ukraine. Then, in September 2022, Moscow annexed the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson following referendums that were deeply flawed, contrary to Witkoff’s view .
Russia demands that Ukraine acknowledge these “ realities on the ground ” by recognizing the four annexed regions and Crimea as Russian — including territory still held by Ukraine. Putin said borders “must reflect the sovereign decision of the people who live on the lands that we name our historic lands.”
Obviously, these two demands are non-starters for Zelensky. Other Russian officials have gone even further, claiming the cities of Kharkiv, Odesa, Dnipro and Kyiv as “Russian.”
Three important roots of the war, according to the Kremlin, can be found in the second half of the 2000s. The first was the launch of the Russian World Foundation to unite the three eastern Slavic peoples and defend Russians and Russian speakers.
The second was the re-unification of the domestic and emigré branches of the Russian Orthodox Church, which infused imperial nationalism into Russia’s body politic. The third was the election of Kirill as Patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church and its promotion of the unity of Holy Rus and the trinity of the three eastern Slavs.
Putin returned to the presidency in 2012 determined to enter Russian history as the latest in the pantheon of “ gatherers of Russian lands ,” a term used for earlier Russian leaders who built the tsarist and Soviet empires.
Ukraine has a central place in this. The core of the Soviet Union was composed of the three eastern Slavic peoples — Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians — who made up two-thirds of the population and the overwhelming bulk of the political, economic and security elites.
The full-scale invasion of Ukraine is the first stage in rebuilding this core. Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian Military History Society who penned Putin’s July 2021 essay on Russian-Ukrainian unity — widely considered to be the ideological treatise of the invasion — even insisted the spring 2022 peace talks be held in the symbolically important Belovezhskaya Pushcha hunting lodge where Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian leaders dismantled the U.S.S.R. in 1991.
The Kremlin’s determination, coupled with Putin’s obsession with Little Russia, pressured Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych to turn Ukraine’s back on European integration. Putin took his revenge against the pro-European demands of the 2013-14 Euromaidan Revolution by initiating Russia’s long-simmering demand to “reunite” with Crimea, invading the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine and setting up proxy enclaves.
Over the next eight years, Putin sought to transform Ukraine into a Belarusian-style puppet state through the Minsk accords. Ukrainian Presidents Petro Poroshenko and Volodymyr Zelensky refused to implement Russia’s reading of these agreements. By 2021, the Kremlin had given up on them and opted for a war, believing Russia would quickly defeat Ukraine because it was an artificial entity and Little Russians would greet the Russian army as liberators. Moscow, which expected a short fight, was unprepared for the resistance they met.
A largely forgotten open letter from August 11, 2009, sent by President Dmitry Medvedev to his Ukrainian counterpart Viktor Yushchenko, reveals the long-term roots of the war. The similarity between Medvedev’s demands and those raised by Putin, Lavrov and Russian officials showcases how the Kremlin’s goals towards Ukraine have remained constant over the last two decades and cannot be ignored by the Trump administration in peace talks to end the war.
Medvedev was never the liberal reformer that the Obama administration and European leaders saw him as. In reality, he held hardline stances towards Georgia, which had been invaded by Russia the year before his open letter, and Ukraine. Medvedev, now deputy head of the Russian Security Council, is one of Russia’s most extreme agitators for military aggression against Ukraine.
Medvedev’s open letter echoed Putin’s view of Russians and Ukrainians as "brotherly peoples" who shared a common history, culture and religion." They both blamed Ukraine for the deterioration in Russian-Ukrainian relations, with Kyiv at fault for refusing to accept that it is a Little Russia.
Medvedev and Putin both have denied that Russia was a threat to Ukraine and therefore brushed aside the need for Ukraine to join NATO. As Medvedev wrote, a Russian threat to Ukraine "does not and cannot exist."
Medvedev in 2009 and Russian leaders since 2022 condemned Ukrainian language, educational, and cultural policies and memory politics. They were, and remain, aghast at a Ukrainian history separate to Russian, “discrimination” against the Russian language in public life, judiciary, education, culture and the media, as well as government interference in the Russian Orthodox Church. Medvedev and Putin denounced Kyiv’s “nationalist interpretation” of the 1933 Holodomor as a “genocide against the Ukrainian people” and glorification of “radical nationalists” and “Nazi collaborators.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov condemned the “racist Kyiv regime” for the “extermination of everything Russian” in the language, media, and cultural domains and the banning of the Russian Orthodox Church. Lavrov viewed the resolution of these “root causes” as a demand to the Trump administration that should be fulfilled before any peace agreement could be reached.
During the spring 2022 and 2025 peace talks, the Kremlin saw the “root causes” of the war refer to long-standing demands that Ukraine can only exist as a Little Russian puppet state akin to Lukashenka’s White Russia.
Russia’s draft peace treaties from March 7 and April 15, 2022, included annexes demanding the repeal of Ukrainian legislation going as far back as 1993 on the status of war veterans, TV and radio, culture, state service, judiciary, education, the Ukrainian language, indigenous peoples of Ukraine and de-communization. Moscow’s demand to make Russian to become a state language in Ukraine is similar to the language’s elevation in Belarus. The objective of "de-nazification" would be taken care of through this Belarusianization of Ukrainian domestic policies.
Next is the war’s goal of “ de-militarizing ” Ukraine through removing the goal of NATO membership from the country’s constitution, replacing it with “permanent neutrality,” ending of Western military assistance and training, and a Ukrainian army reduced to a pale reflection of its current size. Ukraine should also support an end to Western sanctions against Russia and no longer seek justice for the 153,000 war crimes committed by Russia by canceling its claims to the International Criminal Court.
The Kremlin’s demand to “ eliminate the root causes ” of the war reflects a long-standing unwillingness to view Ukraine as a fully sovereign country and, as seen in the Kremlin’s demands for direct negotiations with the U.S., a deeply held belief that Ukraine has no agency. Medinsky described Ukraine as a “phantom state,” while Lavrov spoke about “the country that is now called Ukraine.” Russian representative to the EU Kirill Logvinov called for Ukraine to be placed under the UN’s "Temporary International Administration," a step that went too far for Trump and the UN.
Medvedev, like Putin and other Russian leaders today, believes most Ukrainians hold a pro-Russian or Little Russian, identity that has been marginalized by a small clique of radical nationalists who are propped up by U.S. and EU puppet masters. Vladislav Surkov, the former "grey cardinal" of Russia’s presidential office, described Ukraine as an “artificial quasi-state” that had been taken over by an “aggressive minority” who turned Ukrainians against Russians. Medvedev made the same complaints over a decade ago.
Trump’s growing frustration with Russia’s foot-dragging is rooted in an unwillingness to understand that Moscow will only end its war if Ukraine capitulates and jettisons its identity, sovereignty and independence to become Little Russia. As that is unlikely, a successful outcome to Trump’s peace talks will prove to be little but an illusion.
A plurality of Americans believe Trump is favoring Russia too heavily in peace talks. Nevertheless, accepting the Kremlin’s demand to view Ukraine as a Little Russia is very likely to be a bridge too far for even the Trump administration, and therefore a ceasefire, let alone a peace agreement, is likely to remain out of reach.

title: Russian Politician Admits He’s Been Working Remotely From Ukraine Since 2021
description: A politician in Far East Russia’s Zabaikalsky region said he has been working remotely from Ukraine for the past four years, raising eyebrows over an apparent loophole that allowed him to keep his post during wartime.
content:
A politician in Far East Russia’s Zabaikalsky region said he has been working remotely from Ukraine for the past four years, raising eyebrows over an apparent loophole that allowed him to keep his post during wartime.
Mikhail Nosik, 65, who serves as a local councilman in the Kalarsky district of the Zabaikalsky region, revealed in a recent ethics commission hearing that he has been living in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro since 2021, local media reported Thursday.
Nosik said he moved to Ukraine for cancer treatment after being elected to a five-year term in 2020. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Despite living in a country Russia is waging war against, Nosik has continued to participate in legislative affairs remotely using VPNs and video calls. In a Telegram call with the assembly’s ethics commission in March, he reportedly said he could not return to Russia and claimed he has been working “no worse than the other deputies.”
According to leaked minutes of that call published by the Telegram news channel Baza, Nosik denied holding Ukrainian citizenship and said he is an “active supporter” of President Vladimir Putin and Russia’s war on Ukraine. The politician said he has been “forced to hide” from Ukrainian authorities.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify Baza’s report.
Arkady Gromov, the head of the 15-member Kalarsky district assembly, told local media that Nosik was technically not breaking any laws. “He found himself in a difficult situation. He arrived in Ukraine, where he was born, just before the special military operation,” Gromov said, adding that Nosik is now “trapped.”
Baza reported that a majority of the assembly voted against removing Nosik from office. His term expires in December.
Russian prosecutors reportedly filed a complaint against Nosik in January, which prompted the ethics commission hearing.

title: Former Russian Army General Sentenced to 7 Years in Prison for Bribery
description: A Moscow military court on Thursday sentenced former deputy chief of Russia’s General Staff Vadim Shamarin to seven years in a maximum-security prison on corruption charges.
content:
A Moscow military court on Thursday sentenced former deputy chief of Russia’s General Staff Vadim Shamarin to seven years in a maximum-security prison on corruption charges.
Lieutenant-General Shamarin, who also headed the General Staff’s communications directorate, was arrested in May 2024 on charges of accepting 36 million rubles ($437,600) in bribes from a phone manufacturing plant in exchange for state contracts and “general patronage.”
Shamarin was one of several senior military officials arrested last year in what observers have described as a broader anti-corruption campaign within Russia’s Defense Ministry.
According to the Interfax news agency, his trial was held behind closed doors and without a full examination of evidence, as Shamarin had reached a plea deal with investigators.
Russia’s Investigative Committee, which probes major crimes, said Shamarin was convicted of accepting two bribes and sentenced accordingly. In addition to his prison term, the court stripped him of his military rank and confiscated assets valued at over 35 million rubles ($425,500).
Prosecutors had requested a 12-year sentence and a fine of 107 million rubles ($1.3 million).
The Kremlin has denied that Shamarin’s arrest and others like it signal a sweeping purge of the military following last year’s dismissal of longtime Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, who had faced mounting criticism over Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.

title: Jailed Reporter Ponomarenko Launches Second Hunger Strike Over Prison Conditions
description: Jailed Russian journalist and activist Maria Ponomarenko has gone on a hunger strike to protest her treatment in solitary confinement, her support group said Thursday.
content:
Jailed Russian journalist and activist Maria Ponomarenko has gone on a hunger strike to protest her treatment in solitary confinement, her support group said Thursday.
Ponomarenko, who is serving concurrent prison sentences for spreading “fake news” about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and allegedly assaulting prison guards, is not expected to be released until 2028, according to her lawyer.
Her support group said the hunger strike began Sunday in response to prison authorities’ refusal to install a privacy screen for the toilet in her isolation cell in the Altai region.
“Besides emotional distress, this has led Maria to refuse food so that she would need to relieve herself less often,” the group wrote on Telegram.
Ponomarenko is also protesting the confiscation of her outgoing letters and the prison’s refusal to issue consent forms that would allow supporters to request information about her condition.
She urged supporters to contact Russia’s Prosecutor General Igor Krasnov and presidential human rights commissioner Tatiana Moskalkova, saying that “petitions at the local level are meaningless.”
This marks Ponomarenko’s second hunger strike in seven months. In September, she staged a similar protest after accusing prison officials of fabricating disciplinary reports that landed her in solitary confinement.
Russia’s Memorial human rights group recognizes Ponomarenko as a political prisoner.
The journalist has been diagnosed with histrionic personality disorder and has previously attempted suicide while in police custody. Last month, her employer RusNews reported she was once again at risk of suicide and had launched a hunger strike to demand improved conditions.

title: China Spikes Kremlin’s Proposed Power of Siberia 2 Alternative
description: Moscow’s proposal to transport Russian gas via Kazakhstan as an alternative to the shelved Power of Siberia 2 pipeline has failed to gain traction in Beijing.
content:
Moscow’s proposal to transport Russian gas via Kazakhstan as an alternative to the shelved Power of Siberia 2 pipeline has failed to gain traction in Beijing.
The plan, announced by Moscow in the fall of 2024, envisioned the delivery of up to 45 billion cubic meters (bcm) of Russian natural gas annually to China via Kazakhstan. But Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui said the project would not go forward, citing excessive costs.
“Gas supplies from Russia through Kazakhstan aren’t feasible,” Interfax quoted Zhang as saying to reporters Tuesday. “There’s only one pipeline, and it’s already operating at full capacity. To transport Russian gas via this route, we’d need to build a new pipeline. That’s too expensive. The Russian side is studying this option, but it’s not realistic. In fact, it’s not possible.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak first floated the idea in November 2024, shortly after talks over the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline fell through.
President Vladimir Putin had originally proposed Power of Siberia 2 to Chinese leader Xi Jinping in 2022, a project that would increase Beijing’s purchases of Russian gas to 100 bcm per year to offset the loss of European market share following the invasion of Ukraine.
But despite warm rhetoric about a “no-limits” strategic partnership and Putin’s repeated trips to Beijing, Xi has yet to give the project the green light.
According to the Financial Times, the sticking point has been price: China reportedly asked that Russia sell its gas at domestic Russian rates — about $60 per 1,000 cubic meters. That’s roughly one-quarter of what China currently pays under the Power of Siberia 1 agreement, which delivers gas at $260 per 1,000 cubic meters. Moreover, China was only prepared to buy a fraction of the pipeline’s capacity of 50 bcm, FT reported.
At the end of 2023, Russian officials insisted that Power of Siberia 2 — planned to deliver 50 billion cubic meters of gas per year — was in an advanced stage of readiness, with project documentation expected to be approved in early 2024. But more than a year later, construction has yet to begin.
Mongolia, through which the 2,500-kilometer pipeline would have passed, has not included the Gazprom-led project in its long-term action plan through 2028, The South China Morning Post reported .
Russia has failed to reach final terms with China, confirmed Munkhnara Bayarkhavaa, a former member of Mongolia’s National Security Council.
Last year, Gazprom delivered 31 billion cubic meters of gas to China. That figure is expected to increase this year to 38 billion cubic meters, the full capacity of the Power of Siberia 1 pipeline. However, that still represents only about 15% of Russia’s former exports to the European Union, which peaked at around 200 billion cubic meters annually.
Meanwhile, European demand for Russian gas has collapsed following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2023, exports to the EU dropped to 28 billion cubic meters, and are projected to reach just 32 billion in 2024 — levels not seen since the late 1970s.

title: Putin Meets With Russians Freed by Hamas, Praises Moscow’s Ties With Palestine
description: President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday met with Russian-Israeli national Alexander Troufanov, who was freed earlier this year after being held hostage by Hamas in Gaza, crediting Moscow’s longstanding ties with Palestinian groups for helping secure his release.
content:
President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday met with Russian-Israeli national Alexander Troufanov, who was freed earlier this year after being held hostage by Hamas in Gaza, crediting Moscow’s longstanding ties with Palestinian groups for helping secure his release.
Troufanov, 29, was among the hostages freed in February after 498 days in captivity as part of an Israeli-Hamas ceasefire deal. He appeared at the Kremlin meeting alongside his mother, Yelena Troufanova, and fiance Sapir Cohen, who were also kidnapped on Oct. 7, 2023, and released the following month.
“The fact that you were released is a result of Russia’s stable, long-term relationships with the Palestinian people, their representatives and various organizations,” Putin told the family, adding that he wanted to avoid “political assessments” of the hostage crisis.
“I think we should express gratitude to the Hamas leadership and political wing for meeting us halfway and carrying out this humanitarian act in releasing you,” the Kremlin leader added.
Russia maintains working relationships with both Israel and the Palestinian authorities, as well as with Hamas, which Moscow does not consider a terrorist organization. Putin has repeatedly called for the establishment of a Palestinian state as a long-term resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The Troufanov family emigrated from Russia to Israel in the late 1990s. They were abducted from the Nir Oz kibbutz near the Gaza border during Hamas’ assault on southern Israel in October 2023. Troufanov’s father, Vitaly, was killed in the attack.
During the Kremlin meeting on Wednesday, Troufanov thanked Putin for his role in securing the family’s release and urged him to continue efforts to help free other Israeli hostages still held in Gaza.
Russia’s Chief Rabbi Berel Lazar and the head of the Federation of Jewish Communities of Russia, Alexander Boroda, also attended the Kremlin meeting.

title: Japan Accuses Russia of Restricting Sea Navigation Around Kuril Islands
description: Japan’s government sent Russia a formal letter of protest over the closure of sea navigation around the Kuril Islands, Russian state media reported Thursday.
content:
Japan’s government sent Russia a formal letter of protest over the closure of sea navigation around the Kuril Islands, Russian state media reported Thursday.
Tokyo accused Russia of introducing restrictions on the navigation of foreign military and civilian ships around the southern Kuril Islands from April 16 to May 1, according to the state-run news agency RIA Novosti.
“A protest was lodged to Russia through diplomatic channels,” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshimasa Hayashi was quoted as saying at a press conference.
Both Russia and Japan claim sovereignty over the island chain known in Russia as the Kuril Islands and in Japan as the Northern Territories, preventing the sides from signing a treaty formally marking the end of World War II.
Moscow abandoned talks on a WWII peace treaty and ended visa-free visits for Japanese people to the Kuril Islands after Japan sanctioned Russia over the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Japan also issued a diplomatic protest against what it called an “extremely unjustified” move at the time.
Earlier this month, Russian authorities designated Japan’s Northern Territories Issue Association as an “undesirable organization,” accusing it of promoting revanchist ideas and undermining Russian sovereignty.
Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office claimed the group lobbies for the islands’ return to Japan, distributes “propaganda” and holds educational events, all while being funded by the Japanese government despite presenting itself as an NGO.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry said in its 2024 annual report that Tokyo remains committed to signing a peace treaty with Russia in hopes of reclaiming the southern Kuril Islands.

title: Serbia Says Russian Intel Report Found No ‘Sound Cannon’ Used on Protesters
description: Serbia on Wednesday said protesters' claims that they were targeted by a "sound cannon" were refuted by an investigation carried out by Russian intelligence officers.
content:
Serbia on Wednesday said protesters' claims that they were targeted by a "sound cannon" were refuted by an investigation carried out by Russian intelligence officers.
The officers with Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) concluded no sonic devices were used to violently disperse a March 15 mass demonstration that took place in Belgrade, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said.
That protest — the country's biggest anti-corruption demonstration since a deadly train station roof collapse last year sparked a national protest movement — had gathered between 100,000 and 300,000 people.
But it descended into panic after an unexplained noise triggered chaos and sent hundreds of protesters fleeing.
Participants and activists accused the government of using a "sound cannon" or other sonic weapon, and media published photos of a police vehicle equipped with what appeared to be a U.S.-made LRAD 450XL long-range acoustic device.
While Interior Minister Ivica Dacic confirmed that Serbian police possess such equipment, he denied it was used at the protest.
The Serbian government invited both the United States' FBI and Russia's FSB to investigate.
While the FBI has not commented on the request, signed by Serbia's Interior Ministry on March 18, the FSB responded by sending a team in late March.
Vucic said in a press conference on Wednesday that the FSB report showed there was a "lie about the use of a sound cannon" and he threatened legal action over allegations that one was used.
Serbian civil society groups say they gathered over 3,000 testimonies, in which witnesses at the protest described a noise like a crashing plane or an oncoming car. Some reported lasting health effects.
Last week, activists delivered a petition with over 500,000 signatures to the UN office in Belgrade demanding an international investigation.
The student-led protest movement began after a fatal roof collapse at Novi Sad train station on Nov. 1, 2024, which killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely seen as a symbol of state corruption, has sparked Serbia’s biggest unrest since the 1990s.

title: Dictatorship Isn’t Destiny For Russia’s Indigenous Peoples. They Can Build Independent Democracies.
description: Opinion | In 2023, The Moscow Times published a column by the Indigenous rights advocates Pavel Sulyandziga and Dmitry Berezhkov titled “What Does Decolonization Mean for Russia’s Indigenous Peoples?”  Though the article argues that the Russian state and society must acknowledge the historical fact of colonization and seek more equitable relations between Indigenous peoples and the political center, it also argues that there could be negative consequences if these peoples achieved independence.
content:
In 2023, The Moscow Times published a column by the Indigenous rights advocates Pavel Sulyandziga and Dmitry Berezhkov titled “ What Does Decolonization Mean for Russia’s Indigenous Peoples? ”
Though the article argues that the Russian state and society must acknowledge the historical fact of colonization and seek more equitable relations between Indigenous peoples and the political center, it also argues that there could be negative consequences if these peoples achieved independence. The authors took my homeland, the republic of Sakha (Yakutia), as an example, asking what guarantee there is that the republic would be led by enlightened, liberal, pro-Western nationalists rather than people like its current leader.
It may seem strange to take issue with an article published three years ago. But as a representative of the Sakha people and someone who has devoted his political life to the struggle for the republic’s sovereignty, I cannot leave such an assertion unanswered.
The ideas put forward by Sulyandziga and Berezhkov are constantly repeated by representatives of the so-called good Russians who oppose Moscow’s predatory colonial policies, but refuse at every turn to recognize the root of the problems facing every single region of Russia.
The argument that independence for the national republics will inevitably lead to dictatorships can be heard at conferences held by Russian émigrés, in expert reports on the future of Russia after Putin and in conversations among Western diplomats.
Even in 2026, leaders of the liberal opposition publicly question the very idea of decolonization, demonstrating that they are still not listening to Indigenous voices. When Indigenous activists themselves express such doubts, they sound particularly convincing and are therefore particularly harmful.
The opening paragraphs of the article actually pleased me: Russia’s colonial past is spelled out explicitly and the authors acknowledge Indigenous peoples’ right to self-determination. But then comes a reversal in tone: independence turns out to be too risky and the peoples of Russia turn out to be unprepared for statehood.
I recognize this approach. Political strategists visiting my republic from Moscow always taught the same lesson: start with an argument that resonates with your audience, lower their defenses — and then carefully slip in the opposite argument.
I will not presume to judge the authors’ intentions, but this is precisely how the article is constructed. The result is the same: a reader sympathetic to decolonization comes away convinced that independence is an inevitable path to becoming like Turkmenistan.
It doesn’t have to be that way. The republic of Sakha entered the 1990s with an identity as strong as any former Soviet republic. We adopted our constitution before many of them, too. It still states that the republic of Sakha is a democratic state governed by the rule of law and founded on the people’s right to self-determination. Moscow has forced us to rewrite the text several times to suit its own interests. But in the early 1990s, we established a full set of state institutions: a president (though that term was eliminated in 2014), the Il Tumen State Assembly, a Constitutional Court and a National Bank.
Under an agreement with Russian government, the republic was allowed to retain just 25% of its diamond revenue — and that was enough. Enough for us to build medical centers and social facilities, develop our language and culture and educate our children abroad. A quarter of our revenue came from that single resource — and our budget had a surplus.
Today, Sakha produces a wealth of diamonds, gold, coal, gas, silver and rare earth metals, while Moscow and its oligarchs already control much of the resulting wealth. Our language is being pushed out of schools. Our young people are being sent to die in a criminal war, wiping out entire generations of an already small people. Our land and natural environment are being destroyed with barbaric indifference. And at this moment, we are told that we must cling to the federation. Tell me why.
But the main question I want to ask Sulyandziga and Berezhkov is how they settled on Turkmenistan as the model for an independent Sakha. Why not Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania?
The three Baltic states started in 1991 with the same Soviet legacy as us: a devastated economy, Russification, nomenklatura officials and an absence of market institutions. Over 30 years, they became democracies and members of the European Union and NATO.
Estonia — a country of around 1.3 million people with almost no natural resources — has built one of the world’s most digital states: electronic government, online voting and e-residency. Its schoolchildren consistently achieve the best results in Europe on the international PISA assessments. Estonia gave the world Skype and more technology unicorns per capita than almost any other country in Europe. And, in what is particularly important to me, Estonia restored its language’s status as the state language after decades of russification — precisely what we are fighting for today.
But unlike Estonia, we in Sakha have a vast territory and enormous mineral wealth: the republic produces most of Russia’s diamonds, as well as gold, coal, gas and rare earth metals.
Imagine Estonian institutions — transparent government, high-quality education and digital governance — combined with the resources that now flow to Moscow. This is how Sakha can transform itself from the colonial power’s raw-material-producing appendage into the Kuwait of the Far East: a country where mineral revenues serve its own citizens through a sovereign wealth fund rather than someone else’s oligarchs and someone else’s war.
If we stop dividing our wealth among the Russian Federation’s 140 million citizens, we will increase our concentration of national wealth per capita 140-fold. Just imagine!
Of course, resources alone guarantee nothing. They can be used for good or for harm. That is precisely why we need to learn from those who have managed to build a strong, free and educated society without gas or diamonds.
We have much to learn from Estonia and its Baltic neighbors. I hope that the ties between our peoples, still largely symbolic because of the barriers Moscow has created, will eventually become tangible: in education, digital technology, language policy and the building of state institutions.
Sulyandziga and Berezhkov ask what guarantee there is that an independent Sakha will become a democracy. No one has any guarantees. The Estonians had none in 1991, either. But I know one thing for certain: within Russia, we have only one guarantee — that we will never see a democracy on our soil.
The Sakha people are approaching the third and final stage of their statehood. The first was completed in 1922: we ceased to be aliens without land or recognition and gained autonomy. The second came in 1992: we gained sovereignty and became a state within a federal union.
The third will be the declaration of our independence.
We can no longer trust new agreements with the colonial power sitting in Moscow. Every time the beast grew weak, it persuaded us to stay and promised to treat us well. Every time, it deceived us. It is time to break free of our Stockholm syndrome and look with clear eyes.
An independent Sakha will open to the world. Historically, we had business ties with Manchuria and Japan and the entire Pacific region will be open to us today. I also have no doubt that our Putin-appointed leader Aysen Nikolayev will be the first to flee and, knowing how the Kremlin’s personnel selection favors the worst candidates, the others will follow him.
I am a popularly elected deputy of Sakha. I feel, hear and see my people: strong, freedom-loving and talented. I have seen how far we have come in just the decade since the colonial power’s noose loosened slightly. We established our own state institutions, made Sakha the official language, built hospitals and schools, enabled our children to study at the world’s elite universities.
My people — like the Tatars, Bashkirs, Buryats, Altaians, Erzya and others — are ready to live of their own free will and develop their independent, multiethnic republics themselves, free of Moscow’s chauvinism, xenophobia and imperialism.
This third stage is neither a prediction nor an expectation. Independence is a political task that can be accomplished only through political means. The beast is sick. But its illness will not do the work for us — it merely gives us time to prepare properly for that work. And the model for that preparation is before our eyes — on the shores of the Baltic Sea.

title: Russian Businesses Delay Payments as Cash Squeeze Deepens
description: Russian businesses are increasingly delaying payments to suppliers as slowing economic growth, higher taxes, falling profits and expensive borrowing strain their finances, raising the risk of a chain reaction of unpaid bills.
content:
Russian businesses are increasingly delaying payments to suppliers as slowing economic growth, higher taxes, falling profits and expensive borrowing strain their finances, raising the risk of a chain reaction of unpaid bills.
The growing payment delays highlight strains in Russia’s economy as the full-scale war in Ukraine approaches its five-year mark, raising questions about its ability to sustain military spending while keeping civilian businesses afloat.
Companies’ outstanding payables rose by 32 trillion rubles ($396.8 billion) over the year to June, reaching 155 trillion rubles ($1.92 trillion), according to a report by rating agency Expert RA, citing Rosstat data.
The increase was the largest over any 12-month period since 2004. The total covers outstanding payment obligations, including bills that are not yet overdue.
Expert RA said businesses were increasingly postponing payments because they lacked the cash to cover day-to-day operations and faced difficulties securing affordable financing.
By delaying payments to suppliers, companies effectively obtain interest-free credit. Their outstanding payables are growing roughly twice as fast as bank borrowing, which increased by 12%, and bond debt, which rose by 13%.
Payment delays have become more common among businesses of all sizes.
Among large companies, 23.8% were paying late, up from 20.8% a year earlier. The share delaying payments by more than 60 days rose to 6.5% from 4.1% at the start of 2025.
Among medium-sized businesses, 20.6% were paying late, compared with 17.4% a year earlier, including 6.2% that were more than 60 days behind.
Expert RA warned that high interest rates and shortages of working capital risked triggering a “domino effect,” with suppliers left waiting for payment becoming unable to meet their own obligations.
Falling profits are adding to the pressure. Aggregate corporate profits, after accounting for losses, fell 13.3% in the first half of 2026 compared with a year earlier and were nearly a quarter below their level in the same period of 2024.
The share of loss-making companies rose to 34% from 28% over those two years.
With less cash available and borrowing still expensive, businesses are increasingly spreading out payments. Delaying settlement with suppliers has become cheaper than borrowing money to pay them on time, the agency said.
Expert RA expects credit risks to increase in 2027, when the government forecasts economic growth of just 1.4% and investment growth of 0.2%.
The Central Bank held its benchmark interest rate at 14% on Friday and raised its forecast for the average rate next year to 12.5%-13.5%, from 10.5%-12.5%, signaling that borrowing costs would remain elevated.
Despite the mounting pressure, Expert RA said it did not expect bond defaults to trigger a systemic economic crisis. It forecast that defaults would account for no more than 1% of the bond market by value, with risks concentrated among weaker borrowers.

title: No Prospect of Reviving Black Sea Grain Deal, Russian Diplomat Says
description: Russian officials remain in contact with their Turkish counterparts on issues of maritime navigation through the Black Sea, a senior Russian diplomat told the Interfax news agency on Monday, but Moscow sees no immediate prospect of renewing the Black Sea grain initiative. “We’re considering proposals from various countries.
content:
Russian officials remain in contact with their Turkish counterparts on issues of maritime navigation through the Black Sea, a senior Russian diplomat told the Interfax news agency on Monday, but Moscow sees no immediate prospect of renewing the Black Sea grain initiative.
“We’re considering proposals from various countries. We’re in dialogue with all countries, including Turkey,” Alexander Alimov, deputy director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s department of international organizations, was quoted as saying.
“But for now, I don’t see any prospects for reviving the ‘grain deal’,” Alimov said, referring to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, an agreement brokered by Turkey and the UN in 2022 to prevent a global food shortage.
That original deal enabled the safe transport of nearly 33 million metric tons of Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Russia backed out of the arrangement in the summer of 2023, claiming Western sanctions continued to hamper Russian food and fertilizer exports and alleging Ukraine was using the maritime corridor for military operations.
Since this summer, Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on commercial vessels and port infrastructure in the Black Sea, creating major disruptions to shipping and driving wheat prices higher on global markets.
Turkey, which has maintained good relations with both countries since the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, has for months tried to negotiate a maritime security agreement between the countries.

title: Yandex Supercomputers Unscathed After Ukrainian Strikes, Company Says
description: Yandex said Monday that all three of its supercomputers remained unharmed following a series of Ukrainian drone attacks against its data centers and have been moved to more secure locations. “Once brought back online, the computers will rejoin Yandex’s service infrastructure,” the Russian tech company said in a brief statement. “They will also continue to be used for training foundation language models.” It marks Yandex’s first comments about the three supercomputers — called Chervonenkis, Galushkin and Lyapunov — since Ukraine began launching air attacks against the company’s sites earlier this month.
content:
Yandex said Monday that all three of its supercomputers remained unharmed following a series of Ukrainian drone attacks against its data centers and have been moved to more secure locations.
“Once brought back online, the computers will rejoin Yandex’s service infrastructure,” the Russian tech company said in a brief statement. “They will also continue to be used for training foundation language models.”
It marks Yandex’s first comments about the three supercomputers — called Chervonenkis, Galushkin and Lyapunov — since Ukraine began launching air attacks against the company’s sites earlier this month.
The supercomputers, launched between 2020 and 2021, rank among the most powerful in the world. But as the global AI race has accelerated in recent years, their position on the list has gradually slipped.
Ukraine’s attacks against Yandex data centers have led to temporary outages of the company’s services across Russia, including ride-hailing apps, food delivery platforms and banking. Corporate clients on Yandex Cloud have also been impacted.
The Kremlin has said that, while it is too early to assess the financial losses, Yandex was taking steps to deal with the aftermath of the attacks.
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry said it helped Yandex migrate core systems to external backup servers.
The ministry has also approved recommendations for protecting data centers against Ukrainian drone attacks, the Kommersant business daily reported Monday, citing the document.
The measures include building the most critical facilities underground, installing structures capable of withstanding blast waves, deploying electronic warfare systems and maintaining backup copies of data. They also call for regular coordination with the military and National Guard.
President Vladimir Putin vowed retribution for the attacks and earlier ordered officials to improve Russia’s ability to protect its digital infrastructure. Ukraine said it was responding to Russian attacks on its own data centers.

title: Russia Accuses Ukraine of Launching Strikes Against Oleshky Ahead of Ceasefire
description: Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had prevented the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people from leaving.
content:
Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had prevented the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people from leaving.
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed to a ceasefire in Oleshky that would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing for the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that Ukraine had struck the town 18 times with artillery fire and carried out more than 120 drone attacks on it and the main roads around it in the week since Oct. 19.
Reuters could not independently verify that assertion, and there was no immediate response from Ukraine, which has in the past accused Russia of not letting aid in or people out of the town.
Also on Monday, the Kremlin said that the local humanitarian ceasefire agreed for Oleshky with the United States' help could set a precedent for similar ceasefires elsewhere in Ukraine.
The ceasefire comes as residents of the town, controlled by Russian forces since February 2022 and located close to the front line, have reported ​a deepening food crisis, with both sides accusing each other of blocking supplies.

title: Chief Editor of Independent Belgorod News Outlet Charged With ‘Justifying Terrorism’
description: The editor-in-chief of Pepel, an online outlet covering news in the southwestern Belgorod region, has reportedly been charged by Russia’s FSB security service with publicly justifying terrorism.
content:
The editor-in-chief of Pepel, an online outlet covering news in the southwestern Belgorod region, has reportedly been charged by Russia’s FSB security service with publicly justifying terrorism.
Fonar, another regional news outlet, said Nikita Parmenov stands accused of making statements in support of the Russian Volunteer Corps, a far-right paramilitary group composed of Russians fighting alongside the Ukrainian army.
It was not immediately clear what statements specifically the FSB was referring to, Fonar reported. The criminal charge carries a maximum sentence of seven years in prison.
Pepel suggested that the accusations of justifying terrorism could stem from a YouTube interview in which Parmenov said he was unable to condemn Russians who take up arms to help Ukraine defend itself from invading Russian forces.
Though Parmenov explicitly condemned cross-border shelling that targets civilians in the Belgorod region, Pepel claimed pro-war Telegram channels edited that part out of his interview and circulated it online.
The FSB’s statement, cited by yet another regional news outlet, Belpressa, claimed Parmenov is currently living in exile outside Russia, somewhere in the South Caucasus.
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Parmenov a “foreign agent” in February 2025.
Parmenov founded Pepel in the fall of 2022, months after President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: ‘Still Just a Child’: The Russian Teenagers Fighting and Dying in Ukraine
description: “Why?! A young soldier who’d never seen combat … Still just a child,” Svetlana Serezhkina, a resident of the Moscow region, wrote on social media after news emerged of the death of Alisher Svirin, the first publicly identified Russian soldier born in 2008 to be killed in the war in Ukraine. “It’s such a shame they let him sign a [military] contract,” wrote another commenter, Andrei.
content:
“Why?! A young soldier who’d never seen combat … Still just a child,” Svetlana Serezhkina, a resident of the Moscow region, wrote on social media after news emerged of the death of Alisher Svirin, the first publicly identified Russian soldier born in 2008 to be killed in the war in Ukraine.
“It’s such a shame they let him sign a [military] contract,” wrote another commenter, Andrei. Dozens of similar comments written by residents of Svirin’s hometown of Pavlovsky Posad appeared under the same post.
According to his obituary, Svirin had served as a machine gunner in a motorized rifle brigade. He was just 14 when President Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
More than 200 Russian soldiers aged 18 have been killed in the war, according to a count by the BBC’s Russian service and the exiled news outlet Mediazona.
The real number may be higher, as the tally excludes soldiers listed as missing and fighters from the Russian-backed separatist territories in Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
The pro-war Orthodox Christian VKontakte group Synodik, which has about 50,000 followers, carries dozens of obituaries for soldiers who were teenagers when the invasion began.
In Orthodox Christianity, a synodik is a list of names of the living or the dead who are remembered in prayers and church services. Likewise, Synodik’s members pray for Russian soldiers like they would in a real church. The comments, mostly posted by women, are filled with Orthodox prayers, animated images of icons and cross emojis.
One recent post commemorates Kirill Tretyakov, who was born Feb. 7, 2007, near the end of Putin’s second presidential term. He had just turned 15 when the full-scale war began.
Tretyakov grew up in Kamensk, a settlement of about 6,300 people roughly 100 kilometers (62 miles) from Ulan-Ude, the capital of Russia’s republic of Buryatia. After completing ninth grade at a local school, he enrolled in a vocational college to study construction. He enjoyed kettlebell lifting and football in his free time.
Tretyakov signed a contract with the Defense Ministry six days after his 18th birthday, according to his obituary.
“From an early age, Kirill strove to be a worthy citizen of his country. On Feb. 13, 2025, Kirill made the courageous decision to defend the Fatherland and signed a contract with the Defense Ministry,” the group’s administrators wrote.
The Moscow Times found identical obituaries in a VKontakte group about Ulan-Ude and on the website of Buryatia’s Kabansky district. Tretyakov served as a combat engineer in an obstacle-laying company of the 656th Separate Guards Engineer-Sapper Battalion. He was killed on Sept. 22 of this year.
“Kirill strove to learn everything a real man should know. He was a brave, determined and fearless warrior who always put the common cause above his own,” his obituary reads.
A psychologist in Russia who works with adolescents said that many young people struggle to grasp the reality of going to war.
“The risk of being killed is very high, but young people don’t think about that,” the psychologist told The Moscow Times, speaking on condition of anonymity for safety reasons.
“When you’re young, you feel like life will last forever, like you’re invincible. Teenagers lack the social circle, the word-of-mouth networks, that could help them think critically about the war.”
That illusion of invulnerability is compounded by a broader devaluation of life in Russia, the psychologist said, referencing television propagandist Vladimir Solovyov’s comment on air that “life is greatly overrated.”
The number of “newly departed warriors,” as the Synodik group calls them, rises almost every day. The group also publishes obituaries for soldiers from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Nikolai was a simple guy. He finished school in our village and was open, cheerful and kind,” the head of the Voikovsky rural settlement in annexed Crimea, said of Nikolai Ruzov, 19. Ruzov was six when Russia annexed the peninsula in 2014 and 14 when the full-scale war began.
Like all draft-age men without a deferment, Ruzov completed a year of compulsory military service before signing a contract with the Defense Ministry and going to fight in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. He was killed on Aug. 18, 2026, less than three months after his 19th birthday.
A Crimean news outlet illustrated his obituary with an apparently AI-generated image presented as a portrait of Ruzov that was later reposted by other outlets. The soldier in the image wears a U.S. flag patch on his shoulder. The Moscow Times analyzed the image using Hive’s AI-detection software , which returned a 100% confidence score that it was AI-generated.
Ruzov had been the commander of an assault squad, state media reported .
“Can someone explain how a 19-year-old boy ended up commanding an assault squad?!” one commenter, Maxim Borisov, asked .
Among those offering condolences online were mothers whose own sons had been killed in the war.
“May Nikolai enter the Kingdom of Heaven, and may you find the strength to learn to live with this irreplaceable loss. Our children don’t die … they are joining the Lord’s army. My boy has been there for four years,” Tamara Romanova wrote on the social network Odnoklassniki.
Ruzov was posthumously awarded Russia’s Order of Courage.
Another 19-year-old soldier, David Fedorov, died on Oct. 20 after being sent on an assault mission, according to his mother.
Police stopped Fedorov on the street in Cheboksary, the capital of the Volga republic of Chuvashia, in May and forced him to sign a contract with the Defense Ministry, his mother told the independent news outlet Astra. He was officially assigned to serve as a driver despite having no driver’s license, she added.
The deaths of young soldiers also feature in state efforts to promote the war in schools.
On Sept. 21, materials for “Important Conversations,” a series of state-mandated patriotic lessons, highlighted two soldiers killed in the invasion at ages 20 to 25. One was Nurmagomed Gadzhimagomedov, a soldier from Dagestan who died in the first month of the full-scale war.
“When I see examples of heroism like this young man ... I want to say: ‘I am a Lak, I am a Dagestani, I am a Chechen, Ingush, Russian, Tatar, Jew, Mordvin, Ossetian’,” Putin said after Gadzhimagomedov’s death in March 2022.
Footage of Putin’s remarks was included in a seven-minute video shown to schoolchildren, while pupils were also offered an interactive lesson about Gadzhimagomedov’s life.
Military personnel in their early 20s also visit schools to deliver patriotic lessons. The children’s psychologist said in-person meetings with returning soldiers could have an even stronger influence on teenagers.
“Soldiers are surrounded by an aura of heroism,” the psychologist said. “The person who comes to speak to you is alive. He fought for three years and came back. Now he’s addressing an audience and has a stable position in society.”
“Young people have little to lose,” the psychologist continued. “They don’t yet have families of their own or things they would find painful to give up, so war can seem appealing.”

title: Award-Winning Production Designer Dies at Moscow Hospital After Arrest for Treason
description: Alexander Kondratov, an award-winning production designer for the popular Russian TV series “Liquidation,” has died at a Moscow hospital after being transferred from a detention center where he was awaiting trial on treason charges, the rights NGO Perviy Otdel said Monday.
content:
Alexander Kondratov, an award-winning production designer for the popular Russian TV series “Liquidation,” has died at a Moscow hospital after being transferred from a detention center where he was awaiting trial on treason charges, the rights NGO Perviy Otdel said Monday.
Kondratov, 52, was reportedly hospitalized at the Botkin hospital last Friday for an undisclosed ailment. The cause of his death has not been made public.
Russian law enforcement authorities charged Kondratov with treason on Aug. 5, though he had been held for more than 70 days under so-called “carousel arrests,” a practice of consecutive detentions on charges of disorderly conduct.
Born and raised in Moscow, Kondratov moved to Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2012, where his family currently resides.
Russian border guards at Vnukovo International Airport detained him on May 5, when he arrived to renew his international passport.
His defense attorney Natalia Tikhonova said the treason charges, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison for men, stemmed from “at least six” online posts Kondratov had made. The nature of those posts has not been disclosed.
Kondratov was best known for his work as an art and production designer for the 2007 post-World War II detective drama “Liquidation.” His work on the series earned him two of Russia’s highest honors in television production — the TEFI and Golden Eagle awards.
Perviy Otdel reported that Kondratov’s death marks at least the 11th known case of someone dying in Russian custody this year while standing trial on charges widely viewed as being politically motivated.

title: Kremlin Signals Desire to Maintain Serbia Ties After Vučić Ousted by Student Movement
description: The Kremlin said Monday that it wants to maintain and develop ties with Serbia despite the defeat of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling coalition in this weekend’s parliamentary elections, while noting that building those relations will require effort from both sides. “We deeply value the contribution that Mr.
content:
The Kremlin said Monday that it wants to maintain and develop ties with Serbia despite the defeat of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling coalition in this weekend’s parliamentary elections, while noting that building those relations will require effort from both sides.
“We deeply value the contribution that Mr. Vučić has made to the development of our bilateral relations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters at a daily briefing.
“We know that he will remain on the political stage, and we hope that even in opposition, he will continue to contribute to advancing our ties,” Peskov added.
Vučić, who dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade as prime minister and then later as president , conceded defeat on Sunday night following a historic snap election. The vote pitted his ruling coalition against a student-led movement that had spent months protesting against his government.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
The defeat followed Vučić’s resignation as president in September, a risky political maneuver intended to allow him to reclaim the prime minister post. It also came after nearly two years of anti-government demonstrations triggered by the November 2024 roof collapse at the Novi Sad railway station, an accident that killed 16 people and sparked widespread outrage over state corruption.
During his tenure, Vučić balanced Serbia’s candidacy for EU membership with a refusal to join Western sanctions against Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. He had remained one of the few European leaders to maintain direct contact with the Kremlin and make official visits to Moscow.
Peskov said Monday that Moscow hopes the incoming government in Belgrade will work “constructively” to preserve bilateral relations since, in its view, doing so would bring “tangible benefits to Serbia itself.”
“For our part, we intend to continue doing everything possible to foster our relations with Belgrade. But as you know, it takes two to tango,” he said.
Jovo Bakić, a representative of the Student List, told the Kremlin-backed broadcaster RT Balkan that the incoming government would not impose sanctions on Moscow or abandon Russian gas supplies despite pressure from the European Union.
He argued that sanctions imposed by a country of Serbia’s size would change little but would send a negative signal symbolically.
“ We respect Russia as a great power and as a historically important partner, and in many cases as a protector,” Bakić said. “ There will be no changes on this issue.”

title: Ukrainian Drone Barrage Kills At Least 3 in Voronezh
description: At least three people were killed in a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Voronezh in southern Russia, local authorities said early Monday, with another 29 people being reported injured.
content:
At least three people were killed in a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Voronezh in southern Russia, local authorities said early Monday, with another 29 people being reported injured.
Voronezh region Governor Alexander Gusev said air defense systems destroyed 113 drones in the skies above the region overnight. He said most unmanned aircraft were intercepted directly over the regional capital.
“Unfortunately, two people were killed,” Gusev initially wrote in a post on Telegram, identifying the victims as two men born in 1960 and 1973. At an emergency meeting later in the day, he said the death toll had risen to three people.
Gusev said most of the people wounded in the overnight attack were on a passenger train that was hit.
Falling drone debris also sparked fires at multiple industrial and commercial sites, the governor added, as well as residential buildings and a school’s sports arena.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of black smoke rising over Voronezh to identify one of the targeted industrial sites as a synthetic rubber plant owned by the Sibur petrochemical corporation.
The facility makes rubber and polymers used in military aircraft tires, armored vehicles and solid rocket fuel components for Iskander ballistic missiles.
If confirmed, the strike in Voronezh would mark the third attack on a Russian synthetic rubber factory in as many days, following strikes on rubber plants in the cities of Tolyatti and Omsk this weekend.
Elsewhere, Bryansk region Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said a drone attack killed a train driver on Sunday night.
A passenger train bound from the southern resort town of Anapa to Moscow was also hit in an overnight strike, with Russian Railways reporting that at least five passengers were wounded.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 290 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Civil aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights across all Moscow airports.

title: Over 350 People Killed and Nearly 800 Still Missing in Kursk Region After Ukrainian Incursion, Prosecutor Says
description: More than 350 residents of Russia’s southwestern Kursk region have been killed and nearly 800 remain missing following Ukraine’s months-long occupation of the border area, regional authorities said Tuesday. “The fate of 789 residents of the border regions, including four children, remains unknown.
content:
More than 350 residents of Russia’s southwestern Kursk region have been killed and nearly 800 remain missing following Ukraine’s months-long occupation of the border area, regional authorities said Tuesday.
“The fate of 789 residents of the border regions, including four children, remains unknown. There are 358 dead officially,” the Kursk region’s Prosecutor General Alexei Tsukanov said at a local roundtable.
Ukrainian forces captured dozens of towns in the Kursk region amid their surprise cross-border incursion in August 2024, marking the first time a foreign army occupied Russian territory since World War II.
More than 150,000 residents in the Kursk region were ordered to leave their homes, some of whom later staged protests over poor living conditions and what they described as inadequate government support and compensation for destroyed property.
Russia’s military said last month that it had completely driven out Ukrainian troops from the Kursk region with the help of North Korean troops.
Acting Kursk region Governor Alexander Khinshtein said at the time that the civilian death toll from the nine-month occupation stood at 288.
Neither Khinshtein nor Tsukanov provided details as to how the civilians died.
But Tsukanov said Tuesday that Russian military investigators have recorded 582 crimes allegedly committed by “Ukrainian nazis and their accomplices,” according to the Kursk region broadcaster Seym.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, at least 621 Russian civilians have been killed in Ukrainian attacks in the regions of Kursk, Belgorod, Bryansk, Rostov, Krasnodar, as well as annexed Crimea, according to authorities.
By comparison, the United Nations estimates that more than 13,100 Ukrainian civilians have been killed since President Vladimir Putin ordered troops across the border over three years ago.

title: Putin Says Russia Should ‘Strangle’ Foreign Tech Companies
description: President Vladimir Putin said late Monday that Western tech companies still operating in Russia but acting against the country’s interests should be “strangled,” as authorities seek to replace foreign software and services with domestic alternatives. “We need to strangle them… I say this without hesitation,” Putin told business leaders at a Kremlin meeting, responding to complaints from Iva Technologies CEO Stanislav Iodkovsky, who said local firms were “losing billions” because companies like Zoom and Microsoft had not fully withdrawn from the Russian market. “We must respond in kind, mirror their actions,” the Kremlin leader added.
content:
President Vladimir Putin said late Monday that Western tech companies still operating in Russia but acting against the country ’s interests should be “strangled,” as authorities seek to replace foreign software and services with domestic alternatives.
“We need to strangle them… I say this without hesitation,” Putin told business leaders at a Kremlin meeting, responding to complaints from Iva Technologies CEO Stanislav Iodkovsky, who said local firms were “losing billions” because companies like Zoom and Microsoft had not fully withdrawn from the Russian market.
“We must respond in kind, mirror their actions,” the Kremlin leader added. Asked about Russian consumers who still rely on foreign software and services, Putin said his proposal would help rid them of “bad habits.”
Hundreds of Western companies have left Russia or scaled back their operations in the country since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In response, the Kremlin has imposed steep exit costs on remaining firms.
“We haven ’ t kicked anyone out... we provided the most favorable conditions for them to work in our market, and they are trying to strangle us,” Putin said at the Kremlin meeting.
But, he added, Russia will not “roll out the red carpet” for companies like McDonald’s, which sold its Russian business in 2022. The U.S. fast food chain was quickly replaced by the Vkusno i tochka, a virtual rebranding of McDonald’s.
Amid U.S. President Donald Trump ’s efforts to reset relations with Moscow and mediate an end to the war in Ukraine, rumors have emerged that some Western firms are looking to re-enter the Russian market. Yet, Putin has warned that any return would be met with strict protectionist conditions.
At the same time, business leaders and economic officials in Russia say that they have so far not seen any interest among foreign companies to restart their businesses in the country. Western companies, meanwhile, say they continue to see risks to operating in Russia.

title: Putin Praises Musk, Compares Him to Soviet Space Hero
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk on Wednesday, telling university students he was a pioneer comparable to legendary Soviet rocket engineer Sergei Korolev.
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk on Wednesday, telling university students he was a pioneer comparable to legendary Soviet rocket engineer Sergei Korolev.
The comments came as Russia and the United States forged closer ties under President Donald Trump's administration, of which billionaire SpaceX founder Musk is a key figure.
"You know, there's a man — he lives in the States — Musk, who, you could say, raves about Mars," Putin told students on a visit to Bauman Moscow State Technical University, which specializes in science and engineering.
"These are the kind of people who don't often appear in the human population, charged up with a certain idea."
"If it seems incredible even today, such ideas often come to fruition after a while. Just like the ideas of Korolev, our pioneers, came about in due time," Putin added.
Korolev is considered the father of the Soviet space program, developing the first satellite Sputnik as well as Vostok 1, which carried first cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin into orbit in 1961.
Musk, the world's richest man and Trump's most powerful advisor, is the head of SpaceX — a U.S. company that launches rockets for NASA and owns the Starlink satellite internet network.
Musk has been a frequent critic of Ukraine, which is currently battling a three-year Russian offensive.
The billionaire accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last month of wanting a "forever war," and in February said Kyiv had gone "too far" in the conflict.

title: Russia's Treason Convictions Hit Post-Soviet Record in 2024 – IStories
description: Russian courts convicted a record number of citizens for treason in 2024, as the Kremlin intensified its crackdown on perceived internal threats amid the ongoing war in Ukraine and heightened tensions with the West.
content:
Russian courts convicted a record number of citizens for treason in 2024, as the Kremlin intensified its crackdown on perceived internal threats amid the ongoing war in Ukraine and heightened tensions with the West.
According to the independent investigative outlet IStories, 145 Russian citizens were convicted of treason last year. That figure is nearly four times higher than the number of convictions in 2023 and the highest recorded in modern Russian history, the outlet said.
Russian courts also convicted 23 citizens of espionage in 2024, IStories reported — a 2.5-fold increase over the previous year.
The number of Russians convicted for “ confidential cooperation ” with a foreign state, a charge introduced in 2022 shortly after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, also rose sharply. Twenty-one individuals were found guilty on this charge, marking a tenfold increase from the previous year.
At least 209 people were convicted in 2024 under laws governing the disclosure or mishandling of state secrets, a one-third increase from the previous year.
In December 2024, the news outlet RTVI reported that at least 28 people had been convicted of espionage that year. Of those, 18 were Ukrainian nationals, seven were Russians and two were American citizens.
The same month, President Vladimir Putin called on the Federal Security Service (FSB) to intensify efforts to root out “traitors” and foreign operatives within Russia.
"You must swiftly suppress the activities of foreign intelligence services, actively combat those who orchestrate sabotage and terrorist attacks and detect spies and traitors," he said in a video address to security service officers on their professional holiday.

title: Police Arrest Former Kursk Region Governor Alexei Smirnov
description: Former Kursk region governor Alexei Smirnov and his first deputy Alexei Dedov were arrested and charged with large-scale fraud on Wednesday.
content:
Former Kursk region governor Alexei Smirnov and his first deputy Alexei Dedov were arrested and charged with large-scale fraud on Wednesday.
Moscow’s Meshchansky Court ordered Smirnov to be placed in pre-trial detention for two months. The court’s press service published photos and videos of the ex-governor being led into a glass defendant’s box where he sat as the judge read the charges aloud.
Smirnov and Dedov are accused of embezzling 1 billion rubles ($12.17 million) from the Kursk Region Development Corporation that was meant to be used for constructing defense fortifications along the border with Ukraine, Russia’s Interior Ministry said.
Law enforcement officials suspect that the two men “led the members of an organized group and, together with the management of the Kursk Region Development Corporation, organized the theft of public funds,” Interior Ministry spokeswoman Irina Volk said.
Telegram news channels with purported ties to Russian law enforcement agencies claimed that Kursk Region Development Corporation CEO Vladimir Lukin, who is facing trial in the same embezzlement case, testified against Smirnov.
Smirnov served as governor for just over 200 days before stepping down in December. President Vladimir Putin replaced him with State Duma lawmaker Alexander Khinshtein.
Several months into Smirnov’s tenure, Ukrainian forces launched a surprise incursion into the Kursk region, displacing thousands of residents from their homes near the border with Ukraine. Some of those who managed to flee areas captured by Ukrainian forces staged protests, accusing both local officials and the Kremlin of failing to compensate them for their lost homes.
In recent weeks, Russian troops have taken back much of the Kursk region, though a small portion reportedly remains under Ukrainian control.
Smirnov appeared to fall out of favor with Putin during the early days of the incursion, when the Kremlin leader publicly cut him off mid-sentence as he attempted to brief him on Ukrainian military gains in the border region. When Smirnov resigned in December, Putin said that the former governor had not been successful in “crisis management.”
Scrutiny over the Kursk region’s border defenses has intensified since Ukrainian forces launched their cross-border incursion, reportedly meeting minimal resistance.
In October, police searched the business of controversial regional lawmaker Maxim Vasilyev, who had faced accusations of border defense failures. Vasilyev publicly blamed filmmaker Nikita Mikhalkov for “sensationalizing” the situation.
Independent journalist Farida Rustamova noted Wednesday that construction work on defense fortifications in the Kursk region was completed before Smirnov took office in May, replacing former governor Roman Starovoit, who Putin appointed to head Russia’s Transportation Ministry.
Before being appointed governor, Smirnov served as first vice governor of the Kursk region and chairman of the regional government.
His arrest also comes days after the mayor of the Kursk region ’s capital city announced that he would resign due to “ family circumstances, ” leading to speculation that Acting Kursk region Governor Alexander Khinshtein is purging local elite networks and replacing them with his own.
